He opened the red log, the paper yellowed and damp.

"The Clay-10 polymer," Xiao Feng read aloud, his voice echoing softly in the stone vault. "It was designed to seal the fissures. But it has mutated the pathogen in the water. The cells bind with the clay, creating a waterlogged shell that does not decay and cannot be cut. The water walkers. If the main valve is not shut from the primary station inside the karst caves, the polymer will saturate the entire valley aquifer. Within seven days, the water of Qingping will be poison."

"Seven days," Liang whispered. "We have only a week."

"The primary station is upstream," Li said, pointing to the dark tunnel at the back of the chamber. "The trail leads deep into the karst caves. We must go on foot."

Xiao Feng closed the logbook, tucking it into his jacket. "We must find the valve."

Suddenly, the mechanical ticking sound that had been echoing from the dark tunnel stopped.

*Silence.*

The sudden return of the quiet was a physical shock, the cold air of the vault settling like a stone.

And then, the heavy steel security door behind them slammed shut.

*BANG!*

The iron pipe that had been wedged into the frame fell to the concrete floor with a loud, clattering ring, rolling into the glowing mud.

Xiao Feng and Liang ran to the door, their hands grasping the iron handle. They pulled, but the lock had engaged, the heavy steel bolts sliding deep into the stone frame. It was locked from the oucoarse haire.

They were trapped inside the concrete vault.

"Liang! Help me!" Xiao Feng yelled, trying to leverage the handle with his sword, but the steel was too thick.

From the other side of the door, in the dark corridor they had just cleared, a sound began to echo.

It was not the slow, canvas-shuffling drag of the mummified dead.

It was the heavy, rhythmic stomp of rubber-soled combat boots, walking slowly toward the door. Someone—or something—was standing just on the other side of the metal wall.

And then, in the pocket of the petrified scientist on the floor, a small black radio suddenly crackled to life, a cold, distorted voice speaking through the static.

"Outpost Three," the radio static-hissed. "This is Chengdu Command. The quarantine has failed. The sector is black. Do not open the valves. Repeat, do not open..."

Xiao Feng stood before the closed steel door, his Nandao held tight, his heart hammering in the dark silence, as the heavy footsteps oucoarse haire stopped right at the metal frame.

================================================================================

STORY 5: THE KARST CAVES
CHAPTER 1: THE SHADOW IN THE CORRIDOR


The steel security door of the hydrological vault stood cold and immovable. Inside the concrete room, the red light of Xiao Feng’s flashlight cast a bloody, dancing glow over the massive iron valves and the petrified limestone statue of the scientist.

Liang pulled on the iron handle, his muscles tensing, but the heavy steel bolts remained locked in the stone frame.

"It won't budge," Liang whispered, his breath coming in short gasps. "The lock has engaged from the oucoarse haire."

*Clank... stomp...*

The sound of the combat boots oucoarse haire the door stopped.

Through the narrow, reinforced glass window in the center of the steel door, a shadow fell. The red light of the flashlight caught the outline of a figure standing in the dark corridor. It was a man, tall and broad-shouldered, wearing a dented tactical helmet and a heavy chest rig covered in empty magazine pouches. He held a short-barreled automatic rifle, the barrel pointed toward the floor.

It was a soldier. A survivor from the Chengdu garrison.

But he did not look like a savior. Through the dirty glass, his face was pale, his eyes bloodshot and dark with fever. A thick, grey bandage was wrapped around his neck, stained with black fluid. He looked at the three youths inside the vault with a dull, unblinking stare.

"Open the door!" Xiao Feng shouted, pressing his hands against the glass. "We are from the village of Qingping! The well is contaminated! We must go upstream to shut the valve!"

The soldier did not move. He slowly raised his left hand, holding up a small, hand-held radio. He pressed the button, and his voice carried through the speaker of the radio inside the petrified scientist’s pocket, the static-hissing sound echoing in the concrete vault.

"No," the soldier’s voice said. It was dry, raspy, and interrupted by weak coughs. "I locked it. The vault is closed. The quarantine must hold."

"What quarantine?" Liang demanded, stepping up next to Xiao Feng. "The river is already dry! The water walkers are inside our walls! If we do not shut the valve, our well water will be poison! We have only a week!"

"If you open the door," the soldier said, his voice dropping to a low whisper, "you open the path. The karst caves are not empty. They are a nest. Thousands of them... trapped in the deep tunnels, saturated with the clay. If they hear you, they will pour through this corridor into the reservoir, and from there, down the river to your valley. I locked the gate to keep them in."

"We have the steel," Liang said, patting the hilt of his Nandao. "We cleared the pass, and we cleared the lock. We can navigate the caves."

The soldier let out a dry, hacking laugh that turned into a cough. "Your short swords are nothing in the dark, kid. The clay-zombies don't feel pain, and their skin is hard as stone. You cannot cut them. I had a squad. Twelve men, fully armed. Automatic rifles, grenades, body armor. We went in to seal the leak three weeks ago."

He paused, his red eyes locking onto Liang’s face.

"Only I came out," the soldier whispered. "And I did not come out clean."

He pointed to the grey bandage on his neck. The black stain was spreading, the skin around the edges turning a pale, bruised blue. The infection was in his blood, burning through his veins.

"The fever is rising," the soldier said. "Within an hour, I will be like them. A stone walker. But I will die on this side of the door. I will not let you invite the fire."

Xiao Feng looked at the petrified scientist on the floor, and then at the glowing grey mud that was still spraying from the cracked valve casing. "If you die there, Captain, the valve will continue to leak. The clay will reach the aquifer. The village will die anyway. Is that your quarantine? To let everyone drown in the poison?"

The soldier stood in silence, the radio static-hissing in his hand.

Through the glass, they could see his body trembling, his breath coming in shallow, ragged gasps. The fever was destroying his mind, but the discipline of his training was still holding, a stubborn, final wall.

"We are the boat families of the Grand Canal," Li said, stepping forward, her voice quiet but firm. "For generations, our fathers held the river. We do not run from the water, Captain. We live with it, or we die with it. If the caves are a nest, we will walk them in silence. But we will not sit in a tomb and wait to starve."

The soldier looked at Li, his red-hot eyes tracking her face. The mention of the Grand Canal, of the old discipline, seemed to strike a note in his fading mind. He looked down at the hand-held radio, and then at the heavy steel door.

"The key is in the lock panel," the soldier whispered. "The code is 0-4-1-2. The date of the collapse. But once you go in, you do not come back. The door locks automatically from the inside. The keys to the primary valve room are in my rig."

He slumped against the steel door, his body sliding slowly down the metal plate until his head vanished from the glass window.

*Thump.*

His body lay still in the dark corridor oucoarse haire, the rifle clattering to the concrete.

Xiao Feng ran to the electronic lock panel next to the door. It was dead, but the manual override screen was still powered by the backup battery. He entered the code: *0-4-1-2*.

The lock groaned.

*CLACK.*

The heavy steel bolts slid back. Xiao Feng pushed the door open, the cold wind from the corridor rushing in, carrying the scent of coal dust and decay.

The body of Captain Zhao lay at their feet. He was still breathing, but his eyes were closed, his skin turning a dark, stone-grey.

Xiao Feng knelt down, his fingers searching the soldier's tactical rig. He found a heavy iron ring carrying three keys, and a map of the karst cave tunnels drawn on waterproof paper.

"We have the keys," Xiao Feng said, standing up. "And we have the map."

He looked into the dark corridor ahead. The glowing grey mud ran along the floor like a glowing green path, disappearing into the dark, arched opening of the karst cave tunnel in the distance.

"Into the dark," Liang said, drawing his Nandao.

They stepped over the soldier's body, leaving the concrete vault behind, and walked into the silent mouth of the karst caves.

---

CHAPTER 2: INTO THE LABYRINTH


The air inside the karst caves was a cold, wet hand that gripped their chests.

Unlike the concrete vault behind them, the tunnels were organic, carved by subterranean rivers over millions of years. Huge limestone stalactites hung from the vaulted ceiling like the teeth of a giant beast, water dripping from their tips in a slow, irregular rhythm. On the floor, stalagmites rose like stone columns, their surfaces slick with moisture.

The only light came from the center of the path.

The glowing grey clay mud, leaking from the cracked valve, ran in a narrow, three-inch stream along the floor, casting a faint, phosphorescent green light that illuminated the damp limestone walls. It cast long, distorted shadows that made every rock and column look like a crouching figure.

Xiao Feng kept his red-light flashlight off, tucked into his pocket. "The soldier said the light draws them," he whispered, his hand resting on the hilt of his Nandao. "We use the mud path to guide our feet."

"The mist is heavy here," Li said, her hand holding the iron-pointed boat hook. "I cannot see five feet ahead."

"Keep the line," Liang whispered, his canvas-wrapped boots sliding slightly on the wet limestone.

Xiao Feng pulled Captain Zhao’s map from his jacket. The waterproof paper was cold, and in the green glow of the mud, the lines were difficult to read. The map showed a labyrinth of intersecting tunnels: the Gallery of Columns, the River of Echoes, and the Devil's Chasm, leading to the high-pressure valve dome.

"The Gallery of Columns is first," Xiao Feng said, pointing to a wide section of the tunnel where the rock walls split open. "It is the main passage. We must cross it to reach the river path."

They walked silently, following the green stream.

The silence of the cave was a heavy, physical thing, broken only by the slow *drip... drip...* of water and the low, distant sighing of the wind through the high fissures. The air smelled of wet lime, cold stone, and the sharp, metallic tang of the chemical clay.

They entered the Gallery of Columns.

It was a vast cavern, the ceiling rising forty feet into the darkness. Hundreds of massive stone pillars—formed where the stalactites and stalagmites had met over thousands of years—stood like a forest of grey trunks.

And in the shadows of the pillars, the guard was waiting.

Xiao Feng froze, raising his hand to halt the group.

Through the shifting ribbons of fog, he could see them.

Dozens of clay-zombies—their bodies blackened by the coal dust of the mines, their skin turned to a hard, stone-like grey by the polymer—were standing motionless among the columns. They did not walk, and they did not grovel. They stood like ancient terra-cotta soldiers guarding a tomb, their heads bowed, their arms hanging loosely, their eyes closed.

They were in a state of hibernation, suspended by the cold, damp air of the cave and the complete lack of sound.

"The sleeping horde," Liang whispered, his breath catching in his throat.

"We must walk through them," Xiao Feng said, his voice a low vibration. "The path runs directly between the pillars. There is no other way. Do not touch the stone. Do not breathe loud."

They stepped into the forest of pillars.

The gap between the massive stone columns and the sleeping clay-zombies was narrow—barely two feet wide in some places. Squeezing past them required painful, agonizing precision.

Xiao Feng walked first, his body turned sideways, his chest inches from the calcified chest of a sleeping miner zombie. The zombie’s skin was cold, hard, and smelled of dry rot and lime. He could see the tiny, grey crystals of the polymer glinting in the green light of the mud path.

Li followed, her boat hook held close to her body, her steps silent.

Liang brought up the rear. His boots, wrapped in canvas, were wet from the river. As he stepped over a wet limestone ridge, his heel caught on a loose piece of rock.

*Clack.*

The sound was tiny, a soft click of stone on stone. But in the hollow, vaulted cavern, it did not die. It bounced off the limestone pillars, multiplying in the quiet air, a sharp, echoing ring that traveled through the gallery.

Xiao Feng tensed, his body freezing next to a sleeping zombie.

The silence returned, but it was no longer peaceful.

A low, dry creak of calcified joints echoed from the shadow of the column next to Liang.

The massive miner zombie—its skin a hard, grey limestone shell—slowly raised its head. Its eyelids, stiff with clay dust, opened to reveal two dull, green-grey eyes that began to glow with a faint, hungry light.

Its head turned slowly toward Liang in the dark, the jaw clicking as it prepared to release the first cry.

---

CHAPTER 3: THE THREAD OF HOPE


The miner zombie’s jaw began to click, its dry, calcified throat opening to release the warning cry that would awaken the forest of stone giants.

Liang did not think. He did not raise his sword to strike, knowing that if the blade hit the stone column or the hard shell of the zombie’s head, the ring of metal would be a bell that would destroy them all.

Instead, he lunged forward, thrusting the thick wooden pommel of his Nandao hilt directly into the zombie's open mouth.

*Choke.*

The cry was cut off, turned into a dry, muffled rattle.

Xiao Feng moved from the other side. With a swift, rising thrust, he drove the pointed tip of his Nandao upward, entering the soft, uncalcified pocket of flesh under the jaw, directly beneath the chin. The steel slid through the soft tissue, penetrating the skull and destroying the brain stem.

The zombie’s green-glowing eyes flickered, then went dark.

As the body began to collapse, Liang caught the heavy, stone-hard torso with both arms, his muscles straining as he lowered the three-hundred-pound weight slowly and silently to the wet limestone floor.

They stood still, their breathing stopped, their ears ringing.

Around them, in the dark gallery, the other clay-zombies twitched. A stone miner’s head tilted by an inch; another’s fingers clicked against a column. But the silence held. The warning had not been shouted.

"Move," Xiao Feng whispered.

They slipped out of the Gallery of Columns, entering a narrow, winding fissure that sloped downward. The limestone walls here were close, the ceiling so low they had to crawl in some places.

According to Captain Zhao’s map, they had entered the Maze of Fissures—a network of hundreds of identical water-carved cracks that ran through the mountain. It was a place where a traveler could wander in circles until their water ran out, their bones left to join the limestone.

Li reached into her canvas satchel, pulling out a large, heavy ball of traditional hemp thread—a thick, dark cord her mother had spun for net-mending. She tied the end to a thick stalagmite at the entrance of the passage.

"We unravel the thread," Li said, her voice a low whisper. "If we must retreat, we follow the cord. And if we get separated, we stay on the line."

"Good," Xiao Feng said. "We follow the sound of the water."

In the distance, a low, muffled rumble was carrying through the stone—the sound of the subterranean river.

They walked for twenty minutes, winding through the dark fissures, the green stream of mud on the floor growing thinner, branching into small cracks. Li held the ball of hemp, letting the cord slide through her fingers, leaving a thin brown line along the wet limestone.

Suddenly, the thread went taut.

Li stopped, her fingers feeling the sudden tension in the cord. She pulled gently, but the line did not yield. It was caught.

"Is it caught on a stone?" Liang asked, holding the lantern low.

Li pulled again.

The thread was not caught on a rock. It was vibrating.

A slow, rhythmic tug was coming from the other side of the line, miles back in the dark tunnels they had just traversed. The cord hummed, a low-frequency vibration that ran through Li's fingers.

*Tug... tug... tug...*

Xiao Feng turned, holding the weak red beam of his flashlight back along the line.

Through the mist of the narrow tunnel, the brown hemp thread was suspended in the air, running straight back into the shadows. And in the red light, they saw the cord shift.

Something in the darkness had grabbed the thread. They could hear a soft, wet scraping sound—like multiple bodies crawling along the stone floor, following the line of the thread like a guide rope in the dark.

The thread was leading the dead straight to them.

Li stood frozen, the vibrating cord humming in her hand, as the scraping sounds in the dark corridor grew closer.

---

CHAPTER 4: THE UNDERGROUND RIVER


The hum of the hemp cord in Li’s hand felt like a live wire, vibrating with a cold, rhythmic pulse that seemed to match the pounding of her own heart. In the narrow, limestone tunnel, the silence had been replaced by a wet, sliding scrape—the sound of skinless knees and calcified fingers dragging across the damp stone floor.

"Cut it," Xiao Feng whispered, his voice a barely audible breath.

"If we cut it," Liang hissed, his knuckles white around the hilt of his Nandao, "we have no path back. We’ll be blind in the labyrinth."

"If we don't cut it, they'll climb the line right to our throats," Xiao Feng countered. He did not wait. He raised his short sword, the edge gleaming faintly in the green phosphorescence of the mud path, and brought it down on the taut cord where it met the stalagmite.

*Snap.*

The tension went out of the line, the severed end dropping into the wet clay with a soft, dead splat. For a second, the scraping sound seemed to falter, as if the creatures in the dark had lost the guide. But then, a high-pitched, wet snarl echoed from the dark corridor behind them—a sound like wet leather tearing. The scent of ancient damp and rot grew thick, pushing through the cold draft of the tunnel.

They had not lost the trail. The scent of living flesh and the heat of their breath was a beacon in the cold air of the mountain’s veins.

"Run!" Xiao Feng said.

They turned and fled down the sloping fissure, their canvas-wrapped boots sliding on the wet limestone. Li led the way, holding her iron-pointed boat hook forward to test the ground, while Liang and Xiao Feng brought up the rear, their eyes darting back into the shadows. The tunnel was winding, twisting like the gut of a dragon, the walls closing in until their shoulders scraped the cold rock. The ceiling dipped lower, forcing them to run in a half-crouch, their heads brushing the hanging stalactites.

Behind them, the scraping grew louder, accompanied by the dry, heavy clatter of stone-hard joints. These were not the slow, wandering dead of the plains; these were the miners who had been trapped in the deep shafts, their bodies saturated with the chemical clay that had leaked from the reservoir. The polymer had hardened their skin, but it had also preserved their limbs, making them heavy, solid, and relentless. They did not feel the jagged rocks that tore at their flesh. They simply pressed forward, a mass of stone and bone.

"The sound is changing," Liang gasped, his breath coming in ragged pants.

A deep, low rumble was vibrating through the floor of the fissure, a sound that was not the echo of their footsteps or the pursuit of the dead. It was a wet, heavy roar, like a dragon sleeping in the deep earth.

"The underground river," Li said, her eyes widening in the dim green light.

The fissure ended abruptly, opening into a vast, cavernous canyon. The transition was so sudden that Xiao Feng had to grab Liang’s shoulder to keep him from stepping off the edge.

They stood on a narrow limestone ledge, no wider than two feet, that clung to the wall of a massive subterranean gulf. Below them, a hundred feet down, a black torrent of water was rushing through the stone channel, its surface churning with white foam and green, glowing streaks of the chemical mud. The roar of the river was deafening, filling the cavern with a constant, vibrating hum that made speech almost impossible. The air was thick with cold spray, coating their faces and clothes with a fine, damp mist.

The green mud path they had been following did not cross the river; it ran along the ledge, winding around the shoulder of the cavern wall toward a narrow stone archway in the distance.

"Is that the path to the valve room?" Liang shouted over the roar of the water.

Xiao Feng pulled out Captain Zhao's map, holding it under the weak red beam of his flashlight for a fraction of a second. "Yes! The map calls this the River of Echoes. The primary valve control is in the dome on the other side of the canyon. We have to cross!"

"How?" Li asked, pointing her boat hook into the white mist.

Through the drifting spray, they saw the only link. An ancient, half-decayed suspension bridge spanned the gulf, its ropes made of thick, rusted iron chains and its walkway constructed of weathered pine planks, many of which were missing or hanging loose above the black torrent. The bridge swayed slowly in the cold wind that blew along the river channel, the iron links creaking with a dry, metallic groan.

It was a relic of the old mining operations, built a century ago to carry ore carts across the river. It looked like a spiderweb suspended over an abyss.

"The chains are iron," Liang said, stepping toward the bridge’s anchor point—two massive iron rings driven deep into the limestone wall. "They will hold. But the wood is rotten. We must step on the chains where the planks are gone."

"We go one by one," Xiao Feng said. "Li, you first. Keep the hook low. Liang, watch the rear. They are coming."

As Li stepped onto the first wooden plank, the bridge groaned, dropping three inches under her weight. She gripped the cold, rusted iron chain that served as a handrail, her knuckles turning white. She did not look down at the black water rushing below; she fixed her eyes on the opposite ledge, fifty feet away.

Behind them, the first of the clay-zombies emerged from the mouth of the fissure.

It was a tall miner, his chest bare and blackened by coal dust, his skin covered in a hard, grey crust of dried clay. His left arm was missing below the elbow, but his right hand ended in a cluster of thick, stone-like fingers. His eyes, glowing with a dull green light, locked onto the three survivors. He did not hesitate. He lunged forward, his heavy boots clattering on the ledge.

"Go, Li!" Xiao Feng yelled, drawing his Nandao.

He and Liang stood side by side at the mouth of the bridge, their backs to the abyss. The narrowness of the ledge was their only advantage; the zombies could only approach one at a time. But the weight of the horde was behind them, and more figures were pouring out of the crevice, their stone-hard bodies pressing against one another.

The miner zombie reached them, its stone hand swinging in a heavy, horizontal arc.

Xiao Feng ducked under the blow, the wind of the heavy hand whistling over his head. He brought his Nandao up in a rising slash, targeting the zombie’s neck. The blade struck the hard, clay-encrusted skin with a dry *clack*, leaving a shallow grey groove but failing to sever the head. The zombie did not flinch; it simply lunged forward, trying to grab Xiao Feng’s collar with its heavy fingers.

"The joints!" Liang shouted.

He stepped forward, his Nandao moving in a precise, downward thrust. He drove the point of the blade into the soft pocket of flesh behind the zombie’s knee, where the clay had not fully hardened. The steel sank three inches, severing the tendon.

The miner zombie’s leg buckled, its heavy body collapsing onto the wet limestone. But it did not stop. It crawled forward, its fingers clawing at the stone, its teeth clicking as it reached for Xiao Feng’s ankle.

Xiao Feng stepped back, his boot heel finding the edge of the first bridge plank. "We must retreat! Liang, get on the bridge!"

Li was halfway across. She had reached a section where three consecutive pine planks were missing, leaving only the two rusted iron chains that suspended the walkway. She paused, balancing her feet on the narrow links of the lower chain, her boat hook held horizontally to maintain her equilibrium. The spray from the river was slick, making the iron links like ice.

"The chains are slippery!" Li shouted back, her voice barely carrying over the roar. "Take your time!"

"We don't have time!" Liang yelled.

He stepped onto the bridge, his weight causing the structure to sway wildly. Behind him, three more clay-zombies pressed onto the narrow ledge. One was a woman, her clothes tattered, her head tilted at a broken angle; the others were miners, their bodies heavy and solid. They did not care about the cliff or the water. They simply walked toward the scent of life.

The lead zombie, the woman, stepped onto the wooden planks.

The wood split under her weight, her foot slipping through the gap. She fell forward, her hands grabbing the handrail chains, her body dangling above the roaring black river. But she did not cry out. She simply pulled herself back up, her dead eyes fixed on Liang, her teeth bared in a silent snarl.

"They’re coming onto the bridge," Liang said, his voice tight. "Xiao Feng, cross!"

Xiao Feng stepped backward onto the swaying bridge, his eyes on the zombies that were now crowding the entrance. The bridge was shaking violently now, the rusted iron chains groaning under the weight of five bodies. Every movement was an exercise in balance, the abyss waiting below.

Suddenly, a new sound rose above the roar of the water—a wet, heavy splashing from the dark pools near the opposite bank.

Li, who had almost reached the far ledge, froze.

Through the green-streaked mist, she saw them. The water walkers.

These were the dead who had been carried down from the reservoir and had gotten caught in the deep eddies of the underground river. Their bodies were bloated to twice their size, their skin a pale, translucent green from the chemical clay. They were rising from the water, their dead hands grabbing the wet limestone boulders at the base of the far ledge, pulling themselves upward.

One of them, a massive figure with no hair and eyes that were completely white, reached the far anchor point of the bridge. His wet, bloated fingers closed around the iron rings that secured the chains.

"Xiao Feng!" Li screamed. "They’re at the end! They’re cutting us off!"

The water walker at the far end did not have a weapon, but his heavy, waterlogged body was a solid barrier. Behind him, two more bloated figures were crawling onto the ledge, their wet clothes dripping black water onto the stone.

They were trapped. Behind them was the clay-hardened horde; ahead of them, the water walkers; below them, the roaring abyss.

"Liang! Use the harpoon!" Xiao Feng shouted, his boots sliding on a wet plank as the bridge swung to the left.

Liang reached back, grabbing one of the bamboo harpoons strapped to his pack. He balanced himself on the chains, his knees bent to absorb the swaying of the bridge, and aimed the long shaft at the water walker blocking the far ledge.

"Hold the line!" Liang yelled.

With a powerful, rhythmic thrust of his shoulders—a motion he had practiced a thousand times in the village fields—he threw the harpoon.

The long bamboo shaft flew through the mist, its barbed iron tip striking the bloated water walker in the chest. The iron prongs sank deep into the waterlogged flesh, the barbs locking into the collarbone. The force of the impact knocked the zombie backward off the ledge, but the rope attached to the harpoon’s tail was still wrapped around Liang’s arm.

As the heavy, three-hundred-pound body fell into the rushing river below, the rope snapped taut.

"Liang!" Xiao Feng screamed.

The sudden, violent pull yanked Liang off his feet. He fell forward, his chest striking the wooden planks, his fingers slipping from the handrail chain. The bridge twisted violently, tilting at a forty-five-degree angle.

"Cut the rope!" Li shouted, lunging forward with her boat hook.

But the rope was wrapped tight around Liang’s wrist, the wet hemp biting into his skin. The falling body of the water walker, caught in the fast-flowing current of the river below, was a drag-line that was pulling Liang, and the entire section of the bridge, down into the gulf.

*CREAK... SNAP.*

At the far end, the ancient iron ring that held the left handrail chain began to groan. The limestone around the bolt cracked, sending a shower of grey pebbles into the water.

The chain was pulling out.

Xiao Feng scrambled forward on his knees, his Nandao raised. He reached Liang just as the iron ring at the far wall gave way with a sharp, metallic report.

The left chain snapped free, whipping through the air. The bridge collapsed on one side, the wooden planks sliding off the remaining chain like cards.

Liang hung by the rope, his body suspended in the empty air above the roaring torrent, while Xiao Feng held onto the single remaining chain with one hand, his other hand reaching down to grab Liang’s collar.

"I’ve got you!" Xiao Feng roared, his muscles screaming under the strain.

But above them, on the section of the bridge that still clung to the entrance ledge, the clay-zombies were still walking. The female zombie stepped onto the single chain, her heavy boots sliding along the links toward them, her dead face inches away.

The bridge was falling apart, the last chain groaning under the weight, and Liang was dangling over the black water as the dead closed in from above.

---

CHAPTER 5: THE ECHO OF SILENCE


The roar of the underground river was a physical weight, pressing against Xiao Feng’s ears as he hung from the single remaining support chain of the collapsed bridge. His fingers, locked around the rusted iron links, were numb and slick with cold spray. Below him, suspended over the churning black water, Liang was a dead weight, his feet dangling feet above the foaming current that wanted to sweep him into the dark.

"Hold on!" Xiao Feng roared, but the sound was instantly swallowed by the crash of the torrent.

With a desperate grunt, his shoulder muscles straining to the point of tearing, Xiao Feng pulled. He managed to lift Liang by six inches, just enough for Liang’s free hand to claw at the wet limestone edge of the ledge.

From the far end of the collapsed walkway, Li lunged forward. She did not try to reach for Liang’s hand, knowing she could easily lose her balance on the wet rock. Instead, she extended the long wooden shaft of her boat hook, wedging the curved iron tip under Liang’s canvas backpack strap.

"Pull!" Li screamed, her feet finding purchase in a crevice of the limestone floor.

Working in perfect, silent coordination, Xiao Feng and Li exerted their remaining strength. With a wet scrape of canvas on stone, Liang was dragged over the lip of the ledge, collapsing face-down onto the cold limestone floor. Xiao Feng followed a second later, rolling onto his side, his hands trembling and covered in red rust from the chains.

Behind them, the single remaining chain of the bridge swung violently, hitting the rock wall with a series of dull, heavy clangs. The female zombie, who had been crawling along the links, lost her grip as the chain struck the limestone. She fell silently into the black river below, her grey body instantly swallowed by the foam.

On the ledge below them, the water walkers were still struggling to climb. Their bloated, green-tinged hands clawed at the wet boulders, but the rock was too slick and the current too strong. One by one, they were swept back into the deep pools.

"The tunnel," Xiao Feng gasped, pointing his sword toward the narrow stone archway. "Get inside. Quickly."

They scrambled through the archway, leaving the roar of the river behind. The transition was immediate; the roaring water became a distant, muffled hum, replaced by a silence so profound it felt like a pressure on their eardrums.

They were standing at the entrance of a towering, cavernous dome.

Unlike the rough, limestone fissures they had traversed, this chamber was a natural cathedral of quartz and calcite. The walls were lined with thousands of delicate, needle-like crystal formations that glinted with a cold, pale green light, reflecting the phosphorescence of the chemical mud that had pooled in the center of the floor. The ceiling rose fifty feet, lost in the shadows, but the air was dry and cold, carrying a faint, sweet scent of mountain herbs mixed with the decay.

This was the River of Echoes basin, a geological formation famous among the old miners. The shape of the dome and the crystalline structures on the walls acted as a natural acoustic amplifier. A whisper here would travel along the curved ceiling, growing louder as it bounced off the crystals, until it sounded like a voice speaking directly into a traveler’s ear from across the cavern.

"Do not speak," Li warned in a voice that was a barely audible breath.

Even that tiny whisper seemed to catch in the crystals, repeating itself in a soft, dry hiss that circled the dome three times: *...speak... speak... speak...*

Xiao Feng nodded, raising his finger to his lips.

He pointed to the far side of the dome. The path was a narrow, flat ledge that circled the edge of the crystal walls, passing above the central pool of green mud. But the path was not clear.

Along the ledges and in the natural niches of the crystal walls, hundreds of clay-zombies were resting. They were blackened by the coal dust, their skin coated in the grey, hard shell of the polymer. They stood or sat in silent rows, their heads bowed, their eyes closed, like stone statues in a subterranean museum. The lack of air currents and the complete absence of sound had kept them in a deep, undisturbed state of hibernation for weeks.

To cross the dome, the survivors would have to walk within inches of these sleeping sentinels, and any sound—even the rustle of their clothes or the scratch of a boot on the sand—could wake the entire chamber.

Liang sat against the wall, his head back, his eyes closed in pain. His right wrist was raw and bleeding, the wet hemp rope having torn through the skin to the white muscle underneath during his fall from the bridge. The red blood was dripping slowly onto the stone floor, making a soft, wet *splat*.

*Splat... splat... splat...*

The sound echoed off the crystals, a dry, rhythmic thud that sounded like a finger tapping on a drum.

Xiao Feng tensed, looking at the sleeping zombies. A miner zombie ten feet away tilted its head, its calcified nostrils twitching. The scent of fresh, warm blood was drifting through the cold air of the dome, a sharp trigger that was slowly reaching the dormant senses of the dead.

We must stop the bleeding, Xiao Feng thought.

He reached into his pack, pulling out a roll of clean white cotton bandage—a traditional herbal dressing made by the village healers, treated with dried wormwood and pine resin to prevent infection. He moved with agonizing slowness, trying to keep the fabric from rustling.

*Fffff-t.*

The sound of the bandage unrolling was a sharp hiss in the silence, repeating along the walls: *...t... t... t...*

Liang winced as Xiao Feng wrapped the cotton around his wrist, the resin sticking to the raw flesh. He bit his lip, his teeth drawing blood, to keep from groaning. Xiao Feng tied the knot, his fingers working with delicate precision, and the bleeding stopped. But the scent of blood still hung in the cold air, and the echoes of the rustle were still bouncing off the quartz crystals.

A low, dry creak came from the ledge above them.

Xiao Feng slowly raised his head.

On a crystal shelf five feet above the path, a clay-zombie—a former mine supervisor wearing a rusted iron helmet—was slowly beginning to stir. His eyelids, white with lime dust, twitched open, revealing two cloudy green eyes. His jaw clicked, his neck muscles tensing as he prepared to release the warning cry that would rouse the entire dome.

If he cried out, the echo would multiply the sound a thousand-fold, and the thousands of dormant dead in the caves would descend upon them in a wave.

Xiao Feng did not draw his sword, knowing that the ring of steel would be just as loud as the scream.

Instead, he stepped forward, his feet moving in the silent, sliding pattern of the traditional *baguazhang* martial arts—a style that emphasized circular movement, balance, and quiet footsteps. He reached the base of the shelf in three silent strides.

As the zombie's throat opened to release the first rattle, Xiao Feng lunged upward.

He did not strike the head. Instead, he threw his arms around the zombie’s neck from behind, his right forearm locking under the chin, his left hand pressing against the back of the rusted helmet. Using his body weight and the leverage of his legs, he pulled backward and downward, twisting the neck in a smooth, continuous motion.

*Crunch.*

The sound of the vertebrae breaking was a dry, snapping branch in the quiet room.

*Snap... snap... snap...*

The echo circled the room, a sharp, clean sound that made the other sleeping zombies twitch. Xiao Feng did not let the body fall. He held the heavy, clay-hardened corpse against his chest, his muscles screaming under the strain as he lowered it slowly and silently to the sandy floor behind a crystal formation.

He stood still, his breathing shallow, his ears straining.

Around the dome, the twitching stopped. The green eyes of the dormant dead closed once more, the threat of the echo subsiding into the silence.

Xiao Feng waved his hand, signaling Li and Liang to move.

They walked along the narrow path, their bodies pressed against the crystal walls, their movements slow and deliberate. Every step was a calculation; they had to ensure no loose sand or crystal shards were disturbed under their boots. Liang held his bandaged wrist close to his chest, his face pale from the pain, while Li carried her boat hook like a balance pole, her eyes scanning the ceiling.

They reached the far side of the dome, where a wide, arched tunnel led toward the high-pressure valve vault. The exit was only ten feet away.

But the mountain was not done with them.

In the high, dark ceiling of the dome, a massive stalactite—a three-ton column of solid limestone and quartz that had hung above the center of the chamber for ten thousand years—was failing. The humidity from the leaking reservoir and the sudden vibration from the bridge collapse had reopened an ancient fracture in its root.

*PING.*

The sound of the crystal root snapping was a sharp, musical note that cut through the silence like a silver bell.

Xiao Feng froze, looking up.

Through the darkness, the massive stone column began to slide, dropping silently at first.

"Jump!" Xiao Feng yelled, forgetting all warnings of silence.

They threw themselves forward into the mouth of the exit tunnel just as the stalactite struck the limestone floor of the dome.

*THOOM.*

The impact was a volcanic eruption of sound. The three-ton stone column shattered into a thousand pieces, sending a shockwave of dust and crystal shards through the chamber. The roar was deafening, a physical force that knocked them to their knees, their ears ringing with a high-pitched, painful whistle.

And the echoes did not die.

The sound bounced off the quartz walls, multiplying, amplifying, until the dome was a screaming vortex of noise. The vibrations ran through the stone floor, the walls cracking, sending more stone debris falling from the ceiling.

Instantly, the silence of the nest was shattered.

Around the dome, and in the dark tunnels beyond, thousands of clay-zombies opened their green-glowing eyes. Their heads snapped upward, their dry, calcified throats opening to release a collective, deafening roar that joined the echoes of the stone collapse.

The sleeping horde had awakened.

Behind the survivors, the collapsed stalactite had blocked the entrance to the dome with a pile of massive boulders, cutting off any possibility of retreat. And from the dark corridors ahead, the sound of thousands of clattering boots and scraping fingers began to rush toward them.

---

CHAPTER 6: THE CHASM CROSSING


The thunderous crash of the shattered stalactite was still ringing in their ears, a high-pitched, painful whistle that made their heads throb as they fled down the sloping exit passage. The air behind them was a thick cloud of white limestone dust and quartz shards, flying through the dark corridor like shrapnel.

Behind the dust, the roar of the awakened nest was a collective, scraping wave—thousands of clay-hardened feet scrambling over the newly fallen boulders.

"Don't look back!" Xiao Feng shouted, his voice hoarse from the dust.

They ran blindly, their flashlights casting frantic, sweeping beams of red and white light over the uneven stone floor. The passage was sloping downward at a steep angle, the limestone walls slick with moisture and patches of black coal silt. Liang stumbled, his bandaged wrist held tight against his chest, but Xiao Feng caught his shoulder, hauling him back to his feet before he could slide into the dark.

"The air is getting colder," Li said, her voice shaking as she ran.

A freezing wind was blowing from the depths ahead, carrying the scent of snow and wet stone. It was a clean, sharp draft that did not belong to the stagnant caves, suggesting a connection to a deep, open fissure that ran to the mountain's surface.

The corridor ended abruptly, opening into a gargantuan cavern.

They stood on a wide, sloping platform of rock that looked out over a bottomless chasm. The space was so vast their flashlight beams were lost in the empty air, unable to find the opposite wall or the ceiling. Below them, a howling wind was rushing up from the black depths, carrying a fine spray of icy water. The air was freezing, their breath pluming in the cold light.

This was the Devil’s Chasm, a massive geological split that ran through the heart of the mountain range.

The only way across was a natural stone arch—a thin, slippery bridge of limestone that had been carved by water millions of years ago. The arch was forty feet long, no wider than eighteen inches at its center, and had no handrails or supports. It arched slightly over the black gulf, its surface wet and covered in a thin layer of slippery green clay that had dripped from the roof.

"We have to cross the arch," Xiao Feng said, his flashlight beam tracing the narrow stone bridge to the far platform.

"It's too slick, Feng," Liang said, looking at the bottomless black below. "One slip and we're gone."

"We have no choice," Li said.

From the dark tunnel behind them, the first of the clay-zombies emerged from the dust cloud.

It was a pack of five, their bodies blackened by coal, their skin a hard, calcified shell. They ran in a clumsy, shuffling trot, their green-glowing eyes locked onto the survivors. They did not feel the cold or the wind; they were driven only by the collective hunger of the nest.

"Li, Liang, cross!" Xiao Feng commanded, drawing his Nandao. "I will hold the entrance."

Li did not argue. She stepped onto the natural stone arch, her bare feet finding purchase on the cold limestone. She walked with a low center of gravity, her boat hook held horizontally to balance against the howling wind that threatened to blow her off the narrow path. Liang followed close behind, his boots sliding slightly on the wet green clay. He held his Nandao in his left hand, his right wrist wrapped in the thick cotton bandage.

Xiao Feng stood at the mouth of the arch, his sword raised, his body balanced in the defensive stance of the *wushu* guards.

The first zombie, a heavy miner with a cracked skull, lunged toward him.

Xiao Feng did not try to slash the hard, clay crust of the chest. Instead, he used the zombie's own momentum. As the creature lunged, Xiao Feng stepped to the side, his boot heel finding the edge of the stone platform. He caught the zombie’s wrist with his left hand, pulling it forward while his Nandao executed a quick, horizontal cut behind the knee.

The zombie's leg gave way, its heavy body sliding off the wet rock and tumbling into the black gulf. It fell silently, its green-glowing eyes disappearing into the darkness.

But the remaining four zombies were already pressing forward, their stone-hard hands reaching for Xiao Feng's throat.

On the narrow stone arch, Liang and Li were halfway across.

Suddenly, a dry clatter echoed from the far side of the chasm.

Through the mist, they saw more figures emerging from a series of small, water-carved fissures on the opposite platform. These were clay-zombies that had been wandering the lower tunnels, awakened by the thunderous crash of the stalactite. They were scrambling onto the far landing, blocking the exit.

"Xiao Feng!" Li called out, her voice tight. "They're on the other side too!"

They were flanked. The narrow arch was now a bridge between two threats.

"Liang! Hold them!" Xiao Feng shouted, his sword clashing against the stone-hard forearm of a zombie at the entrance.

Liang tensed, his left hand gripping the hilt of his Nandao. He stepped in front of Li, his boots balancing on the narrowest section of the arch. The wind was howling, spray hitting his face, but his eyes were fixed on the three zombies that were crawling onto the far side of the arch.

The lead zombie, a former mine worker with a heavy iron wrench still rusted to his belt, stepped onto the stone bridge.

Liang did not wait for it to reach him. He lunged forward, his movement limited by the narrow ledge. He drove the point of his Nandao into the zombie's throat, the steel finding the soft pocket of flesh beneath the chin. The blade sank deep, and with a powerful twist of his wrist, Liang threw the zombie’s weight to the right.

The heavy body fell off the arch, dragging the second zombie down with it as it tumbled into the abyss.

But the third zombie was already climbing over the edge, its stone fingers grabbing Liang's ankle.

Liang fell back, his boots slipping on the wet clay. He landed hard on the stone arch, his bandaged right hand instinctively reaching for the handrail that wasn't there. He slid toward the edge, his legs dangling over the black gulf.

"Liang!" Li screamed.

She lunged forward, thrusting the iron tip of her boat hook into the eye socket of the zombie clawing at Liang’s ankle. The iron prongs sank deep, and with a heave of her shoulders, she wedged the wooden shaft under Liang’s arm, pinning him to the stone arch.

At the entrance, Xiao Feng was fighting a losing battle.

Three clay-zombies were pressing him back onto the arch. He had cut the tendons of two, but the third, a massive figure with a heavy iron coal shovel in its hands, was swinging the iron tool in wide, aggressive arcs. The metal shovel struck Xiao Feng’s Nandao with a sharp, ringing clang that echoed through the chasm.

The impact vibrated through Xiao Feng's arm, his fingers nearly releasing the hilt. He stepped back, his heel finding the narrow stone arch.

"Feng! We must collapse the arch!" Liang shouted, his voice hoarse as he pulled himself back onto the stone. "The base on your side is cracked!"

Xiao Feng looked down.

At the entrance of the arch, where the natural stone bridge met the platform, a deep, horizontal fracture ran through the limestone. The weight of the zombies and the vibrations of the fight had widened the gap, and a slow stream of stone dust was falling into the chasm.

If he could strike the fracture with enough force, the arch would collapse, sending the zombies into the gulf and securing the far side. But he was still on the bridge side of the crack.

"Go!" Xiao Feng shouted to Li and Liang. "Cross the landing!"

Li grabbed Liang's arm, dragging him the remaining ten feet to the far platform. They collapsed onto the dry stone landing, their breath coming in short, frozen gasps.

Xiao Feng tensed his legs, preparing for the leap.

Behind him, the massive zombie with the coal shovel lunged, the heavy iron tool swinging toward his head.

Xiao Feng did not jump forward. Instead, he drove his body downward, landing on his knees on the stone arch. He brought his Nandao down with both hands, using all his weight and the momentum of the fall, and struck the cracked base of the arch.

*CLANG.*

The hand-forged steel, tempered in Lao Ma’s forge, struck the limestone fracture with a sharp, ringing report.

The stone split.

A web of black cracks raced through the base of the arch. With a wet, heavy groan, the entire forty-foot limestone span began to sag, the center dipping toward the abyss.

Xiao Feng lunged forward, his legs driving him toward the far platform.

But the stone was already giving way under his boots. The arch broke into three massive sections, the limestone crumbling into dust and falling into the black chasm, carrying the three zombies with it.

Xiao Feng fell short.

His hands slammed into the wet, cold edge of the far platform, his fingers clawing at the slippery green clay. His body swung violently in the empty air, the freezing wind of the chasm catching his legs, pulling him down toward the torrent.

"Xiao Feng!" Liang screamed, scrambling toward the edge on his knees.

But the limestone around Xiao Feng's hands was soft, crumbling under his fingers. The green clay was like grease, his grip sliding inch by inch as the stone gave way.

Xiao Feng hung by his fingertips, the bottomless chasm waiting below, as the stone began to crumble under his hands.

---

CHAPTER 7: THE LOST OUTPOST


The cold wind of the Devil’s Chasm howled like a thousand ghosts, pulling at Xiao Feng’s legs as his fingers slipped from the crumbling edge of the stone platform. The limestone was soft, turning to white paste under his fingertips, and the green clay was a layer of grease that offered no purchase.

"Feng!" Liang’s voice was a desperate rasp.

Liang threw himself face-down onto the wet landing, his left hand lunging over the edge. His fingers locked around Xiao Feng’s right wrist, his grip tight and solid despite his own trembling. From the other side, Li knelt, pressing the thick wooden shaft of her boat hook down next to Xiao Feng’s chest, offering him a solid bar to grab.

"Hold on!" Li gasped, her boots digging into a split in the rock.

With a heavy grunt, Xiao Feng caught the wooden shaft with his left hand, his feet kicking the empty air of the chasm to find a foothold. Working in perfect, desperate synchronization, the two youths hauled him upward. The rotted limestone edge crumbled completely, sending a shower of grey pebbles into the black void, but Xiao Feng’s elbows found the solid rock of the platform.

With a final, chest-heaving pull, they dragged him over the lip. The three of them lay in a heap on the cold, wet stone, their breath pluming in the freezing air, their hearts hammering like drums.

Across the empty chasm, where the natural stone arch had stood only seconds ago, the remaining clay-zombies stood on the platform. They stared across the forty-foot gap, their green-glowing eyes reflecting in the mist, their jaws clicking in frustration. They could not cross; the bridge was gone, and the abyss lay between them.

"Move," Xiao Feng breathed, standing up and wiping the limestone dust from his face. "The noise will draw others to the landing. We must find a shelter."

They gathered their gear, Liang holding his bandaged right wrist close to his chest. The cotton wrap was stained with a dark patch of red, but the bleeding had slowed. They walked quickly down the winding, dark passage that led away from the landing, their flashlights casting long, jumping shadows on the damp walls.

After a hundred yards, the passage split, opening into a vast, dark cavern that felt different from the organic karst caves they had traversed.

The floor was flat, carved by human hands, and the air smelled of rust, old coal dust, and rotted timber. In the beams of their flashlights, they saw the skeletal remains of human industry. Rusted iron rails ran along the floor, half-buried in the sand; rotted wooden support beams lined the walls, and the ruins of several structures stood in the shadows.

It was an old mining outpost, built during the early twentieth century during the first industrial iron boom in the Sichuan hills. The place had been abandoned for decades, forgotten by the outer world, but it had served as a secondary staging post for Captain Zhao's squad before they were lost.

"A barracks," Li said, pointing her light toward a large, rotted wooden building that stood near the center of the cavern, its walls built of thick pine planks.

"The doors are iron," Xiao Feng observed, walking up to the building. The door was a heavy, rusted iron plate secured by a simple slide bolt.

He slid the bolt back, the metal groaning with a dry, screeching slide that made them wince. He pushed the door open, and they stepped inside, closing the door behind them and sliding the inner bolt.

The interior of the barracks was dry, the air stagnant and cold. Rows of rotted wooden bunks lined the walls, their straw mattresses reduced to dust. In the center of the room sat a heavy iron stove, its chimney pipe running up through the rotted wooden roof into the cavern ceiling.

Liang sat on a wooden bench, his head resting against the wall, his face pale from exhaustion. "We have to rest, Feng. My wrist... the rope cut deep."

Xiao Feng knelt next to him, gently unwrapping the bloody bandage. The wound was a raw, red line that circled the wrist, the skin torn by the tension of the hemp cord. "The wormwood is holding, but we need to wash it. Li, is there any clean water left in the flask?"

"Only half a cup," Li said, pulling the metal flask from her satchel. "We must conserve it. We don't know how long it will take to reach the primary valve."

"Use the water," Liang said, his voice quiet. "I can hold the sword with my left hand, but if the infection gets into the blood, I will be a burden. We cannot afford that."

Xiao Feng washed the wound with the clean water, the cold liquid making Liang tensed, but he did not cry out. Xiao Feng reapplied the herbal dressing, wrapping the wrist tight with clean cotton.

As the silence returned to the room, a low, metallic clatter echoed from the back of the barracks.

Xiao Feng froze, his hand dropping to the hilt of his Nandao. Li raised her boat hook, her eyes fixed on the dark hallway that led to the rear of the building—the old ore-sorting facility.

*Clang... scrape...*

It was a slow, heavy sound, like metal dragging on concrete.

"Is someone there?" Liang whispered, his left hand drawing his Nandao.

They walked slowly down the hallway, their boots making no sound on the dusty floorboards. The hallway opened into a large, double-height room filled with rusted iron machinery—sorting screens, iron chutes, and heavy rock-crushing cylinders suspended from rotted timber frames.

And in the center of the room, behind a partition of thick iron bars, they saw the source of the sound.

It was the old holding cage—an iron enclosure designed to keep valuable ore secure before sorting. Inside the cage, four clay-zombies were pacing. They were former miners, their denim work clothes rotted to rags, their skin covered in the hard, grey crust of the polymer. They had been trapped inside the cage when the outbreak began, locked in the dark for weeks.

As the light of the flashlights swept over them, the zombies tensed. Their green-glowing eyes locked onto the survivors, and they threw themselves against the iron bars with a heavy, metallic crash.

*BANG.*

The rotted iron bars groaned, the rust falling like brown snow.

"They are locked in," Li said, stepping back. "We should leave them."

"Wait," Xiao Feng said, pointing his light at the door of the cage.

The door was secured by a heavy iron padlock, but the hinges of the door were completely rusted through. The metal was a paper-thin crust of red rust, and the weight of the four heavy, clay-hardened bodies slamming against the gate was too much.

*CREAK... SNAP.*

The upper hinge snapped with a sharp report, the door tilting outward. The zombies tensed, their collective weight pressing against the loose gate. The lower hinge cracked, and the entire iron door fell forward, striking the concrete floor with a deafening crash.

*CLANG.*

The four miner zombies stepped over the fallen door, their green eyes glowing with a hungry light, their stone-hard hands reaching forward.

"The tracks!" Xiao Feng yelled.

The room was split by a set of iron rails that ran from the sorting chutes toward the exit. On the tracks, ten feet away, sat an old, heavy iron ore cart—a massive steel tub filled with several hundred pounds of iron ore stones, its wheels rusted to the rails.

"Li, Liang! Help me push it!" Xiao Feng commanded.

They threw themselves behind the heavy steel cart, their boots digging into the rotted wooden floorboards that supported the tracks. The cart was a mountain of iron, its rusted axles locked.

"Push!" Liang roared, his left shoulder pressing against the cold steel, his injured right hand held away.

With a dry, screaming screech of metal on metal, the wheels turned. The massive ore cart rolled forward along the tracks, gaining momentum.

The lead zombie, a massive miner with a cracked leather belt, was standing directly on the tracks, his hands reaching to grab the cart’s rim.

*CRASH.*

The heavy steel cart struck the zombie at ten miles an hour. The impact was a dull, wet thud. The force of the heavy machine crushed the zombie against a massive concrete support column at the end of the tracks, pinning its torso to the stone. The creature's head snapped back, its green eyes flickering and going dark as the skull shattered.

But the remaining three zombies were already bypassing the cart, climbing over the rusted chassis to reach them.

"Back!" Xiao Feng shouted.

He lunged forward, his Nandao executing a quick, circular cut that severed the fingers of the second zombie as it grabbed the cart’s rim. The stone-hard fingers fell to the wood like pebbles.

But as they stepped back, a sharp, cracking sound echoed from beneath their feet.

The floor of the ore-sorting room was not concrete; it was constructed of thick pine timbers, suspended over a fifty-foot-deep vertical mine shaft that ran to the lower veins. The rotted wood, weakened by decades of damp and the sudden weight of the iron ore cart and the struggle, was failing.

A massive crack raced through the central timber beam.

*CREAK... SNAP.*

The floorboards tilted, the rotted pine splitting open like paper. A three-foot gap opened in the center of the room, revealing the pitch-black void of the shaft below.

Liang slipped, his boot falling through the gap. He caught himself on the edge of a rotted beam, his left hand holding his Nandao, his injured right wrist screaming in pain as he tried to balance.

"Feng!" Liang yelled as the rotted timbers around him began to crumble.

The heavy ore cart tilted, its wheels sliding off the tracks as the rotted floor collapsed. The steel cart slid into the gap, falling into the shaft with a hollow, echoing crash that did not end.

And the remaining two zombies, sliding on the tilting boards, were falling toward them as the entire rotted floor began to collapse into the dark pit below.

---

CHAPTER 8: THE DOME OF THE DEAD


The screech of splitting pine was a sudden, violent crack that tore through the stagnant air of the barracks. The floorboards beneath Liang’s feet did not merely tilt; they exploded upward, the rotted wood splitting into splintered teeth as the central timber beam snapped under the weight of the steel ore cart.

"Liang!" Xiao Feng lunged forward, his body flying across the tilting floor.

He caught Liang’s canvas vest with both hands just as the floorboards vanished into the dark shaft below. From the other side, Li threw herself onto the narrow concrete footing of the cavern wall, her iron-pointed boat hook wedged behind a rusted conduit pipe, her right hand reaching down to grab Xiao Feng’s collar.

*CRASH.*

The massive steel ore cart, filled with three hundred pounds of iron stones, plummeted into the vertical mine shaft, carrying the rotted timber floor with it. A second later, the two remaining miner zombies, sliding on the wet pine planks, tumbled into the dark void. A long, echoing series of metallic clangs and wet thuds drifted up from the depths as the heavy machine struck the walls of the lower veins, ending in a distant, muffled splash fifty feet below.

A thick cloud of rotted wood dust and black coal silt rose from the shaft, filling the room with a choking grey mist.

Xiao Feng and Li lay on the narrow concrete rim, their arms shaking as they pulled Liang up. His boots found purchase on the concrete footing, and they scrambled back against the cold stone wall of the cavern. They tensed, their chests heaving, their ears ringing in the sudden, quiet draft that blew up from the shaft.

The floor of the ore-sorting room was completely gone, leaving only the three-inch concrete ledge that lined the walls and two horizontal concrete support girders that spanned the empty space above the pit.

"We have to cross the girders," Xiao Feng said, his flashlight beam illuminating the narrow, twelve-inch-wide concrete beams that ran through the dust cloud toward the heavy iron door on the opposite wall.

"We go slow," Li said, her hand tightening around the wooden shaft of her boat hook. "One foot at a time. Liang, keep behind me."

Liang nodded, his face pale, his bandaged right hand held close to his chest. The cotton wrap was dark with old blood, but the bandage was dry. He stepped onto the first concrete girder, his balance compromised by his injured wrist, his left hand holding his Nandao forward to maintain his center of gravity.

They crawled across the empty space, their boots sliding on the damp concrete. Below them, the dark mouth of the mine shaft was a black throat, waiting for a slip. Xiao Feng brought up the rear, his eyes darting back toward the iron door they had bolted. The wood of the barracks was creaking, but the door remained secure; the main nest had not yet found the corridor.

They reached the far wall, Xiao Feng sliding the rusted latch of the heavy iron door. The metal plate was cold, covered in a thick layer of grey condensation. He pushed the door open, and they stepped through, closing the heavy iron barrier behind them and securing the latch.

The transition was immediate, the dry smell of coal dust replaced by a heavy, humid warmth that smelled of wet copper, chlorine, and the sweet, cloying scent of decay.

They were standing on a high, rusted iron catwalk that clung to the curved wall of a gargantuan circular cavern.

This was the Dome of the Dead—the central water purification and pressure-balancing facility for the entire mountain reservoir. The space was a massive cylinder of concrete and stone, three hundred feet in diameter, its ceiling lost in the high shadows where massive iron pipes ran like veins. In the center of the cavern sat three gargantuan steel water purification tanks, each fifty feet tall, their rusted shells covered in green slime and chemical mud.

But it was the floor of the cavern that made their breath catch in their throats.

The bottom of the dome was a crawling, writhing sea of thousands of clay-covered zombies. They had been drawn to the water purification facility weeks ago during the early days of the dam leak, trapped inside the circular basin when the high gates were closed. The chemical clay, leaking from the main pressure valves, had saturated their bodies, hardening their skin into a grey, stone-like crust. They moved in a slow, collective circle around the bases of the tanks, their boots clattering on the wet concrete, their green-glowing eyes a sea of tiny, dancing lights in the dark.

It was a nest of five thousand.

"The catwalk," Xiao Feng whispered, his voice shaking.

The path was the narrow iron catwalk that wrapped around the curved wall of the dome, leading toward a concrete control platform on the far side. From the platform, a vertical iron ladder led down to the primary valve room. The catwalk was suspended fifty feet above the crawling mass of the dead, supported by a series of rusted iron struts driven into the concrete wall.

"The struts are rusted, Feng," Liang whispered, pointing his flashlight beam at the supports. "Look at the brackets. The rust has eaten half the bolts."

"We go light," Xiao Feng said. "Keep to the wall. Do not step in the center of the metal grates."

They slipped along the catwalk, their boots making a soft, metallic *ping* with every step. The structure was fragile, the iron grates creaking and sagging under their weight, sending showers of red rust flakes falling into the dark below.

As they reached the midpoint of the catwalk, above the second gargantuan purification tank, a dry clatter echoed from a side platform.

Two clay-zombies—former engineers wearing faded blue work uniforms and dented hard hats—emerged from a high access corridor. They stepped onto the catwalk twenty feet ahead, blocking the path. Their green eyes locked onto the survivors, their stone-hard hands reaching forward as they began to advance.

"Xiao Feng," Li said, her voice tight. "We can't fight them here. The vibration will tear the catwalk down."

"We have to do it quietly," Xiao Feng said. "Liang, hold the rear. Li, use the hook."

Xiao Feng stepped forward, his bagua steps sliding on the wet iron grates. He did not raise his Nandao to strike, knowing the ring of metal on the iron helmet would be a bell that would wake the five thousand below.

As the first engineer zombie lunged, Xiao Feng ducked under the grasp, his body sliding next to the guardrail. He caught the zombie’s work vest with his left hand, using its own forward weight to slide it toward the rail.

Li moved from behind. She drove the iron tip of her boat hook into the zombie's hip joint, leveraging the long wooden shaft to lift the creature’s center of gravity.

With a collective heave, they rolled the zombie over the rusted guardrail. The heavy, clay-hardened body fell fifty feet, striking the concrete floor below with a wet, heavy thud that was instantly swallowed by the clatter of the mass.

But the second zombie, a massive man with a heavy iron wrench rusted to his belt, was already upon them.

He lunged at Xiao Feng, his stone-hard fingers closing around the collar of Xiao Feng’s tactical vest. The force of the grab yanked Xiao Feng forward, his boots sliding on the wet iron grates. The rusted struts beneath them groaned, the metal brackets cracking under the double weight.

*CREAK... SNAP.*

A support strut ten feet behind them snapped, the section of the catwalk sagging outward by three inches.

"Feng!" Liang lunged, his left hand bringing his Nandao down in a quick, downward cut that severed the zombie's wrist. The stone-hard hand remained locked to Xiao Feng’s vest, but the armless torso was kicked back by Xiao Feng's boot.

The zombie stumbled, its heel catching on the broken strut. It fell backward, its heavy body striking the guardrail.

The rusted iron rail gave way with a sharp, metallic report.

*CLANG.*

The rail snapped, and the massive zombie fell into the abyss, carrying a ten-foot section of the guardrail with it. The impact of the heavy iron on the concrete floor below was a thunderous ring that echoed through the dome.

*THOOM.*

The sound was a signal.

Below them, the sea of five thousand stopped its circular march. Thousands of heads snapped upward, their green-glowing eyes locking onto the rusted catwalk suspended above. Their dry, calcified throats opened to release a collective, deafening roar that shook the very walls of the dome.

They began to climb.

The zombies did not use ladders; they began climbing the rusted iron braces of the purification tanks, their heavy, clay-hardened bodies stacking over one another like a mountain of stone. The vertical ladders of the tanks were packed with climbing figures, their stone fingers clawing at the metal rungs.

"Run!" Xiao Feng roared.

They fled along the sagging catwalk, the iron structure shaking violently under their boots as more support struts snapped behind them. The catwalk was a falling zipper, the sections dropping into the dark as they ran.

They reached the final section of the catwalk, just ten feet from the concrete control platform.

*CREAK... SHREEECH.*

The main anchor bracket of the catwalk section failed with a deafening screech of tearing steel.

The entire ten-foot span broke free from the wall, dropping at a ninety-degree angle. Xiao Feng, Liang, and Li were thrown forward, their hands grabbing the iron handrails of the control platform as the catwalk collapsed beneath them.

They hung by their fingers, their bodies suspended in the empty air above the climbing mass.

Below them, the mountain of clay-zombies was rising. The lead walkers had reached the top of the nearest purification tank, just ten feet below their dangling boots, their stone hands reaching upward, their jaws clicking in the dark.

They were hanging from the platform edge, their fingers slipping on the cold iron, while the dead below rose to claim them.

---

CHAPTER 9: THE CONTROL ROOM FOUND


The cold iron handrail of the control platform was a lifeline that bit into Xiao Feng’s palms as his boots kicked the empty air of the dome. Fifty feet below, the sea of five thousand clay-zombies was a roaring vortex of reaching hands and clicking jaws, their green-glowing eyes a swirling galaxy of hunger in the dark.

"Feng! Swing!" Liang’s voice was a desperate grunt.

Liang, his knees wedged behind a concrete conduit pipe on the platform, reached down with his left hand, his fingers locking around Xiao Feng’s forearm. Next to him, Li lay on her stomach, her boat hook hooked under Xiao Feng’s belt, her muscles tensing as she threw her weight backward.

Xiao Feng tensed his stomach, swinging his legs toward the wall. His boot heel found a narrow concrete support ledge, and with a collective heave, Liang and Li hauled him over the lip of the platform.

They collapsed onto the reinforced concrete landing, their chests heaving, their breath rising in white plumes in the humid air of the dome.

Below them, the vertical iron ladders of the purification tanks were bending under the weight of the climbing dead. The zombies were not using the rungs; they were a mass of grey, clay-hardened bodies, climbing over one another to reach the platform. The lead walkers had reached the top of the nearest tank, their stone fingers clawing at the concrete edge of the landing, just five feet below.

"The door!" Xiao Feng said, scrambling to his feet and drawing his Nandao.

The control room door was a massive, circular steel plate, three inches thick, set into the concrete wall of the dome. Next to the door sat a hydraulic control panel, its glass screens dead, its electronic keys dark. The manual override lever was a heavy iron bar painted a faded yellow, secured by a heavy steel padlock.

Xiao Feng pulled the keys he had salvaged from Captain Zhao’s body. He selected the smallest key, inserting it into the padlock.

*Clack.*

The lock popped open, and he threw the metal latch aside. He grabbed the yellow hydraulic lever, pulling it downward with both hands.

Nothing happened.

The override lever moved, but the hydraulic line was dry. The green fluid had leaked from the cracked pipes weeks ago, and the manual cylinder had no pressure.

"It's dry," Xiao Feng hissed. "We have no pressure."

"They're on the ledge!" Liang yelled.

The first zombie—a former foreman wearing a dirty canvas jacket—climbed over the lip of the platform, its stone fingers clawing at the concrete floor.

Liang did not hesitate. He lunged forward, his left hand bringing his Nandao down in a quick, downward cut that severed the zombie's wrists. The creature collapsed back off the platform, landing on the climbing mass below. But behind it, three more zombies were climbing over the lip, their green eyes locked onto Liang.

"Li! Hold them!" Liang shouted.

Li stepped up next to him, her iron-pointed boat hook moving in a series of quick, rhythmic thrusts. She targeted the soft pockets of flesh behind the knees and in the armpits of the clay-hardened figures, using the long wooden shaft to keep them at bay. Liang, fighting one-handed, stood next to her, his Nandao flashing in the red light of their flashlights.

At the door, Xiao Feng was searching the hydraulic panel.

According to Captain Zhao's map, there was a manual pressure bypass wheel located beneath the concrete floor of the landing—an ancient, hand-cranked pump used to build pressure in the event of a total hydraulic failure.

Xiao Feng knelt, his fingers finding a recessed metal ring in the concrete floor. He pulled, lifting a heavy iron access hatch.

Inside the dark hatch sat a rusted iron wheel, connected to a vertical steel piston. The metal was covered in a thick layer of red rust and green hydraulic grease.

"Liang! Li! Keep them back!" Xiao Feng shouted.

He grabbed the iron wheel, his hands slick with grease, and turned.

*Screeech... clack.*

The metal screamed with a dry, grinding resistance that vibrated through the concrete landing. The piston moved by an inch, a slow hiss of air escaping from the valve.

"It's turning!" Xiao Feng roared, throwing his weight into the next rotation.

On the landing, the struggle was turning desperate.

Dozens of clay-zombies were now crowding the lip of the platform, their heavy bodies pressing against one another. Li’s boat hook was wedged in the shoulder of a massive miner, the wooden shaft bending under the strain. Liang’s left arm was numb from the clashing of his sword against the stone crusts of the dead. He stepped back, his boot heel finding the edge of the open hydraulic hatch.

"Feng! Hurry!" Liang gasped.

Xiao Feng cranked the wheel with frantic speed. The pressure gauge next to the steel door began to rise, the red needle moving slowly from the zero mark toward the green operating zone.

*Creak... creak... creak...*

The hydraulic lines along the wall groaned, the green fluid leaking from a cracked joint, spraying a fine mist of copper-smelling oil over the concrete floor.

The needle hit the green line.

*CLACK.*

Inside the steel door, the heavy locking bolts slid back with a sharp, metallic report.

Xiao Feng lunged up, grabbing the heavy iron handle of the circular door. He pulled, his muscles straining. The three-ton steel plate slid slowly into the wall, opening a two-foot gap.

"Inside!" Xiao Feng yelled.

Liang and Li retreated through the gap, their swords and boat hook held forward to block the entrance. Xiao Feng followed, throwing his shoulder against the inner edge of the door, sliding it shut just as the first clay-zombie slammed its body against the steel plate from the oucoarse haire.

*BANG.*

The door closed, the automatic bolts engaging with a solid, reassuring clang.

The control room was quiet, the roar of the dome reduced to a distant, hollow vibration. The air was dry and cold, smelling of old paper and electrical insulation.

Xiao Feng found the manual lock wheel on the inside of the door, turning it until the steel bar engaged, locking the barrier from the inside. They were safe, for now, behind three inches of reinforced steel.

The room was a large, semi-circular concrete bunker, its walls lined with dead control consoles and dark indicator panels. In the center of the room sat a large, wooden desk covered in technical manuals and maps.

But it was the observation window at the back of the room that drew their attention.

The window was a thick plate of reinforced green glass, six feet wide, looking out into the lower levels of the dome. In the beam of their flashlights, they saw the primary pressure reservoir—a massive, circular steel tank, seventy feet in diameter, that occupied the center of the cavern floor.

The tank was cracked.

A vertical fracture, ten feet long and three inches wide, ran down the side of the steel shell. A heavy, continuous stream of the green chemical clay was spraying from the crack, falling directly into a wide concrete canal that ran through the floor of the dome.

"The main aquifer channel," Li whispered, her hand touching the cold glass. "That water flows straight to the village well."

"We must shut the main valve," Xiao Feng said, pointing to the control console.

He walked to the primary console, his flashlight illuminating a large, red metal lever labeled: *EMERGENCY SHUTOFF - PRIMARY AQUIFER*.

He pulled the lever.

The lever moved smoothly, but the indicator light remained dark. From the depths below the room, a low, grinding rattle echoed—the sound of the gate valve struggling to close. But then, the sound stopped, replaced by a dull, metallic clang.

"The valve is jammed," Liang said, looking through the glass. "It's the clay. It has hardened inside the gate."

Xiao Feng looked at the technical map on the desk. "There is a manual override chamber directly beneath the tank. A flooded vault that contains the mechanical gate piston. If we can reach the vault, we can use a crowbar to clear the clay and force the piston down."

He looked at Liang, and then at Li.

"But the map says the vault is fed by the reservoir intake pipes," Xiao Feng said, his voice dropping. "If the intake locks are open, the vault is flooded. And the water walkers that were carried down from the river... they will be inside the chamber."

He pointed his flashlight down.

Through the observation glass, in the dark water of the flooded lower chamber beneath the tank, they saw several bloated green figures drifting in the current, their dead faces pressed against the lower glass panels, their teeth clicking in the dark water.

To save the village, one of them would have to go into the dark, flooded vault, surrounded by the water walkers, to clear the valve.

---

CHAPTER 10: THE FINAL TURN


The heavy steel hatch in the floor of the control room was a cold, circular lid that looked down into a well of absolute blackness. Through the gap, the sound of sloshing, waterlogged boots and the wet, rhythmic clicking of jaws drifted up, a chilling contrast to the dry quiet of the concrete bunker.

"I go," Xiao Feng said, his hand resting on the hatch handle.

"Feng, no," Li said, her hand reaching out to grab his sleeve. "The water is deep, and you have no line. If the hatch locks behind you—"

"If we don't shut the valve, the village well is dead by Tuesday," Xiao Feng said gently. He unbuckled his tactical rig, letting the heavy plate carrier fall to the concrete floor.
