STORY 7: THE EARTH FORTRESS (YONGDING TULOU, FUJIAN)
CHAPTER 1: THE CIRCLE OF CLAY


The massive outer wall of Chengqi Lou rose forty feet into the misty sky of Yongding, a circular mountain of rammed earth that had stood in the Fujian valleys for over three hundred years. Known as the "King of Tulou," the circular fortress was a self-contained city of clay and timber, its four concentric rings of buildings housing over eighty families of the Jiang clan. From the high hills above, the fortress looked like a giant earthen ring dropped among the terraced tea fields, its solid, windowless lower walls a shield against the world.

In the center of the outer ring’s second-story balcony, Jun stood checking the alignment of a heavy bamboo lever.

He was a young carpenter of twenty-four, his shoulders broad from hauling pine logs, his hands calloused from the chisel. He wore a faded blue cotton vest and trousers, his hair tied back. Next to him, his grandfather, Elder Jiang, a man of seventy-six with eyes that were clear and sharp behind a network of wrinkles, observed the work.

"A Tulou is not a stone castle, Jun," Elder Jiang said, his voice quiet but carrying over the creak of the wood. "It does not fight the earth. It is the earth. The walls are three meters thick, rammed from clay, sand, and lime, reinforced with brown sugar, sticky rice juice, and splits of wild bamboo. It breathes, and it bends, but it does not break. Remember this."

Jun tapped a wooden dowel into the frame, securing the lever. "The wood is seasoned, Grandfather. The pine from the northern slope is dry and strong. The gate will hold."

Chengqi Lou had withdrawn into its circular sanctuary three weeks ago when the first frantic radio warnings spoke of a biological virus spreading through the coastal cities of Xiamen and Fuzhou. The Jiang clan had not hesitated. Under the direction of the elders, they had closed the single entrance—a massive, double-leaved gate of cured pine, six inches thick, reinforced with heavy iron plates and secured by two thick beams of ironwood.

The lower stories, which had no windows facing the outer valley, were sealed. The courtyard in the center of the rings, normally a bustling market square, had been turned into a collective farm. The stone pathways were covered in rich soil from the terraced fields, planted with sweet potatoes, garlic, and green onions. The concentric wooden balconies were lined with hanging racks of drying peppers and salt-cured pork.

They were self-sufficient, a community of four hundred souls living by the old ways of cooperation and ancestral duty. They did not make noise. The central ancestral hall was quiet, the only sound the slow clucking of chickens in the inner ring.

It was three in the afternoon when the horn sounded from the watchtower on the fourth floor.

It was a sharp, clear note made from a brass trumpet, a signal that carried across the valley.

Jun set his tools down, running after Elder Jiang up the narrow wooden staircases that wound along the circular balconies. The steps were dark, polished by the bare feet of generations of Jiangs.

Reaching the fourth-floor catwalk, they looked out through a narrow observation slit in the thick clay wall.

The valley below was a green expanse of terraced tea fields, shrouded in a white, mountain fog. Down the winding dirt road that led to the nearby town of Yongding, a small group of survivors was running.

There were eight of them, their clothes covered in black soot and coal dust. They ran in a frantic, stumbling pack, their hands reaching toward the massive circular wall of Chengqi Lou.

Behind them, emerging from the dark forest of the valley slope, came the infected.

There were twenty of them. They were former workers from the local industrial coal mines, their skin blackened by coal dust, their eyes glowing with a dull, unblinking green light. They moved in a clumsy, shuffling trot, their heavy leather work boots thumping on the dirt path. They did not feel the steepness of the hill; they were driven by the collective hunger of the virus, their jaws clicking in the cold air.

The refugees reached the base of the Tulou’s outer wall, slamming their hands against the three-meter-thick clay.

"Let us in!" a man shouted, his voice cracking with exhaustion. He wore a dirty miner’s jacket, his face streaked with sweat and coal. "We are from the Yongding mine station! The town is overrun! The miners... they have turned! They are right behind us!"

Elder Jiang stood at the observation slit, his hands resting on the clay sill. "We cannot open the gate. The quarantine must hold. If we lift the ironwood beams, we invite the dead."

"We have children!" the miner pleaded, pointing to a young girl of ten who lay on a pile of canvas sacks in the back of a small utility truck they had parked next to the gate.

The truck was a small, three-wheeled agricultural vehicle, its cargo bed loaded with the refugees' remaining supplies: wooden crates of rice, blankets, and a massive, blue steel tank of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) used for cooking.

"The baskets," Elder Jiang commanded, turning to Jun. "Lower the rope baskets from the second-story balconies. We bring them up. But the gate stays closed."

Jun ran to the second-floor balcony, where three large, woven bamboo baskets—normally used for harvesting tea leaves—were secured by thick hemp ropes to the timber columns.

Working with three other young men, Jun lowered the baskets through the high, narrow window slits of the second floor.

"Get in!" Jun called down through the slit. "One by one! We pull you up!"

The refugees did not argue. The miner helped the young girl into the first basket, and Jun’s team hauled the rope, their muscles straining against the weight. The basket rose slowly along the smooth, sloping surface of the rammed-earth wall.

One by one, the refugees were brought through the narrow window slits, their hands trembling as they touched the solid wooden floor of the balcony.

But the mining zombies had reached the base of the wall.

They ignored the baskets; they did not have the intelligence to climb the ropes. Instead, they swarmed around the agricultural truck parked next to the gatehouse, their heavy bodies pressing against the metal panels.

One of the zombies, a massive man wearing a cracked miner’s helmet, had a heavy, battery-powered safety lantern still mounted to his head. The lamp was cracked, its wires sparking with a dry, white spark.

As the zombie slammed its body against the truck's cargo bed, the agricultural vehicle tilted, its fuel tank rupturing against a sharp stone. A dark pool of gasoline began to spread along the dirt ground, running under the massive pine gate.

*Spit... spark...*

The cracked lantern on the zombie’s helmet fell off, striking the wet gasoline pool.

*Fwoosh.*

The fuel ignited with a sudden, orange roar, a wall of flame rising along the front of the gates. The heat blistered the pine planks of the gate, and the fire began to spread toward the massive blue steel LPG tank in the back of the utility truck.

The gate was catching fire, the truck was a bomb, and the explosion was ticking directly against the entrance of the clay fortress.

CHAPTER 2: THE FIRE AT THE GATE


The heat inside the entrance tunnel of Chengqi Lou was a physical pressure, a hot, dry wave that carried the bitter smell of charred pine and bubbling lacquer. The double-leaved wooden gate, six inches of cured pine wood, was already beginning to turn black from the oucoarse haire, the flames from the utility truck's gasoline leak licking the bottom edges.

Jun sprinted down the narrow wooden staircase, landing on the granite slabs of the ground-floor corridor.

His chest was heaving, his face covered in soot. Behind him, Elder Jiang walked with steady, deliberate strides, his hand resting on the shoulder of a young watchman who carried a heavy iron pitchfork.

"The gate is catching," Jun said, pointing at the wisps of white smoke that were rising from the joints of the pine leaves. "The fire is oucoarse haire, but the wood is dry. If the charcoal reaches the core, the ironwood support beams will split."

"The water, Jun," Elder Jiang said, his voice calm. "The bamboo lines from the central spring. We must direct the flow to the gate vault."

Chengqi Lou was equipped with an ancient, gravity-fed water system—a network of thick bamboo pipes that ran from a mountain spring on the northern hills, through the thick clay walls, feeding a stone basin in the central courtyard and several outlet valves in the corridors.

But the valve in the gate corridor had been dead for months, the bamboo connection cracked by the winter frost.

Jun knelt at the wall, his flashlight illuminating the split bamboo pipe. The wood was split along a three-foot section, and a thin stream of cold water was leaking onto the mud floor, wasting the pressure.

"Liang! The hemp!" Jun yelled, calling to the village carpenter's assistant. "And the pine resin pot from the forge!"

Working with frantic, skilled speed, Jun went to work. He did not have the time to replace the three-foot bamboo section. Instead, he wrapped the split wood tight with thick hemp cord, binding the fibers together. He took a small iron pot of melted, hot pine resin from the forge stove, pouring the thick, gold glue over the hemp binding.

The resin cooled instantly in the cold draft of the corridor, forming a solid, waterproof seal that locked the water inside the pipe.

"Turn the valve!" Jun roared.

In the courtyard, a watchman worked the heavy iron wheel of the main spring intake.

*Squeeech... clack.*

The water rushed through the repaired bamboo line, the pipe tensing under the pressure. The valve in the gate corridor opened with a sharp, wet hiss, a high-pressure stream of cold mountain water spraying from the bamboo nozzle.

Jun grabbed the nozzle, directing the stream onto the hot pine gate.

*HISSSSSS.*

The water struck the charred wood, turning instantly to a thick cloud of white steam that rose to the ceiling. The stones of the archway cooled, the wood turning from red ember to black charcoal.

Oucoarse haire the gate, the utility truck was a burning torch.

The flames had reached the cargo bed, and the blue steel LPG gas tank was heating up. The metal of the tank was beginning to turn a dull, crimson red, the gas inside expanding, creating a low, vibrating hum that traveled through the clay wall.

If the tank exploded, the blast would shatter the pine gate, crack the rammed-earth archway, and destroy the timber shoring.

"Cool the tank!" Elder Jiang called from the watch slit. "Through the slot! Jun, lift the nozzle!"

Jun stepped onto a wooden bench, directing the water stream through a narrow, horizontal watch slot above the gate. The water flew thirty feet, striking the red steel of the LPG tank.

*HISSSS.*

The water cooled the metal, the steam rising in a thick cloud that obscured the orchards. The hum of the tank subsided, the danger of the explosion averted for a second.

But the mining zombies, undeterred by the fire and the steam, began to push.

Their bodies were blackened by coal, their skin hardened into a grey crust by the polymer. They did not feel the heat of the burning truck. They pressed their heavy, solid bodies against the rear bumper of the utility vehicle, their boots sliding in the mud as they shoved the machine forward.

The wooden wheels of the truck had burned away, leaving the steel hubs to grind against the stone road.

With a dry, screaming screech of iron on stone, the burning truck was pushed into the narrow gate tunnel.

The front cabin of the vehicle slammed directly into the oucoarse haire of the pine gate, its burning hood wedged against the wood. The heat was immediate, a localized blast that struck the center of the pine leaves.

*CREAK... SNAP.*

The pine planks began to split, the outer layer of wood charring to ash, as a slow, high-pitched hiss rose from the utility truck’s cargo bed.

The relief valve of the LPG tank had failed, and a three-foot jet of burning gas was spraying from the nozzle, acting as a giant blowtorch that was directed straight at the center of the village gate.

The gates were burning from the inside and the oucoarse haire, the blowtorch was melting the ironwood beams, and the horde was pushing the burning vehicle deeper into the fortress's mouth.

CHAPTER 3: THE RAMMED EARTH SHIELD


The gas blowtorch jet that hissed from the utility truck's ruptured LPG valve was a white, screaming needle of fire. The heat struck the center of the pine gate, the gold-lacquered wood blistering and cracking, the char spreading rapidly toward the ironwood support beams inside the corridor.

Jun stood inside the dark gate tunnel, his hands holding the bamboo water nozzle, his eyes watering from the thick pine smoke. The air was a hot, stagnant cloud that stung his lungs.

"The gate is failing, Grandfather!" Jun yelled over the scream of the gas. "The blowtorch is eating the core! The water isn't enough to stop the char!"

Elder Jiang stood next to him, his bare feet planted wide on the mud floor, his hand holding a heavy iron pry bar. "We do not rely on the wood, Jun. The ancestors knew that fire could destroy the gate. The stone is our second skin. Drop the slabs."

Chengqi Lou was built with a traditional defensive system—a double-leaved stone portcullis set inside the gate corridor. Two massive granite slabs, each six feet wide, four inches thick, and weighing over a thousand pounds, were suspended from the ceiling of the gate tunnel by heavy iron chains. If the outer wooden gate fell, these stone slabs could be dropped into vertical slots in the clay walls, creating a solid granite barrier that sealed the entrance.

But the slabs had not been dropped in eighty years, and the vertical guide slots were blocked with decades of accumulated lime dust, bird nests, and dry clay.

"The left slot is jammed!" Jun said, flashing his light into the wall slot. A thick crust of hardened clay and rotted timber debris filled the gap, blocking the path of the stone.

"Clear it, Jun!" Elder Jiang commanded. "Watchmen, to the pulley deck! Hold the chains!"

Four young men ran up the wooden stairs to the second-story gatehouse deck, where the massive iron capstans that controlled the chains were located.

Jun knelt at the base of the left slot, his fingers grabbing his heavy carpentry chisel and a wooden mallet. Working with frantic, rhythmic speed, he drove the iron chisel into the hardened clay crust.

*BANG. BANG. BANG.*

The mallet blows were a desperate, echoing sound inside the tunnel. The dry clay split under the steel, sending a shower of grey dust and rotted wood shards over his face. Jun cleared the first foot of the slot. The second foot.

The heat behind the pine gate was rising, the wood groaning as the ironwood support beams inside began to warp. A thin, red ember appeared in the center of the gate leaves, the fire having burned through the six inches of pine.

"It's through!" a watchman screamed.

"Jun! Now!" Elder Jiang yelled.

Jun drove the chisel into the last pocket of hardened lime at the base of the slot, the iron bar breaking the crust. He scrambled back, dragging his tools. "Clear! Drop them!"

On the second-floor deck, the watchmen released the heavy iron pins of the capstans.

*CREAK... SCREEECH.*

The rusted iron chains ran through the guide blocks with a dry, screaming slide that vibrated through the clay walls.

The two massive granite slabs dropped.

*THOOM. THOOM.*

The impact was a double earthquake that shook the entire gatehouse, the granite slabs striking the stone floor with a force that sent a cloud of dust rising from the joints. The stone slid smoothly down the vertical wall slots, locking into place, a solid, four-inch-thick granite wall directly behind the burning wooden gate.

The corridor fell silent, the scream of the gas blowtorch oucoarse haire reduced to a distant, muffled hiss.

"The stone is down," Liang gasped, his face white with dust.

But the relief was short-lived.

The heat of the burning truck had reached the main body of the blue steel LPG tank. The gas inside, compressed to its limit and heated by the diesel fire, expanded in a final, catastrophic volume.

*BOOOM.*

The explosion was a volcanic eruption of sound and light. The blast blew the utility truck into a thousand pieces of shrapnel, sending a shockwave of pressurized air and fire through the gate tunnel.

The wooden gate was shattered completely, the pine planks turned to charcoal splinters that flew through the corridor.

The force of the blast struck the granite portcullis.

*CRACK.*

A horizontal fracture, two inches wide, split the center of the granite slabs, the stone groaning under the impact. The mortar joints between the clay walls and the stone frame cracked, a stream of red sand falling from the ceiling.

The stone portcullis was cracked down the center, its structure weakened, and behind it, through the smoke of the blast, the massive forest horde from the coal mines arrived.

Thousands of coal-dusted zombies were running down the terraced tea fields, their green-glowing eyes a moving sea of hunger, their heavy bodies heading straight for the cracked stone barrier of the Tulou.

CHAPTER 4: THE BALCONY ARCHERS


The sound of the explosion died away, leaving a ringing, pressurized silence in the gatehouse corridor. For a long, frozen second, the only sound was the patter of falling plaster and the dry, scraping hiss of burning gas oucoarse haire the wall. Then, the dust settled, revealing the jagged black line running down the center of the granite portcullis. The two-ton slabs, which had stood as an unbroken shield for eighty years, had cracked like dry clay. A thin, continuous stream of grey sand and red earth trickled from the fractured seam, pooling at Jun’s feet.

"It's holding," Liang whispered, his face grey with stone dust. "The stone is still in the slots."

"For now," Jun said, his voice tense as he stepped forward to touch the cold granite. He could feel the vibration through the stone—a low, rhythmic thrumming, like the heartbeat of a massive machine. It was the pressure of the horde oucoarse haire, their bodies crowding into the narrow stone archway, pressing against the outer face of the granite. "The crack is clean. If they push together, the slabs will buckle inward. The slots in the clay walls won't hold the lateral force."

Elder Jiang walked up, his eyes fixed on the fractured stone. He did not look panicked; his expression was one of calm, analytical resolve, the look of a master builder assessing a damaged roof. "We do not let the clay carry the load alone. The circle must support itself. Jun, get the brace logs from the ancestral vault. The old pine columns. Liang, fetch the heavy iron chains from the grain store."

"The pine columns?" Jun asked, his eyes widening. "The ones kept under the altar?"

"The very ones," Elder Jiang said, his voice firm. "They were cut from the old forest three generations ago, seasoned in tung oil, and kept for the day the fortress groaned. That day is today. Go."

Jun did not waste another breath. He ran toward the central ring of the Tulou, his boots clattering on the granite flagstones. The courtyard was no longer silent; the air was filled with the urgent hum of voices as families organized their defenses. Women were carrying baskets of heavy, curved clay roof tiles to the upper floors, while older men carried long, fire-sharpened bamboo spears. There was no screaming, no chaotic panic. The collective discipline of the Jiang clan, honed by centuries of mountain isolation and mutual reliance, had taken over. Every person knew their station.

Under the raised wooden floor of the ancestral hall, in a cool, dry vault smelling of incense and dry earth, lay the emergency timber. These were massive trunks of old-growth Fujian pine, twelve feet long and ten inches thick, their wood dark and polished from the tung oil treatment.

Jun and four other young men grabbed the first log. It was incredibly heavy, the dense, oil-soaked wood cold to the touch. They hoisted it onto their shoulders, their muscles straining, and carried it back toward the gate corridor.

Oucoarse haire the outer wall, the forest horde had arrived.

From the fourth-floor catwalk, the view was terrifying. The white fog of the valley was choked with black coal dust, and through the haze, thousands of infected were moving. They had emerged from the deep pine forests of the mountain slopes, drawn by the thunderous blast of the LPG tank. They were not the slow, wandering dead of the cities; these were former miners, their bodies hardened by years of manual labor, their movements driven by a relentless, coordinated frenzy.

They swarmed over the charred ruins of the utility truck, their boots crushing the melted metal. They pressed against the base of the Tulou’s forty-foot rammed-earth wall, their clawing hands scratching at the packed clay. The wall, built with a slight inward batter, was smooth, but the explosion had blown small craters in the outer plaster, creating handholds.

"Draw!" Uncle Chen’s voice echoed along the third-floor balcony.

Chen was Elder Jiang's younger brother, a mountain hunter of sixty-eight who still had the chest of a young man. He stood at a narrow wooden window, holding a heavy, recurved bow made from laminated bamboo and water buffalo horn. Next to him, six other elder hunters held similar traditional bows, their arrows tipped with forged iron points used for wild boar.

*Thwang. Thwang. Thwang.*

The release of the bowstrings was a dry, snapping hum. The arrows flew true, plunging downward into the swarming mass at the base of the gate. An infected miner in a yellow hard hat was struck through the eye, his body collapsing instantly into the mud. Another, climbing onto the hood of the truck, took an arrow through the throat, falling backward into the crowd.

On the balconies above, the women and older children lined the railings. They did not have bows, but they had the clay tiles of the fortress roofs. These were heavy, semi-cylindrical pieces of baked earth, three pounds each, their edges sharp.

"Drop!" a woman shouted from the second ring.

A rain of red clay tiles descended on the horde. The heavy tiles struck with dull, smashing cracks, fracturing helmets and splitting skulls. The zombies at the base of the wall were crushed under the sheer weight of the falling earth, their bodies stacking up in a mound of broken bone and red clay. But more were coming, their green-glowing eyes reflecting the orange glow of the burning truck.

Down in the gate tunnel, the pressure was reaching its limit.

The granite portcullis groaned, a sharp *screeech* of stone on stone echoing through the vault. The horizontal crack in the center of the slabs had buckled inward by an inch, the granite teeth grinding against each other.

"Position the first brace!" Jun shouted, his voice hoarse.

They dropped the heavy pine log, its base wedged against a deep granite socket in the corridor floor, its top angled upward to press against the upper section of the cracked portcullis.

"Now the second!"

They brought the second log, angling it against the lower section. Jun grabbed a heavy wooden mallet and a handful of oak wedges. He crawled under the angled logs, his heart hammering against his ribs as he positioned the wedges between the timber tops and the groaning stone.

*BANG. BANG.*

With each blow of the mallet, the pine logs tensed, their wood fibers creaking as they took the weight of the granite. The inward movement of the portcullis slowed, but the pressure from the oucoarse haire was still growing. Through the two-inch crack in the stone, Jun could see the green glow of the zombies' eyes, could smell the cold, chemical stench of their breath.

Suddenly, a massive impact struck the oucoarse haire of the stone.

A group of coal-dusted zombies, led by an infected supervisor who still wore his heavy steel-toed boots, had climbed onto the chassis of the truck and were throwing their combined weight against the portcullis.

*CREAK... SNAP.*

The first pine brace, the one holding the upper slab, began to splinter. A long, white fracture opened along the grain of the wood, the fibers popping with the sound of breaking bone.

"It's splitting!" Liang yelled, backing away.

"Hold it!" Jun roared. He did not run. He threw his own shoulder against the splintering pine log, using his weight to brace the timber, his face pressed against the rough, oil-slick wood. He could feel the raw power of the horde on the other side of the stone, a relentless, mindless force that wanted to grind everything in its path to dust. "Liang! The wedge! Under the third brace! Drive it in!"

Liang scrambled forward, his mallet swinging in a desperate arc.

*BANG.*

The mallet struck the oak wedge, driving it deep into the joint. The third pine brace, positioned next to the splitting log, caught the load. The splintering of the first log stopped, its wood remaining cracked but stable under the shared pressure.

Jun fell back onto the damp floor, his breath coming in ragged gasps, his shoulder bruised and aching. He looked up at the braced granite. It was solid, a tripod of ancient pine holding the cracked stone in place.

"The gate holds," Elder Jiang said, looking down from the stairs. "But they are no longer just pushing, Jun. Look up."

Jun ran to the watch slot, looking through the narrow opening.

The zombies at the base of the wall were no longer just milling about. They were climbing. Not by ladders, but by using each other. The infected were crawling over the backs of the fallen, stacking their bodies against the three-meter-thick clay wall, their fingers clawing at the window slits of the second floor. The red clay ramp they had built with their own bodies was rising, and the first of the climbing dead was already reaching for the balcony railing.

CHAPTER 5: THE CLAY RAMP


The fog hanging over the Yongding valley had turned from white to a dirty, coal-streaked grey. It clung to the circular facade of Chengqi Lou, dampening the sounds of the struggle but doing nothing to cool the air. From the second-story balcony, the view through the narrow window slits was a chaotic blur of smoke and movement. The fire from the destroyed utility truck had died down to a smoldering heap of black rubber and twisted metal, but the real threat had shifted from fire to flesh.

At the base of the northeastern wall, the dead were building.

They did not use tools; they did not coordinate with words. Driven by the singular, viral impulse to reach the living inside, they piled themselves against the three-meter-thick clay base. The first wave, crushed by the falling roof tiles and pierced by the hunters' arrows, formed a solid foundation. The second wave ran over their bodies, pressing their hands against the rough, hand-rammed earth of the wall, trying to find purchase in the plaster cracks. Those who fell were immediately trampled by those behind, their bodies compacted into a rising slope of grey clay, dark coal dust, and twisted limbs.

It was a ramp of the dead, and it was rising at a terrifying speed.

"They are four feet from the sill!" a young watchman named Ah Bao yelled, his voice cracking. He stood at the window of the twelfth room on the second floor, his hands shaking as he held a long bamboo pole. The tip of the pole was bound with a curved steel blade used for harvesting bananas.

Jun ran up the dark wooden stairs, his shoulder still throbbing from the strain of holding the brace log. He carried a heavy carpenter's axe in his right hand and a bundle of thick pine slats under his left arm. Next to him, Elder Jiang walked with a quiet, rhythmic breath, carrying a basket of iron spikes.

"Keep your footing, Ah Bao," Elder Jiang said, his voice cutting through the noise. "The walls are sloped. They must climb against the gravity of the earth. Thrust, do not swing. Use the length of the bamboo."

Jun leaned out of the adjacent window slit. The window was small—barely eighteen inches wide and three feet high—framed in thick pine timber that was mortised directly into the rammed-earth wall. The wooden shutter, made of two-inch-thick cedar planks, was currently pinned open, allowing the watchmen to fight.

Oucoarse haire, the ramp of bodies had reached the bottom of the window frame.

An infected miner, his face half-crushed by a tile but his green-glowing eyes still wide with hunger, lunged toward the opening. His hand, stained black with coal grease and wet with grey slime, grabbed the granite sill.

*Thrust.*

Ah Bao drove the bamboo spear forward. The steel banana blade caught the zombie in the throat, the curved edge cutting through the vocal cords and muscle. The impact pushed the creature back, its fingers slipping from the stone as it fell into the mass below. But another took its place instantly, its boots stepping on the face of the fallen as it reached for the window.

"Jun, the shutters!" Elder Jiang called. "We cannot hold twenty windows with spears. We must seal the lower ring."

"If we close them, we lose our sight!" Ah Bao protested, thrusting again.

"The third and fourth floors have the sight," Elder Jiang replied calmly. "The second floor must be a wall. Jun, nail them shut."

Jun stepped to the window. The smell was overpowering—a mixture of sulfur from the coal mines, rotted flesh, and the sharp, chemical tang of the virus that seemed to leak from their pores. A zombie’s head appeared in the opening, its teeth clicking frantically as it tried to bite the wooden frame.

Jun swung his carpenter's axe, the heavy steel blade catching the zombie across the jaw with a clean, dull *tock*. The force of the blow sent the creature tumbling backward into the fog.

Before the next one could climb up, Jun slammed the heavy cedar shutters closed.

*CLACK.*

He threw a thick pine crossbar across the iron brackets, locking the leaves together. But he didn't stop there. He took a three-foot pine slat, positioned it diagonally across the frame, and drove a five-inch iron spike through the wood and into the thick timber frame of the window.

*BANG. BANG. BANG.*

The blows of his hammer were loud and rhythmic, a counterpoint to the thumping of the dead against the oucoarse haire of the shutter. He could feel the wood vibrating against his palm as the zombies slammed their chests against the cedar.

"The next room, Jun!" Liang called out from down the balcony.

They moved to the next chamber. The room belonged to an old widow, Grandmother Liu, who sat in the corner holding a brass incense burner, her eyes closed as she chanted a quiet prayer for her ancestors. The window shutter here was already bowing inward, the pine latch groaning under the pressure.

Jun didn't have time to clean the sill. He shoved a table against the frame, but before he could nail the slats, the cedar shutter split with a loud *crack*.

A grey, clawed hand broke through the splintered wood, grabbing Ah Bao’s vest. The young watchman was dragged toward the opening, his throat pressing against the sharp edge of the broken timber.

"Help!" Ah Bao choked out, his hands clawing at the zombie's wrist.

Jun dropped his hammer and grabbed his axe. He swung downward, the blade cutting through the zombie's forearm. The severed hand remained clamped to Ah Bao's vest, its fingers still twitching as the body fell away.

Before the next zombie could scramble through the broken shutter, Elder Jiang stepped forward. With a strength that belied his seventy-six years, he shoved a heavy, clay-fired jar of pickled cabbage into the opening. The jar, weighing eighty pounds, wedged perfectly into the window frame, blocking the gap.

Jun quickly laid three pine slats across the jar, driving spikes into the timber frame to lock the heavy clay container in place.

"It's sealed!" Jun gasped, his shirt soaked in sweat.

But from the floorboards beneath their feet, they heard a new sound.

It was not the thumping of bodies or the scratching of fingernails. It was a low, scraping grind, coming from the central courtyard. Jun and Elder Jiang looked at each other, the same realization hitting them.

The water.

The spring water they had used to cool the gate was still flowing through the bamboo lines, but the drainage system of the Tulou—a network of stone-lined channels that ran under the granite flagstones of the courtyard to exit through the northern wall—was blocked. The water, mixed with the red clay dust and the blood of the fallen oucoarse haire, was beginning to rise through the joints of the courtyard floor, turning the central market square into a red, bubbling mire.

And in the red water, the stones of the ancestral well were beginning to shift.

CHAPTER 6: THE RISING WELL


The central courtyard of Chengqi Lou, normally a clean, stone-paved sanctuary where the Jiang clan dried tea leaves and children played, had become a stagnant pond. The red-tinged spring water, blocked from its underground drainage channels by the debris of the gatehouse collapse, had risen to a depth of two feet. It flooded the ground-floor kitchens, turning the sweet potato storage bins into floating wooden crates, and licked at the bases of the massive timber columns that supported the four concentric rings of balconies.

Jun stood on the lower gallery walkway, his boots submerged in the freezing, muddy water. The air was thick with the scent of wet clay, damp pine, and a faint, chemical smell that made his throat dry.

In the exact center of the courtyard sat the ancient ancestral well.

It was a circular structure, three feet across, built from thick, curved granite blocks that had been fitted together without mortar three hundred years ago. Normally, the water sat ten feet below the stone rim, crystal-clear and sweet. But now, the well was churning.

A low, guttural gurgling rose from the shaft. The water inside did not rise slowly; it bubbled and pulsed, rising and falling like the throat of a great beast. The surface was covered in a thick, iridescent green scum—the phosphorescent clay residue from the karst caves miles away, carried through the deep mountain aquifers directly to the Tulou's water source.

"Grandfather, the well is overflowing," Jun said, his hand tightening around his axe.

Elder Jiang stood on the second-story balcony directly above, looking down into the courtyard. His face was dark. "The karst caves. Xiao Feng closed the primary valve, but the pressure in the mountain aquifer is still shifting. The contaminated water is finding the lowest outlets. Jun, get away from the rim."

Before Jun could step back, the well water erupted.

A violent pulse of green-tinged water shot three feet into the air, splashing across the granite flagstones. With the water came the first of the walkers.

It was a bloated, pale figure, its clothes shredded by the sharp limestone of the subterranean tunnels. Its skin was the color of curdled milk, showing through the translucent water, and its eyes burned with a cold, unblinking green light. The creature’s fingers, swollen and soft from the long immersion, clawed at the granite rim. It pulled its heavy, water-logged body out of the well, landing with a wet splash in the flooded courtyard.

A collective gasp rose from the circular balconies above. For weeks, the clan had felt safe, protected by forty feet of rammed earth. Now, the enemy had risen from the very heart of their home.

"Watchmen, to the courtyard rails!" Uncle Chen’s voice roared from the third floor.

*Thwang. Thwang.*

Two arrows flew from the third-story balcony, striking the water walker in the chest and shoulder. The iron points sank deep into the bloated flesh, but the creature did not fall. The cold, chemical-soaked water in its muscles seemed to insulate it from the pain, and it continued to crawl forward, its jaw clicking as it dragged itself toward the wooden columns of the kitchen ring.

"Target the head!" Chen yelled, his bow string snapping again.

A third arrow struck the walker through the temple. The creature stiffened, then collapsed face-down into the red water, the green glow in its eyes fading to grey.

But the well was still bubbling.

Three more figures rose from the dark shaft. One was a former mine engineer, his blue overalls stained with grease; the other two were villagers from the lower valley who had been lost weeks ago, their bodies soft and swollen. They climbed out of the granite ring, their hands reaching through the water.

"We must seal the shaft!" Jun shouted, wading into the freezing water. The cold was a sharp needle that bit into his thighs, his wet trousers dragging at his movement. "Liang! The heavy seasoned pine planks! The ones we used for the granary floor!"

"They are in the eastern store!" Liang called, splash-running through the flooded corridor.

Jun reached the well rim just as a fourth walker emerged. It was a massive man, his arms thick and white, his fingers clawing at the stone. Before the creature could gain a foothold, Jun swung his axe, the heavy steel back-pommel cracking the zombie's skull. The creature slid back into the dark water, the splash coating Jun's face in green-slick water.

Jun wiped his eyes, his skin stinging from the chemical residue. "Liang! Now!"

Liang and two other young carpenters arrived, dragging three thick planks of old Fujian pine, six feet long, three inches thick, and heavy with tung oil.

"Position them across the rim!" Jun commanded.

They laid the first plank across the granite blocks. The walker below slammed its head against the wood, the impact vibrating through the pine.

"Hold it down!" Jun roared.

He threw his chest onto the first plank, his boots sliding on the wet granite stones of the courtyard. Liang and the carpenters laid the second and third planks, creating a solid pine cap that covered the well opening.

But the water walker below was incredibly strong. The wood began to shift, the planks sliding across the smooth granite rim as the creatures below pushed upward with their combined strength. A stream of green-tinged water sprayed through the joints, soaking Jun's vest.

"The brackets, Liang!" Jun yelled, his muscles shaking under the strain. "The iron spikes! Drive them into the flagstone joints!"

Liang knelt in the freezing water, holding a heavy iron L-bracket against the edge of the pine plank. He positioned a six-inch spike over the joint between two granite paving stones and swung his hammer.

*BANG.*

The sound was a flat, wet thrumming. The spike sank two inches into the packed earth between the flagstones.

*BANG. BANG.*

The bracket held, locking the first plank to the floor. They worked around the circle, driving eight spikes into the joints, securing the pine cap with a ring of iron.

The upward pressure on the planks subsided as the water walkers below were trapped inside the shaft. The green water stopped spraying, settling to a slow, bubbling leak around the edges.

Jun stood up, his body shivering from the cold and the adrenaline. He looked down at the capped well, then looked around the flooded courtyard. The water was still rising, the red pool now reaching his knees.

Then, he heard the grinding.

It was a deep, structural sound, coming from beneath the granite flagstones. The weight of the flooded courtyard, combined with the pressure of the water trapped under the Tulou, was causing the floor to shift. The circular paving stones in the southeastern quadrant were tilting, their edges rising like the scales of a dragon.

"The drainage vault," Elder Jiang said, his voice flat as he walked down the stairs into the water. "The vault under the courtyard is collapsing, Jun. If the arch splits, the entire inner ring will sink into the mud."

***

---

CHAPTER 7: THE SINKING RING


The structural groan of Chengqi Lou was a low, base frequency that vibrated through the soles of Jun's boots. It was the sound of three-hundred-year-old pine timbers under tension—a slow, agonizing dry creak that traveled around the circular balconies of the fortress. In the southeastern quadrant of the courtyard, the red water was no longer stagnant. It was swirling, forming a slow, counter-clockwise drain that sucked in floating wood chips and cabbage leaves.

With a sudden, wet *whoosh*, the earth beneath the flagstones collapsed.

A circle of granite paving stones, fifteen feet wide, sank into the ground. A deep, dark sinkhole opened, instantly filled by the rushing red water. The ancient underground drainage arch, built of dry-laid shale, had completely collapsed under the weight of the flood.

In the center of this shifting zone stood the main support column of the southeastern ring.

It was a massive trunk of Fujian pine, two feet thick and forty feet tall, rising from a granite base slab to support the weight of the four concentric wooden balconies above. As the earth around its base washed into the drainage vault, the granite slab tilted. The column shifted, leaning six degrees toward the swirling sinkhole.

Above, the balconies reacted instantly. The wooden railings warped, the handrails splitting with the sound of gunshots. On the third and fourth floors, families screamed as the floorboards tilted beneath them, their household goods sliding toward the courtyard. The narrow wooden staircases, the only escape routes for the upper levels, were twisted out of alignment, their steps jammed against the support posts.

"Jun! The column is slipping!" Liang yelled, his face white as he held onto a balcony post.

"The chains!" Jun roared, his voice hoarse. "Grandfather! We must tie it to the circle!"

Elder Jiang stood on the gallery deck, his face set in stone. "The Tulou is a ring, Jun! If one part falls, the circle holds the rest, but only if the joints are tied. Tie it to the western pillar! Use the grain capstan chains!"

Jun waded back into the freezing water. It was now waist-deep, the cold a numbing weight that made his legs feel like lead. The current from the sinkhole pulled at his hips, trying to drag him toward the center of the dark pool. Next to him, Liang dragged a heavy, rusted iron chain—normally used for the grain-lifting pulleys—its links clattering against the submerged stone flagstones.

From the capped well, a loud *clack* echoed through the courtyard.

One of the iron spikes holding the pine cap had snapped under the pressure of the water walkers below. The planks lifted by an inch, a spray of green, chemical-slick foam escaping the gap. The creatures inside were hammering their bloated heads against the wood, their pale fingers clawing through the seam.

"Archers! Focus on the well!" Uncle Chen called from the third floor.

*Thwang. Thwang.*

Three archers leaned over the railing, their bows bent. They fired straight down into the green spray, the arrows splitting the cedar planks and pinning the climbing hands of the water walkers to the wood. The cap held, but the wood was groaning.

At the sinking column, Jun worked in the dark, swirling current.

The water was up to his chest now. He wrapped the heavy iron chain around the base of the tilting pine pillar, his fingers slick with mud and cold. The rough bark of the oil-cured pine bit into his palms as he hauled the links.

"Liang! Pull the end to the next column!" Jun yelled.

The next column, fifteen feet away, stood on solid granite that had not shifted. If they could bind the two columns together with the chain, the strength of the solid pillar would hold the leaning one until the water receded.

Jun threw the chain end to Liang, but as he did, the granite slab beneath his feet gave way.

The earth dissolved into a slurry of red mud, and Jun fell into the sinkhole. The current was a physical force, a cold hand that dragged his legs down into the collapsed drainage vault. The water closed over his head, cold, dark, and tasting of sulfur and clay. He clawed at the water, his fingers finding only mud, his lungs burning.

In the darkness, his hand struck the iron chain.

He grabbed the links with both hands, his knuckles turning white as he clung to the iron rope. The current pulled his body horizontally, his legs dangled in the empty void of the collapsed vault.

"Jun!" Liang screamed, chest-deep in the water.

Elder Jiang did not hesitate. The old man climbed over the gallery railing, dropping into the waist-deep water next to Liang. He grabbed the chain, his old hands finding a grip next to the younger carpenter’s.

"Pull!" Elder Jiang commanded, his voice sharp and clear.

Together, the old man and the carpenter hauled the chain. Their muscles strained against the weight of the water and the pull of the sinkhole. Slowly, link by link, they dragged the chain out of the hole, pulling Jun’s head back above the surface.

Jun gasped, spitting out the cold, bitter water, his chest heaving. He climbed onto the solid flagstones next to the columns, his hands still shaking.

"Tie it!" Jun choked out.

Liang wrapped the remaining chain around the solid pillar, driving a heavy iron spike through the links to lock it in place. The chain tensed, the links singing like a wire under tension as the weight of the leaning column settled onto the iron bridge.

The leaning column stopped shifting. The creaking of the balconies above subsided, the wooden structure stabilizing under the shared load. The circle had held itself.

But from the watchtower on the fourth floor, the brass horn sounded again.

It was not a single, sharp note this time. It was a continuous, frantic alarm that wailed over the valley, its sound carrying through the mist.

"The ramp!" Ah Bao’s voice screamed from the second-story watch window. "The ramp has reached the catwalk! They are over the wall!"

***

---

CHAPTER 8: THE INNER GATEWAY


The second-story gallery of Chengqi Lou was a narrow, circular shelf of dark pine boards, just four feet wide, flanking the outer ring of the fortress. Ordinarily, it was a quiet corridor connecting the private bedrooms of the Jiang families. Now, it had become a battlefield.

At the southeastern bend, three coal-dusted zombies had squeezed through the window slit of a storage room, their bodies sliding over the granite sill like grease. They were joined by more climbing over the balcony railing, their hands finding purchase on the wooden posts that had tilted when the main column shifted.

Jun, his skin numb from the freezing sinkhole water and his clothes dripping red mud, scrambled up the southern staircase. He was followed by Liang, who carried a heavy wooden iron-shod shovel, and Ah Bao, whose face was streaked with blood from a splinter cut.

"The stairs!" Jun yelled, pointing to the southern wooden steps that wound up to the third floor. "We barricade the landing! If they reach the third ring, they reach the children!"

Working with the frantic efficiency of men who had spent their lives handling timber, Jun and Liang grabbed a massive, red-lacquered wedding chest that sat in the hallway. The chest, filled with heavy cotton quilts and copper basins, was a family heirloom, but today it was a shield. They slid it across the narrow corridor, wedging it between the clay outer wall and the wooden railing of the gallery.

Behind it, they piled four heavy sacks of rice and a solid oak dining table, creating a chest-high wall that blocked the corridor completely.

*Thump.*

The first zombie, a former miner whose throat was blackened by coal dust, slammed into the wedding chest. The impact slid the heavy box back by two inches, the wood groaning. Jun stepped up to the barrier, his axe held high. He drove the blade downward, the steel cutting through the collarbone of the zombie, pinning it to the chest.

Ah Bao stood next to him, his banana-spear thrusting through the gap between the rice sacks, striking the second zombie in the eye. The creature collapsed, but the weight of the bodies behind them pressed against the barricade. The wood of the wedding chest began to crack under the lateral force.

"Hold them here!" Jun shouted to Liang. "Don't let them clear the sacks!"

But from the northern side of the circular ring, a sharp warning rose.

"Jun! The north walkway!" Elder Jiang’s voice called down from the third-story balcony. "They have broken the shutters of the eighth room! They are climbing the northern stairs!"

Jun looked across the circular void of the courtyard. Through the rising mist and the red water below, he could see the northern wing. A pack of six zombies, their green-glowing eyes reflecting off the wet floorboards, were scrambling up the northern steps. They had bypassed the southern barricade entirely and were heading toward the unprotected rooms of the third floor where the elders were gathered.

"The northern walkway is weak, Jun!" Elder Jiang shouted, his arm pointing at the timber joists that supported the gallery floor. "The tie-beams! Cut them! Drop the section!"

The circular balconies of Chengqi Lou were modular, built in ten-foot sections that rested on projecting pine joists. If those joists were cut, the floorboards of that section would collapse into the courtyard, creating a ten-foot gap that no zombie could cross.

Jun did not hesitate. He ran back along the southern balcony, his wet boots sliding on the boards. He crossed the central gatehouse bridge and entered the northern corridor. The air here was quiet, but he could hear the thumping of boots approaching from the stairs.

He reached the northern walkway section just as the first zombie, a heavy man wearing a torn security uniform, stepped onto the landing.

Jun swung his carpenter's axe at the main support joist—a four-inch-thick pine beam that projected from the clay wall to hold the floorboards.

*WHACK.*

The axe bit deep into the seasoned pine, sending a shower of white chips into the red water below. The wood was tough, cured with tung oil and hardened by eighty years of dry mountain air.

*WHACK. WHACK.*

The zombie was ten feet away, its boots thumping on the pine boards, its hands reaching. The green light in its eyes was a dull, unblinking glare. Behind it, two more were climbing the steps.

"Jun! Faster!" Ah Bao yelled from the southern wing, where the wedding chest barricade was cracking under the pressure of the horde.

Jun swung again, his shoulder screaming with pain, his grip slick with sweat and mud. The blade caught the joist at an angle, the wood splitting with a sharp, screaming *crack*.

The floorboards tilted.

Jun scrambled back, his boots finding purchase on the solid section of the corridor just as the security zombie lunged forward.

The zombie’s boot stepped onto the cut section. Under the weight of the heavy body, the joist failed completely.

*ROAR.*

With a sound like a small landslide, the ten-foot section of the northern gallery collapsed. The heavy pine floorboards, the railings, and the five climbing zombies fell twenty feet into the flooded courtyard below, landing with a massive, muddy splash in the red pool.

The drop worked. The northern stairs were isolated, a ten-foot gap of empty air separating the second-story steps from the third-story landing. The family members on the balconies above cheered, their voices a sudden, emotional relief.

But the relief did not reach Jun.

As the northern section fell, the support column next to it shifted. The timber frame creaked, and a secondary partition wall of cedar laths collapsed behind Jun, blocking his path back to the southern gatehouse bridge.

He was trapped on the northern landing. He looked to his left and saw the gap of empty air. He looked to his right and saw three coal-dusted zombies emerging from the smoke of the corridor, their teeth clicking as they locked their eyes onto the lone carpenter.

***

---

CHAPTER 9: THE LANTERN LEAP


Jun backed away until his shoulders struck the collapsed partition wall of cedar laths. The wood was a splintered barricade behind him, blocking any retreat to the central gatehouse bridge. To his left, the ten-foot gap of empty air where the northern walkway had fallen showed the flooded courtyard twenty feet below. The red water was still churning, and around the pine-capped well, three bloated water walkers were swimming in circles, their pale arms cutting the surface.

To his right, the three coal-dusted zombies were coming.

They moved in a slow, stumbling line along the narrow landing, their boots dragging on the wet boards. The lead zombie, a former mine foreman whose jaw hung loose from a previous blow, was less than six feet away. Its green-glowing eyes were fixed on Jun, its hands reaching forward with a dry, clicking motion of the fingers.

"Jun! The rope!" Uncle Chen’s voice called from the third-floor balcony directly above.

Jun looked up. Chen had thrown a thick hemp rope over the railing, but the line hung eight feet to the right, directly behind the advancing zombies. To reach it, Jun would have to walk straight into their grasp.

"No!" Jun yelled back, his voice tight. "It's too far! Keep the families back!"

He looked out over the central courtyard. Hanging from the high, dark struts of the Tulou's roof, forty feet above, was the great ancestral lantern.

It was a traditional red cloth lantern, six feet tall and four feet wide, built on a heavy frame of split bamboo and iron wire. It was kept for the Mid-Autumn Festival, suspended in the exact center of the circular courtyard by a thick, oil-cured hemp rope that ran through a bronze pulley on the main roof beam. The lantern hung level with the second-story balconies, about ten feet from Jun's position on the railing.

It was a desperate calculation. Jun was a carpenter; he knew the strength of hemp and bamboo. The rope was old, but it had been seasoned in tung oil. The bamboo frame of the lantern could not carry his weight, but the iron collar at the top of the suspension line could.

If he missed, he would fall into the flooded courtyard, straight into the sinkhole current and the waiting water walkers.

"Jun, what are you doing?" Liang screamed from the southern balcony across the gap.

Jun did not answer. He stepped onto the narrow, wet wooden railing of the gallery, balancing his boots on the two-inch pine rail. He braced his left hand against the clay wall, his heart hammering a frantic rhythm against his ribs.

The foreman zombie lunged. Its coal-stained fingers scraped the fabric of Jun’s vest, the chemical stench of its breath hot against his neck.

Jun sprang.

He threw his body outward, away from the railing and into the empty air of the courtyard. For a fraction of a second, he was weightless, suspended between the clay walls and the sky.

His hands reached out, his fingers locking around the thick hemp rope just above the lantern's bamboo collar.

*JERK.*

His weight caught the line with a bone-jarring force that nearly tore his arms from their sockets. The rope tensed, the ancient bronze pulley on the roof struts forty feet above screaming with a dry, metallic screech.

*CREEEAK.*

The main roof beam groaned under the sudden, lateral load, but the pine held.

Jun’s body swung in a wide, sweeping arc across the central courtyard. Below him, the red water rushed by, and the water walkers in the pool reached upward, their bloated white hands breaking the surface, their fingers snapping at the soles of his boots. One of them managed to scrape the leather of his heel, the contact a cold, wet reminder of what lay below.

The momentum of the swing carried him toward the southern balcony.

Liang and Ah Bao were leaning over the rail, their hands reaching out.

"Grab him!" Liang roared.

As the swing reached its peak, the hemp rope—frayed by the sharp bronze edges of the ancient pulley above—began to split. A series of sharp pops echoed from the ceiling as the fibers unraveled.

The lantern began to drop.

Jun released his grip, throwing his body forward toward the wooden deck of the southern gallery.

He hit the wet pine boards chest-first, his breath leaving him in a loud gasp as he tumbled across the floor. Liang and Ah Bao grabbed his shoulders, dragging him back from the edge just as the remaining fibers of the rope snapped.

The great red lantern, along with its bamboo frame and the iron collar, plunged into the center of the courtyard, landing with a loud, hollow splash that sent a wave of red water washing over the gallery walkway.

Jun lay on his back, his chest heaving, his hands trembling. He looked up at the empty sky where the lantern had hung, then at Liang.

"You're mad," Liang gasped, his face white. "You're completely mad."

"It worked," Jun whispered, his throat dry.

But before he could stand, a sharp, electrical crackle cut through the sound of the water.

In the northeastern corner of the courtyard, the water had reached the level of the kitchen generator annex—a low brick structure where the village generator and the winter fuel wood were stored. The floodwaters had submerged the generator's battery bank, and a bright blue arc of electricity shot across the metal frame, sparking against the dry pine logs stacked next to the power box.

*Fwoosh.*

The dry wood, seasoned for winter fires, caught instantly. A wall of yellow flame rose from the kitchen annex, the fire spreading rapidly toward the low wooden eaves of the inner ring.

***

---

CHAPTER 10: THE CIRCLE SECURED


The smoke from the burning kitchen annex was a greasy, black column that rose through the central circular opening of Chengqi Lou, staining the misty sky above Fujian. The fire, fed by the generator's winter woodpile and dry pine kindling, had climbed the wooden support pillars of the kitchen roof, its yellow tongues licking at the decorative eaves of the inner residential ring.

On the third and fourth-floor balconies, families were gathered at the railings, their faces covered with wet cotton cloths to filter the stinging smoke. The wind, blowing hard from the northern mountains, pushed the heat directly toward the residential quarters.

"Jun! The eaves!" Elder Jiang’s voice called down from the fourth-story catwalk, his figure silhouetted against the dark smoke. "The kitchen roof is connected to the first ring! You must cut the bridge, or the fire will take the circle!"

Jun, coughing and shivering in his wet clothes, did not hesitate. He grabbed his heavy carpentry adze—a curved, horizontal blade used for shaping timber—and ran along the gallery. Liang and Ah Bao followed, carrying long pine poles to push away any debris.

They reached the wooden walkway that joined the kitchen annex to the gallery of the first ring. The wood was already hot, the red lacquer bubbling and smoking under the heat.

"Help me up!" Jun yelled.

Ah Bao and Liang locked their hands together, hoisting Jun onto the shingled roof of the connecting walkway. The smoke was a thick, blinding cloud that stung his eyes and made his throat burn. Below him, the red water of the courtyard reflected the yellow glare of the flames.

Jun swung the adze downward, the curved steel blade cutting through the pine rafters.

*WHACK.*

The seasoned wood split under the blows, sending a shower of burning pine shingles into the water below. He could feel the heat through the soles of his boots, the wood beneath him shifting as the rafters weakened.

Suddenly, a figure emerged from the smoke of the generator room.

It was a zombie, its clothes burning with blue-green chemical flames from the spilled generator fuel. It moved with a fast, jerky trot along the roof ridge, its hands reaching toward Jun, its teeth clicking behind a wall of fire.

"Jun! Watch out!" Liang screamed from the courtyard.

Liang did not have a weapon, but he had his heavy iron-shod wooden shovel. He stepped into the waist-deep water, reached up, and drove the flat of the shovel against the burning zombie's chest.

*THUMP.*

The force of the blow pushed the creature off the roof ridge. It fell with a wet splash into the deep sinkhole next to the well. Before it could rise, the current of the collapsed drainage vault caught it, and the bloated water walkers below dragged the burning figure down into the dark, liquid depths, neutralizing the threat.

Jun did not look back. He swung his adze with all his remaining strength, cutting through the main tie-beam that held the walkway to the gallery frame.

*CRACK... SNAP.*

The beam split. Jun scrambled backward onto the solid balcony just as the connecting walkway collapsed.

The ten-foot wooden bridge fell into the flooded courtyard, landing with a heavy crash that sent a shower of sparks and red water rising into the air.

The firebreak had worked. The fire, cut off from the main residential rings, burned itself out in the ruins of the kitchen annex, its flames dying down to a smoldering heap of charcoal and wet ash.

As the fire subsided, a deep rumble shook the ground.

The collapsed drainage vault, which had created the sinkhole, had finally worn a channel through the foundation clay on the northern side of the outer wall. The trapped floodwater in the courtyard, finding a new path, began to drain rapidly through the gap, rushing out into the northern terraced tea fields.

Within minutes, the courtyard was empty of water, leaving only a coating of red mud, broken tiles, and the wet pine cap of the ancestral well, which remained sealed by the iron brackets. The pressure from the aquifer had subsided, and the water walkers inside the shaft were locked in the dark.

Oucoarse haire, the wailing of the watchtower horn stopped.

The horde of coal-dusted miners, unable to climb the slippery clay walls after the tile-droppers had broken their ramp of bodies, and with no new sound to draw them, had begun to disperse. They drifted back into the dark pine forests of the mountain slopes, their green-glowing eyes fading into the mist.

Chengqi Lou had stood. The circle was secured.

By the evening, the courtyard was quiet. The families descended from the upper balconies, their faces tired but relieved. Under the direction of Elder Jiang and Jun, they began the work of cleaning the mud, shoring up the tilted columns, and repairing the broken windows.

In the central ancestral hall, the elders lit incense before the wooden plaques, the sweet smell of sandalwood replacing the scent of pine smoke. The villagers gathered for a simple meal of boiled sweet potatoes and garlic, their voices quiet but carrying a deep sense of shared survival and filial duty.

Jun sat on the steps of the hall, his shoulder bandaged and his clothes dry.

Elder Jiang walked up, his steps steady, carrying a small, battery-powered radio that crackled with static. He set it on the granite step next to Jun.

Through the static, a weak, looping voice was speaking. It was a broadcast from the north, hundreds of miles away in Anhui Province.

"...this is the keeper of the Moon Pond at Hongcun..." the voice crackled, thin and desperate. "...the stone dams have failed. The water walkers from the mountain lakes have flooded the canals. We are trapped in the center of the water labyrinth... they are coming through the stone gates... if anyone can hear this... the water is turning..."

Jun looked up at his grandfather.

Elder Jiang looked toward the northern mountains, his eyes clear and grave. "The circle of Chengqi Lou is safe, Jun. But the water connects us all. The canals of Hongcun are the veins of the valley. If they fall, the dead will flow to every village in the north."

Jun stood up, his hand reaching for his carpentry bag. "I will pack the tools, Grandfather."

"Go, Jun," Elder Jiang said, placing a hand on his shoulder. "Take Liang. Protect the water. Protect the people."

Jun looked north, the dark silhouette of the mountains rising against the clearing night sky, knowing that a new labyrinth of water and stone was waiting for him.

***

STORY 8: THE WATER LABYRINTH (HONGCUN/XIDI, ANHUI)
CHAPTER 1: THE MOON POND


The ancient village of Hongcun lay nestled at the foot of the Huangshan mountains...

*(To be continued in Story 8, Chapter 1)*

================================================================================

STORY 8: THE WATER LABYRINTH (HONGCUN/XIDI, ANHUI)
CHAPTER 1: THE MOON POND


The white horse-head walls of Hongcun rose like stepped stone waves against the dark green backdrop of the Huangshan foothills. Under a heavy, leaden sky, the ancient Huizhou-style village, built in the shape of a giant ox, was drowning in its own blood and water. The sophisticated system of narrow canals that had fed every household for eight hundred years had become a network of veins carrying the contagion.

The mountain lakes above the village had overflowed. The clean mountain water, mixed with the green phosphorescent runoff of the biological leak, rushed down the stone channels, turning the narrow flagstone alleys into waist-deep torrents of dark, freezing water.

Jun and Liang had arrived at the outskirts after a grueling two-day journey north from Fujian, their clothes stiff with dried mud, their carpentry bags heavy on their backs. They stood at the southern entrance of the village, where the South Lake spread like a wide, black mirror reflecting the white walls.

In the center of the village, the historic Moon Pond—the crescent-shaped basin that formed the "stomach" of the ox-shaped layout—was a churning pool.

"Uncle Wang!" Liang called out, his voice echoing off the high brick walls. "We are here from Chengqi Lou! The Jiang clan sent us!"

An old man of seventy-two, his face weathered like the pine bark of Huangshan, stood on the arched stone bridge that crossed the primary inlet canal. He wore a dark blue cotton jacket, his trousers rolled up to his knees, revealing thin, corded legs. He held a long, iron-tipped gaff pole. Next to him, his niece, Meihua, a young woman of twenty-two with her hair tied in a practical bun, held a heavy wooden pole-axe used for clearing canal debris.

"Keep to the high stones!" Uncle Wang called back, his voice hoarse but steady. "The inlet is open! The water walkers are coming down from the upper reservoir! They are using the canals to enter the Moon Pond!"

Hongcun’s water system was designed so that the water flowed from the northern stream, through a system of narrow channels (the "intestines") that ran past every house, into the central Moon Pond, and finally out to the South Lake. The canals were only three feet wide and two feet deep, but the flood had made them deep enough for the bloated, water-logged dead to slide through.

As Jun watched, a pale, green-glowing shape emerged from the narrow canal that ran between two white-walled houses.

It was a water walker, its skin soft and white, its eyes glowing with the dull green light of the virus. It swam with a slow, silent breaststroke, its body aligned with the current, heading straight for the open basin of the Moon Pond. Behind it, two more figures floated in the dark water, their limbs moving in a rhythmic, mechanical crawl.

"If they fill the Moon Pond, they will reach the ancestral hall!" Meihua said, thrusting her pole-axe down into the water. The blade sliced through the neck of the lead walker, pinning it to the stone bottom of the canal. "The hall houses three hundred refugees from the valley!"

The Wang Ancestral Hall, a grand building with carved wooden beams and a wide granite courtyard, stood directly on the northern bank of the Moon Pond. Its doors were closed, but the water was already rising against the threshold.

"We must block the throat," Jun said, his carpenter's eye immediately analyzing the masonry of the arched bridge. "The bridge arch is the narrowest point of the inlet. If we build a wooden sluice gate here, we can block the water walkers while letting the clean overflow run over the top."

"We have the timber," Uncle Wang said, pointing to a stack of seasoned fir planks kept under the eaves of the ancestral hall for bridge repairs. "But we have no way to anchor them against this current. The stone is old and slippery."

"We use the granite joints," Jun said, dropping his bag. "Liang, the heavy chisels and the iron T-bars! We drive them into the bridge abutments to form a vertical guide slot. Meihua, help Liang carry the planks!"

Jun ran to the base of the stone bridge. The current was strong, the freezing water rushing past his thighs, threatening to sweep his boots off the wet flagstones. The water was cold, a biting mountain chill that made his knuckles stiff.

He positioned a heavy steel chisel against the joint between two granite blocks of the bridge arch.

*BANG.*

His mallet struck the steel, the sound a sharp, metallic ring that echoed off the white walls. A small shower of stone dust fell into the water.

*BANG. BANG.*

The joint opened, the ancient mortar splitting under the steel. Jun drove a heavy, T-shaped iron bar into the gap, creating the first anchor point for the wooden gate.

Behind him, in the narrow canal, the water walkers were approaching.

Three bloated figures had entered the bridge channel, their pale hands clawing at the stone walls to drag themselves against the current. Uncle Wang stood on the bridge arch, his iron-tipped gaff pole thrusting downward with mechanical precision, striking the first walker through the throat and holding it back.

"Hurry, Jun!" Uncle Wang grunted, his old muscles straining against the thrashing weight of the zombie. "More are coming from the upper canal! The reservoir gates have failed completely!"

Jun moved to the opposite side of the arch, his hammer swinging in a desperate, rhythmic arc.

*BANG. BANG.*

He drove the second T-bar into the granite wall. The guide slot was ready.

"Planks!" Jun roared.

Liang and Meihua ran forward, carrying the first heavy fir plank, ten feet long and two inches thick. They slid the ends of the wood into the vertical guide slots between the T-bars.

The wood hit the water, the current immediately slamming it against the iron anchors. The plank took the force of the flow, the water level behind it rising instantly by a foot, creating a small waterfall that spilled over the top.

The first plank blocked the lower half of the channel, trapping two water walkers behind the wood. The zombies pressed their white faces against the fir, their fingers clawing at the grain.

"The second plank!" Jun yelled.

They slid the second plank into the slots, doubling the height of the wooden barrier. The water rose to the top of the bridge arch, the inlet channel sealed. The flow was cut off, the water walkers trapped in the upper canals, unable to enter the Moon Pond.

The crescent basin fell quiet, the surface of the pond settling into a smooth, dark mirror.

"It's holding," Liang gasped, leaning on his shovel.

But Uncle Wang did not look relieved. He stood on the bridge, looking north along the winding canals that led to the upper village.

Through the mist, they could hear a low, continuous thrumming. It was not the sound of water; it was the sound of thousands of boots and hands, a collective vibration that traveled through the stone foundations of the village. The upper reservoir had not just leaked; it had collapsed, and the entire northern valley horde was now entering the narrow canals of Hongcun, heading straight for the wooden barrier.

CHAPTER 2: THE SLUICE CHAMBER


The water level behind the two fir planks of the newly built sluice gate was rising an inch every minute. The dark mountain runoff, thick with green phosphorescent slime, pressed against the outer face of the timber, creating a heavy hydrostatic load. The two-inch-thick planks bowed inward, the wood grain groaning under the strain, while streams of green water sprayed through the narrow seam between the boards.

Uncle Wang stood on the granite arch of the bridge, his old eyes scanning the dark, winding canal that disappeared into the foggy alleys of the upper village.

"The water isn't stopping, Jun," Uncle Wang said, his hand resting on the smooth shaft of his iron-tipped gaff pole. "The upper reservoir has three gates, and if the main sluice chamber has failed, the entire lake will drain through these streets. The planks won't hold the weight of the water, let alone the weight of the dead."

"We must brace the center," Jun said, his boots submerged in the shallow overflow that had spilled into the Moon Pond basin. "If we run diagonal struts from the granite bridge abutments to the center of the planks, the timber won't flex. Liang, get the five-foot fir braces and the iron dog-pins from the bag!"

Liang splash-ran to the ancestral hall porch, returning with two thick timber struts and a handful of double-pointed iron staples used in traditional Huizhou carpentry to bind beams together.

Jun waded into the mouth of the bridge arch. The current was a cold, swirling force that dragged at his legs, the green water smelling of sulfur and wet stone. He positioned the first timber brace, its top wedged against the center of the upper fir plank, its base angled downward to press against the granite flagstones of the canal bed.

"Liang, hold the base!" Jun commanded. "Meihua, watch the canal!"

Working with rapid, heavy mallet blows, Jun drove the iron dog-pins into the joints between the granite stones, locking the brace bases in place.

*BANG. BANG. BANG.*

The metallic thumping echoed off the high, white horse-head walls of the narrow alley, a sharp, clean sound that cut through the low gurgle of the flood.

Suddenly, a dry scratching rose from the tiled roofs above their heads.

Jun stopped his hammer, his eyes rising to the stepped black gables of the adjacent merchant houses. The horse-head walls, designed to prevent the spread of fire between the tightly packed houses, rose twenty feet into the foggy air.

Along the steep, black-tiled roof ridge, a shape was moving.

It was a water walker, its bloated body covered in grey mud, its limbs moving in a clumsy, crawling trot. It did not have the slow, stiff stride of the land dead; the chemical contagion had left its muscles loose and flexible, allowing it to crawl along the slick tiles like a massive, pale spider.

*Clack... clack...*

Its fingers, soft and swollen, scraped the clay roof tiles, sending a loose slate crashing into the canal below.

"Look up!" Meihua yelled, her pole-axe raised.

Before Liang could scramble back, the crawling figure on the roof reached the edge of the eaves and dropped.

*SPLASH.*

The zombie crashed directly onto the arched stone bridge, its bloated body striking the granite blocks with a wet, heavy impact just three feet from Uncle Wang. The force of the fall broke one of the creature's legs, but it did not care. It lunged forward on its hands, its jaw clicking, its green eyes locking onto the old gatekeeper.

Uncle Wang reacted with the fluid, practiced movement of a lifelong boatman. He lunged forward with his gaff pole, the iron tip catching the zombie in the throat, pinning it to the stone bridge parapet.

"Meihua! The axe!" Uncle Wang grunted.

Meihua swung the heavy pole-axe in a clean, downward arc. The steel blade split the zombie's skull, and the green glow in its eyes went dark as its body slid off the bridge into the deep water of the canal.

But a second scratching arose from the eastern roof.

Another water walker, its blue overalls torn and soaked in green slime, crawled over the eaves and dropped directly onto the wooden sluice gate.

The impact of the heavy body struck the center of the fir planks. The wood groaned, a loud *crack* echoing through the archway as the lower plank split along a natural knot. The diagonal brace Jun had just pinned began to shift, its iron dog-pins grinding against the granite joints.

"The gate is splitting!" Liang slammed, trying to hold the shifting base of the brace.

Jun did not look up at the zombie clawing at the top of the planks. He threw his own weight against the diagonal timber, his shoulder pressing against the wood to lock it in place. "Liang! The second brace! Under the split! Drive the pin!"

Liang, his hands wet and trembling with cold, positioned the second fir strut under the split section of the plank. He grabbed the mallet and struck the iron staple.

*BANG.*

The mallet struck Liang's thumb, but he did not drop the tool. He swung again, his face twisted in pain and determination.

*BANG. BANG.*

The second brace caught the load. The split plank stabilized, the timber remaining cracked but secured against the pressure.

Above them, Meihua lunged with her pole-axe, the blade catching the zombie on the gate in the shoulder and dragging it off the timber. The creature fell into the rising water behind the gate, its head disappearing beneath the green foam.

Jun fell back, his chest heaving, his clothes soaked in the green-stained water. He looked up at the braced gate. It was solid, a heavy wooden cross holding the water back.

But as he looked up at the high white walls of the alley, his heart sank.

Along the black roof ridges of the village, more figures were appearing. Five, ten, twenty... a silent, pale vanguard of the reservoir horde, crawling along the black tiles, their green-glowing eyes looking down into the narrow, flooded canal like hungry ghosts.
