Jun looked at Liang. Liang said nothing.

"How long until they reach firm ground?" Jun asked.

"Twenty minutes at that pace. Maybe thirty. The outer flat is very soft this time of year — the summer silt."

"South walkway," Jun said. "Can we cut it now?"

"We need it for the net delivery," Granny Yau said immediately. "The mesh weave won't be done for another hour. We need the south walkway to carry the nets to the bridge."

Jun did the arithmetic. The bridge netting was the critical task — without the false floor, the stone arch remained a fully passable crossing and the village's eastern approach was open. But the south walkway was the only route between the net-weaving station and the bridge. Cutting it now would strand the incomplete nets on the wrong side.

"Finish the walkway delivery first," Jun said. "Pull it the moment the last net is across."

Granny Yau nodded once and turned back toward the village at the same quick, short stride.

Jun turned to the bridge.

They had ten slabs still to remove.

"Faster," he said to Liang and Ah Kun.

The remaining slabs came up in eleven minutes — Liang hammering the pry bar with a wooden mallet to break the mortar while Jun levered and Ah Kun dragged the freed pieces to the railing. The last slab went into the channel with a heavy splash, and the full length of the arch deck was bare — a smooth grey oval of algae-slicked concrete, curving gently from abutment to keystone.

From the Tung Chung road side, the bridge now looked, at a glance, like a bridge: concrete railings, open span, a grey surface. The missing road pavement was not apparent unless you were specifically looking for it — the arch deck's concrete was close in color and texture to the stone slabs that had covered it.

The first nets arrived on Jun's left as he worked — two village women carrying a folded section of freshly knotted mesh between them on a bamboo pole, the knots still pale and tight, smelling of the synthetic mesh line. Granny Yau followed with a second pair carrying another section.

"Six sections done," she said. "Thirty-six square meters. We need forty-two."

"The six sections cover the center of the arch," Jun said. "The highest-traffic path — the centerline of the road surface. Lay them now. We'll finish the edges when the remaining sections are ready."

He took the first net section and spread it across the arc of the concrete deck, working from the village end inward. The mesh was a fifteen-centimeter grid — tight enough that a foot placed flat on it would appear to find resistance, but loose enough that a concentrated load — a boot heel, a steel-toed work boot pressing down — would punch through the mesh and send the leg through the gap, down toward the four-meter drop to the channel.

The net was pinned to the concrete railing posts with simple wire loops, pulled just taut enough to hold its position without lifting in the sea breeze but with enough slack in the center to give under load.

Jun spread the second section beside the first, overlapping the edges by half a meter, and wired the overlap to prevent separation.

From the south, a sound reached them that was distinct from the background drone — a series of soft, wet impacts, evenly spaced. The sound of boots moving through ankle-deep mud.

"They're on the approach flat," Granny Yau said from the railing, her binoculars up. "Twelve of them in a line. The front one is thirty meters from firm ground."

"The south walkway," Jun said.

"The last nets aren't across yet."

Jun looked toward the village. The walkway — a meter-wide plank path running along the south channel wall — was still in use: two women carrying another folded net section were halfway across it, moving at a careful pace because the planks were wet and the load was awkward.

"Tell them to run," Jun said.

Granny Yau turned and called across the water in rapid Cantonese. The two women heard her and began moving faster, the bamboo carrying pole between their shoulders, their rubber boots slapping the wet planks.

They cleared the walkway junction and delivered the net to the bridge in ninety seconds.

"Pull it," Jun said.

Granny Yau turned and called again. A teenager at the south walkway junction — a boy of about fifteen, stationed there with a handsaw — began cutting.

The walkway planks were thick hardwood, but the saw was sharp and the cut point had been pre-scored. The boy worked through the first plank in forty seconds, then the second. On the third plank, the structure shifted, the unsupported weight of the walkway pulling the cut downward, the wood fibers separating under the tension.

*CRACK.*

The walkway section dropped into the channel, its planks fanning apart as they hit the water. The gap it left in the south shore connection was three meters wide — too far to jump, too shallow to swim without touching the mud bottom.

Jun turned back to the bridge.

Three more net sections had arrived while he worked. He spread them rapidly, filling in the western end of the arch deck and the edges of the center section, wiring each one to the railings.

The coverage was not complete — two sections still missing from the eastern quarter of the arch — but the visual effect was sufficient from a distance: the entire road surface of the stone arch appeared to be a continuous grey-mesh floor, the gaps in the weave indistinguishable from the texture of old concrete in the morning light.

Jun stepped back to the village-side abutment and looked across the full length of the bridge.

It looked like a bridge.

That was the point.

"They're on the shore path," Granny Yau said, her binoculars fixed south. "Moving toward the bridge access road."

The fourteen bodies from the mud flat had reached firm ground. They were moving north along the narrow concrete path that connected the south beach to the road — a service access route that ran along the base of the seawall, passing under the south arch of the stone bridge and connecting to the Tung Chung approach.

"Can they reach the bridge road from the south service path?" Jun asked.

"Yes. There's a stepped ramp — four steps up from the service path to the bridge road level." Granny Yau lowered the binoculars. "It's been there for sixty years."

Jun looked at Liang.

"The ramp," Liang said, and was already moving.

The ramp was six meters from the eastern abutment — four concrete steps rising from the service path below to the bridge road surface above. Jun reached it in thirty seconds, Liang behind him. The steps were solid cast concrete, mortared into the seawall.

They could not be removed quickly.

But they could be obstructed.

Jun looked at the railing posts on the eastern abutment — iron pipes, thirty millimeters diameter, set into the concrete in lead sleeves. He had driven the wire loops for the net sections around two of them. He pulled the loops off, grabbed the iron post with both hands, and rocked it. The pipe moved — slightly, in its sleeve, the lead packing compressing around it.

Not enough to remove. But enough to bend.

"Ah Kun," Jun said.

Ah Kun had followed them from the bridge. He did not ask. He set his welding bar against the base of the railing post and struck it once with the iron head of his mallet, bending the pipe forty-five degrees outward over the stair opening, blocking the top step.

Jun grabbed a second post — Liang took a third — and they bent them inward across the ramp's upper opening in overlapping angles, creating a lattice of bent iron over the stair head, each pipe crossing its neighbor.

It was not a cage. It would not stop a determined body permanently. But it would slow the crossing from the service path to the bridge road — each body would need to find a way through the bent iron lattice before it could step onto the net surface.

And slow, in Jun's experience, was usually enough.

From below the seawall came the sound of the service path — boot steps on concrete, the heavy, even rhythm of factory workers on a flat, predictable surface.

Jun wired the three bent pipes together at their crossing points with two loops of heavy wire, cinching the lattice tight.

"Done," he said.

They retreated to the village-side abutment just as the first figure appeared on the service path below — a broad-shouldered body in a blue factory overall, its yellow hardhat cracked across the dome, its rubber-soled boots wet with mud. It moved at its characteristic factory-floor pace — purposeful, direct, entirely without hesitation — and reached the base of the ramp steps.

It began climbing.

At the top step, it met the bent iron lattice. It pressed against the pipes, its hands gripping the iron, its weight bearing forward. The wired joints held. It moved sideways, found a gap between two pipes, pushed its arm through, then its shoulder.

Seven seconds to pass through the lattice.

The foot that found the bridge surface felt what appeared to be solid — mesh, tight mesh, the same resistance as a grate. It stepped forward with full confidence.

The mesh gave under its boot heel.

The foot punched through the net opening — a fifteen-centimeter square gap — and the leg followed to the knee. The body's momentum carried it forward, the opposite foot stepping in the same pattern, finding the same false surface.

Both legs went through simultaneously.

The body fell through the net and dropped four meters to the channel.

The water closed over it with a single, flat concussion.

The second figure had already cleared the lattice. It stepped onto the net in the same place — the footprints of the first body had depressed the mesh into a visible trough, the path of least resistance clear even to a thing that followed patterns rather than made decisions.

It fell through in the same way, in the same place.

"They'll follow each other until the bridge is empty," Liang said, watching.

"Until the tide comes in and the channel fills," Jun said. "Then the ones on the channel bottom will be submerged."

Granny Yau stood beside him at the abutment, her binoculars down, watching the bridge with the same flat attention she had given the incoming sampan that morning.

"The bamboo stake path on the south flat," she said after a moment. "The ones who followed it — they followed it because it was marked."

"Yes," Jun said.

She turned to look at him. "If I move the stakes, I can mark a different path. One that leads into the deepest part of the mud flat — the part where the summer silt is two meters deep."

Jun looked at her. "You'd need to do it at low tide. With the horde already on the flat."

"I know the flat," she said simply. "I've been walking it since I was four years old. I know which ground holds and which gives." She paused. "They follow marks."

"They follow marks," Jun confirmed.

She nodded, and her expression did not change, but something in it settled — the look of a person who has identified precisely the tool the situation requires and found it already in her hand.

"High tide is in six hours," she said. "When it comes in, the mud flat will be submerged. Whatever is on the outer flat at high tide stays there."

"Then we have until high tide," Jun said.

"I'll need two people to carry the stakes and keep the path behind me clear," she said. "And a boat standing off, in case."

"Liang," Jun said.

Liang looked at Granny Yau. "I can pole a sampan."

"I know you can," she said. "I watched you come in."

She was already walking toward the boat mooring.

***

---

CHAPTER 3: THE STAKE PATH


The sampan was a nine-foot flat-bottom, painted green, its hull worn to bare wood on the bow where decades of mud landings had stripped the paint. It sat low in the shallows of the tidal channel — low enough that Jun had to step across two mooring ropes to get to the stern without wetting his boots.

Granny Yau stepped in without looking at her feet and settled herself at the bow without sitting — she crouched, her rubber boots flat on the hull planking, her balance adjusted automatically to the boat's movement. A teenage girl named Yan followed her, carrying a bundle of bamboo stakes — each one a meter-and-a-half of straight bamboo culm, its tip sharpened to a point with a billhook. The bundle was tied with a strip of rattan. Yan set it across the bow thwart without instruction.

Liang took the stern and picked up the bamboo pole.

"Straight out," Granny Yau said, pointing south. "Then follow the outer margin of the flat — you'll see where the exposed mud meets the standing water. Don't go over the mud line. Keep the hull in six inches of water at all times."

Liang pushed off from the mooring post and began poling.

The tidal channel between the village stilts and the outer flat was dark green water — murky with suspended silt, smelling of brine and decomposing seaweed, its surface dimpled by the movement of small crabs retreating ahead of the hull. The channel was deep enough to pole through without grounding until they cleared the last row of stilt houses, at which point the bottom shelved rapidly and the water turned grey-brown and shallow.

The mud flat opened in front of them.

Jun had seen coastal mudflats before, but not in the Pearl River Delta, and not at summer low tide. The expanse of grey-brown silt stretched three hundred meters to the south — a vast, nearly featureless plain of tidal mud, its surface broken only by the rills and drainage channels left by the retreating water, by the scattered darkness of crab burrows, and by the line of bamboo stakes that marked Granny Yau's crab-trap path.

The stake path ran from the village's south quay in a gentle curve south and southwest — the line of a path that knew the mud, taking the firm substratum rather than the straight course, avoiding the deep silt pockets by a margin of experience. Each stake was planted two meters from the next, its tip just above the mud surface, tipped with a small white rag that caught the light.

At the far southern end of the stake line, three hundred meters out, a column of figures moved northward.

Granny Yau studied them from the bow for a long moment, her hand shading her eyes against the morning sun. "Nineteen," she said. "Spaced about a meter apart. The front one is at my third stake from the outer edge — that's the point where the path begins its curve north." She lowered her hand. "They've found it."

"How long before they reach the village end?" Liang asked.

"At that pace, on that path — forty minutes."

"Then we need forty meters of new path laid before they get here," Liang said.

"Less than that," Granny Yau said. "We only need to redirect the path at the curve. If I move the stakes at the turning point east instead of north, they'll follow the new bearing." She looked back at him. "We work at the curve — not the far end, not the near end. The middle."

She already had a stake in her hand — drawn from Yan's bundle with the ease of a woman who had been planting them in this mud for seventy years.

"Stop here," she said.

Liang braked the pole and held the sampan stationary. They were at the edge of the mud flat — the hull in eight centimeters of water, the mud surface two meters off the port side.

"I go on foot," Granny Yau said.

"You said to keep the boat near," Liang said.

"Keep it near. Move when I move." She looked at him steadily. "Don't come onto the mud yourself. The paths look the same to an oucoarse hairer."

She stepped off the gunwale onto the mud flat with the certainty of someone stepping onto a familiar floor. Her rubber boot found firm ground — the surface dimpling slightly but holding, the mud not more than three centimeters of wet surface layer over the packed sand substrate. She took a second step. A third.

She moved across the flat with small, deliberate strides, her weight balanced slightly backward, testing each footfall before committing. She was not walking the stake path itself — she was walking a parallel line, slightly to its east, following something in the mud that Liang could not read from the sampan.

Yan watched her go, then looked at Liang. "She reads the mud by its color," Yan said quietly. "The dark patches are wet — they drain slow — the substrate underneath is loose. The pale patches drain fast and the sand underneath is firm. She's walking the pale line."

Liang looked at the mud flat and tried to see it. At first it looked uniformly grey-brown. Then, gradually, he began to see the variation — slightly darker areas where the surface held standing water between the ridges, slightly paler areas where the drainage rills had carried the surface moisture away.

Granny Yau reached the stake path's turning point — the northernmost curve of the crab-trap route, the place where the stakes changed direction from southwest to north. She paused, crouching slightly, studying the column of approaching figures. They were still a hundred and eighty meters south — close enough to see clearly, the yellow hardhats and torn blue overalls of factory workers, their boots lifting high with each step as the mud resisted and released.

She pulled the first stake out of the mud.

One clean motion, straight up, the stake coming free with a soft sucking sound. She turned forty-five degrees east and drove it in two meters away, pressing it down with her palm until it held vertical in the substrate.

Then the next stake: pulled, moved east, planted.

And the next.

She was redirecting the path's curve — not sharply, not abruptly, but in the same gradual arc of the original route. From a distance, from the direction of the approaching column, the path still appeared to be a marked trail leading north. The changed bearing was not visible as a change — it was simply the next section of the path, extending as paths do.

Extending toward the east.

Where the mud was darker.

"She's walking them into the deep pocket," Yan said. Her voice was not exultant or afraid. It was the voice of someone stating a fact about weather or tide.

Liang watched Granny Yau work her way east along the new bearing, pulling and replanting each stake in turn. She had moved nine stakes — an eighteen-meter section of redirected path — when she stopped.

She turned and looked at the column.

The lead figure was now a hundred and twenty meters south, following the stake line precisely, its yellow hardhat steady as it moved. The figures behind it maintained their spacing — a loose, even column of nineteen bodies strung out across the three hundred meters of flat.

Granny Yau looked east from her position. She crouched and pressed the flat of her palm against the mud surface, then lifted her hand and looked at it. She pressed again, slightly east, and her hand sank a centimeter deeper.

That was enough.

She turned and began walking back — not on the stake path, not on the new bearing, but on her pale-mud line, the firm substrate that drained fast. Her steps were quick and light, her weight distributed carefully, covering the forty meters back to the water's edge in under two minutes.

She stepped over the sampan's gunwale without looking down and crouched at the bow.

"Move north along the margin," she said to Liang. "Slowly. Keep the hull in the shallows."

Liang began to pole.

They tracked north, the sampan moving parallel to the flat's edge at a walking pace. From the hull, Liang could now see the approaching column clearly — nineteen figures in blue overalls, yellow hardhats, their heavy boots lifting and sinking in the mud with a rhythmic, adhesive sound, following the stake line with the total commitment of things that had no reason to doubt a marked path.

The lead figure reached the redirected section.

It followed the new bearing east without hesitation. The stake was in the ground. The path went east. It went east.

The second figure followed. The third.

The column turned, nineteen bodies filing along the new bearing toward the darker mud.

Granny Yau watched without expression.

The lead figure stepped off the pale substrate and onto the dark surface. The first step sank to the ankle. The second step sank to the shin. The body continued forward — not pausing, not registering the change in resistance — and the third step sank to the knee, the boot going in and then the leg following as the wet silt closed around it.

The body stopped. Not from decision — from physics. The silt had closed above the knee and the combined weight of the factory overalls and steel-toed boots was pulling the leg down into the substrate at a rate that exceeded the body's capacity to push back up.

The second figure walked into the first figure's position and sank to the shin immediately.

The third figure walked into the second.

One by one, the column entered the dark silt pocket and stopped moving.

The nineteenth figure — the last in the column — was still on the firm ground of the original path when the lead figure had stopped entirely, sunk to the hip, its upper body still upright and moving mechanically but its legs fully embedded in two meters of soft summer silt.

The tide was still four hours from returning.

They would still be there when it came in.

Granny Yau said nothing. She looked at the column in the silt for a moment, her expression the same as it had been when she looked at the incoming sampan that morning — measuring, practical, complete. Then she turned to face the village.

"Three more problems," she said.

"Tell me," Jun said. His voice came from Liang's left.

Liang turned. Jun was standing at the north margin of the flat, at the edge of the outer channel, on a moored sampan of his own — a second, smaller boat that he had borrowed from the stilt house row and poled out alone while Granny Yau worked the south flat.

"You didn't stay at the bridge," Liang said.

"The bridge is finished," Jun said. "Yan's brother counted eleven bodies through the net in the last hour. The channel depth at the impact point is two meters. They're not getting out." He looked at Granny Yau. "Three problems."

"The north gangway," she said. "It's bolted — we can pull it, as I said. But the bolt heads are rusted and two of the eight bolts will need a wrench we don't have aboard the village tools."

"I have a bolt wrench in my bag," Jun said. "What's the second?"

"The rope ferry cable. If they get onto the eastern quay before we cut the ferry cable, the ferry platform itself becomes a bridge. The cable is fixed — it runs on a continuous loop driven by a hand-crank winch. If we cut the cable, we lose the ferry permanently."

"Do we need the ferry after today?" Jun asked.

Granny Yau considered. "No. The boats are our transit now."

"Then we cut the cable. Third problem."

She looked at him steadily. "The stilt posts."

Jun had been expecting this since the morning. He said so.

"The ironwood piles on the eastern row of houses face the shore," Granny Yau said. "The barnacle growth ends at the high-tide line — above that, the poles are clean wood, painted with coal-tar compound. An adult body in factory boots could get purchase on the coal-tar surface. If enough of them pile into the channel from the eastern shore—"

"They don't swim," Jun said.

"They don't swim," she agreed. "But if the channel is shallow enough at low tide — and it is, on the extreme spring tides, barely a meter on the eastern margin — a body that walks into the channel and doesn't stop walking can reach the stilt foundations."

Jun nodded. He had been looking at the pile spacing and the coal-tar surface since they arrived.

"Coal-tar is adhesive when warm," he said. "But it's smooth. A rubber boot sole has very little grip on smooth coal-tar." He looked at the eastern stilt row across the channel. "If we grease the poles above the high-tide line, we eliminate the grip problem entirely."

"We have the fish oil from the drying rack," Granny Yau said. "Two hundred liters. Smells terrible. Lubricates everything."

"Fish oil and coal-tar," Jun said. "The poles become frictionless above the waterline."

She looked at him for a moment. Something in her expression shifted — not warmth, exactly, but the particular acknowledgment that passes between two people who solve problems at the same speed.

"You think like a fisherman," she said.

"I think like a carpenter," Jun said. "Fishermen and carpenters have the same problem. The sea and wood both require you to work with what you have, not what you wish for."

She absorbed this without comment, then turned to Yan. "Go back to the village. Tell my son to start the fish-oil application on the eastern row — every pole from the high-tide mark to the walkway floor level. Don't let him use the oil on the inner rows. We may need it for other things."

Yan stepped off the sampan and walked quickly up the shore path toward the village, her rubber boots flapping on the concrete.

Liang poled the green sampan alongside Jun's smaller boat, and the two vessels drifted together at the flat's margin.

"The north gangway," Jun said. "Now, before anything else comes around the coast. If the Tung Chung road opens—"

"It opened," Granny Yau said. Her binoculars were up, pointed inland. "Twenty minutes ago. I didn't say it immediately because I was counting."

Jun looked at her.

"Two hundred and forty bodies on the road," she said. "Moving south at a steady pace. They'll reach the north gangway in forty minutes."

Jun looked at Liang. Liang was already picking up the bamboo pole.

They poled hard for the north quay.

***

---

CHAPTER 4: THE NORTH GANGWAY


The north gangway was older than the rope ferry and had been built with the confidence of a generation that assumed the land connections to Tai O would never need to be severed. It was two meters wide and four meters long — a stout wooden ramp of ironwood planking on a welded steel frame, the frame bolted to the concrete north quay wall with eight M24 anchor bolts set in cast-iron sleeves. The bolts had been installed in 1962 and had not been removed since.

Jun could see the problem before he was close enough to touch the bolt heads.

The cast-iron sleeves had oxidized around the bolt shafts — not simply rusted in the way of wet metal left in salt air, but galvanically corroded, the iron sleeve and the steel bolt shaft having spent sixty years establishing a tight electrochemical bond. The surface of the bolt heads was coated in a thick, pitted shell of orange-brown ferrite that had flowed into the socket of each hexagonal head, partially filling the wrench engagement.

Six of the eight bolts showed intact hex heads — slightly obscured by scale but still grippable. Two, on the channel-side rail, were so corroded that the hexagonal profile had rounded into a rough, irregular dome. A standard wrench would spin on them.

Jun knelt and looked at the two problem bolts without touching them.

Ah Kun crouched beside him. The blacksmith looked at the bolt heads for three seconds, then reached into the pocket of his canvas jacket and produced a cold chisel — a stub of hardened steel, fifteen centimeters long, its tip still sharp. He set it against the face of the nearest rounded bolt head, angling it forty-five degrees.

"One tap to create a new face," he said. "Then the wrench bites the chisel shoulder instead of the bolt head."

"Will the bolt turn without the sleeve cracking?" Jun asked.

"The sleeve is cast iron. Cast iron is brittle — it won't deform, it'll either hold or fracture." Ah Kun pressed his thumb against the concrete surface around the sleeve. "The concrete is sound. If the sleeve fractures, the bolt comes out with it — the whole assembly just fails outward."

"That works," Jun said.

"Yes," Ah Kun agreed.

Jun looked north along the quay. The Tung Chung road was visible as a pale grey line rising from the waterfront — a two-lane highway on a raised embankment, its surface empty and flat for two hundred meters, then curving slightly east before it disappeared into the scrub vegetation of the Lantau interior. At the curve, barely visible — a dark mass, moving.

"Thirty-five minutes," Granny Yau said from behind them. She had not put down her binoculars since they landed.

Jun handed his bolt wrench to Liang — a heavy, single-piece tool, forged from high-carbon steel, with a long handle for leverage. "Start on the six intact heads. Work from the landward rail first."

He turned to the rope ferry.

The ferry cable ran from the east quay winch station — a hand-cranked cast-iron drum mounted on a concrete plinth fifteen meters north of the gangway — across the main channel to the west bank winch, a distance of forty meters. The cable was twelve-millimeter braided steel, galvanized, looped on itself in a continuous circuit so that cranking the east winch drew the ferry platform west, and cranking the west winch drew it east. The platform itself was a three-by-four-meter raft of ironwood planking on a welded steel pontoon, currently moored at the east bank.

The cable was the problem. As long as it remained taut and connected, the ferry platform was a crossing point — a flat surface sitting at water level, reachable from the east quay and extending to the west bank.

But cutting twelve-millimeter steel cable without bolt cutters required either a hacksaw and time, or a cold chisel and a hammer and less time.

Jun looked at the concrete winch plinth. The cable ran over a cast-iron guide sheave — a grooved wheel that redirected the cable from horizontal to the drum. If the sheave seized or the cable jumped the groove, the system jammed. If the sheave mounting was removed entirely, the cable would drop into the channel.

He looked at the sheave mounting: four bolts, same pattern as the gangway, but these were stainless steel — no corrosion, factory-fresh thread visible at the base of each shaft. Recent maintenance. Ten minutes with the wrench on a clear bolt head.

He did not have ten minutes.

Jun looked at the ferry platform. Then at the channel. Then at the winch drum.

The drum had a ratchet pawl — a spring-loaded catch that prevented the drum from unwinding under load. If he released the pawl, the drum would unspool freely. The cable would go slack. The ferry platform would drift with the current — westward on the incoming tide.

He found the pawl release: a simple lever, spring-loaded, the spring visible as a coil of galvanized wire around a pivot pin. Jun pressed the lever with his thumb. The spring resisted. He pressed harder, feeling the coil compress, and the pawl lifted clear of the ratchet teeth.

The drum turned.

The cable went slack in a long, gradual sag — twenty kilograms of steel wire losing its tension over forty meters, the center of the span dropping until the cable hung in a deep catenary, its midpoint submerged. The ferry platform, freed from the cable's pull, drifted two meters west on the current before catching on its bow line — still moored at the east cleat.

Jun looked at the bow line. A single mooring rope, thirty millimeters of braided nylon, tied to a cleat on the east quay.

He untied it.

The platform drifted.

The channel current — the tidal flow moving east to west on the incoming tide — caught the flat underside of the pontoon and pushed it. Slowly at first, then with gathering momentum, the ferry platform moved west, crossing the channel in ninety seconds, coming to rest against the pilings of the west bank, forty meters from the east quay.

No cable. No platform. No crossing.

From the east quay, the only remaining connection to the village was the north gangway.

"Two bolts clear," Liang called.

Jun walked back to the gangway.

Liang had removed two of the landward-rail bolts — long shafts of oxidized steel, their threads intact below the corrosion, the concrete sleeves still in the wall. The gangway frame had shifted slightly on the remaining six bolts, the steel moving a centimeter outward on the freed side.

Jun picked up the wrench and went to the third bolt. It broke loose in thirty seconds — the threads had not corroded, only the surface, and once the head was engaged the shaft turned cleanly. The fourth bolt the same.

Ah Kun was working on the first of the two rounded heads with his cold chisel, tapping carefully — one measured stroke at a time, angling the chisel to create a new flat face on the corroded dome. The cast-iron sleeve around it had not cracked.

"Almost," Ah Kun said.

"Granny Yau," Jun said without looking up. "The ferry platform is on the west bank. Tell your son to tie it off and keep it there."

A pause. Then her voice, sharp and immediate, carrying a name across the channel.

Five more bolts cleared in four minutes. The gangway was now held by a single bolt on the channel-side rail — the second of the two corroded heads, the one Ah Kun had not yet reached — and the resistance of the steel frame bearing against the concrete wall.

Ah Kun finished his chisel work and set the wrench on the new flat face.

He pressed.

The bolt did not move.

He pressed harder, both hands on the wrench handle, his weight leaning into it. A faint, metallic groan from the sleeve.

"It's going to fracture," Ah Kun said.

"Let it," Jun said.

Ah Kun gave one sharp, short push with his full body weight behind it. The cast-iron sleeve sheared at the concrete face with a sound like a ceramic tile breaking — a single sharp *CRACK* — and the bolt shaft pulled through the fractured sleeve, the entire assembly coming out in Ah Kun's hand: bolt, sleeve, and a disk of cracked cast iron, trailing concrete dust.

The gangway was free.

"Twenty minutes," Granny Yau said.

Jun and Liang grabbed the gangway frame — the steel hot in the morning sun — and pushed. The ramp was heavy, perhaps three hundred kilograms of ironwood and welded steel, but it was balanced on the channel edge, its inner rail now free of the quay wall. They pushed from the landward side, tilting the frame outward.

It went slowly at first. Then the center of gravity passed the pivot point, and the ramp dropped.

*CRASH.*

The gangway hit the channel surface flat — a tremendous, resonant impact that sent a wave rolling across the water. The platform sank nose-first, the heavy steel frame pulling it down, the ironwood planking floating free as the frame submerged. Within seconds only the planks remained at the surface, bobbing in the disturbed water.

The north quay wall was now a blank concrete face above an open channel.

Jun looked at the quay. He looked at the stone arch bridge, fifty meters south — where the net trap was set, where the bodies from the morning were still working through it in ones and twos, each one falling through in turn. He looked at the channel between the eastern quay and the stilt village — forty meters of water, incoming tide, the current moving steadily.

The eastern quay was now an island.

Whatever arrived on it from the Tung Chung road would have the arch bridge to the south — which dropped them into the channel — and the channel to the west — which they could not cross. They would accumulate on the quay. They would stand there. The quay was concrete and solid and could hold ten thousand of them without structural consequence.

But they could not reach the village from it.

"It's enough," Jun said.

A voice came from behind him — not Granny Yau's, not Liang's, not Ah Kun's.

"The ferry cable."

Jun turned. An old man stood at the edge of the north quay, perhaps eighty years old, in a fisherman's blue shirt and canvas trousers, his feet bare on the concrete. He was looking at the slack cable lying in the channel and at the ferry platform resting against the west bank pilings.

"You released the cable without asking," the old man said. His Cantonese was slow and precise.

"There wasn't time to ask," Jun said.

"My wife is on the west bank," the old man said. "She went across this morning to tend to Old Cheung's fish ponds. She will want to come back."

Jun looked at Granny Yau.

"Uncle Fong," Granny Yau said, her voice careful.

"I know what is coming," Uncle Fong said, without heat, without accusation. He had the tone of someone stating his position for the record rather than arguing. "I have seen what is coming for two weeks. I know why you did it. I am telling you that my wife is on the west bank."

The silence lasted four seconds.

"The boats," Jun said. "There are sampans on both banks. She can cross by boat. It's forty meters."

"She is seventy-three years old," Uncle Fong said. "She has never poled a sampan alone."

"Someone will pole it for her," Jun said. He looked at Liang.

Liang was already moving to the mooring.

"Uncle Fong," Jun said. "Tell us her location. Liang will cross now."

The old man looked at Jun for a moment — the measuring look of someone deciding whether to trust — then described the fish pond location in three precise sentences.

Liang pushed off from the mooring with the bamboo pole and crossed the channel without another word, the hull cutting a clean line across the current toward the west bank.

Uncle Fong watched him go.

"The cable can be re-rigged," Jun said to him, not because it was certainly true but because it was true enough to say.

"I know," Uncle Fong said. He turned and walked back along the quay toward the village without looking at the road.

Jun turned north.

The first figures were visible on the Tung Chung embankment — not a vanguard but the leading edge of a column that stretched back around the curve and out of sight. Two hundred and forty bodies, moving in the compressed, purposeful crowd-flow of the factory floor — not the irregular stumbling of the water-logged Anhui dead or the broad formation of the Pearl River Delta delta workers, but a tight, dense column. These were Lantau residents: hotel workers, logistics staff from the cargo hub, airport service crews in high-visibility vests. They had not traveled far. They were compact and fast.

The distance to the quay edge was four hundred meters.

"Twelve minutes," Granny Yau said. "Possibly ten."

The quay wall was blank concrete — nothing to climb, nothing to grip, nothing to breach. The only surface the column would find when it reached the quay edge was water.

Jun watched them come.

He was thinking about the east quay. About how many bodies it could hold before the accumulated weight pressed the rearmost figures over the south edge or the north edge — into the channel on one side, onto the bridge net on the other. About whether the net anchors at the bridge abutment would hold under the lateral pressure of several hundred kilograms of bodies compressing against them.

He was thinking that they needed to reinforce the bridge anchors.

"Ah Kun," he said. "Come with me."

They walked south along the quay toward the bridge at a run.

Behind them, on the Tung Chung road, the column reached the embankment's end and began descending toward the quay.

***

---

CHAPTER 5: THE FUNNEL GATE


Jun had not designed the bridge net for crowd pressure.

He had designed it for individual bodies — one at a time, stepping onto the false floor and falling through under their own weight. That design was sound. Eleven bodies had confirmed it in the three hours since the nets went down, each one following the last through the mesh into the channel below.

But a crowd was not a sequence of individual bodies. A crowd was a fluid — it pressed in all directions simultaneously, and the force it exerted on any fixed structure was not the weight of one person but the accumulated lateral thrust of every person behind them, transmitted forward through the compressed mass of bodies like pressure through water.

The bridge net's anchor points were wire loops around iron railing posts — posts that had been designed to prevent a single pedestrian from falling over the edge, not to resist the lateral force of two hundred and forty bodies compressing against them from one direction.

If the crowd pressed the net from the quay side, the railing posts would bend. If the posts bent far enough, the wire loops would slip. If the loops slipped, the net would peel away from the arch and fall into the channel.

And the bridge would be open.

Jun reached the bridge abutment from the village side and crossed to the east end on the arch deck — walking on the net itself, his feet finding the concrete surface below the mesh, moving carefully. He tested each railing post in turn: took it in both hands, pressed lateral force against it, watched the base where it entered the concrete.

Six of the ten posts on the east end were firm — no movement, the concrete around their bases sound. Three showed a slight rock — a millimeter of play in the base socket, the post mount slightly degraded by decades of salt air. The last one, at the southeast corner where the railing met the abutment wall, was worse: two millimeters of play, the concrete at its base showing a hairline crack.

Nine minutes, Granny Yau had said. Possibly seven.

Jun looked at the crack in the corner post's base and made a decision.

He did not try to fix the cracked post. He removed it.

Ah Kun had the welding bar. Three strikes at the base, angling the blows to exploit the existing crack, and the post broke free at the socket — a clean fracture along the hairline, the post coming out of the concrete in one piece, trailing a disk of broken aggregate.

Jun took the post — a thirty-millimeter iron pipe, one-point-two meters long — and drove it vertically into the arch net immediately adjacent to the corner, pressing the sharpened stub end of the broken base through the mesh and into the expansion gap between the arch deck and the abutment wall. He hammered it down with Ah Kun's mallet until it was set, then bent the top end toward the village side with a sharp, leveraged blow, creating a diagonal strut that pressed the net edge against the arch concrete rather than the railing.

One anchor point improved.

He looked at the remaining eight posts on the east end and thought about crowd dynamics.

The problem was not the posts individually. It was that the crowd would approach the bridge entrance as a wide front — six meters across, the full width of the road — and compress against the net's eastern edge all at once. The net had no resistance to lateral force; it was designed to yield vertically, not horizontally.

What the bridge entrance needed was not stronger anchors. It needed a narrower entrance.

He looked at the bent-iron lattice they had made over the service ramp in the morning — four pipes crossed at angles, wired at the joints. It had slowed the fourteen bodies from the mud flat to a rate of one at a time. Seven seconds per body.

The same principle would work here, scaled up and positioned at the bridge entrance rather than the ramp.

"Ah Kun," Jun said. "Pull every loose railing post from the west end of the bridge. Bring them here."

The west-end posts — on the village side of the arch, where the crowd would never reach — were structurally redundant once the net was in place. Jun had wired some of them as net anchors, but those wires could be moved.

Ah Kun began working at the west end, using the cold chisel to break the base sockets on the posts that were removable, carrying them to the east end one by one.

Jun received each post and drove it into the arch net at the bridge entrance, building upward and inward — not randomly, but in a deliberate geometry: two posts on each side of the entrance, angled inward at forty-five degrees, their top ends crossed and wired together at a height of one-point-five meters, creating an A-frame on each side. Between the two A-frames, the entrance width narrowed from six meters to one-point-two meters — the width of a single body, one at a time.

It was not a gate. It was a funnel.

From the east, the entrance looked like a narrowing of the bridge road — visible as an obstruction, but not as a wall. The crowd pressure would press against the A-frames from the oucoarse haire, compressing inward, but the angled posts would redirect the lateral force downward into the arch deck rather than outward against the net anchors. The net itself would only receive the weight of bodies that passed through the funnel entrance and stepped onto the false floor.

One at a time.

Seven seconds each, at the pace of the ramp this morning.

At that rate, two hundred and forty bodies would take twenty-eight minutes to pass through the funnel. Each one would fall through the net into the channel. After the first thirty, the channel at the base of the arch would begin to fill — the accumulated bodies piling on the channel bottom. After the first hundred, the pile would approach the surface.

Jun thought about this.

"Granny Yau," he called across the channel.

She was on the village side of the bridge abutment, watching through her binoculars.

"The channel depth at the arch base," Jun said. "What is it at high tide?"

"Three meters," she said. "Two-point-five at the keystone center."

"At low tide?"

"One-point-eight. One-point-two at the margin."

"And the tide now?"

"Coming in. Currently two meters at center."

Jun did the arithmetic. At two meters depth, a fallen body in steel-toed boots and heavy factory overalls would be fully submerged. As more bodies fell, they would stack — eventually the stack would approach the surface. At some point, perhaps after a hundred and fifty bodies, the pile would be high enough that the next falling body would not be fully submerged. It would land on the pile and potentially remain upright.

At that point the false floor would stop working.

"We need to clear the channel bed periodically," Jun said, more to himself than to anyone.

"The boat hook," Granny Yau said. She had heard him. "We can push the pile laterally from the sampan — move it east along the channel bottom, away from the arch shadow. The incoming tide current will help."

"Can we work under the arch from a boat?"

"The arch clearance at high tide is two meters. A sampan fits."

"Then we maintain the channel depth from a boat, on rotation," Jun said. "Two people, one sampan, four-hour shifts. Push the pile east whenever the base depth drops below one-point-five meters."

Granny Yau said nothing for a moment. Then: "My son Yau Kin can do the first shift. He knows the channel."

"Done," Jun said.

From the north came the sound of the column arriving on the quay — not a single impact but a sustained, building noise, boots on concrete replacing the previous silence of the empty road. The Lantau dead were faster than the Pearl River Delta workers and lighter on their feet: hotel porters and airport staff, their footwear lighter than the steel-toed factory boots, the sound of their arrival higher-pitched and more rapid.

Jun crossed back to the village side of the arch and watched.

The column reached the north quay edge and stopped.

Not all of it — the front rank stopped, finding the edge, the blank concrete falling to the channel below. The ranks behind pressed forward, and the front rank stepped off the edge and fell into the channel. Not one or two — twenty fell within the first thirty seconds as the column's rear pressed the front forward into the water.

The channel at the quay's north face was four meters deep. The bodies sank.

The next rank stepped off and fell. And the next.

Then the column's pressure resolved itself — the front ranks were gone, and the new front rank, arriving at the quay edge, slowed. Not from recognition but from the physical absence of a surface to step onto. The column compressed, bodies stacking against the rear of the front rank, and the front rank pressed sideways along the quay edge, searching for a crossing.

They found the bridge.

The first body reached the funnel entrance.

It pressed against the A-frame on the left side, trying to pass through. The angled post redirected it into the gap between the two frames. It entered the one-point-two-meter opening and stepped onto the net.

It fell through.

The second body followed.

Jun watched from the village abutment, counting seconds between each fall. Seven. Eight. Six. Eight. The funnel was working — the crowd pressure was absorbed by the A-frame geometry rather than transmitted to the net anchors. The railing posts behind the funnel showed no movement, no lateral flexing, no sign of the base sockets cracking.

The net held.

On his left, a sampan appeared from the west bank — Liang at the pole, a small, white-haired woman seated in the bow, upright and composed, her hands folded in her lap. She was watching the crowd on the quay with the same expression she might use for a distant weather front: noting it, assessing it, filing it.

Liang moored the sampan at the village east-facing dock, helped the woman to the walkway with one hand.

Uncle Fong was there waiting. He said nothing. He took his wife's arm and walked with her back into the stilt house rows without speaking, their rubber-booted feet finding the planks in the same rhythm, the same pace.

Jun watched them go.

On the bridge, the thirtieth body fell through the net into the channel.

He turned back to the bridge and counted the crowd still on the quay. He had underestimated — there were more than two hundred and forty. The column had a long tail that had been out of sight around the road's curve. He revised upward: three hundred, perhaps three-twenty.

At seven seconds per body, through the funnel, that was thirty-seven minutes.

He had thirty-seven minutes of sustained function to maintain.

"The stilt poles," Jun said. "The fish-oil application."

"Kin started it two hours ago," Granny Yau said, from the abutment beside him. She had moved there without him noticing. "Eastern row is done. He's working south on the outer face."

Jun looked at the eastern stilt row — the outermost ring of ironwood piles visible across the channel, their above-waterline sections now dark and wet with oil. The coal-tar was still visible below the oil coat, but the surface sheen above the waterline was new — a wet, reflective film that caught the morning light differently.

"The current?" Jun asked.

"Running east to west on the flood," Granny Yau said. "Any body that enters the channel from the quay side will be carried west and south by the current before it reaches the stilt foundations."

"How far west before it touches bottom?"

"The channel floor drops sharply west of the quay. Four meters, then six. Anything in the channel on the flood tide will be carried past the village perimeter and into the inner harbor before it can walk to the foundation row."

Jun looked at the channel. The current was visible at the surface — a slight directional shimmer, the tidal flow pressing steadily west, moving toward the inner bay.

The water was working for them. The tide was working for them.

He thought about how many of the defenses in the last hours had relied not on what they had built but on what was already there — the mud flat's deep silt pockets, the tidal current, the channel depth, the fish oil over coal-tar, the mooring ropes, the ratchet pawl. Each one a feature of the existing environment, not a new structure.

Tai O had been defending itself from the sea for three hundred years. It already knew how.

His job, he thought, had mostly been to not interfere with what it already knew.

"The outer bay," Jun said. "The north coast. The mangroves."

"The mangrove prop roots are too dense for anything to move through quickly," Granny Yau said. "But dense is not impassable. A body that walks in a straight line, without adjusting for obstacles, will eventually work through a mangrove stand by brute force." She paused. "Three days, maybe four, for the outer edge."

"We have three days," Jun said. "Maybe four."

She looked at him sidelong. "And then?"

Jun looked west across the channel, past the stilt houses, past the inner harbor, past the outer bay to the open South China Sea — blue-grey and featureless and enormous, the horizon a clean line thirty kilometers away.

"The sea," he said.

Granny Yau followed his gaze.

"I have four seaworthy boats," she said. "Two diesel, two sail. The diesel boats carry twenty people each. The sail boats carry twelve. Combined — sixty-four people, if we load carefully."

"The village has three hundred," Jun said.

"I know," she said.

She said it the way she said everything — without inflection, without distress. A statement of the problem's dimensions.

They stood together at the bridge abutment for a moment, the sound of the funnel's work behind them — the metronomic rhythm of bodies passing through the one-point-two-meter gap, seven seconds, eight seconds, seven — the channel below filling slowly with factory blue and airport high-visibility yellow.

On the bridge, the forty-fifth body fell through the net.

Two hundred and seventy-five more to go.

Jun picked up his carpenter's bag and went to help clear the channel.

***

---

CHAPTER 6: THE PAIRED HULLS


The funnel processed its last body at half past noon.

Jun knew it was the last because the quay had gone quiet — the rhythmic shuffle of boots on concrete replaced by the sounds of water and wind and the creak of the stilt houses settling in the midday heat. He crossed to the east end of the bridge arch and looked at the empty quay. The concrete was marked by the passage of the column — dark smears of mud and engine grease in long, compressed streaks — but otherwise unmarked. No bodies remained standing. The quay held nothing that could move.

Below the arch, in the channel, Yau Kin was working from a sampan with a long-handled boat hook, pushing the submerged pile east along the channel bed. The water was cloudy with disturbed silt. The depth gauge — a bamboo pole with painted depth marks that Kin had planted at the arch's center — showed two meters of clear water above the pile. Safe margin.

Jun walked back to the village.

Granny Yau was waiting at the inner quay beside a coil of rope, her binoculars around her neck and a folded sheet of paper in her hand — a hand-drawn map of the village's boat inventory, annotated in small, precise Cantonese characters. She had made it while the funnel was running.

"Forty-three sampans," she said, handing him the paper. "Of those, thirty-one are currently sound — no rot in the hull planking, thwarts intact, able to carry weight. The other twelve are in various states of repair. Eight need caulking. Four need structural work I wouldn't trust in open water."

Jun studied the map. The boat symbols were distributed throughout the inner harbor in clusters — the fishing fleet moored by family, generation, and habit, the same moorings used since the village was built. He counted the symbols.

"In calm weather," he said, "how many people can a sound sampan carry in protected water?"

"Six," she said immediately. "Seven if they sit still and don't shift weight."

"In open water? South China Sea swell, summer conditions?"

"Four. Three if the person is large."

Jun did the arithmetic. Thirty-one sound sampans at four persons each: a hundred and twenty-four people. Added to the four seaworthy boats' sixty-four capacity: a hundred and eighty-eight. The village had three hundred.

The gap was a hundred and twelve people.

"The eight that need caulking," Jun said. "How long to make them sound?"

"Two hours each, with the right cotton and tar. We have the materials."

"Then we caulk them. That gives us thirty-nine sound sampans." He recalculated. "A hundred and fifty-six in the sampan fleet, plus sixty-four in the main boats. Two hundred and twenty total. Still eighty short."

"The twelve are the limit," Granny Yau said. "We cannot build new hulls in three days. Wood needs time to season and the shapes need a boatwright's tools I don't have here." She paused. "My husband was the boatwright. He died six years ago."

Jun looked at the boats in the harbor, then at the bamboo that lined the catwalks and the building frames of the stilt houses — structural bamboo in the walls, decorative bamboo in the railings, utility bamboo in the fishing poles and crab-trap frames stacked on the outer decks. The village was dense with it.

"We don't build new hulls," Jun said. "We join existing ones."

Granny Yau looked at him.

"Pair the sampans," Jun said. "Two hulls side by side, connected by crossbeams — bamboo poles lashed across both gunwales, spaced one meter apart. The space between the hulls becomes a platform. A catamaran."

She was quiet for several seconds.

"A twin-hull carries twice the weight with the same stability as a single hull," Jun continued. "In open water, paired hulls are more stable than a single sampan — the beam width triples, the capsize resistance increases by the cube of the beam change. Two sampans each rated for four persons can carry ten or twelve persons safely as a pair."

"The bamboo crossbeams," she said slowly. "How many? What diameter?"

"Eight crossbeams per pair, at one-meter spacing across a four-meter gap. Each crossbeam carries one-hundred-and-twenty kilograms live load. The bamboo needs to be at least six centimeters in diameter — the structural culm, not the decorative material." He looked at the catwalks. "The catwalk support poles are eighty millimeters. Exactly right."

She looked at the catwalks. "Those poles hold up the walkways."

"The inner walkway poles," Jun said. "The eastern outer row — the poles facing the quay — those we leave. The inner village catwalks have redundant support; if we remove alternating poles, the walkways remain functional. We lose nothing that matters."

Granny Yau was still looking at the catwalks. Her expression was the one Jun had learned to wait for — the expression of a person running the full calculation, not just the immediate arithmetic. She was not thinking about the bamboo poles. She was thinking about which houses they were attached to, which families walked those catwalks each morning, whose grandmother had hung her laundry on which rail.

"How many pairs?" she asked.

"Sixteen," Jun said. "Sixteen paired sampans, plus the original fleet of seven singles — the unpaired ones and the four main boats. That gives us two hundred and ninety-six carrying capacity, minimum. We load carefully and we make three hundred."

"We have thirty-one sound sampans and eight that need caulking," she said. "Thirty-nine total. Sixteen pairs use thirty-two of them. Seven singles from the remaining seven."

"Yes."

"You need the bamboo poles from fourteen sections of inner catwalk." She thought for a moment. "The east-central section. Between the fish store and the market shed. Those catwalks have the highest pole density and the most structural redundancy — the houses on either side have independent deck supports."

"I'll need to see them."

"I'll show you." She folded the boat map and put it in her jacket pocket. "The caulking — who does that?"

"Anyone with steady hands and patience. Do you have cotton batting?"

"In the sail-repair shed. Two full rolls."

"And pine tar or equivalent?"

"Fish tar. Same effect."

"Then set the caulking teams now — two people per boat, rotate them in two-hour shifts. I need the caulked boats floating by tomorrow morning."

Granny Yau turned and called across the walkway in Cantonese — a sequence of names and instructions, rapid and precise, the village organizing itself around her voice the way it had organized around her father's voice and his mother's voice before that. Within minutes, women and teenagers were moving toward the sail-repair shed, carrying cotton rolls and tar pots.

Jun and Liang followed Granny Yau to the east-central catwalk section.

The catwalk poles here were, as she had said, dense — every eighty centimeters along the walkway edge, the bamboo culms standing vertically from the water to the walkway floor level, each one lashed to the deck frame above with rattan binding. The culms were approximately two meters in length above the waterline, their lower ends submerged and anchored to the channel bed.

Jun tested a pole: gripped it and pulled laterally, feeling the rattan binding at the top flex without breaking. The lower anchor held — the bamboo had been planted long enough that its root zone had collapsed into the silt, the natural hydraulic grip of a submerged base.

He would need to cut them, not pull them.

He took his handsaw from the bag. The bamboo culm was eight centimeters in diameter — two passes of a coarse-toothed saw, one horizontal cut thirty centimeters above the waterline, the culm free in forty seconds. He tested the cut end: straight, clean, the hollow interior visible as a series of fibrous chambers, each chamber providing independent buoyancy.

"How many poles do you need from this section?" Granny Yau asked.

"Eight per pair, sixteen pairs. A hundred and twenty-eight poles total." He looked along the catwalk. "This section has approximately eighty poles. I need another catwalk section — the secondary one, the section behind the fish store."

"That one's older," she said. "The poles are mixed — some are nine centimeters, some are five. The five-centimeter ones aren't strong enough."

"I'll sort them," Jun said. "Liang."

Liang already had his own saw out.

They worked through the afternoon — Jun and Liang cutting alternating poles from the two catwalk sections, the walkway surfaces remaining stable because every other pole was left in place, the redundant supports carrying the load without visible deflection. Granny Yau watched the first cuts with the stillness of someone letting go of something she had decided to let go of, and then turned away and did not watch again.

The poles accumulated on the inner quay — a growing stack of green-grey bamboo sections, their cut ends pale and fibrous, their hollow chambers intact. Yan and two other teenagers sorted them by diameter, setting aside the undersized culms for later use as lashing material.

By midafternoon Jun was at the inner harbor, beginning the first pairing.

He had selected two identical sampans — both nine-footers, both green-painted, their hull profiles well-matched. He moored them side by side in the harbor, their gunwales parallel, separated by the width of the bamboo crossbeam platform — approximately one-point-two meters, enough to walk between them with clear footing.

The crossbeams went in pairs: one across the bow thwarts, one across the stern thwarts, then six equally spaced between them. Each crossbeam was a full eight-centimeter bamboo culm, its ends resting in notches that Jun cut into the gunwale rail with a chisel — the notch angled slightly inward so the beam seated under its own weight, the load pressing the beam deeper into the notch rather than lifting it out.

Each crossbeam was lashed to the gunwale at both ends with three wraps of split rattan, the wraps crossing over each other in the traditional Malay pattern that Jun had learned from a book on Southeast Asian boat building, the same pattern used on the traditional outrigger fishing vessels of the Philippine archipelago. It was a pattern that had been developed specifically for the load conditions of open-water swell — the wrapping tightened under lateral force rather than loosening.

He had Liang and Yan test the first crossbeam by standing on its center with their combined weight — two hundred and fifty kilograms — while he watched the gunwale notches and the lashing wraps. No movement. The beam bowed slightly at the center — three millimeters of natural bamboo deflection — but returned to level when the load was removed.

Sound.

Eight crossbeams in: the first catamaran hull was complete. Jun stepped onto the platform between the two hulls — four meters long, one-point-two meters wide, a flat, stable surface suspended two centimeters above the channel waterline. He shifted his weight side to side deliberately, rocking the paired hulls. The platform flexed slightly but did not tip — the wide beam of the paired hulls' combined width resisting the capsize moment.

"Stand on one gunwale," he told Liang.

Liang stepped onto the outer rail of the left hull, his full weight on the edge. The platform tilted — five degrees, eight degrees — then arrested. The paired hulls would not capsize with one person standing on the outermost rail.

In open water, with twelve seated passengers distributed evenly across the crossbeam platform, the platform would be more stable than this — lower center of gravity, more distributed load.

"It works," Liang said, stepping back to the center.

"It works for now," Jun said. "We test the next one and the next. Every pair gets the same load test. Any crossbeam that shows more than five millimeters of deflection under full load gets replaced."

He had twenty-eight sampans still to pair and approximately forty-two hours before Granny Yau's estimated mangrove-breach window.

He picked up the saw.

Uncle Fong appeared at the quay edge at dusk, carrying a coil of rattan — a thick, supple coil of freshly split material, the strips wide and pale. He set it down beside the lashing pile without a word.

Jun looked up from the third catamaran hull he was lashing.

"My wife split it," Uncle Fong said. "She said to tell you the Malay wrap is correct but you should double the forward crossbeam. Bow swell is the worst in summer."

Jun looked at the rattan, then at the old man. "Your wife knows the Malay wrap?"

"Her father was a Thai fisherman," Uncle Fong said. "He came here on a fishing boat sixty years ago and never went back. He built outriggers." He paused. "She watched."

Jun set down his saw.

"Is she willing to check the wraps on the hulls I've done?"

Uncle Fong looked back toward the stilt house rows. "She was already going to. She came out to see the first one and went to get the rattan." He looked at Jun steadily. "She says the bow crossbeam notch angle is wrong. Too shallow — will ride up in bow swell."

Jun looked at the first catamaran hull moored in the harbor. Then at his chisel.

"Which angle?" he asked.

"She'll show you," Uncle Fong said.

He turned and walked back into the stilt rows. A moment later, the old man's wife appeared — small, white-haired, precise — walking to the harbor edge and stepping onto the catamaran platform without hesitation. She crouched at the bow crossbeam and pressed her thumbnail into the notch angle, feeling it.

She shook her head.

She held out her hand for the chisel.

Jun gave it to her.

She recut the notch — a single, angled stroke, deeper and steeper, the cut surface showing the correct geometry immediately. She laid the crossbeam back in and pressed it down. It seated with a solid, definitive click that the previous shallow-cut version had not made.

"All of them," she said, in Cantonese, to Jun.

He understood enough. "Yes," he said. "All of them."

She handed the chisel back, stepped off the platform, and walked back to the stilt rows.

Jun looked at the corrected notch, then at the sixteen pairs he still needed to build.

Behind him, in the direction of the north coast, the wind had shifted slightly. It was coming from the northeast now — off the mainland, carrying the faint chemical smell of burning polymer. Somewhere in the mangrove fringe along the north shore, something had moved closer.

Not yet a breach. But closer.

He picked up the saw and went back to work.

***

---

CHAPTER 7: THE CREEK MOUTH


The smell reached them before the sound did.

Jun woke before dawn to it — not the salt-and-seaweed smell of the bay, not the fish-tar and cotton smell of the caulking work, but the sharp, synthetic odor that had followed the industrial horde from Foshan to the Pearl River Delta and across to Lantau: burned polymer, overheated machine oil, the olfactory residue of ten thousand factory floors compressed into the bodies that had walked through them for years.

He sat up on the folded net he was using as a sleeping mat on the inner quay and looked north.

The sky was the grey-blue of very early morning, stars fading at the horizon. The village was quiet — the catamaran work teams had stopped at midnight, the caulking teams an hour later, the boat channel running its four-hour watch. In the stillness, the north wind carried the smell clearly, without interference.

He found Granny Yau at the north edge of the village catwalk with her binoculars raised, still in yesterday's clothes.

"You slept," she said, without lowering the binoculars.

"Two hours," Jun said. "What are you seeing?"

"Movement in the outer mangroves. The fringe layer — the seaward edge — began shifting about forty minutes ago. Not the whole fringe. One section. Northeast, at the creek mouth." She lowered the binoculars and pointed. "Ah Fai saw it first. He was out checking the crab traps."

Ah Fai was the young man with the aluminum harpoon Jun had noticed on the quay when they arrived — twenty years old, broad-shouldered, with the quick, economical movements of someone who had worked on boats since childhood. He was standing at the catwalk rail ten meters away, watching the north shore. The harpoon was still over his shoulder.

"The creek mouth," Jun said.

"Sheung Pak Creek," Granny Yau said. "It runs from the interior hills to the north bay. At low tide the creek is a meter deep — shallow enough to walk. At high tide, two-point-five meters."

"What's the tide now?"

"Ebbing. We're two hours past high water."

Jun looked at the sky. "Depth at the creek mouth right now?"

"One-point-eight at center. Dropping."

A meter-eighty of depth. Factory workers in steel-toed boots and heavy overalls could cross at that depth — the boots would keep them on the channel bed, the weight of their clothing pulling them down into the current, the current not strong enough on the ebb to push them off course.

"They're crossing the creek bed," Jun said.

"Not yet," Ah Fai said from the rail, his voice careful. "The ones in the mangroves are pressing the fringe from inside. The prop roots are holding them — you can see the fringe layer moving, the roots bending where they push. But they haven't come through to the open water yet."

Jun watched. In the growing light, the mangrove fringe was visible as a dark mass along the north shore — not a wall but a dense, irregular tangle of aerial roots arching from the water surface to the canopy above, the spaces between them close enough to block a standing adult but not close enough to be impenetrable. The fringe layer at the creek mouth, he could now see, was moving slightly — a rhythmic flexing of the outer prop roots, the whole structure trembling with the accumulated pressure of bodies working through from behind.

"The creek mouth is four meters wide?" Jun asked Ah Fai.

"Three-point-five at low tide. The mangroves grow out on both banks — the navigable gap is in the center."

"Current direction on the ebb?"

"East-northeast. It joins the main bay current and runs out past the headland."

Jun considered the geometry. The creek mouth was a gap in the mangrove barrier — a natural opening where the prop roots were absent because the channel had scoured them away. Any bodies emerging from the mangroves would find the creek mouth and enter it, because the creek mouth was the path of least resistance in an otherwise impassable fringe. Once in the creek, they would walk the creek bed toward the village — the direction of least resistance again, following the slope of the channel floor.

The creek's ebb current was running east. The bodies would be walking west, toward the village. The current would work against them but not stop them — a meter-eighty of depth was sufficient for a body to keep its footing on the creek bed against a weak tidal ebb.

Unless the depth increased.

If the creek mouth were deeper — if the channel bed dropped at the entrance — a body stepping off the mangrove mud and into the creek mouth would find itself in water too deep to maintain footing, and the ebb current would take it east.

The creek mouth was not deeper. But it could be made effectively deeper by blocking the shallow margin — forcing the bodies into the navigable center channel, where the depth was greatest.

That was the approach. Not a wall. A funnel — the same principle as the bridge, applied to a waterway.

"Ah Fai," Jun said. "I need two sampans, two anchor stones, and sixty meters of the heaviest rope in the village."

Ah Fai did not ask why. He turned and went.

Jun looked at Granny Yau. "We have an hour, maybe less, before they breach the fringe."

"I know," she said. "Go."

He and Liang followed Ah Fai to the inner harbor, where the boy had already pulled two sampans alongside each other and was coiling rope from the sail-repair shed. The rope was eighteen-millimeter braided nylon — mooring-grade, the heavy material used to secure the diesel boats in the outer harbor. It would hold against anything short of a winch.

They pushed off from the inner harbor and poled north through the village's inner channel, then around the western headland of the bay and along the north shore. The north coast was entirely different from the south — no beach, no mud flat, no open approach. The mangroves came down to the water on both sides of the creek mouth, their prop roots arching into the dark, tidal shallows, their canopies meeting overhead in a dense green vault that blocked the early morning sky almost completely.

The creek mouth opened ahead of them — a pale gap in the dark mangrove wall, three-point-five meters wide, the water in it moving east with the ebb current, the surface showing the slight, directional shimmer of flow over a shallow bed.

From inside the mangroves, the pressure sound was now audible: a sustained, rhythmic creaking of prop roots under lateral load, the mangrove trunks bending and recovering at each push, the percussion of it irregular but continuous.

Jun looked at the creek mouth carefully.

The channel had two deep points: the center, which Ah Fai had said was one-point-eight meters, and the outer margin on the eastern bank, where the current had scoured a slightly deeper trough — perhaps two meters. The western bank was shallower — one-point-two at most. That was where the bodies would emerge first. The shallower, flatter approach on the western bank was the easier foothold.

The boom needed to close the western margin entirely and angle the remaining gap toward the deep eastern trough.

"Right bank," Jun said to Ah Fai, pointing to the eastern bank of the creek mouth. "Anchor there, fifteen meters upstream." He pointed to Liang. "Left bank, same distance upstream from the mouth. Hold station. Don't anchor yet."

Ah Fai pushed his sampan toward the eastern bank and set his anchor stone — a concrete block on a short chain, dropped into the creek bed with a precise throw that Jun recognized as someone who had anchored sampans in current before. The boat swung on the chain, stabilized, fixed.

Liang held station on the western bank by pushing his pole against the mangrove root mass, the boat steady against the slight tidal pull.

Jun ran the rope.

One end: tied to Ah Fai's sampan bow cleat with a bowline, triple-hitched. Jun pulled on the standing end, watching the cleat. The hitch held — the bowline embedding tighter under load.

He fed the rope across the creek mouth in a diagonal line — not perpendicular to the bank, but angled downstream, the rope running from Ah Fai's bow at the east bank to Liang's bow at the west bank and then ten meters further downstream along the western bank, creating a V-shape when viewed from above: a boom that started at the eastern bank upstream, crossed to the western bank at an angle, and terminated downstream of the western margin.

The geometry directed any body entering the creek mouth from the west — the shallower approach — into the angled rope. The rope would deflect them diagonally toward the deep eastern trough, where the two-meter depth would take them off their feet and the ebb current would carry them east.

But the rope alone was not visible enough. Bodies moving through chest-deep water would feel a rope across their chest and try to push through it — the nylon might hold, but they would press against it with their full body weight and the weight of the current behind them, which would eventually overload a single line.

Jun pulled the bundle of cut bamboo sections that Ah Fai had brought — short lengths from the sorting pile, each one sixty centimeters, their hollow interiors intact. He threaded the rope through the hollow chambers of the bamboo sections at half-meter intervals, each section floating free on the rope but captured between two half-hitches that prevented it from sliding. The bamboo floated at the surface, the rope hanging below it — visible above the waterline as a line of floating green-grey cylinders, and below the waterline as a barrier that extended to the creek bed.

Not quite. The rope hung in a catenary — deepest at the center of the span. He needed weights to pull the center down to the creek bed.

"Anchor stones," Jun said.

Ah Fai had two more. Jun tied them to the rope at the boom's center and at the three-quarter point with short drops of cord — the stones descending to the creek bed, pulling the rope down in two points along its span, approximating a flat curtain across the channel rather than a hanging arc.

He looked at the boom. It was not perfect — there were gaps at the bottom where the stones' cords didn't span the irregular creek bed — but it was a barrier. Something with no sense of strategy, following the path of least resistance, would be deflected by it toward the deep trough.

"Secure your bow," Jun told Liang. "Anchor on the west bank."

Liang dropped his anchor stone.

The boom was in place.

From inside the mangroves, a sound louder than the creaking prop roots: a single sharp *CRACK*, then a sequence of smaller sounds — roots parting, a body pushing through the gap the fractured root had left.

The fringe was opening.

The first figure emerged from the mangrove wall at the western bank, exactly where Jun had predicted. It was dressed in grey airport service coveralls — the yellow reflective strips on the shoulders still visible, though the vest was torn and the material was dark with mangrove mud. It stepped from the prop roots into the shallow water of the western margin — ankle deep, then knee deep — and walked toward the creek mouth.

It hit the bamboo boom at chest height.

The floating bamboo sections resisted — the rope underneath tensed, the anchor stones on the creek bed holding the boom in position. The body pressed forward, its weight tilting the boom downstream, the bamboo rolling slightly under the pressure.

The diagonal angle of the boom deflected its direction. It turned, following the boom's surface, walking along the rope toward the east — toward the deep trough.

Its feet left the western shallow bottom. For a moment it stood in one-point-five meters of water, still upright, still moving.

Then the bottom dropped away at the eastern trough edge and it was in two meters.

The current took it east.

The second figure emerged from the mangroves five seconds later, to the left of the first — slightly further into the mangrove fringe, where the prop roots were tighter. It worked through more slowly, its airport vest catching on the aerial roots, tearing free. It entered the creek on a course three meters west of the first.

It hit the boom at shoulder height and followed the same deflection.

A third emerged. A fourth.

Each one reached the boom, followed its angle east, entered the deep trough, and was taken by the current.

"How many are in the fringe?" Jun asked Ah Fai.

Ah Fai was standing at his sampan's stern, the aluminum harpoon held loosely in one hand, watching the mangrove wall. "Can't say," he said. "The fringe is two hundred meters deep. Could be twenty, could be two hundred."

"The boom holds ten before the anchor loads exceed the stones' weight," Jun said. "If they stack up against it—"
