"I'll watch the stone lines," Ah Fai said, moving to the stern and looking down through the clear ebb-tide water at the two anchor cords. They were taut — the boom under load from three bodies pressing against it simultaneously. "Still holding."

"If a stone lifts, call it."

"I'll call it."

Jun looked at the mangrove fringe. More roots were moving now — the pressure behind the fringe was not diminishing. More bodies were working through the prop root maze, following whatever gap the first ones had opened, the forest yielding one fractured root at a time.

"We need a second boom line," Jun said. "Upstream, inside the creek, as a backup if the first fails." He looked at Liang. "How much rope remains?"

Liang measured the coil. "Twenty-five meters."

"Enough for a secondary. Shorter span, same geometry." Jun began tying the secondary anchor, working fast, running the line between the two sampans at a point five meters upstream of the first boom — a shorter diagonal crossing the same channel, backing up the first if the anchor stones dragged.

He was tying the second bamboo section onto the secondary line when Ah Fai said, quietly: "Stone is lifting."

Jun looked. The eastern anchor stone's cord was angling upstream — no longer vertical, the stone dragging across the creek bed as the accumulated pressure of six bodies against the boom overcame its weight.

"Cut the eastern stone," Jun said.

Ah Fai looked at him.

"The boom shifts downstream when you cut it," Jun said. "The downstream angle increases. Bodies following the deflection go further east — away from the secondary." He met Ah Fai's eyes. "Cut it."

Ah Fai crouched at the stern, reached down with the harpoon's edge — the aluminum shaft had a small stripping blade near the base, used for cleaning fish — and drew it across the stone's anchor cord. One clean motion.

The cord parted. The eastern anchor stone dropped to the bed and the boom swung downstream on the remaining stone and the two sampan moorings. The deflection angle increased — bodies at the boom surface now traveling southeast, the current trajectory more direct, the deep-water delivery cleaner.

The three bodies pressing against the boom at the moment of the cut moved with the boom's swing, their deflection accelerated. They reached the deep trough faster.

The secondary line was in place before the next body reached the primary boom.

Jun sat back on the sampan thwart.

The creek mouth was processing. Not perfectly — there were gaps in the lower portion of the boom where the creek bed was irregular — but the deep trough was working, the current was working, and the bodies were moving east rather than west.

"How long does this hold?" Liang asked.

Jun looked at the mangrove fringe. The creaking was still continuous. Bodies still working through. "The boom holds until the pressure exceeds the secondary anchor's weight. The current helps. As the tide ebbs further, the depth at the creek margin drops, the approach shallows further, and more bodies will enter the deep trough directly without needing the boom."

"So it gets better as the tide drops," Ah Fai said.

"Until the tide turns and starts coming in," Jun said. "Then the creek mouth deepens again and the bodies already in the deep trough float east on the flood. New bodies entering from the fringe will be in deeper water — harder to walk, more likely to be carried."

"So the tide works for us in both directions," Liang said.

"The tidal cycle works for us," Jun said. "As long as the boom holds through the transition."

He looked at the secondary line, then at the sky. The sun was up now — fully risen, the mangrove canopy lit from above, the prop roots throwing long shadows across the creek surface. The smell of polymer had not diminished, but it had not intensified either. The fringe was releasing bodies at a steady rate, not accelerating.

They had time.

But time was the catamaran fleet. Time was sixteen more pairs still unfinished, seven singles still uncaulked, forty-two more crossbeam notches to correct at Uncle Fong's wife's angle, and three hundred people who did not yet know the specific hour they would be asked to get into a boat.

"Ah Fai," Jun said. "Can you maintain this from the sampan? Alone, if needed?"

The young man looked at the boom, the anchor lines, the creek mouth, the fringe. He assessed it with the same unhurried attention he probably gave a crab trap in a new location — reading the current, the bottom, the structure.

"Yes," he said.

"If a stone lifts, swing the boom downstream and let it reset. If the secondary drags, call me on the radio." Jun looked at the field radio Granny Yau had sent with them. "I'll come back at tide turn."

He looked at Liang. Liang was already picking up the bamboo pole.

They left Ah Fai at the creek mouth — one young man with an aluminum harpoon, two anchor stones, sixty meters of rope, and a decade's worth of reading this particular piece of water — and poled back around the headland toward the village.

Behind them, the creek mouth worked in the morning light, the boom deflecting each emerging figure east, the current carrying them away, the mangrove fringe creaking steadily under the weight of everything still inside it.

Twelve catamaran pairs still to build.

***

---

CHAPTER 8: THE NIGHT FLEET


The last catamaran pair was lashed by late afternoon of the second day.

Jun set the final forward crossbeam into its notch — the steeper angle that Uncle Fong's wife had shown him, the click of it seating correctly now as familiar as a well-fitted mortise joint — and pulled the rattan wrap tight, crossing it three times over the gunwale in the Malay pattern, the lashing snugging under its own tension as he pulled the free end through the final loop.

He stepped back and looked at the fleet.

Sixteen catamaran platforms floated in the inner harbor in four rows, their paired green-and-blue hulls side by side, the bamboo crossbeam platforms above the waterline carrying the late-afternoon light at a slight angle. The seven unpaired sampans were moored in a separate line at the south quay. Granny Yau's four main boats — the two diesel trawlers and the two rigged sail boats — were anchored in the outer harbor beyond the headland, their hulls already provisioned, their fuel tanks full from the diesel store in the equipment shed.

Three hundred and four people. That was the final fleet capacity, loaded carefully with weight distributed across the crossbeam platforms, the heavier adults at the hull centerlines, children toward the middle.

There were two hundred and ninety-seven people in Tai O.

Three would not go. Jun had learned this the previous evening, from Granny Yau, without surprise on either side.

Two were elderly men who had lived in their stilt houses since the 1940s and had decided, with the same calm precision with which they decided everything, that they would not leave the water they had worked for eighty years. The third was a woman of sixty who had made the same decision on different grounds — she could not leave because she was already sick in a way that a boat journey would not help, and she preferred the familiar smell of her own house to any alternative.

Granny Yau had visited each of them. She had not argued.

Jun had left supplies at each house: five days of rice and dried fish, two fresh-water containers, a field radio set to the emergency frequency.

That was all that could be done.

The fleet capacity now exceeded the departing population by seven, which meant each catamaran platform could carry one fewer person than its rated maximum — a margin that Jun considered essential for open-water conditions and was glad to have.

"The route," Jun said to Granny Yau. They were standing at the outer harbor headland, looking south-southwest across the open bay. The sun was dropping toward the west — an hour above the horizon — the water going from blue to hammered pewter in the changing light.

"Po Toi," she said, pointing south. "Twenty-two kilometers. My family has fished those waters since my great-grandmother. The main island has a natural harbor on the north face — protected from the northeast swell, fresh water from a hillside spring, no land connection to the mainland." She paused. "And there are people there. I spoke with them this morning on the radio."

"How many?"

"Eighty. Fishermen from Aberdeen who got there before the Aberdeen harbor closed. They have two large trawlers and food stores for a month. They said to come."

Jun looked at the bearing. South-southwest. The summer wind was from the southwest — slightly against them, which would slow the catamarans but would not stop them. The diesel trawlers would be unaffected. The sail boats would need to tack.

"The catamarans in open swell," he said. "The South China Sea summer chop — what's the typical wave height at night?"

"Half a meter to a meter, on a calm night. Up to two meters if the wind picks up." She looked at the western sky. "Tonight looks calm. The pressure is steady, the cloud base is high. I'd say half a meter."

"The catamaran beam is wide enough for half a meter without trouble," Jun said. "The forward crossbeam double-lashing handles the pitch. The concern is if the paired hulls diverge under heavy bow swell — the rattan at the bow thwart takes the full spread load."

"Your notch angle handles that," she said.

"If the lashing holds."

"Then make sure it holds," she said, with the same toneless practicality with which she discussed all things. It was not dismissive. It was simply accurate.

Jun had already reinforced the forward lashings on every catamaran platform that afternoon — adding a fourth wrap to each bow crossbeam after Uncle Fong's wife had confirmed the notch angles were correct. He had tested each one by standing on the forward crossbeam alone, his full weight on the center, while Liang pushed lateral force against the bow of one hull with the bamboo pole. Not one had shifted.

"We go at midnight," Granny Yau said. "High water is at eleven-fifteen. By midnight, the ebb is running — the outgoing tide gives us two extra knots of speed south through the channel. It's also dark, which means the approach to Po Toi is less visible from the shore."

"The order of departure," Jun said.

"Diesel trawlers lead. They have the radar and the radio. They set the course and maintain the lead light." She looked at the fleet. "Catamaran platforms in sequence, one every two minutes — the harbor mouth is wide enough for one catamaran at a time without crowding. The single sampans follow, led by Kin. I take the rearmost sail boat with the last group."

"Liang and I take the last catamaran out," Jun said.

She looked at him. "The last catamaran carries the boom ropes from the creek and the remaining supplies from the equipment shed. It will be heavy."

"Then it needs a careful handler," Jun said.

She did not argue.

"The creek mouth," Jun said. "Ah Fai is still there."

"I spoke to him on the radio at midday. The boom is holding. The fringe is still breaching — slowly. He says the count today is approximately forty through the creek mouth, all deflected east." She paused. "He'll stay until the last boat passes the north headland. Then he'll pole to the harbor mouth and join the fleet."

Jun thought about Ah Fai at the creek mouth — one young man in a sampan, alone, in the dark, watching the mangrove fringe creak and yield in the night. Doing the arithmetic that needed doing so three hundred people could sleep a few hours before the departure.

"The loading starts at ten," Jun said. "Two hours to settle the weight."

"I've assigned the platforms," Granny Yau said. She produced a second hand-drawn map — this one showing each catamaran and single sampan labeled with family names and their allocated positions on the platform. The handwriting was small and even and covered both sides of the paper. She had made it last night.

Jun looked at the map. Every family was there — the Fongs, the Yaus, the Kims, the Chens, the boat-builders and the fishwives and the net-menders and the teenagers and the children. The old man who had refused to go was on the map too, crossed through with a single line, his slot redistributed to the family beside him.

Granny Yau had thought through all of it while Jun was counting crossbeam wraps and running notch-angle calculations.

"Ten o'clock," he said.

"Ten o'clock," she confirmed.

She folded the map and walked back toward the village.

The loading took two hours and twenty minutes — longer than planned, because three catamaran platforms required last-minute weight redistribution when the initial loading placed too many adults at one end and the platform listed forward enough to concern Jun, who measured the list with a small spirit level and moved four passengers aft until the bubble centered.

The children, once settled on the crossbeam platforms, were largely quiet — the older ones recognizing that something serious was happening and moderating themselves accordingly, the very young ones asleep on their parents' laps. The harbor was lit by a dozen paper lanterns hung from the catwalk rails — not bright enough to be visible from shore, but sufficient to work by. The light on the water was soft and orange and the stilt houses above reflected it, the faded blues and yellows of the painted siding warm in the lantern glow.

Jun moved from platform to platform during the loading, checking each forward crossbeam, each rattan lashing, each bow cleat and mooring line. He did not hurry the checks and he did not skip any. On the eleventh platform he found a rattan wrap that had worked slightly loose — the rattan had dried since the afternoon and shrunk half a millimeter, the wrap slack enough to turn under lateral load. He re-tightened it with three additional wraps and moved on.

At quarter past midnight, Granny Yau's elder diesel trawler — a forty-foot vessel named *Hung Hing*, the name painted in red characters on the bow — moved out of the outer harbor and took up position at the harbor mouth, its running lights on, its engine at idle. The second diesel trawler followed thirty seconds later, taking a position two boat-lengths behind.

The lead boat's stern light was a green lantern — the departure marker. Every catamaran and sampan in the fleet would follow the green light south.

"First platform," Granny Yau called from the quay.

The first catamaran — twelve people on a crossbeam platform, two children asleep, four adults gripping the gunwales — was untied from its mooring and pushed off by three dock hands. The paired hulls moved slowly into the harbor channel, the bamboo crossbeams flexing slightly as the hulls found the small chop of the harbor entrance, then steadying as the open water smoothed the motion.

It cleared the harbor mouth and turned south, following the green light.

Two minutes. Second platform.

Third. Fourth.

Jun stood at the inner quay and watched them go, each platform moving with a deliberate, flat-bottomed confidence that the individual sampans could not have managed. The doubled hulls cut the small harbor chop cleanly, the crossbeam platforms above the waterline dry and level. He had not been entirely certain, until this moment, that the design would work in motion. The structural calculations had been sound. The load tests had been sound. But there was always the thing that only the water itself could reveal.

The water revealed that the design was sound.

He watched the eighth platform pass the harbor mouth and felt something loosen in his chest that had been tight for two days.

The singles went next — Yau Kin leading in his channel-clearing sampan, the remaining six following in a loose cluster, their bamboo poles raised vertically as they transitioned to open water and shipped the poles for the outboard paddles that each sampan carried for offshore work.

The sail boats went last of the main fleet — their rigs up, the southwest wind light enough that they were moving slowly, their navigation lights steady.

Jun's catamaran was the final vessel in the harbor.

He had loaded it himself: the boom rope coiled in the stern, the remaining tool bag, the field radio from the creek mouth, two caulking rolls, the last of the fish tar, a bundle of cut bamboo sections, the mallet, the cold chisel, the bolt wrench. Enough for wherever they went next.

Liang was at the stern thwart with the paddle. Jun stood at the bow, looking at the stilt village.

The lanterns still burned on the catwalk rails — they would burn until the oil ran out, which would be morning. In the orange light, the stilt houses sat in their familiar configurations: the fish store, the sail-repair shed, the market building, the rows of two-story plank houses on their ironwood piles above the channel, their windows dark now, the laundry lines still strung with drying hairtail and silver-belly in shapes like punctuation. The rope ferry cable lay slack in the channel — the platform already tied off at the west bank, the cable hanging in a deep loop above the water.

The bridge arch was visible at the east channel end — the net still in place, the railing post lattice still in position. A few yellow hardhats were visible on the quay beyond it, moving in their slow circuits, unaware that the thing they had been pressing toward for two days was now empty.

Jun untied the bow line.

The catamaran moved into the channel — slowly, heavily, the full tool load in the stern pulling the bow up slightly. Jun shifted his weight aft, distributing it across the crossbeam, the bow settling.

From his radio came Ah Fai's voice — flat and unhurried, carried on the VHF channel Granny Yau had set.

*"Last platform is leaving the harbor. I'm pulling the boom now."*

"Copy," Jun said into the radio. "Come to the harbor mouth. We'll wait."

*"Two minutes."*

Jun held the catamaran at the harbor mouth, the tidal ebb pushing them gently south, Liang counter-paddling to hold position. The night was warm and moonless, the stars very bright, the South China Sea a dark plain beyond the bay with the faint scattered lights of the fleet visible on it — the green stern light of the *Hung Hing* leading them south, the catamaran platforms behind it as small, dark shapes on the water.

Ah Fai came around the north headland in his small sampan three minutes later, paddling fast, the aluminum harpoon balanced across the bow thwart, the coiled secondary boom rope in the stern.

He pulled alongside the catamaran without a word, shipped his paddle, and looked at Jun.

"The fringe is still going," he said. "Maybe sixty through the creek today total. The boom is down but the trough will keep working — the eastern channel is deep enough that anything coming through will be carried out to sea on the ebb." He paused. "It doesn't need me anymore."

"No," Jun agreed.

Ah Fai looked at the village — at the lantern light on the water, the stilt houses, the rope ferry cable in its long arc above the channel.

Then he picked up his paddle and fell in beside the catamaran.

They pushed south together, out of the bay, into the open water where the fleet lights moved ahead of them in the warm summer night.

Behind them, the green lanterns on the Tai O catwalks burned down one by one as the oil ran out, the last of them fading somewhere around three in the morning — a small, warm light going dark over the stilt houses and the empty harbor and the channel where the ironwood poles stood in their rows in the water, their coal-tar surfaces gleaming in the starlight, the fish-oil coating above the tide line still wet.

The village was still.

The water held it, as it had always held it.

Twenty-two kilometers south, the fleet found the Po Toi harbor in the grey light before dawn — the natural anchorage opening around the headland exactly where Granny Yau had said it would be, the Aberdeen trawlers already lit and waiting, the harbor smell of salt rock and fresh water coming down from the hillside spring.

Granny Yau's *Hung Hing* led them in.

***

---

CHAPTER 9: THE ROCK HARBOR


Po Toi Island rose from the South China Sea like a fist of granite.

The rock face was dark and rough-grained, its southern and eastern cliffs dropping sheer to the swell, the stone worn smooth at waterline by a thousand typhoon seasons and cut above that into angular columns and ledges that caught the morning light in hard geometric shadows. The summit — a hundred and eight meters, by the chart Granny Yau kept rolled under the *Hung Hing's* wheel console — was a bare granite plateau furred with grass and wild pepper, a rusted weather station mast on its highest point. No trees. No soil of consequence. No level ground except the small crescent of the north harbor.

The harbor opened on the north face, sheltered from the northeast swell by a natural rock arm that curved west from the main cliff face — a granite ridge, twenty meters high, that had been catching storm water for a hundred thousand years and did not care about any particular morning's swell. The Aberdeen trawlers were moored against it: two large steel-hulled vessels, their nets in the water on long leads, their cabins lit, their crews watching the Tai O fleet come in from the northwest.

Captain Yip was on the stone jetty when the *Hung Hing* tied off.

He was about sixty, compact and weathered, wearing a plastic-coated orange rain jacket over canvas trousers despite the clear morning. He had the particular stillness of someone who had spent forty years on a working trawler — not restless, not relaxed, but in a state of permanent readiness that had become indistinguishable from calm. He looked at the *Hung Hing*, then at the catamaran fleet coming around the headland in sequence behind it, and then at Granny Yau.

"More than I expected," he said.

"Two hundred and ninety-four," Granny Yau said. "Plus my crew. The carpenter and his man are last in."

Yip looked at the catamaran platforms. He studied the crossbeam lashing, the paired hull geometry, the loaded weight distribution. He said nothing for a moment.

"Bamboo and sampans," he said eventually. Not a question.

"The carpenter's design," Granny Yau said.

Yip looked at the platforms for a moment longer, then back at Granny Yau. "They held."

"They held."

He nodded once — the minimal acknowledgment of a man who had not expected a bad answer and was unsurprised to receive a good one — and turned to direct his crew to help with the mooring.

Jun came ashore from the last catamaran with his tool bag and stood on the stone jetty looking at the island. Liang tied the bow line to a granite mooring ring that had been set into the jetty stone so long ago the iron was buried in lichen. Ah Fai moored his sampan alongside.

The harbor, Jun could see immediately, had a problem.

The natural rock arm on the northeast sheltered the harbor from the dominant swell direction — northeast and east, the direction of the monsoon and the typhoon track. But the western approach was open. The harbor mouth faced northwest, and the northwest was exposed to the South China Sea fetch: open water for two hundred kilometers before the next significant island mass. In a southwest summer typhoon — the track that brought the most severe storms to Hong Kong waters — the swell would enter the harbor mouth from the northwest, unobstructed.

The Aberdeen trawlers could manage it. Their steel hulls and heavy mooring lines would hold in two-meter harbor swell. The *Hung Hing* could manage it.

The catamaran platforms could not. Bamboo crossbeams in two-meter harbor swell would work loose from the gunwale notches within an hour of sustained wave action, the rattan wraps fatiguing and parting. The paired hulls would separate. Twelve people on a separating catamaran platform in a storm harbor were in serious difficulty.

Jun looked at the sixteen catamaran platforms mooring in sequence along the jetty and the inner harbor wall, their crossbeams level and steady in the current morning calm.

"Captain Yip," Jun said, approaching the trawler man. "Your radio — do you have the Hong Kong Observatory frequency?"

Yip looked at him. "Yes. Who are you?"

"Jun. The carpenter. The Observatory frequency."

Yip reached into his jacket pocket and produced a handheld VHF radio. He extended the antenna and pressed the channel selector to 92 — the Observatory weather broadcast frequency.

Static. Then, clearly:

*"...tropical storm Cora has intensified to a severe tropical storm at oh-six-hundred. Current position three hundred and eighty kilometers south-southeast of Hong Kong. Forecast track northwest. The Hong Kong Observatory is issuing Typhoon Signal Number Three. Winds of thirty-five to fifty kilometers per hour are expected in Hong Kong waters..."*

Yip lowered the radio.

"Signal Three now," Jun said. "Track northwest, three hundred and eighty kilometers south. At the standard storm track speed—"

"Thirty-six hours to Signal Eight," Yip said. "Maybe less if she accelerates." He looked at the harbor mouth. "I've been watching the barometer since midnight. It's been dropping."

"The catamaran platforms," Jun said.

"I saw them," Yip said. "They won't survive Signal Eight swell in this harbor."

"No," Jun agreed. "We need a breakwater across the harbor mouth. Something that attenuates the northwest swell before it reaches the mooring area."

Yip looked at the harbor mouth — approximately thirty meters wide between the jetty end and the outer rock arm's tip. He looked at the catamaran fleet.

"You're going to lash the catamarans together across the mouth," he said.

Jun had not said that yet. He looked at Yip.

"I ran a trawler into a floating breakwater off Sai Kung during Typhoon Ellen in 1983," Yip said. "Pontoon sections chained together. They work." He paused. "Not perfectly. But they work."

"The catamaran platforms are already paired hulls," Jun said. "Each pair is structurally similar to a double pontoon. Sixteen pairs across thirty meters — I'll need to overlap them slightly, chain them together at the bow and stern of each pair, anchor the chain to the rock arm and the jetty with heavy mooring line." He was already calculating the spacing. "The wave attenuation won't be complete — some swell will pass under the hulls. But the platforms will reduce the wave height by fifty to sixty percent and break the period of the swell."

"Breaking the period matters more than the height," Yip said.

"Yes," Jun said. "Synchronized harbor swell is what breaks mooring lines. Disrupted period reduces the resonance."

Yip looked at him for a moment with the same measuring expression Captain Chen had used at the Kaiping towers — the assessment of someone accustomed to making rapid decisions about the competence of unfamiliar people.

"My crew knows how to chain pontoons," Yip said. "We used to set the fish farm cages in Sai Kung."

"Then show me the chain," Jun said.

The Aberdeen trawlers carried substantial ground tackle — heavy galvanized chain, shackles, anchor swivels, mooring clamps. Yip's crew produced two coils of thirty-meter chain from the trawler's anchor locker and a canvas sack of heavy shackles, each one sized for chain links the diameter of Jun's thumb.

Jun and Yip stood at the jetty end and planned the chain run together.

The breakwater line would run from a mooring ring set into the rock arm at the harbor mouth's northern end, east across the thirty-meter gap to the jetty's outermost bollard. The sixteen catamaran platforms would be positioned in a staggered line along this chain — their bow lines tied to the chain at two-meter intervals, their stern lines tied to a parallel chain running three meters seaward of the first. This double-chain arrangement would prevent the platforms from pivoting on a single axis under swell — each platform constrained fore and aft, the paired hulls aligned with the swell direction rather than broadside to it.

"The anchor points," Jun said. "The mooring ring on the rock arm — how old is it?"

"Pre-war," Yip said. "Iron. I've used it before. The ring itself I'd trust. The mortar around the shaft I wouldn't."

"We back it up," Jun said. "A second anchor, set further up the rock arm, running a secondary line to the chain's northern end. If the primary ring gives, the secondary carries the load."

"There's a natural crack in the rock arm about three meters up," Yip said. "Wide enough to set an anchor wedge."

"Show me."

They walked to the rock arm — a rough granite ridge rising from the harbor water, its surface covered in barnacles and dry rock lichen above the spray line. The crack Yip had indicated was a natural fracture in the granite, approximately forty millimeters wide and running horizontally for two meters at knee height — a classic stress fracture in the granite formation, the rock face above it overhanging slightly.

Jun looked at the crack. He reached into his bag and took out the two remaining ring-pitons from the Kaiping work — the steel rings with tapered iron shanks. They were sized for mortar joints, not granite fractures. But granite was harder and more grippy than mortar.

He drove the first piton into the fracture with four blows of his mallet — the taper expanding in the crack, the granite gripping the iron shank with a friction hold that would have been insufficient in mortar but was very close to adequate in solid rock.

He drove the second piton three centimeters further along the fracture, at the opposing angle — the X-anchor configuration, same as the Kaiping parapet work.

He clipped a heavy shackle through both rings, locked the shackle pin, and tested the combined anchor by putting his full weight on it plus a hard pull outward.

The pitons did not move.

"Good granite," he said.

"Lantau granite is harder," Yip said. "Po Toi granite is softer. Don't load it more than a thousand kilograms."

"The chain load per anchor point, distributed across sixteen platforms, is approximately three hundred kilograms at Signal Eight swell." Jun ran the numbers in his head. "We're inside the margin."

"Just inside."

"Just inside is inside," Jun said.

Yip made a sound that was not quite a laugh. He called his crew.

The chain-setting took four hours.

Two of Yip's trawler crew went into the water in wetsuits — the harbor clear enough to work in, the current manageable — running the chain along the harbor bottom and attaching the anchor shackles to the mooring points. Jun worked from the jetty end, feeding chain, directing the catamaran platforms into position along the chain run as each link was set.

The catamaran platforms were moved from their harbor moorings one at a time and positioned across the mouth — their bow lines tied to the forward chain with bowlines, their stern lines to the after chain with the same. The platforms were spaced to overlap slightly, each paired-hull set angled three degrees to the perpendicular of the swell direction, creating a staggered zigzag line across the harbor mouth rather than a straight wall.

Jun had learned this from the Sai Kung fishfarm setup that Yip described: a straight breakwater reflects swell at its original amplitude; a staggered breakwater scatters swell in multiple directions, the reflected components canceling each other. The net wave energy reaching the harbor interior was lower from a staggered arrangement than from a rigid wall.

By midafternoon, the last catamaran platform was in position. The breakwater line stretched across the harbor mouth — sixteen double-hull platforms in their staggered arrangement, the chain visible beneath the surface as a dark line between the anchor points, the platforms floating level and stable in the afternoon swell.

Jun stood on the rock arm and looked at the line.

From inside the harbor, the catamaran platforms appeared as a low, continuous structure across the mouth — their crossbeam platforms just above waterline, the paired hulls below. The northwest swell was already running at forty centimeters — the leading edge of Cora's circulation, several hundred kilometers distant. As each wave reached the breakwater line, it struck the outer hull faces of the platforms, its energy partially absorbed by the paired-hull geometry, partially reflected in scattered directions, and partially transmitted through the gaps between platforms as a reduced, disrupted wave.

The harbor interior, behind the line, was noticeably calmer.

Not flat — the transmitted swell still produced a light chop. But the rhythmic synchronized surge that would have driven harbor resonance was gone, the wave period broken into irregular components that did not reinforce each other.

"It works," Liang said from beside him.

"So far," Jun said. "The test is Signal Eight."

"You said we're inside the margin."

"I said just inside." Jun looked at the rock arm anchor. The pitons had not moved. The chain was taut and even, the platforms riding their individual motions without transmitting those motions along the chain as a synchronized load. "When the swell reaches two meters, each platform will be working independently — rising and falling on its own wave cycle. The chain will absorb the differential loads between adjacent platforms."

"Will the rattan hold on the crossbeams?" Liang asked.

"In two-meter swell, the crossbeam notches are taking pitch loads rather than spread loads," Jun said. "The notch angle — the steep angle — handles pitch. That's why the angle matters. The lashing wrap handles spread. In a seaway, they're working together rather than separately." He paused. "Uncle Fong's wife's correction. If she hadn't shown me the angle, the bow crossbeam would have ridden up under pitch and the lashing would have failed."

Liang was quiet for a moment.

"We should tell her that," he said.

"She knows," Jun said.

Captain Yip appeared at the rock arm base, climbing the slope with the careful footing of someone who knew granite. He stood beside Jun and looked at the breakwater line.

"Signal Five is forecast," he said. "Not Eight."

"The track shifted?"

"Slightly east. It'll still hit. But Signal Five is survivable in this harbor with that line." He looked at the platforms. "Without the line, Signal Five would have given us problems."

"Without the line, it would have been Signal Eight equivalent inside the harbor," Jun said. "The northwest aspect—"

"I know," Yip said. "I know this harbor." He looked at the line for another moment. "You set it correctly. The stagger angle is right."

Coming from Yip, Jun understood, this was the equivalent of an extended commendation.

"Where did you learn the stagger?" Yip asked.

"You told me," Jun said. "You described the Sai Kung fishfarm setup."

Yip looked at him. "I told you about pontoons. I didn't say anything about stagger angle."

"You said the Ellen typhoon. 1983. I looked at how the wave was moving at the harbor mouth and the stagger was the next conclusion." Jun shrugged. "Physics doesn't change between fishfarms."

Yip was quiet for a moment. Then: "You're not a fisherman."

"No."

"What are you?"

"A carpenter," Jun said.

Yip considered this. "We need a carpenter here," he said. "The settlement houses on the north slope are half-collapsed. Stone walls, timber roof trusses — all rotted from the salt air. Nobody's lived in them in thirty years. We have three hundred and seventy-seven people who need roofs by tonight."

Jun looked toward the north slope. Above the harbor, on the hillside, a cluster of single-story stone buildings was visible — fishermen's cottages and a small temple, their roof lines irregular, some collapsed inward, some still standing with their original grey tile.

Granite walls. Timber trusses. Materials on site.

"Tell me the worst one first," Jun said. "The one with the most structural load still carrying."

Yip pointed.

Jun picked up his bag.

***

---

CHAPTER 10: SIGNAL FIVE


The worst house was the furthest one.

Captain Yip led him past four stone cottages in varying states of degradation — walls intact but roof tiles missing, walls cracked but load-bearing columns still plumb, walls leaning slightly inward from frost-heave and salt erosion — to the last structure in the row: a single-story building at the top of the slope, its south wall partially standing, its north wall collapsed entirely into a rubble pile from which three granite course-stones the size of bread loaves projected upward like teeth. The roof was gone — not collapsed, simply gone, the timber trusses having rotted completely and slid off the wall plates decades ago, the tiles with them. A thicket of wild grass and creeping fern had grown up inside the roofless shell, filling the interior to knee height.

Jun walked the perimeter of the south wall — the remaining wall — running his hand along the stone face, feeling for the slight warmth of sound masonry versus the cold looseness of compromised mortar joints. The granite courses were hand-cut, each block fitted to its neighbor with thin lime-mortar joints, the overall construction dry enough and compressed enough that the blocks had in most places locked themselves together by weight and friction rather than relying on the mortar. Most of the mortar was gone — washed out by salt air and condensation — but the blocks remained in their courses, held by geometry.

Two meters of wall: sound. He measured the plumb with the spirit level from his bag — two millimeters out of vertical, tolerable. He pressed the corner block at the southwest angle with his palm, feeling for movement.

No movement.

"The south wall carries," Jun said.

"The north wall—" Yip began.

"I saw the north wall," Jun said. "It's rubble. We use what's here." He turned and looked at the collapsed rubble pile. "How far from here to the catamaran bamboo? The surplus poles from the sorting."

"Fifty meters," Yip said. "We left them on the jetty."

"I need twenty poles, eight-centimeter culm, three meters minimum." Jun looked at the south wall's top course, where the wall plate had once sat. "And whatever timber is in the other cottages. Anything that was under cover long enough to stay dry."

"The temple," Yip said. "It's the only building that's kept a roof. The interior has two stacks of salvaged timber from the other cottages — previous occupants left it there."

"Show me."

The temple was a modest structure at the row's center — small, single-room, its exterior walls sound and its roof intact under a heavy stone tile course that had outlasted everything around it by virtue of sheer mass. Inside, stacked against the altar wall: two bundles of timber sections, cut and rough-sorted, some still carrying tenon mortises from their previous lives as roof trusses. Pine and fir, the wood dry and resinous, its grain tight from the slow growth of high-altitude timber.

Jun picked up the longest piece and looked down its length from one end — checking the straightness with the same instinctive eye he had used since his first year of apprenticeship.

Straight. Two meters and forty centimeters. Sound mortise on one end, the tenon cut from the opposing section still wedged in the socket.

He looked at the stack.

"We have enough," he said.

He did not explain the calculation. He went back to the worst house and started work.

The bamboo poles arrived twenty minutes later, carried by four of Yip's crew and three Tai O teenagers who had followed them from the harbor. Jun had them stand the poles vertically at the south wall — propping them at the wall plate level, their bases on the rubble of the north wall to find their footing, the bamboo tops resting against the inside face of the south wall's upper course. Temporary rafter props: not the final structure, but enough to define the roof geometry.

He set the ridge line from two bamboo sections lashed in a T — the vertical post rising from the center of the south wall, the horizontal ridge piece extending north across the open air to where the north wall had been. No north wall to support the ridge's far end. The ridge needed a prop from below.

He cut a king post from the pine stack — a section two meters long, its lower end with a flat saw-cut that he notched with a chisel to seat on a flat granite block from the rubble pile, and its upper end with a saddle-notch that received the ridge bamboo. He drove it vertical and pressed the ridge into the saddle.

The ridge sat at the correct height — one-point-eight meters above the former floor level — and was stable between the south wall's bamboo prop and the king post's base.

Rafters next. He cut eight pine sections from the stack, angling each end with two saw cuts to create a birdsmouth joint — the traditional cut that allowed a rafter to sit flush on a wall plate on one end and meet the ridge cleanly on the other. The birdsmouth geometry was not precisely calculated; he estimated it against the ridge height and the span and cut slightly proud, testing each rafter in position and trimming as needed.

Four rafters on each side. The roof pitch was thirty-five degrees — steep enough to shed the typhoon rain, shallow enough not to generate excessive wind uplift.

"Bamboo purlins," Jun said, pointing to the remaining poles. "One every sixty centimeters, lashed to the rafters. Run them the full length of the roof from south wall to the north overhang."

The teenagers began lashing without needing further instruction — they had been lashing bamboo to timber for two days, and the Malay wrap pattern was by now as automatic as tying a bowline.

Jun moved to the next cottage.

The system became clear to the Tai O teenagers within the first house: assess the remaining walls, set the ridge, establish the rafters, run the purlins, lash. Each cottage varied in what it had and what it lacked — two had partial timber trusses that Jun could supplement rather than replace, three had walls in worse condition that needed temporary bamboo props inside before they could carry a roof load, one had a complete east-west ridge beam still in place, suspended in the air without rafters like a memory of the building it had been.

Jun worked from house to house, never staying at any one building longer than the time needed to set the primary structure. He left each cottage's completion to whoever had followed him there — the teenagers, Yip's crew, Tai O fishwives who had spent forty years doing structural maintenance on stilt houses and recognized a roof geometry when they saw one.

By late afternoon, six of the eight cottages had working roofs. Not permanent roofs — bamboo-purlin structures would need to be replaced with proper timber in the coming weeks, and the missing north walls would need rebuilding once materials and time permitted. But roofs: surfaces that would shed rain, reduce wind, define interior space, make a place habitable for tonight.

The typhoon would come tonight.

Jun heard the signal upgrade on Yip's radio at four in the afternoon, standing on the hillside looking at the harbor below: *Signal Five is in effect for Hong Kong waters. Severe Tropical Storm Cora continues on a northwesterly track. Maximum sustained winds of seventy to ninety kilometers per hour are expected...*

Signal Five. Not Eight. Yip had been right about the track shift.

But seventy to ninety kilometers per hour was enough to lift a roof that wasn't properly weighted.

"Stones," Jun said to the teenagers beside him. "Every roof that's finished. Load the ridgeline and the purlins with the granite from the rubble piles. Flat stones, stacked two courses. Don't block the rain drainage but weight the structure."

They went. He went back to the seventh cottage.

The storm arrived at midnight, not with a single onset but in bands — squall lines rotating around the eye, each one bringing forty minutes of driving rain and gusting wind followed by a brief, deceptive lull before the next band hit. The rain was not Hong Kong rain — it was South China Sea typhoon rain, horizontal sheets of it driven by the wind into every gap and joint and opening, finding weaknesses in minutes that dry-weather inspection would miss in days.

Jun was in the temple during the first band, listening to the roof above him — the old stone tiles carrying the rain sound as a continuous drumming hiss, the timber rafters below them creaking slightly at each gust peak.

He listened to the creak. It was the creak of a structure working as it was meant to — not the sharp report of a joint failing or the sustained groan of an overloaded member, but the ordinary elastic response of dry timber to wind load. The building was old and sound in its bones, and it was doing what old sound buildings do in weather: moving slightly, absorbing the load, recovering.

He fell asleep against the altar wall sometime in the second lull, his tool bag under his head.

When he woke, it was still dark but the rain had stopped and the wind had dropped from its sustained roar to an intermittent buffeting — the typhoon past its closest point, tracking northwest and away. He went oucoarse haire and stood in the wet grass and listened to the harbor.

Quiet. Not the quiet of calm — the quiet of a storm that had finished and left a different kind of air behind it, cool and salt-scrubbed and very clear.

He went down the hill to the harbor.

The breakwater line was intact.

Not undamaged — one of the catamaran platforms had rotated ninety degrees on its bow line, twisting the stern chain into a diagonal, and two of the bamboo crossbeam sections on the outermost platform showed stress cracks where a wave crest had caught them broadside during a particularly heavy band. The X-anchor on the rock arm had held — both pitons still driven to their rings in the granite fracture, the chain taut and true. The jetty bollard had not moved.

The harbor interior was rough with residual chop — the swell still propagating into the protected water from the disturbance oucoarse haire — but the harbor's mooring area, sheltered by the breakwater line and the natural rock arm together, had sustained no more than a meter-five swell at peak. The *Hung Hing* was at her mooring, engine off, hull unmarked. The Aberdeen trawlers the same.

Jun looked at the twisted platform. He waded into the shallows and corrected the rotation by hand — pushing the stern back to its proper alignment on the after chain, resetting the bow line angle, tying off. The stress-cracked crossbeam sections he examined carefully: the cracks were in the outer bamboo wall only, not through to the hollow interior. They had not failed. They had absorbed the impact load and distributed it into the crack rather than shattering. Controlled damage: the right kind.

He left them in place.

Captain Yip appeared at the jetty as the dawn light reached the harbor.

He looked at the breakwater line, then at Jun. He had the expression of someone who had spent a night listening to storm sounds through a steel hull and calculating probabilities and was now comparing his calculations against the observable result.

"Four hours of Signal Five swell," Yip said. "Peak wave period nine seconds."

"I know," Jun said. "I heard it."

"The line held."

"The line held."

Yip looked at the twisted platform and the cracked crossbeams for a moment. "You'll want to repair those."

"Not yet," Jun said. "I want to know what they tell me first."

Yip looked at him.

"A structure that fails completely tells you one thing," Jun said. "A structure that partially fails tells you more. The outer-wall stress crack means the swell was loading the crossbeam from the side rather than end-on — which means the platform's alignment shifted during the storm. Which means the stern chain angle was slightly wrong." He looked at the twisted platform. "I set it three degrees off from the swell direction. It should have been five."

"For next time," Yip said.

"For next time," Jun agreed.

Yip stood at the jetty end and looked at the harbor — the breakwater line, the moored boats, the calm interior behind the platforms' staggered geometry. He looked at the south slope of the island where the settlement houses were, their bamboo-purlin roofs still in place, the stone tile weighting visible as a dark band along each ridgeline.

"The cottages held," he said.

"The cottages are a thousand years old," Jun said. "I just put the roof back."

"You put the roof back in a day," Yip said. "With teenagers and bamboo."

"The walls were already there." Jun looked at the hillside. "The materials were already there. My job is usually to not waste what's already there."

Yip was quiet for a long moment. He looked at the harbor, then at the sea beyond the breakwater, then at Jun.

"We need a permanent breakwater," he said. "Concrete if we can find the materials, stone if we can't. The catamaran line is good for a season — maybe two seasons if you maintain it. But this harbor can't hold three hundred and seventy-seven people long-term without a proper structure at the mouth."

"I know," Jun said. "I've been looking at the rock arm."

"And?"

"The rock arm is the breakwater. It's already half-built." Jun looked at the granite ridge curving westward into the harbor mouth. "It needs to be extended thirty meters. Dry-stone masonry, laid in courses, with a cap of concrete if we can reach Lamma Island for materials." He looked south along the coast. "Lamma has a quarry on the north end. Or did."

Yip followed his gaze south. "Lamma is forty kilometers. In a trawler, eight hours round trip."

"I know," Jun said.

"The quarry may have—" Yip stopped.

"It may," Jun said. "Or it may be clear. The island has no land connection to the mainland. The only access is by boat."

Yip looked at him for a long moment. "You want to go and see."

"I want to go and see," Jun said.

Yip turned and looked at his two trawlers.

"Tomorrow," he said. "After we check the hulls."

Jun nodded. He looked at the harbor one more time — the floating breakwater still performing its quiet work, the morning light coming across the staggered catamaran platforms in long angles, the paired hulls casting double shadows on the harbor floor.

He thought about Tai O. He thought about the stilt houses standing in their channel in the morning light they would be receiving right now — the same morning light at a different angle, the ironwood poles dark in the water, the coal-tar and fish-oil surfaces gleaming, the net still in place on the stone arch bridge, the quay empty. He thought about the three people who had stayed. He thought about the lanterns that had burned until the oil ran out, and the village's three-hundred-year habit of building on the water's edge, and the way Granny Yau had turned away from the catwalk poles when Jun began cutting them.

He thought about the ferry cable in its long arc above the channel. *The cable can be re-rigged.*

He picked up his bag.

Behind him, three hundred and seventy-four people were beginning to wake in the cottages on the slope — the children first, then the women, then the fishermen — their voices carrying down the hill in the cool, washed air, the ordinary sounds of a morning beginning in a place they had not yet learned to call home but were already beginning to.

Liang was waiting at the harbor edge, carrying two bowls of rice from the Tai O stores that Yan had cooked on the temple fire.

He handed one to Jun without a word.

Jun took it. They stood at the harbor edge and ate, looking out over the breakwater line at the South China Sea — flat now after the storm, the horizon clean and hard and very far away.

"The quarry," Liang said eventually.

"Tomorrow," Jun said.

"Forty kilometers."

"Yes."

Liang ate for a moment. "Is there anything at Lamma we'd need besides the stone?"

Jun thought about what a permanent harbor breakwater on a granite island required: cut stone in courses, a hydraulic mortar that would set in salt water, iron tie-rods to key the courses at intervals, a proper foundation trench along the rock arm's extension line. He thought about the quarry and what a working quarry would have had in its equipment shed. He thought about what the quarry might still have, if the island was clear.

"Iron rods," he said. "And lime. If the lime store was under cover."

Liang nodded slowly.

"And a boat hook," Jun said. "I lent Kin mine and he took it to Po Toi in the channel-clearing sampan and I haven't seen it since."

Liang looked at him for a moment, then made the sound that served him as a laugh — short, silent, a compression of breath.

Jun finished the rice.

He set the bowl down on the jetty stone and looked at the sea.

Twenty-two kilometers north, Tai O stood in its channel. Forty kilometers south-southwest, Lamma had a quarry and possibly lime and possibly iron rod. The distance between them was the South China Sea, which was not a wall and was not a barrier and did not care, in any direction, what was on either side of it.

He looked at the breakwater line — sixteen catamaran platforms in their staggered chain, absorbing the morning swell with small, independent motions, each one working alone and together at the same time.

*Whatever the place already has*, he thought. *Start there.*

He picked up his tool bag, walked up the hill to the cottages, and went to look at the seventh one — the one he had not finished before the storm.

The wall was still standing.

---

*End of Story 10: The Stilts of Tai O*

================================================================================

STORY 11: THE BEACON WATCH
Setting: Simatai Great Wall, Miyun County, Beijing

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE RIDGE LINE


The wall appeared in sections.

Jun saw the first tower from the valley road — a grey-brick silhouette on the ridgeline, its crenellations jagged against the morning sky, appearing and vanishing as the road curved between the shoulders of the mountains. Then a second tower, lower, slightly behind the first. Then a long, unbroken run of wall following the ridge's spine east, the walkway visible as a pale line threading between towers, narrowing with distance until it resolved into something indistinguishable from the rock below it.

Simatai. The northeast section of the Ming Great Wall, built on ridges of quartzite that the original surveyors had chosen because they were already a wall — sheer, interlocked, impossible to cross except at the passes. The brick and mortar work had simply formalized what the geology had established.

The access road ended at a chain-link gate across the tourist entrance. The gate was wrapped three times around its central post with heavy chain and a combination lock. On the other side of the gate, a hand-painted sign on cardboard in Mandarin and English: CLOSED. DO NOT ENTER. DANGER.

Behind the gate, on a concrete apron between the ticket booth and the start of the stone staircase, seven people stood watching Jun and Liang approach along the road.

The man at the front was stocky and broad-shouldered, wearing a canvas work vest over a grey shirt, his hair cut short and grey at the temples. He had the look of someone who had spent years outdoors in all weather — his face permanently creased at the corners of the eyes from squinting at distances, his hands large and scarred in the particular way of people who worked stone. He was perhaps fifty-five.

He looked at Jun's carpenter bag. He looked at Liang. He looked at the road behind them.

"You're alone?" he said.

"Yes," Jun said.

"Where from?"

"South. Lantau, most recently." Jun looked at the gate. "I'm a carpenter. We need to get off the road."

The man studied Jun for a moment, then turned and said something to the group behind him. A younger man produced a key and opened the combination lock. The chain fell away and the gate swung inward.

"Wang Shuo," the man said, extending his hand. "Restoration supervisor. Simatai section, Ming Wall Conservation Project."

"Jun."

"Come up," Wang Shuo said. "We'll talk at Tower Seven."

The staircase from the entrance gate to the wall walkway was modern — concrete steps on a steel frame, built for tourist access. At its top, the wall itself began: Ming Dynasty brick over an older core, the walkway surface worn smooth by decades of tourist traffic, the battlements on either side chest-high and solid. The mortar joints between the bricks were tight and dark, pointing that had been maintained by Wang Shuo's crew until eight days ago, when the conservation project had stopped.

Jun walked the walkway slowly, not from fatigue but from attention. He pressed each battlement as he passed it, feeling the mortar joint quality. He looked at the wall's inner face — the side that dropped toward the valley north of the ridge — and at the outer face — the side facing south, toward Beijing. He stopped at each crack and traced it with his finger.

Tower Seven was a two-story structure, its lower chamber a vaulted brick room with arrow slits on three faces and a wooden staircase to the upper platform. The upper platform had a crenellated parapet and a clear view in all directions: west along the wall toward the main tourist access area, east along the steeper section toward the summit ridgeline, north into the valley where a road ran toward Miyun, and south toward the line of mountains between here and Beijing.

Wang Shuo's group occupied the lower chamber — sleeping mats on the brick floor, a camp stove in one corner, water containers stacked against the north wall. Twenty-three people total: eight restoration crew, the rest village residents from the valley communities below. They had been on the wall for six days.

"The Beijing road," Jun said, standing at the tower's south arrow slit. "When did it open?"

"Four days ago," Wang Shuo said, behind him. "The eastern approach from Gubeikou. Three days after that, the northern valley road."

Jun looked south through the arrow slit. The valley below was a green corridor between ridgelines, the road running northeast as a pale grey line. At the road's southern end, barely visible in the morning haze — movement. A sustained, low-amplitude movement, the kind that resolved at this distance into a mass rather than individuals.

"How many?" Jun said.

"We counted eight hundred and forty when the front of the column was at the valley entrance," Wang Shuo said. "That was yesterday morning. The column has a long tail — we don't know the full number. At least a thousand, possibly twice that."

"Beijing workers," Jun said. It was not a question. The haze was at the right altitude for a valley road — the kind of road that fed the northeast corridor cities, the industrial belt that ran from the capital through Miyun to the border.

"Factory district workers, office workers, residential," Wang Shuo said. "Mixed. The construction sites north of the Fifth Ring Road contributed a lot of hardhats."

Jun pulled back from the arrow slit and looked at the chamber.

"Show me the wall from here to the eastern summit," he said. "All of it. The sections that are sound, the sections that aren't, and anything you've already assessed."

Wang Shuo spread a hand-drawn map on the floor — a plan view of the Simatai section, twenty towers marked from west to east, the wall line threading between them along the ridgeline. He had annotated it in pencil.

"Tower One through Tower Six — western section, below the reservoir gorge. Sound but low priority for us because the gorge cuts them off from the eastern section. No crossing available since the bridge was closed."

"What bridge?" Jun asked.

"The Xianxiu Bridge. Iron suspension, spans the gorge between the western and eastern sections. The restoration project used it for supply runs. It's still there — I locked the access gate on our side when we came up." He pointed. "Tower Seven through Tower Fifteen — eastern section, where we are. Tower Seven, Nine, Eleven, Twelve — sound, in good repair, my crew worked on them within the last two months. Tower Eight — partial roof collapse, northeast chamber open to weather, but the walls are carrying. Tower Ten — worst problem. The tower itself has been deteriorating for thirty years and one wall failed in last winter's ice. There's a gap in the wall line at that point — twelve meters of open ridgeline between the tower's remnant and the next intact wall section."

Jun looked at the map. A twelve-meter gap in the wall. On a ridgeline.

"The gap — what's the terrain on either side?" he asked.

"The ridgeline at Tower Ten is the narrowest point in the entire section," Wang Shuo said. "Three meters wide at the crest. The quartzite drops thirty meters on the north face and forty meters on the south face. The only way through is along the crest."

"So the gap is the only viable crossing point," Jun said.

"For anything that can't climb sheer rock," Wang Shuo said. "Yes."

"The horde follows flat surfaces," Jun said. "A ridgeline path."

"We've seen that," Wang Shuo said. "The valley road. They don't vary from it."

Jun returned to the map. Tower Ten's gap was the primary vulnerability. But between the valley floor and Tower Ten's gap, the horde would first encounter the access road, the tourist entrance staircase, and the wall's base.

"The wall base on the north face," Jun said. "How high?"

"Varies. At the staircase entrance, the wall face is eight meters from ground level to the walkway. Further east, as the ridge steepens, the wall base height decreases — at Tower Ten, the wall stands only three meters before the ridgeline takes over."

"Three meters," Jun said.

"Three meters," Wang Shuo confirmed.

Jun was quiet for a moment. He looked at the arrow slit again, then at the map, then at Wang Shuo.

"The Heavenly Ladder section," Jun said. "Between Tower Fifteen and the summit."

Wang Shuo's expression shifted slightly. "You know it?"

"I've seen photographs. The angle is what — sixty-five degrees?"

"Sixty-eight at the steepest. The steps are forty centimeters high and twenty centimeters deep. An adult in normal physical condition can ascend it in about fifteen minutes if they're willing to use their hands." He paused. "A body that doesn't understand the mechanics of climbing would have significant difficulty. But with enough pressure behind it—"

"Enough pressure doesn't need to understand the mechanics," Jun said. "It just needs one body to reach the top by accident and the rest will follow the path." He looked east along the wall. "Is there anything east of the Heavenly Ladder that they could use? After the summit?"

"The wall ends at the summit — Tower Sixteen is a ruin, no walkway connects it to anything. East of the summit is sheer cliff. Nothing can descend that face."

"So the Heavenly Ladder is the eastern boundary of the threat," Jun said. "The gap at Tower Ten is the center. The north-face base height at the staircase entrance is the western boundary."

He straightened up from the map.

"Three problems," he said. "In order of urgency: the gap at Tower Ten, the base height at the staircase entrance, and the Heavenly Ladder."

"We've been sandbagging the gap with rubble," Wang Shuo said. "My crew carried stone from the collapsed tower sections. We've filled about four meters of the twelve."

"Show me," Jun said.

They walked east along the wall toward Tower Ten.

The walkway narrowed progressively as they moved east — the ridge below it steepening, the wall's base diminishing from eight meters to six to four, the drop on either side becoming more severe. Between Tower Nine and Tower Ten the walkway was exposed — no tower cover, the crenellations the only protection from the wind that moved steadily from the north, cool even in summer at this altitude.

Tower Ten was a ruin from the oucoarse haire. Its eastern wall had failed — collapsed inward, the brick courses lying in a heap on the walkway behind the tower shell. The surviving three walls stood, but the eastern face was open to the sky, the tower's vaulted ceiling in the lower chamber exposed and visibly cracked where the missing wall had supported its keystones.

Beyond the tower's eastern remnant: the gap.

Twelve meters of bare quartzite ridgeline, the wall line interrupted entirely. On either side of the gap, the surviving wall ended in cleanly broken brick faces — not gradual deterioration but sudden cessation, the wall simply ending where the ground had shifted in an old freeze-thaw movement and pulled the foundation apart.

Wang Shuo's crew had filled four meters from the western end with rubble — loose stone and broken brick, stacked to shoulder height in a rough pile. It was not a wall. It was a cairn. Under pressure from a crowd moving at any sustained speed, it would shift and scatter.

Jun looked at the gap, then at the rubble pile, then at the broken brick faces on either side.

"The brick faces," he said. "The mortar at the break — is it still sound along the course joints?"

Wang Shuo pressed his thumb against the mortar at the break. "Within thirty centimeters of the break — yes. The failure is local, not systemic."

"Then we have something to key into," Jun said.

He set his bag down and crouched at the break, looking at the course structure. The Ming Wall was not a single wall but a composite: an outer facing of fired brick, a rubble core between the two faces, and an inner facing of brick on the valley side. The outer and inner facings were tied together through the core by header bricks — bricks laid perpendicular to the face, their length extending into the core. The gap had exposed the header brick ends at the break face, the brick cross-sections showing like a grid of rectangular windows in the wall's interior.

He could use those header ends. If he set new brick sections at right angles into the existing header grid — threading new courses through the break face like a dovetail joint — the new section would be mechanically locked to the old wall, not merely abutted against it. The joint would be stronger than a simple butt connection.

He needed brick and mortar. Wang Shuo had both.

"Your conservation materials store," Jun said. "What's on-site?"

"In the maintenance shed at Tower Seven — two pallets of Ming-specification facing brick, three bags of hydraulic lime, one bag of natural cement, two bags of river sand." Wang Shuo counted on his fingers. "Mixing troughs, trowels, pointing tools, scaffolding boards."

"How many bricks on the two pallets?"

"Approximately four hundred."

Jun looked at the gap. Twelve meters of wall, two faces, the wall width approximately one-point-five meters. To fill the gap with a solid double-face wall at the same height as the surrounding sections — one-point-eight meters, chest-high — would require approximately six hundred bricks. Not enough.

"We're two hundred bricks short for a full-height fill," he said. "So we don't fill the full height. We fill to one meter — enough to stop anything walking upright — and cap it with the rubble pack Wang Shuo's crew has already placed. The rubble sits on top of the new course as a second barrier. Something that breaks through the rubble still has to breach the brick below it."

Wang Shuo looked at the gap. At the rubble. At the brick break face.

"That works," he said. "How long to lay four hundred bricks?"

"With four workers who know masonry — six hours for the first half, longer for the second as the new mortar takes initial set." Jun looked at the sky. The horde in the valley was still a kilometer from the wall base. "We have until tomorrow morning at current pace."

"You can't lay brick faster?"

"You can't," Jun said. "Mortar needs time to reach green strength before the next course goes on. Stack too fast and the lower courses slide under the weight before they've set. Six hours per half, with a rest period between." He picked up the bag. "Start the mortar mix now. I'll set the first course while it reaches the right consistency."

Wang Shuo turned and called a name back along the walkway toward Tower Nine. Two of the restoration crew appeared within minutes, carrying a mixing trough between them.

Jun opened his bag.

He had a trowel, two levels, a length of string for coursing, and the cold chisel. He looked at the break face again, identifying the header ends, counting courses. He was planning the dovetail lock, the angle of the first keyed brick, the bed joint thickness.

The horde was a kilometer away. The mortar needed forty minutes to reach workable consistency. The sun was moving west.

He set the string level at the first course height and reached for the trowel.

***

---

CHAPTER 2: THE DOVETAIL COURSE


The mortar took fifty minutes, not forty.

Wang Shuo's hydraulic lime was conservation-grade — slower to activate than building-trade lime, formulated to be reversible and chemically compatible with the original Ming-era mortar. Jun had used it once before, on a different project, and remembered that it had a deceptive consistency: it looked workable before it was, the surface smooth and the body still loose underneath. He tested it every ten minutes by pressing his thumb into the mix and watching how quickly the impression filled back in. At forty minutes it still recovered too fast. At fifty minutes it held the impression for four seconds — the threshold — and he picked up the trowel.

The first course was the hardest and most consequential.

He had decided on a toothed approach to the dovetail lock: at the header grid he exposed in the break face, he would set alternating full bricks and half-bricks — full bricks projecting into the new section, half-bricks set flush with the break face, creating a sawtooth profile that the second course would overlap in the opposite pattern. Course by course, the alternation would create a running bond between old and new masonry that was mechanically interlocked in both the horizontal and vertical planes — not merely glued by mortar but physically unable to pull apart without shearing through brick.

He set the first brick into a bed joint twelve millimeters thick — conservation spec, slightly thicker than modern practice, matching the original Ming mortar joint visible in the surrounding wall. He pressed the brick level with both palms, twisted it slightly to seat it in the mortar, checked it against the string line. Level to the millimeter. He scraped the extruded mortar from the face with the trowel edge and set the next brick.

Wang Shuo crouched behind him and watched without speaking. The two restoration crew who had brought the mixing trough — a young man named Zhao and a woman named Lin, both in their thirties — stood at the rubble pile on the gap's other side, ready to hand bricks forward as needed.

Jun worked steadily. He did not hurry. Speed in bricklaying beyond a certain threshold was counterproductive — the mortar bed needed to be compressed evenly by the brick's weight settling into it, and that required deliberate placement rather than rapid stacking. He had seen apprentices lay brick fast and watched them pull the whole stack apart the next morning when the uneven compression had let the lower courses slide.

Twelve bricks in: the first course was complete across the three meters he was filling on the eastern half of the gap. He cleaned the joints, rechecked the level, and stood up.

"Rest the course," he said. "Thirty minutes. Don't touch it."

Wang Shuo looked at the clock on his phone. "The horde is moving faster than yesterday's pace. They may reach the wall base in eighteen hours instead of twenty-four."

"Then I'll work faster in the places where I can afford to," Jun said. "This isn't one of them."

He left the first course alone and walked west along the walkway toward Tower Nine, examining the wall surface as he went. He had been doing this during the mixing wait — glancing at the inner wall face, the walkway surface, the joint patterns — in the systematic way he examined all structures he was about to depend on. The brick survey habit. His teacher had called it the first obligation: look before you touch.

He was looking at the walkway surface between Tower Nine and Tower Ten when he found it.

A crack.

Not in the brick face — in the walkway paving itself, a coursed granite slab surface approximately two meters wide between the inner and outer parapets. The crack ran parallel to the wall line, about forty centimeters from the inner parapet, continuous for seven meters before it disappeared under the tower's east arch.

Jun crouched and pressed the slab on either side of the crack.

The slab on the parapet side was solid — no movement, no resonance, the stone resting on a sound bed. The slab on the walkway-center side shifted — not dramatically, a millimeter of downward play when he pressed it, as if something beneath it had a small void.

He pressed harder. The slab rocked slightly, the crack widening and closing under the pressure.

He stood up and looked at the inner wall face — the face on the valley side, the north face. At the section corresponding to the crack's location, the brick courses showed a subtle misalignment: the horizontal mortar joints on the upper courses were slightly wider than the joints on the lower courses, the wall face having moved fractionally outward at the top, rotating away from the core on a hinge somewhere below.

Delamination.

The inner wall face was separating from the rubble core — the header bricks that tied the two faces together had lost their grip in this section, the mortar around them deteriorated by decades of freeze-thaw cycling. The inner face was still nominally upright, still carrying the walkway slab edge, but it was no longer bonded to the core. Under crowd pressure from the north — the weight of a thousand bodies pressing against the wall base — it would bow outward and eventually fail. Not quickly. But under sustained load, in the hours after the horde reached the wall base and pressed against it, the delaminated section would be the weakest point in the entire eastern wall.

Jun went back to Tower Nine and looked through Wang Shuo's conservation materials inventory.

Masonry stitching rods: a bundle of six, each one six hundred millimeters long and twelve millimeters in diameter, stainless steel, with expanding anchor heads on both ends. Standard conservation tool for exactly this situation — a hollow-drill installation through the full wall width, the rod inserted and the anchor heads expanded at both faces with a torque wrench, clamping the two faces back against the core.

He held a rod up and looked at the anchor head. The expansion mechanism was a split cone: torque on the central bolt spread the cone's fingers outward against the drill hole wall, locking the rod in place by friction in both the inner and outer faces simultaneously.

Six rods. The delaminated section was seven meters long. Ideally, one rod every meter — seven rods. He was one short.

"Wang Shuo," Jun said. "Where's your hollow-core drill bit?"

Wang Shuo found it in the tool crate: a masonry core drill, twenty-millimeter diameter, six hundred millimeters of extension shaft. Designed for exactly the wall's width.

"You have a hammer drill?" Jun asked.

"Battery-powered. Sixty percent charge."

"Enough for six holes," Jun said. "We'll space them at one-point-two meters instead of one. Closer at the center of the section where the delamination is worst."

"How do you drill through a Ming Wall from the top?" Wang Shuo said. "The walkway slabs—"

"We drill from the inner face," Jun said. "Through the north parapet, angled slightly downward to clear the walkway slab edge above. Six holes, each one through the parapet face and into the wall core — not all the way through to the outer face. The rod anchors in the core, its outer head pulls against the parapet face, the inner head—" He looked at the wall geometry. "We cut the inner head flush with the parapet surface. The rod holds the face to the core. The outer face doesn't need stitching — it's already bonded. Only the inner face is moving."

Wang Shuo looked at the parapet. He ran his hand along the inner face, finding the joint misalignment where Jun had found it.

"My crew drilled anchor holes for safety handrail posts last year," he said. "Same drill bit. I know the technique." He looked at Jun. "We do this while your first brick course is setting."

"Yes," Jun said. "You do the drilling and rod installation. I'll come back when the thirty minutes are done."

Jun set Wang Shuo and Lin at the inner parapet with the drill and the stitching rod bundle, and returned to Tower Ten's gap. Zhao was waiting by the mixing trough. The mortar in the trough was covered with a wet cloth to prevent skinning.

The first course had been resting for twenty-six minutes. Jun pressed it with a fingertip — firm, resisting the press without significant deformation. Not fully set, but stable. He pressed harder, deliberately — the test for green strength, the point at which the course could bear the next course's weight without the lower joints being squeezed.

Adequate. He would add the second course now and let both set together.

He re-tempered the mortar — a small addition of water and a re-knead with the trowel — and began the second course. Here the full-brick and half-brick pattern reversed from the first course: where the first course had set a full brick at the header end, the second course set a half-brick, and vice versa. The course-by-course reversal created the running bond — the stagger that distributed load across the joint plane rather than concentrating it in a single vertical line.

He was halfway through the second course when he heard the drill start up — Wang Shuo working at the parapet, the battery hammer drill loud in the open air above the ridge. The sound traveled clearly in the mountain quiet.

From the valley, he heard nothing yet. But the valley was seven hundred meters away and the ridgeline absorbed sound.

He set the next brick. Pressed it level. Scraped the joint.

The rhythm of it was familiar — not the emergency urgency of the past weeks but the older rhythm, the one that predated everything that had happened: mortar to trowel, trowel to bed, brick to bed, press, level, scrape. He had been doing this rhythm, or one close to it, since he was sixteen. It was the rhythm of making something that would still be there long after the person who made it had stopped caring whether it was.

Wang Shuo's drill stopped after thirty minutes. Jun heard six holes: five in quick succession and the sixth taking longer, the drill stalling twice in what sounded like a harder section of the core rubble before breaking through. Then the sound of the torque wrench — a rapid clicking as each anchor cone was expanded, two per rod, twelve clicks total.

Wang Shuo appeared at the gap with the drill and the empty rod bundle. "Six rods installed. All anchors expanded to specification."

"Any face movement when you torqued them?"

"The fourth rod — there was visible movement when I expanded the inner anchor. About two millimeters of the inner face pulling back toward the core."

"That's the rod working," Jun said. "If the face pulled back, the anchor pulled it. That means the stitching is in contact." He set the next brick. "Give me thirty minutes on the second course, then we start the third."

Wang Shuo crouched and looked at the brickwork. He said nothing for a moment, examining the joint quality, the level, the bond pattern.

"The dovetail in the first course," he said. "The alternating pattern — is that a specific technique?"

"It's called interlocking toothing," Jun said. "Usually used when you're joining a new wall to an existing wall and you want the joint to perform as well as the wall itself. Not usually used for repairs — the books call for a butt joint with bonding agent." He set another brick. "But a butt joint relies entirely on the adhesion between old and new mortar.
