If the old mortar face is contaminated with dust or salt crystallization — which it is, after six centuries — the adhesion is limited. The toothing is mechanical. It holds even if the mortar fails."

Wang Shuo was quiet for a moment. "You learned this from a book?"

"The joint pattern I learned from a book," Jun said. "The logic of why it holds, I worked out on a different wall, on a different problem, years ago." He pressed the next brick level. "A wall tells you what it needs if you look at it long enough."

"I've been looking at this wall for four years," Wang Shuo said.

"Then you already knew the toothing was right," Jun said. "You just hadn't had a reason to use it yet."

Wang Shuo absorbed this without comment. He picked up a trowel and looked at the mortar trough.

"Second face?" he said. The gap had two brick faces — the outer (south-facing) and the inner (north-facing valley side). Jun had been working the outer face. The inner face still needed its own courses, running parallel to the outer, the space between filled with rubble core.

"Set the inner face courses to match mine," Jun said. "One course behind me — don't go ahead of where I am. I'll call the bed joint thickness as I go."

Wang Shuo loaded a trowel and moved to the inner face of the gap.

They worked in parallel for the next two hours — Jun on the outer face, Wang Shuo on the inner, Zhao passing bricks and mixing fresh mortar as each batch stiffened past workable. Lin came back from the parapet work and joined the brick-passing chain. The walkway at Tower Ten's gap began to fill — a new brick section growing course by course from the quartzite ridgeline upward, its freshly laid faces a slightly different color from the surrounding six-century-old wall but its geometry matching exactly: same joint thickness, same course height, same header-and-stretcher bond pattern.

By late afternoon, the new section was eight courses high — ninety-two centimeters. Two courses from the target one-meter height.

Jun stopped and looked at the mortar trough. It was three-quarters empty — the remaining mortar beginning to stiffen past workable, the surface cracking slightly at the edges.

"One more batch," he said to Zhao. "Last mix of the day — just enough for the final two courses."

Zhao began the last batch.

Jun walked to the north parapet and looked into the valley.

The horde was closer. In the late afternoon light, its leading edge was visible as a dark band on the valley road — not yet individual figures at this distance, but dense enough that the road surface was no longer visible through it. The column had reached the valley's midpoint. At the current pace — the same unhurried, unstopping movement he had been observing since arriving — it would reach the wall base at the tourist staircase sometime before midnight.

The brickwork would not be fully set by midnight. Green strength, yes — enough to resist deformation. But not the cured strength that came with twenty-four hours of hydraulic lime hydration.

If the horde pressed against the new section while the mortar was still green, the joint faces might creep — a microscopic deformation that over hours would accumulate into visible displacement. Probably not failure. But possibly.

He looked at the rubble pile that Wang Shuo's crew had built — four meters of it, now consolidated at the gap's eastern end by the new brickwork's presence. The rubble had no mortar. No dovetail. It held by friction and gravity and the particular stubbornness of heavy rocks that had been stacked by human hands and settled into each other over six days.

Under crowd pressure, the rubble would fail before the new brickwork would.

"The rubble," Jun said to Wang Shuo, who had come to stand beside him. "It needs to be consolidated. Something to hold it together so it acts as a mass rather than a collection of individual stones."

Wang Shuo thought for a moment. "Concrete."

"We don't have enough mix for a full pour," Jun said. "But we have the natural cement bag. Half a bag of cement, mixed dry with the remaining sand, packed into the rubble voids and wetted in place — not poured, packed. It'll set slowly but it'll bind the rubble mass."

"The water application," Wang Shuo said. "We'd have to wet it at intervals through the night."

"Twice. Once now, once at midnight." Jun turned to Zhao. "Can you manage a midnight wetting?"

Zhao looked at the rubble pile, then at the valley. He was perhaps thirty, with the particular composure of someone who had accepted the situation sufficiently to make practical decisions within it.

"Yes," he said.

The final two courses went on before the light failed. Jun set them himself, working quickly now that the lower courses had reached green strength and the precision requirement relaxed slightly. The mortar was stiffening in the trough — he had perhaps twenty minutes of workability remaining — and he used it in full, finishing the outer face and then the inner, and scraping the last of the mix from the trough onto the core fill between the two faces and pressing it into the rubble with the trowel handle.

He set the trowel down.

The new section stood one meter above the quartzite ridgeline, connecting the two break faces of the old wall in a continuous line. The dovetail locks were invisible from the oucoarse haire — the bond pattern looked like any other running bond, the alternation of the toothing buried in the joint plane. But the mechanical grip was there.

He looked at it for a moment.

"Point the joints at dawn," he said to Wang Shuo. "Before the mortar fully hardens. The surface joints need filling where I missed them in the fading light."

"I'll do it," Wang Shuo said.

The cement-and-sand dry pack went into the rubble next — Zhao tamping it into the voids between the stones with a pole, Lin wetting it from a water container at measured intervals. Jun watched the first wetting — the dry pack darkening as it absorbed the water, the surface stiffening within minutes as the cement began its long hydration.

Not fast. Not strong yet. But bonding.

When the last light left the ridge, Jun went back to Tower Seven and ate with the rest of the group — rice from the camp stove, canned fish, the particular communal quiet of people who have worked all day toward a shared problem and have not yet learned whether the work was enough.

Wang Shuo sat across from him. "The wall base," he said. "The north face at the staircase entrance. You said eight meters."

"Yes."

"They'll stack against it. If enough stack against it, the upper bodies will be at the battlements."

"I know," Jun said. "That's tomorrow's problem."

Wang Shuo looked at him steadily. "The staircase problem is more urgent than the gap."

"The gap is a hole in the wall," Jun said. "A hole in the wall is an immediate breach. The stacking problem at the base is a slow accumulation problem — it takes time to build a pile eight meters high even with a thousand bodies. The gap had to come first." He looked at his rice. "The staircase is tomorrow. First light."

Wang Shuo nodded, accepting the logic.

From the valley below, faint but distinct in the mountain stillness, the sound of the horde had begun to be audible — not individual sounds but a sustained, subsonic pressure, the way a river sounds from a great distance: not the water itself but the weight of it.

Jun finished his rice.

He needed to think about eight meters of stacking buffer. He had the wall itself, its existing geometry, Wang Shuo's remaining materials, and whatever the original Ming engineers had already put in place for exactly this contingency — because the Ming engineers had built this wall to stop a horde from the north, and they had solved the stacking problem five hundred years ago.

He needed to find what they had already built.

He went to Wang Shuo's survey files and started reading.

***

---

CHAPTER 3: THE DRAINAGE SLUICE


The survey files were handwritten in a blue-lined ledger, the ink faded to the color of dry slate. 

Wang Shuo’s predecessors in the 1980s had been meticulous. They had mapped not just the visible brickwork of the Simatai restoration, but the internal void spaces, the water runs, and the structural anomalies of the Ming core. Jun turned the pages by the yellow light of a battery-powered camp lantern, his finger tracing a cross-sectional diagram of Tower Seven’s foundation.

The Ming designers had faced two enemies: the northern nomads and water. Of the two, water was the more persistent. 

To prevent the core rubble from liquefying during the summer monsoons, the builders had integrated a system of internal drainage channels—*tupin*—running through the heart of the wall. These were not open gutters but rectangular stone conduits, forty centimeters wide, built from granite slabs and sloped at a four-degree angle. They collected water from the walkway sky-wells and channeled it through the wall body, discharging it through carved stone gargoyles—*taotie* heads—projecting from the north face.

Jun stopped at a page showing the base of the tourist staircase.

"Here," he said, tapping the diagram. 

Wang Shuo leaned over his shoulder, the smell of dry lime dust and tobacco smoke coming with him. "The entrance landing. The modern stairs join the wall at the old postern gate site."

"The postern gate was built in a dip," Jun said. "The natural runoff from the ridge collects there. The Ming builders placed three separate *tupin* outlets directly above that gate. They're four meters up from the path. If we block the collection wells on the walkway and divert the channels, we can access the conduits from the interior core."

Wang Shuo frowned, his calloused thumb rubbing his chin. "Access them for what? They’re water runs."

"They're funnels," Jun said. "Four meters high, directly over the bottleneck where the stairs meet the landing. If the dead stack there, we don't fight them over the parapet. We use the conduits to drop stone rubble and dry lime directly onto the staircase landing from inside the wall. It’s a gravity feed. We don't expose ourselves, and we don't waste wood."

Wang Shuo looked at the diagram, then at Jun. The logic was clean, the kind of solution that relied on the existing mass of the structure rather than external materials.

"The conduits are probably choked with dirt and moss," Wang Shuo said. "They haven't been cleared since the Qing Dynasty."

"Then we clear them tonight," Jun said. "And we build the draw-gate at the top of the stairs before dawn."

By midnight, the wind had picked up, howling through the arrow slits of Tower Seven. The temperature on the ridge had dropped to ten degrees, the damp mountain air carrying the smell of pine needle rot and something else—a faint, sour odor of old decay that the north wind was dragging from the valley road.

Jun, Liang, and Zhao stood at the staircase landing. 

The modern tourist staircase was a lightweight steel frame anchored into the rock, its steps wire-mesh treads that let the air and light through. It rose sixty meters from the ticket plaza below, ending at a small concrete platform level with the wall's walkway. A steel guardrail ran around the platform, and a modern iron gate—now locked with a heavy padlock—secured the entrance.

"The iron gate is too light," Jun said, testing it with his heel. The metal rattled in its frame. "The lock will hold, but the hinges are only welded to the steel posts. If two dozen bodies push at once, the welds will shear."

"We brace it," Liang said, holding a six-by-six pine timber.

"No," Jun said. "A static brace just transfers the load to the posts. We build a draw-gate behind it—a drop-bar gate that sits in vertical guide tracks. If the iron gate fails, the drop-bars take the weight. The guide tracks will distribute the force into the brick masonry of the portal arches."

Jun had selected four seasoned pine planks from the restoration scaffolding store—five centimeters thick, twenty centimeters wide, and two meters long. He had also brought two U-channel steel posts that had been intended for handrail repairs.

Working in the dark, with Zhao holding a shrouded flashlight, Jun aligned the first steel U-channel against the inner brick face of the postern arch. He used the hammer drill to sink four eighty-millimeter anchor bolts into the mortar joints, the concrete dust blowing back into his face in the wind. He tightened the nuts with a socket wrench until the washers bit into the steel.

"Liang, the other side," Jun muttered.

Liang aligned the second U-channel, checking the plumb with a brass pocket level. The wind was so strong now that the level's bubble vibrated, but Liang held it steady with his palm until the drill bit bit into the masonry.

The sound of the drill was a sharp, mechanical chatter that seemed to carry for miles. Jun kept his eyes on the dark stairs below. 

At forty meters down, the stairs vanished into the mist. But the sound from the ticket plaza was growing distinct—a rhythmic, metallic scraping, like hundreds of iron-tipped shoes dragging over concrete. The leading edge of the column had reached the valley entrance.

"Hurry," Zhao whispered, his hand shaking slightly on the flashlight.

"The bolts must be full depth," Jun said, not changing his pace. "A shallow bolt will pull out under tension. Let the drill do the work."

They finished the guide tracks at two in the morning. Jun took the first pine plank and slid it into the channels. It dropped with a heavy, satisfying *clunk*, wedging itself tightly between the steel guides at the bottom of the arch. He slid the second plank in, then the third.

The barrier was now sixty centimeters high—a solid wall of treated pine, five centimeters thick, locked into the brickwork.

"Leave the fourth plank out for now," Jun said. "We need to see over it to clear the landing if they get this far. Zhao, where's the dry lime?"

Zhao pointed to three fifty-kilogram paper bags stacked under a canvas tarp. "We brought the conservation lime. It’s non-hydraulic—pure calcium hydroxide."

"Dry lime burns wet tissue," Jun said. "If we dump it down the *tupin* conduits, the moisture in their eyes and mouths will activate it. It won't kill them, but it will blind the front rank and slow the push. Liang, get the iron bars. We need to clear the conduit outlets from the oucoarse haire."

They moved to the north parapet, three meters east of the postern gate. 

Jun leaned over the edge, looking down the face of the wall. In the dim starlight, the carved stone *taotie* gargoyle was visible—a monstrous, blocky face projecting thirty centimeters from the brick, its mouth a dark hole.

Liang tied a safety line around his waist and handed the end to Jun. He climbed over the parapet, his boots finding purchase on the narrow brick ledges of the wall's ornamental plinth. He leaned down, holding a three-meter iron reinforcement bar.

"I see the mouth," Liang called up, his voice muffled by the wind. "It's clogged with bird nests and old mortar."

"Drive the bar straight in," Jun said, bracing his boots against the inner parapet. "The conduit runs straight for two meters before it bends upward toward the core."

Liang swung the iron bar, driving it into the gargoyle's mouth. A dull *thud* echoed from the stone. He pulled the bar back and drove it in again, harder. A shower of dry dirt, dead leaves, and old straw erupted from the opening, blown away instantly by the wind.

"Clear," Liang said. "I can feel the metal sleeve inside. The Ming engineers lined the exit course with cast iron."

"Good. Come up," Jun said.

They cleared the second and third conduits by three in the morning. On the walkway, Jun used the cold chisel to break open the stone sky-well cover—a decorative granite slab with drainage holes. Beneath it, the square opening of the conduit vertical shaft was visible, filled with dry leaves and gravel.

Jun dumped a bucket of water down the shaft. A second later, a wet splashing sound came from the north face below—the water had run clean through the core and out of the gargoyle's mouth.

"The line is clear," Jun said. "Stack the stone rubble next to the sky-well. We want fist-sized quartzite stones. Anything larger will jam the bend."

As they began carrying the stone from Tower Ten's heap, a sound came from the stairs.

It was not the distant scraping they had been hearing. It was local. A sharp, clear *ping* of steel vibrating under weight.

Jun stopped, a fifteen-pound quartzite block in his hands.

"Lights off," he said.

Zhao clicked the flashlight off. The darkness fell over the landing like a blanket.

The wind howled, rattling the wire-mesh steps of the tourist staircase. In the gap between the gusts, the sound came again—a wet, dragging step on the steel treads, twenty meters down the staircase. Then another. Then the sound of a hand rail sliding under a heavy grip.

Jun crept to the pine barrier, his boots silent on the concrete platform. He leaned over the edge, looking down.

The mist was shifting, parting in thin ribbons. 

Ten meters below the landing, a figure was visible on the stairs. 

It was wearing a bright yellow windbreaker, the hood pulled up, but the fabric was torn at the shoulder, revealing pale, bloodless skin underneath. The figure moved slowly, one foot rising and planting itself on the next step with a heavy, mechanical momentum, then the other foot dragging up to match it. It did not look down. Its face was tilted upward, its mouth open, its teeth gleaming white in the starlight.

Behind it, a second figure emerged from the fog—a man in hiking shorts and a blue backpack, his left leg twisted outward at an impossible angle, his hands clawing at the steel handrail as he hauled his weight upward.

And behind them, the mist was dense with shapes—a dark, slow-moving tide rising silently up the mountain.

"They're here," Liang whispered, his hand resting on the hilt of his iron bar.

"Let them reach the gate," Jun said. "We need to know if the guide tracks hold before we use the lime."

The first zombie reached the landing. It did not stop. It walked straight into the modern iron gate, its chest pressing against the bars. The gate rattled. The zombie’s hands rose, its fingers curling around the iron rods, its face pressing into the gap between them. Its breath plumed in the cold air, sour and grey.

It did not try to open the gate. It did not look for a latch. It simply pushed.

A second later, the hiker in the blue backpack reached the landing and pressed against the first zombie's back. The iron gate groaned, the welded hinges creaking under the double load.

"Jun," Zhao whispered, his voice rising in panic. "The welds."

"Wait," Jun said.

A third zombie arrived—a tall man wearing a green hardhat from a Beijing construction site, his face completely ruined by a blast injury, his jaw hanging loose. He did not press against the gate; he wedged his shoulder into the gap between the gate post and the brick archway, his dead weight acting as a wedge.

With a sharp *crack*, the upper weld on the gate hinge split. The gate tilted three inches outward, the iron bar scraping against the concrete floor.

"Drop the last plank," Jun commanded.

Liang slid the fourth pine plank into the guide tracks. It dropped, completing the one-meter barrier.

At that moment, the lower weld sheared. The iron gate fell inward with a loud clang, its weight slamming against the new pine barrier. The three lead zombies stumbled forward, their bodies falling over the iron frame and pressing directly against the pine planks.

The planks bowed. The steel guide tracks groaned, the anchor bolts holding firm in the brickwork but the steel flanges bending fractionally under the sudden load.

The zombie in the green hardhat fell face-first over the top of the barrier, his hands clawing at Jun's boots.

Jun did not step back. He lifted the cold chisel and drove the iron point straight down through the center of the hardhat. The steel split the plastic and the bone underneath with a wet, heavy crack. The zombie went limp, its weight hanging over the pine planks like a sack of wet salt.

"Zhao, the lime!" Jun shouted. "First conduit! Now!"

***

---

CHAPTER 4: THE CHIMNEY DRAFT


Zhao did not dump the bag. He slitted it with his pocket knife, his hands shaking, and tipped the paper mouth into the granite sky-well.

The white powder vanished into the vertical shaft. 

Below, at the gargoyle’s mouth, the dry calcium hydroxide erupted in a silent cloud, falling like a heavy, artificial snow over the heads of the three zombies pressed against the barrier and the dozen others crowded on the staircase landing. 

For three seconds, nothing happened. The dead, lacking nerve endings in their outer skin, felt no pain. They continued to claw at the pine planks, their finger bones clicking against the wood. 

Then the chemical reacted. 

Pure calcium hydroxide is highly basic; when it contacts moisture, it undergoes an exothermic hydration reaction, converting to calcium carbonate while releasing intense localized heat and drawing water from surrounding tissues. The moisture in the zombies’ open mouths, wet throat passages, and exposed eyes activated the powder. 

A low, collective hiss rose from the landing—not a vocal cry, but the sound of steam and escaping air as the lime boiled the fluids in their throats. The hiker in the blue backpack stumbled backward, his blinded eyes white with crusting chemical heat. He collided with the zombie behind him, his boots slipping on the wire-mesh step. 

The weight shifted. The trooper zombie, his jaw already broken, lost his footing as the blinded crowd behind him began to turn and churn blindly on the narrow landing. 

"The stone!" Jun ordered. "Now!"

Liang lifted a twenty-pound quartzite block and dropped it down the sky-well. 

The stone rattled through the cast-iron sleeve and shot out of the *taotie* gargoyle's mouth like a projectile from a mortar. It struck the zombie in the green hardhat directly on the shoulder, breaking the collarbone and dragging him over the edge of the staircase. The body fell twenty meters into the dark gorge below, hitting the steel supports with a dull, ringing clang.

Zhao and Lin dropped more stones, a steady, rhythmic barrage that cleared the immediate landing, sending bodies tumbling down the steel steps into the mist.

"It cleared the landing," Zhao gasped, leaning over the sky-well. "They're falling back."

"They aren't falling back," Jun said, pointing down the valley ridge. "The column is too long. The ones behind are just pushing the blind ones over the side. The steel stairs are becoming greasy with lime and fluids. Eventually, the pile at the base will reach the landing level anyway. We have three hours before the staircase is choked. Move the tools to Tower Eight."

They retreated along the walkway, the cold wind at their backs.

Tower Eight stood three hundred meters to the east, situated on a high quartzite knob where the ridge narrowed to a two-meter spine. 

From the oucoarse haire, the tower was a grey-brick block, six meters square, its lower chamber accessed through a low barrel-vaulted arch. But the restoration project had not finished here. The northeast corner of the upper roof platform had failed during the previous winter's freeze; a large section of the vaulted ceiling had caved inward, leaving a two-meter hole in the floor of the second story and filling the lower chamber with a heap of broken brick and rotted pine rafters.

Jun stood in the center of the lower chamber, looking up at the gray sky visible through the caved ceiling.

"The hole is too large to patch," Wang Shuo said. "We don't have the timbers to span the joists, and we don't have the lime to lay new vault arches."

"We don't patch it," Jun said. "We use the chimney."

He pointed to the south wall of the chamber. 

Like most Ming watchtowers, Tower Eight was equipped with a built-in brick fireplace—*kang* furnace style—designed to heat the guardroom during the brutal winter months when Miyun was buried in snow. The hearth was a low, brick arch built into the base of the wall, connecting to a vertical chimney flue that ran through the core of the masonry to exit through a small brick stack on the roof platform.

"The chimney draft is strong," Jun said. "The wind is from the north. If we open the flue cleanout door at the base and seal the window arches on the north side, the north wind will hit the wall, pass over the top, and create a low-pressure zone on the south face. That will draw air from this chamber up the flue like a pump."

"And?" Wang Shuo asked.

"And we turn the chimney into a fire barrier," Jun said. "We stack the old pine rafters from the ceiling collapse in the hearth. We dry-pack the cleanout with scrap timber. If we light it, the draft will pull the flame and the smoke straight up the flue. The masonry around the chimney stack on the roof will heat to over three hundred degrees. The hole in the northeast vault is right next to the chimney exit. Any body attempting to climb down through the roof collapse will have to cross the thermal column of the chimney. The hot air and the ash will repel them. They can't navigate heat."

"The wood will burn out in two hours," Zhao said.

"Not if we choke the intake," Jun said. "We control the draft at the hearth arch. We use a damp mortar sack over the opening to limit the oxygen. We make it a smolder, not a flash. We need the heat in the stone, not the flame in the room."

Working quickly, Liang cleared the cleanout door with his prybar, pulling out decades of bird nests and soot. 

Lin and Zhao carried the rotted pine timbers from the ceiling collapse, chopping them into half-meter lengths with the carpentry axe. The pine was dry, saturated with resin that had cured over six centuries—*huanghuali* grade density. It smelled of turpentine and old dust as they stacked it inside the hearth.

Jun went to the north window arch—a narrow, stone-framed opening looking out toward the valley. 

He used three scaffolding planks, wedging them horizontally across the stone jambs and locking them with oak wedges driven by his mallet. He packed the seams with wet clay from the water run-off, sealing the opening to prevent the north wind from pressurizing the lower chamber. The only air source now was the low archway from the walkway west.

"Light it," Jun said.

Liang struck a match and held it to a handful of dry pine shavings at the base of the hearth.

The flame caught instantly, a bright orange tongue licking the dark brick of the cleanout. For a minute, the smoke spilled into the room, thick and grey, making Zhao cough. 

Then, as the air inside the vertical flue warmed, the draft took hold. 

With a low, hollow *whoosh*, the smoke was sucked back into the chimney. The sound of the fire changed from a crackle to a steady, deep hum—the furnace roar of a functioning draft. The air in the lower chamber grew clean, drawn toward the hearth opening by the vacuum.

Jun climbed the wooden ladder to the upper platform, his palm resting on the brickwork next to the chimney stack.

Within ten minutes, the stone was warm. Within twenty, the air rising from the chimney exit was invisible, shimmering with heat that distorted the view of the valley below. The draft was pulling so hard that small pieces of charred pine bark were rising twenty meters into the sky before burning out.

The caved-in section of the northeast vault was less than a meter from the chimney stack. The hot air rising from the flue created a thermal wall—a column of air at two hundred degrees Celsius, moving upward at three meters per second.

"It's working," Liang said, standing on the roof platform.

"For now," Jun said, looking at the chimney base.

A sharp, metallic *crack* sounded from the vault below.

Jun scrambled down the ladder.

In the lower chamber, the brick arch above the hearth had split. A horizontal crack, five millimeters wide, had opened across the third course of the cleanout, and a thin line of grey smoke was leaking into the room, curling toward the ceiling.

"Thermal shock," Wang Shuo said, his voice tense. "The brick is old restoration work. They used modern Portland cement for the 1980s repair instead of hydraulic lime. The cement doesn't expand with the heat—it splits the bricks."

The crack was widening. As they watched, another course joint failed, the brick face shifting two millimeters outward under the weight of the wall core above it. If the hearth arch collapsed, the vertical flue would fill with core rubble, blocking the draft and filling the tower with smoke.

"Get the sand," Jun said. "We mix the natural cement now. No lime—we need the fast set."

"The heat will dry the cement too fast," Wang Shuo warned. "It will shrink and crack."

"We wet the brick first," Jun said. "Zhao, water. Keep the face wet while I apply the pack."

Jun mixed the cement bag in a small plastic bucket, using a three-to-one sand ratio and minimal water until the mix had the consistency of stiff clay—dry-pack grade.

Zhao threw water against the hot brick, the liquid turning to steam instantly with a sharp hiss. 

Jun stepped into the heat, his face red, his eyes tearing from the leaking smoke. Using his margin trowel, he drove the cement mix deep into the crack, tamping it with the wooden handle of his chisel. The heat from the brick was so intense that his leather gloves began to smell of scorched hide, but he did not stop, packing course after course, wedging broken pieces of Ming tile into the gap to act as keys.

"More water," Jun muttered.

Zhao wetted the face again. Jun applied the final layer of cement, smoothing it with the trowel face to seal the pores.

The smoke leak stopped. The hum of the draft recovered its deep, hollow resonance.

"It's holding," Liang said from the ladder.

"Keep it wet for thirty minutes," Jun said, stepping back and wiping the soot from his forehead. "If the cement stays damp, it will cure before the heat kills it. If it dries, it's just sand."

He walked to the low archway and looked west along the wall.

The mist had cleared from the ridge.

On the walkway, fifty meters away, the first of the blinded hikers from the staircase was stumbling toward them. His yellow windbreaker was white with lime, his face swollen and dark. He moved by touch, his hands sliding along the inner battlements, his head turning toward the hum of Tower Eight’s chimney.

And behind him, the ridge path was a line of grey-brick and white lime, filled with the slow, unhurried shapes of the dead.

---

CHAPTER 5: THE SIGNALING SMOKE


The beacon was a warning that had not been sent in five hundred years.

Wang Shuo stood in the lower chamber of Tower Seven, holding a wooden crate he had dragged from the deepest recess of the maintenance vault. The crate was stenciled with faded yellow characters: *CONSERVATION DEMOLITION - EXPLOSIVES/FLARES.* Inside lay twelve industrial smoke canisters—remnants of the tourist search-and-rescue inventory—and six old hemp bags filled with a dark, greasy powder.

"Wolf dung," Wang Shuo said, patting one of the bags. It gave off a pungent, musky odor that cut through the smell of coal smoke. "The Ming manual specifies it for a reason. Wolf dung smoke is dense, oily, and rises in a tight column that doesn't disperse in a mountain gale. The restoration project kept a stockpile for historical demonstrations. We have the dung, we have dry straw, and we have five liters of diesel from the generator tank."

"The wind is blowing south-southeast," Jun said, checking the sky. "A signal from Tower Seven will be visible across the entire Gubeikou valley. If there are military outposts or organized rescue zones at the Miyun reservoir, they'll see the column. But a signal also tells the horde exactly where the living are."

"They already know we're here," Liang said, pointing down the ridge. "The noise we made at the stairs drew the front. The smoke won't make them any hungrier, but it might bring help."

"Then we light the beacon on the roof platform," Jun said. "Liang, take the smoke canisters and the straw up. I’ll prepare the diesel-and-dung mix here."

The staircase leading from Tower Seven’s lower chamber to the upper roof platform was not modern. It was a reconstruction from the 1950s—steep, narrow pine steps supported by two heavy timber carriages anchored into the brick vaulting. The wood had not been treated; decades of damp air rising through the tower’s drainage vents had rotted the carriage bases where they met the wet flagstones of the floor.

Liang loaded the canvas sack of canisters onto his shoulder, gripped the pine handrail, and began to ascend.

The wood groaned under his weight. A sharp, dry *tink* echoed from the wall—the iron anchor bolt holding the left carriage to the brickwork had sheared from rust. The entire staircase shifted two centimeters to the right, the top landing scraping against the brick vault arch.

"Hold," Jun said, his hand rising.

Liang froze, his foot suspended over the sixth step. He did not move his head. "The carriage is twisting. I can feel the right stringer bowing."

"Don't back down," Jun said. "If you step back, the dynamic load will push the base outward. Keep your weight centered and walk close to the wall. The wall-side carriage has more anchors."

Liang shifted his weight, his boots pressing against the inner edge of the treads next to the brick wall. He moved slowly, step by step, his body tense. He reached the upper landing and pulled himself through the roof hatch onto the open platform.

"I'm up," Liang called down. "The hatch frame is solid, but the top step is loose. The tenons have pulled out of the mortise."

"Stay on the roof," Jun said. "Don't come down until I’ve braced the stringer. Zhao, get the three-meter pine prop from the scaffold pile."

Before Zhao could reach the door, a sound came from the walkway oucoarse haire.

It was a wet, heavy thud.

Jun turned. 

A zombie—a woman wearing a blue nylon raincoat, her hair matted with dried blood—had reached the tower's entrance arch. She did not stumble. She was being pushed from behind by three others, their bodies wedged tightly in the narrow brick portal. The pressure of the crowd behind them was so immense that the woman's ribs cracked against the stone jambs with a dull, hollow sound, but she kept moving, her hands reaching into the chamber.

"The gate!" Wang Shuo yelled, reaching for his shovel.

"No," Jun said, drawing his axe. "The portal is too wide for a gate now. We let them bottleneck in the arch. Zhao, help Wang Shuo hold the staircase base. Don't let them reach the carriage."

Jun stepped toward the entrance. 

The woman in the raincoat fell forward onto the flagstones, her knees buckling. Jun stepped side-on, avoiding her clawing fingers, and brought the butt of the carpentry axe down onto the base of her skull. The bone gave way with a dry, crunching snap. 

But behind her, two more were already in the arch—a man in a grey business suit, his face half-eaten by his companions, and a younger man in a tourist T-shirt. They were tangled in the raincoat of the first, their limbs interlocking as they scrambled over her body, creating a low, writhing mound of gray flesh in the doorway.

Jun swung the axe again, splitting the shoulder of the tourist zombie, but the steel became wedged in the heavy collarbone. He pulled back, his boots slipping on the wet blood.

"Jun!" Wang Shuo screamed.

From the staircase, a loud *crack* split the air.

The right pine stringer—already weakened by rot and the structural shift—had split down the center under the tension of the twisted carriage. The carriage base slid forty centimeters across the flagstones, the bottom three steps splintering into fragments. The entire staircase collapsed toward the middle of the chamber, hanging by only the two top anchor bolts at the roof hatch.

Liang was trapped on the roof.

"The hatch is shifting!" Liang called down through the opening. "The brickwork around the anchors is cracking!"

"Use the rope!" Jun shouted, kicking his boots free of the tourist zombie's grasp. He abandoned the wedged axe and drew his framing hammer. "Tie it to the chimney stack and drop the tail through the hatch!"

In the doorway, three more zombies pushed through the bottleneck. One of them—a heavy man in a brown leather jacket—stumbled over the mound and fell toward the collapsed staircase carriage. His hand caught the dangling pine stringer, his weight pulling the carriage down another ten centimeters.

The top anchor bolts in the roof hatch began to bend, their nuts clicking against the steel washers as they pulled out of the brick joints.

"Liang! The rope!" Jun yelled.

A coil of white nylon rope dropped through the hatch, the end hitting the floorboards next to the hearth.

Jun grabbed the rope. "Wang Shuo, Zhao, get on the line! We haul him down before the stairs pull the vault jambs apart!"

"We can't go up," Zhao said, his face white as he looked at the invading zombies. "They're in the room."

"We don't go up," Jun said. "Liang, slide down! Now!"

Liang did not hesitate. He threw his legs through the hatch, gripped the nylon rope with his gloved hands, and slid down the line. His boots hit the floor just as the top anchor bolts finally sheared.

With a deafening crash, the remains of the wooden staircase fell into the center of the chamber, the heavy timber stringers splintering into a heap of jagged pine planks. The pile of wood fell directly across the path of the invading zombies, creating a temporary, chaotic barricade of broken boards and iron nails.

The heavy zombie in the leather jacket was pinned beneath the collapsed carriage, his legs crushed by the main stringer. He thrashed blindly, his hands clawing at the wood.

"The door," Jun said, chest heaving. "Block the archway with the remaining planks."

Using the broken timbers of the staircase, Jun and Liang wedged three heavy pine stringer fragments diagonally across the entrance portal, driving the ends into the mortar joints of the archway with the hammer. The barrier was crude, a tangle of jagged wood and rusted iron brackets, but it locked the entrance, trapping the five zombies inside the archway pile and blocking the path for the hundreds waiting on the walkway oucoarse haire.

"The roof," Wang Shuo said, pointing to the open hatch. "How do we get the beacon lit if we can't climb up?"

"We don't need to climb," Jun said. He picked up one of the smoke canisters from the floor—it had fallen from Liang’s sack during the collapse. "The diesel and the dung are already on the roof in the metal drum. We have the rope. We tie a burning flare to the end of the line, haul it up through the hatch, and drop it into the drum."

Liang found a red highway flare in the tool crate. He struck the cap, the chemical igniting with a brilliant, sputtering pink flame that filled the dark chamber with a harsh, sulfurous glare.

He tied the flare securely to the nylon rope.

"Haul it up," Jun said.

Liang pulled the opposite tail of the rope, which he had looped over the chimney stack on the roof before sliding down. The burning flare rose through the hatch, casting long, dancing shadows on the brick vaulting of the ceiling. 

Five meters up. Six. The flare cleared the hatch.

With a sharp pull, Liang jerked the rope, swinging the burning flare over the rim of the metal drum that sat next to the chimney. The flare fell into the drum, landing on the mixture of damp straw, wolf dung, and diesel.

For a second, there was silence.

Then, a deep, oily rumble echoed from the roof.

Through the hatch, a thick, black column of smoke erupted into the sky, so dense and heavy that it blocked the starlight. The smell of burning diesel and acrid dung filled the air, carried south by the wind.

Jun walked to the south arrow slit and looked out.

The black column rose straight and tall, a dark finger pointing toward the heavens, visible for twenty miles across the mountains.

And from the valley below, a mile to the south, a single, brilliant white light flashed twice through the mist. An answering signal.

---

CHAPTER 6: THE FLYING BUTTRESSES


The pressure at Tower Ten was silent, but it was massive.

When Jun reached the gap at four in the morning, the night was at its coldest. The wetted cement-and-sand pack they had tamped into the rubble had cured to a dark, grey crust, locking the loose stones into a solid mass. It had held the first wave. But the main body of the Miyun column had now bypassed the staircase entrance entirely, scrambling up the terraced slopes below the ridge to stack against the base of Tower Ten's outer wall.

The wall stood only three meters high at this point, the quartzite ridge beneath it serving as the primary barrier. 

Thousands of bodies, packed shoulder to shoulder in the narrow draw below, pressed against the north face of the wall. It was not an active assault; it was the slow, hydraulic accumulation of weight—the force of a crowd that had no exit, pushed from behind by the thousands still rising from the valley road.

Jun laid his hand against the inner brick face of Tower Ten's southern remnant.

The masonry was cold, but it was vibrating. A low, rhythmic shudder passed through the courses, corresponding to the wet, heavy thuds of bodies hitting the outer face.

"Jun," Wang Shuo said, pointing to the bed joints at the second course. "The mortar is weeping."

Jun crouched. A thin line of white lime water was oozing from the joint, squeezed out by the pressure. A vertical fracture—a hairline crack—had opened through the headers of the third course, running six meters along the wall base before disappearing into the quartzite bedrock.

The ancient wall was bowing. 

The inner face was separating from the core, rotating outward over the forty-meter drop on the south face. If the base of the wall kicked out, the entire structure would slide off the ridge, taking the new dovetail course and the survivors with it.

"We can't brace it from the inside," Liang said, looking at the narrow walkway. "There’s no room for a deadman anchor. The walkway is only two meters wide."

"We brace it from the south face," Jun said. "We use the scaffolding timbers to build flying buttresses—diagonal struts that anchor into the quartzite shelves below the wall base and press against the bowing face at the third-story line."

Wang Shuo looked over the south parapet, his eyes wide. The drop was sheer—forty meters of vertical quartzite ending in a scree slope of broken stone. "You can't work on the south face. There's no ledge. It's sixty-eight degrees."

"There is a plinth," Jun said. "The Ming builders laid a projecting granite foundation course—the *diyu*—that projects fifteen centimeters from the brick face. We can stand on the *diyu* if we use safety lines. Liang, get the four-meter pine timbers and the heavy steel restoration brackets."

The brackets were T-shaped iron plates, ten millimeters thick, designed to connect timber joists to stone foundations during the arch restoration work. They had four bolt holes on the long leg and two on the cross.

Jun tied a heavy climbing harness made of hemp rope around his waist, securing the anchor line to the iron portcullis frame of Tower Nine. He checked the knot—a double figure-eight—and stepped over the southern parapet.

The wind hit him instantly, cold and clean, rising from the valley below. 

His boots, heavy leather with rubber soles, found the fifteen-centimeter granite plinth. He pressed his back against the bowing brick wall, his chest tensing as he looked down at the dark void of the canyon. The rope was tight against his chest, holding his weight against the wall.

"Liang, drop the drill," Jun called up.

The battery hammer drill came down on a separate line, its twenty-millimeter bit rattling against the steel frame. 

Jun took the drill. He had to work one-handed, his left hand gripping an iron tie-rod he had driven into a mortar joint above him. He leaned out, his body suspended over the abyss, and aligned the drill bit with the quartzite shelf twenty centimeters below the plinth.

He pulled the trigger.

The drill roared, the carbide tip grinding into the hard, grey quartzite. The vibration passed through Jun’s arm, shaking his shoulder and chest. The rock was incredibly hard—quartzite is ninety percent silicon dioxide, resistant to steel—and the progress was slow, a millimeter at a time, a white cloud of stone dust rising in the wind.

After three minutes, the battery indicator on the drill began to flash red.

"Hurry, Jun!" Zhao called from the parapet. "The crack at the base has widened to ten millimeters! I can see the core rubble through the joint!"

Jun pressed his shoulder into the drill body, using his weight to force the bit deeper. The motor whined, smelling of hot copper and ozone. At sixty millimeters, the drill stalled. The battery was dead.

"Change it!" Jun yelled.

Liang hauled the drill up, swapped the battery pack for the last fresh one, and dropped it back down. 

Jun caught the handle, cleared the dust from the hole, and resumed drilling. The bit bit deep, finally reaching the eighty-millimeter depth. He set the drill aside, took an iron expansion bolt from his pouch, and drove it into the hole with his hammer.

He slid the steel T-bracket over the bolt, added the washer, and tightened the nut with the socket wrench. The anchor was set, locked into the bedrock by the expanding steel sleeve.

"First strut!" Jun called up.

Liang and Wang Shuo lowered a four-meter pine timber—ten centimeters square, heavy and wet with preservative. The bottom end of the timber had been notched with a V-cut to fit the bracket.

Jun guided the timber end into the steel bracket, his boots slipping once on the narrow plinth. His heart hammered against his ribs, but he held the wood, aligning the bolt holes. He drove a steel pin through the bracket and the timber, locking the base.

The top of the timber rose diagonally across the south face of the wall, its upper end resting against the brickwork at the height of the walkway.

"Brace the top!" Jun shouted.

On the walkway, Liang used a heavy iron screw clamp—a scaffolding coupler—to lock the upper end of the diagonal timber to the inner parapet wall. He tightened the screw handle with a steel rod, pulling the bracket tight against the brick face.

The diagonal strut tensed. The wood groaned, the grain compressing under the load as it took the outward thrust of the wall.

Jun felt the vibration in the plinth diminish. The wall had stopped moving.

"Second strut," Jun said, moving sixty centimeters to the east along the plinth.

They worked for two hours in the dark, Jun drilling and anchoring the brackets while suspended over the cliff, Liang and Wang Shuo preparing and lowering the heavy timbers. By six in the morning, five diagonal struts were in place, forming a wooden skeletal framework that braced the south face of Tower Ten’s wall against the quartzite bedrock.

The structure was a series of flying buttresses, transferring the hydraulic pressure of the northern horde directly into the mountain itself.

As Jun tightened the last clamp on the fifth strut, a loud *snap* echoed from the third bracket.

The iron T-plate—forged from recycled steel that had been improperly annealed during the restoration project—had sheared across the weld. The diagonal timber slipped outward, its notched end sliding off the rock shelf.

The wall groaned, the brick courses at the base shifting three millimeters to the south.

"Jun!" Liang yelled, reaching over the parapet.

Jun did not look up. He dropped the socket wrench, grabbed his cold chisel, and jammed the steel wedge into the narrow gap between the slipped timber end and the quartzite plinth. 

He swung the three-pound sledgehammer with his right hand, driving the chisel deep into the joint. The steel wedged the wood back against the rock, stopping the slip.

"Hold it!" Jun screamed. "Get a secondary clamp on the stringer!"

Liang dropped a chain hoist over the parapet, hooking the link to the iron tie-rod above and the timber body below. He cranked the lever, the gears clicking rapidly as the chain tensed. The chain took the load, pulling the timber back into alignment and locking it against the wedge.

The wall settled. The groaning stopped.

Jun collapsed against the brick, his forehead resting on the cold stone, his breath pluming in the grey light of dawn. 

From the north face of the wall, less than a meter away through the brick courses, he could hear them—the dry, papery scratching of fingernails on the outer facing, the soft, rhythmic thud of heads hitting the stone, and the low, collective sigh of a thousand bodies that did not know how to stop.

---

CHAPTER 7: THE RIDGE ARCHERS


The wind shifted at seven in the morning.

It did not change gradually. A sudden, cold front swept down from the Inner Mongolian steppe, reversing the ridge current from south to north-northwest. The black, oily smoke from Tower Seven’s beacon, which had been rising in a clean column toward the valley, was flattened against the stone walkway. 

It came down like a heavy shroud, smelling of burnt rubber, diesel, and the bitter stench of wolf dung. 

Jun coughed, his eyes stinging instantly as the smoke filled the narrow gap between Tower Nine and Tower Ten. The visibility dropped to three meters. The valley below vanished, replaced by a swirling, grey-black fog that made it impossible to see the battlements, let alone the stairs or the ridge below.

"Masks!" Jun called out, his voice muffled. He pulled a damp cotton rag from his tool bag and tied it over his mouth and nose. "Use the water bucket! Wet the rags!"

In the middle of the smoke, a sharp, dry *twang* sounded from the parapet.

Lin stood next to Tower Nine, her body tensed in the classic archer's stance—feet perpendicular to the target, hips aligned, her left arm extended straight toward the north battlement. She held a Ming-reconstruction composite bow, its limbs a laminate of mulberry wood, water buffalo horn, and dried deer sinew, bound together with fish-bladder glue.

She released the string. 

A heavy, iron-tipped willow arrow hissed through the smoke, striking a zombie that had just cleared the parapet wall three meters away. The arrow entered the eye socket, the iron point splitting the orbital bone and destroying the brain stem. The body fell backward off the wall without a sound.

"We have four bows from the exhibition display," Lin said, her breath pluming through her mask. Her hands were black with soot, her fingers protected by a simple leather ring. "Zhao and three of the village boys can shoot. But the bows are too stiff—the sinew has absorbed the moisture from the mist."

A composite bow is a biological machine. 

The horn on the inner face resists compression; the sinew on the outer face resists tension. In dry weather, they work in perfect balance, storing twice the energy of a self-bow of the same draw weight. But sinew is animal protein; in the damp, sulfurous air of the ridge, it absorbs moisture like a sponge, softening the fibers and reducing the draw weight from eighty pounds to less than forty.

Worse, the fish glue holding the laminate together was softening.

*Crack.*

The top limb of Zhao's bow split with a dry, splintering sound. The sinew strip peeled back from the wood like wet bark, the horn core snapping in half under the sudden imbalance of tension. The bow whipped out of Zhao's hand, the frayed silk string lashing his cheek.

"The glue is failing," Zhao said, pressing a hand to his bleeding face. "The limbs are delaminating. If we draw them full length, they'll all snap."

"We need dry heat," Jun said, inspecting the broken limb. He peeled a piece of the fish glue with his fingernail; it was soft and gummy, having lost its crystalline rigidity. "The animal glue must be dehydrated to set back into a hard matrix. We use the chimney stack at Tower Eight."

He took the three remaining bows and ran west along the walkway, the black smoke swirling around him.

Inside Tower Eight, the lower chamber was warm and dry, the hearth draft still humming steadily. The cement patch Jun had applied to the cleanout arch had cured to a hard, pale seam, holding the heat inside the flue.

Jun climbed the ladder to the roof platform. 

The air rising from the chimney exit was clean and hot, free of the black diesel smoke because the hearth fire was burning pure pine heartwood. The temperature of the brick stack was eighty degrees Celsius—perfect for curing animal glue without burning the wood.

Jun constructed a makeshift drying rack using four iron-tipped scaffolding brackets. He wedged the brackets into the chimney stack joints, creating a platform directly over the hot air exhaust, and laid the three bows across them.

"How long?" Liang asked, standing guard at the hatch with his iron bar.

"Ten minutes for the surface moisture," Jun said. "Twenty for the glue to recrystallize. If we keep them there longer, the wood will dry too fast and become brittle. We need to watch the limb curve. As the sinew dries, the limbs will reflex—they'll bend forward, away from the string side."

He watched the mulberry wood limbs. 

Slowly, as the heat drew the water from the sinew fibers, the bows began to move. The tips curved forward, the reflex shape returning as the animal protein contracted. The smell of hot horn and warm glue rose from the chimney, dry and organic.

On the walkway below, Zhao let out a sharp cry.

"They're over the wall!"

Jun looked down through the roof hatch.

The smoke was shifting, leaving a temporary pocket of clear air. At the lowest section of the wall—where the masonry met the quartzite knob between Tower Nine and Tower Eight—the zombies had scaled the three-meter facade. 

It was not a climb; they had stacked themselves against the stone plinth until the top bodies were level with the battlements. A woman in a red sweater, her hands raw and bleeding from the quartzite, tumbled over the parapet onto the walkway. Behind her, a man in a blue track jacket scrambled over, his boots hitting the stone with a heavy thud.

Zhao and Lin stood ten meters back, their shovels raised. 

The woman in the red sweater rose, her clouded eyes fixing on Zhao. She lunged, her jaw snapping. Zhao swung the shovel, striking her neck, but the blow was angled—the steel blade cut the muscle but did not break the spine. She caught the shovel shaft, her fingers locking around the ash wood with the mechanical strength of rigor.

She pulled Zhao toward her.

"Bows!" Jun yelled.

He grabbed the first composite bow from the chimney rack. The wood was hot, the sinew stiff and dry to the touch. He strung it with a rapid, practiced motion—bracing the lower limb against his foot, bending the upper limb with his hip, and slipping the silk loop over the horn tip.

He leaped through the roof hatch, landing on the wooden ladder and sliding down to the lower chamber. He ran out onto the walkway.

The man in the blue track jacket was crawling toward Lin, his hands dragging his weight over the flagstones.

Jun drew an arrow from Lin's quiver. He nocked it, drew the string to his ear—feeling the eighty-pound weight of the dried sinew resist his shoulder—and released.

The arrow flew straight. 

It struck the track-jacket zombie in the crown of the skull, the iron point driving through the parietal bone. The body collapsed instantly, going limp on the stones.

Jun nocked a second arrow, drew, and shot the woman in the red sweater who was dragging Zhao toward the edge. The arrow caught her in the temple. She let go of the shovel and fell backward, tumbling over the south parapet into the forty-meter void.

Lin took the second bow from Liang, who had brought it down from the roof.

"Hold the low wall!" Lin shouted to the village youths. "Keep the arrows in the ones that clear the stone!"

For twenty minutes, the ridge was a line of silent, mechanical violence. 

Lin and Jun stood side by side, their composite bows drawing and releasing in perfect coordination. The dry heat of the chimney had restored the bows' power; the arrows struck with enough force to penetrate the thick leather and bone of the Beijing hardhats. 

By eight in the morning, the pile of dead on the walkway at the low wall section was a meter high, creating a secondary barrier that the climbing zombies had to cross, slowing their push.

But the string on Jun's bow was fraying. 

The silk threads at the nocking point had been cut by the iron tips of the arrows, the individual strands unraveling under the eighty-pound tension. 

He drew the string for the next shot, his eye tracking a tall zombie climbing the battlements.

*Snap.*

The string failed at the center loop. The whipped end struck Jun's thumb, cutting through his leather glove and leaving a thin line of red across his palm. The bow limbs straightened with a dull *flunk*, the horn core uninjured but the weapon useless.

He looked at the low wall.

The pile of bodies was shifting. A hand—pale, with black dirt under the fingernails—reached through the gap between two corpses, grabbing Zhao’s boot.

And behind it, the mist was rising again, revealing the full extent of the climb: the entire north slope of the ridge was grey with the rising dead, a slow, crawling carpet of bodies moving up from the valley floor toward the Great Wall.

---

CHAPTER 8: THE HEAVENLY LADDER


"Retreat!" Jun shouted, his voice cracking. "To the ladder!"

They fled east, leaving the pile of bodies at the low wall behind them. 

The ridge rose sharply. The flat, comfortable walkway of the western towers ended, replaced by the vertical spine of the Simatai summit. Here, the wall narrowed until it was barely more than a staircase laid over the rock, its width shrinking from two meters to one, and then to eighty centimeters—the width of a single man.

This was the Heavenly Ladder.

The incline was sixty-eight degrees. The steps were not modern concrete; they were Ming-era masonry, forty centimeters high and only twenty centimeters deep. To ascend, one could not walk upright; you had to lean forward, placing your hands on the step above you, crawling like an animal up the face of the quartzite cliff. On either side, the ground dropped away—sheer vertical drops of thirty meters to the north and fifty meters to the south. 

Jun climbed first, his carpenter's bag slung across his chest, the heavy iron tools inside shifting and clicking with every upward pull. His calves burned, his lungs drawing the cold, thin mountain air in ragged gasps. 

Behind him came Lin and Zhao, then Wang Shuo, his breath rattling in his throat, and Liang bringing up the rear, his iron bar clutched in his hand.

Below them, the horde followed.

They did not crawl. They did not have the balance to navigate the steepness, but the pressure from the rear was so relentless that the front bodies were pushed up the steps like water rising in a pipe. When a zombie fell, it rolled down, knocking three others off the ledge, but the mass behind them simply stepped over the falling corpses and continued the ascent, their nails scratching at the quartzite joints.

"The bottleneck," Jun said, stopping at the tenth step of the ladder.

The wall here was bordered by two towering rock pillars—the Twin Sentinels. The Ming builders had squeezed the steps between these natural stone shafts, leaving a gap only seventy centimeters wide. The brick battlements on either side were gone, replaced by the raw, jagged quartzite of the pillars.

"We build the slide-gate here," Jun said. "Liang, the two remaining two-by-fours and the pine shutter board. We wedge the frame between the two stone faces."

The shutter board was a heavy timber panel, eighty centimeters wide and one-point-two meters long, that had been used as a mixing board for the lime. It was solid pine, saturated with dry mortar crust.

Jun took his framing chisel and began cutting two shallow sockets—mortises—into the mortar joints where the brick of the lower step met the quartzite of the left pillar. He worked with rapid, heavy blows of his mallet, the steel splitting the old lime mortar in showers of white dust.

"Liang, notch the timbers," Jun said.

Liang cut two angled notches—shoulders—into the ends of the two-by-four pine posts, matching the slope of the rock.

They stood on the steep steps, their bodies angled forward at forty-five degrees to keep their balance in the howling wind. Zhao held the shutter board, his back braced against the right rock pillar, his legs shaking from the strain.

Jun aligned the left pine post with the socket he had cut. "Drive it in!"

Liang swung the sledgehammer, striking the top of the timber. The pine notch slid into the brick socket with a dry, grinding crunch. The post was locked at the base.

They aligned the right post, wedging it against the quartzite face of the right pillar.

"Now the shutter," Jun said.

The shutter board was designed to slide vertically down the channel between the two posts, acting as a portcullis. Jun set the board in the top of the guides. It slid down, blocking the seventy-centimeter gap completely.

"Anchor the head," Jun said, reaching for his battery drill.

He aligned the drill bit with the right rock pillar, intending to sink a final anchor bolt through the top of the pine post into the quartzite. 

He pulled the trigger.

The drill bit hit the rock. With a sharp, dry *tink*, the carbide tip shattered against a hidden vein of iron-rich quartz. The drill body kicked back, the housing cracking in Jun's hand. The motor whined, spun once, and died.

The drill was ruined.

"We can't bolt it," Liang said, looking at the dead tool.

"We wedge it," Jun said. "Mallet and iron spikes."

He took three twenty-centimeter steel spikes from his pouch. He set the first spike at the joint where the top of the left post met the brick wall, swinging his mallet.

The spike bit. But the ancient brick—degraded by centuries of frost-thaw cycles and currently carrying the vibration of the climbing horde below—could not take the localized pressure.

*Crack.*

The entire step beneath Jun's left boot split. 

A horizontal fracture ran through the four courses of the brick landing, the stone slabs of the stair tread tilting outward. A section of the wall foundation—three hundred kilograms of brick and core rubble—broke away, sliding off the quartzite shelf and plunging into the fifty-meter void on the south face.

The left post of the gate shifted, its base socket crumbling into red dust. The entire gate frame tilted ten degrees to the south, the shutter board jamming in its guides.

"Jun!" Zhao screamed, grabbing the nylon rope.

The slide-gate was slipping. The weight of the shutter board was dragging the remaining post out of its rock shelf.

Jun lunged. He did not grab the rope. He threw his body across the jammed shutter board, his chest pressing the wood against the right quartzite pillar, using his own weight to friction-lock the frame against the rock.

His boots were suspended over the south abyss, his toes clawing at the empty air. The wind howled beneath him, cold and empty.

"Liang! The chain!" Jun yelled, his face pressed against the pine wood.

Liang did not look at the drop. He dropped his sledgehammer, grabbed the chain hoist, and wrapped the steel links around the top of the right post and a natural knob of quartzite on the right pillar. He cranked the lever, his muscles tensing until the veins stood out on his neck.

The chain clicked. Once. Twice.

The hoist took the load. The sliding timber frame locked back against the quartzite face, the wedge holding the base.

Jun hauled himself back onto the remaining steps, his chest heaving, his hands shaking as he looked down at the empty space where the step had been.

"The gate is locked," Liang said, his voice flat with adrenaline. "But it only has one anchor. If they hit it with any speed, the chain will hold but the wood will split."

"They won't hit it with speed," Jun said, pointing down the ladder. "The incline is too steep. They can only crawl. But they will pile up."

At the bottom of the slide-gate, the first of the climbing dead had arrived. 

It was a woman in a grey wool coat, her face half-destroyed by the lime burn, her fingers clawing at the bottom seam of the shutter board. She could not lift it. She simply pressed her forehead against the pine wood, her dead weight adding to the pressure on the chain.

Behind her, the next zombie arrived, pressing against her back.

And behind them, the line of the dead stretched down the 68-degree stairs, a slow, writhing column of grey flesh and white lime, rising step by step toward the summit of the Great Wall.

---

CHAPTER 9: TOWER SIXTEEN


Tower Sixteen sat like a broken tooth on the highest peak of the ridge.

The wall ended here. Beyond the tower's eastern wall, the quartzite spine of the mountain dropped four hundred meters in a vertical precipice—the East Gorge—where the rock had split during an ancient tectonic shift. There was no walkway beyond, no path, no steps. The only way forward was the sky.

The tower was a roofless shell. The second-story vault had caved in long ago, filling the interior with a two-meter pile of brick rubble, clay mortar, and rotted pine joists that had grown over with mountain grass and dwarf pine trees. 

Jun scrambled through the west portal, his boots sinking into the wet, grassy rubble. The wind here was deafening, a constant roar from the north that whipped the long grass against the brick walls.

"The gate is splitting," Liang said, climbing in behind him. He had left his iron bar at the slide-gate to wedge the lock, carrying only a carpenter's adze. "The wood is bowing. The second carriage anchor has pulled. We have ten minutes, maybe less."

Wang Shuo dropped his pack onto the rubble heap, his chest heaving, his face grey with exhaustion. He leaned against a brick pier, his hand tracing the stone arch of the portal. "This is the end. There's no bridge. No cable car. Gubeikou is five miles east across the gorge, but we can't fly."

"The watchmen didn't fly," Jun said, scanning the floor.

He kicked the grass aside, exposing the floor slabs. Unlike the walkway, which was paved with granite, the interior floor of Tower Sixteen was laid with large, square brick tiles—*jinzhuan*—each one forty centimeters square and ten centimeters thick. 

In the center of the floor, under the grass root mat, the tile pattern changed.

A rectangular border of granite slabs, two meters long and eighty centimeters wide, was set flush with the brick floor. The center of the rectangle was filled with a single, massive slab of grey quartzite, its surface rough-chiseled and gray with lichen.

"A cleanout vault," Jun said, crouching. He cleared the dirt from the seam with his pocket knife. "The Ming garrison didn't stay to die if the pass was lost. Every terminal tower had a *yindao*—a hidden tunnel. It runs through the core of the foundation down to the south-face scree slope below the cliff line."

Wang Shuo crouched next to him, his fingers tracing the quartzite seam. "It’s sealed. Look at the joints. They didn't use lime mortar here—they used molten lead."

The gray seam between the quartzite slab and the granite border was metallic, soft but solid, filling the gap to the millimeter. 

"They poured the lead to keep the moisture out," Jun said. "And to stop the wind from lifting the slab. If the lead is cold, it’s soft. We can cut it."

He opened his tool bag and pulled out his two-inch framing chisel—hardened tool steel—and a heavy wooden mallet.

"Liang, the other side," Jun said.

Jun set the chisel tip at the corner of the seam, angling the blade at thirty degrees to the lead joint, and struck the handle with the mallet. 

The steel sliced through the soft lead with a clean, metallic *shlip*. A strip of grey metal peeled back from the stone like a shaving of pine. He struck again, moving three centimeters along the seam, the mallet blows rhythmic and fast.

Liang worked the opposite side, using a cold chisel and his sledgehammer. The sound of their work—the sharp *clink* of steel on stone and the wet *shlip* of cutting lead—was lost in the roar of the wind.

Zhao and Lin stood at the west portal, looking down the Heavenly Ladder.

The slide-gate was visible three hundred meters below, a tiny wooden block in the narrow rock gap. Through the shifting mist, they could see the column of the dead pressing against it—a dark, slow-moving line that looked like ants crawling up a branch.

"The gate is down," Zhao said quietly.

A distant, wooden crack had carried over the wind. The shutter board had split under the cumulative weight. The dark line was moving again, the ants crawling over the broken pine planks and rising up the steep steps of the ladder.

"They'll reach the summit in five minutes," Lin said. She nocked the last arrow in her composite bow, her fingers trembling on the silk string. "Zhao, get the shovel. We hold the entrance arch. The portal is only eighty centimeters wide."

"Cut the end joints!" Jun shouted, his mallet swinging.

His chisel had cleared the long side of the slab. He turned the corner, the steel cutting the lead cap at the eastern joint. The lead was thicker here, poured into a deep recess to lock the stone. He had to use the mallet with both hands, his shoulders tensing as he drove the chisel through the metallic block.

"Liang, the prybar!"

Liang wedged the flat tip of the iron bar into the long joint where Jun had cleared the lead. He leaned his weight onto the bar, using a brick block as a fulcrum.

The quartzite slab did not move. 

"It’s keyed," Wang Shuo said. "The bottom of the slab must have a rebate joint that fits into the granite frame. You have to lift the eastern end first."

Jun drove a second chisel into the eastern joint, creating a two-millimeter gap. He wedged his cold chisel into the opening, then a steel spacer plate.

"Now, Liang!"

Both men pressed their bars into the joints, their muscles tensing, their boots slipping on the wet grass of the floor. The iron bars groaned under the strain, the steel bending fractionally.

With a wet, sucking sound, the quartzite slab shifted. 

The rebate joint cleared the frame, a thin line of black, dry dust rising from the dark opening below. The slab stood three centimeters high.

"Hold it!" Jun gasped, his shoulder braced against his bar. "Zhao, slide the brick under the lip!"

Zhao shoved a broken Ming brick into the gap, locking the stone in its raised position.

At that moment, the first zombie reached the west portal.

It was a man in a grey wool coat—the leader who had pressed against the slide-gate—his face white with dry lime, his coat torn to shreds. He did not look at the view. He lunged through the archway, his clawing hands reaching for Lin.

Lin released. 

The willow arrow struck him in the throat, the iron tip passing through the neck and locking him against the brick jamb of the door. He did not fall; he thrashed on the arrow shaft, his feet sliding on the flagstones.

Behind him, two more zombies pushed into the portal, their weight slamming against the pinned leader and breaking the arrow shaft with a sharp snap. They fell into the tower chamber.

Lin drew her hunting knife, her back against the brick wall.

"Liang! Hold the arch!" Jun screamed.

He did not drop his bar. He held the lever with his left hand, keeping the quartzite slab from dropping back into the slot, while he reached into his tool bag with his right, pulling out his broadaxe.

He threw the axe to Liang.

Liang caught the handle, stepped toward the portal, and swung the broadaxe in a flat, horizontal arc. The heavy steel blade cut through the neck of the lead zombie, sending the head bouncing into the grass. He did not stop, swinging the axe back, the blade splitting the shoulder of the second zombie and wedging him against the stone door frame.

"We have to lift the slab!" Wang Shuo cried, his hands clawing at the stone lip. "The tunnel is open! I can see the steps!"

Beneath the slab, a steep, narrow flight of stone steps was visible, dropping into the dark core of the wall foundation. The air rising from the tunnel was cold and dry, smelling of ancient clay and dry earth.

"All of us on the bar," Jun said.

He left the cold chisel in the joint, grabbed the long iron prybar with both hands, and stood on the granite frame, his chest aligned with the lever. Wang Shuo and Zhao joined him, their hands locking around the steel bar.

"One, two, lift!"

They pulled. 

The quartzite slab rose, tilting forty degrees, fifty degrees. With a heavy, scraping groan, it rolled over onto the brick floor, landing with a thud that shook the tower walls.

The tunnel was fully open.

"Go!" Jun shouted, pointing to the dark hole. "Lin first! Zhao, Lin, go!"

Lin scrambled into the opening, her boots finding the steep, narrow steps. Zhao followed, his shovel clattering against the stone vaulting.

In the portal, Liang was fighting the third zombie, his broadaxe wedged in a timber rafter as he tried to free the blade under fire. A hand caught his jacket sleeve, pulling him toward the wet pile of the dead in the archway.

Jun dropped his bar, grabbed his framing chisel, and lunged. He drove the steel point through the zombie's temple, the mallet blow driving the chisel three inches into the bone. The zombie went limp.

Jun grabbed Liang by the collar and dragged him back from the arch.

"Into the hole!" Jun yelled.

He pushed Liang into the dark opening of the tunnel. 

He looked back at the portal. 

Through the west arch, the summit platform was a mass of grey shapes—dozens of zombies scrambling over the brick rubble, their white eyes catching the first red light of the rising sun.

Jun stepped into the tunnel, his boots finding the first stone step, and reached up to the brick vault of the entrance.

---

CHAPTER 10: THE SUMMIT ESCAPE


The tunnel did not drop straight down. It wound through the core of the masonry, a spiral of stone steps that had been chopped out of the quartzite foundation by the Ming masons. The air was dead, cold, and smelled of centuries of dry clay dust and the mineral tang of the mountain.

Jun descended five steps, his hand sliding along the arched brick ceiling. 

Above them, at the hatch, a dark shadow blocked the early morning light. A zombie—its face white with lime, its jaw snapping—had tumbled headfirst into the opening. It jammed itself in the narrow throat of the shaft, its arms thrashing blindly.

"We can't pull the stone slab back," Liang said from the steps below. "It’s too heavy from this angle. If they stack in the shaft, their weight will slide the slab off the ledge and seal us in."

"We don't need the slab," Jun said. He turned his flashlight onto the walls of the tunnel throat.

The Ming builders had anticipated a breach. 

Two meters down from the floor level, the masonry of the tunnel walls changed. The granite blocks were notched with two vertical slots—*bolan*—thirty centimeters deep and ten centimeters wide. In the left slot, still resting in its storage recess, was a heavy, square beam of petrified oak. It was black with age, its grain packed with salt and dried pine resin to prevent rot.

"The drop-bar," Jun said.

He reached into the recess, his fingers finding the iron ring set into the end of the beam. The iron was pitted with rust, but the ring was thick. 

"Liang, help me pull," Jun muttered.

Both men grabbed the ring, their boots braced against the steep steps. They pulled, their muscles tensing. The oak beam had not been moved in five centuries; it resisted, the wood fibers sticking to the stone walls of the slot.

With a dry, grinding screech, the beam slid out of its recess. 

It spanned the tunnel throat, its opposite end sliding into the matching slot on the right wall. The barrier was ten centimeters square, solid petrified oak, blocking the passage at chest height.

"Second bar," Jun said, pointing to the slot forty centimeters below the first.

They pulled the second beam. It slid out, locking the lower half of the throat.

At that moment, the jammed zombie above them was pushed through the hatch by the pressure of the horde. It fell, its head hitting the top oak beam with a wet, heavy thud. The body hung over the bar, its hands clawing at Jun's jacket.

Behind it, two more zombies slid down the shaft, their weight landing on the first.

The oak beams groaned, the petrified wood fibers compressing but holding firm in their stone slots. The granite walls of the tunnel throat took the load, distributing the downward force into the main core of the foundation.

"Wedges," Jun said, not looking back.

He took two oak wedges from his pouch, jammed them into the slide slots behind the beams, and drove them home with his mallet. The beams were locked, unable to slide back into their recesses even if the dead thrashed against them for weeks.

"Move down," Jun said, turning the flashlight toward the spiral stairs.

They descended in silence, their footsteps echoing softly in the narrow stone tube. 

The steps went down forty meters, bypassing the vertical cliff face of the north ridge, before the incline flattened. The tunnel became a horizontal corridor, three meters long, its ceiling so low that Jun had to walk bent double.

At the end of the corridor, a faint, golden light was visible.

It was the morning sun.

The tunnel exit was a low, corbeled archway, barely sixty centimeters high, hidden on the south slope of the mountain. The Ming builders had placed it in a narrow crease between two quartzite ribs, overgrown with dense wild rose bushes and dwarf pines. 

Jun crawled through the opening, his boots sliding onto the dry, pine-needle scree of the southern slope.

He stood up, drawing a long breath of the morning air.

The sky was a pale, clear blue, the red light of the rising sun painting the peaks of Simatai in shades of orange and gold. The wind here was gentle, blocked by the main ridge above them.

Behind him, Liang crawled out, then Lin, Zhao, and Wang Shuo. They sat on the dry pine needles, their faces covered in soot, their hands raw and bloodied.

Wang Shuo looked up at the ridge.

High above, on the summit of the mountain, the silhouette of Tower Sixteen was visible against the sky. The ruins of the tower were crowded with shapes—a dark, restless line of figures standing on the roof, their white eyes catching the sun, their hands reaching out toward the void. 

But they could not descend the cliff. The forty-meter sheer wall was an absolute barrier. The Great Wall had held.

"We did it," Zhao whispered, his hand resting on Lin’s shoulder.

"The beacon," Lin said, pointing south.

Through the gaps in the pine trees, the Gubeikou valley was visible, stretching toward the Miyun Reservoir. 

A mile away, along the valley road, a column of dust was rising. It was not the slow, quiet dust of the dead. It was mechanical—a convoy of six military utility vehicles, their headlights cutting through the morning haze. 

And above them, the rhythmic *thud-thud-thud* of a twin-rotor transport helicopter was audible, rising from the reservoir base and heading straight toward the black column of smoke that was still pouring from Tower Seven.

The rescue had arrived.

Jun looked at his broadaxe, the steel blade covered in grey soot and dried blood. He set it inside his bag, next to his levels and chisels, and zipped the canvas shut. He adjusted the strap on his shoulder.

"Come," he said, turning down the mountain path toward the valley. "The road is open."
