CHAPTER 4: THE WIND CHASM


The Wind Chasm was a narrow gap between two towering limestone pillars where the draft from the river valley was compressed into a gale. The wind howled through the notch with a deafening shriek, carrying dust and dry pine needles that stung the eyes.

Here, the trail was nothing more than a ledge sixty centimeters wide, with a vertical drop of five hundred meters.

"No arrows here," Suli said, her voice strained as she fought to keep her balance against the wind. "The draft will carry the light bamboo shafts twenty meters off target. We must hold them with steel."

Jun looked at the gap. "We build a barricade. A *zhaolan*—a traditional timber fence, but we will make it double-walled and pack the center with river stone. The wind will pass through the cracks, but the dead won't be able to push it over."

"We don't have time to stack stone, Master," Liang said, his teeth chattering from the cold wind.

"We use what we have," Jun said. He pointed to several large, flat granite slabs that had fallen from the cliff face. "We will set these vertically, like fence posts, and brace them with horizontal pine poles. Liang, get the drill and the iron expansion plugs."

Using a hand-cranked stone drill, Jun began boring holes into the granite trail bed. The wind tried to tear the tool from his hands, the cold steel freezing his fingers. He worked by touch, his eyes squinted against the dust.

Below them, the horde was approaching the pass. They were no longer scattered; the narrow trail had funneled them into a single, dense line of grey flesh and torn clothing. 

Because they felt no fear of the height, they walked along the very edge of the cliff, their shoulders scraping the rock face, their feet occasionally slipping over the brink. When a zombie fell, it did not scream; it simply drifted down into the white water of the Jinsha like a dropped stone.

"They're coming through the wind!" Liang warned, holding a brace pole.

A zombie in a blue mountain guide jacket reached the entrance of the chasm. The wind caught its loose hood, whipping it over its eyes, but it continued to stumble forward, its hands extended.

Suli stepped forward, her long iron-tipped hunting spear held in both hands. She thrust the spear into the zombie's throat, using the length of the shaft to keep it at bay. But the zombie did not retreat; it pushed forward against the steel point, its hands sliding along the ash shaft toward her.

"Help her!" Jiazhi shouted, drawing a heavy Naxi knife—a short, broad-bladed chopper used for brush clearing.

Jun finished driving the second iron expansion plug into the stone, locking the vertical granite slab in place. "Pass the cross-pole, Liang! Wedge it tight!"

Jun jammed the horizontal pine log between the granite slabs, driving an oak wedge to lock the joint. Suli, with Jiazhi's help, managed to push the guide zombie over the cliff edge, the figure spinning silently into the dark void.

Jun and Liang quickly laid the second layer of poles, creating a sturdy wooden screen. The village youths threw heavy granite cobbles and gravel into the gap between the timber walls, weighting the barrier down until it was solid as the mountain itself.

"The chasm is sealed," Jun said, leaning his weight against the stone-filled wall. The wind whistled through the gaps in the timber, but the heavy frame did not budge.

Behind the barrier, the pressure of the horde began to mount. The grey hands of the dead thrust through the timber slats, their nails scratching the wood. But the double-walled structure, anchored deep into the bedrock with the expansion plugs, held the pass.

"Move on," Elder Jiazhi said, adjusting his gear. "The hydropower station is ahead. If the water there is blocked, the lower village trails will be completely flooded."

CHAPTER 5: THE HYDROPOWER SLUICE


High above the river, a small mountain stream had been diverted into a concrete channel to feed a micro-hydroelectric station—a small turbine house that provided power to the upper Naxi villages. 

The station was abandoned, its windows shattered. The intake reservoir—a five-meter-deep concrete basin—was overflowing, the water spilling across the trail and turning the limestone flagstones into a slick, mossy slide.

The cause of the overflow was visible at the trash rack.

A dozen bloated, water-logged bodies were wedged against the iron intake grate, drawn there by the suction of the penstock. They were covered in river silt, their limbs pale and soft from days in the water. The pressure of the pool had jammed them into the steel bars, blocking the flow and raising the water level.

"The overflow is undermining the trail foundation," Elder Jiazhi said, looking at the cracks opening in the concrete retaining wall. "If the wall goes, the whole terrace will collapse into the gorge. The village above will lose its water source and its path."

"We must open the bypass sluice," Jun said, pointing to a heavy cast-iron gate valve set into the side of the concrete basin. "But the control wheel is submerged under two meters of water."

"I'll go," Liang offered, his face pale but determined.

"No," Jun said, grabbing Liang's shoulder. "The suction at the trash rack is too strong. If you get near the grate, the current will pin you against the bars. I will use the safety ropes and the long timber hook."

Jun tied a thick hemp rope around his waist, handing the end to Liang and Jiazhi. He took a three-meter pine pole tipped with a hand-forged iron log-dog—a sharp hook used for moving timber.

He stepped into the freezing water of the reservoir. The cold was immediate, a sharp pain that took the breath from his lungs. The current pulled at his legs, dragging him toward the dark mass of bodies wedged against the intake grate.

As he waded deeper, one of the water-logged bodies shifted.

The milky eyes of a drowned zombie turned toward him. The mouth opened, releasing a bubble of cold air. The fingers, soft and white from decomposition, began to claw at the iron bars, trying to pull its body free from the suction to reach the living man.

"Hold the rope!" Jun shouted, his voice cracking from the cold.

He raised the timber hook, placing the iron point against the shoulder of the lead zombie. He leaned back, using his weight to pry the bloated figure free from the grate. The zombie tore loose, the current carrying it toward the spillway. But the movement shifted the remaining bodies. Two more active dead, their limbs tangled in the weeds, reached out and grabbed the iron shaft of Jun's hook, their dead weight dragging him down into the freezing pool.

"Pull!" Liang screamed, throwing his weight back on the hemp rope.

Jun went under, the freezing water filling his ears and nose. The darkness was absolute, save for the green glow of the mountain algae. He kicked his legs, trying to find purchase on the smooth concrete floor of the basin. The cold felt like a steel band tightening around his chest, squeezing the air from his lungs.

Above water, Liang and Jiazhi pulled with all their strength, their boots slipping on the wet limestone trail. The village youths joined them, grabbing the rope and hauling it in hand-over-hand.

Jun’s head broke the surface, coughing and gasping for air. He was still holding the pine pole, but his fingers were so numb he could barely feel the wood. He lunged forward, hooking the iron tip into the handle of the bypass sluice gate.

"Now! Pull the lever!" Jun yelled.

With a final, desperate heave, Jun used the pole as a lever, while Liang and the others hauled the rope. The rusted cast-iron wheel on the bypass gate turned with a heavy, grinding groan. A column of dark water shot out from the lower discharge pipe, releasing the pressure on the intake pool.

The water level in the reservoir immediately began to drop, exposing the bloated bodies on the grate. Jun scrambled out of the basin, his limbs shaking violently from hypothermia. Liang wrapped him in a dry wool blanket, while Suli used her knife to clear the remaining dead from the iron bars.

CHAPTER 6: THE CABLE LINE


The gorge narrowed to its most dramatic point—a vertical drop of eight hundred meters where the two mountain walls seemed almost to touch.

Here stood the old mining cable line—a single steel cable that stretched across the abyss to an abandoned copper mine on the Jade Dragon Snow Mountain side. A rusty iron trolley, big enough to hold four people, hung from the cable, controlled by a manual winch and a heavy iron capstan on the eastern platform.

"The elders and the children must cross here," Jiazhi said, looking at the narrow trail ahead, which was blocked by a fresh rockfall. "The path to the high village is too steep for them. But the cable winch has not been greased in ten years."

Jun inspected the capstan. The iron gears were orange with rust, their teeth filled with grit and dried tallow. The main wooden frame—built of heavy fir timbers—had rotted at the ground line, the wood soft and spongy under his thumb.

"The frame will split if we put tension on the cable," Jun said. "We must shore up the base with diagonal struts and replace the rotten sills with fresh timber. Liang, get the oak timber blocks and the jack."

Using a small hydraulic bottle jack they had scavenged from an abandoned truck, Jun lifted the three-ton winch assembly two inches. The rotten fir sill crumbled like bread under the pressure, releasing a smell of damp earth and rot.

"Keep it steady, Liang," Jun warned, sliding a fresh block of seasoned oak beneath the iron baseplate. "If the jack slips, the whole frame will tip into the chasm."

From the trail behind them, a sharp whistle sounded.

Suli was standing on a high rocky outcrop fifty meters down the path. "Father! The scouts say the main group from the town has bypassed the lower barricade! There are hundreds of them, and they are moving fast!"

The wind brought the sound—a collective, dry rustle of feet on stone, like a swarm of locusts moving through dry grass.

"Get the first group into the trolley!" Jiazhi ordered.

Three elderly women and two young children climbed into the rusted iron basket. The basket swayed over the abyss, the wind rattling its sheet-metal sides.

"Jun! The winch!" Jiazhi called out.

Jun grabbed the iron capstan bar—a two-meter pine lever set into the central gear. "Liang! Help me!"

They pushed. The iron gears shrieked, their rusty teeth grinding against each other. The oak frame groaned, the wood fibers compressing under the tension. The trolley moved slowly out from the ledge, suspended over the vast, misty drop.

But the effort was too slow. As the trolley reached the middle of the chasm, the first of the town zombies emerged from the pine scrub, their eyes fixed on the moving basket.

"Keep turning!" Jun yelled, his muscles burning. "Don't look back!"

The zombies did not stop. They trotted down the trail, their limbs stiff but persistent. Suli and the village youths formed a protective circle around the winch platform, their spears held low.

The first zombie—a former tour guide still wearing a faded whistle around its neck—reached the platform. Suli thrust her spear, the iron tip entering its chest, but the figure continued to push forward, its weight sliding down the shaft. Suli was forced to drop the spear and draw her short recurve bow, releasing an arrow at point-blank range into the zombie's forehead.

The figure collapsed, but three more were right behind it.

Jun and Liang strained against the capstan bar. The iron basket reached the far side of the gorge, the elderly refugees climbing out onto the safety ledge of the Jade Dragon Mountain.

"Send it back!" Jiazhi called.

Jun released the winch dog, and the empty trolley slid back along the steel cable under its own weight, its iron wheels screaming.

"Get the next group in!" Jun shouted, his breath ragged. He grabbed the capstan bar again, ready for the next lift. The horde was now at the edge of the platform, their grey hands reaching for the winch cables as the second evacuation began.

CHAPTER 7: THE MOUNTAIN SLIDE


A fresh landslide, triggered by the vibration of the river and the weight of the climbing horde, had swept away a three-meter section of the trail, leaving a sheer limestone face with no footings.

"We are cut off," Liang said, staring at the gap. "We can't go forward, and they are behind us."

"We build a bridge," Jun said, his voice calm. "A *jiadao*—a cantilevered ladder-bridge. We will use two long spruce poles, brace them on this side with heavy stones, and slide them across to the stable ledge on the other side."

"Master, the gap is too wide," Liang argued. "The poles will bend and slide off the opposite ledge under a man's weight."

"Not if we notch them and use a king-post brace," Jun replied. He immediately began cutting a deep V-notch into the center of the first spruce pole. "Liang, prepare the cross-struts. We need five of them, fifty centimeters wide, set into mortise holes."

Working with feverish speed, they assembled the modular ladder-bridge. Jun drove the wooden pegs, securing the joints without the need for metal fasteners.

Below them on the trail, Suli and her father were holding the line. Suli's bow was warm to the touch, her fingers raw from the constant draw and release of the sinew string. She had only five arrows left in her quiver.

The zombies were climbing the scree slope below the gap, their fingers digging into the loose shale. They did not search for handholds; they simply clawed at the rock, their bodies sliding back two feet for every three feet they gained. But they were gaining.

"Jun! Is the bridge ready?" Jiazhi shouted, his knife striking the head of a climbing zombie that had reached his boots.

"Slide it out!" Jun called.

He and Liang lifted the heavy spruce ladder, pushing it across the chasm. The far end of the poles scraped the opposite ledge, sliding three inches before catching in a natural rock crevice.

"It's not anchored!" Liang yelled. "Someone has to crawl across and wedge the ends!"

"I'll go," Jun said.

He lay flat on the narrow timber bridge, his toolbox slung tight against his back. He crawled forward, the chasm yawning beneath him, the wind trying to tilt the spruce poles. As he reached the center, a zombie on the scree slope below lunged upward, its cold, grey hand catching the bottom rung of the ladder.

The bridge tilted violently, the far end slipping from its crevice.

Jun did not panic. He gripped the spruce side rails with his knees, his hands reaching for his heavy framing chisel. He leaned over the edge, the wind whipping his face, and struck a blow directly through the zombie’s wrist. The steel chisel sheared through the dried, leathery tendons and bone with a clean *crunch*. The hand released its grip, and the zombie fell backward, its body tumbling down the scree slope.

"Liang! Tension the rope!" Jun yelled, his voice carrying over the wind.

On the eastern ledge, Liang and Jiazhi threw their weight onto the safety line, pulling the bridge back into alignment. Jun crawled the remaining meter, scrambling onto the stable granite ledge of the opposite side. He quickly retrieved two heavy oak wedges from his belt and drove them between the spruce poles and the rock face, locking the bridge in place.

"Solid!" Jun called back. "Cross, one by one!"

The village archers crossed the swaying ladder, their boots slipping slightly on the wet wood, but they made it safely. Once all were across, Liang chiseled away the pine anchors on the eastern bank, dropping the bridge into the chasm to ensure the horde could not follow them.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE CLIFFSIDE GATE


They reached the outer wall of the high village—a defensive barrier of dry-stacked limestone blocks built across a narrow ridge saddle. In the center of the wall was the gatehouse, a two-story stone structure with a double-leaved wooden gate.

But the gate was in ruins. 

Built of old Yunnan spruce, the timbers had been exposed to the mountain weather for fifty years without oil. The bottom hinges had rusted away, and the wood was dry-rotted and split, with wide gaps that showed the grey mist oucoarse haire.

"The gate won't hold a single push," Elder Jiazhi said, his hand resting on the splintered wood. "The villagers are inside the ancestral hall, but if they get through the gate, the village is dead."

"We must rebuild the gate structure," Jun said. "We don't have time to make new leaves, so we will build a *kailong*—a heavy timber portcullis frame that slides vertically in guide channels. We'll use the village's vertical roof supports as the guides."

"Where do we get the timbers?" Liang asked.

"The village granary," Jun said. "The floor beams are seasoned pine, ten by fifteen centimeters. Go, Liang! Bring the cross-cut saw and the heavy spikes."

While Liang ran to the granary, Jun began clearing the old gate leaves. He used his broadaxe to chop through the rusted iron hinge bands, the metal sparks flying against the stone walls.

The first scouts of the town horde reached the ridge saddle.

They were different from the valley walkers. These were urban refugees—weary travelers in heavy coats and hiking boots, their skin grey and tight, their mouths stained with dried black blood. They moved with a silent, heavy determination, their numbers filling the narrow ridge trail.

Suli stood on the gatehouse roof, her bow drawn. She released her third-to-last arrow, striking the lead zombie in the throat. The figure stumbled but was pushed forward by the crowd behind it, its boots trampling the arrow shaft.

Jun and the village youths dragged the heavy pine granary beams to the gatehouse. Working under a rain of stones and dirt thrown up by the climbing dead, Jun chiseled the guide channels into the granite doorposts.

"Now, Liang!" Jun yelled. "Drop the vertical logs into the slot!"

They slid the first pine log into the channels. It dropped with a heavy *thud*, blocking the bottom thirty centimeters of the opening. They slid the second, then the third, building a solid wall of timber block by block.

But as they lifted the fifth log, the lead zombie reached the opening, its grey arm thrusting through the gap between the timber and the stone arch, its fingers snapping toward Jun's face.

Jun reacted instantly. He caught the zombie's wrist, twisting it back against the stone wall. The dried bones cracked under the pressure. Liang slammed the end of the pine log down, wedging the zombie's arm between the log and the stone post.

"Hold it!" Jun yelled, driving a large steel spike through the log into the wooden guides, locking the barrier.

The zombie thrashed, trapped by its arm, but the portcullis was now four logs high, blocking the entrance. Suli and the archers on the roof fired their remaining arrows, clearing the immediate threat oucoarse haire the wall.

"We need three more logs," Jun said, his chest heaving as he wiped his hands on his apron. "Get them from the granary. We must seal this portal completely before nightfall."

CHAPTER 9: THE TIGER'S LEAP


The main crossing of the Tiger Leaping Gorge was a suspension bridge that spanned the narrowest point of the river canyon—a fifty-meter gap where the water boiled around a massive rock in the center of the channel.

The bridge was the survivors' final defense.

"If we cross, we must destroy it," Elder Jiazhi said, his hand gripping the hemp support ropes. "If the town horde follows us across, the upper sanctuary will be overrun in an hour. There are too many of them for our walls."

"We will cut the ropes," Jun said. "But someone must hold the western ledge until the children are across."

The last of the village refugees scrambled across the swaying bridge, their boots clicking on the pine planks. Liang and Jiazhi stood on the eastern bank, their axes ready to chop the main hemp cables.

Jun stood on the western bank, his broadaxe held in both hands.

The main horde emerged from the gorge trail—a solid mass of hundreds of active dead, their grey faces filling the canyon width. They did not stop; they did not look at the river below. They rushed toward the bridge entrance.

Jun fought them at the threshold. His broadaxe swung in a wide, horizontal arc, the steel blade splitting heads and breaking limbs. He did not fight with anger; he fought with the clean, rhythmic precision of a woodcutter felling a forest.

"Jun! Cross!" Jiazhi shouted from the far side. "The cable is splitting!"

Liang was already chopping the northern hemp cable, the fibers popping under his axe blows. The bridge tilted violently to the left, its planks twisting.

Jun turned to run. But a zombie in a red tour jacket lunged from the scrub, grabbing the strap of his toolbox. The weight pulled Jun back, his boots slipping on the wet granite ledge.

He fell onto his back, the toolbox pinning him to the stone. The zombie crawled over him, its teeth snapping inches from his throat.

Jun reached for his chisel, driving the steel point upward through the zombie's chin into its skull. The thrashing stopped, but the dead weight remained on top of him.

On the eastern bank, Liang’s axe cut through the final strand of the northern cable. 

With a sound like a gunshot, the cable snapped, whipping across the chasm. The bridge rolled completely over, the pine planks spilling into the rushing river below. The remaining southern cable sagged, the bridge hanging vertically against the eastern cliff face.

Jun was trapped on the western ledge. Behind him, the horde was swarming over the rocks.

He scrambled to his feet, discarding the heavy toolbox strap. The only path left was the chasm itself.

In the center of the roaring river, thirty meters below and ten meters out, was the Tiger Leaping Rock—a massive granite boulder that split the current.

Jun did not look down. He ran to the edge of the cliff, used a protruding pine root as a launching block, and leaped into the void.

The wind roared in his ears, a cold, violent force that tried to turn him in mid-air. The spray from the river rose like a wall of white mist, blinding him. For a second, he was weightless, suspended between the two mountains.

*CRASH.*

He hit the wet granite surface of the Tiger Leaping Rock. The impact shot through his legs, sending a sharp, white pain through his left ankle. He fell forward, his hands clawing at the slick moss that covered the stone. The river screamed around him, a brown wall of water three meters high hitting the rock's base, throwing up a spray that nearly washed him off.

Jun lay still for a moment, his chest heaving, his fingers dug deep into a natural crack in the granite. He looked up.

On the cliff above, the zombies reached the edge. They did not stop. Several stumbled over the brink, their bodies falling past him, hitting the water with heavy splashes and instantly disappearing in the foam.

Jun slowly dragged himself up the wet rock face, his left ankle throbbing. He climbed to the highest point of the boulder, out of the river's spray.

Across the water, Liang and Jiazhi were throwing a heavy rope. It fell short, the current sweeping it away.

"Wait!" Jun yelled, waving his arm.

Suli walked to the edge of the eastern cliff. She tied a light guide line to a heavy bone arrow, notched it to her bow, and aimed high. She released the string.

The arrow hissed across the river, passing over the Tiger Leaping Rock and landing on the granite cleft behind Jun.

Jun grabbed the line. He hauled it in, pulling the heavy hemp safety rope across the churning water. He wrapped the rope around his waist and locked it with a double hitch.

"Pull!" Jun shouted.

Liang and the youths hauled the line, dragging Jun through the freezing foam as he leaped from the rock, pulling him onto the eastern landing. Jun lay on the gravel, coughing up muddy water, but he was alive.

CHAPTER 10: THE HIGH SANCTUARY


The air in the high village of the Naxi was clean and cold, smelling of cedar smoke and dry grass.

Nestled in a high alpine valley four thousand meters above sea level, the village was a cluster of traditional stone-and-timber houses, their roofs covered in grey slate tiles. The terraces around the village were green with mountain barley and potatoes, irrigated by the cold meltwater of the Haba Snow Mountain.

The bridge was gone. The western cliffs were silent, populated only by wandering shadows that could not cross the great chasm of the Jinsha River.

Jun sat on the wooden porch of Elder Jiazhi's house, his hands wrapped around a cup of hot barley tea. His body was bruised from his leap, his shoulder bandaged with clean linen, but his fingers were steady.

Beside him, Liang was sharpening a framing chisel on a grey water-stone, the rhythmic *shrrr-shrrr* of the steel a comforting sound in the quiet valley.

"You were lucky, Master Jun," Liang said, without looking up. "If you had hit the water instead of the rock ledge, the current would have carried you to Sichuan before noon."

"A carpenter must know how to measure a drop," Jun said softly, taking a sip of the bitter tea.

Elder Jiazhi stepped onto the porch, carrying a newly finished Naxi bow. The wood was wrapped in red silk, the horn tips carved with the image of the mountain tiger.

"The village is safe for the winter," the elder said, handing the bow to Jun. "Our granaries are full, and our walls are strong. Our young men are practicing with the bows every day, and Suli is teaching the children how to weave the hemp string. But the radio we repaired has received a transmission from the north."

Jun set his tea down. "From where?"

"Gansu Province," Jiazhi replied, looking toward the distant mountain peaks. "Jiayuguan Pass. The keepers of the western gate say they have built a desert coalition of survivors. They are holding the old fortress against the northern migration, but they need builders. Their timber towers are cracking under the dry heat."

Jun looked at Liang. Liang stopped sharpening the chisel, his eyes meeting his master's.

"The Great Wall needs its carpenters," Liang said, a small smile touching his lips.

Jun stood up, his joints popping. He reached for his broadaxe, checking the edge with his thumb. "Pack the tools, Liang. We have a long road north."

================================================================================

STORY 14: THE GOBI GATE
Setting: Jiayuguan Pass, Gansu Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE GOBI WIND


The wind of the Hexi Corridor did not blow; it gouged.

It swept down from the frozen heights of the Qilian Mountains, carrying a fine, amber sand that stripped the paint from road signs and wore the edges of the bricks down to round curves. This was the throat of the desert, a gravel basin squeezed between the mountain ranges, and in the center of the dust-red haze stood Jiayuguan—the "First and Greatest Pass Under Heaven." Its massive gate towers rose thirty meters above the desert floor, their three-tiered tiled roofs upturned at the corners like the wings of giant birds catching the rising heat.

Jun pulled his blue cotton scarf tighter across his nose, the dry wind tasting of alkaline salt and cold dust. His eyes were squinted to narrow slits, the glare of the setting sun reflecting off the gravel plain with a blinding, yellow light.

Beside him, Liang dragged the two-wheeled handcart, his head bowed against the wind. The iron-rimmed wooden wheels ground loudly over the pebbles, the sound lost in the constant whistle of the wind through the rampart battlements. Liang’s cheeks were chapped red, his skin dry and peeling from the lack of moisture.

"The air is like fire, Master," Liang said, his voice a dry rasp. He did not look up. "It sucks the water out of your mouth before you can swallow."

"Keep your mouth shut and breathe through the cloth," Jun said, his voice muffled by the scarf. "The desert doesn't give you water back. We have one kilometer to the western gate."

They had traveled north from the high plateaus of Sichuan, descending the long gravel roads of Qinghai and crossing the dry basin of the Hexi Corridor. Along the way, they had seen how the Gobi had slow-cured the zombie crisis. In the dry, hot air of the north, the bodies of the dead did not rot as they did in the damp south. Instead, they evaporated, the dry winds drying their skin and muscles until they turned to tough, dark leather, hard as old boots. They did not smell of decay; they smelled of dry clay and salt, their stiff, mechanical movements rattling like dry bamboo in the wind.

"Hold!" a voice called from the battlements of the Rouyuan Gate.

Jun stopped, letting the heavy oak chest slide from his shoulder onto the gravel.

On the high brick rampart, a watchman stood behind a crenel. He wore a heavy sheepskin coat over a faded green military jacket, a wide straw hat tied under his chin. In his hands, he held a heavy recurve bow, its limbs made of polished birch wood and wild ibex horn, its string drawn to his ear.

"Who goes?" the watchman called down, the wind carrying his voice.

"Carpenters from the south," Jun shouted back, pulling down his scarf. "We worked on the Great Wall at Simatai and the water gates of Zhejiang. We received the radio signal from the Jiuquan coalition."

The watchman lowered the bow. He turned and gestured to the winch room inside the gate tower.

With a heavy, metallic rattle that shuddered the brick walls, a small side-wicket door inside the massive wooden gate leaves began to slide open.

"I am Commander Ma," the archer said as he descended the stone steps of the barbican to meet them in the dry moat. His face was dark and lined, his fingers wrapped in leather guards. "We have sixty refugees inside the inner courtyard and twenty soldiers. The outer ramparts are holding, but the dry wind is splitting our watchtower timbers. If the corner tower fails, the northern rampart will slide into the sand."

Jun picked up his toolbox, adjusting the strap. "Show me the timber towers first, Commander. In this heat, timber shrinks. If the mortise joints are dry-stacked without wedges, they will slip under the wind load."

They entered through the narrow stone archway. Inside, the barbican was a trap of high brick walls, designed to pen an invading army in a crossfire. Now, it was a silent courtyard, populated by silent guards holding spears. The air was still here, hot and heavy, smelling of woodsmoke, roasted wheat, and the metallic tang of dry iron.

"The northern corner tower is the worst," Ma said, leading them up the brick ramp to the watchtowers. "The columns are leaning two inches toward the desert."

Jun inspected the massive corner column—a log of seasoned northern larch wood, thirty centimeters thick. The timber had split along its grain, a deep crack running from the base to the first floor joist, its fibers dried and brittle under the desert sun.

"The dry air has sucked the moisture from the sapwood," Jun said, running his fingers along the split. "The larch is strong, but when it dries too fast, it shears. We must shore it up with iron collar bands and pack the core with hot pine pitch to stop the split from spreading."

He looked at Liang, who had collapsed onto a stone bench, his chest heaving as he drank from a leather water bladder. "Get the draw-knife and the iron collars, Liang. We have work to do before the night wind rises."

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE EARTHEN WALL


The outer walls of Jiayuguan were not built of stone, but of rammed earth—*hangtu*—a traditional mixture of yellow loess clay, gravel, and glutinous rice water, packed layer by layer into wooden frames.

For six hundred years, these walls had stood against the Gobi. But now, a major fracture had opened in the northern rampart, a five-meter-wide vertical split that reached from the parapet to the stone foundation. The dry wind had evaporated the residual moisture in the clay, and the pressure of the shifting sand dunes oucoarse haire was pushing the outer face of the wall outward.

"If the wall bulges another two inches, the foundation will shear," Jun said, running his hand along the rough, straw-flecked clay of the split. "We cannot use stone to patch it; the weight will only pull the cracked section down faster. We must rebuild it using the traditional *hangtu* method, layer by layer, and tie it back to the stable core with timber anchors."

"Master, we don't have enough timber for the forms," Liang said, looking at their small cart.

"We use the old scaffolding poles from the gate tower," Jun replied. "And we will use the local desert scrub—*suosuo* wood—to reinforce the earth layers. The scrub roots are tough and stringy; they will act like iron rebar in the clay."

Jun and the soldiers set up the wooden forms, lashing the pine planks together with thick hemp ropes. They mixed the yellow loess soil with river gravel and a hot, steaming broth of boiled glutinous rice that they had prepared in a giant iron vat in the courtyard.

Working in the dry heat, they shoveled the damp mixture into the forms in ten-centimeter layers. Then, using heavy wooden rammers—*hangchui*—they pounded the earth until it was compressed to half its original thickness.

"Strike together!" Jun commanded, his voice set to the rhythm of the rammer's fall. *Thump. Thump. Thump.*

Below them, on the gravel flats, the first of the desert dead reached the dry moat. They were dry, their skin brown and cracked like old leather, their joints stiffened by the salt deposits of the basin. They did not run, but they did not stop; they walked into the deep sand of the moat, their boots sinking four inches with every step.

Commander Ma stood on the parapet above, his bow string clicking. An arrow struck the lead crawler in the forehead, the steel head splitting the dried bone with a sharp *crack*. The zombie fell forward, its face burying itself in the yellow dust, its limbs twitching once before going silent.

"Keep ramming!" Jun yelled, his hands raw from the wooden handle. "The clay must be packed before the sun dries the rice water!"

*Thump. Thump.*

The wooden rammers fell in unison, the loess clay turning into a dense, solid mass inside the pine forms. Liang worked beside Jun, his face covered in yellow dust, his shirt soaked in sweat.

Between the layers of clay, Jun laid bundles of dry *suosuo* wood roots, spacing them thirty centimeters apart. He locked the ends of the roots around the vertical larch anchors driven deep into the stable core of the wall.

"This is the *tulao*—the earth tie," Jun explained to the soldiers. "The roots will hold the outer face to the inner core. Even if the wind dries the clay, the wall won't slip."

The outer horde was growing. Drawn by the rhythmic *thump* of the wooden rammers, dozens of Gobi walkers emerged from the sand dunes, their leathered bodies clicking as they stumbled toward the breach. They did not scream, but the dry rustling of their skin and the clicking of their teeth created a dry, whispering wind that blew over the ramparts.

Commander Ma’s archers fired in turns, their bone-tipped arrows splitting skulls, but the sheer numbers were beginning to fill the dry moat.

"The forms are full!" Liang called out, throwing down his shovel.

Jun climbed to the top of the form, inspecting the packed clay. The loess was hard as concrete, the sticky rice broth binding the gravel and loess into a single, seamless block.

"Release the ropes!" Jun ordered.

They cut the hemp bindings, and the pine planks fell away, exposing the new, yellow-brown face of the wall. The split was sealed, the rammed earth flush with the ancient Ming rampart.

The horde reached the base of the wall, their claws scratching at the fresh clay. But the earth was packed too tight, and the suosuo roots held the structure firm. The zombies could find no handholds on the smooth, hard surface.

"It's holding," Commander Ma said, looking down from the parapet. "But the wind is shifting. The sand storm is coming from the north, and the western gate is still unbraced."

Jun wiped his brow, looking toward the dark wall of dust rising on the horizon. "We move to the gate, Commander. Bring the charcoal and the iron forge."

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE SAND TRAPS


The dunes to the north of the pass were shifting walls of fine, yellow loess sand that moved five meters a year under the pressure of the Gobi wind. 

Here, the outer defense line of the fortress was vulnerable. The sand had piled up against the dry moat, creating a natural ramp that allowed the Gobi walkers to bypass the rammed-earth wall and reach the lower catwalks of the northern watchtower.

"We cannot dig a ditch here," Liang said, his boots sinking six inches into the loose sand slope. "The wind will fill it back in an hour. It's like digging in water."

"We don't dig a ditch to keep them out," Jun said, his hand resting on a pile of split pine boards in the cart. "We dig a V-chute. We will build a series of sand-funnel traps—*shalu*—along the ridge of the dune. We'll line the sides with pine boards greased with mutton-fat and anchor them to granite stakes driven deep into the gravel bed beneath the sand. When the dead step on the boards, they will slide to the bottom of the V-pit and be buried under their own weight as the sand slides behind them."

"How deep is the gravel bed?" Liang asked.

"One meter down," Jun said. "We use the iron-tipped crowbar to drive the stakes. Let's move, Liang. The wind is picking up."

Working on the loose sand face, Jun and Liang excavated three V-shaped pits, each four meters wide and three meters deep. The sand constantly slid back into the hole, forcing them to work in short, frantic bursts. They drove six granite stakes into the hard gravel bed at the bottom of each pit, then lashed split pine boards to the stakes, forming a steep, funnel-shaped chute.

Liang heated a large iron bucket of mutton-fat over a small charcoal stove, the smell of hot grease rising in the dry air. Using a wide horsehair brush, he coated the pine boards with a thick layer of the yellow fat. The grease dried instantly in the cold wind, forming a slick, glassy film over the wood.

"Here they come," Suli warned from the watchtower ridge.

Through the rising dust, a pack of thirty Gobi walkers appeared. They were dried to leathery husks, their light cotton hiking trousers and wind-breakers caked in dry salt. They walked with a heavy, swinging gait, their feet clicking on the pebbles before they stepped onto the soft sand of the dune.

The lead zombie—a former construction worker with a faded plastic hardhat still strapped to its head—stepped onto the lip of the first funnel trap.

Its leather boot hit the greased pine board. With a sudden, silent slide, the zombie lost its footing and shot down the V-chute, landing on its back at the bottom of the pit. The sand from the dune lip slid down behind it, burying its legs.

The second and third zombies followed, sliding down the slick wood and piling onto the first. They thrashed, their dry limbs tangling in the narrow bottom of the V-pit. But they could find no traction on the greased pine; their fingers slid off the fat-coated wood, and the constant flow of loose sand from the dune edge buried them deeper with every movement.

"It works," Liang said, watching the sand fill the pit. "They're burying themselves."

"Keep greasing the outer chutes," Jun said, adjusting his scarf. "The sand will cover the fat in an hour. We must set a secondary layer of boards above the first to catch the drift."

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE IRON PORTCULLIS


The Rouyuan Gatehouse was the main portal of the inner fortress, a massive brick structure with double wooden doors clad in thick iron plates.

But the winching system that controlled the heavy iron portcullis—the secondary barrier behind the wooden doors—was jammed.

The portcullis was stuck halfway, leaving a one-meter gap at the bottom. The cause was rust; the main oak axle—a log forty centimeters thick that carried the iron lifting chains—had warped under the extreme dry heat, and the cast-iron guide gears had seized in their granite sockets.

"The gate must close," Commander Ma said, his hand resting on the jammed chain. "The scouts say the main northern migration has reached the dry lake bed. If they get through the outer moat, they will rush this gate. If the portcullis is open, we can't hold them."

Jun inspected the winch room. The iron gears were brown with rust and clogged with sand. The oak axle was bowed, the wood fibers dry and cracked from the heat.

"We must heat the iron collar bearings," Jun said, pointing to the gear sockets in the granite wall. "The metal has contracted around the rusted shaft. If we heat it with charcoal, the iron will expand, and we can force the axle to turn. Liang, set up the portable forge and the bellows."

Liang carried the small clay forge to the winch room, filling the hearth with oak charcoal. He pumped the leather bellows, the air rushing through the nozzle and turning the charcoal into a bright, white heat.

Jun used a pair of long iron tongs to hold hot charcoal blocks against the cast-iron bearing collars. The heat radiated through the stone wall, the smell of hot iron and burning grease filling the small room.

*Hiss.* Jun poured a small stream of wild sesame oil onto the hot metal, the oil smoking and cutting through the rust.

"The wind has arrived," Suli called from the gatehouse window.

Oucoarse haire, the sky had turned a dark, bruised purple. The sand storm was hitting the fortress, the wind carrying a wall of dust that reduced visibility to three meters. In the yellow haze, the shapes of the Gobi walkers were visible, their leathery bodies rattling as they crowded against the half-open wooden gate.

"They're pushing!" Ma warned.

A zombie in a brown sheepskin coat thrust its head under the half-open portcullis, its dried teeth snapping at Ma's boots. Ma used his spear to hold it back, his muscles straining.

"Now, Liang!" Jun yelled, grabbing the iron capstan bar. "Turn the lever!"

They threw their weight against the pine bar. The iron gears shrieked, a shower of rust and sand falling onto their shoulders. The oak axle groaned, its warped wood fibers resisting the turn.

*Clack.*

The gear moved one tooth.

"Again!" Jun roared.

They pushed, their boots slipping on the brick floor. The heated iron bearing expanded, the sesame oil lubricating the rusted shaft. The gear began to turn with a heavy, rhythmic *clack-clack-clack*.

The iron portcullis slid down, its heavy granite bottom slab scraping the stone threshold with a dry rumble. It hit the ground with a solid, room-shaking *thud*, crushing the head of the guide zombie under its weight and sealing the portal.

Jun released the winch bar, collapsing against the brick wall. His face was black with soot, his hands blistered from the hot iron.

"It's closed," Liang said, his voice barely a whisper through his dust-soaked scarf.

"For now," Jun said, looking at the warped oak axle. "But the axle is cracked. If we lift it again, the timber will split. We must build a secondary timber shoring system to support the portcullis weight before the storm ends."

---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE BEACON PLATFORM


The beacon tower—*fengsui*—stood on a high clay ridge two hundred meters north of the main fortress. It was a square, tapered tower built of rammed earth and sundried loess bricks, its roof housing a large iron fire-grate designed to send warning signals across the desert.

But the sand gale was howling.

The wind from the north was so violent that it blew the smoke flat against the ridge, dispersing the soot before it could rise. If the signal could not be seen, the Jiuquan coalition watchmen thirty kilometers away would not know the pass was under siege, and the rescue convoy would not be sent.

"We must block the draft," Jun said, shielding his eyes as the sand whipped over the parapet. "The wind is hitting the grate from the northern notch. We must build a curved timber screen—*difeng*—around the windward side of the grate to create a pockets of still air, allowing the smoke to rise straight."

"Master, the timber will catch fire if it's too close to the grate," Liang warned, his voice muffled by his scarf.

"We will line the inner face of the pine screen with wet clay," Jun said. "The loess silt from the courtyard is thick and sticky. If we smear it four inches thick on the wood, the heat won't burn the planks. Suli, get the youths to carry the wet clay from the well!"

Jun and Liang worked on the narrow, wind-swept roof of the beacon tower. The wind was a constant scream, trying to lift them from the ledge. They set up four vertical spruce posts, anchoring the bottom tenons into the loess brick joints using driven iron pegs. They lashed pine boards horizontally across the posts, forming a semi-circular wall two meters high around the northern side of the grate.

Suli and the youths carried vats of wet loess clay up the tower steps. Jun and Liang worked quickly, slabbing the sticky yellow mud onto the wood face, smoothing it with their trowels. The dry wind immediately began to dry the clay, cracking the surface but locking it into the timber joints.

"Ready!" Jun called. "Light the straw!"

Liang threw a bundle of dry desert straw, diesel oil, and dried wolf dung—the traditional fuel of the border guards—into the iron grate. He struck a match, the fire catching instantly.

A thick, black column of smoke rose from the grate. The curved timber screen blocked the northern wind, creating a pocket of still air. The smoke did not disperse; it shot straight up into the purple storm sky, a dense, wind-resistant pillar of black soot that was visible for miles across the gravel plain.

Through the yellow haze, three kilometers to the south, a small, answering column of white smoke rose from the next watchtower.

"They've seen it," Commander Ma said, his hand lowering from his brow. "The coalition is moving."

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE WELL OF THE PASS


The well of the pass—*guanjing*—was the only water source inside the fortress, a deep shaft sunk thirty meters into the gravel bed where the underground runoff from the Qilian Mountains collected.

But the water was black.

A bloated zombie—a former desert packer who had fallen into the shaft days before—had been caught in the bottom bucket. Its body had decomposed, contaminating the well with a greasy film and a sweet, rotting stench that made the water useless.

"The refugees have no water," Commander Ma said, looking at the bucket of dark, oily water. "If we cannot clean the well, we must evacuate the fort. In this heat, a man dies in three days without water."

Jun inspected the well house. "We cannot clean the shaft under siege. We must build a gravity-fed water filtration tower—*shuilong*—using stacked wooden vats. We will filter the water through layers of willow charcoal, sand, and gravel. It will strip the organic rot and the oil from the water."

"Will it clean the poison, Master?" Liang asked.

"The willow charcoal is the key," Jun said. "It has been charred in a closed kiln without oxygen; its surface is covered in millions of micro-pores that will trap the organic impurities. Go, Liang! Build the fire to char the willow blocks from the creek bed."

While Liang prepared the charcoal, Jun built the filter tower. He stacked three large oak water vats, drilling a series of small outlet holes in the bottom of each. 

In the top vat, he placed a thirty-centimeter layer of coarse river gravel to catch the large sand particles and debris.

In the middle vat, he packed a fifty-centimeter layer of fine desert sand, washed twice in boiling water to clear the salt.

In the bottom vat, he packed a forty-centimeter layer of the hand-charred willow charcoal, locking the bed with a layer of clean cotton cloth they had boiled in the kitchen.

"Pour the water," Jun commanded.

The soldiers emptied the black well water into the top vat. The water seeped slowly through the gravel, then the sand, disappearing into the charcoal bed.

Below the bottom vat, Jun set a clean pine bucket.

For ten minutes, the room was silent save for the *drip-drip-drip* of the water through the wood.

*Plop.*

The first drop of water hit the pine bucket. It was clear as glass, the black silt and the greasy film left behind in the upper vats.

Jun caught the drop on his finger, sniffing it. The stench was gone; it smelled only of clean sand and willow wood. He tasted it. The water was flat and cold, with a faint taste of ash, but it was clean.

"It is pure," Jun said, handing the cup to Commander Ma.

"You have saved the garrison, builder," Ma said, drinking the water in a single swallow.

But as he finished, a loud crash echoed from the northern courtyard. The old corner tower, weakened by the wind and the pressure of the scaling dead, had bulged three inches, and its timber dougong brackets were beginning to split.

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE HORSE ARCHERS


The archers of the Jiayuguan Pass were running out of ammunition.

The defense had consumed over two thousand arrows in two days, and the supply of birch shafts and steel tips in the armory was empty. Without arrows, the watchmen could not defend the outer V-traps or clear the scaling dead from the moat walls.

"We need wood," Commander Ma said, looking at the empty racks. "But there are no forests in the Gobi. The only willow trees are along the dry creek bed three kilometers away, which is surrounded by the dead."

"We don't need willow," Jun said, looking at the old packing crates stacked in the courtyard. "The pine wood of these boxes is seasoned and straight. We can split it into three-eighths-inch square blanks, then shave them down to round arrow shafts using a hollow plane—*dulian*. For the tips, we will use the bones of the sheep we slaughtered for meat. A sheep-bone tip, carved to a three-sided point, will split a zombie skull as easily as steel."

"How do we attach the feathers?" Liang asked.

"Animal glue," Jun said. "We will boil the hide scrapings and hooves in the iron pot until they turn to gel. It will lock the goose feathers to the pine wood so they won't slip in the desert gale."

Jun and the refugees set up an arrow shop in the gatehouse basement. They split the pine crates with axes, then used hand-planes to shave the blanks down to perfect, twelve-gram shafts. Liang carved the sheep-bone tips, using his bench chisel to notch the three-sided heads, while Suli and the women lashed the feathers with silk thread and hot hide glue.

They made three hundred arrows in four hours.

Temur, a veteran horseman from the Gansu grasslands, carried the new arrows to his mount. He led a band of ten horse archers out through the northern wicket gate, their ponies trotting silently over the gravel.

They did not engage the horde directly. Using the speed of their horses, they rode in a wide circle around the flanks of the Gobi walkers, firing their sheep-bone arrows into the crowd. Suli’s bone tips flew straight in the wind, the three-sided points splitting the dried, leathery skulls of the lead walkers.

"Follow!" Temur shouted, his horse turning.

The horsemen drew the horde away from the moat, leading them toward the western basin where the soft sand dunes rose thirty meters high. The zombies, following the sound of the horses, waded into the deep loess sand. Their stiff, dried limbs sank into the dunes, their movement slowing to a crawl as the sand constantly shifted under their feet.

Temur’s men rode along the hard gravel ridges, firing their bows until the basin was filled with trapped, thrashing walkers.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE CORNER TOWER


The northern corner watchtower was a two-story timber structure set on the high angle of the rampart, its heavy hip-roof supported by a complex network of interlocking wooden brackets—*dougong*.

But the corner was failing.

The constant vibration of the sand storm and the weight of the climbing dead had shifted the main corner column, causing the double-layered *dougong* brackets to slip from their mortise seats. The roof truss was sagging four inches, the pine rafters groaning under the weight of the clay tiles.

"The tower will collapse," Liang said, looking at the shifting joints. "If this bracket shears, the whole northern catwalk will fall into the moat, opening a ten-meter gap in our defense line."

"We must jack the roof," Jun said. "And drive oak keys—*sunzi*—into the sliding tenons to lock the bracket set. Liang, get the screw-jack and the oak blocks. We must work from the outer scaffolding."

Jun climbed onto the outer timber scaffold, suspended twenty meters above the dry moat. The sand gale was at its peak, the wind trying to rip the spruce boards from the brackets. Below him, in the dust haze, the remaining Gobi walkers were scratching the brick foundation, their dried claws clicking like stones.

He set the iron screw-jack beneath the main horizontal beam of the watchtower roof, resting the base on a solid block of oak.

"Turn, Liang!" Jun called.

Liang turned the iron screw with a heavy lever. The jack groaned, the steel screw threads compressing the dirt and grease. Slowly, the heavy roof beam rose.

*Creeeeak.*

The sagging rafters straightened, the interlocking *dougong* brackets sliding back into their original mortise slots.

Jun chiseled two flat pockets into the sliding tenons. He took two seasoned oak keys, dipped them in hot pine pitch, and drove them into the slots with his mallet.

*Thwack. Thwack.*

The oak keys bit deep, locking the brackets. Jun driven two horizontal iron pins through the collar joints, securing the frame against the wind.

"Release the jack," Jun ordered.

Liang eased the screw. The beam settled onto the locked bracket set, the timber silent. The watchtower roof was straight, its list corrected.

"It's locked," Jun said, looking at the joint. The oak keys, sealed with black pitch, held the larch columns in a tight grip.

But as he climbed back down to the rampart, Suli called out from the watchtower. "Master Jun! The wind has changed! The storm is dropping, but the main migration is moving through the sand traps! They've filled the dunes with their bodies!"

---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE GOBI STORM


The wind had not dropped; it had folded.

The sand gale from the north met a hot, rising draft from the southern gravel plain, creating a massive, swirling dust storm—a *heifeng* or black wind—that turned the afternoon sky to absolute darkness. The air was thick and yellow, filled with a coarse loess dust that reduced visibility to less than one meter, making it impossible to see the crenels or the person standing next to you.

Under the cover of the storm, the Gobi walkers surged.

They were no longer slow; the sand storm did not affect their milky corneas, and their leathery skin shielded them from the biting dust. They climbed the body ramp at the northern wall, their dried limbs scraping the clay.

With a deafening crash that was muffled by the wind, a five-meter section of the rammed-earth wall—weakened by the previous split and the pressure of the horde—collapsed inward, dropping a mountain of loose loess clay and suosuo roots into the northern courtyard.

"Breach!" Commander Ma's voice was a distant, choked scream.

Jun and Liang were caught in the courtyard, the dust blinding them. The wind carried the dry *clack-clack* of teeth and the rustling of leathery bodies. The zombies were crawling over the rubble mound, their hands reaching through the yellow haze.

"Fight by sound!" Jiazhi yelled, his Naxi knife swinging in the dark.

Jun drew his broadaxe, holding the hickory handle with both hands. He could not see the dead, but he could hear the scrape of their boots on the clay. He swung the axe in a short, vertical arc, the steel head splitting a leathered skull with a solid *tunk*.

Beside him, Liang used his pushing pole to clear the space, knocking the crawlers back down the rubble slope.

"We must block the breach!" Jun shouted, his mouth instantly filling with dust. "We cannot rebuild the clay in this storm! We must drop a timber form and fill it with the stones from the courtyard!"

"Master, we can't see the post sockets!" Liang called out, coughing.

"Work by touch!" Jun ordered. "Feel the granite foundation blocks! Find the anchor slots!"

Working in the swirling loess, Jun and Liang dragged three heavy spruce logs to the breach. Jun knelt in the dust, his hands scanning the granite foundation until his fingers found the chiseled mortise slot. He guided the log's tenon into the socket by touch, while Liang driven the wedges with the mallet.

The wind tried to lift the timber, but the heavy oak wedges locked the post. They slid the second and third poles across, forming a rough wood partition across the breach.

Behind them, Suli and Ma stood on the rubble mound, their weapons striking in the dark. They fought with a desperate, rhythmic precision, clearing the zombies that climbed the loess pile before they could reach the carpenters.

---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE DESERT GATE


The sand storm cleared as suddenly as it had arrived, leaving behind a silent, dust-covered world. The morning sun broke through the yellow haze, its light reflecting off the loess flats.

The breach was sealed.

Jun and Liang had filled the gap behind the spruce barrier with three tons of granite cobbles and dry loam, creating a heavy crib wall (*mutong*) that blocked the entry. The Gobi walkers oucoarse haire were gone, their bodies buried under the shifting sand dunes of the basin or trapped in the sand-funnel pits.

The fortress was safe, its walls standing.

Jun sat on a loess brick steps of the Rouyuan Gate, his face covered in yellow loess, his knuckles raw and bleeding from the stone work. Beside him, Liang was cleaning the screw-jack, using a piece of oilcloth to wipe the sand from the threads.

"We have braced the gate, Master," Liang said, a tired smile touching his face. "The portcullis is shored, and the corner watchtower is straight."

"A gate is only as good as the wood that holds it," Jun said, his voice quiet. He adjusted his scarf, the dry wind still carrying a faint smell of salt.

Commander Ma walked over, carrying a wooden tray of dry mutton and barley cakes. "The scouts say the road south through Sichuan is clear. The migration has moved east toward the yellow river valleys. You have saved the pass, carpenters. Jiayuguan will stand."

"But the rest of the wall is waiting," Jun said, looking toward the distant Qilian peaks. "The Great Wall stretches for thousands of miles, and every pass needs its builders."

Suli walked to the gatehouse landing, her recurve bow slung across her back. She held a small, portable radio receiver, its speaker crackling with static.

"Master Jun," she called. "The radio received a message from Guangxi. Yangshuo. The Li River coalition says their bamboo flotilla is under siege from the delta dead. They need carpenters to reinforce the rafts and build water traps."

Jun stood up, his joints popping in the dry heat. He reached for his toolbox, checking the latch.

"Pack the cart, Liang," Jun said, his eyes turning south. "We head to the green water of Guangxi."

================================================================================

STORY 15: THE RAFTS OF YANGSHUO
Setting: Li River, Yangshuo, Guangxi Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE GREEN RIVER


The water of the Li River was the color of polished jade—clear, cold, and deceptive.

It wound between the towering karst limestone peaks of Yangshuo, which rose vertically from the valley floor like green stone teeth catching the morning mist. For centuries, this landscape had inspired painters and poets, its quiet waters and dramatic cliffs a symbol of natural harmony. But now, the river was a road of flight.

Jun stood on the gravel bank of the river, his hand resting on the hickory handle of his broadaxe. He looked out across the water. The current was slow here, but the surface was marked by constant ripples. Every few minutes, a dark, bloated shape would drift past, suspended just below the surface, its limbs moving with the flow.

These were the delta dead, water-logged zombies that had floated down from the industrial cities of Guangzhou and Foshan. Their skin was pale and swollen, their eyes eaten away by fish, but their fingers still clawed at the water, their jaws snapping with a wet, hollow sound whenever they drifted close to the banks.

Beside him, Liang sat on the handle of their handcart, his head bowed. He was covered in yellow loess dust from Gansu, his throat dry despite the dampness of the river valley. "It feels different here, Master," Liang said. "The air is thick. It sticks to the skin."

"The air is wet, Liang," Jun said, his eyes scanning the opposite bank. "And the river is alive with the dead. We cannot use the land trails; the bamboo groves are thick with shadows."

A low, hollow splash sounded from the reeds twenty meters upstream.

Jun did not turn his head, but his grip on the broadaxe tightened. He chiseled a flat tenon into a pine block on his cart, his fingers moving with practiced ease.

From the green shadow of a giant weeping willow, a long, flat bamboo raft emerged. It was built of ten thick canes of green bamboo (*maozhu*) lashed together, its deck carrying a small wicker shelter and an iron fire-pot. Standing on the deck was Xiaoyan, a young woman of twenty in a blue cotton tunic and trousers, her hair tied up in a clean cloth. In her hands, she held a three-meter bamboo pole tipped with a sharp, two-pronged iron hook—a *yinggou*, the traditional cormorant fishing tool of the Li River.

Beside her, Elder Liu, a man of sixty with a face dark as river silt, steered the raft with a long wooden oar set into an iron pin at the stern.

"Carpenters," Liu called out, his voice low and raspy. "The trail is dead. Come onto the water. The flotilla is waiting at the Xingping bend."

Jun nodded, gesturing to the cart. "We have timber and tools. Can the raft take the weight?"

"The *maozhu* is strong," Xiaoyan said, guiding the raft to the gravel bank. "But the water is rising, and the delta dead are gathering at the lock. Jump in."

Jun and Liang lifted the cart onto the raft deck. The bamboo tubes groaned under the weight, the raft dipping three inches into the green water, but it remained stable. Elder Liu pushed off from the bank, the long oar slicing the current with a silent, rhythmic sweep.

"The river is our only path," Liu said as they drifted into the deep channel. "The land-borne dead have filled the narrow karst passes, but they cannot swim. They sink to the bottom like stones. But the water walkers—the ones that have bloated—are different. They float, and the current carries them straight to our anchorage."

Jun adjusted his tool chest. "We must reinforce the rafts, Liu. If a bloated walker grabs the bamboo, its weight will roll the deck. We need to lash the rafts in pairs, forming a catamaran system with raised decks, and build V-shaped funnels to guide the floating dead away from the hulls."

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE BAMBOO FLOTILLA


The Xingping bend was a deep, quiet basin where the Li River widened, surrounded by five limestone peaks that rose like fingers of a giant hand.

Here, the survivors had built a floating street of thirty lashed bamboo rafts, their decks carrying small wicker huts, vegetable boxes, and cages of fishing cormorants. The flotilla housed eighty refugees, who lived on the water, fishing for food and using the river's current as their main defense.

But the flotilla was sagging.

The green bamboo canes of the older rafts had begun to rot, their chambers filling with water as the organic skin split under the dampness. The hemp ropes used to lash the rafts together were loose, their strands rotting from the constant exposure to the river spray.

"The rafts are too low," Jun said, inspecting the main bridge raft. "The water is washing over the decks, and the split bamboo is losing its spring. We must reinforce the hulls with double-layered *maozhu* poles and spruce cross-beams, locked with swelling oak wedges."

"Master, we don't have enough seasoned oak for wedges," Liang said.

"We split the old oar handles," Jun replied. "And we will use the wild bamboo vines—*zhuban*—to lash the joints. The vine is tough and flexible; when it dries, it contracts, locking the wood tighter than any hemp rope."

Jun and Liang set up a carpentry shop on a large, flat cargo raft in the center of the flotilla. They split the thick green bamboo canes, notches the ends to fit the spruce cross-beams. Jun taught the young fishermen how to carve the * guyin sun*—the traditional interlocking joint that allowed the timber to flex without splitting under the movement of the waves.

They worked quickly, their hand-planes shaving the green wood, the smell of fresh sap and river silt filling the air.

"Water walkers!" Suli called from the lookout gantry on the central peak.

From the reeds at the western bank, a group of ten bloated zombies drifted into the basin. They were industrial workers from the delta, their skin blue-grey and swollen like plastic drums. They floated on their backs, their faces turned to the sky, their fingers twitching as they caught the scent of the living.

The current carried the lead zombie straight toward the main residential raft.

"Xiaoyan! The hook!" Elder Liu shouted.

Xiaoyan ran to the raft edge, her *yinggou* raised. She thrust the iron hook into the zombie's shoulder, using the length of the pole to push the bloated figure away from the bamboo canes. But the zombie’s hand reached out, its fingers locking around the green bamboo. The raft tilted, water washing over the deck.

"Help her!" Liang yelled, grabbing a spear.

Jun ran to the edge. He did not use a weapon; he used his broadaxe. With a single, vertical blow, he chopped through the zombie's wrist against the spruce cross-beam. The hand released its grip, and the bloated body drifted away, its limbs twitching in the green current.

Jun helped Xiaoyan pull the pole back. "The rafts must be lashed in pairs, Liu," Jun said. "We need a wider base. If we link the decks, the lateral stability will double, and the water walkers won't be able to tilt the hulls."

"Do it, carpenter," Liu said, wiping his brow. "The lock of Xingping is only two kilometers, and the scouts say it's jammed with hundreds of floating dead. We must open the gates to clear the channel, or the flotilla will be swamped."

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE CORMORANT HOOKS


The fishing rafts of the Li River were not built for combat.

Their low decks and open sides made the defenders vulnerable to the water walkers, who could swim beneath the bamboo poles and grab the ankles of the crew. The traditional cormorant hooks—*yinggou*—were useful, but holding a three-meter bamboo pole against the drag of the current and the thrashing of a hundred-kilogram body was physically exhausting.

"The poles are too heavy," Xiaoyan said, her arms trembling as she rested her iron-tipped hook against the pine railing. "My shoulders feel like they are filled with gravel. If we face a larger group at the lock, we won't have the strength to hold them."

"We must mount the poles," Jun said, looking at the spruce railing. "We will build a swivel socket block—*shizishu*—from seasoned pear wood and anchor it to the cross-beams. It will act like a rowlock, carrying the weight of the pole and allowing the watchman to guide the iron hook with one hand using leverage."

"How do we lock the pole in the socket?" Liang asked.

"A simple leather collar and a pine key," Jun said. "It will allow the pole to slide forward and back, but prevent it from being pulled out of the mount by the dead. Go, Liang! Cut the pear wood blocks and get the tallow to grease the sockets."

Jun and Liang worked on the bow decks of the five lead rafts. Jun chiseled the swivel sockets, cutting a vertical notch that allowed the block to turn three hundred and sixty degrees, and a horizontal pin seat that carried the pole's weight. Liang wrapped the bamboo shafts in thick cow-hide collars to prevent the wood from wearing down against the pear wood sockets.

They mounted ten swivel hooks on the flotilla bow, five on each side.

To demonstrate, Xiaoyan stepped to the port gantry, placing her hand on the end of the bamboo pole. The mount carried the entire weight of the three-meter shaft, allowing her to swing the iron-tipped hook with a simple flick of her wrist.

A bloated zombie drifted within range, its pale head bobbing in the current. Xiaoyan pushed the pole forward, the collar sliding smoothly in the greased socket. The iron fork caught the zombie's throat, and with a simple downward lean on her end of the pole, she lifted the zombie's head, guiding its body away from the raft with the leverage.

"It's light," she said, her eyes wide as she felt the mechanical advantage. "I can hold it with my thumb and two fingers."

"It's a simple lever," Jun said, his hand resting on his toolbox. "The socket carries the load, and the cross-beam distributes the strain to the entire raft. Now we must prepare the ropes for the sandbar ahead."

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE SINKING SANDBAR


The river narrowed at the Nine Horses Fresco Hill, where the water was compressed into a shallow, gravel-heavy channel.

Here stood a massive sandbar—a submerged bank of loose silt and pebbles that shifted with the spring floods. The current was fast, throwing up a white spray as the river flowed over the shallows.

"Keep to the eastern wall!" Elder Liu shouted, his long steering oar bent under his weight. "The channel is narrow, and the sandbar is rising!"

But the wind was against them.

A sudden gust from the karst peaks caught the wicker shelters of the linked rafts, pushing the flotilla sideways. With a heavy, grinding *shrr-shrr*, the lead paired raft ran aground on the sandbar, its bamboo canes wedged into the loose gravel.

The current immediately began to pile sand around the hull, anchoring the raft in the shallows.

"We're stuck!" Liang called out, his boots already in the water as he tried to push. "The gravel has locked the bottom."

From the dense bamboo groves along the western bank, the dead emerged. They were former villagers from the valley, their clothes caked in dry mud, their skin tight and grey. They waded into the river, the water rising to their knees. Because they felt no cold, they pushed through the current, their boots clicking on the stones.

"They're coming from the bamboo!" Suli warned, her bow raised.

Jun ran to the stern of the aground raft. "We must lever the hull free! We cannot push against the current. Liang! Get the three-meter spruce lever and the oak fulcrum block from the cart!"

Jun set the oak fulcrum block on a flat granite stone in the shallows, sliding the spruce lever beneath the rear cross-beam of the raft. "Heave, Liang! Now!"

They threw their weight onto the lever. The spruce pole bent, the wood fibers groaning under the three-ton load of the wedged raft. Slowly, the stern of the boat rose an inch from the gravel.

*CRACK.*

The spruce lever split down the center, the wood fibers shearing under the immense load. The raft dropped back into the sandbar with a heavy splash, throwing Jun into the freezing current.

"Master!" Liang yelled, lunging forward to grab Jun's arm.

Jun scrambled up, his cotton shirt soaked in green water. The Gobi wind had prepared him for hardship, but the cold of the mountain river was a sharp, physical pain that made his ribs ache. He looked up; the lead wader was only five meters away, its wet fingers reaching for the cart.

"Don't change the pole!" Jun shouted, his teeth chattering. "We don't have another spruce log. Liang, get the hydraulic bottle jack from the cart! We will set it on the granite stone and lift the beam directly!"

"Will the jack work under water?" Liang asked.

"The hydraulic fluid is sealed," Jun said. "It will lift as long as the base is stable. Pour the sand out of the cylinder first!"

Jun waded into the chest-deep water behind the raft, setting the bottle jack on the submerged granite stone. He worked by touch in the green water, his fingers locking the jack’s release valve.

"Pump, Liang!" Jun called.

Liang knelt on the deck, pumping the jack handle with a long iron pipe. The piston rose slowly from the steel cylinder, contact the spruce beam of the raft. The wood creaked, then rose.

*Clack.*

The stern lifted two inches, the current washing the loose gravel out from under the bamboo canes. Elder Liu pushed with his steering oar, and with a sudden slide, the raft floated free into the deep channel.

Xiaoyan and Suli held the line, their spears and arrows clearing the waders that had reached the deck. Jun and Liang climbed back onto the raft, the engine of the current carrying them away from the sandbar into the safe reach of the river.

"That was too close," Liang said, his chest heaving as he wrapped a dry blanket around Jun.

"The river is a road, Liang," Jun said, looking back at the sandbar. "But a road has its stones. We must reach the Xingping lock before the main migration blocks the gates."

---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE KARST LOOKOUT


The Solitary Beauty Peak—*Duxiu Feng*—rose like a single, vertical stone pillar three hundred meters above the Li River basin, its limestone cliffs covered in wild fig vines and dwarf pine trees.

This was the highest vantage point in the valley.

From its summit, a watchman could see ten kilometers down the river channels, monitoring the movement of the delta dead before they reached the quiet water bends. But the path to the top was a narrow, crumbled stone staircase carved by Ming Dynasty monks, now blocked by a massive rockfall that had left a twenty-meter vertical gap of sheer rock face.

"We cannot climb it," Xiaoyan said, looking up the cliff. "The limestone is too slick, and there are no handholds. But without a lookout, we are blind. We won't know if the horde is coming from the main channel or the back creeks."

"We build a gantry hoist," Jun said, adjusting his webbed shoulder strap. "A *tiaodiao*—a cantilevered pine platform projecting out from the top cliff lip, carrying a wicker basket hoist. I will climb the rock face using chiseled hand-holds, anchor the top pulleys, and we will haul the timber frames up using the guide rope."

"Master, the limestone is soft," Liang warned. "If you drill a socket too close to the edge, the stone will shear under the hoist weight."

"We drill deep," Jun said. "And wedge the eyebolts with lead plugs. The lead will expand and fill the micro-cracks in the limestone, locking the metal to the stone. Liang, get the stone chisel and the small bellows. We need to melt the lead plugs over the charcoal stove."

Jun began the climb, his fingers gripping the natural fissures in the vertical limestone. He carried his heavy stone chisel and a steel hand-drill. The wind from the karst peaks buffeted him, trying to pull him off the wall. Every ten feet, he chiseled a narrow pocket into the stone, driving an iron peg to act as a temporary step.

It took him two hours of exhausting climb to reach the top ledge. His fingers were bleeding, his forearms tight from the strain.

He set up a heavy pine tripod frame at the cliff lip, lashing the timbers together with split-bamboo ropes. He drilled two deep socket holes into the bedrock behind the frame, drove the iron eyebolts, and poured molten lead from a small crucible he had carried up. The lead hissed as it cooled, locking the bolts in a permanent grip.

"Haul the pine joists!" Jun called down.

Using a block-and-tackle system with pear wood pulleys, Jun and Liang hauled the heavy timber planks up the cliff. Jun assembled the cantilevered gantry, locking the spruce frame to the lead-anchored eyebolts.

They hung a large, woven bamboo basket from the pulley cable, controlled by a manual wooden capstan on the river bank below.

"Test the lift, Xiaoyan!" Jun called.

Xiaoyan stepped into the basket. Liang and Liu turned the wooden capstan, the basket rising smoothly along the cliff face. In ten minutes, she reached the top gantry, stepping onto the stable pine platform.

From the summit, the entire valley was visible, the jade-green river winding between the peaks like a ribbon. Suli took her place on the lookout platform, her recurve bow ready, her eyes scanning the distant river bends for the first signs of the migration.

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE RIVER NET


The main channel below the watchtower was a deep, fifty-meter-wide reach where the current was slow and silent.

Here stood the primary defensive barrier—a heavy river net made of thick hemp ropes weighted with river stones, designed to block the passage of floating water walkers. The net was anchored to the vertical limestone cliffs on both sides of the river by thick steel cables.

But the net was tearing.

A massive wave of bloated dead from the lower township had drifted into the net, their pale limbs caught in the diamond-shaped mesh. The cumulative weight of forty water-logged bodies, combined with the pressure of the river current, was pulling the cables taut, the steel strands shrieking as they frayed against the rock anchors.

"The anchors are slipping," Elder Liu said, pointing to the western cliff face. "The steel eyebolts are pulling out of the limestone. If the cable snaps, the net will wash away, and the entire delta horde will flood the flotilla anchorage."

"We must set a secondary anchor system," Jun said. "And build a *jiaya*—a timber compression strut wedged horizontally between the cliff face and the cable socket. It will transfer the tension to the solid rock wall and stop the bolts from pulling."

"Master, we can't drill in the deep water," Liang said, looking at the boiling pool below the cliff.

"We work from the raft," Jun said. "We will build a timber crib scaffold on the catamaran deck, push the raft against the cliff face, and drill the sockets from the platform. Liang, get the heavy steel drill and the mallet."

Jun and Liang pushed their paired raft against the western limestone wall. The current was fast, throwing up a spray that coated the wood deck and the tools in a slippery film. Suli and Xiaoyan held the raft steady using long bamboo poles wedged into the rock cracks.

Jun stood on the raised timber scaffold, his stone drill placed against the cliff face five feet above the water line. He struck the steel drill with the heavy mallet, the sound echoing down the canyon like a hammer on an anvil. *Clink. Clink. Clink.*

He chiseled a deep, horizontal pocket into the limestone, thirty centimeters deep and ten centimeters wide.

While they worked, a bloated water walker caught in the net shifted, its arm reaching for the scaffold planks. Suli thrust her spear, the iron point entering its chest, but the movement added to the tension on the frayed cable.

The steel wire shrieked, a single strand snapping with a loud *ping*.

"The cable is going!" Liang warned, his hand on the jack.

Jun did not look back. He took a heavy spruce strut, notches the end to slide over the cable socket, and wedged the other end into the newly chiseled limestone pocket.

"Drive it, Liang!" Jun yelled.

Liang struck the wedge with the mallet, driving the spruce strut home. The timber took the load, compressing under the immense tension. The shriek of the steel cable stopped, the tension transferred directly to the limestone cliff.

The anchor held, the river net stabilized.
