Jun and Liang quickly set two more struts on the opposite side, securing the net barrier. With the river channel blocked, the survivors had time to clear the caught dead using the swivel hooks and prepare the flotilla for the next reach.

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE BAMBOO FUNNEL


The river widened below the cliff, the current slowing as it entered a flat, shallow marsh basin.

Here, the water walkers were difficult to track. They drifted across the entire three-hundred-meter width of the basin, their pale shapes hidden by the tall water reeds and the morning mist. If they bypassed the main channel, they could swim into the shallow coves where the survivors grew their river rice.

"We cannot block the whole basin with nets," Elder Liu said, looking at the wide, marshy expanse. "We don't have enough steel cable, and the silt is too soft to hold anchors. If they scatter, they will overrun our agricultural rafts one by one."

"We don't block it," Jun said, pointing to the main current channel. "We steer them. We will build a V-shaped bamboo funnel wall—*zhufeng*—that extends from the banks to the center channel. The current will guide the floating dead along the bamboo screens, directing them into a narrow side-chute where we will set a submerged oak cage—*shuilong*—to trap them."

"How do we drive the piles in the soft silt?" Liang asked.

"We use the water ram," Jun said. "We will set a vertical spruce pole in the silt, place a heavy granite block on top, and use a pulley rope to lift and drop the stone. The weight of the stone will drive the wood three meters into the silt, forming a solid anchor post."

Jun and the fishermen built the pile driver on a flat cargo raft. They drove twenty spruce piles in a diagonal line from both banks, spacing them three meters apart. They lashed dense bamboo screens made of split green canes to the piles, forming a green wall that projected two hundred meters into the basin.

The V-funnel guided the current, directing the floating silt and debris into the central ten-meter gap. Here, Jun built a large, submerged cage from heavy oak slats, set three meters deep in the water, with a sliding trap-door gate held open by a rope trigger.

"Here they come," Xiaoyan warned from the lead gantry.

A group of fifteen water walkers, swept by the main current, hit the western bamboo screen. They did not try to climb the smooth, wet canes; they drifted along the angled wall, the current guiding them slowly toward the central gap.

The lead zombie—a bloated walker in a faded yellow shirt—entered the oak cage, its body hitting the rear partition. Three others followed, packed tight inside the oak slats.

"Drop the gate!" Jun yelled.

Liang cut the rope trigger. With a heavy splash, the stone-weighted oak gate slid down the granite slots, sealing the water walkers inside the submerged cage.

*Creeeak.*

The split-bamboo brace on the western funnel wall cracked under the pressure of the rising water, the wood bowing three inches.

"Liang! Mallet!" Jun called out.

Jun waded onto the brace deck, placing a thick pine block over the crack. Liang struck the block with the mallet, driving a locking oak key (*sunzi*) into the split, stabilizing the timber. The V-funnel held, the water walkers guided into the trap.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE SLUICE LOCK


The irrigation lock of Xingping was a massive Ming Dynasty granite structure that controlled the water levels between the Li River and the agricultural canals of the valley.

But the lock was jammed.

A five-meter drift log—a seasoned cypress trunk that had washed down from the logging camps—was wedged horizontally across the sluice gates, blocked by twenty water-logged bodies that had been drawn into the slot by the suction of the water. The gates were stuck halfway open, the water level in the agricultural canals dropping by two feet a day.

"The rice fields are drying," Elder Liu said, looking at the mud flats opening in the canals. "If we cannot close the lock, the crop will die in a week. But we cannot clear the log from the deck; the suction is too strong."

"We must cut the log under water," Jun said. "We will dive with a two-man saw, notch the center of the cypress trunk, and let the pressure of the river snap the wood. Suli, hold the gatehouse deck with the archers. Liang, get the saw and the diving ropes."

Jun tied a hemp safety line around his waist, handing the other end to Liang. He took a two-meter cross-cut saw wrapped in oilcloth, its steel teeth filed wide to cut through the wet wood without jamming.

He stepped off the stone pier into the freezing lock pool.

The water was dark and silt-heavy, the current pulling violently at his body. He let himself sink to the bottom of the granite gate slot, his hand finding the rough bark of the jammed cypress log. He worked by touch in the dark water, the cold ice-like against his bare chest.

He positioned the saw, gesturing to Liang through the safety rope with two sharp tugs.

Liang dived, his hand finding the opposite handle of the saw. Together, they began the cut, their arms moving in a slow, rhythmic pull-and-push. The steel teeth ground through the cypress, the sawdust rising in a cloud of yellow silt.

As they worked, a bloated shape shifted in the current above them.

The hand of a water walker, caught in the branch of the drift log, drifted down, its fingers touching Jun’s shoulder. Suli, standing on the granite lock bridge above, fired an arrow through the water, the bone tip entering the zombie's head and stopping its movement, but the body remained wedged against the saw blade.

Jun did not stop. He pushed the saw forward, the steel blade cutting through the water-logged bark and the zombie’s collarbone with a single, crunching stroke.

*CRACK.*

The cypress log, weakened by the deep notch and pressed by the three-ton weight of the river, snapped in half. The two sections shot downstream through the lock gates, releasing the jam.

The iron gate, freed from the log, slid down the granite guide slots with a heavy, metallic rumble, sealing the lock and stabilizing the water levels.

Jun and Liang swam to the stone steps, their chests heaving, their skin blue from the cold. Suli helped them up, wrapping them in dry blankets as the river water behind the gate began to rise, filling the agricultural canals.

"It's closed," Liang gasped, his teeth clicking.

"The canals are safe," Jun said, looking at the rising water. "But the flotilla is still exposed. We must reach the flood sweep at the southern bend before the mountain runoff breaks our main cables."

---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE FLOOD SWEEP


The mountain runoff came in a brown, wall-like wave that swept down the Li River canyon, carrying uprooted bamboo, mud, and river debris.

The current in the river doubled in ten minutes, the green jade turning into a brown, boiling torrent.

At the southern bend, the flotilla was in danger. The main anchor cable—a thick iron chain anchored to a massive granite block on the eastern bank—had snapped under the impact of a drift tree. Ten paired rafts, carrying forty refugees, were torn from the anchorage, swept downstream toward the wild rapids of the lower canyon.

"We're loose!" Elder Liu yelled, his long oar powerless against the brown torrent.

The rafts collided, the bamboo hulls groaning as they slammed together, their wicker shelters collapsing. Suli and the archers on the remaining rafts tried to throw ropes, but the distance was too wide, the current sweeping the loose group away.

"The winch tower!" Jun shouted, pointing to a timber tower on the eastern ridge. "The secondary safety line—the three-inch hemp rope—is still set in the drum! If we can release the winch dog and swing the line across, we can catch the lead raft before the rapids!"

"Master, the winch is jammed!" Liang yelled. "The runoff has collapsed the tower sill, and the iron drum is wedged against the frame!"

"I'll clear it!" Jun said.

He ran to the ridge trail, his boots slipping in the mud. The winch tower was a three-story timber frame of seasoned pine, now leaning five degrees toward the river. The main horizontal sill—a log thirty centimeters thick—had split under the weight, the iron winch drum wedged into the cracked wood.

Jun climbed the tower frame, the wind carrying the roar of the rapids below. He reached the winch deck, his hand finding the heavy iron capstan.

"Liang! Pass the jack and the framing chisel!" Jun called down.

Working on the tilting deck, Jun set the hydraulic bottle jack under the winch drum, jacking it up one inch to relieve the pressure on the split sill. He took his broadaxe, using the steel head to chop through the jammed wood fibers that locked the gear teeth.

The wood chips flew, the sound lost in the roar of the water.

Below him, the loose rafts were only fifty meters from the rapids, their decks tilting as they hit the first white waves. A group of water walkers caught in the drift logs was swept alongside, their arms reaching for the refugees.

"Now, Liang! Release the winch!" Jun yelled.

Jun struck the final blow, splitting the sill block. The iron drum slid free, the gear teeth releasing with a loud, metallic shriek. Liang threw the capstan bar, the hemp safety rope flying across the river like a whip.

The end of the rope caught the railing of the lead paired raft. Elder Liu wrapped the line around the main cross-beam, locking it with a double hitch.

The rope went taut, the hemp shieking as it took the three-ton load of the swept rafts. The timber tower groaned, the pine braces bending, but the lead-wedged anchors held. The rafts swung in a wide, slow arc through the current, coming to rest in the quiet water of the eastern cove.

Jun collapsed onto the wet platform, his hands shaking, his chest heaving. Below, the refugees were safe, their rafts anchored in the quiet water.

---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE LI RIVER SAFEHOUSE


The cove at Xingping was a quiet, limestone basin surrounded by three vertical peaks that rose like walls of green granite.

Here, the water was still, the main current of the Li River bypassing the basin. The only entry was a ten-meter-wide channel, blocked by a heavy river net and three pairs of anchored bamboo rafts.

The flotilla was secure.

The wicker huts were rebuilt, their decks dry. The cormorants sat on their perches, their black wings drying in the sun, while the women washed the rice in clean, filtered water.

Jun sat on the deck of the central cargo raft, his hands resting on his oak toolbox. Beside him, Liang was sharpening a draw-knife, the steel edge reflecting the green water.

"We have built a good gate on the water, Master Jun," Liang said.

"The river is a good wall, Liang," Jun replied. "It drowns the dead and carries the living. But the land is still waiting."

Elder Liu stepped onto the deck, carrying a repaired military radio. The speaker crackled, a voice carrying through the static.

"From Shaanxi," Liu said, his face grave. "Xi'an. The keepers of the ancient city wall say the southern gates are under siege. The horde from the coal mines has bypassed the Moat, and the inner doors are cracking. They need builders who know the brick and the timber."

Jun looked at Liang. Liang stood up, checking the edge of his draw-knife.

"The brick of Xi'an needs its builders, Master," Liang said.

Jun stood up, his broadaxe held ready. "Pack the tools, Liang. We head north to the old capital."

================================================================================

STORY 16: THE RAMPARTS OF XI'AN
Setting: Xi'an City Wall, Shaanxi Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE BRICK WALL


The city wall of Xi'an did not just shelter; it enclosed a mountain of earth.

Built during the early Ming Dynasty on the foundations of the Tang imperial palace, the wall was fourteen kilometers in length, twelve meters high, and fifteen meters wide at the top—broad enough for two carriages to pass. Unlike the thin stone walls of the south, this was a massive earthen rampart, its thick core of rammed loess clay clad in a dense skin of heavy, black-fired bricks (*qingzhuan*). The bricks were set in a mortar of slaked lime and river sand, their surfaces worn to a dark grey sheen by six centuries of wind and dust from the northern deserts.

Jun stood on the broad brick deck of the southern rampart near Yongning Men, his hand resting on the stone parapet. He looked south across the dry moat. 

The city below the wall was a silent grid of grey concrete towers and abandoned streets, now filled with the slow, grey shapes of the dead. But on the wall itself, a community of eighty thousand survivors lived, their tents, cooking fires, and vegetable boxes lining the broad brick walkway. The wall had become a floating city on land, its heights isolating the living from the ruins below.

Beside him, Liang was adjusting the wheels of their handcart, his face caked in the grey dust of the Shaanxi plains. "It feels like a fortress, Master," Liang said, looking down the long, straight line of the rampart. "But there are so many entries. The gates, the ramp arches, the drainage sluices."

"A wall is only as strong as its openings, Liang," Jun said, his eyes scanning the South Gate barbican. "And the pressure is rising. The coal mine horde from the Qinling slopes has entered the southern suburbs. They are moving along the avenues, and their numbers are too many for the watchmen's spears."

Captain Zhang, a man of forty with a close-cropped beard and a faded blue security uniform over a leather breastplate, walked over. He held a heavy iron-tipped halberd (*Ji*), its ash shaft wrapped in cord. "Carpenters," he said, his voice carrying the flat tones of the Guanzhong valley. "The scouts say the outer gates of the South barbican have caved. The horde is now packed inside the circular courtyard, and the inner elm doors are beginning to split under the weight."

Jun walked to the gatehouse edge, looking down into the *wengcheng*—the circular "jar wall" or barbican that sat in front of the main gate.

The courtyard below was a solid mass of hundreds of zombies, their grey heads bobbing in the dark. They had crushed the outer steel-reinforced gates under their collective weight and were now pressed against the inner wooden double-doors. The doors, built of seasoned elm planks ten centimeters thick, were bowing inward, the heavy iron bolt brackets groaning as the wood fibers began to split.

"We must shore them," Jun said, his hand sliding to his broadaxe. "We cannot rebuild the gates while they are pushing. We must construct a *duoji*—a diagonal timber shoring framework anchored into the granite paving stones of the archway. It will transfer the horizontal pressure of the doors directly into the bedrock of the gate portal."

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE SOUTH GATE


The inner portal of Yongning Men was a long, vaulted stone archway carved through the twelve-meter thickness of the wall, its floor paved with heavy granite slabs.

Inside the dark arch, the sound of the horde was a constant, thunderous rumble that rattled the brick vault. The double-doors of elm wood were bowing three inches, the cracks in the wood grain opening and closing like mouths as the zombies thrashed oucoarse haire.

"The bolt is bending!" Liang called out, pointing to the two-inch iron bar that locked the doors. The middle bracket was pulling out of the wood, the lag screws stripping the rot-softened elm.

"Get the pine logs," Jun ordered the soldiers. "We need six poles, four meters long, fifteen centimeters thick. Liang, get the heavy screw-jack and the chisel. We must cut notch seats into the granite floor to anchor the base of the braces."

Using a hand-drill and a plugging chisel, Jun began cutting a series of rectangular sockets into the granite floor stones, three meters back from the doors. The granite was hard as steel, the chisel throwing up sparks and a fine white dust that mixed with the sweat on his face. He worked by the light of a single kerosene lamp, his mallet blows landing with a dry, metallic *clank-clank-clank*.

Liang and the soldiers prepared the spruce braces, notches the ends to fit the granite pockets.

"Watch the door!" Zhang warned.

With a sharp *crack*, the middle elm plank of the left door leaf split, an arm thrusting through the gap. The hand was grey and claw-like, its nails worn down to the bone from scratching the wood. It reached for Zhang's collar, its bared teeth visible through the split.

Zhang thrust his halberd, pinning the arm to the frame, but two more zombies pushed against the split plank, widening the breach.

"Jack it, Liang!" Jun yelled.

Liang set the screw-jack against the split plank, wedging a thick block of oak between the jack and the wood. He turned the lever, the screw rising and pushing the door leaf back into alignment. The gap closed, trapping the zombie's arm in the wood.

Jun set the first diagonal spruce brace into its granite socket, its top end notches to fit the horizontal lock-bar of the door.

"楔子! mallets!" Jun called.

He drove two large oak wedges into the granite socket, compressing the spruce tenon and locking the brace. He set the second, then the third brace, forming a triangular shoring wall that propped the gates from the inside.

The groaning of the iron bolt stopped, the horizontal pressure of the doors transferred to the granite floor. The doors remained bowed, but their movement was halted.

"It's braced," Liang said, wiping his brow.

"For now," Jun said, looking at the split elm planks. "But the middle of the gate is weak. The wood is rotten around the hinge pins. We must build a secondary timber wall behind the doors—a *zhaolan* packed with gravel—before the outer barbican walls split under the pressure of the horde."

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE ROLLING LOGS


The defenders on the high parapets of the South Gate were running out of weapons.

Their iron-tipped spears were splitting under the constant work of pushing scaling zombies off the brick face, and the supply of stones to drop was empty. The Qinling coal mine horde was massive, their bodies stacking against the base of the wall to climb.

"We have no more stones!" Captain Zhang called out, his halberd head nicked and blunt. "And they are climbing the buttresses on the western wall. If they reach the top, they will flank our main watchtower."

"We build rolling log traps—*leimu*," Jun said, looking at the piles of seasoned spruce logs stacked behind the barracks. "We will wrap the logs in iron straps and drive hand-forged steel spikes into the wood. We will hang them from the parapet notches using thick hemp ropes and release triggers. When a group of scaling dead gathers on the brick buttresses, we cut the trigger, letting the spiked logs roll down the wall face to crush them."

"How do we return the logs after we release them?" Liang asked.

"We don't," Jun said. "We set them on a double-rope runner. When the log reaches the bottom, the ropes will hold it at the base of the wall, forming a spiked barrier that stops them from gathering in the corners. Go, Liang! Bring the iron straps and the heavy hammer."

Jun and Liang worked on the rampart decks, preparing the spruce logs. Jun used his draw-knife to shave the larch trunks down to a clean, round cylinder. Liang wrapped three iron collars around each log, driving steel spikes through the metal into the wood. They hung the logs from the granite crenels, locking the ropes with wooden toggle pegs (*mushuan*).

They prepared ten rolling traps along the western wall segment.

"Release the first!" Jun commanded.

A group of forty zombies was climbing the brick buttress of Tower Eight, their dried hands finding purchase on the mortar joints. Liang chiseled the toggle peg of the first log.

With a heavy *thud*, the five-hundred-kilogram spiked spruce log dropped from the parapet. It rolled down the vertical brick wall, the steel spikes grinding the masonry. It hit the climbing pack with a series of wet, heavy *thuds*, crushing skulls and limbs before stopping at the wall base, held by the double-rope runner.

"It works," Zhang said, looking down at the cleared wall segment. "The base is clean."

"Keep setting the next block," Jun said. "The East Moat is still flooded, and the water walkers are swimming."

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE MOAT SLUICE


The East Moat of Xi'an was a wide, brick-lined canal that fed water from the Zhahe River around the eastern ramparts.

But the canal was backing up.

An abandoned coal barge had drifted into the East Moat sluice gate, its iron hull wedged horizontally between the granite piers. The water was rising, flooding the lower canal paths and allowing bloated water walkers to swim directly to the base of the wall where the brickwork was cracked.

"The water is rising three inches an hour," Captain Zhang said, looking at the flooded path. "If the water reaches the lower window grates, the water walkers will crawl into the drainage vaults and enter the city core. We must open the sluice gate to drain the canal, but the barge is jamming the vertical lift iron portal."

"We must lift the barge free from the sluice slots," Jun said. "And clear the debris under water. Liang! Get the hydraulic jack and the steel chains. We must work from the stone pier."

Jun and Liang waded into the freezing, silt-heavy water of the moat. The current was fast, throwing up a spray that tasted of coal dust and rot. Suli and the watchmen stood on the granite bridge deck above, their spears held low to ward off the bloated bodies drifting down the canal.

Jun set the hydraulic jack on the stone ledge of the sluice pier, wrapping a heavy steel chain around the barge's iron rudder frame.

"Jack it, Liang!" Jun called.

Liang pumped the handle, the jack cylinder rising slowly. The iron frame of the barge groaned, the rust popping under the three-ton lift. Slowly, the wedged hull shifted, rising two inches from the granite slots.

*Splash.*

A bloated zombie emerged from the brown water behind the gate, its grey hands catching the steel chain. Suli thrust her spear, the point splitting its temple, but the weight of three more water walkers caught in the flow pulled at the chain, trying to tilt the jack base.

"Hold it!" Jun yelled, his shoulder pressed against the steel chain.

Jun took his heavy chisel, driving it between the barge hull and the granite pier to act as a locking wedge. Liang pump-drove the jack with a final heave, and with a sudden rush of water, the barge slid free from the slots, the current sweeping it downstream.

The sluice gate, freed from the jam, dropped with a heavy rumble, draining the East Moat and lowering the water levels.

Jun and Liang climbed onto the stone steps, their limbs shivering from the freezing water, their hands caked in coal silt. Suli wrapped them in dry blankets as the flooded canal paths went dry.

"The moat is clear," Liang gasped.

"But the southern wall corner watchtower is still shifting," Jun said, looking up at the high brick rampart. "The coal mine horde is approaching the main gatehouse, and we must brace the corner vault before the night attack begins."

---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE WATCHTOWER FIRE


The South-East Corner Watchtower—a massive, three-story fortress of grey brick and heavy pine timbers—sat like a fist where the southern and eastern ramparts met.

For hours, the cold, dry wind from the Guanzhong plain had been rising, carrying with it the smell of coal smoke and the dust of the dry loess fields. From his position on the walkway, Jun could see the orange glow of cooking fires flickering in the survivor camps along the rampart. But at the corner tower, the glow was different. It was too bright, too fluid, and it did not stay within the stone hearths.

A scream cut through the wind—a high, thin sound that was instantly swallowed by the roar of the gale.

"Fire!" a watchman shouted from the tower's second-story gallery. "The lower platform is alight! The oil vats have ruptured!"

Jun ran toward the corner, his heavy toolbox shifting on his back, the iron tools clattering inside. Liang followed, dragging the handcart over the uneven brick pavement, his eyes wide as he looked at the rising column of black smoke.

The corner tower was connected to the main southern rampart by a wooden gallery—a covered bridge fifteen meters long and three meters wide, built of seasoned larch beams and pine planks. It allowed the watchmen to move from the barracks to the tower without exposing themselves to the wind. But now, that gallery had become a chimney.

A group of survivors, defending the tower's lower gate against climbing zombies, had knocked over a large iron brazier filled with burning coal and oil lamps. The fuel had leaked through the floorboards, igniting the dry timbers below. The flames, fed by the dry northern gale, were eating their way along the support joists, moving toward the main wall where the survivor tents were packed.

"The wind is pushing it right at us!" Liang yelled, shielding his face from the flying embers. "If the fire reaches the barracks, the whole southern sector will burn!"

Captain Zhang and Suli were already at the bridge entrance, trying to keep a crowd of panicked refugees from crowding onto the burning walkway. Suli’s recurve bow was bent, her eyes fixed on the smoke-filled doorway of the watchtower.

Through the black smoke, figures appeared. They were not refugees.

They were zombies that had been climbing the tower's outer brick facade. Their clothes were burning, their dry hair gone, their skin charred to a black, cracked leather. Yet, they did not stop. They walked through the flames on the gallery floor, their footsteps leaving greasy, black smears of melted fat on the pine boards. Their teeth clicked in the heat, their white, milky eyes fixed on the living.

"We cannot fight them in the smoke," Zhang said, his hand trembling on his halberd. "And we cannot put out the fire. The well is too far."

"We cut the bridge," Jun said, his voice flat. He walked to the edge of the span, his eyes analyzing the joint where the gallery met the stone rampart.

The bridge was supported by three horizontal spruce joists (*diaoliang*), each twenty centimeters square, anchored into deep sockets in the granite face of the wall. To simply chop them would take too long, and if the timber snapped unevenly, the heavy bridge would pivot downward, acting as a ladder for the dead below.

"We must make V-notches—*xiangtian*—at the critical stress points," Jun explained to Liang, pointing to a spot two-thirds of the way across the span. "We will cut them from the top, halfway through the wood. When the wood is weak, we will attach the ropes to the center and pull from the wall. The bridge will fold in the middle, snapping the joists at the notch, and drop straight into the dry moat."

"But the dead are on the bridge!" Liang said.

"Suli, Zhang, keep them back!" Jun ordered as he unbuckled his toolbox.

Jun pulled out the two-man cross-cut saw, its two-meter steel blade glinting in the firelight. He handed one handle to Liang. "Keep your strokes long and even, Liang. Do not let the blade bind. If the wood heats up, it will pinch."

They knelt on the hot pine deck of the bridge, just five meters from the advancing, burning dead. The heat was intense, blistering the skin on Jun’s cheeks, and the air was thick with the smell of burning pine pitch and roasting flesh.

*Screeech-sccch-screeech-sccch.*

The teeth of the saw bit into the first spruce joist. The wood was dry and hard, throwing up a shower of fine, yellow sawdust that was instantly swept away by the wind. Jun focused on the rhythm of the cut, ignoring the black smoke that stung his eyes and the heat that baked his hands.

Beside him, Liang’s breath came in ragged gasps. "Master... the wood is shifting! It’s pinching the blade!"

"Drive the wedge!" Jun yelled.

Liang reached into his belt and pulled out a small iron wedge. He placed it in the cut behind the saw blade and drove it home with a single blow of his mallet. The cut opened, and the saw moved freely again.

A charred zombie, its face a featureless mass of black charcoal, stumbled out of the smoke. Suli drew her bow, the string twanging in the wind. The bone-tipped arrow hit the zombie’s forehead, splitting the skull. The creature fell forward, its burning body landing two feet from Liang’s knees.

"Keep sawing!" Jun commanded, his shoulder muscles burning as he pulled the handle.

They finished the V-notch on the first joist, then moved to the center one. The fire had already eaten through the roof of the gallery, and burning rafters were crashing onto the deck around them.

"The third one!" Jun called out, his voice hoarse from the smoke.

They set the saw on the final joist. The wood was hot to the touch, and the timber was groaning as the weight of the tilting bridge shifted. They had cut three inches into the eight-inch timber when a massive section of the gallery roof collapsed behind them, blocking the view of the watchtower in a wall of red sparks.

"Out!" Jun yelled. "The bridge is going!"

They scrambled back onto the stone platform of the wall, dragging the saw. Suli and Zhang had already secured the heavy hemp rope to the center frame of the bridge, running the line around a granite capstan on the rampart.

"Pull!" Jun shouted, throwing his weight onto the rope.

Zhang, Liang, and four other watchmen joined him, their boots slipping on the brick deck as they hauled the line. The rope tightened, hummed, and then with a sharp, explosive *CRACK*, the three notched spruce joists sheared.

The bridge folded in the middle, its center dipping downward before the anchors tore free from the wall sockets. The entire fifteen-meter structure, along with the burning zombies on its deck, fell into the dark chasm of the dry moat below, landing with a muffled crash of breaking timber and sparks.

The fire stopped at the gap. The southern rampart was safe.

Jun sat on the brick walkway, his face black with soot, his hands raw and blistered. He looked across the fifteen-meter gap to the burning watchtower. The wind was still howling, carrying the embers away into the night sky.

"We stopped it," Liang gasped, his chest heaving.

"For now," Jun said, pointing to the west. "But the wind is carrying the embers toward the West Gate. If the drawbridge catches, the western sector will be open."

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE DRAWBRIDGE


The West Gate—Anding Men—was the wall's portal to the Silk Road, its massive brick barbican facing the open loess hills.

But the gate was in trouble.

When the western suburbs had been overrun three days prior, a panicked group of refugees had tried to close the gate before their companions had crossed. In the chaos, a soldier had used a fire axe to cut one of the heavy steel lifting cables of the drawbridge (*diaoqiao*), hoping to drop the barrier. The cable had snapped with a sound like a rifle shot, but instead of dropping, the three-ton timber bridge had tilted to a thirty-degree angle, its guide rollers jamming in the granite slots of the masonry portal.

Now, the drawbridge was stuck.

Its lower lip rested against the outer bank of the dry moat, while the upper deck hung ten meters in the air, creating a ramp that was too steep for carriages, but perfect for the dead.

Jun stood on the masonry arch of the gate portal, looking down through the freezing wind. The dry moat below was a churning sea of grey shapes—thousands of zombies that had followed the refugees from the suburbs. They were slow, their limbs stiff from the cold Guanzhong air, but they were persistent. The lead zombies had already scrambled onto the lower lip of the tilted bridge, their grey hands finding purchase on the wooden deck slats as they began to crawl upward toward the gate.

"If they reach the upper lip, they can climb the gatehouse frame," Captain Zhang said, his fingers gripping the iron rail. "We tried to winch it up, but the remaining cable is under too much tension. If we pull any harder, the drum will shear."

"We must splice the severed cable," Jun said, inspecting the broken steel wire rope that hung from the upper pulley. "But we cannot splice it while it is under tension. We must go down to the bridge pier, set a timber shoring frame beneath the deck to take the weight, and use our hydraulic jack to align the cable ends."

"Go down there?" Liang looked at the sea of dead below. "Master, the zombies are right under the bridge. If we fall..."

"We won't fall," Jun said. "We will use the safety harnesses. Suli, you and the archers must keep the deck clear while we work. Liang, get the hydraulic jack, the splicing fid, and the copper binding wire. We have twenty minutes before the main horde from the rail yards arrives."

They rigged two safety ropes to the stone corbels of the gatehouse. Jun tied the hemp line around his waist, checking the knot—a traditional bowline, double-looped for security. He slung his toolbox over his shoulder and stepped over the edge of the parapet, lowering himself into the freezing void.

The wind buffeted him, swinging him like a pendulum over the dry moat. Below, the smell of the dead rose—a sweet, cloying odor of decay and dry dust. The zombies in the moat reached up, their grey arms white with frost, their fingers snapping at his boots as he swung past.

Jun landed on the stone bridge pier—a narrow ledge of granite just two meters wide, projecting from the wall face five meters above the moat floor. The stone was slick with frost.

"Liang! Down!" Jun called out.

Liang descended, his face pale, his knuckles white as he held the rope. He landed beside Jun, instantly crouching to keep his balance on the narrow ledge. He dragged the heavy three-ton hydraulic jack behind him.

The drawbridge deck hung directly above their heads, its massive oak framework groaning under the wind.

"We shore it first," Jun said. He took two thick blocks of pine from the cart rope and set them vertically between the stone pier and the main cross-beam of the bridge deck. "Liang, set the jack between the pine blocks. We must lift the deck just one centimeter to take the tension off the jammed rollers."

Liang positioned the jack, its steel base resting on the granite pier. He inserted the iron handle and began to pump.

*Clack... clack... clack.*

The hydraulic cylinder rose, its steel head pressing into the pine block. The wood creaked, its fibers compressing as it took the weight of the three-ton bridge. The drawbridge groaned, the jammed rollers in the granite slots shifting with a metallic screech.

"The roller is free," Jun said, looking at the guide frame. He turned to the broken steel cable.

The cable was a six-strand wire rope, twenty millimeters thick, made of high-tensile steel wire wound around a hemp core. The cut end was frayed, its steel wires splayed out like a wire brush.

To splice a steel cable under these conditions was a brutal, physical task. Jun pulled out his steel splicing fid—a pointed iron tool with a grooved channel—and his wire cutters. He began by unlaying the six strands of the broken cable for about two meters on both sides, cutting away the damaged, bent wires.

"Hold the upper end, Liang," Jun ordered.

He took the first strand of the lower cable and placed it against the upper cable, using the fid to open the strands of the upper rope. The steel wire was stiff and cold, resisting his fingers like spring steel. He had to use his mallet to drive the fid between the tight strands, his hands freezing as they touched the bare metal.

*Tink. Tink.*

Embers from the watchtower fire were drifting down, landing on the timber deck above. A zombie, its clothes smoldering, crawled onto the bridge deck, its weight causing the structure to creak.

Suli’s arrow whistled from the wall, hitting the zombie in the neck. The creature fell sideways, its body landing on the bridge deck with a heavy thud that rattled the jack.

"The jack is slipping!" Liang warned, his hands holding the pump handle as the pine block below began to tilt on the frost-slick granite.

"Hold it, Liang!" Jun yelled, his fingers working frantically to tuck the second steel strand. He used the fid to lift a strand of the main rope, sliding the free strand through the channel. His knuckles scraped against the sharp steel ends, leaving trails of red blood that froze instantly on the grey wire.

He made the first tuck, then the second. The short-splice pattern required three tucks for each of the six strands to hold the load.

"I need more lift, Liang!" Jun called. "The cable ends are two centimeters short!"

Liang pumped the jack with all his weight, his boots sliding on the granite. The pine block groaned, a long crack opening along its grain.

With a sudden *BANG*, the pine block split. The jack slipped sideways, and the drawbridge dropped two inches, its full weight slamming onto the remaining cable. The spliced section was ripped from Jun's hands, the sharp steel wires scoring his palms.

"Master!" Liang screamed.

Jun licked the blood from his thumb and lunged, catching the safety line as the bridge swung. He looked down—the split block had fallen into the moat, and the zombies below were swarming over it.

"We have no more pine blocks," Liang gasped, his face white.

Jun looked at the split timber. "We use the oak tool chest. Slide it under the beam!"

"But your tools—"

"Do it!" Jun commanded.

They dragged the heavy oak toolbox under the bridge beam. Jun set the jack on top of the chest, using a spare block of hickory to distribute the weight. Liang pumped the handle again.

The jack rose. The oak chest, built by Jun's grandfather, took the three-ton load without a sound, its seasoned grain holding the pressure. The cable went slack again.

Jun knelt over the wire, his hands shaking from the cold and the pain. He drove the fid, tucking the remaining strands with a furious, rhythmic precision. Three tucks on each side. He wrapped the splice with copper binding wire, using his pliers to pull the wraps tight and lock the steel ends in place.

"Release the jack, Liang," Jun said, his voice quiet.

Liang opened the release valve. The hydraulic fluid hissed, and the jack cylinder sank.

The spliced cable took the weight. With a deep, metallic *twang* that echoed off the brick walls, the wire rope tightened. The drawbridge hung level, its guide rollers aligned in the slots.

From the wall above, Captain Zhang yelled, "Wind the winch!"

The heavy iron drums in the gatehouse began to turn, their gears clanking. The spliced cable rose through the pulleys, holding the load without a single strand slipping. The drawbridge rose, its timber deck swinging upward to seal the West Gate portal.

Jun and Liang climbed up the safety ropes, their hands raw, their bodies shivering. Suli pulled them over the parapet, wrapping them in wool blankets as the heavy elm doors of the West Gate closed behind the drawbridge.

Jun looked down at his bleeding palms, then at the closed gate.

"The gates are closed," Liang said, collapsing against the brick wall.

"The outer defenses are secure," Jun said, his eyes scanning the grey sky. "But the wind is turning. The cold is coming, and we must check the inner vault drains before the freeze locks the sluices."

---

CHAPTER 7: THE HALBERD WALL


The interior of the West Gate guardhouse smelled of hot pine sap, coal soot, and wet wool.

A large iron cauldron sat on the coal brazier in the center of the brick room, its contents bubbling and sending up a thick, yellow steam. Jun stirred the mixture with a flat piece of scrap iron, his face red from the heat. In the cauldron, raw pine resin, collected from the mountain trees of Yunnan, was melting together with linseed oil and finely ground charcoal dust. This was *yanyou*—a traditional waterproofing and binding pitch that cured to a leather-hard consistency, resistant to both moisture and the dry Guanzhong frost.

Beside him, Liang was preparing the hemp cord. He ran the thick, three-ply string through a block of beeswax, coating the fibers to prevent them from rotting under the constant moisture of the ramparts.

Captain Zhang sat on a low wooden bench, a pile of broken weapons at his feet. Most were *Ji*—traditional halberds from the museum archives and militia stores, featuring a heavy steel crescent blade and a spear point mounted on a three-meter wooden shaft.

"The shafts are splitting, Master Jun," Zhang said, holding up a halberd whose ash handle had cracked longitudinally for a meter below the metal socket. "The wood is old, dried out by the indoor air of the museum. When the men use them to leverage the heavy bodies over the parapet, the wood shears along the grain. If they push too hard, the blade flies off, leaving them with nothing but a broken stick."

Jun took the split shaft, running his thumb over the crack. Ash wood (*qinmu*) was the choice of ancient wheelwrights and spear-makers for its straight grain and high shock resistance. It could bend without breaking. But once the dry cold of Shaanxi set in, the wood fibers shrunk, and any lateral shear force—like the dead weight of a eighty-kilogram zombie hanging from the blade—would split the grain.

"The iron pins are the problem, Captain," Jun said, pointing to the two small iron rivets that secured the metal tang to the wood. "Iron is rigid. When the blade twists, the iron doesn't yield; it cuts into the ash fibers like a knife, starting the split. We must replace the iron pins with flexible bamboo pegs (*zhushuan*), and wrap the split wood in a composite sleeve of tarred hemp and pitch."

"Bamboo?" Zhang looked skeptical. "A wooden peg to hold a steel blade?"

"A bamboo peg will flex under shear load, Zhang," Jun explained. "It distributes the force across the entire width of the shaft instead of concentrating it on two points. And the hemp wrap will act as a tension band, stopping the split from opening."

Jun set the split shaft in his wood-vice, tightening the screw until the long crack closed. He took a hand-drill with a three-leaf spoon bit and began to drill out the old, rusted iron rivets. The steel bit shaved the ash, throwing up clean white curls that smelled of dry wood.

Once the holes were cleared, Jun took a seasoned rod of winter-cut bamboo (*dongzhu*), which he had shaved down to a twelve-millimeter cylinder. He drove the bamboo peg through the shaft and the metal tang using his mallet, his blows landing with a solid, woody *thud-thud*. He cut the ends flush with his flush-cut saw.

"Now, the wrap," Jun said.

He brushed the bubbling, black pine pitch over the wood, coating the split section in a thick, sticky layer. Liang stepped forward, grabbing the beeswax-coated hemp cord. He began to wrap the shaft, starting ten centimeters below the metal socket.

Liang’s wrapping technique was precise, a skill he had learned during their days on the Grand Canal. He used a "serving mallet"—a small wooden tool with a grooved head that allowed him to apply maximum tension to the cord as he wound it around the shaft. He pulled the cord tight, his knuckles turning white, the hemp burying itself into the black pitch.

*Squeak... squeak... squeak.*

The sound of the rope wrapping was tight and rhythmic. After every ten turns, Liang tapped the wraps with a wooden mallet to compress the layers, forcing the pitch to squeeze out between the fibers. Jun followed behind, brushing another layer of hot pitch over the completed wraps, sealing them in a glossy, black protective skin.

"Let it cool for ten minutes," Jun said, setting the reinforced halberd aside. "The pitch will lock the hemp into a hard sleeve that is stronger than the wood itself. The shaft will not split again."

Suli picked up one of the finished halberds, balancing the three-meter pole on her palm. She thrust it forward, twisting the blade as if catching a shield. The shaft flexed slightly, the bamboo pins yielding just enough to absorb the twist, while the black hemp sleeve held the wood solid.

"It feels alive," she said, her eyes bright. "The old spears were stiff, like they wanted to break in the hand. This one returns."

"We need fifty of these by midnight, Liang," Jun said, picking up the next broken shaft. "The watchmen at the North Gate are reporting that the dead are gathering in the lower arch, and their spears are already failing."

They worked through the evening, the pile of reinforced weapons rising against the brick wall. The heat of the cauldron kept the frost at bay, but from the window, the wailing of the wind was growing louder, carrying with it a new, low vibration—the sound of thousands of boots scraping on the frozen earth below.
