---

CHAPTER 8: THE TUNNEL BREACH


The storm drainage vault of the northern rampart was a dark, vaulted gallery of grey brick, built five meters below the street level to carry the summer rains from the city core to the outer moat.

But the moat was dry, and the drain was no longer carrying water.

Jun led the way down the narrow stone steps, holding a kerosene lamp high. The air was thick and cold, smelling of ancient silt, mold, and the sharp, chemical tang of the river clay. Beside him, Liang carried a canvas bag of granite packing stones and a heavy club hammer. Suli followed, her recurve bow strung, an arrow notched in the string.

"The scouts found the breach two hours ago," Captain Zhang said, his voice echoing in the low brick vault. He held one of the newly reinforced halberds. "The water walkers in the outer moat have been scraping at the discharge grate for weeks. The brick arch at the wall base was already cracked by the winter frost, and the pressure of the bodies has caved it in."

They reached the bottom of the vault. The floor was covered in a foot of freezing, black mud that sucked at Jun’s leather boots with every step.

Ten meters ahead, the tunnel ended in a chaotic pile of collapsed brick and loess clay. The vault roof had sheared, leaving a two-meter gap through which the dark, cold air of the outer moat was blowing. Through the gap, they could hear the low, rhythmic scratching of fingers against the broken masonry.

*Scritch... scritch... scritch.*

A grey hand, its flesh worn away by the rough brick, thrust through a opening in the rubble. It clawed at the air, its fingers searching for a hold.

"They're trying to widen the breach," Jun said, his lamp light illuminating the shifting soil above the cave-in. "If the loess clay shifts, the road above will collapse, and the wall foundation will lose its support. We must seal the breach with a dry-stone granite arch vault before the soil slides."

"We can't lay mortar in this mud," Liang said, pointing to the water dripping from the cracked ceiling. "It won't set."

"We don't use mortar," Jun said. "We build a dry arch—a *shigong*. The weight of the earth above will compress the granite blocks, locking them in place. But we must build a wooden centering arch—a *gongjia*—to support the stones while we set them."

Jun set down his lamp and took three pine boards from the handcart. Using his hand-saw, he cut the boards into segments, forming a semi-circular wooden frame that matched the width of the drainage tunnel. He bolted the pieces together using carriage bolts, creating a temporary arch support.

"Liang, brace the frame," Jun ordered.

They set the wooden centering arch in the mud, wedging it against the remaining brick walls of the tunnel using thick spruce blocks. Liang drove oak wedges under the base of the frame, lifting it until the wooden arch was tight against the vault line.

"Now, the granite," Jun said.

He retrieved the first granite block from the cart—a tapered stone forty centimeters long, twenty centimeters wide, and fifteen centimeters thick. These were *yingshi*—hard granite blocks salvaged from the Tang foundation ruins, their surfaces rough-chiseled to provide maximum friction.

Jun placed the first stone on the left side of the wooden frame, packing the gap behind it with small gravel and dry sand to distribute the pressure. He set the second stone on the right, building the arch upward from both sides simultaneously.

*Groan.*

The rubble pile shifted. A large slab of broken brick fell onto the wooden frame, followed by a slide of wet loess clay. A zombie’s head emerged from the gap—a man with a rusted iron collar around his neck, his jaw hanging open, his white eyes staring through the lamplight.

"Watch the front!" Zhang warned.

Zhang thrust his halberd, the steel crescent blade catching the zombie’s neck and pinning it to the brick wall. Suli drew her bow, her arrow hitting the creature’s eye socket. The zombie went limp, its head blocking the narrow opening.

"Keep setting, Liang!" Jun called out, his hands covered in black mud and granite dust.

He set the third stone, then the fourth. The arch was rising, its stones resting on the wooden centering frame. But the gap at the top—the crown of the arch—was still open. The weight of the loose earth above was pressing down on the wooden frame, causing the pine boards to creak and bow.

"The centering is buckling," Liang said, his shoulder pressed against the support post. "Master, the wood won't hold the weight of the next stone."

"We need the keystone," Jun said.

He searched the cart, selecting a tapered granite block that was slightly larger than the remaining gap. He used his chisel to trim the edges, his mallet blows echoing in the narrow tunnel like hammer strikes on an anvil. *Clink... clink... clink.*

The fit must be perfect. If the keystone was too small, the arch would collapse when the centering was removed. If it was too large, it would not seat deep enough to lock the ring.

"Hold the frame, Liang!" Jun called.

He lifted the heavy granite keystone, his muscles straining as he held it above his head in the cramped space. He placed the wedge-shaped stone into the crown of the arch. It stopped two centimeters short of seating flush.

Jun took his three-kilogram club hammer. "Stand back!"

He swung the hammer in the confined space, the steel head striking the granite keystone with a dull, heavy *THWACK*.

The stone shifted one centimeter.

*Thwack!*

The keystone slid home, its tapered sides wedging tightly between the adjacent granite blocks. With a sudden, solid settling sound, the granite ring locked. The groaning of the wooden centering arch stopped instantly, the horizontal thrust of the stones transferred to the solid brick walls of the tunnel.

"It's locked," Jun gasped, dropping the hammer.

He took his chisel and knocked out the oak wedges at the base of the wooden centering frame. The pine arch dropped three centimeters, leaving the granite vault standing on its own, holding the weight of the collapsed roof and the earth above.

Liang crawled forward, packing the remaining gaps between the granite blocks with small slate wedges (*shise*) to ensure full contact.

The scratching sound from the other side was now distant, muffled by the twenty centimeters of solid granite. The breach was sealed, the foundation secured.

Jun leaned against the cold brick wall, his breath misting in the lantern light. "The arch is good. It will hold for a hundred years."

"But the street above is quiet," Suli said, looking up at the vault ceiling. "Too quiet. If the horde has left the gate, they must be gathering somewhere else."

Zhang looked at the radio in his pocket, which was crackling with static. "Captain! The East Gate... they are breaching the inner wall. The winches are jammed, and we cannot drop the portcullis!"

---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE SIEGE OF YONGNING


The climb from the drainage vault to the South Gatehouse was a sprint against the rising noise of panic.

By the time Jun, Liang, and Suli reached the upper deck of the Yongning Men rampart, the night had been swallowed by the glare of searchlights and the smoke of flare pots. The report had been correct: the East Gate’s inner defenses had been overrun by a secondary arm of the coal mine horde. The zombies, moving in a slow, grey wave, had swept along the fifteen-meter-wide brick walkway of the wall, bypassing the ground-level street barriers. They were now pouring into the South barbican—the circular *wengcheng*—from the upper walkway ramps.

Inside the Barbican courtyard, the defenders were retreating toward the massive three-story inner gatehouse.

"The gatehouse is our last line!" Captain Zhang yelled, his voice cracking as he ordered his men to form a shield wall at the entrance. "We must drop the inner portcullis—the *shigan*! If they enter the gatehouse, they will have access to the stairs that lead down into the city!"

The inner gatehouse was secured by a massive granite portcullis, a slab of solid stone four meters wide, three meters high, and thirty centimeters thick, weighing over four tons. It was suspended in vertical stone tracks inside the gate archway, held in place by two thick hemp cables that ran up to a massive timber winch drum in the second-floor chamber.

Jun and Liang ran up the wooden steps of the gatehouse tower, their tools clattering in their belts. The winch chamber was a dark room of heavy brick and thick timber trusses, dominated by the four-meter oak winch axle (*shenxian*).

The winch was jammed.

A group of watchmen was straining against the cast-iron release lever, their boots slipping on the dusty floorboards. The iron lever was bent at a thirty-degree angle, and the gears were locked.

"The lever won't budge!" a watchman gasped. "Something is caught in the teeth!"

Jun ran to the gear train. He held the lamp close, his eyes scanning the large spur gear. A single tooth from the cast-iron pinion had sheared off under the sudden shock load of the gate's arrest and had wedged itself tightly between the pinion and the main gear, locking the teeth like a steel key.

"The tension is too high," Jun said, his hand touching the vibrating hemp cables that held the granite block. "The weight of the portcullis is pulling down on the axle, packing the sheared tooth tighter into the gears. We cannot back it off, and we cannot force the lever."

"Can we cut the cables?" Liang asked, looking at the thick hemp lines.

"No," Jun said. "If we cut the cables, they will whip. In this small chamber, a snapped cable under four tons of tension will shear a man in half. And the portcullis might drop unevenly, jamming in the tracks halfway down."

"Then what do we do?" Zhang demanded, his boots thudding on the floor as he entered. "They're at the door! We have three minutes before the shield wall breaks!"

"We chop the axle," Jun said, his eyes scanning the oak cylinder.

The axle was a trunk of seasoned white oak, thirty centimeters in diameter, its ends carved into round tenons that rested in heavy timber cradles. The hemp cables were wrapped six times around the center of the drum.

"If we cut the axle in the middle, the tension of the cables will cause the oak to split longitudinally, exploding in a storm of splinters," Jun explained, his voice calm despite the rising screams from the courtyard below. "We must cut a diagonal notch—a *xiechong*—at the left bearing neck, just oucoarse haire the cable wraps. We will cut it two-thirds through. When the wood is weak, the shear force of the portcullis will snap the neck, causing the axle to slide out of its right cradle and drop the cables cleanly."

"It will drop the whole axle," Liang said.

"Yes," Jun said. "But the axle will drop forward, away from us, toward the cable slots in the floor. Go, Liang! Set the guide ropes on the drum to pull it forward when it breaks. Suli, Zhang, hold the stairs!"

Jun unstrapped his broadaxe. The head, forged from a heavy section of railway steel, had a fifteen-centimeter cutting edge, honed to a razor-sharp finish.

He stood to the left of the winch, his feet set wide on the oak floorboards. He looked at the bearing neck of the axle—a section of wood twenty-five centimeters thick, spinning slowly in its greased cradle under the tension of the cables.

Jun raised the axe, his shoulder muscles locking, and swung.

*THWACK.*

The steel blade bit two centimeters into the seasoned oak, throwing up a shower of white chips that smelled of dry tannin. The wood was incredibly dense, the shock of the blow vibrating through the hickory handle directly into the bones of Jun’s forearms.

He swung again, his rhythm steady and powerful. *Thwack... thwack... thwack.*

Each blow landed precisely in the V-shaped notch, widening the cut. The axle grooved deeper, the wood fibers groaning under the shear tension of the four-ton granite slab hanging below.

Below the chamber floor, the sound of combat had changed. The dry, metallic *clack-clack* of Hakka staffs and the wet *thuds* of halberds were accompanied by the sound of boots scraping on the stairs. A zombie, its skull split by a halberd but still crawling, dragged itself through the doorway of the winch room.

Suli stepped forward, her soft-soled shoes silent on the dust. She did not use her bow in the cramped room; instead, she thrust the spear-point of her reinforced halberd through the zombie's throat, pinning it to the brick frame. "Keep sawing, Jun!" she called. "There are more coming!"

Jun did not look back. His face was caked in sweat and wood dust, his shirt clinging to his back. His hands were raw, the blisters from the West Gate drawbridge opening and bleeding onto the hickory handle.

*Thwack!*

The notch was now fifteen centimeters deep. The oak axle began to make a new sound—a series of high-pitched, electric *snaps* as the internal wood fibers began to shear under the tension.

"Liang! Pull the guide lines!" Jun yelled.

Liang and three watchmen hauled on the ropes, pulling the heavy drum forward, guiding its potential fall toward the floor slot.

Jun took a deep breath, raising the axe for a final, two-handed swing. He focused all his weight into the blow, aiming for the back of the V-notch.

*THWACK!*

The axe head buried itself to the socket. Jun let go of the handle and leaped backward, throwing himself flat onto the floorboards.

With a sound like a clap of thunder, the oak axle exploded. The bearing neck sheared along the grain, the wood splitting in a violent flash of white splinters. The four-ton weight of the portcullis dragged the free end of the axle forward, pulling it out of its cradles. The drum crashed onto the brick floor, its iron hoops grinding the masonry before it disappeared down the cable slot.

*SHRRRRRRIP.*

The hemp cables flew through the pulleys, their strands humming.

Below, a deafening *SLAM* shook the entire gatehouse structure, rattling the tiles on the roof and throwing up a cloud of white lime dust through the floor boards. The four-ton granite portcullis had dropped cleanly down its tracks, its bottom edge burying itself five centimeters into the granite threshold of the gate archway.

The screams of the horde were instantly cut off, replaced by the dull, hollow thudding of fists against the stone barrier.

The gate was sealed. The city wall was secure.

Jun lay on the floor, his ears ringing, his lungs breathing in the dry lime dust. He looked up at the ceiling trusses, then at Liang, who was sitting against the wall, covered in white powder, his face wide with relief.

Jun smiled, a dry, tired expression that cracked the soot on his cheeks. "The axle held," he gasped.

"It did," Liang said, wiping the dust from his eyes. "But your axe... it's gone down the slot."

"We'll get it tomorrow," Jun said, closing his eyes. "For now, let the dust settle."

---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE WALLED CAPITAL


The morning sun rose over the Guanzhong plain like a cold, copper plate, casting long, blue shadows across the snow-dusted brick ramparts of Xi'an.

Jun stood on the parapet of the southern wall, his hands wrapped in clean linen bandages. Below him, the dry moat was quiet, the heap of collapsed timber from the watchtower bridge now covered in a thin skin of white frost. The bodies of the dead lay scattered along the wall base, frozen stiff by the northern wind that had come after the storm.

On the broad brick deck, the floating city of the wall was coming back to life.

Families were emerging from their felt tents, their breath misting in the cold air as they lit their small charcoal stoves. Women were checking the wooden vegetable boxes that lined the walkway, scraping the frost from the winter cabbage leaves. The smoke from fifty cooking fires rose straight up into the clear blue sky, a sign of the gale's passing.

Beside him, Liang was cleaning their tools. He sat on a low crate, using a rag dipped in sheep tallow to grease the steel blade of the cross-cut saw, protecting the metal from the winter moisture. The oak toolbox sat open beside him, its brass corners polished, its internal racks organized.

"The dry-stone arch in the drainage tunnel is solid, Master," Liang said, looking up. "Zhang’s men inspected it at dawn. The soil above hasn't shifted an inch, and the road is stable."

"And the halberds?" Jun asked.

"Distributed," Liang replied. "We finished forty-eight of them. The watchmen are calling them the 'corked poles' because of the black pitch wrap. They say they can push three of the dead at once without the wood creaking."

Suli walked over from the gatehouse, her recurve bow unstrung and cased in a sheepskin sleeve. She had changed her torn Naxi vest for a thick wool coat of Shaanxi weave, but she still wore the embroidered Big Dipper circles on her collar.

"Captain Zhang is at the radio," she said, her voice quiet. "He says the signals from the south are dead. But a new voice came through from the west. From the mountains."

Jun turned, his eyes narrowing. "Mount Emei?"

"Yes," Suli said. "A watchman named Ah Feng. He says the Wannian Temple is still holding, but the winter freeze has cracked the foundation of the outer Wannian Hall. The granite retaining wall is shifting. If it splits, the western wing will slide down the Red Mountain into the valley."

Jun looked at his bandaged hands. The Wannian Temple was a masterpiece of stone and timber engineering, built on the steep slopes of Wannian Peak at over three thousand meters. Its walls were built of granite blocks set in a mortar of clay and straw, their surfaces battered inward to resist the seismic shocks of the plateau. If the foundation wall was cracking, it meant the water inside the stone core had frozen, expanding and pushing the masonry outward.

"If the retaining wall goes, the palace will follow," Jun said, his voice low. "And the road to the west will be blocked by the rubble. We must go."

"Master," Liang said, looking at the handcart and the snowy road that stretched west toward the horizon. "Mount Emei is two thousand kilometers. The passes are high, and the cold... it will freeze the grease in the axle."

"We will pack the cart with grease-leather," Jun said. "And we will use the winter path through the Hexi corridor before the snow closes the Qilian gates. Suli, will you come with us?"

Suli looked back at the South Gate tower, where Captain Zhang was organizing the morning watch. The children of the wall were gathering near the gatehouse, their faces clean, their hands holding small bowls of hot millet porridge.

"My place is here, Jun," Suli said, her hand resting on the cased bow. "The watchmen need someone who knows the high trail defenses, and the children... they need to know how to set the traps. I will help Zhang hold the wall."

Jun nodded, a gesture of deep respect. "The wall is in good hands, Suli. Keep the pitch cauldrons hot."

They packed the handcart by mid-morning. Captain Zhang brought them three bags of dried beef, a flask of sesame oil for their tools, and a newly forged iron crowbar to replace the axe they had lost in the portcullis slot.

"The road through the Guanzhong valley is clear of the main packs," Zhang said, shaking Jun’s bandaged hand. "But watch the river crossings. The bridges are old, and the water walkers are still in the mud."

"Keep the gates closed, Zhang," Jun said.

Jun and Liang took their positions at the cart handles. The heavy oak wheels creaked on the frozen brick as they turned the cart toward the western ramp.

Suli stood on the high parapet of Yongning Men, her figure a dark silhouette against the copper sun. She raised her hand in a silent farewell as the two carpenters descended the ramp, leaving the floating city of the wall behind.

The road ahead was a white line of snow and loess dust, winding toward the high peaks of the west. But the oak toolbox was secure on the cart, its tools greased and ready, and the rhythm of the journey began again.

================================================================================

STORY 17: THE SUMMIT SANCTUARY
Setting: Wannian Temple, Mount Emei, Sichuan

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE RED MOUNTAIN


The air in the Emei Valley was like cold glass—so thin and sharp that it burned the throat with every breath.

At an altitude of three thousand seven hundred meters, the Wannian Temple did not look like a building; it rose from the summit of the Wannian Hill, *Wannian Peak*, like a mountain of stone and timber that had grown naturally out of the bedrock. The walls, thirteen stories high, rose at a steep inward angle, their surfaces painted in the sacred colors of white, red, and yellow. The massive white granite blocks of the lower Wannian Hall formed a solid bastion, supporting the crimson walls of the Golden Summit above. The golden roofs, with their upturned corners and copper banners, caught the brilliant, unshielded mountain sun, throwing blinding flashes of light across the valley.

Jun stood at the base of the eastern zigzagging ramp, his hand resting on the stone parapet. He was breathing heavily, his chest rising and falling in a rapid, shallow rhythm. His shoulder muscles were tight, aching from the weight of his oak toolbox, which had felt twice as heavy since they had crossed the high passes of the Qinling Mountains.

Beside him, Liang was bent double, his forehead pressed against the whitewashed stone wall. His face was a pale, chalky grey, his lips tinged with a faint violet blue.

"Take it slow, Liang," Jun said, his voice quiet to conserve his breath. "Do not fight the air. Inhale through your nose, hold it for a heartbeat, and let it out. The mountain has its own pace."

"It feels... like there is nothing to catch," Liang gasped, his fingers clawing at the rough granite surface of the wall. "My chest... it feels like it is clamped in an iron vice."

"The altitude sickness will pass once the blood adjusts," Jun said, though he too felt a dull, thumping pain behind his temples. "We must climb. The ramp is the only way up."

They had spent three weeks traveling west from the ramparts of Xi'an, navigating the ancient trade routes across the loess hills and the high, wind-swept grasslands of Qinghai. As they climbed higher onto the plateau, they had observed a distinct change in the nature of the outbreak. The dead they encountered were different from the bloated, water-logged bodies of the southern canals. Here, the intense dry cold and the lack of moisture had mummified the zombies, turning their flesh into a tough, brown leather.

Their movement was even slower than before. The freezing mountain nights stiffened their joints, and the thin air, while not affecting their lungs, seemed to limit the chemical energy in their dried muscles. They moved with a heavy, dragging shuffle, like clockwork toys running down. Yet, they did not stop. They crawled out of the dry stream beds and the ruins of the valley settlements, drawn by the warmth of the living.

"Amituofo!" a deep, resonant voice called out from the portal above.

A broad-shouldered man with a face darkened to a deep copper by the mountain sun stepped onto the landing of the monastery courtyard courtyard. He wore a heavy wool *padded coat*—a traditional Sichuan coat—wrapped tightly around his waist, the long sleeves tied behind his back. In his hand, he held a heavy granite-carving mallet, its hickory handle worn smooth.

"You are the builders from Shaanxi?" the man asked, his Mandarin carrying the soft, tonal inflections of the Emei Valley. "I am Ah Feng, the watchman of the lower gates. We received the radio transmission from Captain Zhang three days ago. We have been waiting."

"I am Jun," the carpenter replied, adjusting the strap of his toolbox. "This is Liang. We came as soon as the passes allowed."

Ah Feng walked down the steps, his soft-soled bull-leather boots making no sound on the stone. He looked at the heavy handcart they had dragged up the lower trail, then at the toolbox on Jun's back. "The palace is grateful. The winter has been cruel this year. The frost has split the granite bastions of the lower Wannian Hall, and the northern retaining wall is beginning to shift outward. If the wall fails, the assembly halls above will lose their foundation."

Jun looked down the steep, zigzagging ramp. The stone walkway was built of massive granite slabs, two meters wide, rising in a series of sharp turns up the southern face of the hill.

Below, in the shadow of the lower wall, several figures were moving. They were climbing the stone steps with a sluggish, mechanical drag. One was a former tour guide, his blue nylon jacket torn and stained, a rusted megaphone still slung around his shoulder. His legs were stiff, his knees barely bending as he dragged his feet over the granite risers. Behind him, two others followed, their dry, leathery fingers clawing at the mortar joints of the retaining wall as they tried to find a shortcut up the cliff.

"They come up from the valley every day when the sun rises," Ah Feng said, his eyes hard as he watched the slow shapes. "The cold keeps them quiet during the night, but once the heat hits the granite, they wake up. We push them off with poles, but more come from the ruins of the town. Come. Let us look at the bastion before the mist descends."

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE STONE BASTION


The lower bastion of the Wannian Hall was a massive, battered wall of grey granite blocks, rising ten meters from the rocky ledge of the Wannian Hill.

The wall was built at an angle, its face sloping inward to distribute the lateral pressure of the earth and the heavy timber structures of the palace chambers above. The granite blocks were massive, some weighing over half a ton, set in a traditional mortar of clay, slaked lime, and chopped barley straw.

But the frost had destroyed the joint integrity.

Jun knelt on the narrow stone platform at the base of the wall, his fingers tracing a wide, horizontal crack that ran for five meters along the masonry. The granite blocks above the crack had bulged outward by three inches, their edges shearing and leaving a trail of white, crushed lime dust on the path.

"The snowmelt from the upper terraces drains down into the wall core," Jun explained, pointing to the dark moisture staining the stone joints. "During the day, the sun warms the granite, melting the ice. But at night, the temperature drops to fifteen below. The water freezes inside the core, expanding and pushing the outer granite face away from the rammed earth interior. It is frost heave—*dongzhang*."

"We tried to pack it with new mortar," Ah Feng said, shaking his head. "But the pressure is too great. The new joints just crack and pop out the next morning."

"Mortar alone cannot hold this," Jun said, standing up. "The horizontal pressure must be anchored back into the solid core of the hill. We must use the traditional *zongmu* method—internal timber tie-rods. We will drill horizontal holes through the bulging granite blocks, deep into the rammed loess core behind them. Then, we will slide in seasoned poplar tie-beams and lock them with oak wedges and a grout of lime and hot bull-hide glue."

"Poplar?" Liang asked, wiping his nose with his sleeve. "Will poplar wood hold the weight of granite?"

"In this dry air, poplar (*baimu*) will last for centuries without rotting," Jun said. "And it has a long, stringy grain that resists shear stress better than pine. Ah Feng, do you have dry rafters from the old stable buildings?"

"We have plenty," Ah Feng said. "We dismantled the lower roofs last month to make firewood. I will have the men bring them up."

The work began under the harsh, unclouded sun. Jun and Liang set up a simple wooden scaffold against the bulging face of the bastion. Using long iron star-drills—*qianzi*—and four-kilogram hammers, they began the laborious process of boring holes through the granite blocks.

The work was physically devastating. In the thin air of Mount Emei, every blow of the hammer demanded double the effort. The masons worked in pairs, one holding the iron drill and rotating it slightly after each strike, the other swinging the hammer.

*Clank... clank... clink.*

The metallic ring of the steel against the granite echoed off the palace walls. After five minutes of striking, a man’s lungs would burn, his heart racing as he gasped for oxygen. Jun took his turn, his hands gripping the hammer handle, his blows landing with a steady, heavy rhythm. The sweat on his forehead froze as soon as it met the wind, forming a salty crust on his skin.

By mid-afternoon, they had bored six holes, each ten centimeters in diameter and two meters deep, extending through the granite facing blocks into the dense, rammed loess core of the hill.

Liang prepared the poplar tie-beams, shaving them down to a tight, octagonal profile that matched the diameter of the holes. At the end of each beam, he cut a rectangular mortise hole to receive the locking wedge.

"The grout is ready," Liang called out.

In a small copper pot over a charcoal brazier, they had melted raw bull-hide glue (*niupi jiao*) together with slaked lime and river sand. The mixture was a thick, sticky paste that smelled of boiled leather and wet stone, but it was incredibly tough, curing into a waterproof, flexible compound.

Jun poured the hot grout into the first hole, then slid the poplar tie-beam in, using his mallet to drive the timber deep into the rammed earth. He inserted a large wedge of seasoned oak into the mortise slot at the outer end of the beam, driving it home until the wood compressed against the granite block.

"That's one," Jun gasped, leaning against the scaffold. His breath came in ragged white plumes.

"Master, look down," Liang whispered, pointing to the eastern ramp.

The sun was setting behind the western peaks, casting the valley into a cold, purple shadow. With the temperature dropping, the mummified zombies below had begun to move more quickly, their dried joints warming up from the day's heat. A pack of six was climbing the zigzag steps, their grey hands reaching for the stone banisters. One of them—a former soldier in a torn green uniform—had reached the terrace just below the bastion scaffold.

Ah Feng stepped to the edge of the landing, his masonry hammer held low. "Keep working, Jun! I will hold the ramp!"

The soldier zombie scrambled onto the landing, its jaw clicking as it smelled the living. Ah Feng did not hesitate. He swung the heavy stone hammer, the steel head striking the zombie's temple with a dull, cracking sound. The figure collapsed, sliding back down the steps, but two more were already crawling over the ledge.

Jun grabbed the second poplar beam. "Liang! Grout!"

They slid the second beam into the hole, Jun driving the oak wedge with his mallet. His hands were shaking from exhaustion, his knuckles split by the cold granite dust. *Thwack... thwack... thwack.*

With the third and fourth anchors locked, the bulging granite blocks of the bastion were secured, tied back into the solid core of the hill.

The remaining zombies on the ramp were held back by Ah Feng and the watchmen, who used their long staff-shoves to knock the sluggish creatures off the narrow ledge.

Jun climbed down from the scaffold, his limbs stiff, his face white. The wind was rising from the north, carrying the cold of the high plains. He looked up at the massive wall—it was straight again, the bulged blocks pulled back into alignment by the timber ties.

"The bastion will hold for the winter," Jun said, his voice hoarse.

"But the wind is rising," Ah Feng said, looking up at the high roofs of the Golden Summit. "The golden roofs are shaking, and we must secure the plates before the gale tears the metal apart."

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE MOUNTAIN SLINGS


The steep cliffs of the Wannian Hill, *Wannian Peak*, were the palace’s primary defense, but frost and snowmelt had carved narrow clefts and talus slides into the mount. Now, these rocky gullies had become pathways for the mummified dead. In the cold, dry air of the plateau, the corpses of the infected dried out rather than rotting, their skin turning to tough bull leather stretched tight over bone. This mummification slowed their movements to a mechanical crawl, but it also made them durable. They did not feel the freezing cold, and their desiccated bodies could wedge themselves into the rocky crevices, slowly climbing the chimneys.

Standing on the high wooden gallery of the Wannian Hall, Ah Feng looked down into a cleft. Jun stood beside him, hands resting on the cold granite parapet. The wind from the north was rising, whistling through the wooden lintels.

"We cannot defend every gully with spears," Ah Feng said, conserving his breath. "Our watchmen are stretched thin. We have only four old Type 81 rifles, and ammunition is down to three magazines. If we shoot, the report echoes off the mountain walls, drawing more of the dead. We must hold them before they reach the terraces."

"We do not need bullets to hold the heights," a deep, cracked voice said from behind them.

They turned to see Elder Feng, Ah Feng’s grandfather. The old man was eighty years old, his face mapped with sun-blackened wrinkles. He wore a sheepskin coat, its sleeves tucked into a sash of braided red wool. In his hand, he held a woven sling, its pocket worn smooth and dark from contact with grease and stone.

"We use the *mountain sling*," Elder Feng said, holding up the sling. "In the grasslands, the sling is the shepherd's rifle. A boy with a *mountain sling* can drive a wolf from his flock at eighty paces. The wind is our ally here. If we drop stones from sixty meters above, the gravity of the Wannian Hill will do the work of gunpowder."

Jun reached out and touched the sling. The two cords, each about a meter long, were made of coarse, dark bull tail-hair, known as *coarse hair*.

"Bull tail-hair," Elder Feng explained. "It is coarse and stiff. Sheep's wool is too soft; it stretches when you swing, and the stone slips. Cotton rots, and hemp becomes stiff as iron when moisture freezes. But the hair from a bull's tail does not stretch, it does not hold water, and it remains supple even at fifteen below."

Jun nodded, calculating the tensile dynamics. "A stiff, braided bull-hair rope ensures that centrifugal force is transferred directly to the stone at the moment of release. We must make more."

The work began in the courtyard of the *monastery courtyard*. Jun and the women gathered materials, pulling coarse bull tail-hair from salvaged hides. Under the direction of the elder women, the watchmen and monks braided the fibers using nine strands to form a tight, flat braid that wouldn't create drag. For the pocket, the *sling pocket*, Jun chiseled a template from scrap poplar. The pocket was woven in a split-diamond pattern to cradle a stone securely during the wind-up and ensure a clean release. The release cord ended in a small knot—the *release knot*—held between the thumb and index finger, while the retention cord ended in a secure loop wrapped around the middle finger.

"We cannot use just any stones," Jun said to Liang. "A jagged stone will catch the air, hum, and drift in the wind. We will miss."

"But where do we find round stones on a mountain of granite?" Liang asked.

"The Emei River," Jun said, pointing toward the southern horizon, where the *Emei River* wound through the valley. "The water has spent thousands of years polishing the granite. The dry banks are covered in rounded river stones."

To bring the stones up the sheer cliffs, Jun constructed a simple gantry hoist over the western parapet. He bolted two old wooden pulley wheels to a projecting pine timber—a *diaoliang*—anchoring it to the stone roof of the lower guardhouse with iron spikes.

He calculated the load limit. "Our twelve-millimeter hemp rope has a breaking strength of nine hundred kilograms," Jun explained. "But with pulley friction, we must limit the load to one hundred and fifty kilograms per basket. A counterweight basket filled with granite rubble will ease the pull."

Below, a team of twenty survivors worked in coordination, gathering smooth, spherical stones from the dry gravel bars. They loaded them into woven wicker baskets, which were then hoisted up the cliff face.

Jun stood by the sorting table, inspecting the ammunition. He picked up a smooth, egg-sized granite stone.

"This is perfect," Jun said. "It is about two hundred and fifty grams. Liang, sort them by size. We need three classes: the *chen*—heavy stones of three hundred grams; the *zhong*—standard stones of two hundred and fifty grams; and the *ying*—light, aerodynamic stones of one hundred and eighty grams for long-range."

Jun performed the ballistic calculations. "At three thousand seven hundred meters, the air density is about zero point eight two kilograms per cubic meter—thirty percent lower than at sea level. This means the aerodynamic drag is reduced by nearly a third. A stone thrown from here will retain its velocity much longer, striking with greater kinetic energy."

Elder Feng walked over, carrying a wooden bowl of hot ginger tea. "The math is good, carpenter, but the wind does not read your book. The north wind, the *changlu*, blows down from the northern plains at fifteen meters per second. If you throw a stone straight, the wind will take it into the ravine. You must throw into the wind's throat."

"How do you calculate the drift?" Jun asked.

"You look at the temple banners—*wind-flags*," Elder Feng said, pointing to the banners fluttering from the ramparts. "If the blue flag is straight, the wind is three steps strong. You aim three steps to the north. You throw when the wind takes its breath, between the gusts."

Suddenly, the wail of a conch shell echoed from the watchtower, warning that the dead were approaching.

A pack of thirty mummified zombies emerged from the willow thickets, climbing the western ramp. In the bright sun, their skin appeared ash-grey. They moved with a slow, mechanical stride, their stiff joints clicking. One of them, a former monk in a faded saffron robe, led the line, his parchment-like skin stretched tight over his skull.

Elder Feng stepped onto the balcony ledge, sixty meters above the ramp. He took a standard granite stone and nested it into the pocket of his *mountain sling*. He held the cords in his right hand, fingers locked around the release knot.

He began a slow, horizontal rotation above his head. The cords whistled, a rising hum. *Whoosh... whoosh... whoosh.* His body rotated, weight shifting. He watched the lead zombie pass a white prayer cairn, waited for the wind to pause, then released the knot.

With a sharp *crack*, the sling snapped. The granite stone descended sixty meters, curving slightly to the south as it met the crosswind.

*Crack!*

The stone struck the lead zombie in the forehead. The mummified skull split, and the figure stiffened, its momentum broken. It tumbled over the edge, falling fifty meters into the rocky ravine.

"A good stone," Elder Feng said, reaching for another. "The head is the only place. If you hit the chest, the dry leather just bounces the stone away."

The other watchmen and young monks took their places along the balcony, their new slings loaded. Jun and Liang supplied the sorted stones from the wicker baskets.

"Spread your feet," Jun instructed Liang. "Keep your center of gravity low. The wind will try to pull you off balance when you spin."

The air was filled with the rhythmic whistling of the slings. Another stone struck the temple of a zombie in a blue coat, and the zombie collapsed.

The coordination was seamless. The older men directed the fire, calling out wind adjustments based on the prayer flags, while the young monks and women hauled the ammunition. It was a collective effort of mutual aid, each person playing their part to defend the sanctuary.

The climbing line on the ramp began to fragment. Struck by the falling stones, the zombies fell one by one. By the time the sun dipped behind the mountains, the ramp was silent. Only three zombies remained, their legs shattered, crawling uselessly on the granite steps.

Elder Feng wiped his forehead, his breathing steady. "The *mountain sling* will keep the palace safe from the dead."

Jun looked down at the empty steps. The defense had cost them nothing but sweat and river stones. But as the wind grew colder, carrying the scent of snow, he knew the battle was not over. He looked up at the high, shimmering roofs of the Golden Summit. The golden plates were groaning in the gale.

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE GOLDEN ROOF


The Golden Summit was topped by gilded bronze roofs—the *golden roofs*—their upturned corners representing the spiritual heart of the complex. But the mountain winds at this altitude were violent, and the current gale, blowing down from the northern northern peaks at fifty miles an hour, was a destructive force. The wind had torn the copper anchoring plates off the southern slope of the main chapel, leaving the heavy, gilded bronze sheets flapping in the wind with a deafening metallic clatter that vibrated through the wooden rafters below.

Jun stood in the dark attic of the chapel, his hands resting on one of the massive red-painted cedar pillars that supported the roof. He could feel the timber shuddering under his palm.

"The wind will tear the plates off completely," Jun said to Ah Feng. "And if the rain gets under the bronze, the water will run down the interior sheathing. These cedar pillars have stood for four hundred years, but if they rot, the entire assembly hall will collapse."

"What can we do?" Ah Feng asked. "The gold is too slick to walk on in this wind, and we cannot drive iron nails into the gilded bronze without splitting the wood below."

"We must build a *wangjia*—a diagonal timber lattice grid," Jun explained. "We will lay pine laths across the copper plates, forming an interlocking net braced against the main ridge beam and the heavy eaves. The weight of the timber grid and the tension of the anchors will clamp the flapping bronze sheets down without the need for hundreds of new holes in the metal. Liang, get the pine laths and the brass screws."

"Master," Liang said, looking at the trapdoor. "The slope is steep, nearly forty degrees. The gold leaf is polished and slick as ice. If a man slips, he will slide off the edge."

"We will wear the *felt boots*—our felt-bottomed boots," Jun said. "The pressed wool soles will grip the smooth bronze much better than leather. And we will anchor our safety lines of braided bull-hair rope to the heavy iron banners along the main ridge. We work in pairs. No one moves without their anchor locked."

They climbed through the hatchway onto the roof. The transition was a physical shock. The wind hit them like a solid wall of ice, its roar deafening. The sun was brilliant, reflecting off the gilded bronze with a blinding, golden glare. Jun had rubbed charred charcoal soot under his eyes to reduce the glare, but the light was still intense.

Jun stood on the steep slope, his felt-bottomed boots finding purchase on the cold, textured gold leaf. He checked his safety line, which was tied with a secure bowline knot to one of the heavy cast-iron banners on the ridge.

"Liang! Drag the first lath up!" Jun shouted, his voice instantly carried away by the wind.

Liang crawled out of the hatch, dragging a three-meter pine lath. He was breathing in rapid, shallow gasps, his face pale from the high-altitude exertion. He wedged his felt soles against the copper seam to stabilize himself, his hands shaking as he held the wood.

The engineering of the *wangjia* required precision. The laths had to be laid diagonally at a forty-five-degree angle to the roof seams, spaced exactly sixty centimeters apart. This grid spacing was calculated to distribute the aerodynamic lift force of the wind.

Jun explained the physics in a shouted voice. "The wind blowing over the ridge creates a low-pressure zone on the leeward slope. The dynamic wind pressure, $q = 0.5 \\times \\rho \\times v^2$. With our air density $\\rho$ at zero point eight kilograms per cubic meter and the wind speed $v$ at twenty-two meters per second, the dynamic lift force is over two hundred Pascals. A single loose copper sheet of two square meters experiences a lift force of four hundred Newtons. The diagonal pine lattice will distribute this lift force across multiple rafters, securing the plates."

Using a hand-drill—a steel gimlet with a wooden cross-handle—Jun began to bore pilot holes through the copper plates into the underlying cedar sheathing. The work was slow and exhausting. Because of the thin air, every rotation of the drill demanded intense physical effort, his chest burning as his lungs struggled to extract oxygen.

After three holes, Jun's hands were numb, the freezing wind robbing his fingers of dexterity. Liang took over, holding the brass wood screws. The screws were flathead, three inches long, made of solid brass to resist the mountain moisture. Liang placed a screw in the pilot hole and used a heavy screwdriver, twisting it with both hands until the screw head was flush with the pine lath, compressing the wood against the metal sheet.

With each screw driven, the terrible flapping sound of the bronze plates began to subside. The loose metal was clamped tight against the deck, the vibration in the cedar pillars below fading into a steady, quiet hum.

"We have four more rows to lock!" Jun yelled, adjusting his safety line.

But as they reached the middle section of the roof, near the western gutter, a sound rose above the wind—a dry, rhythmic scratching.

Liang looked down toward the edge of the roof, his eyes widening in terror. "Master! Look at the drains!"

Three mummified zombies were emerging from the copper rainwater drains of the adjacent Wannian Hall. These drains, designed to channel seasonal snowmelt, were wide rectangular copper conduits that ran down the vertical stone walls. The zombies, their desiccated bodies lightened by the dry air and their leathery skin providing high friction, had squeezed their limbs into the interior of the conduits, climbing them like chimneys.

They crawled out onto the copper gutter, their movements slow and mechanical. Their joints were stiff from the cold night, but the sun warming the copper had given them just enough energy to move. One of them, a former caravan driver in a tattered sheepskin coat, began to crawl up the steep, gilded slope toward Liang, its black, dried fingers clawing at the seams of the copper plates.

"Keep your balance, Liang!" Jun yelled, reaching for his broadaxe, which was slung across his back. "Do not let your heels slide! The felt must remain flat on the metal!"

The zombie crawled with a silent, spider-like drag. Its mouth was open, the dry tongue shriveled to a black strip behind its teeth. As it reached the second pine lath, its hand lunged forward, grabbing Liang’s ankle.

Liang slipped on the gilded bronze, falling backward.

*Snap!*

The braided bull-hair safety line jerked taut, the bowline knot holding secure against the iron banner on the ridge. Liang hung suspended in the middle of the slope, his hands clawing at the smooth metal as the zombie, still holding his ankle, tried to drag itself up his leg.

Jun did not hesitate. He slid down the slope, using the pine laths as footholds to control his descent. His safety line stretched, but held. He reached the sliding zone, his felt-bottomed boots planting firmly on the diagonal timber. He swung the broadaxe, the heavy steel blade cutting through the cold wind.

*Thwack!*

The axe head struck the zombie’s temple, splitting the mummified skull. The dry, leathery body instantly lost its grip, its fingers releasing Liang’s boot. The corpse slid down the steep golden slope, tumbling over the copper gutter and falling seventy meters into the empty canyon below.

At the same time, Ah Feng appeared at the window, holding a long wooden pole tipped with a curved iron hook. He reached out and pushed the second zombie off the gutter ledge, sending it plunging into the abyss. Jun scrambled down to the third zombie, which was still struggling to climb the copper gutter. With a single, heavy strike of his mallet, he crushed the skull against the metal rim.

Jun hauled Liang back up the slope, their breathing coming in ragged, painful gasps. Their chests heaved in the thin air, their hearts racing wildly.

"Are you whole, Liang?" Jun asked, his hand trembling as he held the carpenter's shoulder.

"I... I have my breath, Master," Liang panted, his lips blue but his grip on the screwdriver tight. "The rope... it held."

"The strength of our materials," Jun said, looking up at the iron banners. "Let us finish the grid before the sun sets."

Working with renewed urgency, the three men laid the remaining pine laths. Jun bored the pilot holes, Liang drove the brass screws, and Ah Feng held the timbers in place. By the time the shadow of the mountains covered the Golden Summit, the *wangjia* lattice was complete. The southern roof of the main chapel was locked in a tight, diagonal embrace of seasoned pine and brass. The gilded plates were silent, the structural vibration gone, and the sanctuary was secure against the winter gales.


---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE WATER CISTERN


The water supply of Wannian Temple, the lifeblood of the eighty-seven survivors on Wannian Peak, depended on the ancient stone cistern set into the rock floor of the inner courtyard. This subterranean reservoir, measuring six by four meters and three and a half meters deep, was fed by a natural cold spring from a fissure in the Mount Emei bedrock. For centuries, its waters remained sweet and clear, insulated by the heavy granite paving slabs above. Flanked by the red timber walls of the temple wings, the courtyard was a quiet refuge beneath the mist-shrouded peaks of Sichuan. But the relentless winter had breached this stronghold.

The air in the courtyard was a thick, freezing fog that hung over the glazed green roof tiles, coating the timber in a glassy glaze of frost. Below the flagstones, the water in the cistern had frozen to a depth of nearly three feet. The expansion of this massive block of ice—which Jun calculated had increased in volume by nine percent as it froze—exerted an immense force against the reservoir's lining. The lining, made of five-centimeter-thick slabs of local slate set against the granite bedrock, could not withstand this pressure. The ice had wedged the slabs outward, cracking the slate along its bedding planes and splitting the joints.

The water seeped down through the porous limestone channels, flooding the basement archives of the lower Wannian Hall. In these damp chambers, the temple's ancient woodblock-printed sutras, written on mulberry paper, were stored in lacquer chests. The dripping water threatened to destroy these treasures while leaving the survivors without clean water. Younger monks worked in a human chain to carry the chests to the main hall, their breath rising in white plumes as they saved their heritage.

Ah Feng, the gatekeeper, stood at the lip of the cistern's access hatch, his breath clouding in the freezing air. He lowered a notched pine rod into the dark pit, his knuckles white as he held the cold wood. When he drew the rod back up, the wet mark was alarmingly low.

"The level has dropped another forty centimeters since the middle of the night," Ah Feng said, his teeth chattering from the damp chill of the courtyard. "We have barely two days of water left in the lower basin. But how do we repair the slate? The spring is still trickling in from the northern wall, keeping the entire crack wet. Any mortar we mix will be washed away before it can set."

Jun knelt beside the hatch, his oil lamp flickering. "Traditional mortar cannot set in moving water," Jun said, his voice steady despite the thin air. "We must use the traditional *composite sealant*—a compound of boiled pine resin, slaked lime dust, and pounded hemp fibers. It cures in the wet, remains flexible, and adheres to slate under hydrostatic pressure."

Liang, rubbing his hands together to warm his numb fingers, looked down into the dark cavern. "But Master, how do we apply a hot resin sealant to a wall that is constantly washed by ice-cold spring water? The moment the hot resin touches the wet stone, it will chill, crystallize, and fail to bond."

"We must isolate the work area," Jun said, pointing to the fissure in the northern corner. "We will build a pine cofferdam—a *weiyan*. We will partition the corner using tongue-and-groove pine planks, seal the base with sandbags of damp loess clay, and use the manual pump to drain the work zone. Once the stone is dry, we will apply the sealant."

In the damp cistern chamber, Jun and Liang hauled planks of seasoned Sichuan pine (*hongsha*) down the steps. The wood was cold, its resin scent mixing with the musty smell of wet earth. Jun used a Chinese frame saw (*juzi*) to cut the planks to the width of the corner. He bevelled the edges at a fifteen-degree angle, ensuring they would jam tightly against the slate walls under pressure.

"We will drive the wedge planks here," Jun instructed Liang, pointing to a narrow groove chiseled into the slate floor.

Using iron chisels and four-kilogram mallets, they cut a channel in the floor to receive the bottom of the pine barrier. In the cramped space, their lungs burned with every swing. The air lacked circulation; their breath formed plumes of vapor that condensed on the stone ceiling, dripping back down like needles of ice.

They slid the pine boards into place, forming a wall that cut off the northern corner. The triangular workspace behind the barrier measured 1.2 meters on each side and three meters high, meaning they had to hold back nearly two thousand kilograms of water. To seal the gaps, they packed the base with hemp bags filled with loess clay. Liang stepped into the water, stomping the bags tight into the corners.

"The partition is set," Liang panted, his chest heaving. "But the water inside the work zone is still at level."

"Set up the suction pump," Jun said.

They carried down a manual wooden pump—a *shuiche*—from the agricultural stores. The pump cylinder was a hollow log of wild plum wood, fitted with a leather-rimmed wooden piston on an iron rod. Liang gripped the handle, his arms shaking with fatigue as he began the pumping motion.

*Squeak-clack... squeak-clack.*

The pump groaned, drawing water from behind the cofferdam and discharging it through a bamboo pipe. Liang maintained forty strokes per minute to keep up with the water leaking past the sandbags. As the water level behind the boards dropped, the hydrostatic pressure from the main tank pushed the timber barrier tighter into the chasm, creating a watertight seal.

While Liang pumped, Jun prepared the sealant on the terrace above. He set up a charcoal brazier with a large iron cauldron, throwing in chunks of raw pine resin (*songxiang*) harvested from the temple cliffs. The golden resin melted, releasing a thick, sweet smoke that filled the courtyard, masking the dry, mummified smell of the valley below.

"We must watch the temperature," Jun said, stirring the amber liquid with a green pine stick. "If the resin gets too hot, it will boil and become brittle when it cools. It must remain thick and viscous, like mountain honey, around one hundred and twenty degrees."

Once the resin liquefied, Jun sifted in slaked lime dust (*shihuifen*). He added the lime in a three-to-two ratio by weight, stirring constantly. Finally, he added chopped hemp fibers (*juma*), which Liang had pounded until fine as hair. The hemp fibers acted like straw in mud bricks, reinforcing the sealant against cracking under the pressure of the winter ice.

"The mix is ready," Jun called out, his face red from the heat of the brazier. "Bring the copper irons!"

He carried the hot cauldron down into the cistern, the steam rising from the golden paste. The rock face inside the cofferdam was now dry, though the cold stone radiated a deep, bone-penetrating chill.

Jun dipped a spatula into the hot, sticky sealant. The paste was thick, smelling of burnt pine and hot lime. He pressed it firmly into the vertical crack, working from the bottom upward. The paste hissed as it met the cold stone, but the hemp fibers held it together, preventing it from running out of the fissure.

"Pass the copper iron," Jun said, his hand cramping from the pressure.

Liang handed him a copper smoothing iron (*luotie*), heated to a dull red glow. Jun pressed the iron against the sealant, remelting the surface to drive it deep into the pores of the slate and smoothing the joint to a glassy finish.

They worked for three hours in the dark vault, their hands blackened by resin and faces streaked with soot. Jun applied the compound in three layers, building a flexible, waterproof patch three centimeters thick that extended ten centimeters on either side of the crack.

"The sealant has set," Jun said, touching the patched slate. The compound had cooled into a tough, leathery barrier that resisted the pressure of his thumb.

"Let us slow the pump and test the seal," Liang suggested, leaning against the timber framing.

Liang stopped the pump. The water level behind the cofferdam rose slightly as the trickling spring began to fill the small space, but the patched slate remained dry. Not a single drop of water seeped through the thick, amber joint. The slate was sealed.

"It holds," Jun said, a faint smile breaking through his exhaustion. He wiped his hands on a piece of greasy wool. "The temple will have its water."

Suddenly, a loud, splintering crash echoed from the lower terraces of the temple, the sound vibrating through the solid stone foundations of the cistern vault.

Ah Feng rushed down the stone steps, his face pale under the soot. "Jun! Liang! The garden ladders have given way! The dead have breached the lower path!"

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE CLIFF-LADDER


The gardens of Wannian Temple, situated on a narrow, fertile terrace sixty meters below the main hall of the Golden Summit, were the survivors' primary source of winter sustenance. There, under the shelter of the south-facing limestone cliffs, they grew hardy winter radishes, broad beans, and Chinese cabbage, which they preserved in salt. But access to these gardens was extremely hazardous, requiring the survivors to descend a series of narrow wooden ladders secured against the vertical, wind-swept limestone cliff face.

These ladders, constructed decades earlier from local fir poles (*shanshan*), had long since succumbed to the damp mountain mist. The wood suffered from dry-rot (*ganlan*), its internal fibers weak and powdery. The freezing of winter had split the rungs, and under the weight of three mummified zombies trying to climb, the main ladder at the second terrace had broken. The fir rails sheared down the middle with a loud crack, leaving the broken upper sections dangling from iron spikes by rotted hemp rope.

When Jun, Liang, and Ah Feng reached the edge of the terrace, they looked down into the grey valley.

The wind howled up the canyon, carrying the scent of damp earth. Below them, clinging to the broken rungs, were two mummified figures. Dried to a dark brown, their skin was stretched tight over ribs like cured hide. They moved with the slow, mechanical drag of the mountain dead, dry joints clicking as they tried to grip the splintered wood.

"We must cut the ladders down immediately," Ah Feng said, holding his iron-tipped guard staff. "If they reach this landing, the gates of Wannian Hall are only thirty meters away. But without the ladders, we lose access to the gardens. We cannot survive the winter on dry barley and preserved cabbage alone."

"We will build a *diaoti*—a timber draw-ladder," Jun said, scanning the cliff face. "A modular ladder of seasoned spruce, counterweighted with stone-mill wheels. We can lower it to harvest and hoist it up when the dead approach."

"Spruce?" Liang asked, wiping sweat from his forehead despite the cold. "A twelve-meter spruce ladder will weigh one hundred and twenty kilograms. How can we raise it in this thin air without exhausting the guards?"

"We will use a counterweight," Jun explained, pointing to the old masonry structures nearby. "We can use two stone gristmill wheels from the grain store. A stone wheel of fifty centimeters diameter and ten centimeters thickness weighs fifty kilograms. Two wheels on a single axle will give us a counterweight of one hundred kilograms. The remaining twenty kilograms of weight can be lifted easily with a simple guide rope, even by a single watchman."

The men set to work on the wind-swept terrace. Jun selected logs of seasoned spruce (*shanshan*) from the yard, which had cured for three years under the eaves of the stable buildings. The wood was dry and straight-grained, smelling of clean sap. Using his long frame saw, Jun ripped the logs into clean rails measuring eight by ten centimeters. He marked the positions for the rungs at intervals of exactly thirty centimeters, using a dry charcoal stick and a wooden carpenter's square, ensuring uniform spacing to prevent missteps in the dark.

"Liang, chisel the mortise holes," Jun directed, handing him a mortising chisel (*zaozi*). "Make them three centimeters wide and five deep, cut at a five-degree upward angle so the rungs won't slide out when the rails flex under load."

Liang knelt on the cold granite paving, his hammer swinging in a tight, rhythmic arc. *Clack... clack... clack.* The steel chisel bit into the wood, releasing a fresh pine scent that was quickly carried away by the wind.

For the rungs, Jun chose seasoned oak (*xiangmu*) for its high tensile strength and resistance to shear stresses. He shaped each rung to an octagonal profile using his drawknife, shaving the ends down with care to form clean tenons that would fit snugly into Liang’s mortise holes.

"We must lock every joint," Jun said, adjusting his spectacles.

With his hand-drill, he bored small pilot holes through the sides of the spruce rails into the center of each oak tenon. He drove in seasoned oak pegs (*muqian*), locking the joints together without iron nails, which would rust and split the timber in the mountain's constant humidity.

Meanwhile, Ah Feng and three young monks hauled the basalt stone-mill wheels from the old kitchen. These wheels, once used to grind wheat and mountain corn, were made of dense volcanic stone. Jun inspected their center holes. "The square eye of the stones is ten centimeters wide," he noted. "We will shape an axle pin of seasoned oak to fit the openings, locking the stones together. Then we will chisel the outer ends of the axle to a round profile, fitting them into bearing blocks of wild plum wood greased with mutton tallow."

They constructed the gantry frame—the *diaoliang*—using pine beams projecting over the cliff. Jun anchored the beams to the stone foundations of the parapet, securing them with iron clamps and rock anchors driven into the granite.

"Safety lines are critical," Jun warned. "The cliff face is slick with frost. No one works near the edge without a harness."

They braided safety harnesses from three-strand hemp rope, securing them to heavy iron rings driven into the temple walls. Jun stepped to the edge of the cliff, the sheer drop of sixty meters opening below him. The mountain wind whipped his wool coat, the freezing draft rising from the canyon floor below making his eyes water. With Liang holding his safety line, Jun leaned over the edge to mount the plum-wood bearing blocks to the pine beams, his numb fingers struggling to tighten the iron bolts.

They threaded a double cable of twisted bull-hair rope—braided by the elders of the monastery—over the basalt stone-mill wheels. One end was clamped to the ladder, the other to the counterweight.

"Lower the ladder," Jun ordered.

Ah Feng released the locking pin. The spruce ladder slid over the edge, its sections unfolding. The basalt millstones rotated in their greased plum-wood bearings, the stone counterweight descending into a protective shaft. The ladder descended ten meters, landing on the path below.

"It works!" Liang shouted, looking over the parapet. "The counterweight has balanced the mass. The ladder is stable."

But as the ladder touched the path, a rasping sound rose from the shadows of the garden wall. A mummified zombie in a tattered blue coat dragged itself toward the ladder. It was a former farm worker, its skin dry as parchment and its joints stiff. Moving with a sluggish, clockwork drag, its dry fingers clawed at the bottom rung.

"Hoist it!" Jun yelled. "Do not let it climb!"

Ah Feng pulled the guide rope. Supported by the counterweight, the ladder rose easily. But the zombie's leathery fingers had locked around the bottom rung with the grip of dried sinew. As the ladder rose, the zombie was lifted with it, legs dangling in the empty air.

"It is hanging on!" Liang cried.

Jun grabbed his clearing chopper—a *guandao*—which had been sharpened to a razor edge. Stepping to the edge, safety line taut, he watched the rising ladder. The zombie was five meters below the landing. Jun waited for the ladder to swing close to the rock face, stabilizing the frame, then brought the chopper down.

The blade cut through the zombie's dry wrists with a clean *crunch*. The figure lost its grip, falling through the mist. It struck the ledge fifty meters below, its dried body splitting on the boulders.

Jun drew the chopper back, gasping for air in the thin atmosphere.

"Lock it!" Jun panted.

Ah Feng pulled the rope, and the ladder folded against the cliff face, its bottom rung suspended six meters above the path. Liang slid the locking pin into the axle.

The draw-ladder was complete, providing a secure, controllable link to the gardens.

"The garden is secure," Ah Feng said.

Jun nodded, leaning against the parapet as the first flakes of snow began to fall, drifting silently through the Emei valley.

CHAPTER 7: THE BULL-HIDE NETS


The draw-ladder was up, but the threat remained. Below the western parapet, the cliffs fell away into the misty ravines of Mount Emei, but the eastern approach was different. Here, the mountain slope was gentler, carved by centuries of pilgrims into the eastern zigzagging stone ramp. The ramp, a wide path built of massive slabs of grey Sichuan granite, wound up the ridge in twelve sharp switchbacks, flanked on both sides by low masonry parapet walls.

As the morning sun broke through the high mist, warming the stone slabs, the dry, thin air began to stir. In the valley below, the mummified dead were waking. The day's heat, absorbing into the dark granite, warmed their desiccated joints. Slowly, with the mechanical, dragging shuffle characteristic of the mountain outbreak, they began their ascent. They did not run. They moved with a slow, relentless stride, their leathery limbs lifting and falling in a rhythmic, clockwork crawl.

Jun stood on the landing of the third switchback, looking down the long slope. Beside him, Ah Feng leaned on his guard staff, his copper-skinned face tight with worry.

"There are more today," Ah Feng said, his breath forming a light mist in the cold air. "The warmth brings them out of the pine forests. If they reach this gate, we will be forced to fight them on the stairs. But the ramp is four meters wide. Our spears cannot hold a line that wide, and our watchmen will tire within an hour."

"We cannot build a stone wall," Jun said, his fingers tracing the rough surface of the granite parapet. "The ramp is too steep, and a solid wall would block our own access to the lower paths. We must construct a flexible trap—a *piwei*. A series of heavy bull-hide nets stretched horizontally across the ramp, suspended above the steps. It will catch their feet, causing them to trip and pile up under their own mass, while we neutralize them from the safety of the upper terraces."

"Bull-hide?" Liang asked, joining them with his toolbox. "Will the leather not rot in the mountain mist?"

"Not if we treat it," Jun replied. "And bovine leather has a tensile strength that pine cannot match. The temple leather-stores have hundreds of dried bull hides, harvested from the animals that died during the early winter. They were meant for boot soles, but now they will serve as our net."

They returned to the lower courtyard of the temple, where the work of preparing the nets began. The survivors—men and women from the surrounding mountain villages—had gathered under the direction of the elder village committee. There was no panic, only the quiet, focused energy of collective mutual aid.

The dried bull-hide sheets were stacked in the open stable yard. They were massive, thick, and stiff as oak boards, smelling of salt, grease, and dried tallow. To cut them cold was impossible; the steel knives would dull after a single foot of slicing.

"We must soften the fibers," Jun instructed the young monks. "Set up the copper cauldrons. We will steam the hides over charcoal braziers to make the leather supple."

They built three large brick hearths in the yard, heating water in wide iron pans. The hides were suspended over the steam, wrapped in heavy hemp blankets to trap the heat. After forty minutes of exposure, the stiff leather softened, becoming pliable and rubbery.

Jun and the leatherworkers went to work. Using heavy drawknives (*pi-dao*) and long steel shears, they sliced the warm hides into long, uniform strips. Each strip was cut to exactly five centimeters in width and eight millimeters in thickness.

Jun performed the engineering calculations on a scrap of pine board. "The tensile strength of dried, vegetable-tanned bovine leather is approximately twenty-five Megapascals," he explained to Liang, who was cleaning a leather punch. "With a cross-sectional area of forty square millimeters per strip, a single leather band can support a tensile load of nearly ten thousand Newtons before shearing. When we weave them into a net, the load will be distributed across multiple joints."

"But what of the wind, Master?" Liang asked, pointing to the banners on the roof that were snapping in the gale. "The north wind on the eastern ridge is violent."

"That is why we must not make a solid barrier," Jun said, showing him the design template. "We will weave the strips into a grid with twelve-centimeter square openings. The solidity ratio of this mesh—the ratio of the solid leather area to the total area of the net—will be approximately zero point three five. A solidity ratio this low ensures that the drag coefficient is minimal. The high-altitude wind, even at twenty-five meters per second, will pass through the net with very little resistance, preventing the gale from tearing the anchors out of the stone."

"And the opening size?" Ah Feng asked.

"A human foot is typically twenty-five to thirty centimeters long," Jun explained. "A twelve-centimeter opening is large enough for the foot of a crawling or walking zombie to fall through, but too small for their ankle to pass when they try to lift it forward. Once their foot is trapped beneath the mesh, their own forward momentum will trip them."

The weaving was a laborious process. The strips were laid out on the stone flags of the yard, crossing at right angles. At every intersection, the leatherworkers punched a hole through both strips using a steel hollow punch (*tian-chong*) and a wooden mallet. They inserted a heavy copper rivet (*tongding*) and a brass washer, hammering the rivet head flat until the joint was locked. The resulting net was ten meters long and four meters wide, a heavy, brown mesh that weighed over eighty kilograms.

To protect the leather from the freezing rain and mist, they rubbed the completed net with a mixture of hot mutton tallow and pine tar. The grease soaked into the warm pores of the leather, sealing it against moisture and keeping it flexible even in the sub-zero temperatures of the summit.

By mid-afternoon, the net was carried down to the second switchback of the eastern ramp. The wind was howling over the ridge, carrying a light spray of ice.

"We must anchor it to the granite walls," Jun said. "The masonry is solid, but we cannot rely on mortar to hold the tension. We must use the *guanqian* method."

Ah Feng and the masons set to work. Using steel star-drills (*qianzi*) and four-kilogram sledges, they bored six horizontal holes into the granite parapet walls—three on each side of the ramp. Each hole was five centimeters in diameter and fifteen centimeters deep. The ring of the hammer on the steel drill was a sharp, clean sound that echoed across the valley.

In a small clay crucible over a charcoal brazier, Liang melted scraps of old lead pipe. The lead melted into a heavy, silver pool.

Jun inserted a hand-forged iron ring anchor (*tianhuan*) into the first hole. The anchor had a flared, ribbed shank designed to grip the stone.

"Hold the anchor straight, Liang," Jun said, his voice quiet.

Using a small iron ladle, Jun poured the molten lead into the gap between the iron shank and the granite wall. The hot metal hissed as it met the cold stone, filling every crevice. Within a minute, the lead cooled and solidified, expanding slightly as it hardened to lock the iron ring into the granite with a permanent, mechanical grip.

They repeated the process for all six anchors. Once the rings were set, they attached the bull-hide net to the walls using heavy iron turnbuckles and braided hemp ropes. The net was suspended horizontally across the ramp, parallel to the steps, but raised exactly twenty centimeters above the stone risers.

As the sun began to sink behind the western peaks, casting the eastern slope into cold shadow, the first of the climbing dead reached the second switchback.

They were mummified figures, their flesh dried to the consistency of old boot leather by the high-altitude air. They moved with a slow, heavy drag, their boots scraping on the granite.

The lead zombie, a former mountain carrier in a torn blue canvas jacket, stepped onto the net. Its right foot slipped through the twelve-centimeter opening, landing on the stone step below. But when it tried to take another step, its ankle caught against the thick horizontal leather strip. Lacking the intelligence to lift its foot vertically back out of the hole, it simply pushed forward.

Its balance broke. The zombie fell forward, its knees striking the granite with a dull thud. Its arms became tangled in the leather mesh as it struggled to rise.

The second zombie followed, walking blindly over the fallen leader. Its foot also caught in the openings, and it tumbled on top of the first. Within minutes, five more zombies were trapped, their dry, leathery limbs thrashing uselessly against the bull-hide grid. The net under the strain, the turnbuckles groaning as they transferred the load to the granite walls, but the lead-sealed anchors did not budge.

On the balcony of the third terrace, Elder Feng stood with the watchmen. Under his direction, the young monks prepared their mountain slings.

"Aim for the temples!" the elder shouted, his voice steady. "They are held fast. Take your time and conserve your stones."

The air was filled with the sharp whistle of the slings. One by one, the stones struck the skulls of the trapped zombies with clean, cracking sounds. The bodies went limp, their weight settling into the leather mesh, but the net held, blocking the ramp and preventing any further ascent.

Jun watched from the gate, his chest rising and falling in the thin air. The *piwei* had worked. The flexible barrier had neutralized the threat without the need for a single bullet or a risky close-quarters melee.

"The net will hold them," Jun said, wiping the sweat from his forehead. "But the wind is rising. We must return to the halls and secure the inner gates. There is much to prepare for the heavy snows."

---
