CHAPTER 8: THE PRAYER HALL


The lower assembly hall of the Wannian Temple, known as the Hall of the Thousand Buddhas, was a vast, timber-framed sanctuary that had stood for four centuries. Its roof, heavy with glazed green ceramic tiles, was supported by a forest of massive red cedar columns—the *nanmu* pillars—painted in deep lacquer crimson. Each column was a single tree trunk, over fifty centimeters in diameter, rising eight meters to the interlocking bracket sets (*dougong*) of the ceiling. The floor was laid with large, square slabs of dark grey basalt, worn smooth by the bare feet of generations of monks.

But the sanctity of the hall had been breached. During the night, four crawling zombies had managed to enter the temple's sub-structures. Having dragged their desiccated bodies through a stone drainage conduit that carried run-off water beneath the hall, they had pushed open a rotting timber floor hatch in the dark center of the sanctuary.

The alarm had been raised by a young monk who had gone to light the morning butter lamps. His screams echoed through the wooden galleries.

Jun and Liang ran into the hall, their heavy toolboxes slung over their shoulders. The air inside the vast chamber was freezing and still, smelling of stale incense, dry wool, and the faint, sweet odor of dried skin. The dim light from the high clerestory windows fell on the giant gilded bronze statues of the Bodhisattvas, their serene faces looking down on the scene below.

From the shadow of the central pillars, the four figures emerged. They were mummified and slow, their joints cracking like dry twigs as they dragged themselves across the basalt floor. One of them, a former pilgrim in a tattered grey coat, was crawling on its stomach, its dried fingers clawing at the stone joints as it pulled itself toward the altar steps.

Ah Feng and three watchmen stood near the entrance, their guard staffs held low, but they were hesitant to advance into the dark, cavernous space.

"We must contain them here," Jun said, his voice echoing in the rafters. "If they escape this hall, they will reach the residential quarters and the upper chapels. But we cannot fight them in the open; the hall is too large. We must build a barrier to block their path and funnel them into a killing zone."

"A wall of sandbags?" Ah Feng asked, his breath rising in white plumes.

"We have no sand here," Jun said. "And bags would be pushed over by their weight. We will use the heavy oak prayer benches—the *chanban*—to construct a V-shaped barrier between the main cedar pillars. We will lock the timbers directly around the columns, using the pillars themselves as the anchors."

"The V-shape?" Liang asked, looking at the long rows of heavy wooden benches that lined the hall.

"A straight wall bears the full force of a crowd," Jun explained, sketching a diagram in the sawdust on the floor. "But a V-shaped barrier, with its apex pointing toward the center of the hall, acts as a double wedge. The horizontal force of their bodies pushing against the arms of the V will be decomposed. The lateral pressure is redirected along the length of the benches as axial compression, transferring the load directly into the massive red cedar columns. The pillars can support tons of lateral force without shifting."

"And the apex?" Ah Feng asked.

"The apex will have a narrow, half-meter gap," Jun said. "It will act as a funnel. The dead will be drawn toward the opening, where a single defender can neutralize them one by one as they try to squeeze through, without being overwhelmed by their numbers."

The work began immediately. The prayer benches were massive pieces of seasoned oak, each three meters long, fifteen centimeters thick, and forty centimeters wide, weighing nearly eighty kilograms. It took two men to lift each bench, their boots sliding on the smooth basalt flags.

"Liang! Mark the notches!" Jun called out, his voice hoarse from the cold air.

They carried the first bench to the central red cedar column. Because the columns were circular, the ends of the benches had to be custom-notched to fit the curvature of the timber. This was the traditional *baozhu*—or pillar-hugging—joint.

Jun used a wooden compass to scribe the arc of the column onto the end of the oak bench. "We must cut a semi-circular notch, ten centimeters deep," he instructed Liang.

Using a hand-saw (*juzi*), Liang cut the shoulders of the notch, the steel teeth biting into the dense oak. The wood was dry and hard, resisting the blade. Liang’s muscles burned in the thin air, his breath coming in rapid, shallow gasps. He had to stop every dozen strokes to rest his lungs.

Once the shoulders were cut, Jun took a heavy adze (*wan-chuan*) to clear the waste wood. With practiced, heavy blows, he chipped away the oak, the pale wood chips piling up around his felt boots. The sweet, sharp smell of oak sawdust filled the cold hall. He finished the curve using a wide mortising chisel (*zaozi*), scraping the wood until it matched the scribed line.

They slid the bench into place. The notch fit snugly around the red cedar column.

"It is a tight fit," Liang said, wiping his brow.

"We must lock it," Jun said.

To secure the bench without driving nails into the historic columns, Jun used a traditional clamping system. He shaped two oak blocks to fit the back of the column, connecting them to the bench with heavy timber tie-keys. He then drove a seasoned oak wedge—a *mulao*—into the joint. As he struck the wedge with his heavy wooden mallet, the oak bench was pulled tightly against the front of the cedar column, the friction locking it in place with a solid, immovable grip.

They stacked the benches four-high, creating a barrier one point six meters tall. The horizontal joints between the stacked benches were secured using notched lap joints. Jun bored vertical holes through the joints using a T-handle auger, his shoulders straining as he turned the steel bit. He drove in heavy oak dowels—*muqian*—to lock the timbers together.

The V-shaped barrier now extended from the left and right walls of the hall, converging at a sixty-degree angle toward the central pillars. At the apex, a narrow opening of forty centimeters was left open.

The physical labor was exhausting. The temperature inside the hall had dropped to ten below, and the cold steel of the tools froze to their bare skin if they did not wear their woolen mittens. Jun’s hands were cramped, his fingers stiff and sore.

As they locked the final dowel of the apex post, the crawling dead reached the barrier.

The lead zombie, the pilgrim in the grey coat, dragged itself along the base of the oak wall. It reached the left wing of the V and pushed its head against the wood, its dried, blackened fingers clawing at the oak grain. But the barrier did not budge. The force of its body was directed down the length of the bench, compressing the timber against the massive red cedar column. The column remained solid and still, its red lacquer surface showing no sign of stress.

The other three zombies, drawn by the sound of the builders, shuffled toward the barrier. Their joints clicked as they moved, their eyes milky and blank. They followed the angle of the V, their bodies sliding along the smooth oak wood toward the central opening.

"They are coming to the gap!" Liang warned, drawing his hand-axe.

"Stand back, Liang," Ah Feng said, stepping forward.

Ah Feng stood at the apex of the V, his heavy iron-pointed staff held in both hands. The lead zombie reached the opening, its head and shoulders squeezing through the narrow gap. Its jaw snapped, its dry teeth clicking in the dark.

Ah Feng did not hesitate. He lunged forward, the steel tip of the staff striking the zombie in the forehead. The mummified skull cracked, and the figure collapsed in the gap, blocking the way for the others.

The second zombie tried to climb over the fallen body, but the narrow space restricted its movement. Ah Feng cleared the gap with a quick pull of his staff, then struck the second zombie in the temple, neutralizing it instantly.

Within five minutes, all four zombies were dispatched, their bodies piled neatly in the narrow killing zone at the apex of the barrier. The main body of the assembly hall was silent again.

Jun leaned against the oak barrier, his heart racing as he breathed the thin, cold air. His hands were shaking from the exertion, but he felt a deep sense of satisfaction. The structure had held. The joinery, designed centuries ago by Chinese master builders, had worked perfectly to redirect the physical force of the dead.

"The hall is secure," Ah Feng said, lowering his staff. "The barrier is solid. We can leave a single watchman here now."

"We must still seal the drainage conduit," Jun said, pointing to the open hatch. "Liang, get the lime and the stone slabs. We must seal the floor before the night returns."

CHAPTER 9: THE WANNIAN CHASM


The cold mountain wind of Mount Emei swept down from the high pine forests of the upper ridges, bringing with it a thick, freezing mist that clung to the grey granite walls of the Wannian Temple. The air at three thousand seven hundred meters was thin and bit deep into the lungs, carrying the damp smell of wet stone, pine resin, and the faint, unmistakable odor of old decay rising from the valleys below. Down on the lower flats, where the Emei River wound through the sandbars, a massive horde of ten thousand infected had crossed the shallow waters. They had crawled up the winding mountain trails, their slow, heavy footsteps dragging over the pine needles. The lower gates of the hill had caved under the relentless pressure of their collective weight, and the circular granite ramps that wound around the steep cliffs were now filled with a rising tide of grey, mummified bodies.

The survivors had retreated behind the heavy timber doors of the Wannian Hall, but the granite steps of the main ramp were too wide to hold with spears or staffs. The ramp rose at a thirty-degree angle, supported by a natural limestone arch that spanned a deep, narrow fissure in the rock.

Ah Feng stood by the heavy lintel of the gate, his face dark with soot and sweat. He leaned on his staff, his eyes scanning the grey mass of the dead shuffling up the lower loop of the ramp. "We cannot hold the gate if they reach the platform," he said, his voice raspy from the cold air. "There are too many of them. The spears will dull, and the brothers will tire. We must cut the ramp. The steps are built over the limestone arch, but the arch itself is braced by a massive timber structure beneath the stone. If we chop through the primary support beam, the granite steps will collapse under their own weight into the chasm below, isolating the temple."

Liang looked over the edge of the parapet, his face pale as he watched the lead figures of the dead climbing the middle ramp, their fingers scraping against the stone. "Who will go down there to cut the beam?" he asked, his voice shaking. "The dead are only twenty meters away from the arch. Anyone below will be crushed if the stone falls, or trapped on the cliff face."

"I will go," Jun said, his voice calm as he adjusted the strap of his wooden toolbox. He pulled his padded coat tight around his shoulders and picked up his heavy broadaxe. The axe head, forged from high-carbon steel and weighing one point eight kilograms, was ground to a razor-sharp edge, its curved hickory handle smooth from years of sweat. "Liang, get the safety ropes ready. Ah Feng, stand at the gate with the slings. Keep the lead dead from reaching the arch before I can finish the cut."

Jun climbed over the stone balustrade, securing a thick, three-strand hemp rope around his waist. Liang held the anchor, wrapping the rope around a solid granite pillar of the balcony. Jun lowered himself slowly into the narrow, dark cleft beneath the granite ramp. The space was cramped, smelling of damp limestone, ancient moss, and the cold draft of the chasm. Above him, the massive granite steps creaked and groaned under the weight of the climbing horde. He could hear the dry, rhythmic scratching of their boots and the heavy, uncoordinated thuds of their limbs.

The primary support beam was a log of seasoned red cedar, forty centimeters in diameter, wedged tightly into hand-carved sockets in the limestone bedrock. It acted as a horizontal strut, resisting the lateral thrust of the masonry arch above.

Jun adjusted his stance on a narrow rock ledge, his boots finding traction on the wet moss. He looked up at the cedar beam, calculating the forces in his head. The span of the stone arch was six meters, supporting a total granite mass of approximately twenty-four metric tons. At a thirty-degree incline, the lateral thrust $H$ acting on the support strut was equal to the weight of the stone multiplied by the cotangent of the angle, split between the two ends. This meant the cedar log was under a massive compressive load of nearly one hundred and twenty kilonewtons, plus the dynamic weight of the climbing zombies above. The shear strength of seasoned red cedar along the grain was only five point two Megapascals. By cutting a deep V-notch in the center of the beam, he would reduce its cross-sectional area, increasing the internal shear stress until the timber split under the compressive load of the arch.

He swung the broadaxe, the steel blade biting deep into the red heartwood of the cedar.
*Thwack.*
The sound was flat and heavy in the narrow cleft, followed by the sweet, sharp smell of fresh cedar sap. A shower of pale red wood chips fell into the dark chasm below. Jun drew the axe back, his muscles tensing in his shoulders as he swung again.
*Thwack. Thwack.*

With each blow, the blade cut deeper into the wood, carving a clean notch at a forty-five-degree angle. He could feel the vibrations of the climbing dead running down through the stone arch and into the cedar log, a low, rhythmic shudder that rattled his teeth. The air was so cold that his breath came in thick white plumes, condensing on the iron head of his axe. His hands were raw, the cold stone of the cleft leaching the warmth from his fingers.

"Jun! The dead have reached the lower steps of the arch!" Ah Feng shouted from the balcony above. A stone, thrown from a sling, whizzed past the opening of the cleft, followed by the dull crack of a zombie's skull fracturing on the ramp above.

Jun did not look up. He focused entirely on the notch, his cuts precise and rhythmic. The notch was now twenty centimeters deep, halfway through the log. He began to cut from the opposite side, creating a matching notch that would leave a thin web of wood in the center.

*Thwack.*

The granite block directly above Jun's head shifted with a loud, grating sound. A shower of dry mortar dust and small pebbles fell onto his shoulders, stinging his face. The load on the cedar beam was increasing as the dense crowd of the dead packed onto the arch.

"Jun! Get out of there! The steps are sliding!" Liang called out, his voice turning into a scream as the rope around the pillar grew taut.

Jun took a deep breath, his eyes fixed on the remaining web of wood. The cedar log was creaking, its outer fibers beginning to splinter under the immense compressive load. He could see tiny hairline cracks opening along the grain. He knew that a single horizontal shear failure would cause the beam to explode outward. He stepped back as far as the narrow ledge allowed, raised his broadaxe over his shoulder, and delivered a final, desperate blow into the heart of the notch.

The steel blade cut through the remaining fibers. With a sound like a thunderclap, the cedar log split down its entire length, the wood grain tearing apart as the compressive force crushed the strut.

Jun threw himself backward against the rock wall of the cleft. Above him, the limestone arch caved inward. The granite steps, losing their lateral support, slid downward in a massive landslide of stone and mortar. With a deafening, echoing roar, the twenty-meter section of the granite ramp collapsed into the chasm, carrying the climbing horde with it. The grey bodies fell silently through the mist, tumbling into the deep, rocky gorge below.

A thick cloud of grey stone dust surged out of the cleft, blinding Jun and coating his clothes in white powder. The roar of the falling stone subsided, leaving only the sound of the wind howling through the newly opened gap.

Jun stood on the narrow ledge, his heart pounding against his ribs. The granite ramp was gone, replaced by a wide, empty chasm that fell away into the grey mist. The temple was isolated, but Jun was trapped on the lower ledge of the cliff, the gap between his position and the main hall gate too wide to jump.

Ah Feng ran to the edge of the Wannian Hall balcony. In his hands, he held a long, thick rope made of braided hemp, its end tied to a heavy banner rope adorned with red cotton flags that had hung from the temple rafters. He swung the rope outward, the red flags whistling in the wind as they cut through the mist.

"Catch it, Jun!" Ah Feng called.

Jun reached out, his fingers catching the rough hemp fibers. He wrapped the rope twice around his forearm, locking it tight.

"Hold on!" Liang shouted from the balcony, helping Ah Feng haul the line.

Jun kicked off from the wet limestone ledge, swinging out over the deep chasm. The wind caught his body, turning him in the air as he looked down at the rocks hundreds of feet below. He swung across the gap, his heavy boots scraping hard against the rough limestone wall of the temple foundation, before Ah Feng and Liang reached down, grabbed his shoulders, and hauled him over the granite balustrade to safety.

Jun lay on the stone balcony, panting as he wiped the grey granite dust from his eyes. The chasm lay silent before them, a clean barrier of empty air that no crawling dead could ever cross. The palace was isolated.

CHAPTER 10: THE HIGH SANCTUARY


The morning sun rose slowly over a silent Mount Emei, its cold, golden rays piercing the heavy mountain mist and illuminating the white stone walls of the Wannian Temple. The deep chasm that now lay below the gatehouse was silent, the fallen granite steps and the bodies of the dead hidden beneath a thick, undulating blanket of white clouds that filled the valley. The air at this altitude was calm, carrying only the clean, frozen scent of pine needles, wet stone, and the distant, faint sound of the mountain stream flowing through the deep ravines below.

Inside the inner courtyard of the temple, the survivors slept. The three hundred souls who had fled the valley were warm, sheltered behind the thick masonry walls of the halls, their water supply secure and their gates locked. The young monks swept the soot and ashes from the stone courtyards, their wooden brooms making a soft, rhythmic scratching sound on the granite flags.

Jun sat on the stone steps of the Wannian Hall, his back resting against a massive red-painted pillar. A flat oilstone lay in his left hand, and his broadaxe rested across his knees. The wooden toolbox beside him was scarred and worn, its pine and cedar panels showing the marks of their long journey through Shaanxi, Gansu, Yunnan, and Sichuan, but the tools inside were clean, dry, and free of rust. He applied a few drops of pale camellia oil to the surface of the grey oilstone, spreading it evenly with his thumb. He then ran the bevel of the axe blade across the abrasive stone in slow, circular motions, maintaining a constant twenty-five-degree angle.

The scraping sound of the steel against the stone was steady and peaceful in the morning air, a sharp contrast to the chaotic roar of the falling masonry the night before.

"The edge must be true," Jun said, his voice quiet as he inspected the blade. He wiped the slurry of oil and steel dust from the metal using a corner of his sleeve, revealing a bright, polished line along the cutting edge. "A dull tool requires more force to cut, which means the builder has less control. In our trade, a loss of control is how accidents happen, and on a mountain cliff, a single slip is fatal."

Beside him, Liang was using a fine-cut steel file to dress the edge of his framing chisel, his fingers moving with quiet, focused precision. The white dust of the granite ramp still clung to the fabric of his padded coat, but his face was relaxed, his breathing even. He ran his thumb lightly across the chisel's tip, feeling for any burrs or nicks in the metal.

"We have built a good wall on the mountain, Master Jun," Liang said, looking up toward the golden roof of the temple, which glistened like fire in the morning sun.

"A wall is only as good as the earth beneath it," Jun replied, setting his oilstone back into its wooden compartment. "And this mountain is strong. The limestone bedrock provides a solid foundation that will not yield to the pressure of the dead. But our work here is finished. The chasm we created by collapsing the arch will hold the dead in the valley. The watchmen have their slings, their baskets of sorted stones, and the safety of the heights. They do not need builders anymore."

As they spoke, Ah Feng walked over from the kitchen courtyard, carrying a wooden tray. On it were three bowls of hot, steaming millet porridge, a plate of salted mountain ginger, and a small, battery-powered radio receiver. The steam rose from the bowls, smelling of sweet grain and clean water.

"Eat," Ah Feng said, handing a bowl to Jun and another to Liang. "You have worked through the night, and the road down the northern slopes is cold. The temple elders have made this from the last of the millet we brought up from the lower granaries."

Jun took the bowl, the warmth of the glazed clay heating his cold, stiff hands. He ate slowly, savoring the thick, hot porridge and the sharp, warming bite of the ginger. The simple food restored his energy, warming his chest after the long hours spent in the wet stone cleft beneath the arch.

Liang blew on his porridge, watching the steam curl in the cold air. "How long do you think the chasm will keep them out, Master?"

"As long as the rain does not wash the cliffs away," Jun said. "The limestone is hard, and the gap is twenty meters wide. A slow-moving zombie cannot jump, and without a solid structure to walk on, their weight will only carry them into the gorge. The physics of gravity is our best defense. The forces are resolved downward, away from the temple walls."

Ah Feng set the radio receiver on the stone step between them. It was a small, rectangular transistor radio in a scratched black plastic casing, its telescoping brass antenna extended to its full length. He turned the volume knob, and the speaker emitted a loud, crackling hiss of static that filled the quiet courtyard. Ah Feng adjusted the tuning dial slowly, his fingers moving a fraction of a millimeter at a time as he searched the empty airwaves.

The static rose and fell, a high-pitched whine that bounced off the red walls of the temple. Then, a faint, cracked voice broke through the noise, its tone raspy and distorted by the distance.

"...calling any survivors... this is Song Shan... the Shaolin Temple in Henan..." the voice said, fading in and out as the signal struggled to cross the mountain ranges. "The mountain passes are under pressure... the dead are climbing from the Henan plains... we have the staffs and the warriors, but our outer watchtowers are out of timber... the main timber gates are buckling under the weight... we need builders to reinforce the portals and construct the barricades... if anyone can hear this..."

The transmission cut off, replaced by a loud, empty hum of static. Ah Feng turned the dial back and forth, but there was only the cold hiss of the wind through the speaker.

Liang set his empty bowl down, his face turning serious as he looked at Jun. "Song Shan is far to the north-east, Master. We would have to cross the northern plains and the rivers."

Jun stood up, shaking the frost and wood shavings from his padded coat. He picked up his broadaxe, sliding the hickory handle into the leather loop of his tool belt. He looked toward the east, where the Min Mountains rose like waves on the horizon, their snow-capped peaks lost in the morning light.

"The road is long, Liang," Jun said, his voice steady and quiet. "But the work does not end. The dead do not sleep, and as long as they wander, the living will need walls to keep them out. Pack the chisels, the saws, and the marking gauges. We have to teach some monks how to build."

Liang stood up and bowed, his hands clasped before him in the traditional builder's salute. "Yes, Master. I will gather the spare handles and the oil stones."

Ah Feng watched them, bowing deeply. "Thank you, builders. The mountain will remember your names."

Jun returned the bow, then lifted his heavy toolbox onto his shoulder. With Liang following close behind, he walked through the temple's rear gate, heading down the steep, icy steps of the northern trail, their boots leaving deep prints in the fresh snow as they began their long journey toward the plains of Henan.

STORY 18: THE MONKS OF SONG SHAN
Setting: Shaolin Temple, Mount Song, Henan Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE MOUNTAIN GATE


The pine forests of Mount Song were silent, their dark green needles dusted with the first dry frost of autumn. The air was thin, cold, and carried the faint, sharp scent of pine resin and wet granite.

Rising abruptly from the plains of Henan, the peaks of Song Shan were a maze of vertical granite cliffs, deep ravines, and ancient stone pathways. Nestled in the shadow of the Shaoshi Mountain, the Shaolin Temple stood as a monument of timber and red plaster, its multi-tiered roofs and ancient stone pavilions worn smooth by the soles of fifteen hundred years of pilgrims.

Jun stood at the threshold of the *Shanmen*—the Mountain Gate. He bent his knees, slowly lowering his heavy oak toolbox to the granite terrace. The wooden box, reinforced with hand-beaten copper corners, hit the stone with a solid, resonant thud that echoed off the high plaster walls. Jun’s chest rose and fell in deep, heavy breaths. The climb from the foothills had been a grueling three-hour ascent up the "Eighteen Turns," a path consisting of over a thousand steep granite steps carved directly into the mountain's face. His leather shoulder strap, darkened and stiff with his own sweat, had cut deep into the muscle of his shoulder, leaving a red, raw welt beneath his quilted cotton coat. He leaned his broadaxe—its ash handle smooth from years of grease, its steel head wide and polished to a mirror finish—against the red-painted brick wall of the gatehouse.

Beside him, Liang collapsed onto the topmost stone step, his legs shaking from the strain. He pulled his legs up, rubbing his aching shins through his bound trousers. "The stairs here... they are wider than the ones we climbed in Mount Emei, Master," Liang panted, his voice thin in the cold air. He wiped a layer of frost and sweat from his forehead with the sleeve of his coat, looking down the winding, dizzying path they had just conquered. "But they are far steeper. The air is so dry it burns the throat. And the plain... the plain below is completely dead."

Jun turned his gaze southward, looking beyond the granite balustrade of the terrace. Far below, the vast plains of Henan stretched out like a yellow-grey shroud under the autumn sky. The yellow-earth valley, usually bustling with the smoke of coal fires and the movement of millions, was silent. In the distance, the national highway lay empty, dotted with abandoned trucks and buses that looked like tiny, frozen beetles. 

"The plains have no walls," Jun said, his voice flat and steady. "The cities down there relied on steel fences and concrete barriers, but when the flood came, those became cages. Here, the mountain itself is the wall. The granite cliffs are better than any brick rampart. But a wall is only as good as its gates." He turned his back to the valley, facing the massive timber gatehouse. "We must check the oak sills of this gate immediately. The constant vibration of the mountain wind, the weight of the clay tiles, and the shifting of the masonry have crushed the rotted timbers beneath the central pillar. If this gate falls, the temple has no front shield."

They had traveled east from the high Sichuan mountains, descending through the jagged gorges of Sichuan and the yellow loess hills of Shaanxi to reach this sacred peak. Along their route, they had witnessed the vast scale of the disaster. Yet, unlike the chaotic collapse described in foreign rumors, they had seen the resilience of the state’s regional defense committees. In Shaanxi and Henan, the remnants of the local garrisons, working alongside civilian volunteer brigades, had established coordinate defense zones. They had redirected resources, moved populations to high-altitude redoubts, and blown key bridges to isolate the infected. The Shaolin Temple had been designated as a secondary mountain sanctuary, a regional watchpoint and communications hub for the central Henan defense sector. 

"Amituofo," a voice called from the shadow of the red entry wall.

Master Shi stepped out onto the granite platform. He was a lean, wiry monk in a faded saffron robe that had been patched at the elbows and hem with coarse grey hemp thread. His face was weathered and dark, lined like carved boxwood that had spent decades in the sun, but his eyes were clear, sharp, and entirely calm. In his right hand, he held a long staff of seasoned white wax wood (*baisha mu*), its wood pale and flexible, its tip capped with a simple iron collar. Behind him, three younger warrior monks stood in silent alignment, their heads shaven, their arms crossed within the wide sleeves of their grey robes.

"You are the master carpenters," Shi said, bowing slightly with a single hand raised in front of his chest. "The Shaanxi watchmen at the Tongguan pass sent word by the shortwave radio. They said you had crossed the yellow-earth ridges. Welcome to Song Shan. The state coordinators told us that only a master of the old joinery could save our timber gates. The lower gates at the valley entrance are holding for now, blocked by the rockslides we blew last month, but the dry wind is splitting our main temple doors. Even worse, the mountain dead are still climbing. They find their way up the dry ravines. They climb through the Pagoda Forest behind the temple walls."

Below them on the stone steps, a quiet sound arose—a dry, scraping sound of feet on stone. 

Jun walked to the edge of the terrace and looked down. A group of five zombies had emerged from the shadow of the pine forest, about fifty steps below the platform. They did not run. They did not leap or growl. They climbed with a slow, heavy, mechanical drag, their movements stiff and sluggish, as if their limbs were made of wood. Their bare feet, calloused and encrusted with dried mud, scraped heavily against the granite steps. They wore the tattered clothes of valley farmers—faded blue canvas jackets and trousers patched with coarse cloth—and their skin was a dry, leathery grey, completely free of the wet rot seen in the humid lowlands. The dry mountain air had mummified their flesh, turning their faces into tight, expressionless masks of dried skin. Their eyes were cloudy, fixed on the red walls of the gatehouse above.

"The bells draw them," Master Shi said, his voice quiet, showing no trace of fear as he looked down at the climbing figures. "We ring them every morning to signal the coordinate watches in the foothills. The dead follow the sound of the chanting and the bells, even if their minds cannot comprehend the words. They climb until they hit a barrier. If the gates are weak, they simply press their bodies against the wood until the structure gives way."

Jun knelt down at the base of the gate's central support column, ignoring the approaching dead. "The monks can handle those five steps below," he said to Liang, who was nervously watching the steps. "But if we do not fix this pillar, the next group will push the entire gatehouse down on top of us. Hand me the inspection chisel."

Liang reached into the canvas tool bag and pulled out a narrow, long-bladed cabinet chisel. Jun took the tool, its ash handle fitting comfortably into his palm, and pressed the steel edge into the base of the massive fir column where it met the stone plinth. The steel sank into the wood like dry bread. Jun shook his head. "Look at this, Liang. The column is hollow. The rot has eaten the tenon, and the weight of the gate is resting on nothing but dust and shadow. We must begin the work immediately."

CHAPTER 2: THE TIMBER GATES


The Mountain Gate was a classic three-bay timber structure, six meters wide and four meters deep, built during the late Ming dynasty. Its double gate leaves were made of seasoned northern pine, ten centimeters thick and reinforced with horizontal iron bands. The doors were locked from the inside by a thick, hand-hewn oak crossbar that slid into deep stone pockets in the flanking masonry walls.

But the sills and the primary column bases had failed.

Over centuries, water from the mountain springs had pooled around the granite base-stones (*zhuchu*) that supported the main structural columns. The drainage channels carved into the circular stone plinths had become clogged with windblown dust and decomposing pine needles. Moisture had drawn upward into the end grain of the massive fir columns, causing a slow, invisible rot that had completely hollowed out the lower tenons. The weight of the three-ton roof truss, loaded with heavy ceramic tiles and thick clay bedding mortar, had crushed the spongy wood at the base. The entire gatehouse had sagged three centimeters to the west, causing the iron shoes (*tiefa*) at the bottom of the double doors to drag heavily against the granite threshold, jamming them halfway open.

"The gate cannot be locked," Jun said, his voice echoing under the timber rafters of the gatehouse. He stood before the jammed doors, running his fingers along the gap where the two leaves met. A gap of nearly three inches remained, through which the cold mountain wind whistled. "The western column has settled. If the dead gather and throw their weight against these doors, the lateral force will slide the column off its granite base. The mortise and tenon joint that anchors it is completely gone. The column will buckle, and the entire roof truss will collapse, crushing the gates and opening the temple to the valley."

"Master, we do not have any seasoned fir logs of this size on the mountain," Liang said, looking up at the column, which was nearly half a meter in diameter. "To find a seasoned fir of this thickness, we would have to descend into the lower valleys, which are controlled by the infected."

"We do not need new fir," Jun replied, opening his tool chest. "We will use the old timbers stored behind the guest hall. They are seasoned wild oak (*gongmu*), dry as bone and twice as hard as this fir. We will perform a *jiagudao*—we will jack up the roof, cut away the rotten bottom of the column, and splice a new oak block onto the healthy fir post using a stepped scarf joint, a *guyin sun*."

Jun turned to Master Shi. "I need six of your strongest monks, two heavy pine logs from your timber yard to serve as temporary shores, and the iron screw-jack we brought from Shaanxi."

Within thirty minutes, the courtyard was a workshop. Liang and the monks carried in two thick pine logs, twenty-five centimeters in diameter. Jun notched the top of each log to fit securely under the horizontal tie-beams (*lan'e*) that spanned the gatehouse columns. 

"We must calculate the load before we lift," Jun said, tracing a sketch with a piece of charcoal on the granite floor. "This column supports two purlins, the western hip rafter, and twelve square meters of tiling. The wet clay mortar adds to the mass, giving us a dead load of thirty-five thousand Newtons—three and a half metric tons. The temporary shores must stand at a sixty-five-degree angle to distribute the load to the solid granite foundation stones."

Jun positioned the cast-iron screw-jack (*luoxuan qianjinding*) at the base of the first shore. The jack, salvaged from a quarry near Tongguan, had a thick steel screw black with graphite grease. It was operated by a meter-long iron tommy bar.

"Place the oak footings under the jack, Liang," Jun ordered. "The wood will bite into the granite and provide friction."

Once the shores were braced and the jack snug, Jun stood back. "Slowly, Liang. Turn the bar. Half a turn at a time."

Liang inserted the bar and leaned his weight against it. The metal creaked under the pressure. Liang's face turned red as he fought the resistance of the three-ton roof, while the monks stabilized the diagonal pine shores. 

*Creak.* The timber frame groaned. High above, the terracotta tiles shifted with a dry, scraping noise. Jun kept his eyes fixed on the base of the column. 

"Another half turn," Jun said.

Liang strained, his boots slipping slightly before a monk stepped behind to brace his back. The screw turned, and a tiny gap appeared between the column base and the granite plinth. 

"Stop," Jun commanded. "The load is transferred."

He knelt and snapped a black line using his carpenter's ink-line (*moxian*), marking the cut exactly eighty centimeters above the stone plinth, where the wood was dry and solid. 

"Liang, get the frame saw."

The frame saw (*jugong*) was a traditional Chinese two-man saw with a thin steel blade tensioned by a mulberry frame. Jun and Liang positioned the blade against the black ink line.

*Shh-shh. Shh-shh.*

The saw bit into the seasoned fir. A fine, pale-yellow sawdust accumulated around their boots, smelling of pine resin. The work was intense; the wood was dense and the angle awkward. Jun’s arms burned with the repetitive motion, while Liang’s breath grew ragged. They cut through the solid outer wood, then hit the soft, wet center, where the blade moved easily through wet rot. Finally, the blade cut through the far side. Jun laid the saw aside and struck the rotten base with a wooden mallet. The lower column section shattered into damp fragments, leaving the top hanging suspended.

Jun immediately set to work carving the stepped scarf joint (*guyin sun*) into the bottom of the suspended column. Using a broad framing chisel (*dazao*) and a mallet, he cut precise vertical and horizontal steps into the heartwood. The joint would interlock in three dimensions, preventing the column from sliding under lateral wind loads. He chiseled a square mortise in the center of the middle step for a hidden wooden key (*tiansun*).

Next, he took the seasoned oak block. Using his broadaxe and a hand plane, he shaped the oak to match the steps of the fir column. The oak was incredibly hard, requiring heavy blows from the mallet. Jun worked with precision, checking the fit of the joints with a wooden square. He carved the key (*tiansun*) from dense red jujube wood (*zaomu*), designed to lock the two sections of the column together.

"Let us fit the block," Jun said.

With Liang's help, they slid the new oak block onto the granite plinth and pushed it under the column. The joints lined up. Jun inserted the jujube key and drove it home with three blows of his mallet. The wedge action of the key pulled the stepped joints together, locking the block to the fir column.

Jun then used a manual breast drill (*bowan zuan*) to drill three horizontal holes through the interlocking steps. He drove seasoned oak dowels (*sunxian*) through the holes, hammering them flush. To provide additional lateral stability, he bolted two iron reinforcing straps (*tiehu*) around the joint, and braced the lower frame by driving diagonal timber struts (*xiecheng*) between the column base and the floor beams.

"Release the jack, Liang," Jun said.

Liang turned the iron bar in reverse. The screw-jack creaked, and the diagonal shores loosened as the roof weight settled back down. The spliced column took the load without a single squeak or sign of compression. 

The double gates, now free, rose two centimeters. Liang pushed them. They moved smoothly, clearing the granite threshold, and shut with a solid *clack*.

Suddenly, a dry, grey hand reached through the remaining gap at the top of the gate, its fingers clawing at the wood. A slow-moving zombie was pressed against the crack, its mouth snapping.

Before Liang could draw his axe, Master Shi stepped forward. His white wax wood staff moved like a snake, sliding through the gap. The tip of the staff struck the zombie's temple with a dry *crack*. The figure slid backward down the stone steps, motionless.

'Close the bar,' Shi said.

Liang dropped the heavy oak crossbar into the iron brackets. The gate was sealed.

CHAPTER 3: THE SHAOLIN STAFFS


The afternoon sun hung low and cold over the western ridges of Mount Song, casting long, sharp shadows across the stone flagging of the temple’s rear courtyard. The air was thin and dry, smelling of frozen pine needles and the faint, bitter scent of coal smoke from the kitchen stoves. The surrounding red plaster walls, weathered by centuries of mountain storms, rose high against the granite cliffs, forming a narrow, protected canyon where the wind whirled in cold eddies.

Master Shi stood near the stone cistern, his patches on his saffron robes fluttering in the breeze. Before him on a low wooden bench lay several white wax wood staffs (*baisha mu*), the traditional weapons of the Shaolin monks. Jun walked over, his heavy woolen coat buttoned tight against the chill, and picked up one of the staffs. He ran his calloused thumb along the shaft. 

The wood felt rough and papery under his fingers. Near the tip, a long, jagged split had opened, running nearly thirty centimeters down the grain, its edges frayed like dry hemp.

"This is the fifth one today, Master Jun," Shi said, his voice flat but carrying a note of deep concern. "During the morning watch on the lower paths, three of our younger brothers were forced to retreat when their staffs split on the first strike. The wood did not bend. It shattered like dry bone."

Jun held the staff up to the light, peering at the split. "It is the air," he said, turning the shaft slowly. "White wax wood—*Fraxinus chinensis*—is one of the finest timbers under heaven for a staff. Its fibers are long, straight, and naturally aligned, which gives it its famous whip-like elasticity. When you strike a blow, the wood bends to absorb the impact, storing the kinetic energy and releasing it at the tip. But that flexibility depends entirely on the natural sap and moisture within the wood's cellular structure."

He tapped the split wood with his knuckle. The sound was high, dry, and hollow, like dried bamboo. "The hot, dry summer we had in the plains, followed by this biting mountain frost, has sucked the moisture clean out of these shafts. The cells have shriveled, leaving the wood fibers stiff and brittle. When you strike the dried, leathery skulls of the dead—which are as hard as cured oak—the wood cannot flex to dissipate the force. The shockwave travels straight down the shaft. Under such compression, the shear stress exceeds the lateral strength of the dry grain, and the growth rings simply tear themselves apart."

"Can we not harvest new canes from the northern slopes?" Liang asked, coming out of the workshop with a bundle of hemp rope. "The valley is full of wild ash groves."

"New wood is green," Jun replied, shaking his head. "It is full of water. If you use it now, it will warp within three days in this dry wind, and it will split even faster once the winter frost sets in. We must treat the wood we have, and we must do it by replacing the lost sap with a drying oil that will lock the fibers together."

Jun stood up and looked around the courtyard. "Liang, go to the temple oil press. They have vats of wild sesame oil (*ye zhima you*) stored for the winter lamps. It is a drying oil, rich in linoleic and oleic acids. When heated, it will penetrate deep into the ash fibers and polymerize, forming a flexible, water-resistant resin inside the wood. We will also need brass wire—*huangtong xian*—about one millimeter in thickness. We will wrap the critical impact zones of the staffs to resist the radial forces that cause splitting."

Within an hour, Liang and two younger monks had constructed a crude boiling hearth in the center of the courtyard. They used old, heavy clay bricks to build a long, narrow trough base, lining it with river sand to insulate the heat. On top of the bricks, they placed a long, rectangular copper trough, normally used for washing dyes in the temple's weaving rooms. The trough was two and a half meters long, forty centimeters wide, and thirty centimeters deep. They poured three large jars of wild sesame oil into the copper vessel, filling it to a depth of fifteen centimeters.

Jun built a small fire of dry pine branches and charcoal beneath the trough. He watched the oil closely as the heat rose. He did not want it to boil violently, which would scorch the wood and make it brittle. Instead, he maintained a steady, low heat. The oil began to shimmer, releasing a thick, rich, toasted scent that filled the cold courtyard, masking the faint, sour smell of decay that occasionally blew up from the valley below.

"The oil must remain at approximately one hundred and forty degrees," Jun explained to Liang, checking the viscosity of the liquid with a split piece of pine. "If it is too cold, it will not penetrate the tight grain of the ash. If it is too hot, it will char the cellulose and destroy the wood's strength. We want the heat to drive out any remaining water vapor, replacing it with the oil."

While the oil heated, Jun and Liang prepared the staffs. For the split staffs, Jun first cleaned the cracks using a fine-tipped scraping tool, removing any dirt or splinters. He then clamped the split sections together tightly using wooden hand-screws, ensuring the grain aligned perfectly.

"Now, the brass wire," Jun said, pointing to a spool of bright yellow wire Liang had salvaged from the temple's maintenance shed. "We cannot simply wrap the wire around the outside of the staff. If we do, the wire will stand proud of the wood. It will catch the monks' hands when they slide the staff through their palms during a strike, and it will slide out of place under impact."

Jun took a small, specialized rebate plane and a scribe tool. He marked out three zones on each staff: one ten centimeters from the tip (*gunjian*), one in the middle (*gunshen*), and one near the butt (*gunwei*). In each zone, he carefully carved a shallow, recessed channel around the circumference of the shaft, exactly one millimeter deep and four centimeters wide.

"This is the bedding," Jun explained to Master Shi, who watched with quiet curiosity. "The wire will sit flush within this recess. The depth of the cut is minimal, so it does not reduce the structural core of the staff, but it provides a shoulder that prevents the wire wrap from sliding up or down when the staff bends."

Once the recesses were carved, Jun set up a simple wire-winding jig. He clamped the butt of the staff into a wooden vise. He wrapped the brass wire around a wooden handle, passing it through a friction peg to maintain high tension. Liang held the staff, slowly rotating it by the tip, while Jun guided the wire into the carved recess.

The wire hummed as it was pulled tight. With each turn of the staff, the wire bit into the shoulders of the recess, laying down a solid, glittering band of yellow metal. The coils were wound so tightly against one another that they appeared as a single, solid sleeve of brass. Once the recess was filled, Jun threaded the tail of the wire back under the last three coils, pulled it taut with pliers, and drove a tiny brass tack into the wood to lock the end in place. He then filed the end flush with a small steel hand-file.

"This brass sleeve acts as a tension ring," Jun said, tapping the metal band. "When the staff strikes a target, the force tries to split the wood outward. The brass wire, which has a high tensile strength, resists this radial expansion. The wood cannot split because the wire holds the grain together under tension."

When the oil reached the correct temperature, Jun and Liang lifted the prepared staffs using iron tongs and lowered them into the shimmering copper trough. The oil bubbled softly as the last traces of moisture within the wood cells escaped as steam. 

They left the staffs in the hot bath for two hours. As the wood absorbed the sesame oil, it darkened, turning from a pale, bone-white color to a deep, warm amber, its grain patterns standing out in rich, dark lines. The wood became heavy, its density increased by the weight of the absorbed oil.

After two hours, Jun lifted the staffs from the trough and laid them on a clean woolen cloth to cool. As the oil cooled, it began to cure and dry within the wood fibers, restoring the natural elasticity of the ash.

Jun picked up one of the treated staffs. It felt cool, smooth, and slightly heavy in his hands. He stepped into the center of the courtyard, cleared his mind, and swung the staff in a wide, horizontal arc, bringing it down against a heavy granite mounting block with full force.

*THWACK.*

The sound was deep, solid, and resonant, like a bronze bell wrapped in felt. The staff did not splinter. It did not crack. The brass sleeves remained perfectly flush and tight against the wood, and the shaft vibrated briefly before returning to its straight, true alignment.

Master Shi took the staff from Jun’s hands. He spun it quickly, the amber wood blurring in the cold air, before delivering a series of rapid thrusts and strikes against the stone. A smile, thin but genuine, appeared on the old monk's weathered face.

"It has the weight of iron and the spring of green bamboo," Shi said, bowing to Jun. "With these, our brothers can hold the paths. The dead will find no purchase against the wood of Mount Song."

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE PAGODA FOREST


To the west of the main temple buildings, nestled in a quiet valley between the high granite cliffs of Mount Song, lay the Pagoda Forest (*Talin*). Here, over two hundred and forty brick and stone pagodas, built over the course of ten centuries, rose from the forest floor like a silent army of ancient pillars. The pagodas—some three stories high, others over fifteen meters—were the tombs of the temple’s most revered abbots and warrior monks. They were carved in various styles, from the simple, circular stone drums of the Tang dynasty to the complex, multi-tiered octagonal towers of the Ming and Yuan, their surfaces covered in worn inscriptions and carvings of lotus blossoms.

The grove was filled with ancient, gnarled pines whose dark needles carpeted the ground, muffling all sound. In the grey, flat light of the autumn morning, the Pagoda Forest was a place of deep shadows and silence. But now, that silence was broken by the dry, rhythmic scraping of feet on stone.

A group of thirty zombies, having drifted up from the lower valleys through the dry ravines of the western slopes, had entered the grove. They moved slowly, their mummified, leather-like bodies unaffected by the biting cold. In the dense layout of the pagodas, they were difficult to spot. The stone structures blocked the sightlines from the temple's watchtowers, allowing the dead to filter through the tombs and approach the low brick wall of the rear vegetable gardens undetected.

"We cannot defend this ground with traditional tactics," Master Shi said, crouching behind the square base of a Song dynasty pagoda. He looked through the narrow gap between two stone towers. Fifty meters away, a zombie in a faded blue cotton shirt was shuffling forward, its hands hanging loose, its hollow eyes scanning the pines. "The spaces are too tight for archery, and if we engage them in hand-to-hand combat among the tombs, they will surround us from the shadows. The ground is uneven, and a single slip on the pine needles means death."

Jun knelt beside him, examining the heavy octagonal base of the nearest pagoda. The base was made of solid, grey Mount Song granite, two meters wide and seventy centimeters high, its surface rough-tooled and green with dry moss.

"We will not fight them on their level," Jun said, tapping the stone base. "We will build a *tianlan*—a horizontal barrier grid of pine poles. The grid will span the narrow alleys between the pagodas, positioned exactly forty-five centimeters above the ground. At this height, the poles will strike the shins of the dead. Because they lack the cognitive reflex to lift their feet or break their stride, their momentum will carry their upper bodies forward, causing them to trip and fall face-first onto the granite pathway. Once they are down, they will be trapped in the grid, and the monks can stand safely on the elevated stone bases of the pagodas, using their long spades to finish them."

"But Master Jun," Liang whispered, his eyes wide as he looked at the ancient stone. "These are the tombs of our ancestors. We cannot drill holes into the sacred granite to mount the barriers. The stone must not be defiled."

"We will not drill a single hole," Jun replied. "We will use friction and leverage. We will construct diagonal timber clamps—*jiashan*—that wrap around the octagonal bases of the pagodas, locking them in place with hardwood wedges. The friction between the wood and the rough granite will be more than enough to resist the lateral force of the dead."

Jun stood up and began to make calculations in his mind, tracing the dimensions on the dry ground with the tip of his chisel. "Let us calculate the force. A wandering zombie has a mass of approximately seventy kilograms. Walking at a slow speed of half a meter per second, its kinetic energy is low, but when multiple bodies press against a barrier, they act as a continuous load. If five zombies crowd into one of these narrow alleys, they can exert a combined static horizontal force of about three thousand five hundred Newtons—three and a half kilonewtons.

"The barrier pole will be forty-five centimeters high," Jun continued, pointing to the base. "This creates a vertical moment arm of zero point four five meters. The clamping frame will wrap around the two-meter-wide octagonal base of the pagoda. The distance between our tightening wedges will be one point two meters. To prevent the clamps from sliding upward or turning under the leverage of the barrier, we must create a clamping force that exceeds the horizontal thrust. By driving our tapered hardwood wedges home with a heavy beetle, we can easily generate a normal force of eight thousand Newtons per clamp. The coefficient of kinetic friction between dry, rough-sawn pine and weathered granite is approximately zero point four. With two clamps per pagoda base, the total resistive force will be over six thousand four hundred Newtons. The barrier will not budge, even if a dozen dead press against it at once."

Jun and Liang set to work, converting the edge of the pine grove into a temporary carpentry yard. The monks brought in long, straight pine logs from the temple's timber yard, logs that had been cut during the previous winter and left to dry. Using their broadaxes, Jun and Liang split the logs into thick planks, eight centimeters thick and fifteen centimeters wide, to form the clamping frames.

They used manual augers to bore two-inch holes through the ends of the planks, and then used their mortising chisels to square the holes, creating clean mortise slots for the heavy tie-bars that would connect the front and back pieces of the clamps.

For the wedges, Jun selected seasoned red jujube wood (*zaomu*), a dense, heavy timber with excellent compressive strength. He cut the wood into long, tapered wedges, twenty-five centimeters long, five centimeters wide, and tapering from three centimeters down to a sharp edge.

"Liang, help me carry the first frame," Jun called.

They carried the heavy pine planks to the base of the nearest Song pagoda. They placed one plank against the front face of the octagonal base and another against the rear face. They slid two thick pine tie-bars through the square mortises, connecting the front and back planks. The frame fit snugly around the stone, leaving a small gap of about four centimeters at the corners.

Jun took two of the jujube wood wedges and slid them into the gap between the tie-bar and the stone base. He picked up his heavy wooden beetle—a mallet carved from a solid block of oak, weighing five kilograms.

He swung the mallet back, his muscles straining under his quilted coat, and brought it down against the head of the first wedge with a loud, hollow *THUD*.

*Thud. Thud. Thud.*

With each blow, the wedge sank deeper into the joint, drawing the pine planks tight against the rough granite base. The wood creaked under the immense tension, its fibers biting into the irregularities of the stone surface. Jun repeated the process on the opposite side, hammering the wedges home until they would not move another millimeter.

He grabbed the heavy pine frame and shook it with all his might. It was rock-solid, joined to the ancient stone as if it were a natural growth of the mountain.

Between these anchored clamps, Jun and Liang mounted the horizontal barrier poles. They used straight pine logs, ten centimeters in diameter. They carved shallow, semi-circular notches into the ends of the poles, fitting them over the tie-bars of the clamps, and lashed them securely using wet hemp rope. As the rope dried in the cold wind, it shrank, locking the poles to the frames with a grip like steel.

They worked quickly but methodically, moving from pagoda to pagoda, bridging the narrow gaps between the tombs until a continuous zig-zag barrier grid—a *tianlan*—spanned the entire western approach to the temple.

As the sun reached its noon height, the first group of zombies reached the outer edge of the grid.

They shuffled forward through the pines, their boots scraping on the dry needles. The lead zombie—a former construction worker in a dusty grey canvas jacket—entered the narrow alley between the Song pagoda and a smaller Ming tower. His cloudy eyes were fixed on the monks who stood on the stone steps of the temple wall above.

He did not look down. His shins struck the heavy pine pole.

Lacking the neural pathways to register the obstacle or adjust his stride, he continued to press forward. The pole held firm. The zombie’s center of gravity shifted past his feet, and his upper body pitched forward. With a dry, heavy crash, he hit the granite path, his forehead striking the stone base of the tomb with a dull crack.

The zombie behind him did not hesitate. It stepped forward, its foot catching on the fallen body, and stumbled over the pole, crashing down on top of the first. Within minutes, the narrow path was blocked by a thrashing, tangled heap of six zombies, their limbs caught in the pine poles, their dry fingers clawing at the empty air.

"Now!" Master Shi called out.

The warrior monks, standing safely on the elevated stone bases of the pagodas, stepped forward. They held their newly reinforced white wax wood staffs and long monk spades. They thrust downward from their secure positions, the steel blades of the spades splitting the skulls of the trapped dead with clean, mechanical precision.

The barrier held. Not a single clamp slipped on the granite bases, and the Pagoda Forest remained silent once more, its ancient tombs undamaged by the conflict.

---

CHAPTER 5: THE WATER MILL


The mountain stream, fed by the high springs of the Shaoshi peaks, rushed down a steep limestone ravine below the temple’s rear garden wall, its water carrying grey granite grit and the scent of frozen earth. Under the grey autumn sky, the turbid torrent surged over the silent waterwheel, a massive three-meter construction of seasoned wild cypress, flooding the lower grain-press room. Inside the mossy granite millhouse, the air was cold and heavy with the smell of wet flour and decaying timber. 

Master Shi stood on the wet catwalk, his patched saffron robe pinned back. "Without the mill, we cannot grind the winter millet gathered by the coordinate volunteer brigades," he said, pointing down. "The axle has slipped from its bearing. A mass of debris and two drowned bodies from the lower ravines have jammed the paddles, and the current has cracked the stone support base."

Jun knelt, peering at the waterwheel's central axle, a massive elm log fifty centimeters in diameter. At each end, a heavy iron gudgeon—a forged spindle with wing-like anchoring straps—was set into the wood, resting in a stone bearing block. The western block had fractured, and the gudgeon had slipped, wedging the axle against the granite housing.

"The current is too swift," Jun said. "We must divert the stream. Liang, get the pine bypass panels."

Jun tied a hemp rope around his waist, handing the slack to Liang and two monks. He stepped down into the freezing stream. The water rose to his waist, its icy current soaking his cotton trousers and numbing his skin. He hammered an iron cold chisel into the silt-choked granite guide slots of the ancient stone abutment, clearing the gravel with rhythmic, bone-jarring blows.

"Drop the panels!" Jun shouted.

Liang and the monks slid three pine boards down the slots. The boards dropped with wet splashes, blocking the flow. The stream surged into the side runoff channel, and the flow into the millrace died to a trickle.

Jun climbed out, his hands blue with cold. He did not stop to warm himself. He grabbed his handaxe and descended into the dry pit. Among the tangled pine branches beneath the paddles lay two mummified bodies, their grey skin tight against their bones from the dry mountain air. Their jawbones snapped sluggishly as the timber shifted. Jun worked with quiet efficiency, splitting the branches and delivering two quick, heavy blows with the poll of his axe to the back of their skulls, neutralizing them. Together with Liang, he hauled the remains out of the pit.

With the pit cleared, the two-ton waterwheel had to be lifted back into alignment.

"We cannot use the iron screw-jack here," Jun said. "There is no flat footing on this wet granite. We must use levers." He pointed to the timber yard. "Bring four seasoned cedar logs, five meters long and fifteen centimeters in diameter."

Jun calculated the mechanical advantage. "The western end of the axle carries ten thousand Newtons. If we place our granite fulcrum forty centimeters from the axle end and use a five-meter cedar log as a lever, we achieve a mechanical advantage of twelve point five to one. A single lever reduces the required effort to eight hundred Newtons—about eighty kilograms. With two levers and three monks on each, we can lift the shaft with complete control."

Liang placed granite blocks to serve as fulcrums. They slid the thin ends of the cedar logs beneath the elm axle, lashing them with wet hemp rope. Three monks stood at the far end of each lever, their hands gripping the bark.

"Heave together!" Jun commanded. "Slowly. Lift!"

The monks threw their weight onto the levers. The cedar logs creaked, bending under the load. The massive axle rose, dripping mud. Jun kept his eyes on the gap. When it cleared, he slid two heavy oak blocks under the shaft as temporary cribbing. "Ease down," he said. The monks released the pressure, and the shaft settled onto the wood with a solid thud.

The axle end was badly damaged. The iron gudgeon had worked loose because the wood had rotted and split under vibration. The original mortise seat was a soft, pulpy cavity.

"We must cut a new seat," Jun said. "We will cut the axle back by fifteen centimeters to reach healthy heartwood, and carve a deeper mortise to receive the iron wings."

Jun and Liang used a two-man frame saw to cut away the rotten timber. The saw bit into the wood, the wet sawdust smelling of vinegar. Jun marked the outlines of the new mortise on the clean heartwood. The mortise had to be perfectly square, with a central round pocket for the spindle and two lateral slots for the wings.

Jun took his mortising chisel and a wooden mallet. He carved the pocket, the chisel biting into the tough elm with a sharp, rhythmic clink-clink-clink. He cleared the chips with a narrow scoop. The wood was dense, but his blows were steady. Liang used a smaller gouge to clean the lateral slots. After an hour of chiseling, the new mortise was complete.

They heated the iron gudgeon over a brazier until it was warm, and then drove it into the mortise. Jun used an oak beetle to hammer the iron wings home. The warm metal fit tightly, the heat sealing the fibers around it. Jun drilled two transverse holes through the timber axle and the iron wings. He drove two seasoned oak pins through the holes, splitting the ends and driving small wedges into them to lock the assembly.

Meanwhile, Liang prepared the hydraulic mortar. In a large cauldron, he boiled five kilograms of sticky rice in ten liters of water, the steam smelling sweet in the cold millhouse.

"The sticky rice water is key," Liang explained. "The amylopectin in the starch reacts with the slaked lime, creating a dense, interlocking crystal structure. Unlike common mortar, this grout cures under damp conditions and becomes harder than the stone itself."

Liang mixed the starch paste with equal parts slaked lime and fine yellow clay from the riverbank, stirring it until it was a smooth, grey grout.

Jun cleaned the loose stone and mud from the fractured granite support pier. He replaced the shifted blocks, aligning them with a spirit level, and poured the hot sticky-rice mortar into the cracks, packing it with a thin steel trowel. The mortar filled every void, binding the granite blocks. They placed the bronze bearing cup into its recess, sealing it with grout.

"We must let the mortar set for three hours before lowering the axle," Jun said, wiping sweat from his brow.

They sat in the quiet millhouse, drinking hot ginger tea. The wind howled outside, but the stone walls kept the chill at bay. The scent of sticky rice and lime filled the air, a clean smell of restoration.

When the mortar had set, Jun called the monks back to the levers. They lifted the axle, Jun removed the cribbing, and they slowly lowered the shaft. The iron gudgeon settled into the bronze cup with a perfect, greasy fit.

Jun walked upstream and pulled the bypass panels. The mountain stream rushed back into the millrace. The water hit the cypress paddles. The wheel stood still for a moment, then, with a deep creak that shook the stone walls, began to turn. The massive axle rotated smoothly in its new bearing, driving the heavy granite millstones to grind flour for the survivors of Mount Song.

CHAPTER 6: THE WATCHTOWER


The rocky ridge of the Shaoshi Mountain was a barren, wind-swept spine of grey granite that rose high above the temple. The wind never stopped, carrying a dry, biting frost that coated the rocks in a thin glaze of ice. To the south and west, the mountain fell away in sheer cliffs of six hundred meters, dropping into shadow-filled ravines. From this height, the defenders could see the entire valley network, making it the critical watchpoint for the Song Shan coordinate. If a large group of the infected climbed from the plains, they would be spotted hours before reaching the gates.

"The stone watchtower we built last year was cracked by the frost," Master Shi said, standing on the edge of the ridge, his hand shielding his eyes. "The ground is too unstable for heavy masonry. When the wind blows, the stones shift. We need a tower that can withstand the gales, but it must be light enough not to slide down the cliff."

Jun stood beside him, leaning on his long ash-handled broadaxe. "A stone tower is rigid," he said. "It resists the wind by force, but when the force exceeds the weight, it cracks. We will build a liaowanglou—a three-story timber watchtower. We will use the traditional sunmao joinery system. The interlocking joints have natural play; they allow the frame to bend and sway in the gale, absorbing the wind’s energy without breaking. The tower will be anchored to the bedrock using iron drift-pins and stabilized by stone ballast at the base."

Jun sketched the framing plan on a flat granite slab using soapstone. "Let us calculate the wind shear," he said to Liang. "The tower will stand ten meters high, with a width of three meters at the base, tapering to two meters at the top platform. The projected surface area of the timber framing and the roof is twenty-four square meters. In a winter gale of eighty kilometers per hour, the wind pressure will reach five hundred Pascals. This creates a lateral wind load of twelve thousand Newtons at the top.

"To resist this shear," Jun continued, "we must use diagonal wind braces—chuanzi—spanning from the corner columns to the horizontal tie-beams. The chuanzi act as tension struts. When the wind blows from the north, the northern braces go into tension, transferring the load down to the granite foundation anchors. By placing the braces at a forty-five-degree angle, we resolve the horizontal shear into a compressive force along the grain of the spruce columns. The wood can easily bear this load. But the joints must be cut with absolute precision. A gap of one millimeter will allow the frame to twist, and under high wind, the joints will shear."

They began by preparing the foundation. Jun used a manual star-drill—a heavy iron rod with a cross-shaped tip—and a four-kilogram sledgehammer to bore four anchor holes into the solid bedrock. Liang held the drill, rotating it slightly after each blow, while Jun swung the sledgehammer.
Clang. Clang. Clang.
The metal rang out over the ridge, sending up granite dust and sparks. It took three hours of hard, bone-jarring labor to drill four holes, fifty centimeters deep and five centimeters in diameter. They drove hand-forged iron drift-pins into the holes, grouting them with a mixture of molten sulfur and sand, which cooled to a rock-hard seal.

Meanwhile, the monks hauled the timbers up the mountain steps. The corner columns were made of four straight spruce trunks, thirty centimeters in diameter and six meters long, which had been barked and seasoned in the temple yard. Jun and Liang laid the timbers on the rocky ground, their chisels and saws ready.

Jun marked out the mortises for the horizontal tie-beams and the slots for the diagonal wind braces. He used his square and scribe, checking the measurements twice. He chiseled the mortises using a wide framing chisel, driving it deep into the soft, resinous spruce. The scent of pine wood rose in the cold air. Liang cut the tenons on the ends of the tie-beams, using his hand saw for the shoulder cuts and a broadaxe to split away the waste wood. He finished the tenons with a shoulder plane, ensuring they were flat and square.

To lift the heavy spruce columns into position on the windy ridge, they constructed a gantry. Jun chose two straight spruce poles, four meters long, and lashed them together at the top to form an A-frame gantry. They mounted a double-block pulley, carved from hard jujube wood, at the apex, threading a thick, three-strand hemp rope through the sheaves.

"We must set the safety lines before we lift," Jun warned the monks. "The wind is strong enough to blow a column off the ridge. We will attach three guide ropes to the head of each post, anchored to the granite pins we drove into the rock."

Jun checked the harnesses worn by Liang and the young monk who would climb the frame. The harnesses were made of thick canvas webbing, secured with iron rings and lashed to safety lines anchored to the bedrock.

"All men to the rope," Jun called out.

Ten warrior monks grabbed the main hoisting cable, their bare arms corded with muscle. They stood in a line along the rocky spine.

"Pull!" Jun commanded.

The monks heaved together, their boots slipping on the frozen stone. The hemp rope grew taut, its fibers humming under tension. The heavy spruce column rose slowly from the ground. Jun and Liang stood at the base, guiding the post with timber poles. The wind caught the rising log, swinging it, but the safety lines snapped taut, holding it in check.

"Lower it down!" Jun shouted. "Slowly!"

The monks eased the rope. The bottom of the spruce column, carved with a square pocket, slipped over the iron drift-pin driven into the bedrock. It settled with a heavy, wooden thump that vibrated through the granite ridge.

They repeated the process for the other three corner columns, stabilizing them with temporary diagonal struts. Once the four main posts were upright, Jun and Liang climbed the frame to install the first-tier horizontal tie-beams. Liang climbed first, his safety line trailing, his hands red with cold. He sat astride the western beam, guiding the tenons into the mortises. Jun hammered the joints home using a heavy wooden beetle, the solid blows echoing off the cliffs.

To secure the joints, they used a three-way interlocking mortise and tenon system. The tenons of the horizontal beams met inside the core of the corner column, their ends cut at a forty-five-degree angle so they locked against one another. Jun drilled a vertical hole through the joint and drove a tapered oak pin through the assembly, locking the beams to the column.

Next, they installed the diagonal wind braces—the chuanzi. These were thick pine planks, ten centimeters wide and five centimeters thick, that crossed the corners of the frame at a forty-five-degree angle. Jun carved shallow notches into the sides of the columns and the tie-beams to receive the ends of the braces. He secured them using heavy iron bolts and tapered oak wedges, hammering the wedges tight until the wood creaked.

"This is the wind shield," Jun said to Liang as they stood on the platform, forty meters above the ravine. The wind howled through the open frame, making the safety lines snap, but the structure did not shake. "The braces distribute the wind force across the entire frame. The joints share the load."

They built the second and third tiers, capping the tower with a simple, four-sided hip roof tiled with split pine shingles. To ensure the tower could not be overturned by a sudden gust, they constructed a heavy timber crib at the base, filling it with two tons of granite boulders. This ballast lowered the tower's center of gravity, anchoring it to the bedrock.

From the top platform, the watchman had an unobstructed view of the Henan plains. The yellow-earth valleys stretched to the horizon, silent and empty. The watchman, a young monk with a brass telescope, stood behind the timber balustrade, his eyes scanning the roads.

"It is a strong tower," Master Shi said, climbing the ladder to join Jun. "It stands like the pines of Song Shan. It bends, but it does not fall."

But as he spoke, a thin wisp of black smoke rose from the foothills to the south, followed by the bright flash of a beacon fire. The southern outpost had lit their warning signal. A dark, slow-moving mass was crawling along the valley road toward the mountain gate. The watchman looked down, his face pale, but his voice steady. "They are coming."
