CHAPTER 7: THE MONK SPADES


The cold wind of Mount Song swept down from the high peaks, whistling through the narrow courtyards and rattling the roof tiles of the temple's eastern workshops. The air was thin, dry, and carried the biting scent of coal smoke and rusted iron. Towering above the red plaster walls, the granite cliffs of the Shaoshi Mountain stood like silent guardians under a leaden sky.

In the courtyard, Master Shi laid out a row of damaged Monk Spades—*Chanyou*—upon a low oak workbench. These double-ended steel weapons were the traditional polearms of the Shaolin warrior monks, designed for both labor and defense. At the front was a broad steel spade with edges ground to a keen sharpness. At the rear of the ash wood shaft was a crescent blade, its tips curving outward. The weapons spanned two and a half meters.

Today, three of the spade heads lay separated from their shafts, their iron sockets split open and their fixing pins sheared flush with the wood.

"We lost three spades during the morning skirmish on the middle steps," Master Shi said, his voice quiet as he picked up a loose spade head. "The metal is not forged for this kind of work. When the brothers strike the heads of the dead, the steel slips. The socket pin shears off, and the weapon is rendered useless."

Jun lifted one of the intact spades, running his hand down the shaft of seasoned white wax wood (*baisha mu*). The wood was dry, its surface rough in the cold air. He tapped the steel head with his knuckle; the ring was high and thin, indicating poorly tempered steel.

"The spades were forged for ceremonial use and light earthwork," Jun said. "The steel collar is too shallow, extending only six centimeters down the shaft. More importantly, in this dry wind, the white wax wood has shrunk, losing its internal moisture and creating play inside the socket. When the blade strikes the mummified, leathery skull of a zombie—which is as tough as dry oak—this play causes a sudden, massive rotational torque at the pivot.

"Let us calculate the force," Jun continued, tracing a diagram on the dusty workbench with his finger. "A spade head weighs one point five kilograms. Swung in an arc, the velocity reaches twenty-five meters per second. When the blade strikes a hard skull and stops in five-hundredths of a second, the deceleration is five hundred meters per second squared, producing seven hundred and fifty Newtons of impact force. If the impact is off-center by two centimeters, it generates fifteen Newton-meters of rotational torque on the socket. For a two-centimeter radius shaft, this requires the locating pin to withstand seven hundred and fifty Newtons of shear force. A soft four-millimeter pin has a cross-sectional area of only twelve point six square millimeters; its shear strength is easily exceeded, causing it to shear and the socket to split."

"Can we not simply drive a thicker pin?" Master Shi asked.

"No," Jun shook his head. "A thicker pin would require drilling a larger hole in the ash wood, which would weaken the shaft precisely where the stress is highest. The wood would split along the grain under a heavy blow. We must change the mechanics of the connection. We must extend the socket using two long flat iron straps—*jiaqiang*—running twenty-five centimeters down the sides of the wooden shaft. We will also forge thick iron collars to slide over the sockets, preventing the metal from expanding. Finally, we will secure the straps with three copper rivets driven through the wood, distributing the shear stress over a much larger surface area."

"Where will we find the iron for the straps?" Liang asked, looking around the sparse workshop. "And copper for the rivets?"

Master Shi turned toward the kitchen courtyard. "The temple kitchen has several old, cracked copper cooking pots that are no longer fit to hold water. And the window grates of the old guest hall are made of hand-wrought iron bars. In these times, the safety of our brothers is the highest priority. Let us use them."

Within the hour, the workshop was transformed. Liang operated the bellows, bringing the coal fire to a bright yellow flare. Jun cut wrought-iron grates from the guest hall into thirty-centimeter bars and placed them into the coals to heat.

With a pair of long iron tongs, Jun lifted the red-hot iron onto the anvil. He swung his cross-peen hammer, drawing out the iron bars, flattening them into thin, uniform straps exactly five millimeters thick and twenty-five millimeters wide. He tapered the ends of the straps to a feather-edge to prevent a sudden change in stiffness, which would create a stress concentration point in the wood.

Once the straps were forged, Jun heated the steel socket of the spade head and the iron straps to a white heat. He applied a small amount of borax as a flux and hammered the straps onto the sides of the socket, forge-welding the two metals together. The hammer blows were light and fast, fusing the wrought iron to the carbon steel until they became a single, solid piece.

Meanwhile, Liang prepared the copper rivets. He cut the old copper pots from the kitchen into narrow strips, heated them in the forge, and hammered them into round rods six millimeters in diameter. He cut the rods into short pins, sixty-five millimeters long, filing the ends flat.

"The copper is ideal," Jun explained. "It is soft enough to be hammered cold, swelling the rivet inside the wood without using heat that would char the ash fibers. Yet, under shear, copper is ductile; it will bend and deform to absorb the shock of an impact rather than snapping like iron."

Jun cleaned the ends of the white wax wood shafts and painted them with a thin layer of pine resin to seal the grain. With Liang’s help, he pressed the modified steel spade head onto the wood. The newly forged iron straps fit snugly along the flat-shaved sides of the shaft. Jun then slid a thick, hand-hammered iron collar over the joint, driving it down until it clamped the socket tightly against the wood.

Using a manual breast drill with a hand-filed steel bit, Jun positioned the spade in a wooden vise. He leaned his chest against the drill's wooden block, his hands turning the double-crank handle. The steel bit groaned as it cut through the iron strap, then sank into the tough ash wood, producing long, curly white shavings. He drilled three horizontal holes, spaced eight centimeters apart, along the length of the iron straps. Liang slid the copper pins through the holes.

Jun placed the shaft onto the flat anvil block. Using a ball-peen hammer, he struck the protruding ends of the copper pin with light, rapid blows. Under the hammer, the soft copper expanded, filling the drilled hole and forming a neat, round head that pulled the iron straps tight against the wood. Jun repeated the process for all three rivets, locking the straps to the ash shaft.

He picked up the completed spade. The weapon was heavier now, its center of gravity shifted slightly toward the head, but the balance was still true. Master Shi took the weapon, stepped into the courtyard, and found his stance on the granite flags.

With a sudden, sharp shout, he thrust the spade forward. The steel blade sliced through the air with a low, whistling hum. He spun the weapon, bringing the rear crescent blade down in a sweeping hook, and then drove the front spade head deep into a seasoned pine log that lay in the corner of the yard.

The blade bit ten centimeters into the solid pine. Master Shi twisted the shaft violently, trying to wrench the blade free. The wood of the log groaned, but the spade head did not budge. The iron straps remained perfectly flat against the shaft, and the copper rivets did not show a single millimeter of play.

"It is stronger than before," Master Shi said, his face relaxed. "The wood and the iron are one. The energy of the strike stays in the blade."

"The force is no longer concentrated on a single point," Jun said. "When you strike, the tension is carried by the iron straps and distributed across three copper rivets. The wood can flex, but the head cannot twist. Use the crescent end to hook the legs of the dead and pull them to the ground. Once they are down, use the spade end to split the skull. Do not waste your strength on wild swings. A single, clean thrust to the temple is all that is required."

"We will reinforce all the spades," Master Shi said, bowing slightly. "The brothers on the watch will have weapons they can trust."

Jun and Liang returned to the forge, their hammers rising and falling as the cold mountain wind continued to blow, their collective work securing the temple's defenders for the days to come.

CHAPTER 8: THE HALL OF ARHATS


The Hall of Arhats—*Luohan Tang*—was a quiet sanctuary situated at the rear of the temple, its silent courtyards surrounded by high brick walls and shaded by ancient cypresses. Inside the hall, the air was dim and cold, smelling of sandalwood incense, aged wood, and damp plaster. Lining the perimeter walls were five hundred painted terracotta statues of the Arhats, their expressive faces—some laughing, some in deep meditation, others fierce with determination—looking down upon the empty granite floor.

But the peaceful silence of the sanctuary was shattered by a low, persistent sound coming from the massive front entry doors. It was a dry, scraping noise of flesh against timber, accompanied by the slow, heavy thuds of mummified bodies pressing against the outer panels.

Outside, a vanguard of the dead had gathered in the stone courtyard. Drawn by the morning bells, they had shuffled through the Pagoda Forest, and now their collective weight was focused entirely on the hall’s entrance. The double doors were made of northern pine (*songmu*), each leaf three meters high, one and a half meters wide, and eight centimeters thick, locked from the inside by a heavy oak crossbar. Yet, under the constant, unyielding pressure of the crowd, the door leaves were bowing inward. A gap of nearly two centimeters had opened at the center seam, letting in a draft of freezing mountain air and the faint, sour smell of decay.

Liang stood near the altar, his hands trembling as he held his broadaxe. "Master Jun, the oak crossbar is beginning to bend. The iron brackets are tearing out from the brick doorframe. If we do not block the doors, they will buckle and shatter."

"Do not panic, Liang," Jun said, his voice calm and steady as he examined the doors. He walked up to the entrance, placing his hand on the pine wood. He could feel the deep, rhythmic vibrations of the dead pressing on the other side. "We cannot block these doors by simply piling heavy objects. The granite tiles are smooth, and the friction would be insufficient. The lateral force would push any loose barriers across the floor. We must construct a diagonal bracing frame to distribute the load directly into the temple's stone foundations."

Master Shi and several monks entered the hall, carrying long monk spades and staffs. "The dead are gathering on the steps," Shi said, his face grave. "More are climbing from the ravines. We can hold the side gates, but if the main hall doors fall, the inner sanctuary is lost."

"We will secure them," Jun said, turning to Liang. "We have the seasoned pine logs—*fangmu*—stored in the side gallery. They are twelve centimeters square. Bring four of them, each three meters long. We will construct a diagonal truss system using the ancient triangulation of forces."

As Liang and the monks ran to fetch the timbers, Jun knelt on the granite floor, examining the stone flagging. Near the center of the hall, exactly two and a half meters from the doors, were several square stone sockets carved into the granite floor. These sockets, eighteen centimeters square and ten centimeters deep, had once held the columns of a decorative wooden partition screen that had been removed decades ago.

"This is our foundation," Jun said to Liang, who had returned with the heavy pine logs. "These stone sockets will act as the heel blocks for our braces. They are cut directly into the bedrock of the mountain, meaning they can bear immense horizontal loads without shifting a single millimeter."

Jun took his carpenter's square and chalk, sketching the calculations on the floor. "We must calculate the load to prevent Euler buckling of our struts. Suppose sixty of the dead are pressing against these doors. If each zombie exerts a static force of five hundred Newtons, the total horizontal thrust $H$ is thirty thousand Newtons. To distribute this load and prevent the door panels from buckling locally, we will run two horizontal pressure beams—*yaoguan*—across the back of the door leaves at one-third and two-thirds height.

"The diagonal braces—*xiecheng*—will run from these horizontal beams down to the stone floor sockets at an angle of forty-five degrees," Jun explained. "At this angle, the horizontal force and the vertical downward force are equal. The axial compressive load $P$ along each diagonal brace is calculated as the horizontal force divided by the cosine of forty-five degrees. For a total force of thirty kilonewtons, the compression along the braces will be approximately forty-two point four kilonewtons.

"Since we are using four braces—two for each door leaf—each timber will bear a compressive load of ten point six kilonewtons," Jun continued. "To ensure they do not buckle under this compression, we calculate the critical buckling load $P_{cr}$ using Euler's formula: $P_{cr}$ equals pi squared multiplied by the Young's modulus $E$ and the moment of inertia $I$, divided by the length $L$ squared. The Young's modulus of seasoned northern pine is ten Gigapascals. For our twelve-centimeter square timbers, the moment of inertia is seventeen point two eight times ten to the minus six meters to the fourth. With a strut length of two point eight meters, the critical buckling load for a single brace is two hundred and seventeen point five kilonewtons. This gives us a safety factor of over twenty. The wood will not buckle."

With the calculations complete, Jun and Liang set to work. They used the frame saw to cut the pine logs to the calculated lengths, their teeth biting into the dry pine with a dry, scraping hum. The sweet scent of pine resin rose into the cold air of the hall.

Jun used his mortising chisel and mallet to carve birdsmouth joints—*yazui sun*—into the upper ends of the diagonal braces. These joints were shaped like an open beak, designed to wrap around the horizontal pressure beams to prevent the struts from sliding upward or turning under pressure. The hammer blows on the chisel echoed under the high timber ceiling of the sanctuary, a steady, rhythmic sound that contrasted with the scraping of the dead outside.

"Liang, prepare the hardwood wedges," Jun ordered. "Use the seasoned jujube wood. We need them tapered from four centimeters down to a sharp edge."

While Liang split the jujube wood, the monks held the horizontal pressure beams against the doors. Jun positioned the first diagonal brace, fitting its birdsmouth joint over the upper horizontal beam. He lowered the bottom end of the brace into the square stone floor socket. A gap of about three centimeters remained between the timber end and the back of the stone socket.

Jun slid two of the jujube wood wedges into the gap. He picked up a heavy wooden beetle—a mallet carved from a solid block of oak.

He swung the mallet, bringing it down against the head of the wedge with a loud, solid *THUD*.

*Thud. Thud. Thud.*

With each blow, the wedge sank deeper, forcing the diagonal brace upward against the horizontal pressure beam. The timber creaked under the immense tension, its fibers compressing as they took the load. The massive doors groaned, and the inward bow at the center seam began to disappear.

Jun repeated the process for the other three braces, hammering the jujube wedges home until the mallets bounced off the hard wood.

The double doors, now supported by the interlocking pine frames, were forced back into their original alignment. The gap at the center seam closed completely, locking the leaves together. The wood was flat and rigid, supported by the diagonal braces that ran down to the stone floor sockets.

Just as the last wedge was driven, a sudden surge occurred outside. A larger group of the dead had reached the steps, throwing their weight against the door panels. The wooden doors rattled, but the bracing frames did not move. The horizontal thrust was transferred down the diagonal spruce timbers, directly into the stone sockets of the granite floor. Not a single joint creaked, and the door leaves remained perfectly straight.

From the high transom windows above the doors, Master Shi and the warrior monks stood on temporary scaffolding. Armed with their newly reinforced monk spades, they thrust downward through the narrow openings. The sharp steel blades split the skulls of the dead pressed against the threshold, neutralizing the threat with clean, mechanical precision.

Inside the hall, Jun stood back, wiping the sweat from his face. He patted the diagonal pine timbers, which were now cool and solid under his hand.

"The carpentry has held," Jun said, looking up at the silent terracotta Arhats. "The triangulation of forces has turned the mountain's own stone into our shield. As long as the stone sockets hold, no force from the plains can push these doors open."

"Amituofo," Master Shi said, descending from the scaffolding. "The gate of the sanctuary is secure. We must now prepare for the road ahead."

CHAPTER 9: THE SONG SHAN PASS


The cold mountain wind of Henan Province swept down from the jagged peaks of Shaoshi Mountain, howling through the narrow, rocky gorges of Mount Song. The air was dry and thin, carrying the bitter scent of frozen earth, dry coal dust, and the stale, sickening odor of decay that rose from the yellow-earth plains below. Down in the valley, a massive horde of five thousand infected, having crossed the Yellow River on the highway bridges, had reached the base of the mountain. The winding dirt trails and stone steps of the pass were now filled with a rising tide of grey, mummified bodies, their slow, uncoordinated movements carrying them inexorably upward. The defenders had retreated to the Mountain Gate, but the rocky trail directly above the Devil's Ravine was too wide to hold with staffs or spears.

The path spanned a deep, vertical cleft in the mountain, crossing over a narrow stone arch bridge that had been built by masonry builders centuries ago.

Master Shi stood at the edge of the ravine, his red robes whipping in the freezing wind. He gripped his reinforced monk spade, his knuckles white in the cold. "We cannot hold them on the open path," he said, his face dark with dust and weariness. "The steps are too wide, and the brothers will be flanked if they are forced back. We must cut the trail. The path crosses the Devil's Ravine over this limestone arch. The entire structure relies on a single wedge-shaped keystone at the center. If we can split or dislodge that stone, the arch will lose its compression, and the twenty-meter section of the trail will collapse into the ravine, isolating the temple complex."

Liang looked down into the dark, yawning chasm, his eyes wide. "Who will climb down to the arch? The dead are already on the lower steps of the bridge. The vibrations alone could collapse it while someone is underneath."

"I will go," Jun said, his voice calm as he opened his wooden toolbox. He took out his heavy steel framing chisel, thirty centimeters long and made of solid tool steel, along with a four-kilogram iron sledgehammer. "Liang, prepare the guide ropes. Shi, keep the monks on the bridge balcony. Use the slings to keep the lead dead back for as long as possible. Once I start striking, the vibrations will draw them, but I must have five minutes."

Jun climbed down the steep limestone cliff face, his boots finding small niches in the rock. The space beneath the arch was freezing, a dark, narrow cavern where the wind howled like a wounded beast. Above him, the limestone blocks of the arch groaned and creaked under the weight of the climbing dead. He could hear the heavy, dragging footsteps and the scraping of dry leather soles on the stone directly above his head.

The arch was built of grey limestone blocks, laid in a semi-circular curve. The blocks were locked together by a single wedge-shaped keystone in the center, which was under immense compressive force from the weight of the bridge and the climbing horde.

Jun wedged himself into a narrow rock chimney directly beneath the keystone. He calculated the forces in his head. An arch transfers the vertical load of the bridge into lateral thrust along the curve of the stones, resolving the forces down to the abutments on either side. The keystone at the center is the pivot; it is under pure compression, wedge-locked by the flanking stones. The compressive stress on the limestone keystone, given the twenty-five-ton mass of the bridge, was approximately three Megapascals. By driving his steel chisel into the mortar joint flanking the keystone, he would split the stone or destroy the friction wedge, causing the arch to fail in shear.

He positioned the tip of the heavy framing chisel against the joint, drew back the sledgehammer, and struck.
*CLANG.*
A high-pitched, metallic ring echoed through the ravine, accompanied by a bright flash of sparks as steel met stone. A smell of dry sulfur and limestone dust rose in the narrow space. Jun adjusted his grip, his shoulders tensing as he swung the hammer again.
*CLANG. CLANG.*

The limestone was hard, but the joint was old, the mortar dry and crumbling. With each blow of the sledgehammer, the chisel sank deeper into the seam, wedging the stones apart. Jun could feel the vibrations of the climbing dead running down through the arch, a low, rhythmic shudder that vibrated through the steel of his chisel and into his arms. His hands were numb from the cold, his breath condensing in white clouds on the dark metal of the hammer.

"Jun! They have reached the center of the bridge!" Master Shi called from the far ledge. The sharp crack of a monk spade striking a zombie's skull echoed from the platform above, followed by a wet, heavy thud as a body fell over the parapet and plunged into the ravine.

Jun did not look up. He swung the hammer with steady, mechanical force, his eyes fixed on the joint. The chisel was now ten centimeters deep. A small hairline crack appeared in the center of the limestone keystone, spreading upward toward the roadbed.

"Jun! The stones are shifting!" Liang screamed, holding the safety rope taut.

A granite block directly above Jun's head slid downward by half an inch, its mortar joint splitting open. A shower of sharp stone fragments fell onto his head, drawing a thin line of blood across his cheek.

Jun took a deep breath, gathered his remaining strength, and swung the sledgehammer in a wide arc, bringing it down against the head of the chisel.

*CLANK.*

The limestone keystone split down the middle with a sound like a cracking whip. The wedge-shaped halves of the stone fractured, losing their grip on the flanking blocks.

With a deafening, grinding roar, the limestone arch caved inward. The twenty-meter section of the stone trail collapsed, carrying the climbing zombies down into the Devil's Ravine in a massive landslide of rock and dust. The grey bodies tumbled through the air, disappearing into the dark chasm.

The roar of the falling masonry subsided, leaving only the sound of the wind howling through the newly opened gap.

Jun was trapped on the lower ledge of the cliff, the twenty-meter gap too wide to jump. He clung to the rock face, his fingers dug into a narrow seam.

Master Shi ran to the edge of the far ledge. In his hands, he held a long, thick hemp rope, its end tied tightly around a heavy, woven white wax wood staff. He swung the staff in a wide, circular motion, launching it across the chasm like a harpoon.

"Jun! Catch the staff!" Shi shouted.

The staff flew through the dust cloud, its pale wood visible against the grey stone. Jun reached out, his hand locking around the smooth wax wood. He wrapped the hemp rope around his forearm, securing his grip.

"Pull!" Shi commanded.

Liang and the monks heaved the rope, their boots slipping on the stone. Jun kicked off from the cliff face, swinging out over the deep ravine. The wind caught him, spinning him in the air, but the white wax wood staff held firm, its flexible fibers absorbing the shock of his weight. He swung across the gap, his boots scraping the limestone wall before Shi and Liang hauled him over the ledge to safety.

The temple was isolated.

---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE SACRED FOREST


The morning sun rose slowly over a silent Mount Song, its golden rays piercing the cold, dry mountain air and illuminating the red plaster walls of the Shaolin Temple. The deep chasm of Devil's Ravine, which now cut across the ancient stone trail below the Mountain Gate, was silent and empty. The fallen limestone blocks and the bodies of the climbing dead were buried beneath a thick layer of grey dust at the bottom of the gorge. The air was calm, carrying only the clean, sharp scent of frozen pine needles, coal smoke from the temple workshops, and the distant, faint sound of the mountain stream flowing through the deep valleys below.

Inside the temple gates, the survivors slept. The four hundred refugees who had fled the surrounding villages were warm, sheltered behind the heavy brick walls of the inner courtyards, their water mill repaired and their gates braced against the threat. The young novices swept the stone steps of the Mountain Gate, their wooden brooms making a soft, rhythmic scratching sound on the granite flags.

Jun sat on the stone steps of the Shanmen, a flat oilstone held in his left hand and his broadaxe resting across his knees. The wooden toolbox beside him was scarred and worn, its pine and cedar panels showing the marks of their long journey, but the steel tools inside were clean and sharp. He applied a few drops of pale camellia oil to the oilstone, spreading it with his thumb. He then ran the bevel of the axe blade across the abrasive stone in slow, circular motions, keeping his wrist steady at a twenty-five-degree angle.

The scraping sound of the steel against the stone was steady and peaceful in the morning air, a welcome silence after the thunderous roar of the falling bridge.

"The edge must be true," Jun said, his voice quiet in the cold air. He wiped the slurry of oil and steel dust from the metal with a piece of dry rag, revealing a clean, polished line along the cutting edge. "A dull tool requires more force to cut, which means the builder has less control. In our trade, a loss of control is how accidents happen, and on a mountain cliff, a single slip is fatal."

Beside him, Liang was using a fine-cut steel file to dress the edge of his framing chisel, his fingers moving with quiet, focused precision. The white dust of the limestone arch still clung to the fabric of his padded coat, but his face was relaxed, his breathing even. He ran his thumb lightly across the chisel's tip, feeling for any burrs or nicks in the metal.

"We have built a good gate on the mountain, Master Jun," Liang said, looking toward the ancient pines of the Pagoda Forest, which stood like silent sentinels under the morning light.

"A gate is only as good as the men who hold the staff," Jun replied, setting his oilstone back into its wooden compartment. "And the monks are strong. The watchtower stands firm, and the gates are braced with diagonal struts. The forces are resolved down to the granite foundation. They do not need builders anymore."

As they spoke, Master Shi walked over from the courtyard, carrying a wooden tray. On it were two cups of hot green tea, a plate of salted mustard greens, and a small, battery-powered radio receiver. The steam rose from the cups, smelling of wild chrysanthemum and clean water.

"Drink," Shi said, handing a cup to Jun and another to Liang. "You have worked through the night, and the road is cold. The temple has little food, but the tea is warm."

Jun took the cup, the warmth of the clay heating his cold, stiff hands. He drank slowly, the hot tea restoring his energy, warming his chest after the long hours spent in the wet stone cleft beneath the arch.

Liang blew on his tea, watching the steam curl in the cold air. "How long do you think the chasm will keep them out, Master?"

"As long as the cliffs do not crumble," Jun said. "The limestone is hard, and the gap is twenty meters wide. A slow-moving zombie cannot jump, and without a solid structure to walk on, their weight will only carry them into the ravine. The physics of gravity is our best defense. The forces are resolved downward, away from the temple walls."

Shi set the radio receiver on the stone step between them. It was a small, rectangular transistor radio in a scratched black plastic casing, its telescoping brass antenna extended to its full length. He turned the volume knob, and the speaker emitted a loud, crackling hiss of static that filled the quiet courtyard. Shi adjusted the tuning dial slowly, his fingers moving a fraction of a millimeter at a time as he searched the empty airwaves.

The static rose and fell, a high-pitched whine that bounced off the red walls of the temple. Then, a faint, cracked voice broke through the noise, its tone raspy and distorted by the distance.

"...calling any survivors... this is Hubei Province... the Wudang Mountains..." the voice said, fading in and out as the signal struggled to cross the mountain ranges. "The Purple Cloud Temple is holding, but the mountain dead are climbing the cliff paths... our timber gates are buckling under the weight... we need builders to reinforce the timber portals and construct the barriers... if anyone can hear this..."

The transmission cut off, replaced by a loud, empty hum of static. Shi turned the dial back and forth, but there was only the cold hiss of the wind through the speaker.

Liang set his cup down, his face turning serious as he looked at Jun. "Song Shan is far from Wudang, Master. We would have to cross the northern plains and the Han River."

Jun stood up, shaking the frost and wood shavings from his padded coat. He picked up his broadaxe, sliding the hickory handle into the leather loop of his tool belt. He looked toward the south-west, where the peaks of Hubei rose like waves on the horizon, their snow-capped peaks lost in the morning light.

"The road is long, Liang," Jun said, his voice steady and quiet. "But the work does not end. The dead do not sleep, and as long as they wander, the living will need walls to keep them out. Pack the chisels, the saws, and the marking gauges. We have to teach some Taoists how to build."

Liang stood up and bowed, his hands clasped before him in the traditional builder's salute. "Yes, Master. I will gather the spare handles and the oil stones."

Shi bowed deeply. "Thank you, builders. The mountain will remember."

Jun returned the bow, then lifted his heavy toolbox onto his shoulder. With Liang following close behind, he walked through the temple's rear gate, heading down the steep, icy steps of the mountain trail, their boots leaving deep prints in the fresh snow as they began their long journey toward the peaks of Hubei.

================================================================================

STORY 19: THE TAOIST HERMITS
Setting: Wudang Mountains, Hubei Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE PURPLE CLOUD


The mist of the Wudang Mountains was different from the cold, dry fogs of the northern plains; it was thick, blue-tinted, and heavy with the scent of damp pine needles and wild ginger. It rose from the deep, forested valleys of Hubei Province, clinging to the vertical cliffs and wrapping around the green stone columns that rose like fingers from the earth. The humidity was a physical weight, settling into the wool of Jun’s coat and bead-coating the eyelashes of his apprentice, Liang. Every step up the thousand stone stairs felt like lifting a sodden log. The stones themselves, slabs of weathered green limestone quarried from the lower ravines centuries ago, were slick with moisture and patches of dark, velvety moss. 

Jun stopped on a wide landing, resting his hand on a carved stone balustrade that was shaped like a writhing dragon emerging from clouds. His chest heaved, the thin mountain air burning his lungs. At his feet sat his heavy oak toolbox, its iron-reinforced corners dark with oil and sweat. In his hand, he carried a long framing chisel, its forged iron blade wrapped in a oiled cloth to protect it from the mountain damp. Beside him, Liang dropped his own burden—a larger, coarse pine chest containing their roughing tools, saws, and a heavy wooden mallet. Liang bent over, his hands resting on his knees, his breath venting in rapid white plumes that immediately dissolved into the blue fog. 

"Master," Liang gasped, looking upward through the shifting steam of the mountainside. "The mountain is quiet. Too quiet. On the road from Mount Song, we could hear the temple bells from miles away. Here, there is nothing. No chanting. No drums. Only the wind in the pines."

Jun looked up. Above them, emerging and disappearing in the mist like a phantom city, lay the Purple Cloud Temple, *Zixiao Gong*. It was a vast complex of green-glazed roof tiles and yellow plaster walls, built in tiers that clung to the steep slope of the mountain. The green tiles glistened under the damp sky, looking like the scales of a great beast coiled against the red-cliff face. The yellow plaster of the walls was cracked and streaked with soot and minerals, showing the decades of mountain storms it had weathered. In the center of the main courtyard, visible through the arched entrance, stood several ancient bronze incense burners, their metal oxidized to a pale verdigris green. 

"The Taoists believe in silence," Jun said, his voice quiet but steady. "They say the mountain speaks when the mouth is closed. We did not come here to listen to bells, Liang. We came to work. The mountain air is wet, and where there is moisture, there is rot. We must check the cedar posts of the main gate before the night damp sets in."

They had traveled southwest from Mount Song, crossing the yellow rivers of Henan and entering the green, rugged hills of Hubei. Along the way, they had seen how the infection—what the provincial authorities called the *bingbian*, the outbreak of the stagnant blood—had scattered through the countryside. It was not the chaotic collapse that some had feared in the early weeks; the state had established quarantine zones along the main rivers, and here, in the mountains, the local civil committees and the monks had organized a network of collective mutual aid. The survivors worked together, pooling their grain reserves and maintaining watch along the steep passes. The dead they encountered were not like the fresh, aggressive infected of the crowded cities. Here, they were the "mountain dead"—slow, silent figures that had wandered up from the flooded valleys. Their leather-like skin, dried by the mountain winds and damp from the valleys, was often covered in green moss and yellow lichens. They moved with a slow, heavy drag, their bodies following the natural contours of the land like water seeking the lowest point.

Jun picked up his toolbox, the leather strap biting into his shoulder, and walked toward the *Zixiao* gate. The gate was a massive timber structure, its double-eaved roof supported by four giant posts of ancient cedar, each nearly a meter in diameter. 

"Look here," Jun said, kneeling at the base of the eastern pillar. Liang knelt beside him, pulling a small brass-bound pocket ruler and a steel testing awl from his apron. Jun tapped the base of the cedar post, where the circular end-grain rested on the carved stone plinth—the tenon seat, or *dongguan*. Instead of the clear, ringing sound of healthy heartwood, the blow produced a soft, hollow thud. Jun took the steel awl from Liang and pressed it into the timber. The steel sank two inches into the wood with almost no resistance. When he pulled it out, the tip was coated in dark, spongy wood fibers that smelled of sweet cedar rot.

"The roof of this gate weighs over three thousand catties," Jun explained, pointing to the heavy clay tiles and the massive spruce rafters above. "The vertical load is distributed across these four posts. But because the stone plinth has a slight indentation that holds rainwater, the bottom of this cedar post has been soaking in moisture for decades. The outer sapwood is still intact, but the inner heartwood at the tenon joint is rotting. Under the weight of a winter snowfall, the tenon will shear. The entire gate will twist, the mortises in the lintels will split, and the roof will come down."

"Can we wedge it, Master?" Liang asked, tracing the crack that ran vertically up the base.

"No," Jun said. "A wedge would only split the dry shell. We must cut away the rotten base—a process of *chazhu*, or pillar-splicing. We will support the main load with temporary spruce shores, cut out the rotten bottom foot of this cedar pillar, and fit a new foot of seasoned larch wood, joined with a double-stepped tenon locked with copper pins."

"A respectful plan," a soft, clear voice said from the shadow of the gatehouse.

Jun and Liang stood up immediately, Jun bowing from the waist, his hands clasped before him. Daoist Master Chen stepped out from the grey mist. She was a woman of sixty, her face lined with the clean, dry wrinkles of a life spent in the mountain wind. Her silver-streaked hair was tied in a neat bun on top of her head, secured by a simple hairpin carved from wild plum wood. She wore a robe of indigo-dyed cotton, patched neatly at the sleeves with darker blue thread, and a wide woven belt. Across her back was slung a long, double-edged steel sword—a *Jian*—in a scabbard of weathered black wood. Behind her stood two young disciples carrying wooden staves.

"I am Chen," she said, returning the bow with her hands folded inside her long sleeves. "The representatives of the Song Shan committee sent word through the shortwave radio that you were coming. We are grateful for your skills, Master Jun. The temples of Wudang have become a sanctuary for three hundred souls from the valley, but our walls are old and the mountain is unkind."

"We are honored to assist, Master Chen," Jun said, his voice full of respect. "The preservation of these temples is the preservation of our ancestors' work. How stands the lower pass?"

"The barricades at the lower gate are holding," Chen said, her eyes turning toward the misty path below. "But the timber has split under the damp, and the mountain dead are persistent. They do not think, they do not feel pain, but they keep walking. Some have climbed the cliff paths, attempting to reach our herbal gardens on the southern slopes. We have organized watch patrols, but we are short of iron and wood."

As if summoned by her words, a low, scraping sound rose from the stone steps below. Through the veil of blue fog, a figure appeared, dragging its boots against the wet limestone. It was a man who had once been a farmer, wearing the remnants of a blue cotton shirt, now shredded and stained. His skin was the color of wet clay, and across his back and shoulders, a thick carpet of green star-moss had taken root. He moved with a slow, mechanical gait, his head hanging low, his jaw slack. He did not growl or cry out; there was only the dry, rhythmic scrape of his feet on the stone steps.

Liang reached instinctively for his axe, his knuckles turning white, but Jun placed a hand on the boy’s shoulder. "Do not waste your breath or your steel on the stairs," Jun said softly. "He is slow. Let him climb."

Master Chen watched the figure approach. "The *bingbian* is a tragedy of the flesh," she said, her voice showing neither fear nor hatred, but a deep, philosophical calm. "The breath of life has departed, yet the stagnant blood refuses to rest. It is an imbalance of Yin and Yang, a block in the natural flow of the mountain's Qi. They follow the paths of least resistance—the streams, the steps, the open gates. They do not run, but they never tire. We will set the spruce shores tomorrow morning, Master Jun. Tonight, we will prepare the larch block and check the tools. In times of trouble, the work of our hands must remain steady."

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE GOLDEN PAVILION


The Golden Pavilion, *Jingding*, stood at the absolute summit of Mount Wudang—Tianzhu Peak—at an elevation of over sixteen hundred meters. It was a marvel of Ming Dynasty metallurgy and engineering: a small, exquisite temple constructed entirely of cast-bronze plates gilded with thick gold leaf, sitting atop a stone platform three meters square. In the bright sun, it was said to glow like a beacon of solid gold, but today, enveloped in the racing grey clouds of the upper peaks, it was a muted, metallic yellow, its gilded eaves dripping with condensation. 

The wind here did not blow; it howled, a relentless force that swept up from the sheer canyons, threatening to rip the clothes from a man’s back and throw him into the abyss. The platform upon which the pavilion rested was shifting. 

Jun stood on the narrow ledge of the platform, a hemp safety rope tied around his waist and anchored to a bronze column of the pavilion. The cold was different up here; it was dry and biting, numbing his fingers within minutes of removing his thick wool mittens. He held a bronze plumb bob on a thin linen line, suspending it from the northern eave of the pavilion down to the granite base. 

"How much has it moved, Master?" Liang called out, his voice nearly carried away by the wind. He was crouched near the small charcoal stove they had carried up the peak, shielding the embers with his leather apron.

Jun squinted at the plumb line, waiting for the heavy bronze weight to stop swinging in the draft. "Two inches," Jun called back. "The northern foundation block has slid fifty millimeters outward. The freeze-thaw cycles of the winter rains have opened the joint between the outer retaining wall and the core platform. The north-facing bronze sill of the pavilion is now bridging a void."

Jun hauled the plumb bob back up, coiling the line around his hand. He stepped carefully to the edge, looking down the vertical cliff face that dropped six hundred meters into the mist. He pointed to the gap between the two massive granite blocks that formed the platform’s edge. 

"The bronze hall weighs several thousand catties," Jun explained to Liang, who had crawled closer to watch. "It is built of interlocking bronze panels, held together by bronze pins. It is a rigid cage. But a rigid cage cannot survive if its foundation is uneven. If the granite blocks slide another half-inch, the northern sill will lose its support. The weight of the roof will cause the walls to warp, the interlocking joints will shear, and the entire pavilion will slide off the peak into the gorge. We must lock the blocks using the *tiehe* method."

The *tiehe*, or iron union, was a traditional Chinese masonry technique used to bind large stone blocks in areas subject to high seismic activity or structural shifting. It involved cutting matching dovetail slots across the seam of two stones and driving a double-dovetailed iron key into the slot, which was then sealed with molten sulfur.

"We will cut three slot channels across the seam," Jun said, laying his hand on the cold granite. "Each slot must be four inches long, two inches wide in the middle, and three inches wide at the ends. Liang, bring the star-drills and the three-pound mallet. We must finish the drilling before the charcoal burns out."

Jun took a heavy iron star-drill—a solid rod of iron with a cross-shaped, hardened steel tip—and placed the point exactly across the seam of the two granite blocks. Liang stood beside him, his legs braced against the wind, holding the three-pound iron mallet with both hands. 

"Strike," Jun said.

Liang brought the mallet down. The iron met the steel drill with a sharp, metallic ring that echoed off the gilded walls of the pavilion. Jun felt the shockwave travel up his arm, vibrating the bones of his hand. He rotated the drill forty-five degrees. 

"Strike."

Another blow. A small puff of white granite dust rose from the point, instantly whipped away by the gale. Jun rotated the drill again. The work was slow, tedious, and physically demanding. Every strike of the mallet had to be delivered with absolute precision; a single misplaced blow could shatter the edge of the granite block or break the apprentice’s wrist. As they worked, the friction heated the tip of the steel drill, but the freezing wind cooled it just as quickly. Jun’s hands grew numb, the skin of his knuckles turning red and then white from the cold. He had to periodically blow on his fingers and rub them against his wool coat to maintain his grip on the drill.

After an hour of rhythmic striking, they had rough-drilled a series of holes along the dovetail template. Jun then took a flat-nosed stone chisel and a smaller mallet, carefully chipping away the granite webs between the holes to create the clean, double-dovetailed slot. 

Meanwhile, Liang turned his attention to the charcoal stove. From the temple’s medicinal store, Daoist Master Chen had provided them with several bags of yellow sulfur powder. In normal times, the monks used the powder to prepare ointments for skin diseases or scattered it around the foundations of the lower temples to keep venomous snakes away. Now, it was their mortar.

Liang poured the granular yellow powder into a heavy cast-iron ladle. He placed the ladle directly onto the glowing charcoal. Jun watched the ladle closely as he finished cleaning the third stone slot. 

"Watch the heat, Liang," Jun warned. "Sulfur is a delicate spirit. If it remains too cold, it will not flow. If it gets too hot, it will turn dark red and thick like tar, and then it will catch fire. You want it to flow like oil, pale yellow and clear."

As the heat from the charcoal rose, the yellow powder began to melt at the edges, turning into a clear, amber-colored liquid. A faint, sweetish, choking odor began to rise from the ladle. Liang adjusted the air vents of the stove, pulling the ladle slightly back from the direct heat as the liquid began to turn a deeper orange. A tiny blue flame flickered on the surface of the liquid—the sulfur was beginning to ignite. Liang quickly covered the ladle with a flat piece of slate, smothering the flame.

Jun took the three wrought-iron keys they had carried up from the forge—heavy, bowtie-shaped iron bars that had been seasoned to resist rust. He aligned the first key with the slot and tapped it down with his wooden mallet. It fit snugly, the iron bridging the gap between the two granite stones.

"Bring the ladle," Jun ordered.

Liang wrapped a thick leather rag around the handle of the cast-iron ladle and lifted it from the stove. He carried it carefully across the wind-swept platform, his boots searching for traction on the damp stone. Jun held a small iron funnel over the slot. 

Liang tilted the ladle. The molten sulfur, now a rich amber liquid, poured in a thin, steady stream into the funnel. It ran down into the slot, filling the small tolerances between the iron key and the granite walls. The heat of the liquid hit the cold stone, releasing a sharp, suffocating plume of sulfur dioxide gas. Both men coughed, their eyes watering instantly, but they did not flinch. Liang kept his hand steady until the yellow liquid rose to the very brim of the slot, level with the granite surface.

As the sulfur cooled, it underwent a rapid transition, changing from a dark amber liquid to a bright yellow, crystalline solid. Because sulfur expands slightly as it crystallizes, it packed itself into every microscopic pore of the granite, locking the iron key in an airtight, moisture-proof seal that would prevent water from reaching the iron and causing it to rust and expand.

While the second key was being poured, three figures emerged from the mist at the base of the final stone stairway. 

These were not the moss-covered dead of the forest valleys; these were the "cliff dead"—zombies that had climbed from the high limestone quarries. Their skin was dry, grey, and caked with the white dust of the limestone cliffs. They moved with a slow, mechanical crawl, their fingers worn down to the bone from clawing at the vertical rock faces. The lead figure, a tall man in the tattered remnants of a laborer's tunic, dragged himself up the steps, his boots scraping dryly against the rock.

Daoist Master Chen, who had been standing watch at the entrance of the platform, stepped forward. She did not draw her sword immediately; instead, she stood at the head of the steps, her posture relaxed, her weight centered in her hips. Her hands were loose at her sides, her eyes calm as she watched the slow progress of the dead.

When the lead zombie reached the third step from the top, its grey hand reaching out to grab the carved stone post, Chen moved. 

With a motion that was fluid and seamless, she drew her steel *Jian*. The blade slid from its wooden scabbard with a soft hiss. She stepped forward, her body turning in a circular motion that deflected the zombie’s reaching arm with the flat of her blade. Without stopping, she rotated her wrist, driving the tip of the sword directly into the zombie’s left temple. The steel entered the skull with a clean, muffled crunch. 

The zombie’s body went limp instantly. Chen did not try to pull the sword straight back; instead, she stepped to the side, using the momentum of the falling weight to swing the body outward. With a gentle push of her foot, she sent the figure rolling over the edge of the steps. It fell silently into the grey clouds below.

The remaining two zombies, moving with the same slow, relentless impulse, continued their climb. Chen met them with the same calm precision. Her sword moved in quiet arcs, the steel reflecting the grey light of the peak. Within moments, the steps were clear again, the dead dispatched with minimal effort and no wasted movement, their bodies reclaimed by the mountain valleys below.

Jun finished pouring the third sulfur joint, smoothing the cooling yellow surface with the flat of his trowel. He stood up, stretching his aching back, and looked at Master Chen, who was wiping her blade with a clean silk cloth.

"The keys are set," Jun said. "The platform will not slide again in our lifetime."

Chen sheathed her sword and bowed. "The mountain is stable because the work is true, Master Jun. Let us return to the lower temple. The wind is rising, and we have much to do before the night."

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE WUDANG BLADES


The mist in the courtyard of the Purple Cloud Temple did not lift with the rising sun; instead, it settled into the open forge like a cold shroud, carrying the wet smell of pine needles. The forge was a crude stone hearth, built of dry-stacked river boulders and lined with refractory clay. Liang, his face blackened with charcoal dust and his hands raw from the rough hemp rope, operated the wooden box bellows, the fengxiang, in a steady cadence. With every stroke, the bellows hissed, sending air into the bottom of the hearth, causing the charcoal bed to glow from a dull cherry red to a brilliant yellow-white. Beside the stone anvil, Master Chen stood over three ruined Jian—traditional double-edged straight swords of the Wudang sect. One blade was bent at a grotesque thirty-degree angle near the midpoint. The second had its wooden hilt scales split completely in half, the blade's tang rattling loosely within the guard. The third was snapped clean two inches above the guard, the fracture face showing a coarse, grainy crystalline structure.

"The steel is too thin, Master Jun," Chen said, her voice low over the sighing of the bellows. "These were forged for the flowing forms of the Tai Chi sword, light and balanced to the weight of a breath. But when our disciples strike the skulls of the dead on the lower steps, the blades bend like reeds, losing the impact force in the flex of the steel. And when they strike with full force, the soft hilt pins snap, leaving the sword useless."

Jun knelt by the bench, picking up the bent sword to run his thumb along the central ridge, the jianji. The blade was scarcely three millimeters thick at the base, tapering to less than a millimeter and a half near the tip. It was forged from a medium-carbon steel, likely recycled agricultural iron that had been carburized and folded, but it lacked the structural mass required for heavy impact.

"A sword acts as a beam under impact, Master Chen," Jun explained, tapping the flat of the blade to produce a dull, vibrating hum. "In engineering, the stiffness of a beam under a bending load is proportional to the cube of its thickness. If you double the thickness of a blade, you do not merely double its resistance to bending; you increase it eightfold. These blades are three millimeters thick. By forge-welding a thick spine along the center, we can increase the thickness to eight millimeters, making the blade nearly twenty times stiffer. It will not bend, and the force of the strike will be directed entirely through the edge."

He picked up the second sword, sliding the loose wooden grip scales off the flat steel tang. He pointed to two small holes drilled through the tang, where the sheared remnant of a soft, lead-tin pin lay. "The blacksmiths who made these used cast lead pins because lead is cheap and easy to file flush with the wood. But lead has a shear strength of less than fifteen megapascals. When the blade strikes a skull, the sudden deceleration creates a massive rotational force around the guard, shearing the lead pins instantly. We must replace them with hand-hammered copper wire rivets. Red copper has a shear strength ten times greater, and as we hammer it cold, the metal work-hardens, locking the hilt with a force that no strike can break."

To find the materials, Jun salvaged square wrought iron window bars from the temple's old scriptorium. While Liang retrieved them, Jun heated the bent sword to a dull red heat—about eight hundred degrees Celsius—and carefully straightened the warp on the anvil with light, precise blows of his hand hammer. When Liang returned with the bars, Jun cut a section of the wrought iron to match the length of the blade, tapering the ends to sit flat along the central ridge. He ground both surfaces until the metal was bright and clean. Any rust or dirt left between the two pieces would prevent the molecular bonding of the forge-weld, causing the blade to delaminate under stress.

Liang brought a mixture of crushed borax and fine silica sand to act as a flux. Jun bound the iron bar to the center of the sword blade using thin iron wire, wrapping it tightly at three points. He then placed the assembly into the heart of the forge, burying it deep under the glowing charcoal.

"Pump, Liang," Jun said. "Slowly at first, then build the draft."

The bellows creaked, and the fire shifted from orange to a brilliant, blinding white. The temperature rose past eleven hundred degrees, melting the borax flux into a glassy liquid that sealed the clean metal from oxygen. As the heat climbed toward thirteen hundred degrees, the steel began to "sweat"—small droplets of liquid metal appearing on the surface. Jun gripped the tongs, pulling the white-hot composite blade from the fire. He laid it flat on the anvil.

"Strike, Liang! Quick and light!"

Liang swung the four-pound sledgehammer precisely where Jun indicated. Thwack. The sound was a dull, wet thud, indicating that the two semi-liquid surfaces had met and fused. They worked down the length of the blade, welding the iron spine to the steel core. Jun returned the blade to the fire for a second heat, drawing out the iron spine under the hammer and tapering it toward the edges to create a clean, diamond-shaped cross-section. The blade was now a heavy, rigid wedge of iron and steel, eight millimeters thick at the spine and tapering down to the original steel edges.

Jun heated the entire blade to a uniform cherry red—about eight hundred and fifty degrees—to transform the iron structure into austenite. They did not use water for the quench, as the aggressive cooling could crack the composite blade along the weld line. Instead, they plunged it vertically into a long trough of rapeseed oil, heated slightly to reduce its viscosity. A cloud of dark smoke billowed up with a violent sizzling. After a minute, Jun pulled it out; the steel was straight and hard. A file run along the steel edge slid off with a high-pitched skitter, leaving no mark. Jun then tempered the blade over the warm mouth of the forge, watching the oxide colors crawl across the clean steel until the edge reached a deep purple-blue, indicating a hardness of about fifty-two Rockwell, before quenching it in water.

While the blade cooled, Liang split a block of seasoned pear-wood into two halves, carving a channel in the center of each to accommodate the thick tang. Jun took a coil of thick copper wire, four millimeters in diameter, and annealed it over the fire to make it soft and malleable. He drilled two holes through the pear-wood scales and the steel tang using a hand-drill with a spoon bit, slid the copper wire through, and cut it with a cold chisel, leaving two millimeters protruding on either side.

"Watch closely, Liang," Jun said, taking a small ball-peen hammer. "Do not strike hard, or you will split the wood. You must tap the copper repeatedly, working in a circle to spread the metal and form a rivet head while the compression hardens the copper inside the hole."

Jun's rapid tapping caused the soft copper to expand, filling the hole completely and tightening the grip scales against the tang. The ends of the pin mushroomed into neat, rounded copper domes that pressed firmly against the wood, locking the hilt into a single, solid unit.

Master Chen took the finished sword. The weapon was heavier, its center of balance shifted forward, but it felt solid and purposeful. She performed a slow, circular deflection before bringing the blade down with a sudden, whistling crack onto a thick spruce log. The blade bit four inches deep into the wood, splitting it cleanly along the grain. The steel did not flex, and the hilt remained absolutely solid.

"It is a weapon of the earth now, Master Jun," Chen said, her fingers tracing the hammered copper rivets. "It has the weight to meet the dead, and the strength to endure the road."

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE CLIFFSIDE PATH


The path to the Nanyan Temple was a narrow scar carved into the vertical face of the cliff, sixty centimeters wide, with a drop of six hundred meters into the gorge. The limestone wall rose above it like a grey barrier, its surface wet and slick with ice in the shadows, while the valley floor below was buried under a sea of boiling white clouds. A week ago, a heavy rainstorm had loosened a shale outcrop on the upper peaks, causing a landslide that obliterated a three-meter section of the trail. In its place remained a steep, unstable slope of loose scree at its angle of repose. Any step sent gravel sliding into the abyss. Worse, three slow-moving dead from the valley—their damp bodies covered in green star-moss—were stuck on the far side of the slide, their feet sliding in the gravel as they tried to climb toward the temple gate.

"The scree cannot be cleared," Jun said, looking at the gap. "The moment we touch the base, the upper slope will release. We must build a jiadao—a cantilevered timber gallery—to bypass the slide area entirely."

"How do we anchor the beams, Master?" Liang asked, holding the heavy toolbox, his knuckles white as the mountain wind buffeted his shoulders.

"We will drill three horizontal sockets into the limestone below the slide," Jun explained, pointing with his chisel. "We will insert three cantilevered spruce brackets, tiaoliang, each fifteen centimeters square, projecting one point one meters from the face. To support a design load of two thousand Newtons—the weight of two men carrying tools—with a safety factor of three, the brackets must penetrate the rock by at least forty-five centimeters. This one-to-three ratio of penetration to overhang is the minimum for spruce in dense limestone. We will drill the sockets at a three-degree upward angle. This critical incline ensures that gravity and downward loads force the bracket deeper into the rock rather than pulling it out."

Jun wrapped a thick hemp safety rope twice around his waist, securing it with a bowline, and handed the end to Liang and Brother Faxian. Faxian wrapped the rope around a massive, ancient pine tree growing from a nearby rock fissure, using the rough bark for friction.

"Hold the line tight," Jun said. "If I slip, let the rope catch the weight, then haul me up slowly."

Jun stepped off the path into the open air. The wind whipped his coat, and below his boots hung six hundred meters of grey mist. He hung against the cold limestone wall, using his boots to stabilize himself against a narrow rock projection. Jun took a heavy iron piton from his belt, drove it deep into a natural vertical fissure with three hammer blows, and clipped his safety lanyard to it to stop himself from swinging.

"Drills!" Jun called up.

Liang lowered a basket containing two star-drills and a six-pound iron sledgehammer. Jun took the first star-drill—a heavy, octagonal steel bar, fifty millimeters in diameter, with a hardened, cross-shaped cutting tip. He placed the tip against the limestone, three feet below path level, aligning it to the three-degree upward angle. Holding the drill with his left hand, he swung the sledgehammer with his right. The impact sent a sharp vibration through his arm, numbing his fingers. A tiny puff of white stone dust rose, instantly swept away by the wind. He rotated the drill forty-five degrees to prevent the tip from binding, striking it again.

Jun worked with a slow, mechanical efficiency. Strike, rotate, strike, rotate. His muscles began to burn within minutes; holding the heavy steel bar in one hand while swinging a four-pound hammer with the other was exhausting. Sweat poured down his face, mixing with the dust. After twenty minutes of continuous drilling, the hole was only three inches deep. The limestone of Wudang was dolomitic, high in magnesium, making it exceptionally dense and tough.

"Clear the hole, Liang!" Jun called.

Liang lowered a hollow bamboo tube. Jun inserted it into the socket and blew hard, clearing the bottom of the hole so the drill could strike fresh stone. He switched to the second star-drill, which was slightly longer, and resumed the rhythmic striking. It took nearly two hours of grueling labor to drill the first forty-five-centimeter socket. When it was finished, Jun's right arm was trembling with fatigue, his hand so cramped he could barely open his fingers. He rested for ten minutes, hanging in his harness, listening to the wind and the slow, scraping sound of the zombies on the far side of the slide. They were closer now, their moss-covered hands reaching toward the edge of the gap.

Over the next four hours, Jun drilled the second and third sockets, spaced exactly one point two meters apart. By the time the third hole was complete, the sun had dipped below the western ridges, casting long, purple shadows across the canyon.

"Prepare the brackets!" Jun called up.

Liang and Faxian prepared the spruce beams. The ends that would slide into the sockets had been charred over the forge fire to dry the wood and resist rot, then wrapped in several layers of hemp cloth soaked in hot pine pitch. This tarred wrap acted as a gasket, sealing out the moisture seeping through the limestone. They lowered the first bracket. Jun guided the heavy timber into the socket. It was a tight fit; he had to use his sledgehammer to drive the beam home, the wood grooving slightly against the rough stone walls of the hole.

"Wedges," Jun said.

He took several dry oak wedges, shutu, which he had cut from seasoned heartwood. He slid them into the gaps around the spruce beam inside the socket. Using his hammer, he drove the wedges in with full force, compressing the spruce fibers and locking the beam against the limestone with immense frictional force. The bracket was now rigid; Jun stood on the cantilevered beam, bouncing his full weight on it. Within an hour, all three brackets were installed, projecting like three thick fingers over the abyss.

"Planks," Jun ordered.

Liang lowered the deck planks—heavy spruce boards, five centimeters thick and thirty centimeters wide. Jun laid them across the brackets, overlapping the joints at the center bracket. To secure the planks without iron nails, which would rust and split the timber, he used a hand-auger to drill two-centimeter holes through the planks into the spruce brackets below. He then drove seasoned oak pegs, muding, through the holes, locking the deck to the frame.

As Jun hammered the last oak peg home, a low, scraping sound rose from the far side. The lead zombie, a tall man whose skin was caked in dried grey clay and whose chest was covered in green star-moss, had stepped onto the edge of the new wooden deck. It moved with a slow, heavy drag, its boots making a dry, hollow sound on the spruce planks. Its eyes were milky and blank, its jaw hanging loose as it caught the scent of the living. Jun was still hanging in his safety harness, his boots resting on the outer bracket, his tools in his hands. He could not climb up in time to meet the threat.

From the rock platform above, Suli stepped forward. She was a watchwoman of the temple, her face calm, her posture balanced. In her hands, she held a heavy ash recurve bow, its string pulled back to her ear. The arrow was tipped with a point carved from sheep bone, polished and sharp. She took a slow, deep breath, matching the rhythm of the mountain wind. She waited until the zombie reached the middle of the bridge, where the spruce planks met.

*Twang.*

The bowstring released with a sharp, musical snap. The arrow flew through the mist, striking the zombie directly in the left eye socket, shattering the orbital plate and entering the brain. The zombie stopped instantly. Its arms fell to its sides, its knees buckled, and it collapsed onto the wet spruce deck. Because of the three-degree incline of the brackets, the body slid slightly to the side. With a soft, wet scrape, it rolled off the edge of the bridge, disappearing into the grey sea of clouds below without a sound.

The remaining two zombies, moving with the same slow, unthinking impulse, continued their climb, but Faxian and Liang hauled Jun up to the safety of the path. Jun took his framing chisel and, standing on the solid rock, prepared to meet them if they crossed. But the path was now secure, the gap bridged by the true work of their hands.
