CHAPTER 5: THE SACRED SPRING


The blue mist of the Wudang Mountains settled thick and heavy over the inner courtyard of the Purple Cloud Temple, turning the green-glazed roof tiles into slick, dark shingles that dripped with continuous condensation. In the center of the flagstone courtyard, the Dragon Spring—*Long Quan*—lay silent. The stone basin, carved from a single block of grey-green limestone centuries ago and decorated with high-relief carvings of water dragons, was empty. At the bottom of the basin, a thin layer of damp silt was starting to dry and crack under the cool mountain air. The wooden ladle that usually floated on the surface of the spring water lay discarded on the stone flags, its split pine cup warped by dry drafts.

Master Chen stood by the dry basin, her indigo robe damp from the mist. Her face was grim as she looked down at the empty stone dragon heads from which the water usually flowed. "The water supply is the blood of this temple," she said, her voice quiet but carrying the heavy weight of responsibility. "Three hundred souls are sheltered within these walls. The elders, the children from the valley, the injured watchmen. We have enough dried sweet potatoes and millet for three months, but without water, we will have to abandon *Zixiao Gong* in two days. The nearest other source is the stream in the Nanyan ravine, and that path is too dangerous to traverse with water buckets."

Jun knelt by the basin, rubbing a pinch of the dry silt between his fingers. "The blockage is not here," he said, looking up toward the high red walls of the temple's outer boundary. "The spring is fed by an underground stone conduit that taps the aquifer on the upper slopes of Tianzhu Peak. A landslide of wet clay and uprooted pines must have choked the inlet grate outside the walls."

"We cannot clear it," Liang said, pointing to the high red wall. "The valley beyond the wall is crawling with the *bingbian* victims. They wander along the stream beds, their bodies green with moss and their minds gone. If we send a work detail outside the wall, they will be trapped in the narrow ravines with no room to swing an axe or draw a sword."

Jun stood up, dusting the silt from his knees. He looked at the vertical drop of the mountainside and then at the upper terrace of the temple, where a small mountain stream fell from a high cliff before draining into the valley. "Then we do not go to the spring," Jun said. "We bring the stream to us. We will build a bypass channel. We can tap the stream at the upper terrace, route it over the southern red wall using split bamboo conduits, and discharge it directly into the Dragon Spring basin."

"The stream water is not like the spring," Master Chen warned, shaking her head. "The spring water is filtered by the deep limestone of the peak, coming out sweet and pure. The stream water runs over open soil; it is turbid with clay from the recent rains, and higher up, the mountain dead wander. If they fall into the stream, the water will carry their sickness into our very kitchen. We cannot drink it."

"Then we will build a filter," Jun replied. "We will build a gravity-fed sand and charcoal filtration bed—a *shilüchi*—inside the courtyard. It will clean the water, trapping the clay and adsorbing any foul humors or decay before the water reaches the basin."

Jun took his brass ruler and drew a sketch in the damp dust on a flat stone slab. "To feed three hundred people, we must calculate our daily demand. Each person requires a minimum of three liters of water daily for drinking, cooking, and washing wounds. That is nine hundred liters—nearly one cubic meter of water every day. If we use a slow sand filtration method, the water must sink through the filter bed at a controlled rate to ensure proper contact time. A standard slow sand filter operates best at a hydraulic loading rate of about zero point one five meters per hour. If we build three cascading stone filtration chambers, each with a surface area of zero point seven two square meters—one point two meters long and zero point six meters wide—we can process about one hundred and eight liters of water per hour. In nine hours of operation, we will yield nine hundred and seventy-two liters of clean water, which safely meets our needs."

Liang went to work immediately, retrieving the heavy tools. To build the filter chambers, they salvaged large, flat slabs of green limestone from the ruins of an old storage shed near the western gate. Jun used a iron square and a heavy pitching tool—a wide, flat-edged stone chisel—to trim the edges of the slabs so they would fit together with tight, square joints. Liang mixed the mortar, combining slaked lime with a thick paste made from boiled sticky rice. The sweet, starchy scent of the rice paste mixed with the pungent, alkaline bite of the lime, creating a dense, white mortar that would resist water penetration for decades.

They constructed three rectangular stone boxes, stacking them in a stepped cascade against the inner courtyard wall. Each chamber was one point two meters long, zero point six meters wide, and zero point five meters deep. The bottom of each chamber was drilled with three holes, two centimeters in diameter, into which Jun fitted short bronze tubes salvaged from old incense burners to act as drains.

Next came the preparation of the filter media, a task that required meticulous care. Jun explained the physical mechanism of the filter to Liang and the young Taoists who had gathered to help. 

"A filter is not a sieve," Jun said, his voice echoing in the damp stone courtyard. "It works by three distinct principles: mechanical straining, physical adsorption, and contact sedimentation. We must grade our materials from coarse to fine, so the water is progressively cleaned without clogging the bed."

For the bottom layer, they collected coarse river gravel from the dry streambeds, washing it in wooden tubs until the water ran clear. Liang sieved the gravel through a woven willow basket, selecting stones between fifteen and thirty millimeters in diameter. They laid this coarse gravel fifteen centimeters deep at the bottom of the stone chambers, directly over the bronze outlet pipes. Above this, they placed a ten-centimeter layer of medium gravel, with stones sized between five and ten millimeters. 

"This gravel does not filter the fine clay," Jun explained to Liang, who was shovel-loading the stone. "Its purpose is structural. It forms a supportive bed. If we placed the fine sand directly over the drain holes, the water would carry the sand through, clogging the pipes and ruining the filter. The medium gravel holds the sand, and the coarse gravel holds the medium gravel."

Above the gravel, they laid the most critical layer: twenty-five centimeters of activated pine charcoal. To make the charcoal, Liang and the temple woodcutters burned dry pine logs in a closed earthen kiln, sealing the air vents to starve the fire of oxygen. The wood carbonized slowly, turning into dense, black charcoal that retained the cellular structure of the pine. Jun had them crush the charcoal into small granules, between two and five millimeters in diameter. To activate it, they heated the granules in a large, sealed iron pot over the forge fire, injecting steam through a small pipe.

"The heat and steam clear the tar from the carbon pores," Jun said, holding a handful of the black granules. "It creates millions of microscopic cavities. A single Liang of this activated charcoal has a surface area larger than the entire temple courtyard. When the water passes through, the organic impurities, the odors of decay, and the invisible poisons are drawn into these cavities by physical adsorption, locking them to the carbon surface while the clean water passes through."

The final, top layer was twenty centimeters of fine river sand. They sieved the sand through a fine brass wire screen, selecting grains between zero point one five and zero point three five millimeters. They washed the sand three times, rubbing it between their palms in the cold spring water to remove all traces of silt and organic loam. 

"The sand is the mechanical strainer," Jun said as they smoothed the top layer. "The spaces between the grains are small enough to trap the suspended clay particles. As the water sinks, the clay is caught in the upper two inches of the sand, forming a dense layer that filters even finer particles. We must pour the water gently so we do not disturb this sand bed."

While the filter chambers were being filled, Liang and the Taoists worked on the bypass channel. They harvested giant green bamboo from the northern grove, selecting canes that were ten centimeters in diameter. Using their axes, they split the long canes down the center, creating U-shaped half-pipes. Jun used a long-handled chisel to knock out the internal nodes, smoothing the inner surface of the bamboo to prevent friction and turbulence. They lashed the bamboo half-pipes together end-to-end using wet hemp twine, creating a fifty-meter conduit. They suspended the conduit on timber A-frames, routing it from the upper mountain stream, over the high red-plastered wall, and into the courtyard, positioning the outlet directly over the top of the first filtration chamber.

Jun installed a flat stone splash plate beneath the bamboo outlet to distribute the falling water, preventing it from digging a hole in the fine sand bed. 

"Open the flow," Jun ordered.

On the upper terrace, Liang slid back a wooden gate valve in the bamboo conduit. The turbid, brown mountain water rushed down the split bamboo channel, gurgling as it ran over the wall and poured onto the stone splash plate. It spread across the surface of the first filter chamber, a muddy pool that slowly began to sink into the grey sand.

For several minutes, there was silence. The dry sand and charcoal absorbed the water, the air escaping in tiny, hissing bubbles. Jun watched the bronze outlet tube at the bottom of the third chamber.

Then, a single drop of water appeared at the tip of the bronze tube. It hung for a second, clear and bright, before falling into the stone channel that led to the Dragon Spring basin. Another drop followed, then a steady, pencil-thin trickle of crystal-clear water.

Jun caught the water in a white celadon tea bowl. He held it up to the grey mountain light. There was no silt, no cloudiness, and no smell of damp earth. He handed the bowl to Master Chen. She took a sip, her eyes closing as she tasted the cool, clean water.

"It is pure," she said, a smile breaking through her tired face. "It has the taste of the mountain wind, but none of its clay. You have saved the spring, Master Jun."

But as the water began to fill the Dragon Spring basin with a soft, musical splash, a dry, metallic scratching sound rose from the stone flags near the corner of the courtyard.

It came from the drainage vault beneath the floor—an ancient stone channel that carried rainwater runoff out of the temple complex and into the western ravine. The heavy iron grate that covered the drain was old and rusted. Through the slots of the grate, a grey, moss-covered hand appeared, its fingers clawing at the rusted iron bars.

"The dead," Liang whispered, reaching for his hand axe.

A figure emerged slowly from the dark opening. It was a man who had been a local woodcutter, his skin dried to the color of wet slate, with thick patches of green star-moss growing across his neck and shoulders. He had crawled up the dark, wet drainage pipe, drawn by the sound of the running water. His movements were slow, stiff, and mechanical, his jaw hanging open as he caught the scent of the living.

Master Chen did not hesitate. She stepped forward, her posture relaxed, her weight centered. She drew her reinforced Wudang sword, the steel blade reflecting the grey light of the mist. With a single fluid, circular step, she deflected the zombie's reaching arms and drove the heavy, stiff tip of her sword directly through the temple of the skull. The steel entered with a sharp, clean crunch. The zombie collapsed instantly, its body going limp on the wet stone flags.

"The drains must be sealed," Jun said, his voice steady as he wiped a splash of dirty water from his face. "We will cut a heavy limestone plug to seal the runoff grate, leaving only small weep holes that the dead cannot pass. The water must flow, but the temple must remain closed."

Liang nodded, already reaching for his stone hammer. The work was far from over, but the spring was flowing, and the three hundred souls of Wudang had water to drink.

CHAPTER 6: THE HERBAL GARDEN


Below the massive stone foundations of the Purple Cloud Temple, the herbal terrace—*caoyuan*—clung to a steep, south-facing slope of Mount Wudang. Here, under the protective gaze of the red cliffs, the Taoist hermits cultivated the medicinal plants that were essential for the survival of the mountain community: wild ginseng, goldthread, yellow aconite, and the bitter mountain ginger. The air in the garden was a fragrant mixture of damp loam, resinous pine needles, and the sharp, medicinal scent of crushed leaves. The terrace was supported by an ancient, dry-stacked limestone retaining wall that had stood for generations.

However, the relentless autumn rainstorms had saturated the mountain soil, and the water, unable to escape through the choked weep holes of the masonry, had built up a massive hydrostatic pressure. Two days ago, a three-meter section of the stone wall had failed, collapsing down the slope in a heap of broken limestone and wet earth. The breach left a raw, muddy gap in the terrace, exposing the delicate medicinal beds to the wild forest below, where the slow-moving mountain dead wandered through the mist.

Jun stood at the edge of the breach, his boots sinking into the wet loess soil. In his hand, he held a heavy iron-headed adze, its blade coated in sticky mud. Beside him, Liang carried a framing square and a basket of oak pegs. Master Chen and several young disciples stood nearby, looking down at the ruined terrace with concern.

"We cannot simply stack the stones back up," Jun said, pointing to the water seeping from the raw clay face of the slope. "The earth behind the wall is saturated. If we build another rigid stone wall, the weight of the masonry combined with the hydrostatic pressure will only cause it to collapse again. A retaining wall must be able to breathe. It must allow the water to drain while holding back the soil. We will build a timber crib wall—a *mutong*—to repair the breach."

"Where do we get the timber, Master?" Liang asked.

"The old construction sheds below the Nanyan gate," Jun said. "There are dozens of seasoned spruce logs, three meters long and ten centimeters thick. We will notch the ends to build an interlocking rectangular cage. We will fill the cage with coarse river gravel at the back to act as a drainage layer, and pack the front with dry soil and gravel to anchor the structure."

Jun calculated the forces acting on the wall. "The height of the caved slope is approximately one point eight meters. The wet loess soil weighs about eighteen thousand Newtons per cubic meter. With an active earth pressure coefficient of zero point three three, the lateral thrust exerted by the soil against the breach is nearly nine thousand six hundred Newtons per meter of wall. If we build a timber crib with a width of one point two meters and fill it with dense river gravel, the resisting weight of the crib will be over forty-three thousand Newtons per meter. The gravity of the gravel-filled crib will easily overcome the sliding and overturning forces, locking the slope in place."

They worked through the morning. Jun and Liang prepared the spruce logs, cutting interlocking lap joints—*tongkou*—at each end using their broadaxes and hand-saws. The physical work was hard and rhythmic; the sound of the axes splitting the spruce fibers echoed off the red cliffs, and the clean, sweet scent of fresh wood sap rose with every blow. They stacked the logs in an interlocking grid, forming a sturdy timber cage over the breach. They lined the back of the crib with woven straw mats to prevent the fine soil from washing through, then filled the center with coarse gravel and dry earth, ramming it down with heavy wooden pestles until the timber frame was rock-solid and flush with the terrace.

But though the retaining wall was secure, the herbal terrace remained open to the forest. The wandering dead, moving with their slow, mechanical drag, could easily climb the loose slope below the wall and trample the precious herbs.

"We must build a protective fence around the entire exposed perimeter of the terrace," Jun said, looking at the fifty-meter boundary that bordered the pine forest. "A wooden fence would be too heavy and would rot in the mountain damp. We will build a split-bamboo screen fence—a *zhuliba*—using green bamboo poles and woven bamboo strips. It will be light, flexible, and strong enough to withstand the pressure of the dead."

They harvested fresh green bamboo from the lower groves, selecting poles eight centimeters in diameter for the vertical posts and horizontal rails. Using a heavy steel splitting knife—a *zhudao*—Jun split the poles down the center to create light, rigid slats.

"The key to a strong bamboo fence is not rigidity," Jun explained to Liang as they set the vertical posts. "A rigid structure will snap under sudden loads or the constant pressure of a crowd. Bamboo survives because it yields. The Taoists say, *yi rou ke gang*—use softness to overcome hardness. The fence must be flexible, absorbing the force of a strike and distributing the load across the entire structure."

They drove the vertical bamboo posts sixty centimeters deep into the rammed earth of the terrace, spacing them one point two meters apart. To connect the horizontal rails to the posts, Jun did not use iron nails or wire, which would rust and slip in the humid mountain air. Instead, they used wet split-bamboo strips, a traditional binding method that relied on the natural shrinkage of the wood.

Liang and the young disciples split thin ribbons from the outer layer of the fresh bamboo—the green skin, or *zhuqing*. This outer layer was rich in dense cellulose fibers, giving it a tensile strength that rivaled mild steel. They soaked the strips in water to make them completely pliable.

"Watch the grain, Liang," Jun said, demonstrating the technique. "We wrap the wet strip around the post and the rail in a double-cross lashing, pulling it as tight as our muscles allow before tucking the end under the wrap. While the bamboo is wet, the fibers are lubricated and can slide, allowing us to tie a tight knot. But as the wind dries the bamboo, the moisture content drops from fifty percent to about twelve percent. The cells collapse, and the strip shrinks by nearly eight percent in thickness and width."

Jun did some calculations in his head. "This shrinkage creates a massive tensile hoop stress within the dried wrap, reaching up to twenty megapascals. With a cross-sectional area of ten square millimeters, each strip exerts a clamping force of over eight hundred Newtons on the joint. Because the coefficient of friction between the green bamboo surfaces is high, this clamping force prevents any relative movement between the vertical posts and horizontal rails. The joint becomes a rigid node, yet the individual poles can still flex under bending loads."

They worked along the terrace, their fingers raw and red from pulling the wet bamboo strips tight. The physical sensation of the cold, wet green bamboo, the sharp edges of the split ribbons, and the sweet, grassy smell of the fresh wood filled the garden. By afternoon, they had woven a dense, grid-like fence, one point five meters high, along the entire edge of the terrace. The green bamboo glistened in the mist, looking like a living wall that grew naturally from the mountain soil.

As the sun began to set behind the western peaks, casting a cold, violet light over the forest, the watchmen on the terrace raised their hands.

Through the grey pines below, five figures emerged. They were the "valley dead," their skin dried to a pale leather, their hair matted with leaves, and their shoulders covered in a carpet of green star-moss. They moved with a slow, heavy drag, their bare feet scraping against the wet limestone boulders. They did not growl; there was only the dry, rhythmic sound of their breathing and the snap of dry twigs under their boots.

They approached the terrace, drawn by the scent of the living. When they reached the edge of the garden, they pressed their bodies against the new bamboo fence.

The fence groaned. Under the weight of the five zombies—a static force of nearly three thousand Newtons—the vertical bamboo posts bent outward, yielding to the pressure. Liang watched with his hand on his axe, his heart pounding.

But the woven joints did not slip. The dried bamboo wraps held fast, the tension distributing the load across all fifty vertical posts. The fence acted as a single, flexible diaphragm, absorbing the force without a single split or break. The zombies clawed at the green slats, their fingers slipping on the smooth, waxy surface of the bamboo skin, unable to find purchase.

"Now," Master Chen said.

Standing on the dry soil of the terrace behind the fence, she and the watchmen stepped forward. Through the narrow gaps in the bamboo grid, they thrust their reinforced Wudang swords. The heavy, stiff blades slid between the bamboo slats, driving into the temples of the trapped zombies with a clean, dry crunch.

One by one, the five figures went limp, their bodies leaning harmlessly against the flexible bamboo fence.

Master Chen sheathed her sword and bowed to Jun. "The fence yields, but it does not break, Master Jun. It is a true reflection of the Tao. The garden is safe, and our medicines are secure."

Jun returned the bow, his hands clasped before him. The mountain wind blew cold, but the timber crib and the bamboo fence stood firm, a testament to the strength of their hands and the ancient wisdom of their craft.

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE BAMBOO SHIELD


The damp mountain mist of Mount Wudang settled thick and heavy over the temple's eastern courtyards, transforming the green-glazed roof tiles of the Purple Cloud Temple into slick, dark surfaces that glistened in the grey morning light. The air at three thousand seven hundred meters was saturated with moisture, carrying the sharp, cold scent of wet stone, green pine needles, and the faint smell of decay rising from the lower valleys. In the open workshop of the temple, Master Chen stood beside a row of cracked wooden shields. These traditional shields, made of thick oak planks clamped with hand-forged iron bands, had been the primary defense of the temple watchmen. But the constant humidity of the mountain and the frequent rainstorms had saturated the timber, causing the wood to swell, warp, and split along the grain. The iron bands were rusted, their fixing screws loose in the soft, rotted wood.

"The wooden shields are too heavy," Master Chen said, lifting one of the warped oak boards. "They weigh nearly six kilograms each. The watchmen cannot hold them for more than an hour during a skirmish on the steep steps without their shoulders cramping. And in this dampness, the wood splits under the claws of the dead. We need a lighter, more durable shield that can deflect their strikes."

Jun picked up one of the cracked shields, inspecting the split seam. He ran his fingers along the warped wood grain. "The wood is rigid," he said. "When a zombie strikes with its full force, the energy is absorbed entirely by the local fibers, causing them to shear. We must build a flexible shield that distributes the impact across its entire structure. We will weave dome-shaped shields—*tengpai*—from split green bamboo. We will coat the woven mesh with a mixture of hot pine pitch and charcoal dust. This will create a light, water-resistant shield that yields under pressure without splitting. The secret of the bamboo shield is its flexibility. When a blow lands, the individual woven slats bend slightly, acting as a network of springs that distribute the force of the strike across the entire diameter of the shield."

Liang looked toward the northern slopes, where the bamboo groves grew dense. "Where will we find enough pitch, Master?"

"The old pine trees in the valley," Jun said. "We can tap the trunks to collect the sap. We will boil it in the large iron kettle to evaporate the water and concentrate the resin. Go, Liang! Set the kettle and gather the dry pine bark for the fire."

Within the hour, the workshop was filled with the pungent, sweet scent of boiling pine resin. Liang stirred the thick, black pitch in the iron kettle, adding fine charcoal dust to increase its density and heat resistance. The heat of the fire warmed the cold workspace, and the black, bubbling mixture began to thicken.

Meanwhile, Jun and the women of the temple prepared the bamboo. They selected fresh green culms of moso bamboo, ten centimeters in diameter. Using a heavy splitting knife, Jun split each culm down the center, then divided the halves into thin, flexible ribbons exactly three millimeters thick and twelve millimeters wide. He used a scraper to remove the soft, white inner pulp—the *zhuru*—leaving only the strong, fibrous outer green skin—the *zhuqing*.

"The outer skin has the highest tensile strength," Jun explained to the disciples as they began to weave. "It is rich in cellulose fibers that run longitudinally. We will weave the ribbons in a tight, circular herringbone pattern, starting from the center and spiraling outward to create a dome-shaped disk, sixty centimeters in diameter. The dome shape is structurally superior; it resolves a direct impact into compressive forces along the curved ribs of the bamboo, preventing the shield from flattening. By using a herringbone weave, we ensure that every ribbon is locked by its neighbors, so a single break in one slat will not cause the entire shield to unravel."

They wove the bamboo ribbons tightly, overlapping each course to create a dense, interlocking mesh. To reinforce the perimeter, Jun bent a thick, unsplit bamboo rod into a circle, lashing it to the edge of the woven dome using wet split-bamboo bindings. The process was slow and demanded great physical effort, as they had to pull the wet ribbons tight with their fingers, leaving their palms raw and red in the cold mountain air.

Jun showed the disciples how to lay out the warp and weft, maintaining a constant tension so the circular dome would remain symmetrical. "The strength of this shield lies in the tension of the weave," he said. "Each intersection must be locked. When a zombie claws at the shield, the friction between the bamboo ribbons prevents them from sliding, converting the local thrust into a tension that spreads through the entire structure. The wood does not split because it is not locked in a single rigid plane; it yields, distributing the load."

Once the shields were woven, Jun used a wide brush made of hemp fibers to paint the hot, liquid pine pitch over the bamboo surfaces. The black pitch steamed as it met the cold green wood, penetrating deep into the joints and crevices of the weave.

"The pitch serves two purposes," Jun said, his hands black with the sticky resin. "First, it seals the wood, preventing the mountain damp from softening the bamboo fibers. Second, as the pitch cools, it contracts, pulling the woven ribbons tighter against one another. It locks the herringbone pattern in place, turning the flexible mesh into a single, cohesive diaphragm. The resulting shield is both light and incredibly tough, capable of absorbing the impact of a heavy blow without splintering."

They wove forty shields over the next two days, the workshop humming with the sound of knives splitting bamboo and the crackle of the boiling pitch fire. The smell of pine resin and wet grass hung thick in the air, a clean, natural scent that helped mask the stale odor of decay from the lower valleys.

To make the shields easy to carry, they mounted handles on the inner side of the dome. Liang braided thick ropes from three-strand hemp, wedging them through the weave and tying them to the outer reinforcement ring. He added a padded canvas sleeve to protect the watchman's forearm from friction.

When the pitch had dried to a hard, glossy black finish, Jun handed one of the shields to Master Chen. The shield was remarkably light, weighing only one point eight kilograms, less than a third of the weight of the old oak boards.

Master Chen took the shield, fitting her arm through the canvas sleeve and gripping the rope handle. She stepped into the courtyard, where Liang stood ready with a heavy wooden quarterstaff.

"Strike it," Chen commanded.

Liang swung the staff with both hands, bringing it down in a wide arc against the face of the black shield.
*THWACK.*

The impact was loud, but the shield did not crack. The curved bamboo dome flexed slightly under the blow, absorbing the kinetic energy and distributing it across the circular frame, before springing back to its original shape. Liang's staff bounced off the slick, pitched surface, leaving only a faint grey mark.

"It yields, but it does not break," Master Chen said, her eyes bright with satisfaction. "And it is so light that the watchmen can carry it all day on the ridge. We will weave forty of these shields immediately."

Jun nodded, his hands already reaching for the next green bamboo culm. The work was slow, but every woven ribbon was another shield for the defenders of the mountain.


---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE HALL OF TAI CHI


The Hall of Tai Chi—*Taiji Dian*—stood at the very center of the temple complex, its massive timber structure rising above the surrounding courtyards like a silent mountain of stone and cedar. Inside the hall, the air was dim and cold, smelling of ancient sandalwood, damp plaster, and the faint, sweet scent of wild herbs drying in the side galleries. On the high ceiling, a large, black-and-white symbol of the yin-yang looked down upon the empty granite floor, representing the eternal balance of forces and the harmony of opposites. The green stone columns, thirty centimeters in diameter, rose to the high roof rafters, supporting the heavy green-glazed tiles of the roof structure.

But the peaceful silence of the sanctuary was broken during the night. A group of four crawling zombies, having climbed the wet limestone runoff pipe that drained the rear courtyard, had managed to bypass the outer gates and emerged in the dark center of the hall, their dry boots scratching against the cold flagstones. They moved with a slow, mechanical drag, their skin dried to a pale, slate-grey leather, and their shoulders covered in patches of green star-moss. Their fingernails were worn down to the bone from their long crawl up the stone masonry. The sound of their movements was a dry, scraping rasp, like dry leaves blowing across the stone floor.

"We have them inside!" a Taoist watchman screamed, his voice echoing under the high rafters, filled with panic.

Jun and Liang ran to the hall, carrying their axes and a lantern. The chamber was pitch-black, the beam of the lantern cutting through the dust motes and illuminating the four grey figures shuffling between the massive columns.

"We must build a barricade to isolate this section of the hall," Jun said, his voice steady as he assessed the situation. "We cannot let them reach the inner chambers where the children and elders are sleeping. We will use the heavy oak chests—*baoxiang*—that hold the temple's ceremonial robes. We will wedge them horizontally across the doorway, locking them with diagonal timber braces against the central columns."

"Master, those chests are old," Liang said, looking at the carved panels of the massive chests that lined the side walls. "They are part of the temple's history, carved by master carpenters of the Ming Dynasty."

"The living are older," Jun replied, grabbing the corner of the nearest chest. "And their history is not finished yet. Liang, help me clear the robes. We must keep them clean."

Liang and the young disciples quickly opened the chests, lifting out the ceremonial silk robes. The fabrics were dyed in deep indigo, green, and black, embroidered with gold and silver threads representing stars, dragons, and Daoist trigrams. They piled the silks carefully on the altar tables, out of reach of the damp floor and the dust.

Once cleared, they began the heavy work of moving the chests. Together with the Taoist watchmen, they shoved the heavy oak chests across the granite floor. The friction of the wood against the smooth granite tiles created a loud, scraping screech that echoed through the high timber rafters. Each chest was one and a half meters long, one meter high, and made of solid, four-centimeter-thick oak planks. Empty, they still weighed over eighty kilograms, and when loaded with stone blocks for ballast, they exceeded one hundred and fifty kilograms. They lined three of the chests end-to-end across the inner doorway, creating a solid oak barrier that stood one meter high.

To ensure the barrier could not be pushed back by the weight of the dead, Jun constructed a diagonal bracing system. He selected two thick spruce poles, twelve centimeters in diameter, from the construction stack in the gallery.

He chiseled shallow notches—birdsmouth joints—into the rear corners of the oak chests and the bases of the massive green stone pillars that supported the roof. He wedged the spruce poles into the notches, creating a diagonal truss at a forty-five-degree angle.

"The diagonal braces resolve the horizontal force of the dead into a compressive force along the grain of the spruce poles," Jun explained to Liang as he hammered the wedges home. "The green stone pillars can easily bear this load without shifting. The coefficient of friction between the oak chests and the granite tiles is about zero point four; with a mass of four hundred and fifty kilograms, it would require a horizontal force of nearly two thousand Newtons to slide the barrier. With the spruce braces installed, that capacity is increased tenfold. The weight of the chests combined with the structural strength of the diagonal struts locks the barrier in place, ensuring that even a large crowd of the dead cannot push it open."

Jun used his mallet to drive tapered oak wedges between the bottom of the spruce poles and the granite floor joints.
*Thud. Thud. Thud.*
With each blow, the wedge sank deeper, forcing the diagonal brace upward and clamping the oak chests tightly against the doorframe. The wood creaked under the tension, its fibers compressing as they took the load.

"Notice the angle, Liang," Jun said, his breath rising in white plumes. "At forty-five degrees, the horizontal thrust $H$ and the vertical downward force $V$ are equal. The vertical force increases the normal force acting on the chests, which in turn increases the static friction between the wood and the stone floor. The calculation is simple: $f_s = \mu_s (W + V)$. By increasing $V$, we make it impossible for the chests to slide. The joinery works with physics to double our safety."

Jun continued to hammer the wedges, the solid blows echoing off the high stone walls. The spruce timbers creaked, taking the load. Jun checked the alignment, ensuring the birdsmouth joints were seated perfectly. "If there is any play in the joints," he warned Liang, "the force will not be transferred instantly. The chests will shift, the momentum will build, and the impact will shear the timber. A tight joint is a safe joint."

The four zombies, drawn by the light of the lantern, shuffled toward the barrier, their dry, leathery limbs scraping against the oak panels. They pressed their mummified bodies against the wood, their weight pushing the chests, but the barrier did not budge a single millimeter. The spruce poles remained rigid, transferring the horizontal thrust directly into the stone pillars. Not a single joint creaked, and the door leaves remained perfectly straight.

From behind the safety of the oak chests, Master Chen and the watchmen stepped forward. Armed with their reinforced Wudang swords, they thrust downward through the narrow gaps between the chests. The heavy, stiff blades slid through the openings, driving into the temples of the trapped zombies with a clean, dry crunch.

One by one, the four figures went limp, their bodies leaning harmlessly against the oak panels.

Inside the hall, Jun stood back, wiping the sweat from his forehead. He patted the solid oak chest, which was cool and stable under his hand. He looked at the diagonal spruce braces, noting that they had not shifted or split.

"The barrier has held," Jun said, looking up at the yin-yang symbol on the ceiling. "The woodwork has turned the temple's own structure into our shield. The hall is secure. The load is safely carried by the stone column, and the joinery has held without a single nail."

"The temple is safe," Master Chen said, sheathing her sword. "But the valley below is still filled with the dead. We must prepare for the final descent. The main gates are under pressure, and the western path is threatened."

Jun nodded, already looking at his tools. "We will make more braces, and we will secure the side entrances before the night returns. The wood and the stone are our best allies."


---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE NANYAN DESCENT


A massive horde of three thousand infected, having climbed the western valley paths through the pine forests of the lower slopes, had reached the ruins of the Nanyan Temple. The lower gates of the ravine had caved under the pressure, and the narrow, winding cliffside trails were now filled with a rising tide of grey, moss-covered bodies. The survivors had retreated to the Purple Cloud Temple, but the cantilevered timber bridge that spanned the deep chasm was too wide to hold with swords or bows.

"We must cut the bridge," Master Chen said, her face pale as she stood on the edge of the terrace, looking down at the climbing horde. "If they cross the chasm, the Purple Cloud Temple is lost. There are too many of them to fight in the open. The bridge is the only path that connects the western ridge to our sanctuary. If we destroy it, we isolate the temple entirely. It is a harsh choice, but a necessary one to preserve the three hundred souls within these walls."

"Who will cut the anchor?" Liang asked, looking at the bridge that hung over the six-hundred-meter drop. "The dead are already on the western steps. The bridge is vibrating under their feet, and the spruce planks are beginning to creak under the shifting load."

"I will go," Jun said, his voice calm.

Jun climbed down the limestone cliff face, carrying his framing chisel and sledgehammer. The wind was violent, howling through the deep chasm and threatening to tear him from the rock face. Above him, the pine planks of the bridge shuddered and groaned under the weight of the climbing dead. The space beneath the bridge was tight and dark, smelling of damp limestone, ancient moss, and the cold draft of the chasm. Jun's fingers were numb, turning red and stiff as he clung to the rock, the freezing wind whipping his hair and tugging at his padded coat. He had to wedge his body into a narrow rock pocket directly beneath the primary support gantry to avoid falling.

The cantilevered bridge was supported by three massive spruce logs, forty centimeters in diameter, set deep into the limestone rock face and locked in place by a single, wedge-shaped oak key.

Jun wedged himself into the pocket. He could hear the heavy, dragging footsteps of the dead directly above his head, and a shower of dry moss, mortar dust, and small pebbles fell onto his shoulders. He looked up, his eyes tracing the joints of the spruce beams. The spruce logs were under a massive bending moment, their upper fibers in tension and their lower fibers in compression. The wedge-shaped oak key was the critical locking member, resisting the tension that pulled the beams out of their rock sockets.

He positioned his heavy steel chisel against the joint of the oak key, drew back the sledgehammer, and struck.
*CLANG.*
A sharp, metallic ring echoed through the gorge, followed by the smell of dry spruce sap as the hammer met the wood. Jun swung again, his shoulders tensing as he delivered blow after blow.
*CLANG. CLANG.*

The oak key was hard and seasoned, resisting the steel blade. But Jun did not stop. His cuts were precise and rhythmic, his muscles burning from the exertion in the thin mountain air. He could feel the vibrations of the climbing dead running down through the timber gantry, a low, rhythmic shudder that rattled his bones.

"The key is under tension," Jun shouted to Liang, who was watching from the terrace above. "The weight of the bridge is pulling the spruce beams out of the rock socket, and the oak key is resisting this tension. By splitting the key, we remove the resistance, and the gravity of the bridge will pull the beams out, collapsing the structure. The force is immense; the oak key is compressed at over ten megapascals. The wood must split along the grain if we hit it with enough velocity. Liang, hold the safety line taut! If the gantry drops, the rock face will slide!"

Jun took a deep breath, his hands shaking from the cold and the vibration. He raised the sledgehammer, aligning his swing. The wind howled through the cleft, blowing granite dust and dried leaves into his face. He struck the chisel with a massive, two-handed blow, focusing all his weight and momentum into the strike.
*CLANG.*
Sparks flew from the steel head, and a deep split opened down the center of the oak key. The seasoned wood groaned, its fibers tearing apart under the immense tension of the cantilever.

"Jun! The bridge is shifting!" Master Chen called from the far terrace. A pine block above Jun's head slid downward, its joint splitting open. The lead zombies had reached the center of the span, their mummified weight adding to the bending moment on the spruce beams. Jun could see the spruce wood fibers beginning to buckle at the bottom of the logs, while the upper fibers sheared. He knew he had only seconds before the entire structure collapsed. He struck the chisel one last time, the impact vibrating through his entire skeleton.

With a roaring, grinding crash, the cantilevered gantry collapsed. The twenty-meter section of the timber bridge fell into the six-hundred-meter chasm, carrying the climbing zombies down into the sea of clouds below. The heavy spruce beams slipped from their stone sockets, tumbling silently into the mist before striking the rocks far below. The sound of the collapse was a massive, echoing rumble that shook the cliff face, followed by the silence of the empty air.

Jun was trapped on the lower ledge of the cliff, the gap too wide to jump. He clung to the cold limestone rock face, his fingers dug into a narrow seam. The chasm was a wide, empty space of swirling mist, completely separating the temple from the western ridge. His boots scraped the loose limestone, looking for purchase.

Master Chen ran to the edge of the terrace. In her hands, she held a long hemp rope, its end tied tightly around the hilt of her steel Jian. She launched the sword across the chasm like a harpoon.

"Jun! Catch the sword!" she shouted.

The sword flew through the dust, its steel blade reflecting the grey light. Jun reached out, his hand locking around the leather-wrapped hilt. He wrapped the hemp rope around his forearm, securing his grip.

"Pull!" Chen commanded.

Liang and the watchmen heaved the rope, and Jun kicked off from the cliff face, swinging out over the deep chasm. The wind caught him, turning him in the air, but the steel Jian held firm, and they hauled him over the granite balustrade to safety.

The temple was isolated. Jun stood on the terrace, his hands shaking, but the chasm was clean and empty before them. The dead could not cross. Jun looked back down the cliff, watching the last of the dust settle in the clouds.

Liang sat on the terrace edge, his heart beating in his throat as he watched the dust clear. The survivors from Nanyan were silent, looking down into the massive chasm. Master Chen walked up to Jun and handed him a clean linen cloth to wipe the sweat and grime from his forehead. "We have cut the last path," she said, her voice steady. "The temple is safe. The chasm is our wall, and the peaks are our sanctuary. The dead cannot climb the sheer rock faces, and they cannot bridge the gap. We have won this night."

"The bridge is gone," Jun said, his voice raspy. "The chasm is our wall now."

"Thank you, Master Jun," Master Chen said, bowing. "The sanctuary stands."

CHAPTER 10: THE HIGH HERMITAGE


The morning sun rose slowly over a silent Tianzhu Peak, its cold, golden light illuminating the Golden Pavilion and the deep chasm that now separated it from the valley below. The air was calm, carrying only the clean scent of frozen pine and the distant, faint sound of the mountain stream flowing through the deep ravines. The white mist slowly cleared, exposing the green valleys of Hubei Province far below, peaceful and isolated under the morning sky.

The paths were gone. The temple was a fortress in the sky, its garden secure, its survivors warm in the inner courtyards.

Jun sat on the stone steps of the Purple Cloud Temple, his hands resting on his wooden toolbox. The toolbox was scarred and worn, its panels showing the marks of Yunnan pine, Gansu loess, Shaanxi clay, Sichuan cedar, Henan ash, and Hubei spruce, but the steel tools inside were clean and sharp. He applied a few drops of camellia oil to the oilstone, then ran the bevel of his broadaxe across the abrasive surface in slow, circular motions. The scraping sound of the steel was steady and peaceful in the morning air.

Beside him, Liang was cleaning his chisel, his fingers moving with quiet precision. He used a flat steel file to clean the rust from the chisel's collar, then rubbed the bevel on a fine whetstone.

"We have built a good gate on the mountain, Master Jun," Liang said, looking toward the distant peaks.

"A gate is only as good as the steel that holds the pass," Jun replied, his voice quiet as he tested the axe edge with his thumb. The steel was cold and sharp. "And the temple is secure. They do not need builders anymore. Our work here is finished. The chasm will keep the dead in the valley, and the survivors are safe."

"We have used the mountain's own strength to protect it," Liang said, running his finger along the flat side of his chisel. "The stone, the bamboo, and the wood. They are all here, and they have all held. But what about the other places?"

"The other places will have to build their own walls," Jun said. "But if they have the tools and the timber, we can teach them how. We have the knowledge, and we have the steel."

Jun looked at Liang, noting the alignment of his chisel edge. "Liang, do you understand the forces that held the cantilever bridge? The gantry acted as a lever. The deflection of a cantilever beam under a point load at the free end is $\delta = rac{PL^3}{3EI}$. Notice that the length of the span $L$ is cubed. If the bridge had been twice as long, the deflection would have been eight times greater, and the tension on the oak key would have exceeded its shear strength. By keeping the span short and the beams thick, the master builders of old ensured the structure could bear the load. When we design a wall, we must always balance the span against the material's elastic modulus."

Liang nodded, tracing the formula on his slate board. "The geometry determines the limit. If we exceed the limit, the material fails, no matter how strong the wood is."

"Exactly," Jun said. "A builder must work with the material, not against it."

Jun took a clean piece of oiled cloth, wrapping each of his chisels and saws carefully before placing them back into the custom compartments of the pine toolbox. He checked the brass hinges of the box, ensuring they were free of grit and lime dust. He wiped down the bronze marking gauge and the carpenter's square, ensuring they were dry to prevent rust in the mountain mist.

Master Chen walked over, carrying a wooden tray with hot tea and a radio receiver. The steam rose from the cups, smelling of ginger and clean water. The cups were made of thin, celadon-glazed porcelain, their rims decorated with a faint crackle pattern that reflected the morning light.

"Drink," Chen said, handing a cup to Jun and another to Liang. "The road is cold, and the journey is long."

Jun took the cup, the warmth of the clay heating his hands. He drank slowly, the hot ginger tea restoring his energy.

Chen set the radio receiver on the stone step. It was a small transistor radio, its antenna extended. She turned the dial, the speaker emitting a loud hiss of static before a faint, cracked voice broke through.

"...calling any survivors... this is Hong Kong... Lion Rock..." the voice said, fading in and out. "The keepers of the road tunnels say they are blockading the main highway to Kowloon using concrete and bamboo barriers, but they need builders to reinforce the timber portals. The community has rallied together, constructing massive bamboo scaffolding grids across the highway to trap the dead. People from the city have brought their own timber, concrete sacks, and tools, working side-by-side to build a secondary wall to defend Kowloon from the urban horde. If any builders can hear this... we need your help to secure the main portals before the tide reaches the city. The neighborhood associations are coordinating the labor, and the residents are sharing their food and resources to keep the construction crews going. We are holding the line, but we need engineers..."

The signal faded into static. Chen turned the dial, but there was only the empty hum of the airwaves.

The morning mist began to drift away, revealing the green valleys of Hubei Province far below, peaceful and isolated under the blue sky. Jun stood up, looking at the distant horizon where the hills folded into the plains. He felt the cold air in his chest, a clean, sharp sensation that washed away the fatigue of the long night. The red walls of the temple stood solid, a testament to the strength of their hands and the ancient joinery of their craft. Liang gathered the saws and the oil stones, packing them carefully into the side compartments of the pine toolbox. "The tools are clean, Master," he said. "And the path is ready." Jun picked up the toolbox, the heavy wood cold against his shoulder. He looked at Master Chen and bowed, then turned toward the southern steps. The journey ahead was long, but as long as there were walls to build and people to defend, the road would have a purpose.

Jun stood up, shaking the mist from his padded coat. He picked up his broadaxe, sliding the handle into the leather loop of his toolbox. He looked toward the south-east, where the distant sea lay beyond the mountains.

"The sea is wide, Liang," Jun said, his voice steady. "But the road is longer. Pack the tools. We head to Hong Kong."

Liang stood up and bowed, his hands clasped before him. "Yes, Master. I will gather the saws and the oil stones. The toolbox is ready."

Chen bowed deeply. "Thank you, builders. The mountain will remember."

Jun returned the bow, then lifted his heavy toolbox onto his shoulder. With Liang following, he walked through the temple's gate, heading down the steep trail, their boots leaving prints in the damp earth as they began their long journey toward the sea.

STORY 20: THE TUNNEL BLOCKADE
Setting: Lion Rock Tunnel, Hong Kong

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE TUNNEL PORTAL


The concrete vault of the Lion Rock Tunnel was dark, silent, and smelling of cold diesel exhaust, damp rock, and old water leaks. Running for one point four kilometers through the solid granite core of the Lion Rock ridge, the twin tunnels were the primary highway artery linking the crowded, high-rise urban districts of Kowloon with the residential valley of Sha Tin in the New Territories. The Sha Tin portal stood like a massive concrete snout set into the steep, jungle-covered slope, its circular entrance flanked by heavy retaining walls of grey granite blocks and overgrown with wild ivy, ferns, and banana trees.

Jun stood at the threshold of the southbound portal, his broadaxe resting against his boot, his hands grease-slicked from their long journey. Beside him, Liang was cleaning a hand-cranked breast drill, the metal filings falling into the dry dirt of the road shoulder. They had traveled south-east from the Hubei mountains, crossing the southern provinces by train and foot, and taking a fishing junk from Shenzhen to reach the New Territories of Hong Kong. Along the way, they had seen how the urban density of the territory had turned the crisis into a wall of numbers; Kowloon and Hong Kong Island were overrun, their millions of dead wandering the narrow streets and concrete canyons, while a small band of local workers, transit employees, and watchmen held the transport tunnels to protect the northern valleys.

"The wind is blowing from the south, Master Jun," Liang said, looking into the dark, yawning mouth of the tunnel. "It carries the smell of the city. It's like a cold cellar, but filled with the scent of old gasoline and dust."

"A cellar with only one door," Jun said, his eyes scanning the concrete arch. "We must check the ceiling hangers of the ventilation ducts. The vibration of the massive fans over decades has cracked the concrete anchors in the roof. If the overhead ducts drop, they will block the evacuation path and crush the scaffolding barrier we are building below. We must analyze the shear stresses on the hanger bolts before we begin lashing."

Jun stepped under the shadow of the concrete portal. The arch was built of reinforced concrete, cast in-situ against the blasted granite of the ridge. He looked up at the ceiling, where the massive circular ventilation housings hung like steel barrels, three meters in diameter. Each housing was suspended by four threaded steel hanger rods, twenty-four millimeters in diameter, drilled into the overhead rock. Jun took a small brass hammer from his pocket and tapped the base of the nearest hanger rod.
*Tink.*
The sound was high and clear, indicating a solid connection. He moved to the second rod and tapped it.
*Thud.*
"Listen to that, Liang," Jun said, pointing his finger at the concrete collar where the rod met the roof. "A dull sound. The anchor has slipped inside its expansion shell. The vibration of the fan, combined with the dampness of the seepage water, has caused chemical spalling in the concrete around the sleeve. If we assume the fan housing weighs three metric tons, each of the four rods must support a static load of seven point five kilonewtons. But when the fan starts, the dynamic load increases by thirty percent due to torque. With one rod slipping, the remaining three must absorb ten kilonewtons each, increasing the shear stress on the concrete anchors beyond their safety margin."

"We must install secondary safety hangers, then," Liang said, adjusting his spectacles. "We can drill new sockets three hundred millimeters away from the damaged zone, using expansion bolts, and link them with steel cable slings."

"Yes," Jun agreed. "We will use twenty-millimeter steel wire rope, looped around the main housing and clamped with dual U-bolts. But first, we must coordinate with the people at the toll plaza. We need electricity for the heavy rotary hammer, or we must drill the rock by hand using star-drills and sledges."

Behind them, the toll plaza of the Lion Rock Tunnel had been transformed into a bustling refugee sanctuary. Hundreds of local citizens—taxi drivers in their short-sleeved shirts, minibus operators, high-school students, and entire families—had gathered to defend the pass. A row of blue and green canvas tents lined the concrete lanes, and in the center, several large metal woks were set up on portable gas burners. Volunteer grandmas, their hair tied back in nets, stirred giant pots of hot noodle soup and ginger tea, distributing bowls to the watchmen and workers. The air was filled with the clatter of metal ladles, the steam of boiling broth, and the soft, reassuring murmur of Cantonese folk songs being sung by families huddled around the campfires. It was an uplifting scene of mutual aid; everyone contributed what they could, sharing blankets, medicine, and tools.

A group of high-school volunteers, wearing their school uniforms with orange safety vests, were busy stacking plastic crates of bottled water and canned fish that had been brought up from the Sha Tin shops. An elderly man, retired from the transit department, sat on a plastic stool, using a grindstone to sharpen kitchen cleavers and fire axes for the tunnel guards. There was no panic here; instead, the community had organized itself into a tight, efficient collective, determined to keep the horde from crossing the ridge.

"Oi! Builders!" a voice called from the scaffolding balcony above the portal.

Officer Chan, a local watchman in a green police jacket over a heavy high-visibility vest, stood on the bamboo walkway. He held a long riot shield of clear polycarbonate, its surface scarred by deep scratches, and a heavy iron-pointed crowbar.

"I am Chan," he said, descending the steel ladder. "The Wudang watchmen radioed that you were coming. Welcome. The bamboo barrier we built inside the tunnel is holding, but the pressure of the Kowloon crowd is building by the hour. The scouts say they have found a way through the upper ventilation shafts on the ridge. We need your engineering eyes to help us reinforce the structure before the tide pushes through."

Jun nodded, picking up his toolbox. "Show us the barrier, Officer Chan. Let's see what the community has built."

They walked into the northbound tunnel, their flashlights casting long, dancing beams against the damp walls. The air grew colder, the smell of diesel exhaust giving way to the dry, musty odor of the dead. Fifty meters inside, the tunnel was completely blocked by a towering structure.

"It is a dapang," Officer Chan explained, his flashlight beam scanning the grid. "The local scaffolding construction union built it. They used the materials from a high-rise construction site in Sha Tin. It is light, flexible, and can be erected in hours, but we are worried it cannot withstand the constant, unyielding weight of the horde."

Jun examined the structure. The scaffolding was ten meters high, spanning the entire width of the two-lane tunnel. It was built of vertical moso bamboo poles, ten centimeters in diameter, crossed by horizontal ledger poles and reinforced with diagonal bracing. The joints were bound not with iron bolts, but with black nylon strips, wrapped six times and tied with a traditional clove hitch. Behind the grid, the dark shapes of the infected could be seen, their dry, leathery faces pressed against the gaps, their hands reaching through the bamboo lattices, their nails scratching against the green bark.

"The structure is well-designed," Jun said, his voice echoing in the concrete vault. "Bamboo has an ultimate tensile strength of one hundred and eighty megapascals along the fiber, which is comparable to structural steel. But its modulus of elasticity is only twenty gigapascals, which means it will deflect significantly under load. The nylon lashings are the weak point; they are elastic and will stretch under the continuous static pressure of a packed crowd. We must reinforce the base and install timber shoring to transfer the horizontal thrust directly into the roadbed."

"We will help," Officer Chan said, nodding toward the tunnel mouth. "The community has plenty of hands. Tell us what you need, Master Jun, and we will build it together. We have more bamboo poles in the depot, and we can strip utility poles for heavy timber if needed."

Jun looked at Liang and smiled. "Then let us begin. We will calculate the load capacity and make this bamboo gate as strong as a city wall."

CHAPTER 2: THE SCAFFOLDING WALL


The primary barrier inside the Lion Rock Tunnel was not a gate of iron or stone, but a massive wall of traditional Hong Kong bamboo scaffolding—*dapang*—set fifty meters inside the Sha Tin mouth. Built of six hundred green moso bamboo poles, ten meters long and ten centimeters thick, the scaffolding was an interlocking grid of vertical posts and horizontal rails, lashed together with thin, flexible strips of black nylon. The wall was three layers deep, with diagonal braces—*paoliang*—anchored into the concrete drainage gutters of the tunnel floor.

But the nylon lashings were stretching under the constant pressure. Under the weight of the thousands of zombies packed into the dark tunnel behind the barrier, the bamboo poles were creaking and bowing outward, the nylon strips showing white stress lines where they had been pulled tight.

"The bamboo is too dry," Jun said, running his chisel along the smooth green bark of a brace. "And the nylon slips under constant, dead pressure. We must reinforce the grid using spruce timber struts—*tuchen*—and lock the joints with wooden wedges and iron dog-irons driven into the concrete walls of the tunnel."

"Master, we don't have enough pine logs for the struts," Liang said, looking around the dark tunnel.

"We use the utility poles from the highway shoulder," Jun said. "They are seasoned fir, twenty centimeters thick. Go, Liang! Ask the community at the plaza for help. We need a hauling crew."

Within minutes, Liang returned with a crew of twenty local volunteers. Among them were minibus drivers in their blue uniforms, construction workers in orange helmets, and young university students. Among the volunteers was a taxi driver named Ah Sing, who had driven routes through this tunnel for over thirty years. "I know every pothole in this road, Master Jun," Ah Sing said with a grin. "And I know the people who live at the ends of it. We won't let this tunnel fall. In the old days, I would carry families from Kowloon to Sha Tin. Now, we carry the wall that protects them."

Beside him was Ying, a young civil engineering student from the University of Hong Kong who had been evacuated from her dormitory. She looked at the sagging bamboo frame with a mixture of academic interest and practical resolve. "If we assume the mass of the crowd behind the barrier is roughly five hundred kilograms per square meter, the total horizontal thrust on this wall is close to two hundred kilonewtons," Ying calculated, writing figures in a small notebook. "Our nylon ties have an ultimate tensile strength of only three kilonewtons each. Even with six wraps per joint, the safety factor is less than one point two under dynamic surges. The material is reaching its yielding point. The physical friction between the smooth green bark of the bamboo and the synthetic nylon is insufficient under this load. As the nylon warms from the friction of the micro-movements, it elongates by up to ten percent, allowing the joints to slip."

Ying also pointed out that the bamboo poles had been treated by the scaffolding union. "They boiled the bamboo in a saline solution before erecting the frame," she explained. "This is a traditional Cantonese technique. The salt water extracts the soluble sugars and starches from the wood fibers, which prevents the local bamboo beetle—*dinoderus minutus*—from boring into the core and weakening the structural integrity of the walls. It also leaves a microscopic salt deposit within the cellulose matrix, which absorbs moisture from the air, keeping the bamboo slightly hydrated and preventing it from becoming brittle and splitting under the dry, windy conditions of the tunnel."

"Exactly," Jun said, looking at her with approval. "The moso bamboo itself has excellent flexural strength—its hollow cylindrical shape provides a high second moment of area relative to its weight, which prevents local buckling. But a structure is only as strong as its connections. We must bypass the nylon ties by installing timber struts that act as direct compression members, transferring the load directly into the rock walls of the tunnel."

They worked in a coordinated line, shouting out timing cues in Cantonese—"Yat, yi, sam, pull!"—as they dragged the heavy utility poles into the dark tunnel. The creosote-treated fir poles were heavy and slick, their smell mixing with the cold dampness of the tunnel. To make the hauling easier, Ah Sing suggested pouring soapy wash-water from the communal kitchens onto the asphalt roadbed, creating a low-friction slide. The logs glided smoothly over the soapy path, the volunteers laughing and singing Cantonese work songs to keep their rhythm steady. Everyone contributed, from the strongest laborer to the teenagers who guided the cables.

Jun and Liang prepared the timber. Jun used his broadaxe to carve diagonal notches into the concrete tunnel walls, three meters back from the barrier. He worked with rapid, precise blows, the steel blade cutting through the plaster and chipping the aggregate stone, sending up sparks and a dry smell of masonry dust. Jun carved a precise birdsmouth seat on the ends of the fir utility poles. "We must cut this seat with a flat bearing surface perpendicular to the grain of the wood," Jun showed Liang, using his adze to shave the seat flat. "Fir has a compressive strength parallel to the grain of forty megapascals, but perpendicular to the grain, it is only six megapascals. If we don't align the seat perfectly with the force vector of the diagonal strut, the wood fibers will crush and allow the strut to slip inside the notch, reducing the structural efficiency of our bracing."

To ensure the notches would not shear under the immense thrust, Jun calculated the angle of the cut. "The utility poles must meet the concrete wall at an angle of forty-five degrees," he explained to Liang. "This ensures that the horizontal thrust from the bamboo wall is resolved into equal horizontal and vertical force components. The vertical component is absorbed by the roadbed, while the horizontal component is resisted by the shear strength of the concrete notch. By cutting the notch five centimeters deep into the structural concrete lining, we create a bearing area of one hundred square centimeters. The shear strength of the concrete is three megapascals, giving us a safety factor of more than two."

Liang nodded, using a chalk line to mark the exact angle on the concrete wall. "I will prepare the timber ends, Master. We must cut a matching birdsmouth joint on the utility poles so they sit flat against the concrete bearing surfaces."

They set the first fir strut, its bottom end wedged into the concrete notch, its top end resting against the central bamboo cross-beam. Jun positioned the heavy iron dog-irons, linking the two structures together.

"Wedges, Liang!" Jun called out.

The volunteers passed the seasoned oak wedges down the human chain, their hands moving in a rapid, coordinated flow. Liang placed the wedges into the notches at the base of the fir struts, and two construction workers, swinging heavy steel sledges, drove them home.
*Thud. Thud. Thud.*
With each blow, the wedges forced the fir struts forward, tightening the frame. The bowing bamboo wall began to straighten, the lateral thrust of the zombie crowd transferred directly through the diagonal timbers into the solid granite bedrock of the mountain. The creaking of the bamboo subsided, replaced by the solid, rigid silence of the reinforced frame. The volunteers cheered, wiping the sweat from their faces and passing around cups of hot ginger tea.

An elderly woman, Auntie Wong, who lived in the public housing estates near the Sha Tin entrance, walked through the line carrying a basket of warm pineapple buns. "Eat, eat, young men," she said, her voice warm and maternal. "You are doing the work of ancestors. The city below is dark, but here we have bread and fire."

Jun took a bun, the sweet, crunchy sugar crust crumbling in his calloused fingers. "Thank you, Auntie Wong," he said, bowing his head. "The warmth of your kitchen is the strongest brace we have."

"As long as the concrete notches do not shear," Jun said to Chan, his voice quiet. "But we must monitor the ceiling. The rock above is shifting."

Officer Chan shone his flashlight beam upward. "The mountain is old, Master Jun. But the community is young, and we will hold it."

CHAPTER 3: THE CONCRETE SHORING


The scaffolding wall was reinforced, but the pressure inside the tunnel was increasing as the Kowloon horde was pushed forward by the crowds behind them. The constant, heavy thumping of mummified bodies against the barrier vibrated through the structure, and the concrete ceiling lining above the wall was beginning to crack.

"The concrete is buckling," Officer Chan said, pointing the beam of his flashlight toward the roof vault. "The weight of the earth above and the constant vibration has cracked the old plaster lining, and the steel rebar is showing. If the roof collapses, it will crush the scaffolding wall and block our only path."

Jun walked under the cracked section, his face grave. He shone his light on the longitudinal cracks that ran for five meters along the crown of the arch. "This is a structural shear failure," he said, using his chisel to pry away a loose flake of concrete. "The tunnel was blasted through granite, but this section has a faulted seam of highly weathered mudstone above it. The concrete lining here is only thirty centimeters thick, and it was designed to resist a radial load of fifty kilopascals. The vibration of the crowd, combined with the blockages in the mountain drainage channels, has increased the hydrostatic pressure behind the lining. We must build a vertical timber shoring system—*tuchen*—using heavy spruce logs and hydraulic jacks to support the crown before the concrete shears completely."

"We must build a concrete shoring frame," Jun said, looking at the fracture lines. "A vertical support system using heavy timber posts and hydraulic jacks set directly under the cracked vault to prevent a cave-in. Liang, go to the highway department warehouse at the plaza. They have three hydraulic shoring jacks. Take the handcart and some volunteers to bring them here."

Liang ran to the plaza, returning with a team of ten young volunteers pushing a heavy iron handcart loaded with the hydraulic jacks. The volunteers had also brought thick split-pine planks to build a flat deck—*muban*—that would rest against the concrete ceiling, distributing the pressure over a larger surface area.

To help stabilize the vault permanently, the community organized a concrete mixing crew. They gathered near the portal, mixing concrete by hand on a sheet of plywood. They used shovels to combine Portland cement, dry sand from the highway depot, and crushed granite aggregate in a strict one-to-two-to-four volume ratio. Ying supervised the mixing, ensuring they added only enough water to trigger the chemical hydration reaction. "If we add too much water, we will increase the workability but create microscopic capillary pores in the matrix as the excess water evaporates," Ying explained to a volunteer who was holding a hose. "This would reduce the final compressive strength of the cured concrete from thirty megapascals down to less than fifteen. We need the tricalcium silicate to react fully and form a dense calcium silicate hydrate gel that will crystallize around the granite aggregate, locking it in place." The volunteers carried the heavy buckets of wet concrete in a human chain into the dark tunnel, their voices echoing in a steady chant: "Left side, pass! Right side, pass!"

Jun and the carpenters laid out the spruce timbers, cutting them to length using the cross-cut saw. The scent of fresh wood sap rose in the damp tunnel, mixing with the smell of old grease. They built a rectangular frame, lashing the joints with hemp rope and reinforcing them with steel brackets.

They positioned the vertical posts under the ceiling deck, placing the hydraulic jacks at the base of each post. To ensure the load was distributed evenly, Jun insisted on building a header plate and a sill plate from split pine logs. "If we apply a point load of sixty kilonewtons directly to the cracked concrete crown, we risk punching a hole through the damaged lining," Jun explained to Ying, who was assisting with the alignment. "By placing a two-meter pine header plate between the jack piston and the concrete ceiling, we distribute that sixty kilonewton force over an area of six thousand square centimeters. The resulting compressive stress is only one hundred kilopascals, which is well below the crushing strength of weathered concrete."

"All men to the jacks," Jun commanded.

The volunteers worked in pairs, pumping the handles of the jacks in unison. Jun stood back, monitoring the pressure gauges, his eyes fixed on the cracked concrete ceiling. The jacks creaked under the weight, their steel cylinders extending as they lifted the two-ton timber frame. The pressure gauge needle climbed steadily from ten megapascals to twenty-five, indicating that the jacks were taking the weight of the overhead vault.
*Clack. Clack. Clack.*

Slowly, the timber deck pressed against the concrete vault. The cracks closed fractionally, the loose plaster held in place by the pine planks. The ceiling was stabilized, the vertical load transferred down the spruce posts directly to the asphalt roadbed.

But as the last jack was locked, a loud *crack* sounded from the central bamboo barrier.

One of the horizontal bamboo poles, weakened by the constant pressure, split down the center. A grey, leather-like arm thrust through the split, its fingers clawing at the air, trying to find purchase. Behind it, the dry, mummified faces of the dead pressed against the gap, their jaws hanging open.

Zhang, a retired minibus driver in his sixties, stood on the scaffolding balcony, his iron-pointed crowbar ready. "Hold the line!" he shouted in Cantonese. He thrust the steel point downward, splitting the skull of the lead zombie with a clean, mechanical strike. The other watchmen stood behind him, using their bamboo shields and spears to hold the gap.

Officer Chan and Ying formed a shield wall using clear polycarbonate riot shields and sheet-metal road signs salvaged from the highway. They stepped into the breach, their shields locked together in a tight phalanx, their shoulders pressed against the metal to absorb the impact of the dead. The coordination was seamless; when one watchman grew tired, another stepped forward to relieve him, the volunteers passing fresh spears and water down the line. It was an inspiring display of community solidarity; transit workers, students, and elders stood shoulder-to-shoulder, refusing to yield an inch.

"Keep pumping!" Jun called out, his voice steady. "We must lock the jacks before the frame shifts!"

Jun and Liang worked rapidly to drive additional oak wedges into the shoring frame, securing the base plate. With a final heave of their combined strength, the volunteers locked the hydraulic valves, stabilizing the shoring. The watchmen held the breach, their shields deflecting the claws of the dead until the opening could be reinforced with a split-bamboo patch. The line was held, the ceiling secure, and the community stood firm against the dark tunnel.

A young volunteer, a student from the nearby university, sat down on the asphalt, his chest heaving as he caught his breath. "We did it," he whispered, looking at the massive spruce logs supporting the ceiling. "We actually held it."

"We held it because we worked as one," Zhang said, placing a hand on the boy's shoulder. "In Hong Kong, we say *lion rock spirit*—we help each other, no matter how hard the storm. Now, let us go back to the plaza and get some of Auntie Wong's soup. We will need our strength for tomorrow."
