CHAPTER 4: THE VENTILATION SHAFT


The Lion Rock Tunnel was ventilated by a massive vertical shaft that ran from the center of the tunnel roof to the top of the ridge, fifty meters above. The shaft, blasted through solid granite, was three meters in diameter, lined with a smooth layer of shotcrete. At the top of the ridge, the shaft emerged into a small concrete structure set with steel louvered grates, designed to prevent rain and debris from entering the tunnel.

But the shaft was breached. A secondary pack of the dead, wandering along the hiking trails of the Lion Rock Country Park, had gravitated toward the humming of the exhaust draft. Pushing against the weathered steel louvers, several of the dry, mummified figures had fallen through the intake opening. They fell down the vertical shaft, their bodies bouncing off the concrete walls before sliding down the steep sloping chute that fed the main air ducts above the southbound lane.

"They are in the ceiling ducts," Officer Chan said, pointing his flashlight toward the rectangular sheet-metal chambers that ran along the tunnel roof. "We can hear them scraping. If they break through the thin sheet-metal, they will drop directly behind our scaffolding wall, cutting off our watchmen and opening a second front inside our secure zone. The situation is critical because the air ducts run over the entire length of the active command center."

Jun examined the air duct. The sheet-metal was only two millimeters thick, held together by standing seams and supported by steel strap hangers. The dry, scratching sound of fingernails on metal was clear, a rhythmic, metallic rasping that grew louder by the minute.

"We must seal the throat of the shaft," Jun said, adjusting the strap of his toolbox. "We will climb the main access ladder to the ventilation mezzanine chamber and build a heavy timber grid—*yinzha*—across the base of the concrete shaft. We must anchor it directly to the rock to resist the impact of falling bodies."

"Master," Liang said, looking up the dark shaft. "The concrete is vertical. How do we hold the timber in place while we drill the rock sockets?"

"We will use a cantilevered design," Jun replied. "We will notch three main spruce timbers to act as cantilever supports. Two-thirds of their length will rest on the concrete floor of the mezzanine chamber, anchored by heavy iron weights, while one-third projects over the shaft opening. This will create a stable platform from which we can drill the rock and install the transverse locking beams."

Jun, Liang, and four volunteers from the plaza climbed the vertical iron ladder to the mezzanine chamber. The chamber was a cold, cavernous room filled with the smell of old soot, grease, and damp granite. The wind howled down the vertical shaft, bringing with it a freezing draft from the ridge above. At the center of the floor, the three-meter opening of the shaft yawned like a black well, the sound of the scraping dead rising from the depths. Among the volunteers was Uncle Wah, a retired dockworker who had spent thirty years operating container cranes at the Kwai Tsing terminals. He carried a heavy coil of steel-reinforced cable and a set of pulley blocks, his eyes sharp and analytical. "We need a mechanical advantage of at least four to hoist the timbers into this wind," Uncle Wah shouted, his voice echoing in the concrete vault. "The aerodynamic drag from the chimney draft is pulling upward with a force of nearly two hundred newtons."

Jun laid out three seasoned spruce logs, twelve centimeters square and four meters long. He used his broadaxe to cut deep notches into the center of the logs, preparing them for an interlocking half-lap joint.

"We must calculate the bending stress on the cantilever," Jun said to Liang, his voice competing with the wind. "If a body weighing eighty kilograms falls fifty meters, it will reach a terminal velocity of approximately thirty meters per second before it hits our grid. The kinetic energy at impact will be thirty-six kilojoules. To absorb this energy without shearing the wood, our spruce timbers must have a safety margin of at least four. We will space the timbers three hundred millimeters apart, creating a grid that will catch the torso of any falling figure while letting smaller debris pass."

Using a hand-cranked breast drill with a carbon-steel bit, Liang drilled guide holes through the spruce logs. The volunteers, working in pairs, held the timbers steady while Jun used a star-drill and a heavy copper mallet to sink rock sockets into the granite walls of the shaft collar.
*Clink. Clink. Clink.*
The steel tool bit into the hard granite, sending up white stone dust that was carried away by the rushing air. Jun rotated the drill ten degrees after each strike, ensuring a perfectly circular hole. It was slow, back-breaking work, his muscles burning from the overhead angle, but his blows were steady and rhythmic. To clear the stone dust from the deep sockets, Liang used a small leather bellows, blowing a sharp jet of air into the hole after every ten strikes, revealing the clean granite face.

Uncle Wah rigged the pulley blocks, attaching them to a heavy iron H-beam overhead. Using a hand-winch, he and the volunteers lifted the heavy spruce timbers, coordinating their movements with short whistles. "Yat, yi, sam!" Wah called, and the winch gear clicked, drawing the spruce log upward into the mouth of the shaft.

After two hours of continuous labor, they had drilled six sockets, fifty millimeters deep. Jun inserted steel expansion sleeves into the holes, then positioned the transverse spruce beams across the opening, aligning them with the sockets.

"Drive the anchor bolts, Liang!" Jun called out.

Liang set the threaded bolts through the iron brackets and turned them with a heavy box wrench. As the bolts drew the expansion shells tight against the granite, the timber frame locked into place. The grid was completed, its spruce bars forming a solid barrier across the mouth of the shaft.

Suddenly, a loud *thud* shook the frame.

A mummified figure, its skin black and leathery, slid down the concrete chute from the ridge. It hit the spruce grid with a heavy impact, the timber creaking but holding firm. The figure's limbs became tangled in the three-hundred-millimeter gaps, its head hanging downward, its dead eyes staring at the workers below.

"Hold the frame!" a volunteer shouted, grabbing the safety rope.

Jun stepped onto the edge of the cantilever platform, his broadaxe raised. With a single, precise downward stroke, he split the skull of the trapped figure, neutralizing the threat. The body hung silently in the grid, its weight now supported by the locked spruce beams.

"We must clear the grid periodically," Jun said, wiping the steel blade of his axe. "But the barrier is solid. The air can flow, but the dead cannot pass."

Mei, a young volunteer who had helped carry the tools, handed Jun a canteen of warm water. "You did it, Master Jun. The watchmen below are safe now."

Jun took a drink and smiled. "We did it together, Mei. Go down and tell Officer Chan that the ceiling is secure. We will leave a watchman here to monitor the grid."

CHAPTER 5: THE TOLL PLAZA


The toll plaza of the Lion Rock Tunnel was a wide, flat concrete expanse, flanked by the offices of the highway department and the steep jungle slopes of the ridge. Normally filled with the rush of traffic, it was now a fortress of necessity.

"They are coming over the ridge," Officer Chan said, pointing his telescope toward the southern slope. "A secondary pack of fifty zombies has bypassed the tunnel mouth, climbing down from the Lion Rock trails to reach the plaza. We must hold them before they reach the barracks where the families are sleeping."

"We cannot use timber here," Jun said, looking at the wide, open lanes of the plaza. "We need a heavy, stable barrier that can resist lateral impacts over a wide front. We will build *shazhan*—sand-filled highway barriers."

"Master, we have the red plastic barriers," Liang said, pointing to the water-filled traffic barriers stacked along the road shoulder. "But we have no water to fill them. The pumps are dry."

"We will fill them with dry sand from the construction yard," Jun replied. "Water is fluid and will leak if the plastic is punctured by claws or bullets. Sand has an internal friction angle of thirty-five degrees. When packed into the barriers, it forms a cohesive mass with a density of sixteen hundred kilograms per cubic meter. Even if the plastic shell is torn away, the sand will remain in a stable heap, absorbing the kinetic energy of any impact. We will use Rankine's earth pressure theory to calculate the active thrust. By setting the barriers in a double row, the front row will absorb the initial shock, while the back row, offset by half a width, will resist the sliding shear. The total weight of each sand-filled unit will be one point six metric tons, providing an enormous resisting force against sliding friction. The sliding resistance is equal to the weight multiplied by the coefficient of friction of rubber against asphalt, which is zero point six five. This gives each barrier a resisting force of ten point four kilonewtons."

To ensure the barriers were properly filled, the volunteers kept track of the sand weight. "We must fill each container with exactly eighty buckets of sand," Jun instructed Ah Sing, who was managing the filling line. "If we under-fill them, the center of mass will remain too high. A dynamic surge from the horde could generate a overturning moment that exceeds the resisting moment, causing the plastic container to tip forward on its skid. By packing the sand fully and dampening it slightly with whatever residual water we can spare, we increase the density and lower the center of gravity, ensuring maximum stability."

They discussed the physical properties of the sand itself. Ying explained to the high-school students that the coarse-grained sand they salvaged from the roadworks yard had a higher angle of internal friction than fine river sand. "The angular grains of coarse sand interlock with each other under compression," she said, showing them a handful of the rough, grey grit. "This increases the shear strength of the sand barrier, making it behave like a solid block under sudden impact, whereas fine round sand would flow and slide."

"But how do we move them when they are full?" Officer Chan asked. "A single barrier filled with sand weighs over one metric ton. We cannot lift them into position."

"We will build wooden skids," Jun explained. "We will place the empty barriers on pine skids, fill them with sand using a human chain, and then use the manual hand-winches from the tow trucks to drag the skids into a zigzag defensive line across the toll lanes."

The community responded immediately. Taxi drivers, construction workers, and students formed three parallel human chains from the sand depot to the toll lanes. They used plastic buckets, metal woks, and even old oil tins to pass the sand. The air was filled with the rhythmic sound of shovels hitting the sandpile, the clatter of buckets, and the encouraging shouts of the workers. Several young school girls, who had been separated from their school group, sang upbeat Cantonese pop songs to keep up the morale of the older taxi drivers. The cooperation was absolute; if a bucket split, another was passed forward without a pause, and the elders managed the water distribution.

Jun and Liang constructed the skids. They used thick pine planks, twelve centimeters wide, salvaged from concrete formwork. They notched the planks to create a simple rectangular frame, locking the corners with half-lap joints and securing them with heavy iron spikes.

The empty plastic barriers were placed on the skids. Liang stood inside the toll lane, coordinating the filling. "Keep the sand dry!" he called out. "If it gets wet, it will clump and double the weight before we can drag the skid!"

As the sand filled the red plastic containers, the skids settled onto the asphalt. Jun attached the steel cable of a hand-cranked winch to the front tow ring of the first skid.

"All together on the winch!" Jun commanded.

Three volunteers—a retired bus driver, a school teacher, and a young athlete—grabbed the winch handle. They turned the gears in unison, the steel cable grooving into the drum with a metallic whine.
*Creak. Creak. Creak.*
Slowly, the one-ton sand barrier slid across the asphalt, its pine skids smoking slightly from the friction. They positioned it at a thirty-degree angle to the toll booth, creating a funnel that would force any advancing figures into a narrow bottleneck.

By mid-afternoon, six sand barriers were locked in place, forming a solid, zigzag breastwork across the main approach.

The dead emerged from the jungle brush at the edge of the plaza, their boots sliding on the damp grass. They were dry, their skin scratched by the thorns of the mountain vines, their eyes cloudy. They rushed toward the toll plaza, drawn by the smell of the campfires.

"Get behind the barriers!" Officer Chan shouted, raising his riot shield.

The watchmen took their positions, their bows and spears ready.

Suli, a local archer who had trained with the youth sports team, stood on the roof of the central toll booth. She pulled the string of her composite bow, her fingers steady. She released the arrow, the steel point slicing through the air to strike the lead zombie in the temple. The figure fell silently, its body rolling onto the concrete.

The horde pressed against the sand barriers, their hands clawing at the red plastic. The plastic split under the pressure, but the packed sand remained solid, a heavy wall that did not budge. The watchmen thrust their bamboo spears through the gaps, their strikes coordinated and precise.

From the communal kitchen behind the line, Auntie Wong and the other women passed around bowls of hot chicken and ginger congee. The steam rose from the woks, carrying a rich, savory aroma of toasted sesame oil and fresh green onions. "Eat while it's hot, watchmen," she said, her voice steady. "The wall is holding, and we have plenty of sand left. A full stomach keeps the heart brave."

They sat in brief shifts behind the barriers, sharing bowls and talking in low, comforting tones about their old life in Kowloon, their favorite tea houses, and the hope of rebuilding. The line was held, the plaza secured, and the community stood firm under the shadow of the Lion Rock.

---

CHAPTER 6: THE CABLE LINE


During the night, a high-voltage power cable inside the northbound tunnel, damaged by the shifting rock overhead, short-circuited. The electrical arc ignited the wooden cable trays that ran along the concrete wall, sending thick, black smoke billowing through the vault.

"The smoke is thick," Chan said, coughing as he ran out of the portal, his face smeared with black soot. "It is filling the southbound tunnel as well, and if we cannot clear it, we will have to abandon our scaffolding wall. The draft is drawing the smoke toward Sha Tin."

Jun ran to the portal, his eyes stinging from the acidic fumes of burning PVC insulation. "The fire is feeding on the wooden cable trays," he said, examining the blueprints of the tunnel. "It acts as a fuse, carrying the fire toward the main transformer room. We must build a firebreak. We must go inside, cut away the wooden trays on the Kowloon side of the barrier, and seal the upper ventilation damper to stop the chimney effect that is drawing the smoke. The combustion of cross-linked polyethylene insulation releases toxic hydrochloric acid gas, which, when combined with the humidity in the tunnel, will corrode our lungs in minutes. The cable trays are built of structural timber, five centimeters thick and thirty centimeters wide, running along the wall for over two hundred meters."

The brackets holding the trays were anchored into the concrete vault walls using steel expansion bolts. As the fire raged, the heat caused the steel brackets to expand. Jun explained the rock mechanics of the failure to Liang: "Steel has a coefficient of thermal expansion of twelve times ten to the minus six per degree Celsius, while concrete is only eight times to the minus six. Under the intense heat of the electrical fire, the steel brackets expand faster than the surrounding concrete, creating massive internal radial shear stresses. This induces localized concrete spalling, causing the anchors to lose their grip and the heavy trays to sag toward the roadbed."

The heat inside the vault was intense, radiating from the concrete crown. Near the ceiling, the air temperature was close to sixty degrees Celsius. Jun could feel his sweat evaporating instantly, his skin stinging from the acidic fumes of the burning cables. He wrapped a wet felt blanket around his head and shoulders, which acted as a temporary thermal shield. "The wet felt absorbs the heat by vaporizing the water, keeping the air around my face at a breathable temperature for a short time," Jun explained to Liang. "But we must work fast. Once the water in the felt evaporates, the thermal shield is gone."

"But the smoke is toxic, Master Jun," Liang warned, holding a wet cloth to his face. "A man cannot breathe in there for more than three minutes without losing consciousness."

"We will work in shifts," Jun said. "We will use wet felt blankets as masks, and we will construct a manual blower using a car radiator fan and a hand-cranked pulley to force fresh air along the floor of the tunnel."

Jun and the transit workers quickly assembled the blower. They mounted a plastic fan shroud onto a wooden frame, linking it to the rear wheel of a stationary bicycle using a V-belt salvaged from an alternator. A young volunteer named Ah Ming climbed onto the bicycle and began to pedal, his legs moving in a steady rhythm. The fan spun, creating a narrow stream of fresh air that cut through the lower layer of smoke. Jun calculated the air flow: "The bicycle has a gear ratio of fifty-two teeth on the chainring to eighteen teeth on the rear sprocket," he explained to Liang. "At eighty pedal revolutions per minute, the alternator pulley will spin the fan at close to twelve hundred RPM. This delivers approximately four hundred and fifty cubic meters of air per minute through our makeshift duct, providing a positive pressure zone along the asphalt floor." Ah Ming pedaled with sweat dripping down his face, a wet rag tied over his mouth. When his legs locked with cramps, two taxi drivers lifted him off the bike and another volunteer jumped on without missing a beat, keeping the fan spinning. The community support was continuous, ensuring the blower never stopped. The cool wind from the blower felt like a clean breath of life against their stinging skin as they pushed deeper into the dark vault, the forced airflow facilitating the rapid evaporation of sweat from their faces and helping to maintain their core body temperatures in the sweltering heat. This mechanical ventilation was critical, preventing heat exhaustion and carbon monoxide buildup in the workspace.

"I will go first," Jun said, grabbing his hand axe and a wet felt blanket. "Liang, prepare the timber wedges. If the tray falls, it will drop the cables. We must support them with temporary dry-pine props so they do not touch the wet road shoulder and electrify the water."

Jun entered the smoky tunnel, his body hunched low to stay within the fresh air stream. The heat was intense, the concrete walls radiating the warmth of the electrical fire. The smoke was a solid wall of grey, illuminated only by the dull orange glow of the burning wood trays ten meters ahead.

He reached the scaffolding wall. On the other side, the dead were crowded, their silhouettes dark against the smoke, their movements slow and confused by the heat.

Jun climbed the bamboo frame, his axe held in his right hand. The wooden cable tray, built of pine boards, was bolted to the concrete wall three meters above the floor. The wood was charred, small tongues of blue flame licking the edges.

He swung his axe, the steel blade cutting into the dry pine bracket.
*Thwack. Thwack.*
The wood split, sending down a shower of red sparks. He moved to the second bracket and chopped it. The tray began to sag, the heavy electrical cables grooving into the wood.

"Now, Liang!" Jun shouted through the wet cloth.

Liang and two volunteers rushed forward, carrying three-meter pine poles. They wedged the tops of the poles under the sagging cables, locking the bottoms into the asphalt roadbed. The cables were supported, isolated from the damp ground.

Jun took a final swing, splitting the main connector block of the tray. With a loud crack, the burning section of the tray dropped into the wet drainage gutter, where the water extinguished the flames with a hiss of steam.

He then climbed higher to the ventilation damper. Using his crowbar, he forced the rusted iron valve shut, sealing the duct. The chimney effect stopped immediately; the draft died, and the black smoke began to drift back toward the Kowloon portal, carried by the natural south-to-north wind of the ridge.

Jun stumbled back to the portal, gasping for fresh air as he collapsed onto the road shoulder. Liang poured cold water over his head, washing away the soot.

"It's out," Jun whispered, his voice hoarse. "The firebreak is complete, and the air is clearing."

The volunteers cheered, passing around cups of hot chrysanthemum tea to soothe their throats. Officer Chan patted Jun on the back. "You saved the line, Master Jun. The watchmen can return to their posts. The air is safe again."

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE SCAFFOLDING LADDER


The watchmen on the bamboo scaffolding balcony defended the portal, but the structure was built of round bamboo poles, which were slick and difficult to stand on for long periods, especially during the cold, damp nights when condensation coated the green bark.

"We need a safer platform," Officer Chan said to Jun. "The watchmen must stand for hours with their bows and spears. If their boots slide on the wet bamboo, they cannot aim their strikes, and they risk falling into the crowd below. A single fall into the darkness means death. We must establish a stable platform that can support three watchmen simultaneously."

"We will build *jiaban*," Jun said, examining the scaffolding joints. "Timber platform decks. We will split spruce logs into flat boards, notch the ends to fit snugly over the round bamboo ledgers, and lock them with wooden pegs driven through the frame. This will create a rigid, level walkway that will not slip or rotate under a man's weight."

"Where do we get the spruce logs?" Liang asked.

"The highway department has a stack of temporary bridge timbers at the depot," Officer Chan said. "They are four meters long and fifteen centimeters thick. We can use them."

Jun and Liang set up a sawing station at the toll plaza. They used a two-man cross-cut saw, its long steel blade set with deep M-teeth. Two young volunteers, a carpenter's apprentice named Chun and a physics student named Ying, worked the saw, their bodies swaying in a rhythmic, coordinated motion.
*Shree-shree, shree-shree.*
The saw cut through the seasoned spruce, sending up a pile of yellow sawdust that smelled of pine resin. Chun, who had spent his youth working with traditional mortising tools, discussed the value of manual hand tools. "A nail gun is fast, Master Jun, but it splits the grain of seasoned spruce," Chun said, wiping his brow. "A chiseled joint, locked with a hand-shaved peg, allows the timber to expand and contract with the humidity inside the tunnel without losing its grip. The wood fibers wrap around the peg, creating a tight seal that increases in friction over time."

Jun took the split boards and used his drawknife and a spoke-shave to shave the surfaces flat, removing any splinters. He then chiseled semicircular notches, ten centimeters in diameter, into the bottom faces of the board ends. These notches would fit over the horizontal bamboo poles of the scaffolding wall.

To prevent the boards from sliding laterally along the bamboo, Jun designed a locking peg system. He drilled vertical holes, twenty millimeters in diameter, through the notched ends of the boards. Liang used a three-to-one gear-ratio breast drill with a carbon-steel twist bit, turning the hand-crank while pressing his chest against the headplate to drill the holes. The wood fibers smoked slightly from the friction, and Liang must back out the drill to clear the spiral chips. Chun explained the mechanical properties of oak pegs: "Oak is a ring-porous hardwood with high shear strength across the grain—over ten megapascals. When driven into the soft spruce and compressed against the bamboo ledger, the peg undergoes local plastic deformation, swelling to fill the grain structure and locking the joint with a force that cannot be undone without splitting the timber. When you drive the tapered peg with the mallet, you compress the fibers of the oak, storing potential elastic energy. This energy acts like a continuous spring, pressing the components together and preventing slippage even under constant vibrations from the crowd below." Liang also used his chisel to chamfer the leading edges of the pegs, allowing them to slide smoothly into the drilled holes without shearing the structural fibers of the spruce boards.

To ensure the bamboo scaffolding columns themselves would not slip under the weight of the new timber decks, they checked the lashings. The scaffolding union volunteers explained the physics of the clove hitch and the timber hitch they used for the primary load-bearing joints. "The clove hitch provides two parallel wraps that grip the bamboo bark, and the tail is tucked under the turn so that any increase in load pulls the tail tighter, increasing the radial friction force," one worker showed Liang. "We add a secondary timber hitch for diagonal braces, wrapping the tail three times around the standing part. This wraps the cordage tightly around the irregular nodes of the bamboo, preventing any sliding along the length of the column."

"We will drive oak pegs through these holes," Jun explained to Liang. "The pegs will pass through the boards and wedge against the bamboo joints, locking the entire deck into a single, cohesive unit. The friction between the wet oak and the bamboo will prevent any rotation, even under a lateral load of three kilonewtons. We must calculate the bending stress of the spruce boards under a three-point load. For a spruce board with a span of two point five meters and a thickness of five centimeters, a concentrated load of one point five kilonewtons—representing a watchman carrying heavy gear—creates a maximum bending stress of five megapascals. The allowable bending stress of seasoned spruce is twelve megapascals, giving us a safety factor of more than two. The deflection at the center will be less than six millimeters, which is well within the structural limit of L/360."

They also calculated the bending moment of the main bamboo ledgers under the weight of the new timber deck and three watchmen. Ying pointed out that moso bamboo has a modulus of rupture of eighty megapascals. "With a two-meter span and a ten-centimeter outer diameter, the ledger can support a maximum bending moment of one point five kilonewton-meters before failure," Ying noted. "The actual bending moment under the combined load of the timber platform and three watchmen is only zero point six kilonewton-meters. This gives us a safety factor of two point five. To increase the stability further, we can install diagonal bamboo struts—*paoliang*—anchored to the vertical scaffolding columns, which reduces the effective span of the ledgers to one point five meters and increases the load capacity by fifty percent."

The community volunteers gathered to help carry the planks. A team of high-school students, working under the guidance of Chun, carried the finished boards into the tunnel mouth using a simple wooden yoke. They joked and shared stories, their laughter bringing light into the dark, damp vault.

They carried the prepared boards into the tunnel. The watchmen stood aside as Jun and Liang climbed the bamboo frame to install the first deck. Jun positioned the board, its notched ends dropping over the round bamboo ledgers with a solid *clack*.

"Pegs, Liang!" Jun called down.

Liang passed the oak pegs up the line. Jun set them into the holes and tapped them home with his mallet.
*Tap. Tap. Tap.*
The pegs wedged tight, the timber deck locking onto the bamboo frame. Jun stood on the board and bounced his weight; the platform remained perfectly level, with no creaking or shifting.

The watchmen took their positions on the new platform, their boots finding solid, dry purchase on the flat spruce boards. They could now stand with their backs braced against the concrete tunnel wall, their bows and spears held steady.

"It's like standing on a stone floor," Zhang said, testing the platform with his spear. "Now we can hold this gate forever."

Jun smiled as he climbed down the ladder. "A good deck makes a good soldier, Zhang. Keep your eyes on the dark. The wind is shifting again."


---

CHAPTER 8: THE UNDERPASS


An underpass beneath the toll plaza, used for pedestrian access to the hiking trails on the ridge, had been breached by crawling zombies. The underpass was a concrete barrel vault, three meters wide and two point five meters high, running directly under the northbound lanes.

"They are in the floor!" a watchman screamed, running from the underpass entrance.

Jun and Liang ran to the underpass entry. From the concrete stairs, three zombies were crawling, their hands reaching toward the plaza. Behind them, the dark tunnel of the underpass was filled with the scraping of boots and the low, dry rattle of the infected.

"We must seal it," Jun said, his voice firm. "We will build a dry-stone wall—*shiqiang*—across the arch, using granite blocks from the toll plaza's retaining wall, and wedge them tight."

"Master, we have no mortar," Liang said. "How will the wall hold the pressure?"

"Dry-stone walls do not need mortar if the stones are selected and laid correctly," Jun explained. "We will use the weight of the gravity wall to resist the horizontal thrust. By designing a wall with a thickness of eighty centimeters at the base and a slight batter of one-in-ten on the face, the line of thrust from the gravity load and the lateral pressure will remain within the middle third of the wall's thickness. This prevents any tension from developing in the joints, ensuring the structure cannot overturn. The friction between the rough granite blocks, which have a coefficient of friction of zero point seven, will prevent any sliding. We will follow the rule of 'two-over-one and one-over-two'—every stone must cross the joint below it to distribute the vertical load. Continuous vertical joints are planes of weakness that would buckle under the impact of the dead."

Jun explained the math of the thrust line to the volunteers. "A semi-circular concrete arch with a three-meter radius generates a horizontal thrust at the spring line of approximately fifteen kilonewtons per meter of width," he said, drawing a diagram on the concrete wall with a piece of chalk. "To counter this, our dry-stone wall must have sufficient weight to keep the resultant force vector within the middle third of the base width, which is twenty-six centimeters from the center. If the vector falls outside this zone, tension will develop on the windward side, causing the joints to open and the wall to fail by overturning. The weight of the granite blocks we are laying—approx twenty-four kilonewtons per cubic meter—provides the vertical force needed to keep the thrust line safely centered."

Jun used a rock chisel and a heavy steel mash hammer to square the edges of the granite stones. He worked with short, controlled blows, the steel chisel ringing against the hard granite. "We must make the contact surfaces between the blocks as flat as possible," he explained to Liang. "If the stones meet at sharp points, the concentrated compressive stress will exceed the crushing strength of the granite, causing the stone to split and settle. A flat contact area distributes the load evenly, maximizing the frictional resistance between the courses." To maintain a uniform batter of one-in-ten on the wall's face, Jun set up a mason's line suspended from temporary pine stakes. "The batter ensures that gravity pulls the stones back toward the centerline of the vault," Jun pointed out. "This gravity component resists the horizontal thrust from the underpass, acting as a passive stabilizer that keeps the joints closed."

To block the final section of the arch, Jun selected basalt blocks instead of granite. "Basalt has a compressive strength of over one hundred and twenty megapascals," Jun noted to Liang. "This is significantly higher than the granite's eighty megapascals. At the top of the arch, where the concrete vault curvature generates massive concentrated compression vectors, we need basalt's high density and hardness to resist crushing and prevent long-term settling from the highway traffic above." Jun chiseled the basalt blocks so their joints aligned perfectly with the radial vectors of the arch. This ensured that the thrust line passed straight through the center of each joint, preventing any offset that could cause a block to slide or pop out under pressure.

Jun and the volunteers formed a stone-moving crew. Men, women, and even children joined a double-line human chain stretching from the retaining wall to the underpass arch. The chain consisted of old neighbors from Sha Tin who used to gather at the local tea houses; they passed the stones while sharing news about their families, offering support and encouragement. Among them were a husband and wife, who had run a popular bakery in Kowloon before the evacuation. "Our shop is gone, Master Jun, but our hands are still strong," the baker said, wiping sweat from his forehead as he passed a heavy granite block. "We are glad to be here helping the community. If we protect this pass, we can build a new bakery in Sha Tin." They passed granite blocks weighing up to thirty kilograms hand-to-hand, their muscles straining but their coordination perfect. They sang Cantonese work chants to synchronize their movement, the heavy blocks passing smoothly from hand to hand. A young boy named Kai, whose father was a bricklayer, ran back and forth carrying small chinking stones—*pinning stones*—to fill the minor voids between the larger blocks. "You must place the pinning stones from the outside," Kai explained to a helper. "If you pack them from the inside, the pressure of the earth will push them out, causing the main stones to settle and rock. The grandfather of my family taught us that a dry wall relies on these small pins to lock the structural joints, distributing the load across the entire face."

Jun laid the foundation course, selecting the largest, flattest granite blocks. He set them directly onto the concrete floor, packing the gaps with smaller crushed aggregate to prevent any rocking. As the wall rose, he placed long binder stones—*tiezi*—that ran through the entire thickness of the wall, locking the front and back faces together.

"Pass the hearting stones!" Liang called out.

The younger volunteers passed buckets of gravel and small stones, which were used to pack the interior core of the wall, creating a dense, self-draining mass that settled under its own weight.

By the time the wall reached the spring line of the concrete arch, they had laid four metric tons of granite. Jun prepared the final course, selecting wedge-shaped blocks to form a tight seal against the ceiling vault.

"We need the keystone," Jun said, examining the gap at the center of the arch.

Liang chiseled a wedge of hard basalt, shaping it to fit the final central opening. Jun positioned the block and used a heavy spruce log as a battering ram, swung by three volunteers, to drive it home.
*Thud. Thud. Thud.*
The keystone wedged tight, transferring the lateral thrust of the vault directly into the side walls of the underpass. The wall was locked, a solid barrier of granite that sealed the underpass completely.

"It is done," Jun said, wiping the stone dust from his eyes. "The underpass is a tomb now. The dead cannot break this stone. The community has built a wall that will last."

CHAPTER 9: THE LION'S ROAR


A massive horde of ten thousand infected, having pushed down from the Kowloon peninsula, reached the southbound portal of the Lion Rock Tunnel. The pressure of the crowd inside the tunnel was immense, the bodies packed shoulder-to-shoulder for hundreds of meters.

They pushed a public double-decker bus, which had been abandoned in the tunnel, ahead of them. The massive steel and aluminum vehicle was a Volvo B9TL model, weighing nine metric tons. Forced forward by the sheer weight of the crowd behind it, the vehicle acted as a massive battering ram. It wedged against the bamboo scaffolding wall with a force that split three main bamboo columns.
*Crack. Crack.*
The sound was like rifle fire in the concrete vault. The vertical columns split down their fibers, the nylon lashings snapping with sharp pops as the aluminum panels of the bus buckled and sheared under the pressure.

"The wall is caving!" Officer Chan screamed, his voice filled with panic. "If the bus breaks through, the horde will flood Sha Tin and overrun our encampment!"

"We must drop the concrete safety gate," Jun said, his voice calm but loud. "The portal is fitted with an emergency concrete fire-gate, but the winch cable is jammed in the control tower."

"Who will cut the winch axle?" Liang asked.

"I will go," Jun said. "Liang, coordinate the watchmen. Keep the shield wall braced against the bamboo barrier. We must hold them for five minutes."

Jun ran to the control tower, climbing the narrow spiral staircase, his axe held ready in his right hand. The control room was a small concrete box overlooking the portal, its windows shattered, smelling of dust, burnt insulation, and old grease. The main winch axle was a massive log of seasoned oak, forty centimeters in diameter, wrapped in steel cables that held the six-ton concrete fire-gate suspended above the entrance. The brake mechanism had seized, and the steel cable had overlapped on the drum, jamming the gear.

The safety gate itself was a massive slab of precast reinforced concrete, six meters wide, four meters high, and thirty centimeters thick. Inside, the gate was reinforced with a grid of twenty-millimeter high-yield deformed steel bars, spaced at one hundred and fifty millimeters in both directions, to resist any structural shear stress from a dynamic impact. Jun calculated the drop dynamics: "Under free fall, the gate will accelerate at nine point eight meters per second squared," he muttered, examining the cables. "However, the friction of the steel guide channels will reduce the net acceleration to approximately six meters per second squared. With a four-meter drop, the gate will hit the asphalt roadbed at an impact velocity of nearly seven meters per second, generating an instantaneous impact force of over five hundred kilonewtons. To prevent the gate from fracturing upon impact, the bottom of the steel guide channels has been packed with a half-meter layer of dry sand and recycled truck tires to absorb the kinetic energy and distribute the reaction force."

Jun examined the axle. The wood was under immense tension, the fibers groaning under the weight of the suspended gate. The six-ton gate was supported by two twenty-millimeter steel cables, generating a static tension in each cable of approximately thirty kilonewtons. This put the oak axle under a shear stress of five megapascals and a bending moment of twelve kilonewton-meters. If he cut the axle, the gate would drop, but the release of tension would be violent, potentially shattering the axle and sending splinters through the room.

To reduce the risk of a sudden, catastrophic failure that could break the axe blade or injure him, Jun used a cold chisel and his mallet to cut a deep groove into the overlapping steel cable loops on the winch drum. By weakening the outermost loop, he allowed the cable to slip slightly, transferring a portion of the load to the secondary safety brake and reducing the tension in the oak axle.

The steel tracks guiding the gate were bolted directly to the granite walls of the portal using twenty-millimeter structural steel anchor bolts. Jun calculated the shear vectors acting on these tracks during the drop: "The lateral wind resistance and the sliding friction generate a horizontal shear force of seventy kilonewtons," he analyzed, checking the bolt heads. "Each steel anchor bolt has an ultimate shear capacity of eighty kilonewtons, meaning the twelve bolts along the tracks provide an immense safety factor, preventing the guides from twisting or ripping away as the heavy concrete slab falls."

The control tower itself was a structural marvel of reinforced concrete columns, built to resist wind shear and ground vibration. Jun knew that the tower could support the dynamic load of the release, but the structural foundations would groan as the six-ton gate dropped. He braced his legs against the concrete base plate, ensuring his center of gravity was stable before he swung.

"I must cut the tension side," Jun muttered to himself. He stood back, adjusting his stance. He raised his broadaxe and delivered a heavy, vertical blow to the center of the oak log. He chose to cut a wide V-notch on the top tension surface of the log, rather than a straight cut, to control the direction of the split and prevent the log from kicking back.
*Thwack.*
A clean notch appeared, the wood fibers splitting. He swung again, his movements precise and rhythmic, his axe blade biting deeper with each blow. The steel of the axe vibrated, the shock traveling up his arms to his shoulders, making his muscles ache, but he kept his focus. He could feel the tension in the log, the way the wood vibrated after each strike, the grain splitting under the blade. The sweat ran into his eyes, his breath coming in gasps as he worked in the close, dusty air of the tower.

Below, Officer Chan, Zhang, and the watchmen formed a tight phalanx. They locked their clear polycarbonate riot shields and sheet-metal highway signs together, bracing their feet against the asphalt. They stood shoulder-to-shoulder, absorbing the massive shocks as the bus pressed forward, their bodies straining under the load. It was a test of pure collective will; they passed reinforcements to the front line, holding the shield wall together with their combined weight.

Jun ignored the noise. He focused entirely on the wood, watching the grain separate. He took a deep breath, raising his axe for the final blow. He delivered a final, powerful strike to the center of the V-notch.

With a loud *bang*, the oak log split in two. The steel cables unreeled from the drum with a scream of friction, and the six-ton concrete gate dropped down the steel guide channels of the portal.
*Crash.*
The ground shook as the concrete gate hit the asphalt floor, sealing the southbound tunnel completely. A cloud of grey dust and dry leaves rose into the air, obscuring the portal.

Jun was trapped inside the control room, the concrete gate having blocked the main exit staircase.

He ran to the ventilation window, using his chisel to pry away the concrete louvers. He squeezed through the narrow gap, sliding down the retaining wall to land on the soft soil of the slope just as the dust began to settle.

Liang and Chan ran to meet him, helping him to his feet. "You did it, Master Jun," Liang said, his face pale. "The gate is down. The horde is sealed inside the mountain."
