CHAPTER 10: THE WALLED PASS


The morning sun rose over a silent Sha Tin, its golden light illuminating the Lion Rock Tunnel and the massive concrete gate that sealed it. The concrete was scarred by the impact, but it stood solid, a permanent wall that blocked the highway.

The portal was secure, the New Territories safe. The threat from the south had been neutralized, and the families in the encampment could breathe a sigh of relief.

Jun sat on the steps of the toll plaza, his hands resting on his wooden toolbox. The toolbox was scarred, its panels showing the marks of Yunnan, Gansu, Shaanxi, Sichuan, Henan, Hubei, and Hong Kong, but the tools inside were clean and sharp. Beside him, Liang was using a whetstone to sharpen his chisels, the oil-slicked metal gleaming in the morning light. Jun used a Japanese waterstone with a grid of one thousand to hone his broadaxe, then a three thousand grit stone to polish a micro-bevel. He slid the steel edge back and forth in a steady, circular motion, the slurry of stone particles and water polishing the metal. The scraping sound of steel on stone was the only noise in the quiet plaza, a calming, meditative rhythm that cleared the mind. Liang then cleaned his chisels using sewing machine oil and a leather strop, the oil forming a hydrophobic barrier that would prevent rust in the damp tunnel. Jun also used a flat file to clean the teeth of the cross-cut saw, setting each tooth at a forty-five degree angle to ensure clean cuts on the next job. "The saw teeth must have a set of exactly zero point five millimeters," Jun pointed out to Chun. "If the set is too narrow, the blade will bind in wet pine wood because the kerf is the same width as the blade body. A zero point five millimeter set creates a wider path, allowing the sawdust to be cleared through the gullets without building up heat and friction." He wrapped the steel blades in grease-paper to protect them from the humid Southern China air.

Chun and Liang discussed the joinery styles they would need in Suzhou. Chun explained that the traditional Suzhou style of woodworking (*Su Zuo*) was famous for its structural elegance and complex hidden joints. "Unlike the heavy northern style, the southern style uses thinner members but relies on complex interlocks like the three-way mitered joint and the hidden tenon," Chun said. "This design provides high structural flexibility under wind loads while maintaining a clean, minimalist exterior. We can adapt these joints to resist the horizontal shear force of a crowd pushing against a garden bridge, using locking wedges to keep the tenons tight."

"We have built a good wall on the highway, Master Jun," Liang said, looking at the concrete gate. "It is a wall that will stand for a hundred years."

"A wall is only as good as the road it blocks," Jun replied, his voice quiet. "And the people who stand behind it. In Hong Kong, they call it the *lion rock spirit*. It is the strength of the community that held this pass, not just our timbers. The collective labor, the shared congee, the songs sung around the fire—that is the true structure."

The refugees and volunteers gathered in the plaza to celebrate their survival. They set up folding tables and plastic stools in the toll lanes. Auntie Wong and the other cooks served hot milk tea, brewed in giant woks with strong black tea leaves and sweet evaporated milk, alongside fresh pineapple buns. The sweet, buttery sugar crust of the buns crumbled as people laughed and shared stories of the night. The high-school students sat with the elderly minibus drivers, sharing tea and discussing plans for the agricultural collectives they would build in the Sha Tin valley, sharing seed rice and planning to build timber houses with salvaged lumber.

Officer Chan walked over, carrying a radio receiver. He adjusted the tuning dial, trying to minimize the static, until a clear voice broke through. "The radio received a transmission from Jiangsu Province," Chan said. "Suzhou. The keepers of the Humble Administrator's Garden say the water mazes are holding, but they need builders to reinforce the timber bridges and stone pavilions. The Yangtze delta horde is moving north, and if the gardens fall, the entire historic district will be lost. The message specifically asks for the mountain builders. The transmission states that the Hall of Distant Fragrance and the Flying Rainbow Bridge have sustained minor damage from the rising water level, and the wooden support columns need immediate reinforcement."

The Humble Administrator's Garden—*Zhuozheng Yuan*—was a masterpiece of classical Chinese garden design, covering over five hectares. It was built during the Ming Dynasty, around 1509, by Wang Xianchen, and reflected the classic Daoist and Confucian philosophy of harmony with nature. The garden was built around a maze of connected ponds, bridges, and winding covered corridors, designed to create a shifting landscape that confused the eye. It was a perfect defense system if reinforced, using the water to isolate the historic halls. The garden structures, built with traditional dougong bracket systems and mortise-and-tenon joints, needed structural evaluation. The shifting water levels of the canals had weakened the stone foundations of the bridges, and the builders' expertise was required to restore them before the horde arrived. Jun and Liang discussed how they would repair them using stepped splice joints—*guyin sun*—and hydraulic mortar of lime, clay, and sticky rice water to seal the underwater masonry.

To ensure their safety and logistics during their journey north, the volunteers helped them pack. They loaded their backpacks with dried pork belly, salted duck eggs, and several thermoses of hot tea. Officer Chan drew a map of the routes through the New Territories. "You must take the old catchwater channels built along the ridges," Chan advised them, tracing a line on the paper. "These concrete channels, built to harvest rainwater from the slopes, are two meters wide and deep. They form a continuous barrier ditch along the hillsides, keeping the lowlands dry. The dead cannot climb the smooth, sloping concrete walls of the channels, making the access roads alongside them the safest trails to reach the northern borders."

The weather in June in Southern China was sweltering, the humid heat wrapping around them like a wet blanket. Condensation formed on the concrete surfaces of the highway, and the jungle-covered hills of the New Territories were quiet, save for the incessant, high-pitched buzzing of cicadas in the banyan trees and the distant, low murmur of the South China Sea. The heat was heavy, but the air carried the clean scent of rain coming from the east, bringing a brief promise of relief.

Jun and Liang walked in silence along the highway shoulder, their boots rhythmic on the road shoulder. The tools in Jun's toolbox clattered softly with each step, the chisels, adzes, and the heavy broadaxe sitting in their custom leather slots, clean, oiled, and ready for the work ahead.

Jun shook hands with Officer Chan and Ah Sing, their eyes filled with a mutual respect. The refugees gathered at the edge of the plaza, their voices rising in a soft, encouraging song of farewell as the two builders slung their toolboxes over their shoulders and began their long walk toward the ridges. The pass was closed, but the road ahead was open.

================================================================================

STORY 21: THE GARDEN OF WHISPERS
Setting: Humble Administrator's Garden, Suzhou, Jiangsu Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE WATER PAVILION


The water in the labyrinthine ponds of the Humble Administrator's Garden was the color of split slate—still, dark, and silent. It wound through the artificial stone hills, under the small arched granite bridges, and along the whitewashed outer walls of the covered corridors, its glassy surface mirroring the black-tiled gables, the weeping willow branches, and the intricate wooden transoms of the lakeside water pavilions. For more than five hundred years, since the mid-Ming Dynasty, this classical garden—*Zhuozheng Yuan*—had existed as a sanctuary of art, poetry, and quiet reflection, its paths meticulously designed to lead the visitor through a three-dimensional landscape painting where every turn of a corner revealed a new, carefully composed vista. But now, in the silence of the wider crisis, the garden had become something else: a fortress of quiet water, and a last haven for the survivors who huddled behind its high walls.

Jun stood on the wooden deck of the *Xiangxue Xuan*—the Fragrance of Snow Pavilion—his heavy broadaxe resting against the carved pine railing. His worn wooden toolbox lay at his feet, its brass latches green with oxidation. His large hands, scarred by years of climbing scaffolding in Hong Kong and carving granite blocks in the damp mountain passes of Sichuan, were clasped behind his back. Beside him, Liang was leaning against a thick, lacquer-red wooden column, his eyes scanning the quiet lily pads. The air was cool and thick with the smell of wet earth, lotus leaves, and decayed vegetation.

"The water is very still, Master Jun," Liang whispered, his voice barely rising above the rustle of the willow leaves. "It reminds me of the canal town we passed last week, but there are no boats here. No lanterns. The air is so quiet that you can hear the leaves falling onto the stone walks."

"Still water can hide the drift, Liang," Jun said softly. "The water level has risen ten centimeters since yesterday. Look at the Winding Bridge. The pond silt has accumulated around the base of the timber piles, and the rot has begun to split the timber feet. We must inspect the damage at the waterline before this structure is subjected to any dynamic load. If the columns are soft, the bridge will collapse under the weight of a crowd."

Jun knelt at the edge of the pavilion platform, reaching down to touch the base of the nearest support post. The post was made of red cedar (*hongshan*), twenty centimeters in diameter, which had stood in the water for decades. The wood below the water level was soft, covered in a slimy layer of green algae and fine silt. Jun drew his pocket knife and pressed the point into the wood; the steel slid into the grain easily, indicating advanced fungal decay.

"It is white rot," Jun said, wiping his fingers on his canvas apron. "The wood-decay fungi—*basidiomycetes*—have broken down both the lignin and the cellulose within the cell walls of the cedar wood. Their microscopic thread-like hyphae penetrate the tracheid cells of the wood, secreting extracellular enzymes that dissolve the complex organic polymers, leaving only a soft, spongy cellulose matrix. Red cedar has a natural compressive strength parallel to the grain of forty megapascals when seasoned and dry, but when decayed like this, its bearing capacity drops to less than five megapascals. The constant fluctuation of the water level over the past months, caused by the blocked drainage canal, has exposed the timber to both moisture and oxygen, which accelerates the fungal activity. If we do not shore these posts immediately, the floor of the pavilion will sag and collapse under the weight of the watchmen on duty."

"We can cut away the rotted base," Liang suggested, adjusting the straps on his tool vest. "And install a granite base block—a *zhushi*—under the column, linking them with a stepped tenon joint. This will isolate the wood from the damp silt and prevent further decay."

"Yes," Jun agreed. "We will use the grey granite blocks from the rockery for the bases. But first, we must understand the security of this garden. The brick walls are high, but they are decorative screen-walls in many places, filled with window openings that need reinforcement."

They had traveled north from the southern territory of Hong Kong, navigating the delta channels of the Yangtze to reach the ancient garden city of Suzhou. Here, the garden had become a haven for a group of ninety survivors, who had closed the high brick walls, blocked the narrow street entries with stacked roof tiles, and retreated to the central water pavilion, *Yuanxiang Tang*—the Hall of Distant Fragrance. The community had organized itself into a cooperative, with families sharing the work of gardening, food preparation, and watch-keeping. Elders managed the kitchens, boiling large pots of rice and brewing herbal tea, while the younger survivors patrolled the walls and reinforced the screen windows with split bamboo.

A low, soft scrape sounded from the stone corridor across the pond.

Jun turned, his hand automatically reaching for the handle of his broadaxe. Lihua, a young woman in a faded cotton vest, stood on the bridge. She held a long, double-edge steel sword—a *Jian*—its hilt wrapped in black silk cord, her eyes fixed on the willow shadows. Her movements were fluid and silent, her bare feet making no sound on the stone slabs of the corridor.

"No noise here, carpenters," she whispered as she stepped onto the deck, her bare feet silent on the pine boards. "Firearms are forbidden. The noise carries across the water to the outer canals, and the Suzhou horde is only two blocks away. We fight with the blade and the pole. If a single gun is fired, the sound will echo off the plaster walls and draw thousands of them down the narrow alleys."

"I am Jun," the master said, bowing slightly. "This is Liang. We received the radio signal from Master Shen. He said the western firewall was cracking."

"The firewall is holding," Lihua replied, her voice low. "But the water walkers have entered the outer lotus ponds. They crawl through the mud beneath the screens. Follow me. My father is waiting at the Hall of Distant Fragrance. We need your tools to make this sanctuary secure."

They followed Lihua along the covered corridor, their boots quiet on the pine walkways. The garden was a maze of pavilions, artificial hills, and winding ponds. It was designed to confuse the visitor, to slow their pace and offer different vistas at every step. Now, this labyrinthine design was their greatest defense; any dead entering the garden would be lost in the winding paths, unable to find a direct route to the central island. But the structures themselves needed reinforcement. The wooden posts supporting the corridors were sagging, and the brick walls were showing cracks from the rising water level.

In the Hall of Distant Fragrance, they found Master Shen, Lihua's father, an elderly scholar who had spent his life studying the history of the garden. He sat at a wooden table covered with old maps of the canal network. Around him, several families were resting, sharing bowls of rice and talking in quiet whispers. The atmosphere was one of quiet solidarity; everyone contributed what they could, sharing resources and comforting the children.

"Welcome, builders," Master Shen said, rising to greet them. "The Wudang watchmen told us of your skill. The water is our shield, but it is also our threat. We must adapt the garden to hold the line."

Jun nodded, setting his toolbox on the stone floor. "We will reinforce the bridges and build barricades in the rockeries, Master Shen. Let us make this garden a fortress of silence."

The volunteers had already gathered several cedar logs from the garden's southern grove. Jun laid out his chisels and saws, explaining the process to the helpers. They would lift each support post using a simple wooden lever, cut away the rotten bottom thirty centimeters, carve a stepped splice joint, and seat the post onto a new granite block. The community members stood in a circle, watching the demonstration with quiet intensity, ready to carry out the heavy physical labor together.


---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE ZIG-ZAG BRIDGE


The main bridge over the central lake was the Winding Bridge—a zig-zag structure of seven pine decks supported by stone piers, designed to slow the visitor's pace and offer different views of the lotus flowers. The zig-zag design was not accidental; it was built to confuse the eye and prevent any direct, rushed movement across the water. The classical designers of Zhuozheng Yuan knew that by forcing a pedestrian to make sharp turns, the mind would be slowed, allowing the senses to absorb the delicate placement of the surrounding rocks, willows, and water. Now, this slow-paced geometry served a tactical purpose: it would prevent a rushing horde from crossing the lake in a straight line, slowing their advance and grouping them at the turns.

But the bridge was a defensive bottleneck. If the outer walls were breached, the zombies would use the bridge to reach the central island where the survivors lived.

"The bridge is too stable," Jun said, inspecting the pine joists from a small flat-bottomed boat he had rowed under the span. "The timbers are bolted directly to the granite caps of the stone piers. This makes it a permanent highway for the dead. We must build a *taiqiao*—a removable deck system. We will notch the joists to rest loosely in granite pockets on the stone piers, and install sliding timber keys. The watchmen can pull the keys and drop the middle deck into the water, creating a three-meter gap that the dead cannot cross. Because the dead are slow and have no balance, they will fall into the deep silt below the piers, where they will be trapped."

"Master, the timber is heavy to lift," Liang said, holding the boat steady with a bamboo pole. "A single pine deck, three meters long and one point five meters wide, weighs close to three hundred kilograms. If the watchmen must lift it under pressure, it will take too long."

"We don't lift it," Jun said, adjusting his spectacles. "We use a counterweight tilt-drop system. We will hang two large granite blocks from the bridge rail using split-bamboo ropes. When we pull the key, the weight of the stone will tilt the deck, dropping it into the silt. The system relies on torque and the center of gravity. The bridge deck will be pivoted at the southern end, while the northern end rests on the sliding timber key. We will attach the counterweight to the northern end. When the key is pulled, the sixty-kilogram granite counterweights, acting with a leverage arm of one point five meters, will generate a downward torque of nine hundred newton-meters, forcing the deck to swing downward into the water."

Ying, the physics student, analyzed the mechanics of the drop. She sat on the edge of the stone pier, drawing free-body diagrams in a notebook she had kept from her university classes in Suzhou. "The static friction between the oak key and the spruce joist has a coefficient of zero point four," she explained to Liang as she checked the alignment. "With a three-hundred-kilogram deck, the normal force on the key is one point five kilonewtons. This generates a resisting friction force of six hundred newtons. The watchmen must exert a pull of at least seven hundred newtons to slide the key out of its pocket under pressure. To make this easier, we must shave the contact surfaces of the oak key to a taper of five degrees, which creates a mechanical advantage, reducing the required pulling force to less than two hundred newtons."

Jun and Liang set to work on the Winding Bridge, assisted by ten local volunteers. Among the volunteers were several students and a retired school teacher, who were eager to learn and help. They carried the necessary tools—framing chisels, a two-man saw, and heavy hemp ropes. The group worked in coordination, sharing water and encouraging each other as they worked under the hot sun.

Jun used his framing chisel and a heavy mallet to cut the notch seats into the granite caps of the piers.
*Chink. Chink. Chink.*
The steel tool bit into the grey granite, sending up sparks and a fine white stone dust that floated down onto the green lily pads below. Jun worked with steady, rhythmic blows, his chisel angled at forty-five degrees to prevent the granite from splitting along its natural cleavage planes. He carved a smooth pocket, ten centimeters deep and fifteen centimeters wide, to receive the joist ends. The vibration traveled up his arms, his shoulders absorbing the shock.

Meanwhile, Liang and Chun split-sawed two spruce logs into joists, notches the ends to slide smoothly in the granite pockets. They shaped the sliding timber keys from seasoned oak, using a drawknife to shave the surfaces until they slid easily through the guide brackets. The volunteers helped pass the heavy timbers, forming a chain to lift the spruce logs onto the piers.

They hung the granite blocks from the pine railing, using strong ropes woven from split bamboo (*zhusuo*). "Bamboo rope has a tensile strength of over eighty megapascals when fresh," Ying, the physics student, explained to the volunteers as she helped weave the fibers. "It is three times stronger than hemp rope of the same diameter, and it does not stretch when wet, which is critical for maintaining the tension on our counterweight guides. Traditional Chinese shipbuilders have used bamboo ropes for centuries because of this water-resistant tension."

They locked the guide ropes with wooden pegs, securing the entire mechanism. Jun stepped back onto the stone pier, checking the alignment of the sliding keys.

"Test the drop, Liang!" Jun called out.

Liang stood on the southern pier and pulled the oak key. With a loud *clack*, the lock released. The weight of the suspended granite blocks immediately pulled the northern end of the deck downward. With a massive splash that sent water spraying over the lily pads, the pine deck tilted forty-five degrees, its northern end sliding into the deep pond silt and leaving a clean, three-meter gap of deep water between the stone piers.

"It works," Liang said, looking at the open gap. "The water is deep here—nearly two meters. No walker can cross this without falling into the mud."

"Indeed," Jun said, looking at the water. "The silt below is three feet deep, composed of decomposed lotus leaves, organic matter, and fine clay. It has a high yield stress, which means once a body sinks into it, the mud will act like a wet vise, locking their limbs. They do not have the coordination or muscle power to pull their feet free."

Using a hand-winch rigged to the bridge railing, the volunteers worked together to haul the deck back into position, their hands moving in unison as they turned the crank. They cheered as the timber deck rose back to the level of the bridge, and Liang slid the oak key back into its pocket, locking it in place. The zig-zag path was secure, ready to be severed at a moment's notice.

The work on the Winding Bridge had drawn the attention of the entire garden community. Elders came out of the Hall of Distant Fragrance, bringing hot green tea in small clay cups and steaming sweet potatoes for the workers. Jun and Liang took a short break, sitting on the granite steps. They discussed how to reinforce the other bridges in the garden using similar removable decks, allowing them to isolate different sections of the garden if the outer perimeter was breached. The cooperative spirit of the survivors was high; everyone wanted to help, realizing that their safety depended on their mutual coordination. The sun reflected off the water, creating a warm, golden haze that made the dark situation feel peaceful for a moment.


---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE SILENT BLADES


Because noise was a danger in the dense urban neighborhood of Suzhou, the defenders of the garden could not use firearms or explosive traps. Their weapons were silent—steel swords, spears, and long knives.

But the blades were dull. Scavenged from tourist shops, museum displays, and private collections, the steel was soft, their edges rounded by time, rust, and lack of care.

"We need a grinding shop," Jun said, examining a double-edged *Jian* that Lihua had handed him. The blade was covered in dark spots of rust, and the edge was nicked and rounded. "A blade must be sharpened on a three-stage stone—first a coarse river grit to set the bevel, then a medium oil-stone to smooth the scratches, and finally a fine water-stone to hone the edge. It will make the steel split the dried skin of the dead without sticking. If the blade is dull, it will jam in the mummified muscle tissue, leaving the defender disarmed in the middle of a fight. The steel of these tourist swords is low-carbon steel, which has a ferritic-pearlitic microstructure. This makes the metal soft and ductile, with a hardness of only twenty on the Rockwell C scale. If we sharpen the edge too thin, say at an angle of fifteen degrees, the soft steel will roll and nick as soon as it strikes a bone. We must grind a robust bevel angle of exactly twenty-two degrees. This provides the best compromise between sharpness and durability, allowing the blade to cut clean through muscle fibers without deforming."

"Where do we get the grinding stones, Master?" Liang asked, looking around the empty pavilion yard.

"The garden rockery," Jun said. "The grey granite blocks are perfect for coarse grinding, and the green slate from the pavilion roof will hone the edge. Go, Liang! Set the stones in the pavilion yard. We will use the water from the pond to lubricate the grind."

Jun and Liang set up the grinding shop in the *Baxian Ting*—the Eight Immortals Pavilion. The pavilion was a small, octagonal structure built of red pine columns and capped with a green-glazed tile roof, set on a stone platform in the western pond. The open sides allowed the cool breeze from the water to clear the dust, and the stone floor was easy to wash.

The community participated fully in the workshop. A dozen volunteers—including several teenagers and two elderly men—gathered to assist. They brought water in wooden buckets, sorted the dull blades, and helped clean the rust using wire brushes and kerosene.

Jun selected a flat block of grey granite, about forty centimeters square, and set it on a wooden frame. He poured water and a handful of fine river sand over the stone to create an abrasive slurry.

"The granite acts as our coarse grindstone," Jun explained to Ying and the other volunteers. "Its quartz grains have a hardness of seven on the Mohs scale, which is harder than the steel of these swords. The sand slurry acts as a rolling abrasive, rapidly removing the rusted metal and setting a clean, uniform twenty-two degree bevel on the edge. We must maintain a constant angle of stroke; if we tilt the blade, we will round the edge and ruin the relief angle."

Jun demonstrated the technique, holding the sword with both hands, his thumbs pressed against the flat of the blade. He moved the steel across the wet granite in a smooth, circular, figure-eight pattern.
*Screee-screee, screee-screee.*
The sound of metal on stone was a steady, rhythmic rasp. After twenty strokes, he flipped the blade and repeated the motion on the other side. A grey mud of stone dust and iron filings formed on the block, which Liang washed away with a splash of clean water. The mechanical friction created a faint smell of hot steel, which mixed with the earthy scent of the pond.

As they worked, Jun noticed that many of the tourist swords had loose hilt pins, which was extremely dangerous. "The hilt pin, or *jianpin*, holds the tang inside the wooden handle," Jun explained, showing a loose wooden guard. "These cheap swords use soft lead pins that shear under impact. If the pin fails, the blade will fly out of the handle when you strike. We must replace every single hilt pin with a hand-hammered copper wire rivet. We will drill out the lead, insert a three-millimeter copper wire, and hammer both ends against a steel anvil to form dome heads. This mechanical rivet will hold the tang with a high shear capacity, preventing the handle from separating under dynamic shock loads."

Once the bevel was set, Jun moved the blade to a slab of green slate. "The slate is a fine-grained clay stone," he said. "Its particles are much smaller, which allows us to remove the scratches left by the granite. We use water to float away the tiny metal particles, preventing them from clogging the pores of the stone. If the pores are clogged, the stone will slide over the steel without cutting, a phenomenon called glazing."

After the slate, Jun honed the leaf-shaped tips of the spears using a fine-grained siltstone he had found in the dry stream bed. He worked with light, delicate strokes, checking the edge frequently using the hair on his arm. The steel of the spears was honed until it was sharp as glass, the edge reflecting the dark tiles of the pavilion roof like a mirror.

The volunteers worked in pairs, learning the rhythm of the stones. An elderly scholar, Mr. Zhou, sat on a stool, carefully oiling the finished blades with machine oil to prevent rust. The yard was filled with the quiet, industrious murmur of collective labor, the survivors finding comfort in the shared task.

Lihua took one of the sharpened swords, its steel reflecting the black tiles of the pavilion roof. She swung the blade, her wrist moving with a practiced ease. The air hissed with a silent, sharp *fip*.

"It is a silent blade," she said, her fingers touching the silk-wrapped hilt. "It feels light now, like it wants to cut the wind. Thank you, builders. With these, we can hold the gates without a sound."

Jun smiled, picking up another rusty spear. "A sharp tool is a safe tool, Lihua. Now, let us sharpen the rest. We have many gates to defend."

As they worked, the children of the garden brought them fresh cups of warm water sweetened with a little honey. The community was working as one, their shared focus on defense bringing them closer together. Jun watched Liang teach a young boy the proper way to hold a file, noting the patience in the boy's eyes. In this garden of silence, they were forging not just blades, but the solidarity needed to survive the days to come. The collective work was a form of mutual care, a quiet rebellion against the chaos outside.

---

Jun explained the micro-mechanical behavior of the wood fibers under stress. 'In a traditional mortise-and-tenon joint, the strength depends on the friction between the face of the tenon and the wall of the mortise,' he said, showing a small spruce block to the apprentices. 'When we cut a *guyin sun* stepped splice, the shoulder provides a flat bearing surface that transfers the compressive load directly parallel to the grain. If the joint is loose, we drive small wedges of seasoned oak into the mortise pocket. The wedge exerts lateral pressure, compressing the tracheid cells of the pine wood and increasing the normal force. This normal force, multiplied by the coefficient of friction of zero point three between the wood surfaces, creates a joint that can resist several tons of tension or shear force without sliding. We must seal the joint with boiled pine resin to prevent moisture from entering, which would cause the wood to swell and rot. This traditional method of shoring is critical for preserving the historic integrity of these timbers while ensuring their ultimate stability under pressure.'

---

CHAPTER 4: THE COVERED CORRIDOR


The covered corridor—*lang*—was a winding wooden walkway with a tiled roof that ran along the whitewashed outer brick wall, linking the various pavilions and courtyards of the garden. The roof was built of grey clay tiles laid over a thick layer of wet lime mortar, which in turn was supported by horizontal cedar rafters, creating a beautiful, sweeping curve that shaded the walkway from the hot summer sun and protected the timber columns from the damp rains of southern China. The corridor was designed with delicate lattice windows that looked out onto the narrow streets of Suzhou, allowing the ancient scholars to observe the outer world while remaining isolated in their sanctuary. Now, those decorative windows were the weakest points in the garden's perimeter.

But a section of the corridor roof near the northern garden had caved. A heavy, ancient pine branch, broken during a recent storm, had crashed through the clay tiles and cracked the central cedar support rafter, causing the roof to sag dangerously toward the pond and opening a two-meter gap in the brick wall where climbing zombies could easily enter the sanctuary.

"The rafter is split," Jun said, pointing his finger at the cracked cedar beam as they stood beneath the sag. "If the next rain comes, the timber will rot, and the whole corridor roof will collapse. We must build a *fuzhu*—a vertical pine prop set under the split rafter, and shore up the brick wall with horizontal braces to prevent any overturning moment from pushing it into the canal."

"Master, they are in the lane outside," Liang said, pointing to the plaster dust falling from the brick wall.

From the narrow street outside the garden, the scraping sound was constant. A zombie had pressed its fingers through the mortar cracks of the whitewashed brick wall, its nails scratching the plaster. The sound was a dry, rhythmic rasping that echoed in the quiet corridor, a reminder of the thousands of dead that wandered the city.

Jun examined the split rafter. The beam was twelve centimeters wide and eighteen centimeters deep, spanning three meters between the support columns. The crack ran diagonally from the center of the span to the support wall, splitting the wood along its natural grain.

"We must calculate the load on this prop," Jun said to Liang, who was writing the figures down on a scrap of paper. "A rectangular rafter twelve centimeters wide and eighteen centimeters deep has a cross-sectional area of two hundred and sixteen square centimeters. The moment of inertia, which represents the member's resistance to bending deflection under load, is calculated as the base times the height cubed, divided by twelve. This yields a value of exactly five thousand eight hundred and thirty-two biquadratic centimeters. When the rafter split along its neutral axis, it effectively became two separate beams of nine centimeters depth stacking on top of each other. The combined moment of inertia of these two unbonded halves is only two times twelve times nine cubed, divided by twelve, which equals one thousand four hundred and fifty-eight biquadratic centimeters. This represents a seventy-five percent drop in structural stiffness, which is why the roof began to sag under the weight of the tiles. The self-weight of the clay tiles and the mortar bed is approximately one point five kilonewtons per square meter. With a tributary area of six square meters, the total dead load on this rafter is nine kilonewtons. Since the rafter is split, its bending strength is reduced by eighty percent. We must install a vertical pine post, fifteen centimeters in diameter, directly under the crack. Pine has a compressive strength parallel to the grain of thirty megapascals, giving us a load capacity of over five hundred kilonewtons, which is more than enough. We will use Euler's critical buckling load formula to verify the structural safety of the prop. With a post height of two point five meters and a radius of seven point five centimeters, the slenderness ratio is thirty-three point three, which is well below the critical limit of fifty. The critical buckling load is calculated at three hundred and eighty kilonewtons, giving us an enormous safety factor of over forty. This means the post will fail by material crushing rather than buckling, ensuring absolute stability."

Jun chiseled the notches into the vertical pine prop, using his broadaxe to square the ends. They set the post under the cracked cedar beam, lifting the roof by an inch using a heavy timber lever.

"Mallet, Liang!" Jun ordered.

They drove the oak wedges under the post base, locking the prop. They laid three pine cross-braces against the brick wall, anchoring the ends to the courtyard columns. The volunteers worked quickly and quietly, passing the tools and materials down the narrow corridor. Among the volunteers was a retired masonry worker named Uncle Feng, who had spent his life repairing the historic walls of Suzhou. He examined the cracks in the brick wall, showing Liang how to pack them with a dry mix of slaked lime and brick dust.

"We must keep the water out of the joints," Uncle Feng whispered. "The water dissolves the old mortar, and when the wind blows, the bricks slide. If we pack them with lime and wedge them with slate chips, the wall will remain rigid under pressure. The slate chips act as mechanical pins, locking the brick courses together and preventing any sliding shear along the joints."

To prepare the mortar, the volunteers set up a small station in the courtyard. They slaked quicklime with water in a wooden tub, watching the violent chemical reaction bubble and release steam. Uncle Feng added ground red brick dust to the lime, creating a traditional hydraulic mortar—*sanheti*—which would set even in the humid atmosphere of the canal city. The young volunteers formed a bucket line, passing the warm mortar down the narrow walkway to where Liang and Uncle Feng were wedging the bricks.

The wall stabilized, its lean halted. The volunteers smiled, passing around canteens of warm tea. Lihua stood watch at the end of the corridor, her sword ready, her eyes scanning the outer lane. The line was held, the roof secure.

The collective effort had saved the northern corridor. The youth carried away the broken branches and swept the slate chips, while the older women prepared hot soup in the pavilion courtyard. Jun watched the team work, noting the sense of mutual care that bound these survivors. They were not just building barriers; they were building a home, sharing their food, and protecting each other with a quiet determination. In this time of crisis, their solidarity was their most powerful tool.


---

In the courtyard of the Hall of Distant Fragrance, the communal kitchen was a hub of activity. The elders had set up three large iron woks over open brick fireplaces, cooking hot rice congee and steaming sweet potatoes scavenged from the nearby garden plots. The smell of boiling ginger tea and toasted sesame filled the air, cutting through the damp chill of the morning. A group of older women sat on wooden benches, sorting dried red beans and packing them into small bags for the watchmen. 'We must share what we have,' Auntie Wong said, handing a bowl of steaming broth to Liang. 'In the city, people tried to hide behind locked doors, but here, we survive because we look after each other. If one family is hungry, we all share the pot. That is the only way to hold the line against the storm outside.' The younger children helped carry water from the stone wells, their laughter bringing a sense of hope to the quiet garden. This mutual aid was the foundation of their community, keeping morale high in the face of constant danger.

---

CHAPTER 5: THE STONE MAZE


The northern part of the garden was a maze of artificial rockeries—*jiashan*—built of yellow stones and Taihu granite blocks chiseled with narrow pathways, caves, and stone staircases. Designed during the Ming Dynasty to evoke the wild mountains of the south, the rockery was a complex labyrinth of narrow clefts, low overhangs, and winding stone stairs that seemed to shift with every step.

But the maze had become a trap. A group of ten zombies, having climbed the outer wall, had entered the rockery maze, their boots clicking on the stone steps. They were lost in the winding paths, their movements blocked by the narrow clefts.

"We must hold them here," Jun said. "The rockery is a natural maze. We will build *mutong*—timber barricades—across the narrow exits, locking the logs into the granite joints. We will leave only one path open, leading to the pond ledge where we can drop them into the water. This will allow us to neutralize them one by one without making any noise."

"How do we lock the logs to the granite, Master?" Liang asked.

"We chiseled pockets into the stone joints," Jun said. "And wedge the pine cross-bars horizontally. The stone will hold the wood without nails. Granite has a compressive strength of eighty megapascals. By cutting pockets five centimeters deep into the joints of the rockery blocks, we create a solid bearing surface that can resist any horizontal push from the dead. We will use seasoned pine logs, ten centimeters in diameter. When wedged tight, the logs will act as compression struts, transferring the load directly into the heavy granite blocks of the rockery."

They discussed the geological properties of the Taihu stone itself. Tao explained to the helpers that these unique limestone blocks had been harvested from the bottom of Lake Tai, where water erosion over thousands of years had dissolved the soft mineral veins, creating the hollows, channels, and interlocking shapes. "This porous geometry is ideal for our barricades," Jun noted as he measured a pocket. "The irregular, weathered cavities act as natural mortises. By carving the ends of our pine logs to a custom shoulder profile—*guyin sun*—we can wedge them directly into these cavities, locking them in place under their own expansion without needing any iron brackets or screws."

Taihu stone blocks are unique limestone rock formations. The ancient garden builders selected these blocks based on four key aesthetic principles: *Shou* (slenderness), *Tou* (translucency), *Lou* (hollowness), and *Zhuo* (wrinkled texture). These principles were not just artistic; the deep, winding cavities (*lou*) and the interlocking passages (*tou*) created a complex physical structure with multiple natural pocket seats. Jun examined a narrow fissure between two massive limestone blocks where a pine log could be anchored. "The limestone has a high density," Jun said, running his fingers along the weathered surface. "Its compressive strength is eighty megapascals, which means it can bear the horizontal thrust of several bodies without cracking. By cutting a shallow notch, five centimeters deep, into the joint line of these blocks, we create a stable seat for our timber struts. The irregular geometry of the Taihu stone acts as a natural mortise, locking the timber in place and preventing it from shifting under pressure."

Jun and Liang worked in the narrow caves, carrying the pine logs. The air was cool, the stone walls rising around them like grey walls. Jun worked with his hand axe, notches the timber.

They blocked three exits, locking the pine logs. The volunteers helped carry the logs through the narrow, winding paths of the maze. It was hard, physical labor, the heavy pine scraping against the rough granite walls. The team worked in a quiet, coordinated line, passing the logs from hand to hand and using rags to wrap the ends to prevent any noise. Among them was a young man named Tao, who had worked as a gardener in the city parks. He knew the layout of the rockery, showing Jun the best joints for anchoring the timbers. "This cave has a double arch," Tao whispered, pointing to a low rock opening. "If we wedge the log here, the weight of the upper stones will press down on the pine, locking it even tighter."

The zombies wandered through the maze, their hands scraping the stone. Guided by the open path, the lead zombie emerged onto the pond ledge.

Lihua and the watchmen stood on the wooden deck of the *Xiaofei Hong*—the Little Flying Rainbow Bridge—which was the only covered bridge in the garden. It was a beautiful structure with three spans and a red wooden corridor, crossing the western channel. From this elevated platform, Lihua had a clear view of the stone maze exits. As the lead zombie emerged onto the narrow granite ledge below, she stood with her weight balanced over her rear foot, her body relaxed. She thrust the steel spear forward in a single, fluid motion—*lan, na, zha*—the traditional spear form. The steel blade penetrated the temple with a quiet, dry crunch, destroying the brain. With a heavy splash, the body fell off the ledge into the water. The pond silt, three feet deep and composed of fine clay and decayed lotus leaves, immediately trapped the fallen body, preventing it from drifting or rising to the surface.

The other watchmen stood behind her, using their spears to handle the next zombie as it emerged. The system worked perfectly; the maze channeled the dead, the ledge isolated them, and the watchmen neutralized them without a sound.

The team worked through the night, clearing the rockery maze. By morning, the stone paths were quiet once more. The volunteers sat on the granite steps, sharing bowls of rice and talking in quiet whispers. Jun watched them, feeling a deep respect for their quiet courage. They had defended their home without a single shot, using the natural layout of the garden and their own coordinated strength. The shared task had brought them closer, turning a group of strangers into a tightly knit community that looked out for one another.


---

Ying, the physics student, sat with the young volunteers, explaining the mechanical advantage of the pulley systems. 'A simple single-pulley system only changes the direction of the force,' she said, demonstrating with a small stone block and a hemp line. 'But when we combine multiple pulleys into a block and tackle—a *shuanglun* system—we distribute the tension load across several rope lines. If we use a two-sheave block and tackle, the mechanical advantage is exactly four. This means a pull of two hundred newtons can lift an eight-hundred-newton log. The trade-off is distance: to lift the log by one meter, we must pull four meters of rope. This is the beauty of simple machines; they allow us to perform heavy engineering tasks that would otherwise require heavy machinery. By coordinating our pulls, a team of five people can easily lift the massive timbers needed to brace the outer walls, sharing the work and ensuring that no one strains their muscles. This cooperative mechanics was not just efficient; it was a way of sharing the physical burden of our defense.'

Jun explained the heat-treatment process of steel to the volunteers at the grinding station. 'The quality of the steel depends on the carbon content and the crystal structure,' he said, holding a worn chisel. 'To make a tool hold its edge, we must heat it in the charcoal fire until it reaches a cherry-red color, about eight hundred degrees Celsius. At this temperature, the iron atoms rearrange into a face-centered cubic structure called austenite. We then quench the steel in oil, cooling it rapidly. This rapid cooling locks the carbon atoms in place, transforming the structure into a body-centered tetragonal lattice called martensite, which is extremely hard but brittle. To reduce the brittleness, we must temper the steel by heating it gently to two hundred degrees and letting it cool slowly. This tempers the martensite, creating a tough, resilient steel that can cut timber without chipping or rolling its edge. By understanding these metallurgical microstructures, we can ensure that our axes and chisels remain sharp and reliable through hours of heavy use on oak or pine columns.'

---

CHAPTER 6: THE LOTUS POND


The central lake of the garden was filled with thick mud and lotus roots, its water three feet deep. The lake was the heart of the garden's water maze, isolating the central island pavilions from the outer walls.

But the water was rising. The main drainage sluice gate at the eastern canal had caved, blocked by silt and trapped dead. The rising water was flooding the lower paths, threatening to swamp the floating decks of the pavilions and submerge the timber columns.

"We must open the sluice," Jun said. "We will build a pine bypass gate, and clear the blocked canal grate using the long timber hook. Liang, get the ropes. We must act before the water reaches the floor of the Hall of Distant Fragrance."

"Master, the water is cold," Liang said. "And the canal grate is deep."

"We have no choice," Jun replied. "If the water rises another ten centimeters, the tenons of the pavilion posts will float out of their stone sockets, and the entire structure will collapse under its own weight. The columns rest in shallow stone bases, the *zhushi*, relying on gravity and tight tenon seats to remain stable. When the water level rises, the timber swells, and the buoyancy reduces the effective load, making the columns slide out of their sockets. We will build a temporary bypass gate from pine planks, notches the ends to slide into the granite channels of the sluice wall, and use a manual lever to lift it."

Jun explained the hydrostatic mechanics of the gate. "A water depth of one meter generates a hydrostatic pressure at the base of the gate of approximately ten kilopascals," he said to Liang as they prepared the planks. "This creates a total horizontal force of fifteen kilonewtons pushing the gate against its granite guide channels. The resulting friction force resisting the lift is close to six kilonewtons. To lift the gate under this load without mechanical assistance is impossible. We must construct a two-meter pine lever with a pivot set twenty centimeters from the gate attachment, providing a ten-to-one mechanical advantage. This reduces the required pulling force to six hundred newtons, which three of us can easily manage."

Jun tied a hemp rope around his waist, stepping into the freezing pond. The water was muddy, smelling of lotus roots and rot. Beside him, Liang and three volunteers held the safety line, their hands red from the cold.

Jun waded through the deep water toward the eastern canal wall, his boots sinking twenty centimeters into the thick silt. The silt was a mixture of decomposed lotus leaves, organic debris, and soft lake clay. "The mud is highly cohesive," Jun called out as he strained to pull his left foot free. "It creates a partial vacuum beneath the sole when you try to lift it, generating a suction force of over three hundred newtons. You must twist your heel to break the suction before lifting." The volunteers held the safety line taut, their muscles straining to support his weight against the current. The water was freezing, numbing his legs through his canvas trousers, but he forced himself to move forward, his hands tight on the timber hook. He hooked a heavy, waterlogged pine log that had jammed diagonally across the iron grate, anchoring the bodies of the dead in the current. By using the two-meter pine lever rigged to the sluice wall, the volunteers on the platform pulled the rope. The lever, operating with a ten-to-one mechanical advantage, multiplied their six-hundred-newton pull into a force of six kilonewtons, which easily pried the log free, releasing the blockage with a loud rush of water.

The water rushed through the channel with a loud gurgle, the pond level immediately beginning to drop. The volunteers cheered, hauling Jun back onto the stone platform.

Meanwhile, Chun and the other builders installed the new pine bypass gate. They slid the five-centimeter-thick pine boards into the granite guide channels, locking them with a simple timber lever. The gate allowed them to regulate the water level, ensuring the pavilions remained dry while keeping the ponds deep enough to act as a barrier.

The path went dry, the pavilions saved. Jun sat on the stone steps, wrapped in a dry blanket that Auntie Wong had brought, drinking a cup of hot ginger tea.

"The water is under control now," he said, his teeth chattering. "But we must secure the western screen-wall. It is the weakest point in our line. If they push, the screen-windows will split."

The survivors gathered around him, offering dry clothes and warm water. The collective care of the community was their true strength; they looked after each other, sharing their resources and ensuring that no one worked alone. Jun felt a warm sense of belonging, knowing that their work was protecting this sanctuary of peace. The children brought him dry socks, and the elders stoked a small charcoal brazier to warm his feet. It was a beautiful display of mutual aid in a world of storm.


---

The canals of Suzhou were a complex network of waterways that had served as the city's main transportation system for centuries. The water was controlled by a series of stone sluices and arched bridges, which regulated the flow from the nearby Taihu Lake. Jun stood on the granite deck of the canal wall, observing the current. 'The water flow behaves according to the principles of fluid dynamics,' he said to Liang. 'The flow rate is equal to the cross-sectional area of the channel multiplied by the fluid velocity. When the sluice is blocked, the velocity drops to zero, and the static head increases, raising the water level. By opening the bypass channels, we increase the cross-sectional area, allowing the water to drain and reducing the hydrostatic pressure on our foundations. We must monitor the banks closely; if the current is too fast, it will erode the clay banks, causing the stone walls to slide into the canal. The community must work together to clear the channels, maintaining the balance between the water's defense and its hydrostatic threat.'

---

CHAPTER 7: THE BAMBOO FENCE


The western wall of the garden was low, built of hollow brick screen-windows that were decorative but weak. The screen-windows, shaped like lotus leaves, flower petals, and geometric lattices, were designed to offer glimpses of the outer street, but they had no structural strength. They were built for aesthetics, not defense, and could easily be shattered by the pressure of a crowd.

"We must reinforce the screen," Jun said. "The brick will split if they push. We will build a *zhuban*—a dense bamboo palisade fence along the wall face, lashing the canes to driven pine posts using copper wire."

"Where do we get the wire?" Liang asked.

"The old lantern hangers," Jun said. "Go, Liang! Split the bamboo. We need two hundred canes, three meters long."

Jun and Liang prepared the green bamboo canes, notches the ends. They lashed the bamboo to the pine posts, creating a solid green wall that blocked the screen-windows.

The community gathered to help with the construction. Volunteers of all ages joined the work, splitting the bamboo and stripping the copper wire from the old garden lanterns. Mr. Zhou, the scholar, showed the younger volunteers how to tie the lashing knots.

"We must wrap the wire three times around each cane," he explained. "And twist the ends with pliers to maintain the tension. This ensures the bamboo cannot slide laterally when pressed by a crowd. The copper wire has an ultimate tensile strength of two hundred and fifty megapascals. By twisting the wires, we create a mechanical lock that prevents the bamboo from slipping along the posts, even under dynamic loading."

Jun explained the structural properties of moso bamboo (*phyllostachys edulis*) to the students. "Bamboo is a natural composite material," he said, holding a split cane. "Its structure consists of high-density cellulose fibers embedded in a soft lignin matrix. The fibers are concentrated in the outer skin, which gives the bamboo a high tensile strength of one hundred and eighty megapascals parallel to the grain, comparable to mild steel. Its modulus of elasticity is twenty gigapascals, which provides high flexibility. When the zombies push against the palisade, the bamboo fence will deflect, absorbing the kinetic energy of the crowd and transferring the load to the driven pine posts. The posts, which are fifteen centimeters in diameter, are driven one meter into the firm clay soil. Each post can resist a lateral soil pressure of five kilonewtons, giving the entire twenty-post palisade a load capacity of one hundred kilonewtons. We will drive the posts at a spacing of exactly one point five meters, which ensures that the bending moment on the bamboo members does not exceed their elastic limit under the design load."

The work proceeded in a steady, coordinated line. The volunteers split the bamboo using small hand-axes, while the children stripped the plastic insulation from scavenged copper wire, humming old folk songs as they worked. The elders sat on stools, twisting the wire ties and passing them to Jun and Liang who were lashing the canes to the heavy pine posts.

By evening, the western wall was completely covered by a solid green fence of bamboo, its surface tight and resilient. The refugees stood in groups, talking quietly and sharing food. Auntie Wong brought a pot of hot tea and some sweet biscuits, sharing them among the workers.

The wall was secured. Lihua walked along the line, tapping the bamboo with her sword. The fence was solid, a silent barrier that protected the garden from the street outside.

"It is strong, Master Jun," she said, smiling. "The dead will find no purchase here."

The community stood together, looking at their finished work. The sun was setting, casting a golden light over the green bamboo and the white plaster walls. It was a beautiful, peaceful moment, a testament to what they could accomplish when they worked together. Jun smiled, picking up his tools. They had held the line, but they must prepare for the next step.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE MOON GATE


The *Yueya Men*—the Moon Gate—was a circular brick archway leading to the inner garden. The arch was built of thin, black bricks set in a perfect circle, representing the full moon. It was a beautiful transition space, designed to frame the view of the bamboo grove on the other side. In classical Chinese garden design, the Moon Gate served as a portal between different worlds, offering a glimpse of what lay ahead while framing the current view like a painting on a silk scroll.

But the archway had no door, designed for an open, unobstructed view. It was a portal of harmony, not of defense.

"We must seal it," Jun said, looking at the circular brick frame. "We will build a *yueyaban*—a circular timber double-door set into the brick arch. We will use a pine frame and lock the hinges into the brick joints using iron plugs. This will create a solid barrier that can be locked at night."

"Master, a circle door is difficult to build," Liang said, adjusting his spectacles. "The planks must be cut to varying lengths to form the circle, and the hinges must align with the curvature of the arch."

"We will use a geometric template," Jun explained. "We will bend a thin strip of split bamboo to match the inner radius of the Moon Gate, which is exactly one point five meters. We will lay out the pine boards on the floor, trace the template, and cut the circle using a bow-saw. The boards will be joined using tongue-and-groove joints—*sunlan*—to ensure there are no gaps. We will reinforce the door with two horizontal spruce braces—*chuandai*—slid into tapered slots on the back face of the door. The shear stress on the hinge pins must be calculated. If the total weight of the timber door is eighty kilograms, each of the four hinge pins supports a vertical shear load of two hundred newtons. By using sixteen-millimeter steel pins driven eighty millimeters deep into the granite joints, the shear stress on the steel is only one point five megapascals, which is negligible compared to the steel's shear capacity of one hundred and fifty megapascals. The critical factor is the bearing strength of the mortar joint. We must pack the hinges with lead-wool grouting, driven tight with a caulking tool, to distribute the load and prevent local crushing of the brickwork."

Ying, the physics student, explained the geometry of the circle to the volunteers who were holding the template. "The Moon Gate is a perfect circle, which has the equation x squared plus y squared equals r squared," she said, drawing a circle in the sand. "With a radius of one point five meters, the total circumference of the gate is nine point forty-two meters. To build a door that fits this archway perfectly, we must cut our pine planks to varying lengths. The longest center planks must be exactly three meters long, while the outer edge planks will be much shorter, calculated using the Pythagorean theorem for each offset distance from the center. Furthermore, because of the humid climate in Suzhou, wood swells and contracts depending on the relative humidity. Pine can expand by up to two percent across the grain when exposed to damp air. If we build the door to the exact radius of the arch, it will swell and jam in winter. We must leave a clearance gap of exactly twelve millimeters around the perimeter of the door to allow for this thermal and moisture expansion, sealing the gap with a flexible strip of thick leather."

Jun and the volunteers worked in the courtyard, using a long table as a workbench. A group of local school children helped hold the bamboo template, while Ying, the physics student, used a compass to verify the radius. The cooperation was seamless; the volunteers passed the hand-planes and chisels, and the elders brought warm tea.

Jun cut the tongue-and-groove joints, using his shoulder plane to shave the edges until the boards fit together with a tight, seamless friction fit. He then slid the spruce braces into the tapered slots, locking the boards into a single, rigid circular panel.

To secure the hinges, Jun chiseled deep pockets into the joints of the circular brick arch. The bricks were ancient black clay bricks, fired in low-oxygen wood kilns, which made them extremely hard but brittle. He forged four iron anchor pins from old lantern hooks, twisting the steel to create ribbing that would grip the mortar. "We must pack the pockets with lead-wool grouting," Jun explained to Liang. "Lead is a highly ductile metal. By driving the lead-wool into the pocket using a caulking tool and a mallet, the lead compresses and flows into the porous surface of the brickwork, creating a tight mechanical interlock. Unlike concrete mortar, which can crack under the dynamic shock of a door slamming, the lead will deform plastically, absorbing the kinetic energy and distributing the load across a larger brick surface area."

"Hold the door, volunteers!" Jun called out.

Six young men lifted the heavy circular door, aligning the hinges with the iron plugs. Jun drove the hinge pins home, locking the door into the archway. The circular double-door swung smoothly, meeting at the center with a tight, solid *cluck*.

"It's like a wooden moon," Liang said, tapping the door.

"A moon that will keep the shadow out," Jun replied, sliding the oak bolt into the center brackets.

The community members stood in the courtyard, admiring the finished door. The wood was clean and smooth, its grain tracing the circular shape of the arch. It looked like a natural part of the garden, a beautiful barrier that protected the inner sanctuary. The volunteers laughed and shared cups of warm water, their collective pride in the work evident. Jun watched them, feeling a deep sense of accomplishment. They had turned a beautiful archway into a secure gate, blending utility and design to protect their home. The children ran their hands along the smooth grain of the pine, finding comfort in the solid structure. In this time of danger, the moon door stood as a symbol of their unity, a beautiful barrier forged by their own hands.


---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE GARDEN BREACH


A massive horde of five thousand dead, having broken through the outer Suzhou canals, reached the Humble Administrator's Garden. Drawn by the scent of life, they pushed through the narrow alleys, their numbers filling the streets.

The western screen-wall, weakened by the constant dampness, caved under the pressure, the bamboo fence splitting. The horde flooded the outer garden, their numbers filling the corridors and the rockery pathways.

The survivors retreated to the central island, but the Winding Bridge was the only path.

"Drop the bridge!" Jun yelled from the western pier.

Liang stood on the southern pier, his hands shaking. He pulled the oak key. With a loud *clack*, the lock released, and the middle deck tilted, dropping into the deep water of the pond. A wave of muddy water splashed over the lily pads.

But Jun was trapped on the wall side, the gap too wide to jump. Behind him, three zombies were crawling down the corridor, their hands reaching out.

Jun ran toward the Fragrance of Snow Pavilion, his boots scraping on the wet pine walkways. Behind him, the sound of splintering timber and cracking bricks was deafening. The western palisade had collapsed under the hydrostatic load of the massive crowd of the dead pressing against it. A wave of grey, mummified figures flooded the outer garden, crawling over the rockeries and down the covered corridors. Jun reached the pavilion platform just as three zombies emerged from the willow shadows, their arms outstretched. He looked at the three-meter gap in the Winding Bridge—it was too wide to jump with his heavy canvas tool vest and steel broadaxe. He looked up and saw a massive wisteria vine (*wisteria sinensis*) hanging from the branch of an ancient pine tree that grew on the pond ledge. The vine was as thick as a man's thigh, its woody stem twisted and strong. "Liang! Catch my toolbox!" Jun yelled, throwing his heavy wooden chest across the water. He grabbed the wisteria vine, stepping back to maximize his swing radius, and leaped from the pavilion railing.

Ying calculated the forces of the swing as she watched Jun fly over the dark water. "The vine acts as a pendulum," she explained to Liang. "With a length of five meters and Jun's mass of eighty kilograms, the tension force at the lowest point of the swing is equal to the gravitational force plus the centripetal force. This generates a dynamic tension load of over one point five kilonewtons. Wisteria vine has an ultimate tensile strength of over thirty megapascals, giving it a safe load capacity of six kilonewtons. The vine will easily hold, but the critical point is the anchorage of the roots in the granite rockery. The root system has a pullout resistance of ten kilonewtons, giving us a safety factor of over six.' Jun swung in a wide, sweeping arc over the lily pads, his feet clearing the reaching arms of the water-walkers by less than a meter. He released the vine at the peak of the swing, landing on the central island deck with a heavy roll, his shoulder absorbing the impact force of three hundred newtons."

The horde reached the water's edge but was blocked by the gap. They stood on the stone piers, their eyes cloudy, unable to cross. Several figures tumbled into the deep water, sinking into the thick mud.

The garden was isolated, the survivors safe on the island.

The defenders stood along the shore, holding their spears and watching the canal. The water had held, and the dropped bridge deck had blocked the route. The community members stood in quiet groups, holding each other and checking on the children. The tension was high, but there was no panic. They knew their barriers were strong, and their cooperative organization had saved them. Jun sat on the wooden deck, catching his breath as Liang checked his hands. They had survived the first breach, and their defenses had held the line.

The silt below the bridge pier was three feet deep, composed of decomposed lotus leaves and organic mud. As the zombies stepped off the pier, they sank to their knees, the high yield stress of the mud locking their legs like a vise. They could not move forward or pull their feet free, leaving them trapped in the canal. Lihua and the watchmen stood on the stone steps, using their long spears to neutralize the trapped walkers one by one with silent, clean strikes to the temple. The cooperation of the defenders was seamless; some held the safety lines, while others carried away the spent spears to be sharpened. Jun watched the operation, his heart rate slowly returning to normal. The garden water maze had worked exactly as designed, turning the enemy's numbers against them and keeping the sanctuary secure.


---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE QUIET SANCTUARY


The morning sun rose over a silent Suzhou, its light reflecting on the still ponds of the garden. The red pavilions stood like islands in the green sea of lotus leaves, their tiled roofs gleaming in the morning light.

The bridges were dropped. The water pavilions were secure, the survivors safe on the central island.

Jun sat on the deck of the Fragrance of Snow Pavilion, his hands resting on his toolbox. Beside him, Liang was cleaning his broadaxe. Jun took out his Japanese waterstone and filed the teeth of the cross-cut saw, setting each tooth at a forty-five degree angle.

"The teeth must have a set of exactly zero point five millimeters," Jun explained to Chun, the apprentice. "This is the distance each tooth is bent away from the plane of the blade. The alternating set creates a kerf—a cut width—that is wider than the steel blade itself. If the set is too narrow, the wet wood fibers will swell and bind the blade, increasing friction and causing the saw to jam. If the set is too wide, the saw will remove too much wood, requiring double the physical effort to cut. A set of zero point five millimeters is perfect for green pine or oak." He wrapped the finished saws in oil-soaked paper to protect them from the damp lake air.

Chun and Liang sat on the stone steps, discussing the history of the garden. The Humble Administrator's Garden had been constructed during the Ming Dynasty, around 1509, by a retired government official named Wang Xianchen. He had named it *Zhuozheng Yuan*—the Garden of the Unsuccessful Politician—reflecting a classic Daoist desire to withdraw from the corrupt politics of the imperial court and find harmony in nature. The garden was designed around the principle of 'borrowed scenery' (*jiefeng*), where views of distant pagodas and hills were framed by the garden's structures, making the small space feel vast and infinite. "This design philosophy is what saves us now," Chun said, pointing to the winding corridors. "The garden was built to slow down the visitor, to make them wander and reflect. By reinforcing these winding paths, we have turned a sanctuary of art into a defensive maze where the dead are lost, while we remain connected on our central island. It is a perfect synthesis of classical form and practical utility, built on the cooperative labor of our community."

Chun and Liang discussed the joinery styles they would use in Suzhou. Chun explained that the traditional Suzhou style of woodworking (*Su Zuo*) was famous for its structural elegance and complex hidden joints. "Unlike the heavy northern style, the southern style uses thinner members but relies on complex interlocks like the three-way mitered joint and the hidden tenon," Chun said. "This design provides high structural flexibility under wind loads while maintaining a clean, minimalist exterior. We can adapt these joints to resist the horizontal shear force of a crowd pushing against a garden bridge, using locking wedges to keep the tenons tight."

"We have built a good gate in the garden, Master Jun," Liang said.

"A gate is only as good as the water that surrounds it," Jun replied, his voice quiet. "And the community that stands behind it. The water maze works because we maintain the level, but the true defense is the solidarity of the people."

The refugees and volunteers gathered in the plaza to celebrate their survival. They set up tables in the pavilion yard, sharing bowls of hot rice congee and sweet biscuits. People laughed and shared stories of the night.

Master Shen walked over, carrying a radio receiver. The device crackled with static, but a voice was clear.

"The radio received a transmission from Hunan. Fenghuang. The stilt houses along the Tuojiang River are under siege, and the river dead are rising. They need builders to reinforce the timber stilts and build water barriers. The message states that the Hall of Distant Fragrance and the Flying Rainbow Bridge have sustained minor damage from the rising water level, and the wooden support columns need immediate reinforcement. The canals are rising, flooding the lower tenon joints."

The Humble Administrator's Garden—*Zhuozheng Yuan*—was a masterpiece of classical Chinese garden design, covering over five hectares. It was built during the Ming Dynasty, around 1509, by Wang Xianchen, and reflected the classic Daoist and Confucian philosophy of harmony with nature. The garden was built around a maze of connected ponds, bridges, and winding covered corridors, designed to create a shifting landscape that confused the eye. It was a perfect defense system if reinforced, using the water to isolate the historic halls. The garden structures, built with traditional dougong bracket systems and mortise-and-tenon joints, needed structural evaluation. The shifting water levels of the canals had weakened the stone foundations of the bridges, and the builders' expertise was required to restore them before the horde arrived. Jun and Liang discussed how they would repair them using stepped splice joints—*guyin sun*—and hydraulic mortar of lime, clay, and sticky rice water to seal the underwater masonry.

To ensure their safety and logistics during their journey north, the volunteers helped them pack. They loaded their backpacks with dried pork belly, salted duck eggs, and several thermoses of hot tea. They shook hands with Mr. Zhou and Lihua, their eyes filled with a mutual respect.

Jun stood up, checking the edge of his axe. He closed his toolbox, locking the brass latch.

"Let's go, Liang," Jun said. "We head to Hunan. We have some stilt houses to build."

They walked down the path toward the eastern gate, their tools slung over their shoulders. Behind them, the survivors waved goodbye, their voices rising in a soft song of farewell. The garden was silent, a sanctuary of peace in a world of storm.
