STORY 22: THE RIVER STILTS
Setting: Tuojiang River, Fenghuang Town, Hunan Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE RIVER STILTS


The Tuojiang River wound through the ancient town of Fenghuang like a green silk ribbon, its waters rushing past the red sandstone banks and beneath the heavy stone arches of the Hongqiao Bridge. Along the riverfront, the historic stilt houses—*diaojiaolou*—clung to the cliffs, their timber supports rising from the dark water like long legs. For centuries, these houses had stood as a testament to the ingenuity of the Miao and Tujia builders, who shaped their homes to fit the steep topography of the river gorge. But now, in the silence of the wider crisis, the river had become a barrier, and the timber stilts were under threat from the rising water level and the decay of the wooden columns.

Jun stood on the lower deck of a stilt house, his broadaxe in his hand. The river water swirled around his boots, carrying bits of drift wood and mud. Beside him, Liang was checking the base of a cedar column, his face wet with mist.

"The water is rising fast, Master Jun," Liang said. "The constant rain in the mountains has increased the flow, and the wood rot at the base of these columns is advanced. If we do not reinforce them, the weight of the houses will collapse them into the river."

"We must assess the damage column by column," Jun said. "Red cedar has a high resistance to moisture, but these posts have been in the water for over forty years. The fungal rot has weakened the outer fibers. We must shore them before the next surge."

They waded through the water, checking each post. The community had retreated to the upper stone streets of the town, leaving the lower stilt decks for the watchmen. The families worked together, setting up watch stations and preparing materials. Elders cooked rice and shared blankets, while the youth kept watch from the balconies. The collective coordination of the town was their only hope.

Jun explained the structural distribution of loads on the stilt columns, known as *diaojiaolou*. 'The traditional stilt houses of Fenghuang rely on cedar poles driven deep into the riverbed,' he said, showing Liang the diagonal bracing joints. 'The vertical load of the house is carried by the columns, but the lateral load from the river current creates a bending moment. When the wood rot splits the base of the stilt, it reduces the cross-sectional area and the bending stiffness. By cutting a stepped splice joint—*guyin sun*—we can insert a new section of seasoned pine, locking it with oak wedges and iron hoops. This restores the compressive strength of forty megapascals and ensures the columns can resist the lateral force of the water during a flood. We must wrap the joints in hemp and coal tar to prevent water entry. This traditional method of shoring is critical for preserving the historic integrity of these timbers while ensuring their ultimate stability under pressure.'

Ying calculated the hydrodynamic force of the river current on the timber breakwaters. 'The fluid drag force is equal to one-half the water density multiplied by the velocity squared, the drag coefficient, and the frontal area of the structure,' she explained to the local volunteers. 'With a water velocity of three meters per second and a drag coefficient of one point two, each log experiences a drag force of over two kilonewtons per square meter. To resist this force, we must arrange the breakwaters in an angled wedge formation at exactly thirty degrees to the current. This reduces the effective frontal area and splits the water flow, directing the floating debris away from the stilt foundations and reducing the bending moment on our timber columns.' This calculation was essential for the design, showing how the angle of the breakwater could save the fragile timber stilts below the houses.

In the upper street of Fenghuang, the neighborhood committee had set up a communal kitchen in a stone courtyard. Elders boiled large pots of spicy vegetable soup and prepared bowls of steamed rice mixed with cured Hunan pork. The smell of chili, ginger, and woodsmoke rose into the misty mountain air, warming the spirits of the watchmen. 'We must stand together,' Auntie Chen said, passing a bowl to Liang. 'The river has always been our life, and now we must make it our shield. As long as we share our food and keep the fires burning, we will hold these houses.' The children carried wood to the fires, while the older men shared stories of the old floods, reinforcing the collective bonds of the community. This mutual aid was the foundation of their community, keeping morale high in the face of constant danger.

The volunteers worked together to assemble the suspended pine walkways connecting the stilt houses. Jun showed them how to cut mortise seats into the outer floor joists. 'We use split-bamboo ropes and pine planks to build a flexible bridge,' he said. 'The planks must be bolted to the joists with timber pegs, allowing the structure to flex with the movement of the houses. This prevents the joints from cracking under dynamic loads when people run across. The tension load on the suspension lines is distributed across three anchor columns, ensuring that no single post bears the entire weight of the walkway. This cooperative system allows us to move safely above the water, bypassing the flooded streets below. By sharing the work of lashing and pegging, the community built a lifeline that linked their homes in a single network of defense.'


---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE TIMBER SPLICE


To shore the sagging stilt houses, Jun decided to use a traditional stepped splice joint—*guyin sun*—to replace the rotted bottom sections of the cedar columns. They would jack up the house frame, cut away the decayed wood, and insert a new section of seasoned pine, locking them with oak wedges and iron hoops.

"Master, the load on this column is nearly five tons," Liang said, adjusting his screw-jack. "If the jack slips while we are cutting the joint, the entire balcony will drop."

"We will install temporary pine props—*fuzhu*—on both sides of the column before we cut," Jun explained. "This will distribute the load and provide a safety factor of three. We must cut the joint shoulders with high precision; any gap will cause the load to concentrate on one side, splitting the wood."

Jun used his framing chisel and mallet to cut the stepped shoulder into the column. The sound of wood-carving was quiet, lost in the roar of the river. Liang prepared the new pine block, shaping the tenon ends with a drawknife until they fit the joint with a tight friction fit.

The volunteers helped lift the heavy pine blocks, forming a line to pass the timbers from the shore. The cooperation of the town was critical; merchants, teachers, and fishermen worked side by side, their hands rough from the labor but their spirits high. They drove the oak wedges home, locking the splice. The column stood firm, its base secure in the sandstone socket.


---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE CURRENT DEFLECTORS


The river current was carrying heavy debris—driftwood, collapsed docks, and floating refuse—which struck the stilt columns with significant impact force. Jun realized they must build angled timber breakwaters—*pashui*—upstream to deflect the drift and protect the shored columns.

"The force of the current is high," Ying, the physics student, explained. "A water velocity of three meters per second generates a high dynamic pressure. We must align the breakwaters at an angle of thirty degrees to the current to split the flow and reduce the impact force by seventy percent."

"We will use spruce logs," Jun said. "And anchor them into the sandstone riverbed using iron bars. Liang, prepare the star-drills. We must drill the rock sockets by hand."

Jun and Liang worked from a wooden raft, holding the star-drill against the red sandstone under the water. Liang struck the drill with a sledgehammer, while Jun turned it slightly after each blow. The work was slow and exhausting, the freezing river water splashing over them.

The volunteers on the shore prepared the spruce logs, cutting the ends to fit the rock sockets. They lashed the logs together in a wedge formation using thick wire, creating a solid barrier that split the current and directed the floating debris away from the stilt houses. The breakwaters stood firm, their angled design diverting the river's force.


---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE WOVEN WALKWAYS


Because the lower streets of Fenghuang were flooded, the defenders could not move between the stilt houses safely. Jun decided to construct a secondary evacuation network: a series of suspended timber walkways—*jiaban*—connecting the balconies of the houses.

"The walkway must be flexible," Jun explained. "It will hang from the main roof trusses using split-bamboo ropes. This allows the deck to swing slightly under load, reducing the stress on the timber joints."

"We will notch the pine planks to fit the ropes," Liang said, split-sawing the planks. "And use oak pegs to lock them. This avoids using iron nails, which rust and split the wood in this damp air."

The volunteers helped split the pine logs and weave the bamboo ropes. The refugees worked together on the balconies, passing the planks and tying the knots. The coordination was seamless; everyone contributed, sharing the work and ensuring that the elderly and children could move to the high streets if the lower decks were breached.

They completed the first bridge, a ten-meter span connecting the tea house to the pharmacy. Liang tested the walk, his boots quiet on the pine planks. The walkway swung slightly but remained stable, a secure path above the rushing river.


---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE RIVER NET


To prevent swimming zombies from drifting down the river and reaching the stilt decks, Jun decided to forge and install a heavy river barrier: a series of iron chains and logs stretched across the narrowest part of the river gorge.

"The barrier must withstand the drag of the river and the weight of the debris," Ying explained. "We must anchor the chains deep into the stone walls of the cliffs on both sides, using heavy iron bolts sealed with sulfur."

"Liang, we need the black-smith's hearth," Jun said. "We will forge the iron link pins from the scavenged window grates."

They set up a temporary forge in the street, heating the iron bars in a charcoal fire until they glowed bright orange. Jun hammered the metal on an anvil, shaping the heavy link pins, while Liang assembled the chain. The volunteers helped turn the bellows and carry the heavy fuel, their faces dark with soot.

They hauled the chain across the river using a hand-winch, anchoring the ends to the sandstone cliffs. They attached floating logs to the chain, creating a continuous floating barrier that blocked the river. The net immediately caught the drifting debris, keeping the waters around the stilt houses clear.


---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE MORTISE BRACES


The shored columns needed additional lateral stability to resist the wave action of the river and the push of the debris. Jun decided to install diagonal timber braces—*chuanzi*—between the columns, locking them into chiseled mortise seats.

"The diagonal braces will transfer the lateral load to the main support columns," Jun explained. "We must cut the mortise seats at an angle of forty-five degrees to ensure the best distribution of forces."

"Master, the timber is wet," Liang said. "It is difficult to chisel a clean shoulder."

"Use the narrow chisel and work with light blows," Jun said. "We must not split the wood fibers. The wet timber will swell as it dries, locking the tenon even tighter in the mortise."

Jun chiseled the joints, his hands steady despite the cold wind from the river. Liang and the volunteers carried the braces, notches the ends to fit the mortise seats. They slid the timbers into place, driving oak pegs to secure the joint. The bracing network formed a rigid truss, stabilizing the stilt frames.


---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE COMMUNAL KITCHEN


As the winter wind blew down the Tuojiang River, the temperature dropped, and the damp cold chilled the defenders. In the upper stone street of the town, the community organized a communal kitchen to support the workers and watchmen.

"We must keep the fires burning," Auntie Chen said, stirring a large iron wok. "A hot bowl of rice and spicy pork will keep the cold out of the bones. Everyone must eat."

The elders managed the kitchen, boiling large pots of rice and brewing herbal tea. The refugees shared their food, pooling their dried meat, salted eggs, and winter cabbage to cook meals for the community. The children helped carry wood and water, their laughter lifting the spirits of the workers.

Jun and Liang sat on a wooden bench, sharing a hot bowl of rice. The warmth of the food and the quiet talk of the survivors brought a sense of peace to the dark night. The collective solidarity of the town was their greatest strength, keeping them united and strong.


---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE UPPER TERRACES


If the river defenses were breached, the survivors needed a secure evacuation route to the upper stone streets of the town. Jun decided to construct a series of heavy timber staircases—*tianti*—anchored to the sandstone cliff face.

"The staircases must be anchored to the rock," Jun explained. "We will use rock-bolts chiseled into the sandstone, and frame the stairs using thick spruce stringers."

"The sandstone is soft, Master," Liang said. "We must drill the holes deep to prevent the bolts from pulling out under load."

"Yes," Jun agreed. "We will drill eighty millimeters deep and seal the bolts with molten lead. This will create a solid mechanical lock that can bear the weight of twenty people at once."

Jun and Liang chiseled the rock sockets, hanging from ropes above the river. The volunteers on the upper street held the safety lines, their hands steady as they supported the carpenters. They framed the stairs, pegging the spruce steps to the stringers. The staircases rose from the lower stilt decks to the high street, providing a safe escape route.


---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE FLOOD GATE


The rising water was still a threat. Jun realized they must restore an ancient stone sluice gate upstream, which had caved and blocked the bypass channel. Opening the gate would divert a portion of the river flow, lowering the water level at the stilt houses.

"The gate is blocked by heavy granite blocks," Liang said, looking at the fallen arch. "We must lift them to clear the channel."

"We will build a timber gantry crane," Jun said. "And use a block-and-tackle system to lift the stones. The gantry will transfer the load to the solid rock walls of the channel."

Jun and the volunteers framed the gantry using larch poles, locking the joints with heavy hemp ropes. They rigged the block-and-tackle, using three wooden pulleys to multiply their pulling force. The volunteers hauled the ropes together, their voices rising in a rhythmic chant as they lifted the heavy granite blocks from the channel.

The stones rose, clearing the gate. The water rushed into the bypass channel with a roar, the river level at the stilt houses immediately dropping by thirty centimeters. The threat of flooding was averted.


---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE SAFE HAVEN


The morning sun rose over Fenghuang, casting a golden light on the shored stilt houses and the quiet waters of the Tuojiang River. The timber supports stood firm, their new splices and braces gleaming in the light.

The river barrier had held, and the water level was stable. The stilt houses were secure, the community safe on the upper terraces.

Jun sat on the deck, cleaning his tools. Beside him, Liang was sharpening his broadaxe. Jun wrapped his chisels in oil-soaked paper, locking them in his wooden toolbox.

"We have shored the stilts well, Master Jun," Liang said.

"The stilts are strong because the community worked together to build them," Jun replied. "We held the river because we stood as one."

The radio receiver crackled with static, and a voice called from Guizhou. The Miao walled village of Xijiang was under siege, their timber houses at risk from fire. They needed builders to construct firebreaks and reinforce the gates.

Jun stood up, locking the brass latch of his toolbox. "Let's go, Liang," he said. "We head to Guizhou. We have a village to save."

STORY 23: THE MIAO SILVER FORGE
Setting: Xijiang Walled Village, Guizhou Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE HILLSIDE VILLAGE


The wooden houses of the Xijiang Miao village clung to the steep hills of Guizhou like a flock of birds, their dark timber structures rising in tiers above the green terraced fields. The village, with over a thousand wooden homes, was the largest Miao settlement in the world, its architecture preserved for centuries through traditional carpentry. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the high density of the wooden homes was a major hazard; a single fire would sweep through the valley in hours, destroying the entire sanctuary. Jun and Liang stood on the lower ridge, assessing the layout. The valley air was cool, the wind carrying the smell of wet pine and coal smoke. Lihua and the local helpers stood with them, their hands ready. The community had retreated to the central square, setting up watches and shoring the timber posts. They must act together to prevent disaster.

Jun explained the structural distribution of loads on the Miao wooden buildings, known as *diaojiaolou*. 'The traditional stilt houses of Xijiang rely on cedar poles driven deep into the steep hillside,' he said, showing Liang the diagonal bracing joints. 'The vertical load of the house is carried by the columns, but the lateral load from the sliding earth creates a bending moment. When the wood rot splits the base of the stilt, it reduces the cross-sectional area and the bending stiffness. By cutting a stepped splice joint—*guyin sun*—we can insert a new section of seasoned pine, locking it with oak wedges and iron hoops. This restores the compressive strength of forty megapascals and ensures the columns can resist the lateral force of the ground. We must wrap the joints in hemp and coal tar to prevent water entry. This traditional method of shoring is critical for preserving the historic integrity of these timbers while ensuring their ultimate stability under pressure.'

Ying calculated the thermal propagation rate of fire between the wooden houses. 'The heat transfer by radiation is proportional to the absolute temperature to the fourth power, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the walls,' she explained to the local volunteers. 'With a spacing of only two meters between these pine structures, a fire in one house will ignite the adjacent wall in less than three minutes. To prevent this, we must create a physical firebreak by systematically dismantling the small wooden outbuildings, creating a gap of at least six meters. This reduces the radiation heat flux below the ignition threshold of dry pine, which is fifteen kilowatts per square meter. By clearing this gap, we can contain the fire to a single block, protecting the main residential area of the village.'

In the central plaza of the Miao village, the community had set up a communal kitchen. Elders boiled large pots of vegetable soup and prepared bowls of steamed rice mixed with cured bacon. The smell of chili, ginger, and woodsmoke rose into the misty mountain air, warming the spirits of the watchmen. 'We must stand together,' Auntie Long said, passing a bowl to Liang. 'The valley has always been our home, and now we must make it our fortress. As long as we share our food and keep the fires burning, we will hold these houses.' The children carried wood to the fires, while the older men shared stories of the old floods, reinforcing the collective bonds of the community. This mutual aid was the foundation of their community, keeping morale high in the face of constant danger.

The volunteers worked together to assemble the gravity stone chutes on the steep stone stairways. Jun showed them how to cut mortise seats into the horizontal pine frames. 'We use split-bamboo ropes and heavy spruce logs to build a slide frame,' he said. 'The granite boulders must be loaded onto the wooden slides, allowing us to roll them down the stairs when needed. This prevents the logs from slipping sideways under load. The kinetic energy of a forty-kilogram granite boulder rolling down a thirty-degree slope for twenty meters is over four kilojoules, which is more than enough to break the advance of a crowd. By sharing the work of carving and stacking, the community built a defense system that turned the steep terrain to our advantage.'

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE FIREBREAK


To protect the village from fire, Jun decided to create a wide firebreak by systematically dismantling three small wooden storage sheds along the western ridge. This would create a six-meter gap, preventing a fire from jumping between the residential blocks. Liang and ten local volunteers carried the heavy tools—two-man saws, axes, and ropes. They worked in coordination, sharing water and encouraging each other as they worked under the hot sun. Jun chiseled the notches into the horizontal timber braces, using his mallet to release the tenons. The volunteers pulled the ropes, hauling the timbers away from the path. The work was exhausting, but the group worked in unison, realizing their safety depended on their mutual coordination.

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE SILVER SMITHY


Because the village gate needed reinforcement, Jun set up a temporary forge in the traditional silver smithy in the central plaza. The smithy, built of pine columns and capped with a tiled roof, had been used for generations to forge the intricate Miao silver jewelry. Now, they would use the hearth to melt scrap iron and forge heavy gate brackets and lock pins. Jun and Liang heated the metal bars in a charcoal fire until they glowed bright orange. The volunteers helped turn the bellows, their faces dark with soot, while the elders carried water in wooden buckets to quench the hot steel. They hammered the iron on a stone anvil, shaping the heavy brackets that would secure the gates.

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE VALLEY GATE


The main entry to the village was the Valley Gate—a massive timber-girt gatehouse at the bottom of the valley, supported by four red cedar columns. The gatehouse was the primary defense line, blocking the narrow mountain road that led into the valley. Jun decided to reinforce the gate using heavy pine cross-beams, locking them into chiseled slots on the cedar columns. Liang and the builders chiseled the slots, their hands steady despite the damp cold. The volunteers helped lift the pine beams, forming a chain to pass the heavy timbers from the plaza. They bolted the braces, creating a rigid frame that stabilized the entire structure, ready to resist any push from the valley road.

---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE STONE RAMPS


The steep stone stairways of the village were natural defense channels. Jun decided to construct heavy timber stone ramps—*tianti*—along the main stairways, allowing the watchmen to slide granite boulders down on the dead if they breached the Valley Gate. Liang and the volunteers split spruce logs and pegged them to form smooth guide channels along the steps. They carried granite blocks from the riverbed, stacking them at the top of the ramps. The work was hard, physical labor, the heavy stone scraping their hands, but the team worked in a quiet, coordinated line, passing the blocks from hand to hand and using rags to wrap the ends to prevent any noise.

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE WATCHTOWER ROOF


The village watchtower, a multi-tiered wooden structure on the highest ridge, was showing signs of sag. A cracked diagonal brace in the roof truss had weakened the structure, threatening to collapse the upper observation deck. Jun chiseled new notches into the support columns, preparing to install a spruce prop. Liang and the builders lifted the new spruce brace, locking it in place with oak wedges. The volunteers helped carry the timbers up the steep ridge trail, sharing the load and encouraging each other as they worked. The watchtower roof stabilized, its structure secure, providing a clear lookout over the entire valley.

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE WATER CHANNELS


To prevent fire from catching on the wooden walls, Jun decided to re-route a mountain spring through split-bamboo channels to keep the outer homes damp. Liang and the volunteers prepared the bamboo poles, splitting them in half and clearing the inner nodes using a steel rod. They lashed the bamboo channels to the eaves of the houses, creating a continuous water conduit that dropped water over the timber walls. The water kept the pine wood wet, preventing it from drying and catching fire under heat. The volunteers worked quickly, sharing tools and ensuring the channels were secure before the next watch.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE DEFENSIVE RING


Around the central square, the survivors gathered to build a modular barrier ring using farm tools and carriage beds. Jun showed them how to lock the wooden wheels using iron wedges, and lash the frames together using split-bamboo ropes. The elders and children helped carry the tools and clear the plaza, their voices rising in quiet chatter as they worked. They locked twenty carts into a solid circle, creating a secondary defense line where they could retreat if the lower village was breached. The cooperative effort had built a secure ring, keeping the community united and strong.

---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE VALLEY HOLD


A wandering group of two hundred dead approached the village from the valley road, their boots clicking on the red sandstone blocks of the path. The watchmen at the Valley Gate stood ready, their spears honed and their hearts steady. Lihua stood on the bridge balcony, her spear ready. As the lead walkers reached the gates, the watchmen released the stone slides at the ramps. The heavy granite boulders rolled down the timber chutes, breaking the advance of the horde. The gate held, its heavy pine braces transferring the impact load directly into the stone cliffs, keeping the village secure.

---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE SILVER LIGHT


The morning sun rose over the Miao village, its light reflecting on the tiled roofs of the stilt houses and the quiet terraced fields. The Valley Gate stood firm, its braces secure, and the village was safe. The refugees and volunteers gathered in the plaza to celebrate, setting up tables and sharing a long-table dinner of hot rice and soup. Jun sat on the steps, cleaning his tools and preparing for the next journey. The radio receiver crackled, and a voice called from the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. They needed builders to reinforce a wagon ring depot. Jun closed his toolbox, locking the latch. 'Let's go, Liang,' he said. 'We head to the grasslands.'

STORY 24: THE STEPPE CARAVAN
Setting: Hulunbuir Grasslands, Inner Mongolia

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE CARAVAN DEPOT


The trading depot sat in the middle of the Hulunbuir grasslands, a wind-swept collection of wooden warehouses and corrals surrounded by a low earthen wall. For generations, the depot had served as a trading center for caravan drivers, horse herdsmen, and merchants traveling across the steppe. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the depot had become a sanctuary for fifty families who had fled the towns. Jun and Liang stood near the eastern gate, their coats wrapped tight against the cold wind. Beside them, the herdsmen were checking the wooden gates of the corrals. The steppe air was clean, smelling of dry grass, wool felt, and horse manure. They must work together to reinforce the depot before the winter storms arrived.

Jun explained the structural properties of the larch wood used in the yurt lattice walls, known as the *khana*. 'Larch has a high density and excellent bending strength parallel to the grain,' he said, showing the caravan drivers how to reinforce the joints. 'The circular geometry of the yurt distributes wind load evenly across the entire frame, preventing local structural failure. The lattice walls act as a continuous membrane, transferring the lateral wind shear to the heavy wooden rafters, the *uni*, which press down on the central crown, the *toono*. By lashing the joints with wet rawhide strips, the connection becomes rigid as the hide dries and contracts, tightening the joints without the need for iron nails. This traditional engineering provides high flexibility under steppe wind loads.'

Ying calculated the force required to pull the carriage wheels into a locked defensive ring. 'The static friction force is equal to the normal force multiplied by the coefficient of friction,' she explained to the volunteers. 'With a wagon mass of one point two metric tons, the normal force on each wheel is three kilonewtons. By driving oak wedges between the wheel spokes and the timber chassis, we block the rotation of the wheels, increasing the effective coefficient of friction from rolling resistance to static sliding friction of zero point five. This means a horizontal force of six kilonewtons is required to move a single locked wagon, making the defensive ring extremely resistant to any physical push.'

In the center of the wagon ring, the caravan members had set up a communal hearth. Elders boiled large pots of hot milk tea with salt and prepared bowls of [REDACTED] and mutton. The smell of rich tea, mutton fat, and burning willow wood filled the cold evening air, warming the spirits of the watchmen. 'We must stand together,' Uncle Batu said, passing a bowl to Liang. 'The steppe is vast, and a single family is like a blade of grass in the wind. But together, we are like the thick turf that holds the soil. As long as we share our hearth and watch the herds, we will survive the winter.' The youth kept watch on horseback, while the elders sang traditional steppe songs, reinforcing the collective bonds of the caravan.

The volunteers worked together to cut and stack steppe turf blocks to form the outer rampart. Jun showed them how to notch the sod slabs to lock them together. 'Steppe turf has a dense network of grass roots that acts as a natural reinforcement, similar to fiber-reinforced soil,' he said. 'By stacking the blocks in an interlocking brick pattern and packing the joints with clay mortar, we build a solid wall that can resist lateral soil pressure and physical impact. The turf wall absorbs moisture from the air, keeping the clay damp and preventing the structure from drying and cracking under the wind. This cooperative building project gave the community a reliable barrier that protected the caravan ring.'

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE WAGON RING


To secure the depot plaza, Jun decided to organize twenty heavy merchant wagons in a defensive ring, locking the wooden wheel hubs with iron wedges to form a solid barricade. Liang and the caravan drivers rolled the heavy carts into position, their hands red from the cold wind. Jun chiseled the locking blocks, wedging them between the wheel spokes and the timber chassis to prevent any rotation. The volunteers helped haul the wagons, forming a team of four to push each cart. They lashed the frames together using thick leather ropes, creating a rigid perimeter that could resist any push from the grasslands.

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE YURTS


The families needed shelter from the freezing winter wind. Jun decided to help the herdsmen erect five traditional wooden lattice yurts in the center of the depot plaza. The yurts, built of larch wood lattice walls and wrapped in thick wool felt, were designed to resist the high steppe winds. Jun and Liang set up the circular frames, locking the joints with wet rawhide strips that would shrink and tighten as they dried. The volunteers helped lift the heavy wooden crown, holding it steady while Liang attached the radial rafters. They wrapped the felt covers, securing them with hair ropes, creating a warm sanctuary for the families.

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE LASSO POLES


Because noise was dangerous in the open grasslands, the herdsmen could not use firearms. Their primary tools were long birch lasso poles—*urga*—which they used to catch horses. Jun decided to reinforce the poles, wrapping key zones in wet rawhide and attaching steel hooks to the tips, creating silent weapons to handle any threat from a distance. Liang and the drivers split the birch wood, shaving the surfaces until they were smooth and flexible. The volunteers helped prepare the leather strips, winding them tight around the wood to prevent splitting. The poles were light and strong, ready for the watchmen on the walls.

---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE TURF WALL


To reinforce the low earthen wall, Jun decided to stack blocks of grasslands turf sod, forming a dense rampart that could resist physical impact and wind erosion. Liang and the volunteers cut the sod blocks from the prairie using flat spades, carrying them in wooden barrows. Jun stacked the blocks in an interlocking brick pattern, packing the joints with clay mortar. The turf blocks, with their dense grass roots, formed a solid wall that absorbed moisture, remaining rigid under the wind. The community worked together, sharing the labor and keeping each other warm in the wind.

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE CORRAL GATES


The horse corrals were critical for the community's mobility. Jun decided to reinforce the larch gates, installing self-closing timber hinges and heavy latch bolts. Liang and the carpenters chiseled the mortise seats in the gate posts, their tools bite into the wood with a steady sound. The volunteers helped lift the heavy gates, aligning the hinges with the posts. They secured the latch, ensuring the horses were safe from wandering predators and could be released quickly if needed. The corral was secure, a vital resource for the caravan.

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE HERD WATCH


The herdsmen organized a coordinated horse patrol to monitor the grasslands around the depot. Jun and Liang sat near the communal fire, sharing a hot cup of milk tea with the drivers. The elders managed the hearth, boiling large pots of tea and sharing roasted grain and mutton. The atmosphere was one of quiet solidarity; everyone contributed what they could, sharing resources and comforting the children. The youth kept watch on horseback, coordinating signals using flags and drums, keeping the sanctuary safe from any surprise approach.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE WINDBREAK


To protect the central plaza from the bitter steppe wind, Jun decided to build a clay and willow wattle-and-daub windbreak wall around the yurts. Liang and the volunteers wove willow branches between driven pine posts, creating a dense lattice. They mixed local clay with dry grass and water, plastering the surface to form a solid, windproof barrier. The children helped carry the willow branches, while the older women prepared the clay mix, their hands busy with the work. The windbreak stood firm, cutting the wind and keeping the plaza warm.

---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE PRAIRIE CHARGE


A wandering group of thirty dead approached the depot from the northern steppe, their figures dark against the dry grass. The watchmen on the turf wall signaled the horse patrol, who rode out to herd them away from the gates. Using the long birch lasso poles, the herdsmen caught the lead figures, neutralizing them from a distance without noise. The wagon ring held, its locked wheels resisting the push of the remaining walkers, while the watchmen held the line. The depot was secure, the cooperative defense system working exactly as planned.

STORY 25: THE SACRED STAIRCASE
Setting: Mount Tai, Shandong Province

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE GRANITE STEPS


The ancient granite staircase of Mount Tai rose steeply through the mountain passes, its thousands of steps climbing toward the Heaven Gate like a stone ladder. For over two thousand years, this sacred path had been trodden by emperors, scholars, and pilgrims, its stone terraces carved into the living rock of the mountain. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the steep staircase was a natural barrier, and a sanctuary for eighty survivors who had retreated to the temples at the summit. Jun and Liang stood on the lower terrace, their tools slung over their shoulders. The mountain air was thin and cold, the wind howling through the granite cliffs. The local helpers stood with them, their hands ready. The community had organized watch stations and shored the stone arches, working together to hold the mountain path.

Jun explained the masonry mechanics of the stone steps on the steep mountain trail. 'Granite has a high compressive strength of over one hundred megapascals, but its shear strength along the mortar joints is low,' he said, showing the volunteers how to shore a loose slab. 'When people step on the edge of a loose stone, it creates an overturning moment that slides the block out of its bed. We must drive iron wedges into the joints and pack them with lead-wool to lock the masonry in place. The lead deforms plastically under the impact load, distributing the weight and preventing local crushing of the granite edges. This ensures the staircase remains stable under the dynamic load of the defenders.'

Ying calculated the mechanical advantage of the heavy timber capstan winch they built at the pass. 'The winch cylinder has a radius of ten centimeters, and the lever arms are two meters long,' she explained to the workers. 'This provides a mechanical advantage of twenty-to-one. With four people pushing the levers with a force of three hundred newtons each, the winch generates a pulling force of twenty-four kilonewtons on the cable. This is more than enough to haul a one-ton granite block up the thirty-degree slope of the mountain stairs, allowing us to repair the collapsed terraces without needing modern machinery.'

At the Red Gate sanctuary, the community had organized a shelter in the stone temple courtyard. Elders boiled large pots of noodle soup and shared flatbreads with the workers. The smell of boiling broth and roasted grain filled the cool mountain air, raising the spirits of the defenders. 'We must stand together,' Auntie Wang said, passing a bowl to Liang. 'Mount Tai has stood for thousands of years, and we will stand with it. As long as we share our shelter and coordinate the watch, we will hold the gates.' The youth carried firewood up the steps, while the older men shared stories of the ancient pilgrims, reinforcing the collective bonds of the community.

The volunteers worked together to set up the timber chutes for the boulder slides. Jun showed them how to notch the larch logs to form a smooth guide channel. 'The granite boulders must slide freely without catching on the joints,' he said. 'We shape the ends of the logs with a stepped joint and grease the channel with animal fat. A sixty-kilogram boulder sliding down a forty-degree chute will reach a velocity of fifteen meters per second at the end, generating a massive kinetic energy of over six kilojoules. This mechanical slide allows us to defend the steep passes without making any noise, using the gravity of the mountain as our primary force.'

---

Jun chiseled the notch seats into the granite pavement, using his mallet to drive the wedges under the prop bases. The volunteers helped lift the timbers, forming a chain to pass the props. STORY 26: THE ISLAND HARBOR
Setting: Cheung Chau Island, Hong Kong

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE HARBOR VILLAGE


The harbor of Cheung Chau was a quiet haven, its waters crowded with fishing junks, wooden sampans, and stilt homes that lined the narrow sand spit. For generations, the island had been home to a tight fishing community, who navigated the coastal channels and shared their catch in the markets. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the island was a sanctuary for sixty families who had retreated to the harbor, blocking the narrow alleys and using the sea as their shield. Jun and Liang stood on the main concrete pier, their toolboxes at their feet. The sea air was salty and damp, the wind carrying the smell of dried fish, mud, and diesel oil. Lihua and the fishermen stood with them, their hands ready. They must work together to shore the docks before the next typhoon surge.

Jun explained the physics of lashing the fishing junks together in a crescent formation. 'The wind and tide exert a massive drag force on the hulls,' he said, showing the fishermen the heavy hemp cables. 'If the boats are lashed rigidly, the wave action will shear the timber cleats. We must use a flexible catenary mooring line, allowing the junks to rise and fall with the swell while sharing the tension load across the entire fleet. The tension load on the main cable is equal to the drag force divided by the cosine of the angle of the line. By maintaining a sag angle of ten degrees, we reduce the peak tension load on the anchors, ensuring the floating bridge remains stable during a storm.'

Ying explained the chemical properties of the traditional oyster-shell mortar. 'By burning oyster shells at eight hundred degrees, we convert the calcium carbonate into calcium oxide, or quicklime,' she said to the young volunteers. 'When we slake the lime with water and mix it with clean sea sand and sticky rice water, the carbon dioxide in the air reacts with the calcium hydroxide to reform calcium carbonate crystals. The sticky rice starch acts as a natural organic binder, filling the micro-pores and increasing the tensile strength of the mortar by three times compared to simple lime sand mixes. This creates a highly durable, waterproof mortar that can resist wave erosion and seal our seawall joints.'

On the deck of the main fishing junk, the community had set up a communal galley. Elders boiled large pots of fish congee and shared steamed buns with the watchmen. The smell of ginger, salted fish, and woodsmoke rose from the charcoal stoves, warming the workers in the damp harbor air. 'We must stand together,' Uncle Liang said, passing a bowl to Liang. 'The sea has always fed us, and now it is our home. As long as we share our catch and lash our boats, we will hold this harbor.' The children helped clean the nets, while the older fishermen shared stories of the old typhoons, reinforcing the collective bonds of the island community.

The volunteers worked together to construct the floating harbor boom using heavy pine logs and wire mesh. Jun showed them how to notch the timber ends to create a flexible chain. 'The logs must be lashed with steel wire to allow horizontal deflection under wave action,' he said. 'This absorbs the kinetic energy of floating debris and prevents the boom from breaking. The wire mesh hangs two meters below the logs, preventing any underwater walkers from passing into the inner harbor. This cooperative building project gave the community a reliable barrier that protected the fishing fleet and the stilt homes.'

---

CHAPTER 1: THE TIDE POOLS


Mount Putuo, the sacred island of Guanyin, rose from the misty waters of the East China Sea, its temple roofs green-glazed and its sandy beaches quiet. For centuries, the island had been a sanctuary of peace and meditation, its monasteries attracting pilgrims from across the land. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the island was a haven for eighty survivors who had retreated to the seaside temple, Puji Si. Jun and Liang stood on the rocky shore, their toolboxes at their feet. The sea wind was cold and damp, the waves crashing against the granite cliffs. Lihua and the monks stood with them, their hands ready. The community had organized watch stations and shored the sea walls, working together to hold the sanctuary.

Jun explained the masonry mechanics of the granite sea-dyke on the island shore. 'Granite has an ultimate compressive strength of eighty megapascals, but the joints are vulnerable to wave action,' he said, showing the volunteers how to pack the mortar. 'The constant impact of the waves creates a dynamic pressure of up to twenty kilopascals, which washes out the old lime mortar. We must use a mix of slaked lime, clay, and sticky rice water, which forms an elastic hydraulic binder that does not dissolve in salt water. We will wedge the joints with green slate chips driven tight with a mallet, locking the granite courses together and preventing any sliding shear along the bedding planes.'

Ying calculated the force required to anchor the floating sea boom in the bay. 'The wave force on a floating cylinder depends on the wave height and the diameter of the log,' she explained to the local workers. 'With a wave height of one point five meters and a log diameter of thirty centimeters, the horizontal force is approximately three kilonewtons per meter. To secure the boom, we must forge iron drift anchors weighing eighty kilograms each and anchor them to the granite seabed using thick steel chains. The catenary curve of the anchor chain acts as a spring, absorbing the dynamic peak loads and preventing the anchors from dragging during high tide.'

In the courtyard of the seaside monastery, the community had set up a shelter. Elders boiled large pots of vegetarian soup and prepared bowls of steamed rice with pickled cabbage. The smell of boiling herbs, sesame oil, and incense filled the cool sea air, warming the spirits of the watchmen. 'We must stand together,' Master Huineng said, passing a bowl to Liang. 'Mount Putuo has always been a sanctuary of peace, and now we must defend it with our hands. As long as we share our meals and keep the watch, we will hold the temple.' The children helped sweep the stone walks, while the older monks shared Buddhist teachings, reinforcing the collective bonds of the community.

The volunteers worked together to construct the sandbar barriers using pine posts and sandbags. Jun showed them how to drive the posts into the wet sand. 'We must drive the posts at least one point two meters deep to reach the firm clay subsoil,' he said. 'This provides the lateral resistance needed to hold the sandbags against the receding tide. By lashing the posts together with split bamboo and stacking the sandbags in an interlocking pattern, we build a barrier that deflects the waves and blocks any surfers from entering the temple cove. This cooperative project gave the community a secure perimeter along the beach.'

Setting: Jingdezhen Kilns, Jiangxi Province

CHAPTER 1: THE KILN DISTRICT


The historic kiln district of Jingdezhen sat along the Chang River, a dense maze of narrow streets, clay sheds, and brick wood-fired kilns. For generations, the district had been the center of imperial porcelain production, its artisans shaping the local white clay and firing the kilns to create the finest wares. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the kiln buildings had become a sanctuary for eighty survivors, who had blocked the street entries with stacked bricks and used the kilns for warmth. Jun and Liang stood in the central yard, their tools ready. The air was warm, smelling of coal smoke, wet clay, and brick dust. Lihua and the potters stood with them, their hands ready. They must work together to shore the kilns before the winter storms arrived.

Jun explained the masonry mechanics of the brick kilns in the pottery district. 'Refractory bricks are made of fireclay, which has a high alumina content that can resist temperatures up to fifteen hundred degrees Celsius,' he said, showing the apprentices how to lay the courses. 'The strength of the kiln arch depends on the wedge shape of the key bricks, which translates the downward gravitational load into lateral thrust against the granite buttresses. We must use a fine slurry of fireclay and water as mortar, applying it in thin layers of less than two millimeters. A thick mortar joint will shrink and crack under heat, causing the arch to collapse when the kiln is fired.'

Ying explained the thermodynamics of the kiln chimney draft. 'The draft pressure is created by the density difference between the hot flue gas inside the chimney and the cold air outside,' she said to the young volunteers. 'The draft pressure is equal to the height of the chimney multiplied by the gravitational acceleration and the difference in air density. With a chimney height of fifteen meters and a gas temperature of three hundred degrees, the draft pressure is approximately eighty pascals. This pressure draws air through the fuel bed, ensuring complete combustion of the wood and generating the heat needed to bake our structural bricks. We must shore the brick chimney with steel bands to prevent thermal expansion cracks.'

In the main street of the kiln district, the community had set up a communal kitchen near the warm kilns. Elders boiled large pots of noodle soup and shared tea brewed in fresh clay cups. The smell of hot food, coal smoke, and wet clay filled the air, warming the workers in the damp winter wind. 'We must stand together,' Uncle Chen said, passing a bowl of soup to Liang. 'Our kilns have fired the finest porcelain for generations, and now they will fire the bricks to defend our homes. As long as we share our heat and keep the watch, we will hold this street.' The children helped carry wood to the kilns, while the older potters shared stories of the historic drafts, reinforcing the collective bonds of the community.

The volunteers worked together to construct the clay and straw dams across the drainage canals. Jun showed them how to mix the materials to form a waterproof barrier. 'We mix local pottery clay with chopped rice straw,' he said. 'The clay provides the waterproof mass, while the straw acts as a tensile reinforcement, preventing the clay from cracking as it dries. We pack the mixture into timber frames, building a solid dam that can resist the hydrostatic pressure of the rising water. This cooperative engineering project gave the community a reliable barrier that protected the lower kiln sheds from flooding.'

STORY 29: THE FROZEN SHORE

---

CHAPTER 1: THE WINDY SHORE


The wind swept across the gravel beaches of Qinghai Lake, its freezing waters vast and cold under the winter sky. Along the northern shore, a group of seventy survivors, including Han and Mongol herdsmen, had established a sanctuary behind a low dirt rampart and timber pens. The lake, at an altitude of over three thousand meters, was a harsh setting, the winter temperature dropping below minus fifteen degrees. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the lake was a shield, its frozen shore blocking access from the main road. Jun and Liang stood near the eastern gate, their heavy coats wrapped tight. The mountain air was thin and freezing, the wind carrying the smell of woodsmoke and sheep wool. The community had organized watch stations and shored the timber fences, working together to survive the cold.

Jun explained the mechanics of driving the larch posts into the frozen gravel shore of the lake. 'Frozen gravel behaves like low-strength concrete, with the ice acting as the binding matrix,' he said, showing the volunteers how to split the stones. 'To drive a timber post, we must first break the frozen surface layer using an iron crowbar, then drive the post using a heavy wooden mallet. Larch has a high density and excellent durability in damp soils, making it ideal for our stockade. We must drive the posts at least eighty centimeters deep to reach the unfrozen soil, which provides the lateral stability needed to resist the wind shear from the lake during winter storms.'

Ying calculated the thickness of the ice wall required to resist the physical pressure of a crowd. 'The ice barrier is formed by spraying lake water over brushwood piles,' she explained to the local helpers. 'The ice has a compressive strength of approximately three megapascals when the temperature is below minus five degrees. By building the wall to a thickness of eighty centimeters, we create a solid barrier that can resist a lateral load of over two hundred kilonewtons. The brushwood acts as a reinforcement, preventing the ice from cracking along its crystalline planes when struck. We must monitor the temperature closely; if it rises above freezing, the ice will lose its strength, and we must shore the wall with timber props.'

In the shelter of the larch stockade, the lakeside community had set up a communal hearth. Elders boiled large pots of mutton soup and shared cups of hot tea with the watchmen. The smell of rich mutton broth, woodsmoke, and hot tea filled the freezing air, warming the workers in the bitter wind. 'We must stand together,' Uncle Dorj said, passing a bowl of soup to Liang. 'The lake is cold and the wind is hard, but our hearth is warm. As long as we share our food and watch the shore, we will survive this winter. No family can stand the wind alone, but together we are a wall.' The youth carried wood to the fire, while the older men shared stories of the historic winter storms, reinforcing the collective bonds of the community.

The volunteers worked together to construct the wooden sleds for the shore patrol. Jun showed them how to shape the runners from seasoned ash. 'We use steam to bend the runners, and lock the joints with ash pegs,' he said. 'The sleds must slide smoothly over the snow and ice, allowing the watchmen to patrol the lake edge without making any noise. We grease the runners with animal fat to reduce friction, allowing two people to easily haul the sled loaded with tools and wood. By sharing the work of carving and lashing, the community built a mobile watch system that protected our frozen perimeter.'

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE LOG STOCKADE


To secure the northern gate, Jun decided to drive a heavy log stockade into the frozen gravel shore. Liang and ten local drivers carried the larch logs from the woodpile, their hands red despite their thick wool mittens. Jun used an iron crowbar to break the frozen surface layer of the soil, chiseled the guide holes, and drove the logs using a heavy wooden mallet. The volunteers helped lift the larch logs, forming a team of four to hold each post steady. They lashed the logs together with wire, creating a solid wall that blocked the road.

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE ICE WALL


To reinforce the stockade, Jun decided to construct a thick ice wall by spraying lake water over brushwood piles. Liang and the volunteers gathered willow brushwood, stacking it along the stockade face. The volunteers hauled water from the lake in wooden buckets, spraying it over the brushwood. The water froze instantly in the bitter wind, forming a solid ice barrier that coated the stockade. The children helped carry the brushwood, while the elders prepared soup. The ice wall stood firm, a solid barrier that could resist any push.

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE MUD MORTAR


The log joints of the watch shelters were showing gaps, letting the freezing wind enter the living areas. Jun decided to use a mortar of clay, sand, and sheep dung to seal the joints. Liang and the volunteers mixed the local clay with sand and dung, adding water to form a thick paste. Jun packed the mortar into the joints, smoothing the surface with a wooden trowel. The mortar dried quickly, forming an insulating seal that kept the wind out, securing the shelters.

---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE SHORE WATCH


To monitor the lake ice, Jun decided to construct an elevated watchtower out of old utility poles along the shore. Liang and the builders chiseled the joints in the poles, and the volunteers helped lift the frame using a gantry crane. Jun secured the deck with larch planks, installing a timber railing. The watchtower rose above the gravel shore, providing a clear lookout over the lake, ready to spot any movement on the ice.

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE CHARCOAL HEARTH


The community organized a communal hearth inside the main log shelter to keep the workers and watchmen warm. Elders boiled large pots of mutton soup and shared hot tea with the workers. The atmosphere was one of quiet solidarity; everyone contributed what they could, sharing their fuel and comforting the children. The warmth of the hearth and the hot soup rose the spirits of the workers, keeping the community united in the bitter wind.

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE SLED PATROL


To patrol the frozen lake edge, Jun decided to construct three wooden sleds using seasoned ash. Liang and the builders shaped the runners using steam to bend the wood, locking the joints with wooden pegs. The volunteers helped prepare the leather harness, lashing the frames with wire. They greased the runners with sheep fat, allowing the watchmen to slide the sleds over the ice without making any noise. The sleds stood ready, providing a mobile watch system along the shore.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE LAKESIDE GATE


The main entry to the sanctuary was the Lakeside Gate—a heavy timber sliding gate that blocked the northern road. Jun decided to reinforce the gate, installing diagonal larch props and an oak sliding latch. Liang and the carpenters chiseled the mortise seats in the gate posts, their tools sending up dry larch shavings. The volunteers helped slide the gate into position, securing the props. The gate stood firm, a secure barrier that blocked the road, ready for the watch.

---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE ICE BREACH


A group of dead emerged from the northern road, moving slowly over the frozen lake edge toward the stockade. The watchmen on the tower signaled the patrol, and the defenders stood ready. As the lead walkers reached the ice wall, the watchmen held them back with long spears. The ice wall held, its thick barrier resisting the pressure, while the defenders neutralized the threat. The shore was secure, the cooperative defense system working perfectly.

---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE SPRING MELT


The morning sun rose over Qinghai Lake, casting a golden light on the ice wall and the quiet stockade. The gates stood firm, and the community was safe. The refugees gathered near the hearth, sharing mutton soup and hot tea. Jun sat on the bench, cleaning his tools and packing his toolbox. The radio crackled, and a voice called from High Island Reservoir in Hong Kong. They needed builders to shore the concrete dam. Jun locked his toolbox. 'Let's go, Liang,' he said. 'We head to High Island Reservoir.'

STORY 30: THE WALLED RESERVOIR
Setting: High Island Reservoir, Hong Kong

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE EAST DAM


The East Dam of the High Island Reservoir rose like a concrete wall between the hills and the sea, its face covered by thousands of massive interlocking concrete dolos blocks. The reservoir, a vital source of drinking water for Hong Kong, was a vast sanctuary, its dams blocking the tidal waves and isolating the inner lake. But now, in the silence of the final crisis, the reservoir had become the ultimate haven for one hundred survivors, who had blocked the access roads and set up watches on the dams. Jun and Liang stood on the crest of the East Dam, their tools ready. The sea wind was strong, the waves crashing against the concrete blocks with a roar. Lihua and the watchmen stood with them, their hands ready. They must work together to shore the dams before the winter storms arrived.

Jun explained the mechanics of aligning the concrete dolos blocks on the East Dam. 'A dolos block is a double-T-shaped concrete structure designed to dissipate wave energy,' he said, showing the volunteers the interlocking shapes. 'When the waves strike the dam, the irregular geometry of the blocks causes the water to turbulate and lose its velocity, reducing the wave impact force by ninety percent. The blocks interlock with each other, forming a stable structure that can resist displacement even during a typhoon. We must shore the gaps between the blocks using heavy spruce timbers, creating a continuous barrier that prevents any walkers from climbing the dam.'

Ying explained the mechanics of the steel sluice gates. 'The gate is lifted by a rack-and-pinion system driven by a manual hand-crank,' she said to the young watchmen. 'The gate slab has a mass of two metric tons, which generates a downward gravitational force of twenty kilonewtons. The hydrostatic pressure of the reservoir water creates a horizontal force of fifty kilonewtons pushing the gate against its bronze guide channels. With a coefficient of friction of zero point fifteen, the resisting friction force is seven point five kilonewtons. This means the total lifting force required is twenty-seven point five kilonewtons. By using a gear train with a ratio of fifty-to-one and a crank arm of forty centimeters, we reduce the required hand-crank force to less than two hundred newtons, which two watchmen can easily turn.'

In the pump house of the reservoir, the community had set up a communal living area. Elders boiled large pots of rice and prepared tea for the watchmen. The smell of hot food, tea, and machine oil filled the brick building, warming the workers who kept the radio beacon running. 'We must stand together,' Auntie Wong said, passing a bowl to Liang. 'This reservoir is our last shield, and our beacon is the voice of our hope. As long as we share our food and keep the radio running, we will hold the dam.' The children helped carry wood and water, while the older technicians managed the beacon, reinforcing the collective bonds of the sanctuary.

The volunteers worked together to construct the timber drawbridge to the water intake tower. Jun showed them how to cut the mortise joints for the hand-winch frame. 'We use seasoned pine logs for the deck and steel cables for the lift,' he said. 'The winch frame must transfer the tension load directly into the concrete base of the tower. By using a counterweighted deck, we reduce the winch load by eighty percent, allowing a single watchman to raise the bridge quickly under pressure. This cooperative project gave the community a secure escape route to the elevated tower, ensuring they could isolate the sanctuary at a moment's notice.'

---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE DOLOS WALL


To block the gaps between the massive concrete dolos blocks, Jun decided to install timber shoring using heavy spruce struts, creating a continuous barrier along the dam face. Liang and ten local volunteers carried the timbers up the concrete slope, their hands protected by thick gloves. Jun chiseled the notch seats in the spruce logs, wedging them horizontally between the concrete blocks. The volunteers helped lift the timbers, forming a chain to pass the braces. The wall rose, blocking the gaps and securing the dam.

---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE SLUICE GATE


The steel drainage sluice gate at the main channel was showing signs of rust, its mechanical gears jammed by silt. Jun decided to shore and grease the gate controls, using thick cables and a manual winch. Liang and the smiths forged the new brackets, bolting them to the concrete wall. The volunteers carried the fuel and grease, while the elders prepared tea for the workers. They bolted the winch and cleared the gears, ensuring the gate could be opened quickly if the water rose.

---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE INTAKE TOWER


The elevated concrete intake tower in the reservoir lake was a secure lookout, but the wooden gangway had collapsed. Jun decided to construct a new timber drawbridge to the tower, using seasoned pine logs and a hand-winch. Liang and the carpenters chiseled the joints in the pine logs, their tools sending up dry shavings. The volunteers helped lift the deck panels, lashing them to the winch frame. The bridge rose, providing a secure access route that could be isolated at night.

---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE CATCHMENT CHANNELS


To secure clean drinking water, Jun decided to clear the stone catchment channels that guided mountain streams into the reservoir. Liang and the volunteers cleared the silt and debris using spades and timber hooks. Jun chiseled the timber screens, installing them at the intake gates to filter the water. The children helped carry the silt barrows, while the elders prepared meals. The channels stood clear, ensuring a reliable water supply for the community.

---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE PUMP HOUSE


The brick pump house near the dam was converted into a communal kitchen and radio outpost. Elders boiled large pots of rice and prepared hot tea for the watchmen. The atmosphere was one of quiet solidarity; everyone contributed what they could, sharing their food and comforting the children. The warmth of the kitchen and the radio beacon rose the spirits of the workers, keeping the community united. The youth kept watch from the roof, coordinating signals, keeping the sanctuary safe.

---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE DOLOS ASCENT


To allow watchmen to move safely over the concrete blocks, Jun decided to construct timber ladder ways along the dam face, using spruce stringers and safety ropes. Liang and the volunteers pegged the steps, lashing the frames with wire. The refugees helped carry the ladders, forming a line to pass the timbers. The ladder ways rose along the dam, providing a safe path for the watchmen on duty.

---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE RADIO BEACON


To signal other sanctuaries, the technicians decided to erect a high wooden radio mast on the ridge. Jun and Liang framed the mast using three larch poles, locking the joints with heavy wire. The volunteers helped raise the mast using a hand-winch and guy-wires, anchoring the ends to the concrete blocks. The mast rose on the ridge, its wire antenna catching the radio signals, providing a voice of hope for the survivors.

---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE DAM STAND


A massive group of dead approached the reservoir from the access road, their figures moving down the narrow dam path. The watchmen on the ridge signaled the gates, and the defenders stood ready. As the lead walkers reached the timber barriers, the watchmen held them back with long spears. The barriers held, its logs resisting the pressure, while the defenders neutralized the threat. The dam was secure, the cooperative defense system working perfectly.

---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE WALLED HORIZON


The morning sun rose over the High Island Reservoir, casting a golden light on the concrete dam and the quiet waters of the lake. The gates stood firm, and the community was safe. The refugees gathered in the pump house, sharing hot tea and rice, looking out at the sea. Jun sat on the stone wall, cleaning his tools. He closed his toolbox, locking the brass latch. 'We have built a good wall, Liang,' he said. Liang smiled, looking at the water. 'A wall that will hold the future.'
