STORY 31: THE WALL DEFIANT
Setting: Mutianyu Great Wall, Beijing

---

---

CHAPTER 1: THE GREAT RAMPART


The Mutianyu section of the Great Wall wound along the high, rugged ridges of the mountains north of Beijing like a giant stone dragon, its crenellated brick parapets and heavy watchtowers rising from the green pines and granite cliffs. For five hundred years, since the Ming Dynasty, this wall had stood as a defensive barrier, its stone walkways designed to move armies quickly across the rugged terrain. But now, in the silence of the crisis, the wall was a last haven for ninety survivors—local villagers, farmers, and wall restoration workers—who had blocked the passes and turned the brick towers into a secure sanctuary. Jun and Liang stood on the roof of Tower Four, looking down at the steep northern slopes. The mountain air was cold and thin, the wind howling through the arrow slits.

"The position is strong, Master Jun," Liang said, adjusting his tool vest. "The cliffs are vertical on the northern side, and the only path up is the narrow stone steps from the valley. But some sections of the wall walkways are shifting, their granite foundations undermined by the summer rains."

"We must shore the listing walls before the winter freezes the water inside the joints," Jun said. "If the water freezes, it will expand, splitting the granite blocks and bringing down the parapets. Let us inspect the foundations of the loop-holed wall."

They waded through the dry leaves along the walkway, checking the mortar joints. Lihua and the watchmen stood with them, their spears ready, their eyes scanning the forest below. The community had retreated to the lower vault chambers of Tower Four, setting up watch stations and a communal hearth. Elders cooked hot noodle soup and shared blankets, while the youth kept watch. The collective coordination of the survivors was their only hope in this storm.

Jun explained the masonry mechanics of the Wall's brick parapet, known as the *nüqiang*. 'The brickwork is laid in an interlocking dovetail pattern that distributes lateral forces across multiple courses,' he said, pointing to the cracked joints. 'When the zombies scale the wall, their weight and movement exert a dynamic lateral force. By driving iron wedges into the joints and packing them with hydraulic lime mortar, we restore the joint rigidity and prevent the bricks from sliding. The dovetail pattern transfers the load horizontally into the adjacent towers, preventing any local collapse. We must also inspect the drainage channels, the *tupin*, to ensure water does not accumulate behind the wall, which would freeze and crack the masonry during winter. This traditional method of restoration is critical for preserving the historic integrity of these brick ramparts while ensuring their ultimate stability under pressure.'

Ying explained the chemistry of the hydraulic lime mortar mixed with sticky rice water. 'The amylopectin in the sticky rice starch reacts with the calcium carbonate crystals of the slaked lime, forming a compact organic-inorganic composite structure,' she said to the volunteers. 'This micro-structure reduces the pore size and increases the density, making the mortar highly resistant to water penetration and freeze-thaw cycles. Its compressive strength is increased by three times, and its flexibility allows it to absorb the dynamic shocks of climbing dead without cracking. This traditional recipe is the reason the Ming Dynasty walls have survived for five hundred years, and it is our best material to seal the shored gates, ensuring the masonry remains completely impervious to environmental decay.'

Inside the thick brick watchtower, the communal kitchen was a warm refuge from the cold ridge winds. Elders boiled large pots of mutton soup and shared plates of hot dumplings (*jiaozi*) filled with cabbage and pork. The smell of boiling dough, garlic, and hot tea filled the arched chamber, raising the spirits of the watchmen on the parapets. 'We must stand together,' Auntie Ma said, handing a bowl to Liang. 'This wall was built to protect the land, and now it protects our families. As long as we share our hearth and watch the passes, we will hold this ridge. No single tower can stand alone, but together we are a line.' The children carried wood to the fire, while the older men shared stories of the wall's history, reinforcing the collective solidarity of the sanctuary. This mutual aid was the foundation of their community, keeping morale high in the face of constant danger.

The volunteers worked together to assemble the traction catapult (*mangchuan*) on the watchtower platform. Jun showed them how to notch the heavy spruce logs to form the A-frame. 'The catapult utilizes the principle of leverage and tension,' he said. 'By pulling the ropes together, the team translates their collective force into high angular velocity at the arm tip, throwing thirty-kilogram stones over eighty meters. The leverage arm ratio is exactly six-to-one, multiplying the velocity of the pull. This allows us to strike the incoming crowd at the foot of the ridge before they reach the stairs. The winch system on the ridge platform uses a block-and-tackle with a mechanical advantage of four, allowing three workers to haul the granite blocks up from the ravine. This cooperative mechanical design was essential for their defense, turning the steep slope into an active asset.'


---

---

CHAPTER 2: THE DOVETAIL JOINTS


The brick parapet—*nüqiang*—along the eastern walkway was listing three inches outward, its old mortar cracked by tree roots and dampness. Jun realized that a single push from a crowd of the dead scaling the wall would collapse the bricks, opening a gap in the defenses.

"We must shore the wall," Jun explained to Liang. "We will drive iron T-bars into the granite pavement and wedge the brickwork horizontally using pine braces. The original bricks are laid in an interlocking dovetail pattern that distributes lateral forces across multiple courses."

"Master, the granite is hard to drill," Liang said, holding the star-drill. "It takes many blows to make a socket."

"Work with steady, light blows, Liang," Jun said. "Granite has a high compressive strength, but if we strike too hard, we will fracture the stone along its natural cleavage planes. The star-drill must be turned slightly after each strike to create a round hole."

Jun chiseled the guide sockets, his mallet striking the steel with a rhythmic sound. Liang and the volunteers prepared the pine braces, notches the ends to fit the T-bars. They wedged the timbers home, locking the braces. The parapet stabilized, its outward list halted, its structure secure against any lateral load.


---

---

CHAPTER 3: THE LIME KILN


To repair the cracked granite joints of the wall walkway, Jun decided to rebuild an ancient brick-making station and kiln on the ridge, mixing hydraulic lime mortar with sticky rice water.

"The mortar must be hydraulic," Jun explained. "Simple lime sand mortar will wash out in the winter rains. By mixing slaked lime with sticky rice water and ground brick dust, we create a binder that sets even in damp conditions, its strength increasing over time."

"Where do we get the quicklime, Master?" Liang asked.

"The limestone ravine below," Jun said. "We will burn the stones in our kiln, slaking the lime with pond water. Liang, prepare the fire wood. We need a constant temperature of eight hundred degrees to burn the limestone."

The volunteers helped carry the limestone blocks and wood fuel, forming a chain up the steep ridge trail. They fired the kiln, watching the white stone turn to quicklime under the heat. They slaked the lime in a wooden tub, watching it bubble and release steam. They mixed the mortar, passing the buckets to Jun and Liang who were repointing the joints. The mortar set, sealing the walkway.


---

---

CHAPTER 4: THE STONE CATAPULT


The northern approach was a steep ravine where a road wound through the valley. Jun decided to construct a heavy wooden traction catapult—*mangchuan*—on the roof of Tower Four, allowing the defenders to throw granite boulders at any approaching horde before they reached the steps.

"The catapult arm must be flexible," Jun explained. "We will use two lashed spruce logs, wrapping the joints in wet rawhide to prevent splitting under tension. The leverage arm ratio is exactly six-to-one, multiplying the pull of our team."

"How do we trigger the arm, Master?" Liang asked.

"We use a traction crew," Jun said. "Ten volunteers pulling ropes together on the short arm, while the long arm throws the stone. This provides a simple, reliable launch system that does not rely on steel springs."

Jun and Liang framed the A-frame support structure, locking the joints with mortise-and-tenon. The volunteers helped haul the spruce logs, their hands rough from the ropes. They rigged the ropes, testing the swing. They loaded a thirty-kilogram granite boulder, and the crew pulled the ropes. With a loud *whoosh*, the boulder flew through the air, crashing into the valley below. The catapult was ready.


---

---

CHAPTER 5: THE IRON GRATES


The watchtower archways had no doors, designed for open access. Jun realized that if the walkways were overrun, the dead would flood the tower chambers. He decided to reinforce the archways with heavy iron grates forged in a temporary hearth on the wall.

"The grates must be anchored to the brickwork," Jun explained. "We will forge iron plug pins from old road signs and drive them eighty millimeters deep into the mortar joints, sealing them with molten lead."

"We need more coal, Master," Liang said. "The hearth is cooling."

"Use the dry pine wood," Jun said. "It burns hot and quick, which is what we need to forge the iron pins. The volunteers will help turn the bellows."

Jun and the smiths heated the iron bars in the charcoal hearth, hammering the metal on a stone anvil. The volunteers helped turn the bellows, their faces dark with soot, while the elders carried water in wooden buckets. They assembled the iron grate, aligning the frames with the plug pins. Jun drove the pins home, locking the grate in the archway. The gateway was secure, a solid barrier that could be locked at night.


---

---

CHAPTER 6: THE RIDGE WINCH


To haul granite stones and timber logs up the steep ridge face to Tower Four, Jun decided to erect a timber gantry crane and winch system on the ridge platform.

"The gantry must transfer the load to the bedrock," Jun explained. "We will anchor the guide poles to the quartzite rock using steel guy-wires, and use a block-and-tackle to multiply our pulling force."

"Master, the winch drum is cracked," Liang said, adjusting the axle. "The wood has split along the core."

"We will wrap the drum in brass wire and drive steel wedges into the split," Jun said. "This will restore its torsional strength and prevent the axle from sliding inside the wood."

Jun and Liang repaired the winch drum, lashing the wood with wire. The volunteers helped raise the gantry, aligning the guy-wires with the rock anchors. They rigged the block-and-tackle, using three wooden pulleys to multiply the force. The winch turned smoothly, hauling the heavy logs up the cliff face, securing the materials needed for repairs.


---

---

CHAPTER 7: THE WATCHTOWER HEARTH


The temperature on the ridge dropped as winter approached, the wind carrying the first snow. Inside the thick brick vault of Tower Four, the community organized a communal hearth and kitchen to support the workers and watchmen.

"A hot bowl of dumpling soup will keep the cold out," Auntie Ma said, stirring a large metal pot. "Everyone must eat together. We share what we have."

The elders managed the kitchen, preparing Beijing dumplings and boiling hot tea for the watchmen. The refugees shared their food, pooling their flour, dried pork, and winter cabbage to cook meals. The children helped carry wood and water, their voices rising in quiet chatter near the fire.

Jun and Liang sat near the hearth, sharing a bowl of hot soup. The warmth of the fire and the quiet talk of the survivors brought a sense of peace to the cold night. The collective solidarity of the community was their true wall, keeping them united in the face of the storm.


---

---

CHAPTER 8: THE GRAVEL CHUTES


The stairs of the wall walkways were steep and narrow. Jun decided to construct timber log chutes—*mutong*—along the main stairways, allowing the watchmen to slide heavy gravel bags and granite blocks down on any climbers.

"The chutes must have smooth guide joints," Jun explained. "We will shape the ends of the logs with a stepped joint and grease the channel with mutton fat. The gravel bags will slide freely without catching."

"Master, the gravel is heavy to carry," Liang said. "We must fill fifty bags."

"The volunteers will form a chain," Jun said. "Passing the gravel from the ridge plaza. We will work together."

The volunteers formed a line along the walkway, passing the gravel bags from hand to hand. The work was hard, physical labor, the rough canvas bags scraping their hands, but the team worked in a quiet, coordinated line. They stacked the gravel bags at the top of the chutes, ready for the watch.


---

---

CHAPTER 9: THE WALL DEFIANT


A massive horde of ten thousand dead, having moved south from the northern valleys, reached the Mutianyu ridge. Drawn by the scent of life, they swarmed up the mountain trails, their figures dark against the snow.

The watchmen on the towers stood ready, their spears honed and their hearts steady. Lihua stood on the tower roof, her spear ready.

"Release the slide!" Jun called out.

The watchmen released the gravel bags and granite blocks down the timber chutes. The heavy blocks slid down the steep steps with a roar, breaking the advance of the scaling walkers. The catapult on the roof launched stones into the valley, dispersing the main crowd. The wall held, its shored parapets and iron grates resisting the pressure, keeping the sanctuary secure.


---

---

CHAPTER 10: THE GOLDEN RIDGE


The morning sun rose over Mutianyu, casting a golden light on the stone walls and the quiet watchtowers. The snow-covered ridge was silent, the air clean and cold.

The gates stood firm, and the community was safe. The refugees gathered in the tower courtyard, sharing hot tea and dumplings.

Jun sat on the stone ledge, cleaning his tools. Beside him, Liang was sharpening his broadaxe. Jun wrapped his chisels in oil-soaked paper, locking them in his wooden toolbox.

"We have built a good wall, Master Jun," Liang said.

"The wall stood because the people stood together to hold it," Jun replied, looking out at the mountains. "A wall is only stone. The true strength is the solidarity of the community."

They stood up, looking out over the winding ramparts. Behind them, the survivors waved goodbye, their voices rising in a soft song. The Great Wall stood defiant, a monument of stone and human cooperation, secure against the storm.
